units.title: Clean code's goal is understandability
units.detail: Clean code rules (like max 3 nesting levels) exist to reduce complexity and make code understandable, not as dogma. Breaking a rule is acceptable if the code still clearly conveys its intent.

units.title: Use early returns to reduce nesting
units.detail: Instead of checking the happy path and nesting deeper, test for the failure case first (e.g., different ingredient counts) and continue/return early, keeping the rest of the logic flat and unindented.

units.title: Extract nested logic into named functions
units.detail: Break deeply nested conditionals into separate well-named functions (e.g., PlateHasIngredient, PlateMatchesRecipe) so each level of logic is isolated and the nesting depth drops.

units.title: Tutorials are starting points, not the only way
units.detail: Tutorial code achieves the demonstrated result but is not the only valid solution; every game has unique constraints, so adapt the approach to your specific scenario.

units.title: Make a game or make an engine
units.detail: Ask yourself whether your goal is making a game or building a game engine; unless you are exceptional, you cannot do both at the same time, so choose one path.

units.title: Low-level graphics needs heavy math
units.detail: Building engines or low-level graphics requires substantial matrix/transformation math, whereas normal game dev with an engine needs only basic trigonometry and vector math.

units.title: Custom engine specializes your game type
units.detail: A self-built engine can be tailored exactly to one kind of game (e.g., Factorio's massive particle scale), while general-purpose engines trade that specialization for flexibility.

units.title: One engine spans 2D and photoreal 3D
units.detail: Unity successfully shipped stylized 2D hits like Cuphead and realistic 3D blockbusters like COD Mobile, so engine choice does not lock you into one visual style.

units.title: Viral gifs can launch an indie game
units.detail: Untitled Goose Game went viral from early-development gifs before release; a visually striking, interesting concept can market itself with almost no budget.

units.title: Launch demo months before Next Fest
units.detail: Publish your demo on the Steam page about 4 months before Next Fest, gather feedback, and polish it so the demo is solid when Next Fest gives it mass exposure.

units.title: Email content creators before Next Fest
units.detail: Kickstart the Steam algorithm by releasing a demo and emailing content creators before Next Fest (not during), so they promote the game when the festival hits.

units.title: Let content creators do the marketing
units.detail: The best social media promotion is none: make a great demo and get it into content creators' hands to promote for you, though you still market to attract their attention.

units.title: Launch 1-2 months after Next Fest
units.detail: Pick the Next Fest closest to your planned release date, join it, then launch roughly 1-2 months afterward to convert wishlists into sales.

units.title: Join every non-Next-Fest Steam festival
units.detail: Steam holds many smaller festivals with no per-game limits (unlike the single Next Fest slot); join as many as possible to build wishlists and feedback before Next Fest.

units.title: Instanced drawing batches many sprites
units.detail: Replace per-entity DrawMesh calls with one DrawMeshInstanced call fed by arrays of matrices and UVs, dramatically cutting draw calls for thousands of animated sprites.

units.title: DrawMeshInstanced 1023 mesh limit
units.detail: DrawMeshInstanced draws at most 1023 meshes per call; when exceeding that, split the entity list into slices of 1023 and issue one draw call per slice.

units.title: Batched drawing bypasses sort order
units.detail: Instanced drawing skips the engine's entity sorting, so you must sort matrices and UVs yourself (e.g., by Y position) to keep render order correct with transparency.

units.title: Parallel sort by screen slices
units.detail: Instead of sorting every entity against every other (O(n^2)), split entities into horizontal screen slices with jobs, sort each slice in parallel, then merge into full arrays.

units.title: Expand game jam games into releases
units.detail: Superhot started as a game jam prototype; a strong jam concept with a unique hook (time moves only when you move) can be fleshed out into a commercial game.

units.title: Grab momentum when success arrives
units.detail: Among Us was quietly successful until streamers made it explode years later; when an indie finally finds traction, cancel side plans and pour all effort into the hit.

units.title: Use inspiration as a jumping-off point
units.detail: Genshin Impact borrowed heavily from Breath of the Wild but expanded the mechanics beyond the source, showing that heavy inspiration can yield an original-feeling hit.

units.title: Mixing genres creates unique games
units.detail: Enter the Gungeon combined bullet hell with roguelike dungeon crawling into a fresh, successful combo; unusual genre mashups can help a game stand out.

units.title: One codebase ships desktop and mobile
units.detail: Unity builds the same codebase to both desktop and mobile, enabling games like Hearthstone to be played identically on both platforms from a single project.

units.title: Design co-op for cooperation or failure
units.detail: Overcooked designs every mechanic to demand maximum cooperation, turning small failures into cascading chaos, which creates fun and memorable co-op moments.

units.title: Cache lookups out of Update
units.detail: GetComponent, Find, and Camera.main carry real per-frame cost; cache the results in member fields once (in Awake/Start) and reuse them instead of calling every frame.

units.title: Block UI clicks with invisible image
units.detail: Add an empty UI Image with alpha 0 and Raycast Target enabled over UI elements to silently block clicks during tutorials, avoiding special disable logic.

units.title: Subtract timerMax instead of resetting
units.detail: When a timer exceeds its max, subtract the max rather than resetting to zero; this preserves the overflow amount and keeps repeated timers perfectly in sync.

units.title: Replace magic numbers with named locals
units.detail: Give magic numbers meaningful local variable names (e.g., goldCost, maxBuildingRadius) so code reads as its intent instead of requiring deciphering.

units.title: Avoid float sentinel values
units.detail: Special values like -1f meaning 'no timer' are brittle (any math can produce -1.1); use a small class that is null when absent instead of guessing magic numbers.

units.title: Integer division silently truncates
units.detail: Dividing an int by an int yields an int, cutting off decimals (40/100 = 0), so cast at least one operand to float before normalizing ratios.

units.title: Fire events safely with null-conditional
units.detail: Use the ?.Invoke() null-conditional operator to fire events that may have no subscribers, avoiding NullReferenceException in one compact line.

units.title: Test at low target frame rate
units.detail: Set Application.targetFrameRate low during testing to reproduce frame-rate dependent bugs (like movement overshooting a target), ensuring the game works on weak machines.

units.title: SerializeField keeps fields private
units.detail: Make fields private and add [SerializeField] to expose them in the editor while preventing other classes from modifying them, preserving encapsulation.

units.title: System.Serializable enables JSON conversion
units.detail: Adding [System.Serializable] to custom classes lets them appear in the Inspector and converts correctly to/from JSON with JsonUtility, including nested objects.

units.title: Reviews estimate sales with 40x multiplier
units.detail: Multiply a game's review count by roughly 40 to estimate copies sold; about 50 reviews implies ~2000 copies, or ~$20k gross for a $10 game.

units.title: Don't benchmark against all Steam games
units.detail: The ~19,600 yearly Steam games include hobbyist first projects, asset flips, and AI slop; a professional developer with real skills competes only with other professional games.

units.title: Successful game count rises yearly
units.detail: Games reaching 100+ reviews slowly increases year over year; more games fail entirely, but simultaneously more games find real success, so the odds for serious devs are stable or improving.

units.title: White pixel texture for sprite placeholders
units.detail: Keep a 1x1 white pixel texture to assign to sprite renderers so they become visible, then stretch and tint it into any shape or color in the editor.

units.title: Lambdas for compact button listeners
units.detail: Attach button click behavior with compact lambda functions instead of writing a separate named function per button, keeping UI wiring tight.

units.title: Destroy a component, keep the object
units.detail: Call Destroy(this) inside a script to remove just that component while the game object persists, e.g., stopping AI logic on death but keeping death animation visuals.

units.title: Debug.DrawLine visualizes paths
units.detail: Draw Debug.DrawLine between path points to visualize pathfinding routes and internal state; remember to enable Gizmos in the game view or nothing shows.

units.title: Fade health bar damage effect
units.detail: Duplicate the health bar as a hidden damage bar behind it. On damage, set its fillAmount to the pre-damage value, alpha to 1, and reset a fade timer; when the timer runs out, fade alpha down to 0.

units.title: Shrink health bar damage effect
units.detail: Keep a damage bar behind the main bar. On damage, reset a shrink timer to max; when it elapses, decrease the damage bar's fillAmount toward the current bar fill. On heal, move the damage bar's fill up together with the bar.

units.title: Cut and fall health bar damage effect
units.detail: Keep a disabled damage-bar template anchored to the left. On damage, instantiate a copy, position it at the current bar edge using fillAmount * bar width, set its fill to the damage delta, then let it fall down and fade before destroying it.

units.title: Re-hit during visible damage window
units.detail: If the damage bar is already visible when hit again, only reset the timer and alpha instead of resetting its size, so rapid consecutive hits render as one continuous bar rather than flickering.

units.title: Notify health UI via events
units.detail: Have the health system expose OnDamaged/OnHealed events plus a normalized health getter, and let the UI subscribe and update in response instead of polling or coupling UI logic to damage code.

units.title: Trigger collider targeting
units.detail: Add a trigger collider on the attacker and react in OnTriggerEnter, verifying the entering object has the target component before attacking. Needs two colliders plus one rigidbody for events to fire.

units.title: Distance-based targeting from a list
units.detail: Keep a list of live targets; each frame test the distance between this transform and each target against a range and attack the first in range. Simple, code-only, works without colliders, but is O(n) over all enemies.

units.title: Physics overlap targeting
units.detail: Query all colliders within a circle around the attacker each update, iterate the results, and check for the target component. Scales to many enemies but requires colliders on targets and periodic queries.

units.title: Choose targeting by cost model
units.detail: Trigger colliders are event-based and efficient but clutter the scene with colliders; list-distance is portable and versatile but degrades with many entities; physics overlap handles crowds but needs colliders. Pick based on entity count and context.

units.title: Rate-limit expensive targeting queries
units.detail: Instead of running distance checks or overlap queries every frame, run them on a simple timer roughly 10 times per second to cut cost without noticeable behavior change.

units.title: Toggle door via enable/disable
units.detail: The simplest door: disable the game object to open (collider vanishes, player passes) and re-enable to close. Instant but visually abrupt.

units.title: Animated door moves its colliders
units.detail: Animate the door's child objects so the box colliders placed on them slide with the visuals, letting the player pass when open. Never animate the parent holding a static collider.

units.title: Hinge joint door with limits
units.detail: Connect the door to a hinge via a joint with angle limits. Lock it by setting min/max limits to zero and unlock by restoring the open limits, ideal for top-down games where the player pushes doors.

units.title: Colliders must move with animated parts
units.detail: If the collider stays on the parent while child visuals animate, the door remains solid. Put the collider on the moving pieces so collision follows geometry.

units.title: Transform-driven projectile
units.detail: Store a normalized shoot direction, move transform.position along it each frame scaled by speed and deltaTime, rotate to face the direction, and schedule a destroy after a fixed lifetime.

units.title: Physics-driven projectile
units.detail: Use a dynamic rigidbody and AddForce as an impulse along the shoot direction with zero gravity and drag; the physics system handles movement and collisions.

units.title: Hitscan raycast projectile
units.detail: For instant projectiles, fire a ray from the shoot position along the direction and check the hit collider for the target component. No moving object is needed at all.

units.title: Distance-check hit detection
units.detail: Each frame, query the closest target to the bullet position within a radius from a registered target list; damage the target and destroy the bullet on a hit. Works entirely without the physics system.

units.title: Fast projectiles need continuous collision
units.detail: A kinematic rigidbody moved via the transform can tunnel straight through thin targets; enable continuous collision detection and interpolation on the bullet to catch targets reliably.

units.title: Despawn projectiles after a lifetime
units.detail: Destroy spawned bullets after a fixed time (e.g. 5 seconds) so the scene does not accumulate endless projectiles flying off-screen.

units.title: Zoom camera via field of view
units.detail: Access the virtual camera's lens FOV, accumulate a target FOV from scroll input, clamp it between min and max, and smooth toward it each frame with Mathf.Lerp.

units.title: Zoom by moving follow offset
units.detail: Get the CinemachineTransposer and drive m_FollowOffset along its normalized direction, clamping the offset magnitude between min and max, smoothed with Vector3.Lerp.

units.title: Vertical zoom by lowering camera
units.detail: Modify only the follow offset's Y between clamped min/max to lower the camera toward the ground, giving a close-up low-angle view rather than pushing straight in.

units.title: 2D zoom uses orthographic size
units.detail: In 2D mode there is no field of view; zoom by changing the lens orthographic size using the same clamp-and-lerp logic.

units.title: Scroll wheel as zoom input
units.detail: Use Input.mouseScrollDelta.y to read positive/negative wheel movement; invert the sign to taste since 'forward to zoom in' is personal preference.

units.title: Scope zoom via FOV
units.detail: Zoom the whole camera by lowering FOV and lerping to a target value; extremely cheap and simple, but it magnifies the entire screen rather than just the scope.

units.title: Shader-based scope zoom
units.detail: Place a flat object inside the scope and use a scene-color shader that offsets the UV tiling to zoom only the area behind it; the rest of the screen stays normal and it renders only once.

units.title: Shader zoom pixelates at high magnification
units.detail: The shader only enlarges the fixed-resolution image, so deep zooms become blurry and pixelated. Fine for small zoom amounts, bad for sniper-style high magnification.

units.title: Render-texture scope
units.detail: Render a second camera into a render texture displayed on a quad inside the scope; add an alpha-clip circular mask for the round lens. Best visuals with unlimited crisp zoom, but renders the scene twice.

units.title: Per-scope post-processing
units.detail: Because a scope uses a separate camera, apply different post-processing to it than the main camera, e.g. depth of field on the world and clear focus in the scope, or night-vision/thermal in the lens.

units.title: Raycast ground check
units.detail: Raycast downward from the collider center for half its height plus a small extra margin against a platform layer mask; the player is grounded when the ray hits.

units.title: Center raycast fails on slopes and edges
units.detail: A single center raycast misses when only a corner of the collider touches the ground, breaking jumps on slopes and edges; increasing the ray distance only partially fixes slopes.

units.title: Box cast ground check
units.detail: Cast a box the size of the collider straight down by a small margin on the platform layer; it handles slopes and edges reliably and is the recommended ground-check method.

units.title: Ground check hits own collider
units.detail: A downward raycast from the player's collider hits the player itself; filter it with a layer mask that only includes the ground/platform layers.

units.title: Trigger-based ground check
units.detail: Add a child trigger collider at the feet and track grounded in OnTriggerStay/OnTriggerExit against the platform layer mask. Very visual and simple but requires an extra game object.

units.title: Angle mask shader
units.detail: Use the surface normal direction to output a black/white mask so effects like snow only appear on surfaces facing a given direction (e.g. upward), regardless of object orientation.

units.title: Interior cube mapping
units.detail: Fake interior rooms and depth on flat surfaces with a cube-mapping shader and no extra geometry; famously used for Spider-Man's city windows and looks like real depth.

units.title: Scroll UVs in vertex stage
units.detail: Scrolling UVs in the vertex stage produces visually identical results to fragment-stage tiling/offset but is much cheaper, especially on large objects with animated UVs.

units.title: Parallax mapping for surface depth
units.detail: Parallax techniques add perceived detail and depth to a flat surface in the shader without adding geometry, and come in variants (normal-only, parallax, parallax occlusion) with different quality.

units.title: Interface decouples interaction from door type
units.detail: Define an interface with Open/Close/Toggle so button, key, pressure plate, and automatic interaction scripts work with any door implementation (set-active, animated, hinge).

units.title: Interfaces can't be dragged in inspector
units.detail: Interface types don't show up as inspector fields in Unity, so serialize a GameObject reference and GetComponent the interface in Awake instead.

units.title: Distance-limited button interaction
units.detail: On button press, query all colliders near the player with an overlap-circle and toggle the first that implements the interaction interface, so the player must be close to a door to use it.

units.title: Automatic door via trigger
units.detail: A trigger zone calls Open when a collider enters and Close when it exits, verifying the entering object is the player (or implements an interaction interface).

units.title: Pressure plate with stay-and-timer
units.detail: Keep the door open while a collider stays inside the plate's trigger (OnTriggerStay); when it exits, run a countdown and close after the timer elapses, creating timed puzzle pressure plates.

units.title: Sleeping rigidbodies stop trigger events
units.detail: Physics objects that fall asleep stop firing OnTriggerStay, so the door closes while the player still stands on the plate; set the rigidbody's sleeping mode to never sleep to keep events firing.

units.title: Key door via key-type matching
units.detail: Keys carry a color/type, the player holds a key list, and a door consumes the matching key on open; a UI component subscribes to key-change events to refresh the display.

units.title: Reuse interaction system for any object
units.detail: The same interface pattern generalizes beyond doors: lights, elevators, or any togglable object can be driven by the identical button, auto, pressure, and key systems.

units.title: Watch playtesters silently
units.detail: Don't guide testers or rely on what they say; just observe where they struggle, because actions speak louder than words and reveal the real usability issues.

units.title: Friends and family give biased feedback
units.detail: Close people are usually too nice to give honest critique; real players are more brutal, so weight external/stranger feedback more when evaluating your game.

units.title: Launch a Steam page early
units.detail: Publish a public store page as early as possible so people can start wishlisting and you build an audience and following before the game releases.

units.title: Reuse audience across similar genres
units.detail: Sticking with the same or similar management/simulation genres lets wishlist and audience interest carry over from one game to the next, compounding your following over time.

units.title: Learn from experts over trial-and-error
units.detail: To improve at any skill, study what top practitioners do differently and apply it. Learning directly from someone more skilled is much faster than random trial and error.

units.title: Break big problems into tiny pieces
units.detail: Any large task (e.g. making an MMO) can be broken into manageable sub-problems like character controller, then NPC, then quests, then networking. Practice this as a thinking exercise; it enables building anything.

units.title: Never stop learning
units.detail: Knowledge builds on itself: each thing learned unlocks more advanced topics. Treat skill as a never-ending path rather than a finite checkbox.

units.title: Don't blame the computer
units.detail: Computers are deterministic: same code always gives same output. If your code fails, the bug is in the code, not the machine. Debug by re-reading and adding logs instead of getting frustrated.

units.title: Read the error message carefully
units.detail: Error messages contain the info needed to solve the problem. When asking for help, describe the exact error; vague 'I have an error' reports are unhelpful.

units.title: Get your hands dirty with simple tasks
units.detail: Never consider any task beneath you; writing simple systems still yields experience. Help others by mentoring juniors, as guided learning beats solo trial and error, and the cycle compounds.

units.title: Illusion of intelligence beats real AI
units.detail: Half-Life 2 made AI seem to 'predict' players by placing invisible bullseye targets on windows the AI prioritizes shooting. Fake cleverness is often better than genuinely smart AI.

units.title: AI is a show, not a simulation
units.detail: What makes AI fights interesting is putting on a compelling show, not perfect aim/tactics. Perfectly accurate AI is trivial to build and not fun to fight.

units.title: Satisfy different player types (Bartle)
units.detail: Players split into Achievers, Explorers, Socializers and Killers. In vehicle sections, speed-runners need fast-fun tools/challenge while explorers need every inch of the map filled with optional rewards.

units.title: Cut what doesn't work
units.detail: Valve cut the entire Borealis level after playtests showed close-quarters ship combat was unsatisfying. A game with less content but higher quality beats one with filler; don't let sunk cost keep broken content.

units.title: Iterate everything, constantly
units.detail: Final game products are the result of endless iteration on levels, weapons, art and story. Watch players struggle silently, take notes, and fix repeatedly; never assume your first idea is best.

units.title: Mechanics interaction grid
units.detail: Build a grid of all items, weapons, enemies and mechanics, then ensure something interesting happens at every intersection. Fill empty cells with new designed interactions to create emergent gameplay.

units.title: Perfectionism blocks shipping
units.detail: Half-Life 3 was never made because Valve felt it needed innovation beyond a story continuation. High standards help, but at some point launch beats chasing perfection; a game doesn't have to be perfect to be great.

units.title: Crafting = inputs and outputs
units.detail: A crafting system is simply defined recipes of input items producing an output. Dinky Guardians tosses the crafted output item into the air because watching it fly is more fun than spawning in a container.

units.title: Linking buildings creates ownership
units.detail: Have machines require separately-built container buildings the player links together, rather than self-contained machines. Interlocking systems give players ownership and agency over the world.

units.title: Building capsules for controller UI
units.detail: Instead of a button overlay (bad for controller play), represent building blueprints as physical capsule objects the player carries and throws, so any carryable object can construct a building.

units.title: Tiered resource spawn areas
units.detail: Define resource nodes in the world with spawn rates: basic resources spawn constantly, advanced ones require the player to place a fracking machine on the node to extract them.

units.title: Heat mechanic as dynamic difficulty
units.detail: Spawn enemy zombies based on loose physics objects on the map. More clutter means more/stronger enemies, making it self-correcting: getting overrun destroys colony and reduces future difficulty, letting players rebuild.

units.title: Dinkies spawn from houses
units.detail: Refactor the house to track spawned units; a spawner cycles houses with valid positions and emits a new unit every interval. Simple clean data structure drives the spawning loop.

units.title: Rewriting code is normal
units.detail: Even experienced developers refactor the same system repeatedly (the building-link UI was rewritten 5 times). Don't expect perfect first-pass code; leave room to iterate.

units.title: Render textures show linked buildings
units.detail: Use render textures to display nearby container buildings in a building's UI for selecting link targets. (Also covers red/blue boxes/raycast selection from a prior video.)

units.title: Steam first-build manual review
units.detail: Steam manually reviews your first uploaded build (checks it works, no malware); after that, updates upload freely. Plan deadlines around this gate before festivals or demos.

units.title: Make a game you genuinely want
units.detail: Don't chase trends; making a game is a marathon and you can't force passion through the whole journey. Ask if you're excited to play the final version.

units.title: Verify a market exists
units.detail: Use SteamSpy to gauge genre size and be brutally honest about audience. Don't tell yourself an adventure game appeals to Counter-Strike players.

units.title: Compare against realistic successes
units.detail: Success is relative: point-and-click needs far fewer sales than FPS. Look at similar-quality games' sales, not top sellers like Dead Cells, and define what success means for your budget.

units.title: Balance uniqueness with clarity
units.detail: Be unique enough to hook players in 5 seconds but not so weird your target audience is confused. Crowded genres (platformers) need far more uniqueness than sparse ones.

units.title: Validate scope with a prototype
units.detail: Ask honestly if you can finish it given team/skill. Prototype the hard parts (special AI, fancy shaders) early to confirm feasibility before committing months.

units.title: Don't spend years on your first game
units.detail: Make quick games (1-2 weeks, like Flappy Bird) early; you learn far more finishing many small games. Reserve multi-year projects for your 5th or 6th game with solid experience.

units.title: Stay focused, brain-dump new ideas
units.detail: Write every new idea down (paper, text file, notes) to remove it from your head so it stops distracting you. Don't jump projects; revisit the idea list when the current game is done.

units.title: Work from checklists
units.detail: Keep to-do lists for daily tasks, monthly goals and your current game. Working from a list beats staring at an empty project; do one item at a time.

units.title: Do the non-fun parts too
units.detail: Music, sound, steam page art and trailers are necessary to ship. Concept art and lore create the illusion of productivity; allocate dedicated time for the boring-but-essential backend work.

units.title: Devlogs are marketing
units.detail: If you want financial success, marketing is mandatory and devlogs are the most straightforward channel. They also give free feedback: no views may signal a weak game idea worth reconsidering.

units.title: Game-dev audiences don't convert to players
units.detail: A game-dev YouTube audience rarely becomes game players; entertainment channels convert far better. Twitter is the worst place to find players - it's full of devs, not gamers.

units.title: Polish everything evenly
units.detail: Don't hyperfocus one aspect (e.g. gunplay) while enemies stay prototype-level; the game must work as a whole. Match quality across systems, then polish broadly.

units.title: Cultivate discipline, not motivation
units.detail: Motivation is ephemeral; discipline carries you through. Work from lists whether you feel like it or not, but accept occasional off-days without self-punishment.

units.title: Keep first-game scope tiny
units.detail: Design something for one month, then cut it in half. Beginners should clone classics (Space Invaders, Pac-Man, Arkanoid) to learn tools, then expand with new weapons, enemies or modes.

units.title: Build on your strengths
units.detail: Artists should make mechanically simple games (platformers, point-and-clicks) where art shines; programmers should make systems games (sims, strategy) with minimal art. To finish a project, favor strengths.

units.title: Search for answers effectively
units.detail: Knowing how to Google is a core game-dev skill. When stuck, search for someone who solved the same problem instead of banging your head against it.

units.title: Be consistent, avoid burnout
units.detail: Creating a game is a marathon; go slowly and make it part of your routine, moving a step closer daily with a to-do list. Burnout and week-long breaks kill progress.

units.title: Finishing beats prototype-churning
units.detail: Most people quit mid-game; finishing puts you ahead. Completing games teaches progression, flow, balancing, juice, menus and save/load - things prototypes never cover.

units.title: All-in-one sprite shader
units.detail: A single shader combining dozens of effects (glow, outline, gradients, hue shift, UV distortion) that works on any renderer - sprites, particles, tilemaps, UI. Add one component and animate properties.

units.title: Color space affects glow intensity
units.detail: Glow effects look different in gamma vs linear color space. Set bloom threshold/intensity appropriately (e.g. ~1) per color space; the shader supports both with different settings.

units.title: Tight sprite meshes break effects
units.detail: Outline/distortion effects need extra space; a 'tight' mesh cutting off alpha breaks them. Switch mesh type to Full Rect (or leave sprite atlas padding) so effects have room to render.

units.title: Drive shader props via code
units.detail: Modify effects at runtime like any shader property: material.SetFloat("_Glow", 30) on pickup, back to 0 on expiry. Wrap in Mathf.Lerp in Update for smooth transitions.

units.title: 60 days is enough for a prototype
units.detail: An hour a day for 60 days (~60 hours) can produce a working prototype of any modest idea, or complete a beginner course one lecture per day. Start now, don't wait for New Year.

units.title: DOTS for complex voxel systems
units.detail: Complex simulated systems like Teardown-style destruction likely can't be built with plain GameObjects but may be possible with DOTS (Unity's Data-Oriented Tech Stack).

units.title: Prototype gameplay before art
units.detail: Art-first development wastes time since assets get redrawn as skills improve. Build an ugly gray-box prototype first: if it's fun ugly, it'll be even better polished. (Exception: art-driven genres like visual novels.)

units.title: Playtest with strangers, not just friends
units.detail: Friends/family give positively-biased feedback. Get strangers (Reddit, Discord, itch.io, your own audience) to test early and often; collect initial impressions, favorites, least favorites and missing features.

units.title: Don't implement every idea
units.detail: Scope creep from adding every requested feature yields a mishmash. Ask whether a new mechanic fits your core design; if unsure, prototype and playtest it before committing.

units.title: Prototype individual systems
units.detail: You can prototype single mechanics, not just whole games: get the core of one idea working just enough to test whether it improves the final game.

units.title: Borrow mechanics by analyzing why
units.detail: Study the games you love with a designer's eye to understand why their systems work, then apply those lessons. Don't copy-paste; adapt the underlying reason.

units.title: Vertical slice for funding
units.detail: After the prototype phase, polish a tiny slice of the game as much as possible to secure publisher funding or promote a Steam page.

units.title: Set deadlines and announce them publicly
units.detail: Committing to a 6-month deadline and telling other people creates accountability that keeps you working even on low-motivation days.

units.title: Reserve final month for polish and bugs
units.detail: Leave the last month of a 6-month project empty for balancing and polish because unexpected problems always surface at the end, and polish is what separates good games from great ones.

units.title: Cut scope in half twice
units.detail: Initial scope estimates are wildly unrealistic, so cut them in half then half again. Multi-genre mashups produce half-baked systems; focus on 1-2 genres done perfectly.

units.title: Finish projects instead of restarting
units.detail: Feeling like restarting after learning a lot is normal, but finishing teaches you real costs (balancing, localization) and guarantees a release; apply lessons to the next game.

units.title: Keep a living roadmap, re-estimate often
units.detail: Reorganize your roadmap every day and week since time estimates are imprecise; a detailed to-do list keeps you focused and shows how far the finish line is.

units.title: Build dev tools to skip long test setup
units.detail: A save system that loads mid-game states means you never replay 20 minutes to reach a state you want to test; build tools alongside the game itself.

units.title: Keep gameplay loop under 20 minutes
units.detail: Short runs (like roguelikes) make constant iteration and balancing easy; a quick-to-play loop lets you tell whether a feature is fun within minutes.

units.title: Game design is a skill to train separately
units.detail: Being good at programming is not the same as good game design; study what makes favorite games (e.g., FTL, Into the Breach) fun and train design like any other skill.

units.title: Play games as research, analyze mechanics
units.detail: Feed creativity by playing similar games, but analyze why a mechanic works rather than copy-pasting it; apply the underlying reason uniquely to your own game.

units.title: Invest in solid architecture early
units.detail: A clean core built from game programming patterns means adding new content stays easy, you never refactor, and iteration is fast; quick-and-dirty code becomes a mess at the end.

units.title: Developers get blinded to non-intuitive UI
units.detail: After months of development controls seem obvious only to you; real playtesters reveal missing tutorial guidance and which mechanics players ignore or love.

units.title: Use Steam playtest feature for feedback
units.detail: Steam gives a free playtest app ID so you can hand out keys; player feedback redirects effort to mechanics people enjoy and cuts ones nobody cares about.

units.title: Even great games need marketing
units.detail: Post as often as possible on as many platforms as you can and hope something sticks; without any marketing, even an awesome game goes unheard.

units.title: Steam Next Fest vs themed fests
units.detail: Next Fest runs twice a year with no approval (participate once, ideally right before release); themed fests require theme-based approval but allow unlimited participation.

units.title: C# offers speed, tutorials, and job skills
units.detail: Unity uses C#, a fast language with continual updates, a huge tutorial and library ecosystem, and strong career opportunities outside game dev.

units.title: Unity is strong in both 2D and 3D
units.detail: Unity keeps adding 2D features (pixel-perfect, 2D IK) and can make anything from pixel art to massive 3D worlds in a single engine.

units.title: One-click builds to many platforms
units.detail: Unity exports to Windows, Mac, Linux, Android, iOS, consoles, VR and web with a button push, giving native builds that reach more players.

units.title: Unity services cover the business side
units.detail: The dashboard provides collaboration, ads, analytics, and cloud diagnostics (automatic error reports from players), plus a revamped multiplayer stack.

units.title: Asset store speeds up development
units.detail: The asset store provides models, textures, sounds and complex tools for quick starts; just adapt assets to fit your game instead of shipping a straight asset flip.

units.title: Make small weekly games for volume
units.detail: Spend 1-2 months building simple one-mechanic prototypes across varied genres (Pong, top-down shooter, racing), prioritizing volume and continuous learning over unique ideas.

units.title: Watch tutorials above your skill level
units.detail: Follow both engine-specific and standalone C# tutorials, including intermediate content you can't fully follow, to expose yourself to advanced concepts and learn faster.

units.title: Complete a simple game in about 4 weeks
units.detail: A complete game needs a main menu, gameplay loop, end state, near-bug-free code plus sound and music; recreating an existing game with a small twist frees time to learn the engine.

units.title: Read Clean Code early
units.detail: Clean code makes projects more organized, performant, and adaptable; it is essential as projects grow, e.g., a 90,000-line game requires constant structuring discipline.

units.title: Publish a 3-month game to Steam
units.detail: Make a small tight game with one core experience, play to your art or programming strengths, and learn the whole Steam publishing, player-feedback, and basic marketing process.

units.title: Read Code Complete after Clean Code
units.detail: Code Complete is ~900 pages and deeper than Clean Code; reading and applying it makes you a better programmer than most and is a must before bigger projects.

units.title: Write a design doc for the 6-month game
units.detail: Spend 2-3 weeks on a written high-level design with main pillars and detail on core mechanics; keep it short, not a 100-page document, so it guides without over-constraining.

units.title: Keep game playable and fix debt as you go
units.detail: Fix bugs rather than deferring them, keep the build stable and playable while adding mechanics, and write level managers with multi-level expansion in mind from the start.

units.title: Build wishlists before release
units.detail: Make the coming-soon page as early as possible, publish good screenshots, and do pre-launch marketing so you have thousands of wishlists by the time you launch.

units.title: Polish is what separates good from great
units.detail: In the final months, focus solely on polishing existing mechanics and game feel instead of adding more, and aim for a tight 5-hour experience rather than 40 hours of content.

units.title: Engage the community after launch
units.detail: Watch Steam forums and reviews closely, fix technical issues fast to avoid negative-review spirals, and send keys to curators, YouTubers, and your newsletter.

units.title: About 90% of game makers never finish a game
units.detail: Completing a full game in six months already puts you ahead; simply finishing at all is a huge differentiator in this industry.

units.title: Own-site launch with no audience sells near zero
units.detail: An unknown first-time dev self-publishing on their own site sold about $300 total over six months; discoverability, not the game, was the real bottleneck.

units.title: A Steam launch can transform results
units.detail: The same game earned $15k in its first month on Steam vs ~$300 self-published, partly because fewer games competed back then and the storefront gave visibility.

units.title: Perseverance can create a second chance
units.detail: After a flop, the dev saw slow greenlight votes as hope, spent five months fixing bugs and polishing, got approved, and turned the game into a career.

units.title: Unity hides useful GitHub tools
units.detail: NavMeshComponents, 2D extras, photo mode, and starter FPS/third-person controller assets exist only as GitHub projects or single blog posts, so most users never discover them.

units.title: Don't deprecate before a replacement is ready
units.detail: Deprecating networking and pushing new render pipelines before parity with built-in caused pain; newer tools like the input system should coexist with legacy ones rather than remove them.

units.title: DOTS equals ECS plus Burst plus Job System
units.detail: Only ECS is still in preview; the Burst compiler and Job System are stable and verified, so claims that all of DOTS is stuck in preview are inaccurate.

units.title: Know tool relationships: upgrade vs side-grade
units.detail: VFX Graph and particle system are side-grades (GPU vs CPU), input system is an upgrade of input manager, TextMeshPro is a straight upgrade over legacy text, ECS does not replace GameObjects, and URP/HDRP have reached parity with built-in.

units.title: Custom shader assets break in render pipelines
units.detail: Assets using custom shaders do not auto-convert to URP/HDRP, so verify pipeline support before buying and only highlight pipeline-compatible assets in sales.

units.title: Hide legacy features by default
units.detail: Keep legacy text mesh and animation systems supported but hidden by default (like preview packages) so beginners aren't confused about which tool to use.

units.title: Post-processing massively improves visuals
units.detail: Adding post-processing and ambient occlusion is one of the easiest ways to make a game look great and feel grounded; ambient occlusion is always worth adding.

units.title: ProBuilder gray-boxes levels in-engine
units.detail: ProBuilder lets you model 3D geometry directly inside Unity, ideal for quickly blocking out new levels without external 3D tools.

units.title: Assembly definitions speed compilation
units.detail: Splitting code into multiple assemblies means only the changed assembly recompiles, saving significant time on large projects.

units.title: Use Addressables for complex asset loading
units.detail: The Resources folder is simple but limited; Addressables give full control over when to load and unload, including remote URLs for live events without updating the executable.

units.title: Remote config changes game without a rebuild
units.detail: Define parameters or asset overrides in the dashboard (e.g., boss health, Christmas event) and the game fetches them live, avoiding executable updates.

units.title: Cloud diagnostics captures player errors
units.detail: Toggle one setting and Unity automatically receives errors and crashes from players' machines, solving the hard problem of getting bug reports.

units.title: Localize text, audio, and images
units.detail: Unity's localization package supports any asset type and TextMeshPro fallback fonts, making proper localization surprisingly easy.

units.title: Every game is 90% the same
units.detail: Core fundamentals (player controller, interactions, UI, data, physics) apply to any genre, so learn general basics rather than hunting for a tutorial for your exact dream game.

units.title: Simulator genre is low-risk for indies
units.detail: Take the proven 90% (look around, interact) and change only the theme (supermarket, car shop, gas station); players already enjoy the core loop, so risk drops versus original ideas.

units.title: Improving existing games beats originality
units.detail: Start from ~80% proven mechanics so players are guaranteed to enjoy the core, then add a 20% twist; fully original games risk players not understanding why they are interesting.

units.title: Difficulty means you're at the edge of knowledge
units.detail: When tutorials suddenly get hard, it is normal, not a sign you are doing something wrong; push through and your edge of knowledge advances.

units.title: Each game made increases success odds
units.detail: First games are rarely hits (almost no popular Steam releases are a developer's first game); each game removes mistakes and raises your odds, so keep making more.

units.title: Self-discipline beats motivation
units.detail: Motivation is random; discipline is doing the work whether you feel like it or not. It is a skill you build by gradually extending forced work time from 10 minutes to 8-10 hours.

units.title: Clone classic arcade games to learn
units.detail: Flappy Bird, Arkanoid, Snake, Asteroids, Lunar Lander (then Space Invaders, Pac-Man, Angry Birds, Missile Command, Fruit Ninja) each teach distinct skills like physics, AI, and input.

units.title: Launch Steam page when ready to showcase
units.detail: Publish the coming-soon page once the game idea and visual style are locked and you can show several visually different environments; screenshots can be dummy visuals with no logic.

units.title: Reuse genre and assets across games
units.detail: Spiderweb Software made dozens of similar CRPGs for 25+ years, reusing sprites and mechanics; fans carry over so each new game starts with an audience (see GDC talk Failing to Fail).

units.title: Validate game ideas before building
units.detail: Track monthly Steam releases to develop a sense of what sells, and post gifs on Reddit or Twitter to measure engagement; friends and family are too biased to trust.

units.title: Game dev isn't a lottery
units.detail: Nothing is guaranteed, but choosing a popular genre (e.g., simulator) over oversaturated ones (2D puzzle platformers) clearly shifts the odds in your favor.

units.title: Idea theft is rare; obscurity is the enemy
units.detail: Everyone has too many ideas and bare ideas are not valuable; only games that already made millions get ripped off. Talk about your game everywhere instead of hiding it.

units.title: Define your own success
units.detail: Making $0 is not failure if your goal is hobby fun or just finishing; decide your goals first and measure against them, like running for fitness rather than income.

units.title: Angry Birds was Rovio's 52nd game
units.detail: Rovio made 51 games before Angry Birds; expect your first game to be learning, with success odds growing from roughly 0.1% on game one toward ~10% by game ten.

units.title: Success is not linear game to game
units.detail: Survivor Squad made ~$100k in 6 months but its objectively better sequel made ~$10k; expect hits and flops, keep savings, and rely on making more games to smooth revenue.

units.title: Run logic a few times per second, not every frame
units.detail: Use a timer counted down with deltaTime; when it hits zero, reset it and run expensive logic (e.g., find-target sphere casts) 2-5 times/sec instead of every frame for a large performance win.

units.title: Avoid string-based object lookup
units.detail: Transform.Find uses strings, which are terrible identifiers (an invisible whitespace character causes silent null refs); use [SerializeField] and drag-and-drop so the correct reference is guaranteed.

units.title: Awake for local init, Start for external refs
units.detail: Awake runs before all Start calls, so initialize the object's own state (e.g., singleton Instance) in Awake and only access other objects' references in Start; this prevents order-dependent null refs.

units.title: Test your game at a low frame rate
units.detail: Frame-rate-dependent bugs (e.g., an object overshooting and jittering around a target) only appear on slow machines; force a low targetFrameRate and play through the whole game.

units.title: Singleton: static Instance set in Awake
units.detail: Expose a public static Instance property with a private set, assign it in Awake so only the class can set it, and read Player.Instance from other classes in Start.

units.title: Observer pattern with C# events
units.detail: Raise events like OnDamage with a null-conditional invoke (onDamage?.Invoke) so the player never knows about listeners like health bars; subscribing with += keeps systems decoupled.

units.title: Programming is logic, not memorization
units.detail: You don't need to memorize syntax; knowing the logic lets you build the same systems in any language, looking up syntax (e.g., PHP arrays, foreach) on demand.

units.title: Don't obsess over learning speed
units.detail: Learning C# or gamedev takes anywhere from a week to a year depending on the person and starting point; steady incremental daily progress matters more than pace.

units.title: Claim Unity's weekly free asset
units.detail: The publisher-of-the-week sale on the asset store includes one free asset each week; add it to the cart and use the coupon code at checkout to drop the price to zero.

units.title: Pick one engine and master it
units.detail: Unity, Unreal, and Godot (even Lua-based LÖVE) can all ship excellent games like Balatro; deep knowledge of one tool beats hopping between a dozen engines.

units.title: 3D may be easier than 2D via asset packs
units.detail: For non-artists, buying style-matched 3D model packs and mixing them is often easier than matching 2D sprite styles; the code logic differs only by adding an axis.

units.title: Buy vs build: value your time
units.detail: Always frame asset purchases against your hourly rate; if a $36 toolkit saves ~300 hours of building, buying wins whenever your time is worth more than about $0.12 an hour.

units.title: Use the latest LTS or support Unity version
units.detail: Pre-release versions are only for the beta program; use the newest LTS or support version in production, back up before minor upgrades, and definitely before major-version upgrades.

units.title: Vote on Unity's public roadmap
units.detail: At unity.com/roadmap you can see released, planned, and under-consideration features and vote on the ones that matter to you to influence the engine's direction.

units.title: Unity Assistant gives project-specific AI help
units.detail: Unity's AI assistant was trained on the docs and has context of your whole project, making it more accurate than generic chatbots for Unity and tutorial questions.

units.title: Participate in a Steam festival
units.detail: A Next Fest/Steam festival is a must for indie devs: it can deliver tens of thousands of wishlists. You can only participate once per game, so pick the festival right before release.

units.title: Demo should be a polished vertical slice
units.detail: A small, highly polished ~30-minute demo is far better than 10 hours of mediocre content. Treat the demo as a super-polished vertical slice even if the full game isn't finished.

units.title: Fast tutorial onboarding for demos
units.detail: Festival demos are short, so players must learn the game instantly. A great tutorial that gently teaches mechanics is crucial since players abandon anything slightly annoying when thousands of free demos compete.

units.title: Demo playtime benchmarks are medians
units.detail: From Chris Zukowski's How To Market A Game: demo median playtime benchmarks are ~7 min (bronze), 18 (silver), 38 (gold), 65 (diamond). These are medians, not averages, so a strong 65-min demo is extremely hard.

units.title: Missing tutorial tanks playtime
units.detail: A demo without a tutorial had ~9-minute median playtime; after adding a proper tutorial and changes it rose to ~13 minutes with an upward trend. Onboarding directly drives retention.

units.title: Instrument tutorial stages with analytics
units.detail: Track events at every tutorial stage; most players won't give written feedback, so analytics reveal the 'silent majority'. Adding more flashing arrows at a high-drop-off step raised stage completion from 91% to 94%.

units.title: Automated crash/cloud diagnostics
units.detail: Add automated cloud diagnostics (e.g. Unity's) to see crashes and bugs without direct player reports, so you can fix root causes or add guards before issues break the game.

units.title: In-game feedback form with screenshot
units.detail: Few players write feedback, so make it trivial: an in-game feedback window (optionally with auto-attached screenshots) beats expecting players to use YouTube/Steam forums. Many store assets exist for this.

units.title: Push marketing right before festival
units.detail: Unconfirmed theory: pre-festival performance may affect festival visibility. Posting shorts/devlogs in the 1-2 weeks before the festival gathered ~150 wishlists, though it's stressful alongside demo deadlines.

units.title: Livestream dev sessions during festival
units.detail: Steam festivals allow two live events promoted on the homepage; streaming development rather than gameplay stands out from other devs. Two streams drew ~6k and ~5k views with good avg view duration, though wishlist impact was unclear.

units.title: A* costs: G, H, and F
units.detail: G is the walking cost from the start node, H is the heuristic estimate to the goal (e.g. ignoring walls), and F = G + H. Always expand the node with the lowest F since it's most likely close to the goal.

units.title: Open list vs closed list
units.detail: The open list holds nodes queued for searching; the closed list holds already-searched nodes. Loop until the current node is the goal or the open list empties (meaning no path exists).

units.title: Use integers for A* costs
units.detail: To work with ints instead of floats, multiply: straight movement costs 10 and diagonal costs 14 (sqrt(200) rounded), giving clean integer arithmetic for G costs.

units.title: Retrace path via parent references
units.detail: Each node stores a 'came from' parent reference. Once the goal is reached, walk backwards from goal to start following parents, then reverse the list to get the final path.

units.title: Tentative G-cost relaxation
units.detail: For each neighbor, compute a tentative G (current node G + movement cost). Only update the neighbor when this is lower than its stored G — meaning you found a faster route — then update H and F.

units.title: Empty open list means no path
units.detail: If the open list runs out before reaching the goal, the map is fully searched with no valid route — return 'no path' rather than a partial/invalid result.

units.title: Mark and skip unwalkable nodes
units.detail: Give each node a walkable flag; during neighbor expansion, nodes that aren't walkable are added to the closed list and skipped so the path routes around obstacles.

units.title: Linear lowest-F search is slow
units.detail: Scanning the whole open list for the lowest F is fine on small grids but scales badly. Use a binary heap, and pre-compute each node's neighbors when building the grid instead of recalculating them every search.

units.title: Visualize the algorithm for debugging
units.detail: A step-by-step debug view (G/H/F values, open list in blue, closed list in red) makes A* behavior obvious and catches logic errors far faster than reading code.

units.title: Convert grid to world positions for movement
units.detail: Expose a find-path function that takes world positions, converts them to grid coordinates, runs A*, then converts path nodes back to world positions (grid index × cell size) so units can follow a plain list of waypoints.

units.title: AI 'game engines' generate frames, not games
units.detail: A diffusion-based 'AI game engine' (like the Doom demo) generates video/images with no code or real world underneath. It learned from people playing Doom, so the game must exist before the AI can mimic it.

units.title: Short AI memory causes hallucinations
units.detail: The AI only kept ~3 seconds of context, so moving forward erased what was behind it — rooms visibly changed layout. Frame-generating models have no persistent level or logic, only an assumption about the next image.

units.title: Use AI hallucinations for brainstorming
units.detail: Train an AI to play a bare-bones prototype and crank the hallucination to max: it generates new areas, items, and enemies beyond what it saw — a positive use of a usually-bad failure mode.

units.title: AI can't replace game devs yet
units.detail: Building a full game needs programming, design, art, sound, etc., so an AI that builds a whole game from one prompt would basically require AGI. Treat such AI as a working-alongside tool, not a replacement.

units.title: The training environment is the hard part
units.detail: For ML-Agents projects the code is trivial; the tricky part is designing what the AI needs to know. Before coding, decide observations (rays, walls, checkpoints) and rewards that define the task.

units.title: Ray perception sensor for observations
units.detail: A ray-perception sensor fires rays (configurable count, angle range up to 360°, sphere-cast radius, length, vertical offsets) and feeds hit distance and type into the observations automatically.

units.title: Asymmetric collision rewards
units.detail: Give a large negative reward on first wall contact plus a small per-frame penalty while touching; this prevents the AI from just sliding along walls. Checkpoint rewards signal progress.

units.title: Instant-loss episodes prevent learning
units.detail: Making the agent lose on wall touch made every episode tiny, so it rarely explored forward to find the first reward. Making walls solid and disabling episode-end gave it room to learn.

units.title: Curriculum: simple track first
units.detail: Train on easy scenarios first (left turns), then right turns, then a complex track. Space checkpoints evenly and add extra ones on hard turns so the AI gets frequent reward feedback where it matters.

units.title: Bootstrap RL with imitation learning
units.detail: Record demo playthroughs and enable BC + GAIL near strength 1 to clone behavior; then lower imitation strength and raise extrinsic rewards so it surpasses the demos. Train per-track, then on all tracks with pure RL.

units.title: Layer masks and tags filter ray hits
units.detail: Set the sensor's layer mask so rays only collide with relevant layers (walls/checkpoints) and use detectable tags so the agent learns distances to different object types and can increase/decrease distance accordingly.

units.title: Train on multiple tracks to generalize
units.detail: A brain trained across several track shapes (with built-in walls/checkpoints) lets cars race any custom player-created track; more training steps (e.g. 50M) yield more robust generalization.

units.title: Curriculum learning for RL agents
units.detail: Train bit by bit: first no pipes / huge gap, then shrink gaps and add randomness as the agent improves. Brute-forcing the final difficulty needs GPU farms; curriculum needs only one machine.

units.title: Imitation learning bootstrap, then taper
units.detail: Start with high BC+GAIL strength so the agent clones your demos, then lower it (0.4, then 0.1) while raising extrinsic reward strength so it learns beyond you. Expect the reward to dip after big difficulty jumps, then recover.

units.title: Max-step cap masks agent skill
units.detail: A 2000-step episode cap caps the max reward, hiding true performance. Only after setting max steps to 0 (episode ends only on loss) did scores jump from ~20 to 220+, showing the cap was the limiting factor.

units.title: Train RL on standalone builds
units.detail: When a game can't support multiple parallel environments, train on normal builds: set the agent to default behavior, make the build require no input, and use --inf to point at the build plus --num-envs for instance count.

units.title: Many training instances eat disk space
units.detail: 20 parallel training instances used almost 30GB of disk; 8 instances still trained fast enough. Watch memory, disk, and CPU when scaling --num-envs.

units.title: Server/headless builds speed up training
units.detail: If the game logic doesn't depend on visuals or camera input, build a server (headless) executable so training runs much faster without rendering overhead.

units.title: Debugging is a top skill — protect it
units.detail: Debugging took the author ~20 years to build and is one of the most valuable skills; leaning on AI to explain every error erodes it. Read every error message fully, even when AI is available.

units.title: AI as explainer, not replacement
units.detail: Use AI to understand code ('why does this line work?') and to learn — it's excellent at line-by-line explanations. The danger is using it to auto-solve problems so you never build the skill yourself.

units.title: Short-term AI speed trades away understanding
units.detail: Copy-pasting AI solutions optimizes for today's commit at the cost of tomorrow's ability: you become a 'middleman' who can ask good questions but can't understand the answers, helpless when the AI goes down.

units.title: Rules of engagement for AI coding
units.detail: No AI for problems you haven't tried to understand first; read and understand every AI suggestion before using it; do regular no-AI coding sessions; focus on learning patterns, not just immediate fixes. Beginners especially should follow these.

units.title: Self-discipline is the key skill
units.detail: The temptation to take the easy AI answer is real, especially for beginners and kids who lack discipline. Deliberately not taking shortcuts is what preserves problem-solving skill long-term.

units.title: Error-free coding means no learning
units.detail: Every error you solve yourself teaches something; if AI 'magically' fixes errors you learn nothing and stay dependent. Seeing many errors is a sign of active learning as long as you solve them yourself.

units.title: Unity best-practices hub has free resources
units.detail: Unity's best-practices hub (y.com/howto) offers detailed free ebooks (profiling, DOTS, C# style, optimization) and deep blog posts (2D lights, UI Toolkit, design patterns, mobile perf) kept updated to Unity 6.

units.title: Define a code style and stay consistent
units.detail: There's no single objective best code style; any style works as long as you're consistent. Pick a style you like and follow it to the letter.

units.title: Set a frame budget and profile
units.detail: Performance work starts by setting a frame budget (ms per frame) and knowing whether you're CPU-bound or GPU-bound. Mobile is trickier; reduce memory access operations and learn the profiling tools.

units.title: 2D lights massively improve visuals
units.detail: Adding 2D studio lights (point, freeform, sprite) transforms a 2D game's look — the difference between no lights and proper lighting is gigantic and worth learning via the sample projects.

units.title: Unity Muse grounds answers in docs
units.detail: Muse's text assistant searches documentation/training/support content to give structured, up-to-date answers with source links — an explicit attempt to fight AI hallucination. Answers can still be vague (e.g. 'implement match-3 mechanics').

units.title: Text-to-animation drafts
units.detail: Generating draft animations (e.g. 'do a backflip') from text is valuable when you have no animator skills; follow-up refinement (more intense, jump higher) would make it truly useful.

units.title: Sketch-region generation for variations
units.detail: Selecting image regions to generate (rather than one prompt for the whole image) is a much better workflow for creating variations, e.g. replacing one sprite or texture area at a time.

units.title: Sentis runs AI locally on-device
units.detail: Sentis embeds a trained AI model in the runtime across all Unity platforms — no cloud hosting, no per-user server costs, and low latency. Question remains: how do you train the model (vs. the old Barracuda)?.

units.title: AI training data/copyright unclear
units.detail: Unity's AI tools answered vaguely about their training datasets (a 'licensed LLM' + Unity docs; art tools unclear). Before using AI assets in commercial games, verify dataset provenance and copyright — this is essential for serious devs.

units.title: Verify AI outputs — don't trust confidence
units.detail: Chat-style AIs confidently produce wrong answers (hallucination); prefer tools that cite sources and always verify generated code and content, using AI for brainstorming and design rather than authoritative output.

units.title: Decouple hotkey input from game logic
units.detail: Move raw key-input handling out of the MonoBehaviour into a dedicated plain C# class (no MonoBehavior) that receives the player reference via constructor, then call its Update from the MonoBehaviour. This keeps the UI/input code separate from game logic and makes the system reusable.

units.title: Bind keys to actions via Action delegate
units.detail: Store abilities as objects holding an enum ability type plus a System.Action delegate. Map each hotkey index to a list entry instead of hard-coding function calls, so reassigning what a key does is a one-line data change rather than editing input code.

units.title: Enum + Action pattern for extensible abilities
units.detail: Modeling each ability as a struct/class of (type enum + activation Action) makes the system data-driven: swapping which ability a key triggers, or moving abilities between slots, only requires changing list data, never the input/UI code.

units.title: Duplicate a hidden UI template to populate bar
units.detail: Keep a disabled template slot as the visual spec for every item, then instantiate copies of it to populate the bar dynamically. Re-enable the copy after instantiation since the template starts disabled.

units.title: Destroy children (except template) when refreshing UI
units.detail: When regenerating dynamic UI, loop through all children, skip the template, and destroy every other one. This prevents stale/duplicate slots from lingering after a re-order.

units.title: Drop event fires on self, not target
units.detail: When dragging UI over another slot, the drop event fires on the dragged object itself (capturing both events), so it swaps index with itself. Fix: add a CanvasGroup to the template and disable raycast target while dragging.

units.title: Divide drag delta by canvas scale factor
units.detail: When moving a dragged RectTransform with event delta, divide by the canvas scale factor to convert screen-space delta to UI-local space. Grab the canvas by walking parents until one is found.

units.title: Dragged UI appears behind others
units.detail: UI render order follows sibling order, so the dragged item can slide under other slots. Fix by calling transform.SetAsLastSibling at drag start to raise it above everything.

units.title: Fire event when data changes to refresh UI
units.detail: After modifying the ability list (e.g., swap), invoke a C# event (event handler). The UI subscribes once and re-renders on every event, so visuals stay in sync without the data layer knowing about the UI.

units.title: Swap by object reference to support off-bar items
units.detail: Store an 'extra abilities' list for items not on the bar (e.g., inventory). Swap logic compares ability objects rather than indexes so it can tell which list each item lives in, moving an item onto the bar and the displaced one off it.

units.title: Clickable UI via IPointerDownHandler
units.detail: Implement IPointerDownHandler from UnityEngine.EventSystems on a slot to receive clicks and trigger the assigned ability's Action directly, giving UI and keyboard the same activation path.

units.title: Game simulation playtests in the cloud in parallel
units.detail: Unity Game Simulation runs your build in the cloud using parameter combinations, letting you playtest a game hundreds of times quickly (e.g., 30 min of wall-clock time ran 1700 min of simulation). Use it to test level difficulty at scale.

units.title: Write a bot to get a difficulty baseline
units.detail: A simple bot that listens for state events and makes legal moves gives a baseline measure of level difficulty. Bot skill affects results, but any working bot yields values to compare and bounce around.

units.title: Enumerate all possible match-3 moves
units.detail: Generate possible moves by swapping every grid cell with each neighbor, attempting the swap, and checking whether a match of 3+ results. Collect all that match into a list for the bot to choose from.

units.title: Bot picks move based on goal type
units.detail: Let the bot optimize for the level's goal: for score goals pick the move producing the most matches; for glass-destroy goals pick the move destroying the most glass. Simple bots are enough for a repeatable difficulty metric.

units.title: Parameterize level loading for simulation
units.detail: Fetch configuration parameters (e.g., a level name string) at awake and load the matching scriptable object level, falling back to a default if not found. This lets one build run every level via parameter combinations.

units.title: Use counters to record simulation results
units.detail: When the bot wins or loses, set counters (e.g., level_win_moves_used with the move count, level_lose to count losses) then end the simulation. Aggregate reports give average/max/min/std-dev per counter across runs.

units.title: Measure difficulty with unlimited moves
units.detail: Give the bot a target score and unlimited moves to measure how many moves it takes to win, then run a second simulation with a limited move budget to measure win/loss rate. Both reveal difficulty level.

units.title: Rebalance levels from aggregate data
units.detail: Use average moves-to-win per level to adjust difficulty (change move budget, number/type of blocks, or gem types) aiming for a smooth difficulty curve rather than big jumps between levels.

units.title: Re-run simulation after adding features
units.detail: Adding even one mechanic (e.g., an exploding gem) can significantly change level difficulty, sometimes breaking previously balanced levels. Clone the prior simulation with a new build to rebalance in minutes instead of manual playtesting.

units.title: Design on paper before writing code
units.detail: Write down the list of systems/mechanics to build before coding, then prioritize them by importance and ease of implementation so the first prototype delivers high-value features fast.

units.title: Use a stripped-down dev scene for testing
units.detail: Duplicate the complex game scene and delete everything non-essential (level layout, scripting, extra entities) so you can run and test new systems in the simplest possible setup.

units.title: Generic interactable via interface
units.detail: Make any object interactable by implementing a shared interface, and let units run an 'interact action' against it. Because the action is interface-based, it can be anything (open door, blow crate, construct building), so new mechanics like construction are trivial to add.

units.title: Clean extensible code makes features fast
units.detail: A mechanic built on well-abstracted code (e.g., construction) can take ~30 minutes, whereas hacky systems would take hours or days. Investing in clean interfaces is what enables rapid feature iteration.

units.title: Leader system for controlling many units
units.detail: For games with lots of units, mark some as leaders and only allow direct control of non-leaders within a distance check of a leader. This splits units into manageable teams (defense, outpost building, etc.) and keeps turn flow fast.

units.title: Modular unit actions via components
units.detail: Make unit capabilities depend on which action components are attached. A turret is just a unit with the move action removed; you reuse all other logic and it behaves correctly.

units.title: ScriptableObjects as item data
units.detail: Represent item data (prefab, icon, name) as ScriptableObjects; they are ideal for defining item types. Use placeholder visuals (cubes + random icons) while developing systems.

units.title: Stackable inventory for consumable resources
units.detail: One-item-per-slot inventories are too limiting for crafting/building/ammo. Define item types as stackable or not with a max stack, and implement consume/merge/split logic so players can carry meaningful resources.

units.title: Decouple UI from logic with events
units.detail: Inventory UI should only listen to events and update itself; no direct connection to inventory logic. The code still compiles if you delete the UI class, proving clean separation.

units.title: World-space canvases for many world objects
units.detail: When many units/objects exist, regular screen UI is impractical. Attach a world-space canvas to each unit/object to show relevant data near the object itself.

units.title: Item transfer action via interface
units.detail: Implement item transfer as an interface-based action that works with anything holding an inventory (units, storage, crafting stations, loot crates). Interfaces let the action ignore concrete object types.

units.title: Power system as generator/transporter/consumer
units.detail: Model power with three building types (producers, transporters, consumers) connected through an interface any building can implement. It interlinks with crafting, building, and defense, driving interesting gameplay (guard your power lines).

units.title: Conveyor-style item transport routes
units.detail: Build item transporters, define a route (from/to + item types), and move items a set distance automatically each turn. Transport must be powered and can be destroyed, connecting automation with survival/defense.

units.title: Automated grab/drop machines via interfaces
units.detail: An automated machine that grabs items from any inventory and drops onto any inventory only needs to know the interface, not the concrete object type. Keeping systems interface-generic lets them all interlock.

units.title: Automated turn for passive resource gathering
units.detail: Add an 'automated turn' after the player's turn where AI-controlled automated actions (e.g., gather from an area, drop in storage) run if the unit has spare action points. Players can still manually override, keeping control while removing tedious micromanagement.

units.title: Diagram your systems before pausing development
units.detail: Before stepping away from a project, draw a diagram of all systems, their purpose, and connections while the code is fresh. It makes resuming after weeks/months far faster.

units.title: Re-watch your own tutorials as a refresher
units.detail: When relearning a framework, re-watch your own tutorials/courses at 2-3x speed. They present the exact teaching style you like, and serve as a fast, complete refresh before starting integration work.

units.title: Adding multiplayer basics with NGO
units.detail: Adding NetworkObject, NetworkTransform, and NetworkRigidbody components to networked objects is often sufficient for syncing basic behavior. Convert key scripts to NetworkBehavior and add isOwner checks.

units.title: Don't reparent objects in multiplayer
units.detail: Changing an object's parent (used to carry items in single player) breaks networking. Replace it with a small follow-script that snaps to a target transform each frame instead.

units.title: Unpack prefab to fix NGO spawning bug
units.detail: When everything worked then suddenly stopped for no apparent reason, the fix was unpacking the prefab in the scene. NGO prefab-spawned objects can misbehave while unpacked instances work.

units.title: Re-add NetworkObject to fix scene prefabs
units.detail: Objects placed directly in the scene sometimes break with no code change; removing and re-adding the NetworkObject component fixes them even though nothing else changed.

units.title: Pause game while a client connects
units.detail: If a client connects mid-spawn, that client may try to spawn and destroy objects, throwing errors clients cannot fix. Pause the game during connection approval and resume once the client is connected.

units.title: Serialize ScriptableObjects as indexes for RPCs
units.detail: You cannot pass ScriptableObject references in RPC calls. Create a list registry of all scriptable objects and write custom serialization (read/write extension methods) that converts the object to its list index int and back, so any scriptable object works in RPCs and network variables.

units.title: Reuse scene-flow code from prior projects
units.detail: Clean, self-contained scripts (main menu, lobby, character select) copy across projects with minor renaming. Reusing good code built a whole menu flow in ~1 hour instead of a week.

units.title: When to add multiplayer depends on experience
units.detail: Beginners should add multiplayer from day one, taking tiny steps and verifying each feature in both single and multiplayer. Experienced devs can build single-player systems first and convert later, but that creates a mountain of debugging at once.

units.title: Draw sprites pointing right for rotation math
units.detail: In Unity, angle zero points right, so always draw aiming sprites (weapons, characters) facing right. Otherwise LookAt-style rotation math will be visually wrong.

units.title: 2D aim rotation via Euler Z and atan2
units.detail: In 2D, don't use LookAt (it rotates in 3D and hides the sprite). Compute direction = mouse - position (normalized), get angle with atan2(Y, X), convert radians to degrees, and set only the Z Euler angle to the result.

units.title: Separate aim pivot and gun endpoint transforms
units.detail: Make a parent aim pivot (rotates toward target) with an empty gun endpoint child positioned where the bullet leaves. Effects reference the endpoint position, so visuals and fire origin stay aligned after rotating.

units.title: Decouple shoot effects via on-shoot event
units.detail: Define an event with custom EventArgs carrying gun endpoint and shoot position. The player class fires it on click; separate effect scripts subscribe to add screen shake, bullet tracers, muzzle flash, and shell particles without touching the player class.

units.title: Trigger shoot animation with an animator trigger
units.detail: Store the animator reference on the aim transform and call SetTrigger on left click to play a shoot animation. Use a simple idle-to-shoot animator with a trigger transition.

units.title: Custom cursor with hotspot and cursor mode
units.detail: Use Cursor.SetCursor with a texture, a hotspot (offset in pixels from top-left, e.g., the arrow tip at 10,10), and a cursor mode. Automatic mode prefers hardware cursor which looks correct even at low frame rates, unlike software cursor.

units.title: Animate cursor by cycling textures
