units.detail: Animate a cursor by storing a texture array, a current-frame index, and a frame timer. Count down timer with delta time; when it hits zero, advance the frame (wrapping with modulo) and re-set the cursor.

units.title: CursorAnimation data class with [Serializable]
units.detail: Hold cursor data (type enum, texture frames, frame rate, hotspot offset) in a [Serializable] class exposed as a list in the inspector. Without [Serializable], custom classes don't appear in the Unity editor.

units.title: Cursor switching via OnMouseEnter/Exit
units.detail: Give hoverable objects a small script implementing OnMouseEnter/OnMouseExit that calls the cursor manager's SetActiveCursorType with the appropriate type. Colliders drive the detection.

units.title: Override cursor with an on-cursor-changed event
units.detail: Fire an event whenever the active cursor changes. External logic (e.g., the RTS controller) subscribes and overrides the cursor (show move cursor instead of arrow when a unit is selected), keeping the manager generic.

units.title: Singleton for global managers
units.detail: Expose a static instance for cross-script access to the cursor manager (and similar managers). Set it in Awake so other scripts can call SetActiveCursorType from anywhere.

units.title: No built-in DOTS animation toolset yet
units.detail: Unity DOTS has no first-party animation toolset, so you must either use a third-party asset or build a custom animation system yourself. This is one of the trickiest areas of DOTS.

units.title: Mesh-swapping sprite-sheet style animation
units.detail: Bake different animation frames into separate meshes and swap the rendered mesh each frame via code to fake animation. This works within DOTS' value-type constraints and avoids object references.

units.title: Blob assets for immutable fast DOTS data
units.detail: Blob assets let DOTS store immutable data in a super-fast accessible way, including blob arrays. Build an array-of-arrays structure (animation type index -> array of meshes) as a 'dictionary' of animation frames.

units.title: DOTS only stores value types
units.detail: DOTS components/systems work with value types only, so object references like Mesh instances cannot be stored directly. You must serialize them into blob data (e.g., indexes into shared asset arrays) instead.

units.title: DOTS is not a beginner topic
units.detail: Skip DOTS until you fully understand beginner-to-intermediate C# and regular GameObjects; learn the basics with a GameObject-based course first, then DOTS. Concurrency/jobs are far easier to understand with solid foundations.

units.title: Steam festival timing dictates launch window
units.detail: You can only participate in one Steam Next Fest; register before the deadline (months in advance). Choosing the festival constrains your launch to a narrow window that avoids major Steam sales, so plan your release date around it.

units.title: Wishlist-to-sales conversion math
units.detail: Roughly 20% of wishlists convert to sales in week one, and year-one sales are typically 3-5x week-one sales. ~10K wishlists is the soft target that gets a game into Steam's New & Trending page.

units.title: Net revenue is ~40% of gross
units.detail: After chargebacks, refunds, Steam's cut, and taxes, net revenue is roughly 40% of gross revenue. Always plan financial goals in net revenue and back-calculate the gross/copies needed.

units.title: Price multiplayer games for population, not margin
units.detail: Multiplayer games need enough players to matchmake, so selling more copies matters. Don't underprice below the general recommendation (~$10); balance price against the need for a healthy player population.

units.title: Announce early and gather wishlists immediately
units.detail: Set up a public Steam page and trailer as soon as you have something to show, and start gathering wishlists from day one. Wishlists drive Steam's algorithm; a good launch starts months before release.

units.title: Small scoped game as a full launch rehearsal
units.detail: Deliberately build a smaller game to completely practice the full Steam launch process (page, trailer, festival, wishlists, release) so you're prepared and remember everything needed for a bigger project later.

units.title: Adapt plans when scope slips
units.detail: When courses/time push a complex game past its festival registration deadline, adapt: shelve it on hiatus and ship a shorter, simpler game first to hit a yearly launch goal, then return to the complex project.

units.title: Good hooks need uniqueness plus familiarity
units.detail: A strong game hook must be unique enough to stand out yet familiar enough to understand. A safe fallback is making the hook the combination of many well-known genres/systems (XCOM + open world + survival + automation).

units.title: Announce with a concept trailer, not gameplay
units.detail: An announcement trailer should sell the game idea, so it's fine to use mockups and smoke-and-mirrors scenes built just for the trailer (like Elder Scrolls' teaser approach), as long as you don't mislead about the actual genre.

units.title: Steam page can launch with minimal assets
units.detail: You only need five screenshots to publish a Steam page, but a proper trailer greatly increases conversion. Create the page early with minimal assets so you can start collecting wishlists immediately.

units.title: Set goals via price and conversion math
units.detail: Estimate goals by chaining: target monthly income -> net revenue goal (~40% gross) -> copies needed at chosen price -> week-one sales target -> wishlists needed (20% conversion). Always aim above the minimum because first estimates are overly optimistic.

units.title: Price from 10-20 based on visual quality
units.detail: A well-made indie game shouldn't go under ~$10 or above ~$20. Players judge value largely on visual presentation, so price closer to $10 if visuals are weaker and toward $20 if quality is high.

units.title: Low cost of living as an indie advantage
units.detail: Living in a lower-cost-of-living country dramatically lowers the sales bar needed to sustain game development as a career, enabling an indie solo dev to be profitable with modest sales numbers.

units.title: Two multiplayer stacks: NGO vs Netcode for Entities
units.detail: Netcode for GameObjects is for GameObject-based games (Call of Duty-style not needed), while Netcode for Entities targets fast-paced/complex games built with DOTS entities. Both share core concepts (positions, players, score) but differ in syntax and implementation.

units.title: Netcode for Entities core concepts
units.detail: RPCs are simple client-server messages; ghosts are objects auto-synchronized across the network (spawned on server, clients see them); ghost fields sync custom data continuously. Mark a connection 'in-game' when it is ready to receive constant data like spawning and transforms.

units.title: DOTS forbids native C# events
units.detail: DOTS is data-oriented, so normal C# events (objects) can't be used. You must build a custom DOTS-compatible event system, e.g., one based on components/entities and queries, to communicate between systems and UI.

units.title: Use GameObjects for UI even in DOTS games
units.detail: Even when game logic runs in DOTS entities, build the UI with normal GameObjects/canvas and update it via events and DOTS queries. UI rarely needs ECS.

units.title: Watch both stack courses to learn faster
units.detail: Remaking the identical game (e.g., Tic-Tac-Toe) with both GameObject and DOTS stacks lets you learn each faster by seeing the same core concepts implemented two ways side by side.

units.title: Hardware failures delay solo dev work
units.detail: A broken motherboard/CPU can freeze a project for a week. Solo devs should keep projects/versions backed up (cloud/course projects are recoverable) so hardware failure loses little work and progress can resume on replacement hardware.

units.title: NGO small-scale limit is bandwidth
units.detail: Netcode for Game Objects syncs all data in a single packet when a player joins; past a threshold of network objects that packet times out. The fix is splitting large packets into smaller ones, or building custom network variables/RPCs so you control what gets synchronized.

units.title: Adding multiplayer after game completion
units.detail: Adding multiplayer to an already-finished game can be trivial or nearly impossible depending on code quality and coupling. Design for multiplayer from the start if you intend to have it, or be prepared to rewrite large parts (or all) of the game.

units.title: Pick authoritative model by game type
units.detail: Default NGO behavior is server-authoritative (only server can move transforms), but client-authoritative components exist. For casual co-op, trusting the client is fine; for competitive PvP never trust the client.

units.title: Multiplayer tool choice by scale
units.detail: NGO is great for small-scale games (2-player turn-based card games, co-op, survival with few players); Netcode for Entities targets huge simulations; for hundreds of concurrent players (battle royale) use something like Photon Fusion instead.

units.title: Unity multiplayer cost model
units.detail: NGO and Unity Transport are free; you can self-host a server build anywhere (it's just an executable) or use peer-to-peer with IP/port forwarding. UGS Relay is free up to 50 concurrent users then $0.16 per additional user; dedicated servers are billed per hour with an $800 starting credit per account.

units.title: Swap NGO transport layer
units.detail: Netcode for Game Objects lets you swap the underlying transport, e.g. replace Unity Transport with Steam Transport, and the game-objects networking layer keeps working unchanged.

units.title: Prototype before committing to edge cases
units.detail: For scale edge cases (large RTS, many units) the NGO limit is bandwidth-driven, so how much you send matters. Build a quick prototype that pushes your design to the limit to see if it works before committing.

units.title: Pick one networking tool and learn it
units.detail: Without strict requirements (extreme accuracy, many players), all major multiplayer solutions (Photon, Mirror, Fishnet, NGO) are decent; pick one and learn it deeply instead of endlessly comparing.

units.title: Five questions before choosing a game
units.detail: Ask yourself: is it a game you want to make, is there a market for it, have similar games succeeded, is your idea unique enough to stand out, and can you make it. These force honesty about motivation, audience, differentiation, and feasibility.

units.title: Boxleiter sales estimation from reviews
units.detail: Estimate game sales by multiplying Steam review count by ~50 (average sales per review). Rough but sufficient to size a market before committing to a project.

units.title: Familiar core plus one unique twist
units.detail: To stand out, pair a well-understood genre core (familiar to the target audience) with a single unique hook, expressed as a one-line tagline like 'Roller Coaster Tycoon but with shooting arenas'. Unique enough to differentiate, familiar enough to not confuse.

units.title: Solo devs need smaller sales targets
units.detail: A solo developer doesn't need 100k copies to succeed; compare against games in the same genre built by similar-sized teams. Complex genres like management have fewer competitors and per-game average sales that are enough for a small studio.

units.title: UI bar with Image fillAmount
units.detail: Make a health bar by setting the Unity Image type to Filled (horizontal, origin left) so a single fillAmount 0..1 field controls the displayed amount. Keep the filled bar on top of a dark duplicate for the empty background.

units.title: Shield segments as discrete bars
units.detail: Model segmented shields as separate fill bars, each mapping to a range of shield points. For each segment compute min=max index * points-per-segment and set fill to 0, 1, or (current - min) / points-per-segment.

units.title: Color can't be const in C#
units.detail: UnityEngine.Color cannot be a const; use a static readonly field to make a color behave like a constant.

units.title: Cast int to float when normalizing
units.detail: Dividing one int by another yields 0 in C#. Cast at least one operand to float when computing normalized fill amounts (e.g. health / maxHealth).

units.title: Separate mechanics from visuals with events
units.detail: Keep gameplay state in a plain class (no MonoBehaviour) and push updates to the UI via a C# event (e.g. OnHealthShieldChanged), letting the view subscribe and redraw. This keeps logic testable and visuals decoupled.

units.title: Damage flash bar shows last hit
units.detail: Keep a red duplicate bar that snapshots the previous health value when hit, stays visible while a timer runs, then fades alpha over ~0.5s. Reset the timer (not the size) when hit again so repeated hits extend the display.

units.title: Shield absorbs damage before health
units.detail: Apply damage to shield first: if damage < shield, subtract from shield; else subtract the remainder (damage - shield) from health and zero the shield. Clamp healing to max so overhealing never spills into the other resource.

units.title: One button yields many ping types
units.detail: Apex's ping system derives rich context from one input: single-click = move ping (or item-aware when hovering loot), double-click = enemy spotted, hold = radial wheel. Context detection turns simple inputs into full non-verbal team communication.

units.title: Double-click detection by timestamps
units.detail: Detect double-click by storing the previous ping time and type; if the current input lands within a threshold (e.g. 500ms) of the last matching one, upgrade to the special ping and destroy the previous visual.

units.title: SetActive(false) kills off-screen UI updates
units.detail: For off-screen indicator UI, calling SetActive(false) stops Update so the element can never reappear. Instead keep the GameObject active and only toggle the Image/Text components' enabled state.

units.title: Screen-space off-screen marker
units.detail: Project the world ping position to screen space (WorldToScreenPoint) and test whether its X/Y exceed screen bounds. If off-screen, position a UI arrow along the direction vector at a fixed radius from screen center and hide it when the target is on-screen.

units.title: Static singleton via static instance
units.detail: For a single global manager like a ping system, make the class static or use a static instance field set in Awake so any script can call manager functions without finding the object first.

units.title: Store ping data in a typed class
units.detail: Model each ping as a plain data class (type enum + position) instead of passing raw positions; add an OnDestroyed event on it so world and UI visuals can subscribe and despawn together.

units.title: Steam personalized calendar replaces popular upcoming
units.detail: Steam replaced 'popular upcoming' with a per-user personalized calendar; early data shows it can outperform the old system (33% click-through rate vs 1.3M impressions that barely converted). You stay listed ~1 month after launch, extending post-release visibility.

units.title: Set your Steam release date early
units.detail: The personalized calendar is visible ~2 months ahead and many days have no games listed; setting an official release date now puts your game on those empty slots for free visibility even with only ~1k wishlists. Most developers don't do this, so it's an easy win.

units.title: Wishlist-to-followers ratio ~10-15x
units.detail: Wishlists are far more casual than follows (roughly 10-15 wishlists per follower). A spike in wishlists without followers suggests drive-by traffic, so watch conversion quality, not just count.

units.title: 7k wishlist target still holds
units.detail: Analysis of the new personalized calendar shows games listed with 8k-66k wishlists, so the old ~7k goal remains a valid target and the meta has not fundamentally changed: put your page up early, grow wishlists, ship a demo ASAP, maintain momentum, and don't shadow-drop.

units.title: Know your goal before learning marketing
units.detail: If your goal is making games for fun, marketing knowledge is optional; if you want financial success or many players, learning how the platform (e.g. Steam algorithm) works is crucial and massively increases your odds.

units.title: C#/Mono games decompile almost perfectly
units.detail: Mono C# assemblies can be decompiled so closely that most of your code is readable. As an indie dev, don't obsess over protecting it — it's educational and generally not worth the effort; rely on gameplay being hard to replicate.

units.title: Wishlist-to-followers ratio ~10-15x
units.detail: Aim for density of useful, actionable content (Steam algorithm posts, DOTS samples/ebooks, conference talks) and curate rather than skip — but if you only read one thing, prioritize your own game's goal and platform best practices.

units.title: Outliers are outliers by definition
units.detail: Games like Stardew Valley or Baldur's Gate 3 combine huge resources or luck; expecting your game to be an outlier risks your livelihood. Try your best, but don't stake everything on replicating a masterpiece — different scales and quality levels all have a place in the market.

units.title: Beware manufactured outrage narratives
units.detail: Stories like 'devs angry about BG3' were built on one non-negative tweet twisted by click-driven media; verify claims against actual sources before believing or acting on community drama. The real dev reaction was praise and warnings about scale/crunch, not anger.

units.title: Core language and engine concepts age well
units.detail: Variables, classes, functions, physics queries, basic AI, and state machines barely change — a 7-10 year old C# or Unity tutorial is still ~99% valid. Only specific tools (e.g. Animator State Machine 2→3) get breaking rewrites, so the core knowledge rarely goes obsolete.

units.title: Match tutorial version, then upgrade
units.detail: Use the exact same engine version as a tutorial so menus and behavior match 100%, then upgrade the completed project to the newer version to learn the differences — typically minor.

units.title: Template duplication for segmented bars
units.detail: Build one disabled bar template (background + filled child) and instantiate duplicates at runtime, re-enabling each clone. Store created bars in a list; each bar knows its own image so Update only sets fillAmount per segment.

units.title: Per-bar min/max range math
units.detail: For N bars each covering a fixed amount, bar i represents [i*amount, (i+1)*amount). Compute the current value's position: below min = empty, at/above max = full, else (value - min) / amount for the partial fill.

units.title: Re-enable instantiated disabled templates
units.detail: When instantiating from a disabled template, the clone inherits the disabled state — you must set gameObject.SetActive(true) on the clone before it appears.

units.title: Auto-fit bars inside a container
units.detail: Compute per-bar width from the container rect minus padding: (totalWidth - padding*(barCount-1)) / barCount, then lay bars left-to-right adding width+padding each index. Keeps any count of bars filling the same space.

units.title: Sprite slicing prevents border stretching
units.detail: For rounded/cornered UI borders, open the Sprite Editor and set a border on each side so corners don't stretch, then use Image type Sliced instead of Simple for clean scaling at any size.

units.title: UI draw order follows hierarchy
units.detail: In a UI canvas, later siblings render on top. When instantiating bars and helmets together, keep bar clones low (SetAsFirstSibling) so helmets always draw above the bars regardless of instantiation order.

units.title: Set pivot before scaling a bar
units.detail: A fill bar that grows from one end needs its pivot on that side (e.g. Shift+click left-center); with a center pivot, changing width stretches both ways instead.

units.title: Fill spills between bars by normalization
units.detail: To move a single value across multiple bars, store total max, per-bar max = total / barCount, and for each bar set fill to (value - i*perBarMax) / perBarMax, clamped 0..1. Turn a segment's icon red only when its fill reaches 1.

units.title: Compose bar from bar + helmet classes
units.detail: Wrap each bar's UI elements (fill bar + icon) in a small private class holding its rect transforms and an image reference, with a SetFillAmount method. A parent manager creates them from templates and owns the list.

units.title: Static class for single game-wide system
units.detail: Make a resource/system a static class with static fields so there's exactly one instance and it's globally accessible, avoiding a MonoBehaviour lookup. Initialize it once at game start via an Init() call.

units.title: Clamp resource after adding
units.detail: When adding to a capped resource like adrenaline, always clamp against the maximum after incrementing so state can never exceed its cap. Store amount, amountMax, and derive amountMax from a per-bar constant times bar count.

units.title: Integer division truncates before FloorToInt
units.detail: amount / amountPerBar using ints truncates, so 30/25 becomes 1 correctly but edge values behave unexpectedly with FloorToInt. Multiply by a float first to convert to float division, then floor, to get correct filled-bar counts.

units.title: TryRemove returning bool for gating
units.detail: Wrap a resource spend in a bool-returning TryRemove function (only removes if enough exists, returns success). Callers gate actions on the return value, which keeps spend logic in one place and less error-prone.

units.title: Reward only meaningful actions
units.detail: For a dodge-based resource gain, only award bonus adrenaline when an enemy in range is actually attacking you, not for spamming dodge. Tie resource rewards to deliberate, meaningful play to prevent degenerate farming.

units.title: Indicator reflects spendable resource state
units.detail: Show a HUD/world indicator that is only active when the player has at least one full bar they can spend. Recompute visibility every frame from the resource state so UI can never desync from logic.

units.title: Busy state blocks all input
units.detail: Add a 'Busy' state to the player state machine that does nothing, and enter it when starting a long ability like a kick. This blocks re-triggering and other movement logic while the animation plays, then transitions back to normal on animation end.

units.title: Animation impact-frame callbacks
units.detail: Play animations with callback hooks fired on the impact frame and on completion, then apply damage, knockback, or movement inside the impact callback. This synchronizes gameplay events with the visual animation timing.

units.title: Snap attack direction to nearest target
units.detail: Compute a target position by projecting toward the mouse, find the closest enemy within range of it, and if found recalc the direction exactly toward that enemy. Aiming feels precise because the hit connects with the actual target instead of the cursor point.

units.title: Knockback via timer + destroy countdown
units.detail: Apply knockback by moving the victim along the knockback direction each frame at a speed, while a countdown timer destroys it after it leaves the screen. Set the victim to a Busy state so its normal AI doesn't run while flying.

units.title: Gate powerful abilities behind resources
units.detail: Require spending a resource (e.g. a filled adrenaline bar) to use an overpowered ability. The TryRemove pattern naturally gates the action and prevents spamming.

units.title: Screen shake adds impact feedback
units.detail: Add a small camera shake on the ability's impact frame to make damage feel satisfying. Cheap polish that dramatically improves juice for hits.

units.title: Curse of knowledge blinds developers
units.detail: After hundreds of hours building a game, everything seems obvious to you but not to new players. The only way to know what players struggle with is constant playtesting with fresh eyes.

units.title: Animated main menus improve first impressions
units.detail: A static main menu signals unfinished to players; even a looping particle effect or subtle floating element adds life before the player presses start. Cheap, high-impact polish.

units.title: Tutorial must match player's input device
units.detail: If you support both controller and keyboard, show input prompts for the device the player is actually using, including correct controller glyphs. Wrong device hints confuse players.

units.title: Never ship broken content even in demos
units.detail: Cut broken or janky sections rather than publishing them in a demo. A short polished 20-minute demo beats an hour of gameplay that degrades after 30 minutes.

units.title: Put game name on main menu
units.detail: Players downloading many demos forget what each game is; always display the game's name/logo on the main menu so it's identifiable.

units.title: Too little and too much content both fail
units.detail: Players prefer a shorter experience that's excellent over one padded with busy work. Aim to leave players wanting more.

units.title: Players take 3-4x longer than the developer
units.detail: A dev who knows their game can finish it in 5 hours, but a new player might take 15-20. Judge game length from the player's pace, not your own.

units.title: Punishing mechanics must be earned
units.detail: Difficulty is good, but death should feel like the player's fault, not the game's (e.g. an insta-kill block ignoring health felt arbitrary). Preserve player agency in wins and losses.

units.title: Kill your darlings
units.detail: If a mechanic you love isn't fun when implemented, cut it. Developers overlook flaws because of attachment; players judge the game objectively and leave negative reviews.

units.title: Show, don't tell in tutorials
units.detail: Text walls are as bad as no tutorial; teach through clever level design (like Mario 1-1) or short in-game videos. Give optional hints since players learn at different speeds.

units.title: Progressive playtesting pipeline
units.detail: Scale testing from friends/family to Reddit/Discord to Steam playtesting, then publish a polished free demo, iterate on feedback, and only then go to Next Fest and release. Watch people play live when possible.

units.title: Mashup: city builder meets tower defense
units.detail: Combine resource-gathering city building with wave defense for a fresh genre hook: place harvesters near resource sources to afford more buildings while defending your HQ from escalating enemy waves.

units.title: Proximity-based resource generation
units.detail: Make buildings gather resources only when placed near the matching resource type (wood harvester near trees). Placement becomes a spatial puzzle and adds strategic depth.

units.title: Buildings show construction progress
units.detail: Newly placed buildings take time to construct, shown by a visual progress element. This paces gameplay and communicates state clearly to the player.

units.title: Data-driven building types via scriptable objects
units.detail: Define building types (name, prefab, visual, dimensions) as data assets so adding new types requires no code changes. Clean modular architecture makes the game easily expandable.

units.title: Gradient texture + step node reveals progressively
units.detail: A construction-print effect is just a gradient texture (0→1) sampled through a step node driven by a progress slider. The step output multiplies the sprite alpha so only part is visible, sweeping across as progress rises.

units.title: Split effect into discrete segments
units.detail: For per-segment construction, multiply progress by segment count, floor it, then divide back to normalize. This converts a smooth progress value into discrete steps that only advance when a full segment threshold is crossed.

units.title: Isolate top segment by subtracting shapes
units.detail: To animate only the topmost segment, subtract the one-segment-behind filled shape from the one-segment-ahead shape. Boolean subtract of masks isolates exactly one segment.

units.title: Wrap mode Clamp breaks mirrored offset
units.detail: Shifting a texture by -1 offset with default Clamp wrap mode outputs black. Switch the texture import wrap mode to Mirror so the gradient reflects and the direction can be flipped.

units.title: Alternate scan direction per segment
units.detail: Make even segments scan left-to-right and odd ones right-to-left using modulo 2 of the floored segment index feeding a Branch node that picks one of two duplicated horizontal logics.

units.title: Printing head glow via progress offset
units.detail: Duplicate the reveal logic with progress advanced by a tiny 'head thickness' amount, then subtract the un-offset version. The difference is a glowing band at the print head.

units.title: Think in discrete operations for shaders
units.detail: Build complex shader effects from simple numeric operations (step, floor, modulo, subtract, multiply) on normalized values rather than attempting the whole result at once. Debug each mask independently.

units.title: Mesh-swap customization with single material
units.detail: When an asset pack bakes colors into vertex UVs under one shared material, swap out just the mesh field of a skinned mesh renderer to change a body part's look. No bones or material juggling needed.

units.title: Data class array replaces per-part fields
units.detail: Instead of copy-pasting a skinMeshRenderer + mesh array for every body part, wrap them in a serializable BodyPartData class and use an array of them. Editing one part is a single array element.

units.title: Custom classes need [Serializable] to show in inspector
units.detail: Plain C# classes used as serialized fields don't appear in the Unity inspector until marked [System.Serializable]. Without it the field silently shows nothing.

units.title: Enum over hardcoded indices
units.detail: Referencing body parts by magic index (0=color, 1=hat) silently breaks if array elements are reordered in the inspector. Use an enum field inside the data class and a helper that searches the array by enum value.

units.title: Serialize index, not the mesh reference
units.detail: Unity can't serialize a mesh into a JSON save object, so persist the body part type plus the selected array index, then re-apply the mesh on load. Saving indices keeps saves small and portable.

units.title: Separate UI from character logic
units.detail: Keep the character customizer component (mesh swapping) independent from the customization UI script that calls it. This lets you load a customized character into any scene without depending on the editor UI.

units.title: Damageable interface over concrete checks
units.detail: Define an IDamageable interface with a Damage(amount, position) method instead of testing for a specific destructible component in hit code. Any object that implements it becomes damageable, keeping hit logic decoupled and reusable.

units.title: Intact and broken pivots must match
units.detail: When swapping an intact wall for its broken parts, the prefab pivots must sit at the exact same world position, otherwise parts spawn offset and physics explodes wrong. Match pivots before instantiation.

units.title: Explosion force + VFX hides swap transition
units.detail: On death, instantiate the broken prefab at the same transform, apply AddExplosionForce from the stored last-damage position to every child rigidbody, and spawn VFX at the hit point to mask the transition.

units.title: Generalize destructibles with exposed tuning
units.detail: Rename the specific DestructibleWall into a generic DestructibleObject and expose health and explosion-force fields so any object (crates, walls) gets destruction just by attaching the component and setting values.

units.title: Split models into parts with boolean tool
units.detail: Cut a 3D model into randomized destruction chunks using a boolean/subtract tool with positioned cubes repeated many times. Gives believable break-apart geometry.

units.title: Distance-based speed with min/max clamp
units.detail: Make hookshot pull speed proportional to remaining distance (fast start, slow finish) then clamp it between min and max values. Prevents both sluggish arrival and a final-distance crawl.

units.title: Gravity velocity accumulates when never grounded
units.detail: If downward velocity only resets on landing, a character that hooks off ledges never resets it and gravity grows each frame. Reset the gravity velocity whenever you transition back to the normal state.

units.title: Carry momentum with dampening on jump
units.detail: When the player jumps mid-hookshot, store hookshot direction x speed as a momentum vector, add it to movement each frame, and dampen it toward zero over time. Preserves flow so the hookshot feels continuous.

units.title: Scale-from-edge visual via pivot offset
units.detail: To make a visual grow from its start point, put it in a parent, shift it forward by half its length, and scale the parent. Scaling then extends from the edge rather than the middle.

units.title: FOV kick sells movement speed
units.detail: Widen the camera field of view while the player is being pulled and ease it back when the action ends. A cheap perceptual cue that makes traversal feel much faster.

units.title: Re-press the key to cancel an action
units.detail: Use the same input that started a movement ability to cancel it mid-flight, returning to the normal state. Gives players immediate control without new keybindings.

units.title: Snap world position to grid cell
units.detail: Convert a mouse world position to grid coordinates (grid.GetXZ) then back to a world position so buildings land exactly on cells. Consistent snapping makes placement feel precise.

units.title: Per-cell occupancy data with CanBuild
units.detail: Store a reference on each grid cell object to what's placed there, with a CanBuild check (empty if the stored transform is null). Prevents two buildings on one cell.

units.title: Overlap bug: check every occupied cell
units.detail: Testing CanBuild only on the clicked cell lets multi-cell buildings overlap neighbors. Compute the full grid-position list the building would occupy and verify every cell before placing.

units.title: Corner-pivot rotation needs position offset
units.detail: Rotating a building whose pivot is at a corner swings it out of its occupied footprint. After rotating, offset the placed world position by a direction-dependent amount (width/height x cell size).

units.title: Track origin and direction for demolish
units.detail: A placed object can't be cleanly removed from a grid if you only know the cell you clicked. Store the building type, origin, and rotation direction on the object itself so demolish can clear every occupied cell.

units.title: Scriptable objects define building types
units.detail: Define each building as a scriptable object holding name, prefab, visual, width, height, and rotation helpers. Swapping types or adding new ones requires no code, and multi-size footprints come from the width/height data.

units.title: Move by remove, test, restore
units.detail: To move a grid item safely, remove it first, test if the target position is valid, move if yes, otherwise place it back. Removing first lets the new position overlap the old one and guarantees the item is never lost.

units.title: Separate domain logic from manual input
units.detail: Refactor so the core inventory-tetris logic (placement, rotation, bounds) is one script and the manual mouse placement is another. You can then duplicate inventories without duplicating input handling.

units.title: Canvas and world space share the same grid math
units.detail: A 2D UI canvas and a 2D world space are both 2D coordinate spaces, so the same grid class works for both. Only the mouse-position input (screen-to-canvas vs world ray) and the renderer type (Image vs SpriteRenderer) change.

units.title: Cross-inventory drop via local mouse position
units.detail: To drag items between inventories, iterate all inventory instances, compute the mouse position local to each, and treat it as a valid target if it's inside that inventory's bounds. Then run the same remove/test/restore move logic.

units.title: Rotate visual and offset for corner origin
units.detail: Grid items rotate around their lower-left origin, so while dragging you must both rotate the visual and offset its position by the rotated footprint. Grab point vs origin mismatch is the usual source of bugs here.

units.title: Save inventories as JSON save object
units.detail: Persist an inventory by defining a plain save object and serializing it to a JSON string; loading parses it back and re-places items on the grid. Simple, readable, and reusable across systems.

units.title: Reuse assets and systems across projects
units.detail: Rebuild a new system (inventory tetris) on top of an existing, battle-tested grid system, and reuse item art from older games. Reusing prior work is the fastest path to new features.

units.title: Pulse radar via scaling sprite
units.detail: Create a pulse radar by scaling a fading-circle sprite over time; when range exceeds max, reset to zero and repeat. Store range and range-speed as serialized fields so the effect is easily tunable.

units.title: localScale vs radius mismatch
units.detail: When applying range to transform.localScale the circle grows on both sides (doubling effective size), but a circle-cast radius only measures one side. Divide range by 2 for the physics cast so pings land on the correct objects.

units.title: Track hit colliders, clear on reset
units.detail: A circle cast every frame hits the same object many times. Keep a list of already-hit colliders, only ping objects not in the list, and clear the list whenever the pulse resets so objects ping again on the next pulse.

units.title: Single circle cast stops at first hit
units.detail: CircleCast/Raycast return the first collider only, so objects behind others inside the radius are missed. Use the 'All' variants (CircleCastAll/RaycastAll) and loop over every result to detect all targets.

units.title: Fade-out ping prefab
units.detail: Use a small ping prefab with a script that lowers sprite alpha over a disappear timer and destroys itself at zero. Spawn it at the hit point and set its color to communicate what was detected.

units.title: Color-code radar pings by target type
units.detail: Identify what was hit by checking for a distinguishing script component (e.g. enemy vs item handler) and set the ping color accordingly (red enemies, blue items). Component presence is a robust object-type tag.

units.title: Radar layer + render texture minimap
units.detail: Put radar visuals (ping, pulse) on a dedicated 'radar' layer. The main camera excludes that layer while a second camera renders only the radar layer into a render texture shown in a UI Raw Image, and the radar follows the player.

units.title: Rotating sweep radar
units.detail: Build a radar sweep from a line sprite with a fading trail, rotated by adding to Euler Z each frame. Convert the rotation angle into a direction vector and raycast along it every frame to detect targets in range.

units.title: Unity Euler angles rotate counterclockwise
units.detail: In Unity, increasing a Euler angle rotates counterclockwise. Negate the speed (subtract instead of add) to make the sweep rotate clockwise.

units.title: Clear hit list on half rotation
units.detail: To avoid pinging the same object every frame while still re-pinging it next pass, store the previous rotation and clear the detected-collider list when the sweep crosses a half-rotation boundary (computed via angle modulo 360 minus 180).

units.title: Filter radar targets with layer mask
units.detail: A radar raycast will hit walls and anything else with a collider. Expose a LayerMask field on the radar and use it in the cast so only enemy/item layers are detected.

units.title: Tie ping lifetime to sweep speed
units.detail: Set each ping's disappear timer to the time of one full sweep (e.g. 360 / rotationSpeed) so pings vanish before the radar returns. Multiply by a factor to keep pings alive for multiple sweeps, leaving a trail of enemy positions.

units.title: Sorting layers for radar visuals
units.detail: Place the radar background, trail, and sweep on distinct values of a custom sorting layer so the sweep always renders above the trail above the background.

units.title: Aim camera via virtual camera priority
units.detail: Duplicate the follow camera as an aim camera with higher Cinemachine priority and slightly lower FOV and closer distance for zoom. Toggle aiming by SetActive on the aim camera's GameObject, giving a snappy transition.

units.title: Separate aim and walk mouse sensitivity
units.detail: Zoomed aiming feels too sensitive with the same mouse sensitivity. Expose a SetSensitivity method on the base controller and apply a lower aim sensitivity while aiming, restoring the normal value when not.

units.title: Aim raycast needs something to hit
units.detail: Raycasting from the screen center to find the aim point fails when looking at the sky because there is no collider. Add invisible colliders around the world (collider without mesh renderer) so the aim ray always lands.

units.title: Aim point from screen center ray
units.detail: In a third-person shooter the camera is offset from the player, so firing along player forward misses the crosshair. Raycast from the exact screen center point to get the world-space aim target, then aim the weapon/projectile there.

units.title: Aim rotation fights move rotation
units.detail: When aiming, the base controller still rotates the character toward the move direction, breaking the aim. Expose a 'rotate on move' boolean on the base controller and disable it while aiming so the character only faces the aim target.

units.title: Hitscan vs projectile weapons
units.detail: Two options: spawn a real projectile that flies and collides, or hitscan where a raycast directly applies damage to the first target. Choose based on game feel; both still need the aim raycast to know where the shot goes.

units.title: Rigidbody projectile
units.detail: A bullet prefab with a kinematic-free rigidbody (interpolation on, dynamic collision detection), a trigger collider, and a script that sets velocity forward on spawn and destroys the object on trigger enter.

units.title: No-UI world-space crafting
units.detail: Recreate Hydroneer-style crafting: instead of an inventory, items physically exist in the world and are consumed when they sit inside a detection volume. Provides strong immersion with no virtual inventory or menus.

units.title: Physics overlap box for crafting
units.detail: On the craft action only, run a physics OverlapBox at the anvil area and check returned colliders against required items. Querying physics just once per craft (instead of always-active triggers) is more performant with many physics objects.

units.title: Disable the detection volume collider
units.detail: If the overlap box's collider stays enabled, dropped items rest on an invisible box. Use a disabled collider object purely as a data source (position/size reference) so detection works but physics ignores it.

units.title: OverlapBox center is world space
units.detail: OverlapBox expects a world-space center, but a BoxCollider's center field is local. Convert via transform.position + boxCollider.center, and pass boxCollider.size as halfExtents (deprecated 'extents' equaled twice the size).

units.title: Recipe check by list removal
units.detail: Copy the recipe's required-item list, then remove each found item from the copy. If the copy is empty afterward, all requirements are satisfied. Track matched colliders in a list so only the required objects get destroyed on craft.

units.title: Tag items by component presence
units.detail: Attach a simple ItemHolder component (holding a ScriptableObject item reference) to pickable objects. Identifying objects by which component they carry is simpler and more robust than string/name checks.

units.title: HDRP needs full texture maps to shine
units.detail: HDRP is about maximum fidelity options, not automatic beauty. It only visibly improves things when assets use the full set of PBR maps (AO, normal, displacement, roughness, metal, etc.). Low-poly assets look nearly identical switching from URP.

units.title: Low light sells graphics
units.detail: Horror and night-time games showcase visuals best because claustrophobic scenes need fewer high-quality assets and low light hides imperfections. When demoing or designing for visuals, favor limited, dense, low-light scenes.

units.title: Research engines via SteamDB
units.detail: On SteamDB a game's page shows which engine and render pipeline (URP/HDRP) it uses via the library tags. This is a fast way to research how impressive Unity games achieved their look.

units.title: Game simulation for balance testing
units.detail: Unity Game Simulation runs your game thousands of times in parallel on the cloud, letting you gather data to balance levels and systems automatically rather than by manual playtesting.

units.title: ML agents for testing and balance
units.detail: Train an AI to play your game (even win it), then use it to test more efficiently and tune balance. Imitation learning and reinforcement learning both work for teaching game-playing agents.

units.title: Remake classics to learn
units.detail: Rebuilding an old game (e.g. Doom) in Unity teaches deep mechanics and design by replicating exact behavior, and doubles as portfolio content.

units.title: Draw anything via dynamic meshes
units.detail: A drawing/doodling system in Unity is just dynamically creating meshes from line points in code; the same technique powers marking the world or a drawing tool.

units.title: State machines for enemy behavior
units.detail: A simple state machine is the standard structure for enemy AI (idle, patrol, chase, attack) and scales to boss fights with multiple stages; keep logic per-state instead of one giant update.

units.title: Modular controllers via interfaces
units.detail: Build a player controller from swappable modules (movement vs pathfinding, player vs enemy AI) using C# interfaces, so behavior can be combined or replaced without rewriting the whole controller.

units.title: Marketing matters more than code quality
units.detail: For indie success, marketing is the most important skill and wishlists are a primary success metric before release. A good game alone rarely succeeds without active marketing strategy.

units.title: ScriptableObjects not for persistence
units.detail: ScriptableObjects are fine for read-only data and even read-write, but unsuitable for saving persistent player data because asset values mutate and get written back into the project. Keep them for config/data, not saved state.

units.title: Assets are fine; players want good games
units.detail: Research showed players rarely call games 'asset flips'; they just want a good game. Using store assets to realize your vision is normal and acceptable.

units.title: Demos are powerful marketing
units.detail: Steam now lets demos have their own store pages, reviews, and wishlist notifications when launched. Positive demo reviews boost interest and signal your game, while negative demo reviews are early polish feedback.

units.title: Steam description link rules
units.detail: Steam store-page descriptions now forbid external links (including Discord/socials), images mimicking store UI/buttons, and links to other games. Instead enable the built-in 'More from developer' widget and the follow button on your developer page.

units.title: Keyboard-only code navigation
units.detail: Ctrl+arrows move word-by-word, Home/End jump line start/end, and Ctrl+Home/End jump file start/end. Combining these with Shift selects text so you can edit an entire codebase without touching the mouse.

units.title: Jump between symbol references
units.detail: Ctrl+Shift+Up/Down moves the cursor between all usages of the symbol under the cursor within the file; right-click 'Find All References' shows every usage across the whole codebase (works for classes, fields, events, interfaces).

units.title: Global rename with Ctrl+R R
units.detail: Ctrl+R R renames any symbol (variable, function, event, even a whole class) and automatically updates every reference across all files. A quick way to improve naming without manual find-replace.

units.title: Cut-line and clipboard history
units.detail: Ctrl+X with the cursor on a line cuts the entire line for quick moves/duplicates, and Ctrl+Shift+V opens clipboard history to paste any previously copied snippet, not just the last one.

units.title: Multi-line editing and quick comment
units.detail: Shift+Alt+Up/Down creates multiple cursors to edit several lines at once (e.g. add/remove a prefix). Ctrl+K C comments and Ctrl+K U uncomments the selection.

units.title: Static list to track all instances of a class
units.detail: Keep a private static List<T> and add each instance in Awake (lazily instantiating the list on the first one). This lets any other system query all live instances of a building type without finding them in the scene.

units.title: Return closest instance to a position
units.detail: Expose a public static function that takes a position and returns the closest object from a static instance list. Track a 'closest' variable; set it on the first element, then replace it whenever a later element is closer. Workers use this to find the nearest storage for drop-off.

units.title: Prefab instantiation via static create method
units.detail: A static Create function instantiates a prefab, grabs the component, and calls a Setup method to inject constructor-like parameters (position, size, tick max, completion callback). This is the Unity-friendly substitute for constructors since MonoBehaviours can't be new'd.

units.title: Construction progress via tick counters
units.detail: Model construction as an integer tick counter. Workers call AddConstructionTick, and when the count exceeds the max, fire a completion Action and destroy the construction area, which then spawns the real building. Normalize ticks/max to a 0-1 float for progress bars, casting to float explicitly.

units.title: Worker behavior as a state machine
units.detail: Give the worker explicit states (idle, going to construction area, building construction area). Each state has an enter check (move until close enough, then switch state) and a done check (after animation, add tick; go back to idle if built). This keeps AI behavior modular and easy to extend.

units.title: Build a damage ring with sprites
units.detail: Compose a damage circle from a ring sprite (transparent inside, red outside) plus four white one-pixel rectangles tinted red and stretched into the sides. Because the side panels are separate transforms, the whole ring is easy to resize dynamically with a single SetCircleSize function.

units.title: Sprite size is diameter, not radius
units.detail: When testing whether a position is outside the circle, distance must be compared against the radius. Since the stored size is the diameter (e.g., 200 x 200), multiply by 0.5f to get the radius or the damage zone will be twice as large as the visible ring.

units.title: Static instance exposing world-wide queries
units.detail: Store a private static reference to the singleton-ish object (the damage circle) and expose static helper methods like IsOutsideCircle(position). Any other system (e.g., the player) can then ask a global question without holding a direct reference.

units.title: Lerp toward a target over time
units.detail: To shrink/move a zone, compute the delta between current and target, multiply by a shrink speed and Time.deltaTime, and apply it each Update. Introduce a shrink timer that counts down before movement starts, and when both size and position are near their targets, generate the next target.

units.title: Randomize next shrink target
units.detail: A GenerateTargetCircle function randomizes the shrink amount (e.g., Random.Range 5-40), derives the new position from the current position plus a randomized offset, and picks a random delay before the next shrink. Keeping the randomness in one function makes the whole shrink loop easy to tune.

units.title: Move a container instead of individual parts
units.detail: Put the ring sprite and all four side panels inside a container GameObject. Repositioning the container moves the entire circle, so scaling and positioning logic stays in one place instead of updating five transforms individually.

units.title: Keep code cleanly separated for complex games
units.detail: The most complex game the author made stayed maintainable because underlying systems were implemented separately and cleanly separated from each other. Clean separation between systems is what lets a project scale in complexity without collapsing.

units.title: Incremental progress builds complete games
units.detail: A game that took 17 months was finished by constant incremental progress, starting from nothing. Reading user feedback during early access measurably improved the final product; treat feedback as a feature source.

units.title: Clean code enables adding features over time
units.detail: Even near release, adding tons of features remained doable because the codebase was cleanly separated. Good organization pays off at the end of a project, when code quality often degrades if it wasn't maintained.

units.title: Scriptable Objects don't persist runtime writes in builds
units.detail: Changes made to a Scriptable Object during play appear to persist in the Editor but are lost in a standalone build, because runtime writes only affect memory and never write back to the asset file. Never build a save system on Scriptable Objects; use them as read-only data containers for items, recipes, and stats.

units.title: Editor tools may write to Scriptable Objects
units.detail: Writes to Scriptable Objects are safe for editor-only tools (e.g., a level editor) because those run inside the Editor. When doing so, call EditorUtility.SetDirty(target) so the editor knows the asset was modified and actually saves it.

units.title: Persist data with JSON files instead of Scriptable Objects
units.detail: To actually save data, serialize a plain C# data class with JsonUtility.ToJson and write it to a regular file, then read it back. At that point a Scriptable Object wrapper is unnecessary; a simple class plus JSON is the robust save approach.

units.title: Editor vs build behavior diverges
units.detail: Systems that rely on Editor-only persistence (like Scriptable Object writes) will work for months in the Editor and silently break in the final build, which is very hard to diagnose. Test save/persistence features in an actual build, not just Play Mode.

units.title: Always write explicit access modifiers
units.detail: Never omit access modifiers like private even though C# infers private by default. Being explicit removes doubt about member visibility and is a cheap way to improve readability.

units.title: Suffix collection names with List
units.detail: Don't name lists/arrays by the plural of the element type (coins vs coin); at a glance the singular/plural is easy to mix up. Use a suffix like 'coinList' so a collection and a single instance are visually unambiguous.

units.title: Awake for self-init, Start for external refs
units.detail: Initialize the object's own fields in Awake; use Start only for logic that accesses external references. Following this single rule avoids a whole class of timing bugs where things initialize in the wrong order.

units.title: Decouple UI from gameplay via events
units.detail: Instead of a player script directly updating a coin text, fire an event like OnCoinAmountChanged and let a separate UI class subscribe and update itself. The gameplay object should work whether or not any UI exists.

units.title: Centralize input in one class
units.detail: Have a single game input class that is the only class touching the input system; everything else subscribes to its events or asks it for input state. Changing input system then only requires editing one place.

units.title: Use physics overlap queries instead of list cycling
units.detail: For pickup logic, drop a collider and use a physics overlap query (OverlapCircle) to find nearby objects each frame instead of maintaining and iterating a list of every coin. This removes per-frame list management and the coupled bookkeeping that goes with it.

units.title: Removing while iterating skips elements
units.detail: If you remove an item from a list while iterating it with an index, all later elements shift back and the iterator skips the one that moved into the removed index. Decrement the iterator (i--) after a removal so it rechecks the same index.

units.title: A hash is a signature for data
units.detail: A hash deterministically summarizes data: identical input always yields the same hash, while any tiny change (even case of one letter) produces a completely different hash. This property is what lets the network detect any tampering.

units.title: Blocks chain via previous hash
units.detail: Each block stores the hash of the previous block, and its own hash is computed from its data plus the previous hash. Modifying any block changes its hash, which invalidates every following block, making the chain immutable unless you re-mine everything.

units.title: Genesis block anchors the chain
units.detail: The very first block in a blockchain is the genesis block and has a special previous-hash value since no prior block exists. Every other block must reference the hash of the one before it.

units.title: Decentralization via consensus
units.detail: No central authority holds the blockchain; every user keeps a copy. If one actor tampers with their copy, the network ignores it because consensus follows the state agreed on by the majority of users.

units.title: Proof of work makes mining expensive but verification cheap
units.detail: Miners must try nonce values until the block's hash starts with a required number of zeros (the difficulty). Finding a valid nonce takes lots of work, but anyone can verify it in one hash computation, and difficulty is adjusted so blocks take ~10 minutes on average.

units.title: Forks resolve to the longest chain
units.detail: Two miners can produce valid blocks at the same time, creating a fork. The network waits for more blocks and the longest chain (most work) wins; the other fork is discarded. Newly mined blocks shouldn't be fully trusted until several blocks are added on top.

units.title: Security relies on a 51% attack being impossible
units.detail: Rewriting history requires re-mining all subsequent blocks faster than the rest of the network. If one actor controlled a majority (51%) of mining power they could eventually overtake the real chain, which is why very large networks are effectively immutable.

units.title: 90% of games share the same core systems
units.detail: Player control, input handling, interactions, data/state, UI, audio, cameras, game flow, saving/loading, and events appear in almost every game regardless of genre. Learning these core fundamentals transfers across projects, so avoid searching for hyper-specific tutorials that exactly match one game idea.

units.title: Learn by doing, not copy-pasting
units.detail: Blindly copy-pasting tutorial code produces a working project but no retained knowledge. The only real way to learn is to actively implement and solve objectives yourself, then apply the core concepts to your own unique 10%.

units.title: Custom inspector showing fields by logic
units.detail: Create an Editor class extending Editor, tag it [CustomEditor(typeof(MyClass))], and override OnInspectorGUI to draw serialized properties with EditorGUILayout.PropertyField. Switch on the selected enum value to show only the parameters relevant to the current action type, hiding all others.

units.title: SerializedObject lifecycle for editor scripts
units.detail: In OnInspectorGUI, call serializedObject.Update() first, then FindProperty to locate fields, and finish with serializedObject.ApplyModifiedProperties() so changes write back. Custom classes that should appear in the inspector need the [Serializable] attribute.

units.title: OnDrawGizmos vs OnSceneGUI
units.detail: OnSceneGUI (in the Editor script) only draws when the object is selected, while OnDrawGizmos (on the MonoBehaviour) draws at all times. Use OnDrawGizmos for persistent scene visualization such as arrows linking an action to its target object.

units.title: Scene handles for editing transform-like values
units.detail: Use Handles.PositionHandle inside OnSceneGUI (wrapped in EditorGUI.BeginChangeCheck) to let designers drag a position in the scene view instead of typing numbers. Record the object state with Undo.RecordObject before changing so Ctrl+Z works.

units.title: Data-driven scripting with serializable action types
units.detail: Model scripted behavior as an enum action type plus separate serializable parameter classes, and dispatch with a switch. This makes content building designer-friendly: the inspector and scene gizmos expose exactly what each action needs, and adding a new action type is a small, localized change.

units.title: Evaluate assets by performance and extensibility
units.detail: When picking tools/assets, weigh factors the video highlights: job system/burst compiler support for performance at millions of objects, editor-driven customization, integration with other assets, and long-term maintenance (constant updates over years). These determine whether the asset fits a real game.

units.title: Prototype vs Art HD asset pipeline
units.detail: Unity Snaps packs come in two identical-shape versions: lightweight Prototype and high-definition Art HD. Build and test the level with cheap prototypes (runs on weak PCs), then one-click swap every asset to HD for the real build, and swap back for editing.

units.title: Grid snapping with ProBuilder
units.detail: Enable ProBuilder snapping to place snapped assets on a perfect grid; objects snap to valid positions automatically and you can adjust the grid scale. This eliminates gaps between level pieces.

units.title: Asset Swap Tool for prototype/HD swap
units.detail: The free Asset Swap Tool scans the scene, lets you pick the Prototype pack and the Art HD pack, and replaces every matching prefab in one click. Use it to bounce between lightweight editing and polished presentation.

units.title: Use real-world units for mixable assets
units.detail: Snapped assets are modeled to real-world unit proportions, so your own real-unit assets can be dropped into the level and mixed seamlessly. Standardizing on real units is a design decision that enables asset mixing.

units.title: Customize snapped assets with ProBuilder
units.detail: Prebuilt snap assets are ProBuilder-compatible, so select any prefab, click ProBuilderize, and edit the mesh in-engine to adjust pieces that don't fit your level exactly.

units.title: Community-built game via public roadmap
units.detail: Unity Open Projects pairs an official team with community contributors using a public GitHub repo and roadmap. Individuals contribute one system or feature and see it land in a real shipped game.

units.title: Single-system contribution as learning step
units.detail: Contributing one focused system to an ongoing community game is a stepping stone between game jams and full solo development. The game design wiki changes over time as more systems are contributed, so expect iteration.

units.title: Microgames as beginner starting points
units.detail: Unity microgames (2D platformer, Kart, FPS, LEGO) are small complete playable games plus guided tutorials that teach editor windows and basic modifications. They're designed for beginners to learn by modifying a working game.

units.title: Snap placement to valid positions
units.detail: The brick-building system previews a dragged brick under the cursor and auto-snaps it into all geometrically valid connector positions, letting users connect pieces by simply clicking over a valid spot.

units.title: Behavior bricks as physical visual scripting
units.detail: LEGO behavior bricks put logic physically in the world: each brick does one action (hover, rotate, explode, shoot, triggers), and stacking them on an object composes complex behaviors without code. Like visual scripting but placed as objects.

units.title: Compose triggers to build complex behavior
units.detail: Pair trigger bricks (touch, timer, nearby) with action bricks (explode, rotate, elevator) by dragging an action reference into the trigger's target slot. Example: touch trigger wired to an explode brick destroys a mountain when the player touches it.

units.title: Write the game design before coding
units.detail: A builder-defender mix: place buildings, gather wood/stone/gold, defend against enemies that walk to a building and explode on contact; lose if the HQ is destroyed. A clear one-paragraph design makes implementation and course structure obvious.

units.title: Building placement rules
units.detail: Valid placement rules: buildings can't spawn on top of other objects, can't be too close to the same type, and can't be too far from any building. Enforce rules before allowing placement, then show a ghost preview.

units.title: Design is a starting point for iteration
units.detail: Treat the initial design doc as a starting point; as you build and play, iterate on what works and doesn't. Structure code so new building types, resources, and enemy types can be added easily (e.g. ScriptableObjects).

units.title: Plain class with constructor injection
units.detail: Make gameplay logic a plain C# class (not a MonoBehaviour) whose constructor receives its dependencies: a waiting queue, a list of positions, and an exit position. The game handler constructs it and passes real references in.

units.title: Event-driven queue processing
units.detail: Subscribe to the queue's 'guest arrived at front' event; on fire, try to grab an empty slot and pull the first guest from the queue. The building requests guests when it can serve them instead of polling.

units.title: Sub-class tracks state with null check
units.detail: Use a small private sub-class that holds a position plus the guest currently using it; `IsEmpty()` returns whether the guest reference is null. This cleanly models which slot is free.

units.title: Chain actions with callbacks
units.detail: Sequence behavior with callbacks: move to slot, then on arrival fire an animation, on animation complete clear the slot and move the guest to the exit, then on exit arrival request the next guest. Callbacks make sequential state machines readable.

units.title: Visualize internal logic with debug sprites
units.detail: Spawn colored debug sprites whose color updates every frame to reflect internal state (e.g. green = empty, red = occupied). It makes invisible object logic immediately visible for debugging.

units.title: Namespace prefix to avoid collisions
units.detail: Prefix custom classes (e.g. 'cm') to avoid name clashes when your code coexists with a real game's class library. Useful when writing tutorials/modules on top of existing codebases.

units.title: Buy vs build is time vs money
units.detail: Don't ask 'can I build it' but 'how long and is my time worth it'. A $40 asset built yourself at $20/hr must take under two hours to break even; feature-complete tools routinely take 80-100 hours. Build for fun, buy when the feature is a means to an end.

units.title: Tick system runs logic at fixed rate
units.detail: A timer triggers logic every X seconds (e.g. 10 ticks/sec) instead of every frame, cutting work and garbage while staying imperceptible to players. Best general optimization: find-target logic at 5/s is indistinguishable from 60/s.

units.title: Server tick system via RPC
units.detail: Run the same tick timer on the server and fire a client RPC on each tick to run logic on all clients. This sharply cuts bandwidth for multiplayer logic that doesn't need per-frame updates, which matters since multiplayer is billed per byte.

units.title: Tag components over string tags
units.detail: Strings as object identifiers are brittle: one capitalization, space, or dot silently breaks matching. Instead use an empty MonoBehaviour tag component and check it with TryGetComponent, so a typo becomes a compile error instead of a runtime mystery.

units.title: Profile before optimizing
units.detail: Use the profiler to find actual hotspots; it's the one optimization technique that applies to every game. In the hierarchy view check per-function timings and GC alloc per frame to locate garbage sources.

units.title: Reference types generate garbage, value types don't
units.detail: GC happens when C# collects dead objects, and a local value-type variable creates no garbage at all. Minimize allocations of reference types (objects) and selectively call System.GC.Collect at load points to avoid gameplay stutters.

units.title: Mark static objects to enable batching
units.detail: Mark every object that never moves (entire environments) as static so Unity batches draw calls, giving a large rendering win. Static flag can be toggled for all components or per-component via the inspector dropdown.

units.title: Object pooling avoids instantiate stutter
units.detail: Instantiate causes stutter from allocation; pre-instantiate pools during a loading screen and reuse objects for projectiles, enemies, particles, and dynamic UI. Avoid it only when a single tiny VFX spawn — don't over-optimize trivial cases.

units.title: Disable unused collision pairs
units.detail: In physics settings, the Layer Collision Matrix defines which layers collide. Untick pairs that should never collide (e.g. player vs enemies in some games) so the physics engine skips those checks entirely.

units.title: Split canvases by update frequency
units.detail: Any change to a UI element rebuilds its entire canvas. Separate constantly-updating UI onto its own canvas and rarely-updating UI onto others so frequent changes don't repaint everything every frame.

units.title: LODs and billboards for far objects
units.detail: Render far-away objects with fewer vertices: LODs step down vertex count with distance, and billboards replace a mesh with a textured quad (e.g. 11,000 triangles down to 2). Both are invisible to the player at distance and massively cut triangle count.

units.title: Bake lighting and use occlusion culling
units.detail: Precompute/bake lighting into textures (generate lighting in the Lighting window) since runtime GI won't run on normal PCs, and enable occlusion culling so hidden meshes behind walls are not rendered at all.

units.title: Don't run logic every update
units.detail: Most gameplay logic doesn't need 60Hz. Run find-target at 5Hz or offset different tasks across different frames (frame 1 targets, frame 2 collisions, frame 3 mesh info) to spread cost and keep the game smooth.

units.title: Remove debug.log from final builds
units.detail: Debug.Log on every Update has a measurable frame-rate cost. Use a custom easily-disabled logging script instead; keep occasional logs that help trace bugs in the field, but strip per-frame logging from release builds.

units.title: Multiplayer setup: manager, transport, prefab list
units.detail: To set up Netcode for Game Objects: one NetworkManager, a Network Transport (modular, swappable), a player prefab assigned to the manager, and every spawnable prefab registered in the Network Prefabs list — objects not on the list don't exist on the network.

units.title: Server vs host vs client roles
units.detail: A server has no player, a client connects to a server, and a host is both server and client (the 'player-host' model for games without dedicated servers). Many logic decisions depend on understanding which role you're running as.

units.title: Spawn player prefab dynamically
units.detail: Leave the player prefab out of the scene; the NetworkManager spawns it for each player who connects. For games without a single character (strategy), leave the field empty or assign a visual-less prefab to carry player logic.

units.title: Extend NetworkBehaviour and gate with IsOwner
units.detail: Extending MonoBehaviour, movement code runs on every replica, moving all players at once. Extend NetworkBehaviour and check `IsOwner` before reading input so only the owning player's object runs the logic.

units.title: NetworkTransform syncs only changing data
units.detail: Add NetworkTransform and untick every channel that never changes (scale, rotation, Y position) to minimize bandwidth. Sending unnecessary data is the classic multiplayer mistake.

units.title: Server authoritative movement blocks clients
units.detail: Netcode is server-authoritative by default: a client's movement is reverted each tick because the server never moves. Either trust the client with ClientNetworkTransform (fine for casual co-op), or have the client request movement via RPC and let the server move it (required for competitive).

units.title: Test multiplayer with windowed builds
units.detail: Set the build to windowed mode and set Company/Product names (they locate the player.log). Run one build and an editor instance side by side, using an in-game console to read logs from builds where the editor console isn't visible.

units.title: Iterate and throw away what doesn't fit
units.detail: Experiment with mechanics early and be willing to discard ones that don't fit the game; a 2D puzzle platformer needs a strong mix of tested mechanics and varied levels. The final name and polish can come later — prototype first.

units.title: Custom engine means rebuilding it
units.detail: Building your own engine is so complex you'll miss features you only learn about later, often forcing a full engine rebuild mid-project. Ask yourself: build an engine or build a game — doing both well is the exception, not the rule.

units.title: Release prep checklist
units.detail: Before launch: make a website, prepare images and captions, cut a trailer, set up the Steam backend, announce a release date, and fix a batch of tiny bugs. A long devlog series doubles as a bug-testing community.

units.title: Release is another milestone, not the end
units.detail: Launch begins post-launch support: more bug fixing, feature requests, and content updates can be as hectic as pre-release. Successful launches also bring review/feedback pressure, so expect continued work after day one.

units.title: Reviews drive Steam visibility and learning
units.detail: Steam reviews power the store algorithm and teach you what worked and what to improve, so encourage players to leave them at launch. As a player, leave reviews to help indie developers.

units.title: Find any package field via source code
units.detail: To modify a package value through code, right-click its inspector field, Edit Script, or browse the Packages folder in the project window (toggle the hidden-packages button). Search the source for the value you want to change to learn the exact field path.

units.title: Modify Cinemachine FOV through LensSettings
units.detail: Field of view isn't a direct property; it lives in the camera's lens: `cinemachineVirtualCamera.m_Lens.fieldOfView`. No FOV/fov/vertical search will find it — look up the LensSettings struct in the package source.

units.title: GetCinemachineComponent to edit body/aim
units.detail: Cinemachine is component-based; the body/aim scripts (Transposer, Composer, etc.) are separate components. Use `GetCinemachineComponent<CinemachineTransposer>()` to reach fields like `m_FollowOffset` and change them at runtime.

units.title: Edge scrolling with mouse position
units.detail: Detect when the mouse is within an edge-size pixel margin of the screen by comparing Input.mousePosition against Screen.width/height minus edgeSize, then move the camera in that direction.

units.title: Camera follows a modifiable follow position
units.detail: Keep a Vector3 follow position that the camera lerps toward, and modify that position with input rather than moving the camera transform directly. This decouples input from camera movement and makes the system reusable for keyboard, edge scrolling, and other sources.

units.title: Multiply movement by deltaTime
units.detail: Scale input-driven movement by Time.deltaTime so speed is frame-rate independent and behaves the same regardless of hardware performance.

units.title: Feature toggle with inverse keypress
units.detail: Add a boolean that toggles on a single keypress by setting it to its own inverse, and give visible feedback (text popup at the mouse position) so the player knows the state changed.

units.title: Orthographic zoom is camera size
units.detail: In an orthographic camera, zoom is controlled by orthographic size: lower size zooms in, higher size zooms out. Adjusting the size value is the whole zoom mechanic.

units.title: Clamp zoom values
units.detail: Clamp the zoom variable between min and max values so players can't zoom into degenerate or useless ranges, and so invalid values are handled in one place.

units.title: Mouse wheel zoom via scrollDelta.y
units.detail: Read Input.mouseScrollDelta.y: positive scrolls in, negative scrolls out. The wheel fires per notch rather than every frame, so per-event change amounts need a larger magnitude than per-frame key input.

units.title: Split update logic into named methods
units.detail: Move distinct input groups (manual movement, edge scrolling, zoom) into separate private methods and call them from Update, which keeps a growing input handler readable and easy to extend.

units.title: Server authority for object spawning
units.detail: Only the server/host can spawn network objects, so client-triggered spawns must be requested via a ServerRPC. This is the core pattern for synchronizing any dynamically created object.

units.title: Sync transforms and animations
units.detail: Add a network transform component to synchronize movement and a network animator to synchronize animations. Most object types need no custom sync code beyond these components.

units.title: Run logic only on the owner
units.detail: Guard movement and input logic so it only executes on the owning client, and disable the camera on non-owner copies of the player. Otherwise every client tries to control every player instance.

units.title: Merge entities into the player prefab
units.detail: Instead of spawning two linked objects (player and vehicle) which is hard to manage in multiplayer, embed the vehicle inside the player prefab and enable/disable it. Reduces spawning complexity to a simple toggle.

units.title: Wide FOV sells speed
units.detail: Using a very wide field of view makes an object look dramatically faster, a cheap smoke-and-mirrors trick for speed games. The same object can look slow to an outside observer and fast to the pilot.

units.title: Single-player assumptions are the real cost
units.detail: Adding netcode itself was fast; most multiplayer-conversion time went to refactoring single-player assumptions like singletons and code that assumes exactly one player exists. Architect early for the possibility of multiple instances.

units.title: First-person needs a visible body for others
