units.detail: In first-person multiplayer, remote players see your local model, so you need both a first-person view (own body hidden) and a third-person visual for other players, otherwise others see a floating camera.

units.title: Streaming open world by terrain tiles
units.detail: Split a large world into separate terrain tiles sized by a defined world size, then stream tiles in and out of memory based on player position. Tools like Gaia handle this automatically, saving months of custom work.

units.title: Swap the skybox to transform mood
units.detail: Changing the skybox and directional light colors is one of the simplest high-impact visual upgrades, instantly re-theming a scene (e.g., to a dark alien sci-fi planet).

units.title: Euler angles break multi-axis rotation
units.detail: Rotating an object that can spin on any axis (like a plane) by directly changing Euler angles causes it to break down; rotate using quaternions instead.

units.title: Asset pack animations are read-only
units.detail: Animations imported from asset packs often can't be edited directly. Duplicate the animation clip first and edit the copy, e.g., trimming first frames to make an attack wind-up snappier.

units.title: Recolor low-poly meshes
units.detail: Use a recolor tool or shader that changes colors per mesh part and adds emission to selected parts (like plane engines), an easy way to customize store assets to fit your art direction.

units.title: Simple state machine for enemy AI
units.detail: A minimal state machine (find player, move toward it, attack, trigger animation) is enough for functional enemy AI and can be extended as needed.

units.title: Minimap from a world screenshot
units.detail: Instead of rendering a second camera for the minimap, take a screenshot of the entire world as a texture and manually place icon markers on it. Cheaper and simpler for games with a fixed map.

units.title: World reacts to territory capture
units.detail: Change the global look (lighting and post-processing volume weight) based on player distance to a captured landmark, making capture progress visible across the whole world without per-object work.

units.title: Wishlists are ~10x Steam followers
units.detail: As a rule of thumb, a game's wishlist count is about ten times its Steam follower count, letting you estimate wishlists from SteamDB follower charts.

units.title: Wishlists don't guarantee success but absence guarantees failure
units.detail: Wishlists do not guarantee sales (some games with 10k+ wishlists flopped), but launching with almost no wishlists almost certainly fails. Mega-hits like Vampire Survivors and Phasmophobia that launched with tiny wishlists are lottery-level exceptions, not the rule.

units.title: Aim for ~7000 wishlists before release
units.detail: Roughly 7,000 wishlists is the threshold needed to appear on Steam's Popular Upcoming list, which is the gateway to a successful launch for most games.

units.title: Estimate sales from review count
units.detail: A common heuristic: a game's total sales are roughly 40x its number of Steam user reviews (e.g., 500k reviews implies ~2M copies sold). Useful for gauging how well a competitor or your own title did.

units.title: Shady wishlists don't convert
units.detail: Wishlists gathered through giveaways or paid mechanical-turk style schemes inflate the count but don't convert to purchases, destroying the metric's predictive value. Organic wishlists from content and marketing predict success accurately.

units.title: Marketing is mandatory, not optional
units.detail: For indie games, doing marketing before release is required for financial success. Useful channels include blog posts, Twitter, devlogs, memes, shorts, and tutorials.

units.title: Top-down GTA scale is solo-achievable
units.detail: GTA 1/2-style top-down games (drive, shoot, wanted system, gang AI) are achievable today by an experienced solo dev thanks to modern engines and the Asset Store, though it took a ~30-person team and millions of dollars 25 years ago.

units.title: Content volume, not tech, is the solo bottleneck
units.detail: For games like GTA 3+, the core mechanics are still solo-buildable, but filling a huge world with animated cutscenes, voice acting, story, and props is the part that becomes impossible for one person regardless of tools.

units.title: Marketability beats feasibility
units.detail: Just because you can build something (e.g., a top-down shooter like GTA) doesn't mean it will be commercially successful; that genre sells poorly on Steam. Consider marketability before committing a solo project.

units.title: AI tools speed up art and writing
units.detail: AI can generate simple sprites (2D top-down era quality) and accelerate quest/character writing, though a human still needs to review everything AI produces.

units.title: JSON save file pattern
units.detail: Create a save object containing all game state, serialize it to JSON, and write it to a file on device. Load by reading the file and deserializing with JsonUtility.FromJson. This pattern stays valid for years and is the standard way to persist data.

units.title: Aggregate state into a single save object
units.detail: Build one global save object that contains smaller save objects from each system (resources, buildings, metadata) and serialize that whole thing as one file, giving each system ownership of its own save data.

units.title: Unique save slots via timestamps
units.detail: Name save files using DateTime.Now so each save is automatically unique (one new name per second). 'Continue' then finds and loads the most recently written file by scanning the save folder's write times.

units.title: Pack screenshot, JSON, and metadata into one file
units.detail: Combine multiple data types into a single binary save file by converting JSON to bytes, the screenshot to bytes, and adding a small header (e.g., header size as the first two bytes). Load by reading bytes, slicing the header size, then the JSON, then the image. Enables screenshots plus data in one file.

units.title: Store metadata for the load UI
units.detail: Add non-gameplay metadata (date, resource snapshot) to the save file and display it in the load menu, so players can identify saves before committing to load.

units.title: Define entity types with ScriptableObjects
units.detail: Represent building/economy types as ScriptableObjects that store the prefab and rules, so placement logic stores a type reference and stays generic rather than hard-coding each building.

units.title: Learning by doing beats watching tutorials
units.detail: You only truly learn by attempting the work yourself; pausing and building a demo before seeing the solution is the point of practice challenges. Progress comes from attempting, not from watching.

units.title: Render textures make camera views reusable
units.detail: A camera can render to a texture instead of the screen; that texture can then be shown anywhere (UI thumbnails, big monitor views, in-world screens), enabling CCTV/surveillance systems. Render textures are expensive, so using intentionally low resolution also matches a CCTV aesthetic.

units.title: Active feed plus clickable thumbnails
units.detail: Present many camera feeds as a large active view with smaller thumbnails for the rest; clicking a thumbnail promotes it to the active view. A standard, intuitive pattern for multi-camera UIs.

units.title: Camera visibility and motion detection
units.detail: Detect whether an entity is currently visible to a camera (e.g., by checking what the camera sees) and drive a motion-detected indicator, so the system reports which camera sees a character at any moment.

units.title: Consistency in naming conventions
units.detail: Which casing convention (PascalCase, camelCase, snake_case) you use matters less than being consistent across your codebase. Pick a style and stick to it.

units.title: Never make fields public
units.detail: Public fields give every other class read AND write access, creating thousands of places that could corrupt your values. Keep fields private/properties; the exception is public fields on ScriptableObjects treated as read-only data containers.

units.title: Lerp interpolates vectors, Slerp interpolates directions
units.detail: Lerp between a vector pointing right and one pointing left shrinks through zero and flips; Slerp rotates through the angle. Use Slerp when the meaning is a direction/orientation, Lerp for plain vector interpolation.

units.title: Animator bindings are name-based
units.detail: A yellow 'missing' property on an animation means there is no child object with that exact name (e.g., renamed 'head' to 'head2'). Fix by renaming the object to match the animation binding; the same mismatch silently stops the animation from playing.

units.title: OverlapBox vs BoxCast semantics
units.detail: OverlapBox only detects colliders at the final target position, so it misses obstacles along the path; BoxCast sweeps a virtual box from A to B and detects anything between. Choose BoxCast for movement blocking, OverlapBox for area tests.

units.title: Z-fighting from coplanar objects
units.detail: Two objects on the mathematically exact same position cause the GPU to flicker between them (z-fighting). Fix by offsetting one object by a tiny amount like 0.01.

units.title: One base class, many interfaces in C#
units.detail: A class can only extend one base class but can implement multiple interfaces, which is a strong reason to prefer interfaces for shared behavior. Interfaces are also great for capabilities that only some objects have (like IHasInventory).

units.title: Default interface implementations
units.detail: C# 7+ lets interfaces declare default implementations, so you can add members to an interface without forcing every existing implementer to update.

units.title: Function signature is types only
units.detail: A function signature consists of the return type and parameter types; the function name and parameter names are not part of it. Names just need to make the code readable.

units.title: Clean code is guidelines, not rules
units.detail: Clean code principles exist to help you finish the game, not as commandments to obey rigidly. Don't obsess over perfection to the point of no progress, but don't ignore it entirely either; the number one goal is completing the game.

units.title: Compiler ignores style, developer doesn't
units.detail: The compiler produces the same executable no matter how messy the code is, but messy code creates technical debt that drowns you before you finish. Code quality affects the developer, not the machine.

units.title: Correlation isn't causation for messy code
units.detail: Successful games like Far Cry and Sunless Sea ship huge, messy player classes (5,000-7,000 lines), but they succeeded despite the mess because their developers were skilled enough to manage the complexity, not because of it.

units.title: Unity can handle AAA open-world scale
units.detail: Immortals Fenyx Rising, Valheim, and Satisfactory (galaxy-scale factories) prove Unity can ship massive interconnected open worlds, given a skilled team. Engine capability is rarely the limiting factor.

units.title: LOD for terrain and detail distance
units.detail: Hide behind-the-player geometry, limit grass/detail draw distance, and unload far meshes to keep polygon count low while preserving the illusion of a huge view distance. Invisible to players unless actively looked for.

units.title: Dynamic resolution and render scale
units.detail: When a huge area is on screen, drop render scale or use dynamic resolution (finer-grained control) to reduce pixel load while falling/flying over large distances, then restore it in normal gameplay.

units.title: World streaming without built-in support
units.detail: Unity has no built-in world streaming, so build it yourself by combining very low-res terrains for far-away areas with additive scene loading. Doable but requires real work.

units.title: AI LOD by player distance
units.detail: Run simple patrolling AI for distant enemies and only enable complex behaviors when the player is close. Big worlds rarely have many active enemies at once, so most entities can stay cheap.

units.title: Huge scale needs smoke and mirrors
units.detail: Games like Tears of the Kingdom only run on limited hardware by hiding work: LOD, limited terrain detail, reduced render scale during big-view moments, and AI LOD. Implement these techniques and similar scale becomes achievable.

units.title: Capture area system using trigger colliders
units.detail: Define capturable zones with trigger colliders on a dedicated layer. OnTriggerEnter/Exit tracks which players are inside, and progress toward capture only accumulates while at least one player is present.

units.title: Compose one map area from multiple colliders
units.detail: Make each logical area a parent object holding several trigger collider children. This lets you build arbitrary shapes (L-shapes, split zones) without a single matching box, and the parent script aggregates all child collider state.

units.title: Deduplicate players across overlapping colliders
units.detail: If colliders overlap, one player can be counted by two colliders, inflating the player count and doubling capture speed. Fix by collecting unique players into a list and only adding if not already contained.

units.title: Normalized capture progress drives state transition
units.detail: Store capture progress as a normalized 0..1 float increased by playerCount * captureSpeed * deltaTime. When progress reaches 1.0, switch state from neutral to captured. Normalizing makes capture duration easy to tune (0.5 => 2 seconds).

units.title: Simple state machine: neutral then captured
units.detail: Model each capture area with an enum state (neutral/captured). On neutral, run the capture-progress logic; once captured, stop all updates. Keep the state machine tiny and explicit rather than flag booleans.

units.title: Events notify UI of area state changes
units.detail: Expose C# events (e.g. OnCaptured) on the map area and invoke them when the state changes. The UI subscribes and updates visuals, keeping gameplay and presentation decoupled.

units.title: White overlay textures tintable to any color
units.detail: Author map-area overlay textures in white so a single sprite can be tinted to any team color at runtime by setting the UI Image color. Avoids baking per-team textures.

units.title: Radial fill image shows capture progress
units.detail: Represent capture progress in the UI with a filled Image (radial 360 fill method) and set image.fillAmount to the normalized progress. Cost: zero and reads instantly.

units.title: Overlapping colliders break enter/exit event order
units.detail: A player can exit collider A after entering overlapping collider B, so firing exit on the first trigger hides the UI while the player is still inside. On exit, check all colliders; only fire exit if the player is in none of them.

units.title: Isolate capture colliders on their own layer
units.detail: Put gameplay-only trigger colliders on a dedicated layer so they never interfere with player movement, raycasts, or other physics interactions elsewhere in the scene.

units.title: Read input in Update, move physics in FixedUpdate
units.detail: Capture raw input every frame in Update into a stored vector, then apply it to the Rigidbody in FixedUpdate (which runs at the physics tick rate). Keeps input snappy while respecting the physics loop.

units.title: Set velocity instead of MovePosition for movement
units.detail: Driving a character by setting Rigidbody.velocity lets the physics system decide whether motion is legal and naturally produces wall collisions and object pushing. MovePosition can cause jitter when the target is inside geometry.

units.title: Enable Rigidbody interpolation to remove jitter
units.detail: Physics-driven movement appears stuttery at high frame rates. Set Rigidbody interpolation mode to Interpolate so the render smooths between physics steps.

units.title: Dash via MovePosition validated with raycast
units.detail: For an instant dash, MovePosition to a target offset, but first raycast from the current position along the dash direction; if the ray hits, clamp the destination to the hit point so the dash stops at walls. Use a LayerMask to ignore the player's own collider.

units.title: Dodge roll = state machine with decelerating velocity
units.detail: A dodge/roll locks the character into a 'rolling' state that ignores normal input, applies velocity in a fixed direction, and decays speed each frame until below a minimum, then returns to normal state. Simple enum state machine keeps the two modes from fighting.

units.title: Cache last move direction for idle abilities
units.detail: Dashing/rolling while stationary produces a zero direction vector and does nothing. Store the last non-zero move direction and use it as fallback when activating dash or roll.

units.title: Top-down 2D: freeze rotation, zero gravity
units.detail: For a top-down physics character, disable gravity (gravityScale 0) and freeze rotation on the Rigidbody2D so the sprite never tips or falls and only translates.

units.title: Render texture + extra camera for portrait window
units.detail: Create a second orthographic camera whose target texture is a RenderTexture, then display that texture with a RawImage inside a UI window. The result is a live mini-view of a character or building without affecting the main camera.

units.title: RawImage shows textures, Image shows sprites
units.detail: Use RawImage (accepts Texture2D/RenderTexture) instead of the normal Image (sprite-based) whenever the UI must display a dynamic texture like a render texture or camera feed.

units.title: Position portrait camera over target each frame
units.detail: Each Update, snap the portrait camera's transform onto the followed character's position (using the main camera's Z for distance). This makes the portrait automatically track a moving character.

units.title: DOTS = ECS + Jobs + Burst for ~100x speed
units.detail: Unity's DOTS is a tool stack combining the ECS entity component system, the job system for multithreading, and the Burst compiler. Cache-friendly memory layout and parallelized jobs are what produce dramatic speedups, not magic.

units.title: Mix DOTS with regular GameObjects
units.detail: You do not need an all-DOTS game. Use DOTS for the hot performance-critical simulation and keep normal MonoBehaviour/GameObject code for UI, input, and other cold paths, wiring them together.

units.title: Baking converts GameObjects into entities
units.detail: The DOTS baking system lets you keep authoring with familiar GameObjects and components, which are automatically converted into entities at build time. You get a familiar workflow plus DOTS performance.

units.title: Steam app as launcher hub for games/tutorials
units.detail: Ship a single launcher app containing all completed games plus an interactive tutorials section. It gives you a distribution channel to update builds and push new content, including multiplayer or livestream clients, without shipping separate games.

units.title: Expect estimates to slip; budget extra time
units.detail: A self-confessed example: a project estimated for release in May shipped in July. Schedule conservatively and add buffer, especially for first-time builds like shipping a launcher app.

units.title: Triggers need at least one Rigidbody to fire
units.detail: OnTriggerEnter never fires if neither object has a Rigidbody. Only one side of the interaction needs one (e.g. the player); static pickup items with a trigger collider alone still work.

units.title: Kinematic Rigidbody ignores static collisions
units.detail: A kinematic Rigidbody is unaffected by outside forces, so it passes straight through static walls while still pushing dynamic objects. If the player should be blocked by walls, use a dynamic body; reserve kinematic for script-driven motion.

units.title: Trigger vs solid collider usage
units.detail: Set Is Trigger when you only want an event (pickups, zones, doors) and the object must be passable. Leave it off when the collider should physically block or push. Combined with a Rigidbody this decides collisions vs trigger callbacks.

units.title: OnTrigger vs OnCollision event callbacks
units.detail: OnTriggerEnter/Exit/Stay fire between a Rigidbody and a trigger collider; OnCollisionEnter/Exit/Stay fire for solid collisions and receive a Collision with contact points and velocity instead of a Collider. Use the right pair for the behavior.

units.title: Deliver features as follow-up updates
units.detail: Instead of delaying a release to finish every feature, ship the core product then add a major new module (here, a full FPS) as a later update. Keeps initial release on schedule and gives the feature proper dev time.

units.title: Visual scripting can build complete games
units.detail: A full game (FPS with weapons, enemies, pickups, doors, keys) can be built using only Unity Visual Scripting with zero written code, showing node-based logic is viable for full gameplay systems, not just prototypes.

units.title: Keep game systems decoupled and modular
units.detail: Architect the game with cleanly decoupled, modular systems so adding new resource types, building types, or content is easy. Loosely coupled code pays off as scope grows and when you reuse patterns across projects.

units.title: Scope small for your first course/project
units.detail: A 'quick' project ballooned to 6000+ lines of written content. For an unfamiliar pipeline, start with a small scope to validate the process before investing in something massive.

units.title: Sub-scenes auto-convert contents to entities
units.detail: In DOTS, place scene content inside a sub-scene instead of attaching ConvertToEntity scripts: everything in the sub-scene is converted to entities automatically, keeping the scene clean. Toggle a checkbox to open it for editing as GameObjects.

units.title: Tag components identify entities for systems
units.detail: Give entities empty tag components (e.g. Ground, Cloud) and query systems by tag plus the data they need. This is how movement/rendering systems locate specific entity types without string names.

units.title: ECS singleton: read, modify, then SetSingleton
units.detail: GetSingleton returns a copy; modifying it only changes the local copy unless you call SetSingleton to write it back. Always write back after changing singleton component data.

units.title: Bridge DOTS events to UI via C# events
units.detail: DOTS systems can't directly drive UI, so fire C# events from ECS jobs using a trigger object that's safe inside Entities.ForEach, then capture them on the main thread and let normal MonoBehaviour UI subscribe. Keeps object-based UI working with data-oriented code.

units.title: BlobAssets are immutable; rebuild shape to resize
units.detail: DOTS physics colliders store their shape in a BlobAsset which cannot be modified. To resize a collider (e.g. dynamic pipe sizes) you must create a brand-new ColliderShape BlobAsset and assign it to the physics collider component.

units.title: Toggle systems on/off to control game state
units.detail: Drive game state (menu/playing/game over) by enabling or disabling the relevant systems. Stop spawners and controllers when dead, re-enable them on restart, instead of complex branching inside each system.

units.title: Infinite parallax by snapping layers back
units.detail: Move background layers left at different speeds and teleport each layer back to the right when it crosses a threshold. Slower layers create depth; the snap is invisible when off-screen.

units.title: Blend trees choose animation from parameters
units.detail: Blend trees group related clips (walk left/right, idle variants) and automatically pick/interpolate the correct one from float parameters. A handful of parameters replaces a web of state transitions.

units.title: 1D vs 2D blend tree types
units.detail: 1D blends along a single parameter (left/right). For full directional movement use 2D Simple Directional (one clip per direction), 2D Freeform (multiple clips per direction), or Freeform Cartesian (clips not direction-based).

units.title: Drive blend trees from code via SetFloat/SetBool
units.detail: Connect gameplay to animation by setting animator parameters each frame: SetFloat with the movement vector components and SetBool for is-moving. Transitions (idle->move) then trigger off those parameter conditions.

units.title: Transitions with conditions on bool parameters
units.detail: Wire idle-to-movement with a bool parameter (isMoving) and transitions containing conditions (isMoving true/false). Set zero exit time and zero duration for instant, fully parameter-driven switching.

units.title: Task stores only what executor needs
units.detail: When defining a task, store the minimal data the worker needs (a target position) plus a callback Action for the outcome, instead of storing raw object references. This keeps the task reusable across different implementations.

units.title: Separate task creator from task executor
units.detail: The class that creates a task is responsible for filling in implementation details (like how to clean up), while the worker only executes position + animation + callback. This cleanly separates responsibilities and means worker code never changes when visuals change.

units.title: Storing a transform tightly couples a task
units.detail: Storing a Transform field in a task forces the worker to know what a Transform is and how to dispose of it, so the task breaks if the visual is instead a particle system or other representation. Replace it with a position + Action to remove that coupling.

units.title: FunctionUpdater runs an action each frame
units.detail: A FunctionUpdater executes a supplied action every frame until the action returns true, then destroys itself. Useful for one-off effects like fading a sprite's alpha via deltaTime instead of hard-coding destruction.

units.title: Workers request, execute, then request again
units.detail: A simple task loop: each idle worker requests a task from the system, executes it (move + animate + callback), then immediately requests another. Tasks are dispatched to whichever worker grabs them first.

units.title: Test resources before spending them
units.detail: Before performing a costly action (building), verify the player has enough resources, and only remove the resources after the check passes. Test the check and the removal separately before wiring up the visual spawn.

units.title: Encapsulate cost check and spend together
units.detail: Put the resource cost logic in a static TrySpendResources(cost) on the object's class. Callers just do if (Tower.TrySpendResources(cost)) then construct, so cost testing and removal live in one place instead of inline in the controller.

units.title: Static factory Create keeps caller clean
units.detail: A static Create(position, prefab) function instantiates the prefab, wraps it in a plain object, and returns the fully-constructed instance. The controller stays tidy and the construction details are hidden from callers.

units.title: Tick counter swaps construction sprites
units.detail: Model construction as a tick counter: increment on a periodic timer, switch the sprite based on the current tick (one sprite per stage), and consider the build done when tick reaches tickMax.

units.title: Normalized value drives progress bar
units.detail: Compute progress as tick * 1f / tickMax (a float in 0..1) and feed it to a world-space bar's SetSize. Progress bars and other gauges need this normalized value rather than the raw counter.

units.title: Building triggers an injected completion action
units.detail: Pass an onConstructed Action into the building's factory. The building just fires the action when built and never knows what should happen (e.g. spawning a unit), keeping the building class generic.

units.title: Seed resources for faster testing
units.detail: Starting resources at zero forces you to wait for gatherers each test. Temporarily initialize with a large amount (999) so you can validate build logic immediately, then restore the real starting value.

units.title: Click-to-select via static click event
units.detail: Each unit fires a static event when clicked, and a central controller subscribes to route clicks into its selection logic. This decouples units from the RTS controller so the controller knows which unit was clicked.

units.title: Selected circle shows the chosen unit
units.detail: Add a circle sprite under each unit, disabled by default, and toggle it active when that unit is selected. The visual indicator should mirror the controller's selected reference.

units.title: Single selected reference; orders target it
units.detail: Keep one 'selected unit' reference in the controller and apply orders only to it. Clicking a resource node routes the order to the currently selected unit; if none is selected, ignore the order.

units.title: Hide old selection sprite before showing new
units.detail: If you only show the selection indicator on the newly clicked unit, the previously selected unit keeps its indicator too. Hide the old unit's indicator (only if one exists) before displaying the new one.

units.title: ButtonSprite + BoxCollider2D for clicks
units.detail: A reusable ButtonSprite helper component on a BoxCollider2D fires a click callback when clicked. Attach it to selectable objects so the game handler can capture mouse clicks on them.

units.title: ComponentSystem for input-driven ECS
units.detail: In Unity ECS, logic lives in a ComponentSystem with an OnUpdate loop that listens to input (mouse press/release) and issues structural changes through PostUpdateCommands.

units.title: Selection area from mouse start and end
units.detail: Store the mouse position on button down; on button up compute the rectangle via min/max of start and end points. Test each entity's translation against these bounds to find what's inside.

units.title: ECS systems need a static instance for refs
units.detail: ECS systems cannot have serialized fields pointing to scene objects. Expose a static instance on a MonoBehaviour (set in Awake) and have systems access shared transforms/meshes/materials through it.

units.title: Tag components mark selection state
units.detail: Use an empty tag IComponentData (e.g. unitSelected) to mark selected entities, adding it via PostUpdateCommands inside the selection bounds and removing it when deselected.

units.title: Deselect all, then select inside the area
units.detail: On each selection gesture, first remove the selection tag from every currently selected entity, then add it to entities inside the new area. This guarantees empty clicks clear the selection.

units.title: Tiny drags can't select a single unit
units.detail: Clicking exactly on a unit produces a zero-size area that matches nothing. Fix by expanding the bounds when the drag distance is below a minimum size, or treat it as a single-unit click.

units.title: Formation positions in concentric rings
units.detail: Generate distinct move targets by taking an array of ring distances and an array of position counts per ring, then distributing positions around each circle at evenly spaced angles.

units.title: Single click selects one overlapping unit
units.detail: When the selection area is below the minimum size, set a flag so only a single entity (the first found) is selected. This lets players separate units stacked on top of each other.

units.title: OverlapAreaAll finds units in a box
units.detail: Use Physics2D.OverlapAreaAll(start, current) to get every 2D collider inside the drag rectangle, then filter the results by which objects carry the unit component.

units.title: Filter selection by component, not collider
units.detail: The selection area returns all colliders including rocks and scenery. Filter by asking GetComponent for the unit marker: only objects that have the unit component get added to the selected list.

units.title: Offset child sprite makes custom pivot
units.detail: Place the selection-area sprite as a child offset up and right by half its size so the parent transform pivot sits at the lower-left corner. Then position at the min corner and scale by the drag delta.

units.title: Clear and deselect before re-selecting
units.detail: Deselect every currently selected unit (hide their indicators) before applying the new selection. Otherwise stale selections persist across drags and empty clicks don't clear.

units.title: Rotating index spreads units across positions
units.detail: Keep an index that cycles through a list of move positions (index = (index + 1) % count) and assign one position per selected unit. Prevents all units stacking at a single point.

units.title: Angle-to-direction generates circle positions
units.detail: For each index, compute an angle across the circle, convert it to a direction vector, and build the target as start + direction * distance. Scale up with multiple ring distances and counts.

units.title: Each unit gets a distinct target position
units.detail: When issuing a move order to many units, hand each unit its own generated position around the target instead of the raw target. This keeps squads visually clean and avoids total overlap.

units.title: Paste JSON as classes in Visual Studio
units.detail: Copy a JSON payload, then in Visual Studio use Edit > Paste Special > Paste JSON as Classes. It auto-generates the complete nested C# class/struct structure for the clipboard JSON in one step.

units.title: dynamic keyword for untyped JSON access
units.detail: An alternative to hand-writing classes is using json.net's dynamic keyword, which lets you access JSON fields directly without defining the structure up front.

units.title: Most 2D systems port to 3D easily
units.detail: Almost any system shown in 2D works in 3D with a few tiny changes, because the underlying logic is independent of dimension. Don't limit yourself to one perspective when solving a problem.

units.title: 3D mouse position needs a raycast
units.detail: ScreenToWorldPoint only works in 2D. In 3D, shoot a ray from the camera through the mouse screen point and intersect it with a collision plane (on a dedicated layer) to get a world position.

units.title: Flat quad mesh + material for ground
units.detail: Build 3D ground from a 3D quad rotated 90 degrees to lie flat with a material applied, rather than a sprite renderer. Place it at y=0 and scale as needed.

units.title: Flat sprites look squished in 3D
units.detail: Sprite-based objects lying in the XZ plane appear squished. Either add a slight rotation so they face the camera more, or make them billboard by looking at the main camera.

units.title: Swap grid axes from XY to XZ
units.detail: Convert a grid class for 3D by duplicating it and replacing every Y coordinate with Z in world-position conversions, while keeping internal logic identical. The logic itself needs no other change.

units.title: Perspective camera plus depth of field
units.detail: Switch the camera from orthographic to perspective for a 3D feel and add a volume with a depth of field profile so distant content blurs, selling the 3D depth.

units.title: Logging is the superpower of programming
units.detail: Unlike physical crafts, software lets you add a debug.log at any point to see exact state and find bugs quickly. It's the main reason programming has such a fast debug loop.

units.title: Iteration speed beats raw skill
units.detail: Code compiles and reruns in seconds, so you can test, rewrite, and retest constantly with zero material cost. Physical activities are limited by redoing real materials, so don't take this speed for granted.

units.title: Learn the why behind each decision
units.detail: When following tutorials, research why each design choice exists (e.g. why interfaces) instead of blindly copying code. Understanding the why lets you build your own tools and solve new problems.

units.title: Heatmap from a per-cell custom mesh
units.detail: Render a heatmap by creating a custom dynamic mesh with one quad per grid cell, then updating quad UVs so each cell shows a color from a gradient texture based on its underlying value.

units.title: Gradient texture with normalized UV
units.detail: Use a 1x64 horizontal gradient texture (black, red, yellow, green) and map color by UV.x = value / maxValue. Normalized UV lookup gives a smooth value-to-color interpolation automatically.

units.title: Clamp grid values to a valid range
units.detail: Clamp stored grid values between a min and max constant (e.g. 0..100) inside the set-value function so values can never run away and normalized math stays valid.

units.title: Diamond area effect from mirrored triangles
units.detail: Apply an area-of-effect as a diamond by looping X over the range and Y over (range - X) to make a triangle, then mirroring it on the X and Y axes (skipping zero axes to avoid doubling).

units.title: Value falloff toward the effect edge
units.detail: Split the radius into a full-value range and a total range; beyond the full range, subtract a linearly decreasing amount as radius approaches total. Produces a hot center cooling to the edges.

units.title: Per-cell events rebuild the mesh too often
units.detail: If every cell add fires a value-changed event that rebuilds the mesh, one click with a radius triggers roughly a hundred mesh updates in a single frame. Batch or coalesce updates so the visual refreshes once per frame.

units.title: Value-changed event drives the visual
units.detail: Fire an event whenever a grid value changes and let the heatmap visual subscribe and redraw. This decouples the data grid from its display, and shows the power of events.

units.title: Copy component values from play mode
units.detail: Tune values live while playing (paused), then right-click the component and choose Copy Component, stop the scene, and Paste Component Values to commit the runtime values back to the prefab/scene.

units.title: Runtime-only visuals make edit-mode tuning guesswork
units.detail: Values that only become visible at runtime (e.g. a collider matched to an animated character) can't be set accurately in edit mode. Play the scene, pause, adjust, copy, stop, and paste the values.

units.title: Wrap each data point in a visual object
units.detail: Instead of returning a list of GameObjects from a graph-visual factory, return a single object that owns and manages each data point's GameObjects. This wrapper enables per-point updating later because the owner knows exactly what each child object represents.

units.title: Factory returns visual object interface
units.detail: Rename the factory from 'add graph visual' to 'create graph visual' and change its return type to an interface (IGraphVisualObject) implemented by each visual (bar, line). The graph class stores these in a list and calls a shared set-info method to configure position and label.

units.title: Old visuals overlap when not destroyed
units.detail: After switching from a raw GameObject list to visual-object wrappers, re-rendering the graph stacked new bars on top of old ones because cleanup only destroyed the old GameObject list. Fix: give the wrapper a cleanup method that destroys its own objects and call it during re-render.

units.title: Encapsulate per-element UI in the wrapper
units.detail: Move per-element setup such as button/tooltip wiring and RectTransform positioning into the visual object's set-info method. This guarantees the element is fully configured correctly every time its data changes, not just on creation.

units.title: Visual object links to previous element
units.detail: A line-graph dot stores a reference to the previous visual object so it can draw its connecting line. The connection is recomputed from the direction, distance, size delta, and rotation between the two dot positions.

units.title: Next point's connection needs notification
units.detail: Updating a dot fixes its own line to the previous dot but leaves the NEXT dot's line stale. Fix: the visual object fires a change event, and each object subscribed to its predecessor's event updates only its connection, avoiding an event cascade.

units.title: Common interface keeps graph code unchanged
units.detail: Because the main graph consumes only the IGraphVisualObject interface, adding a new visual type (bar, line, later ones) requires zero changes to the core show-graph code. Interface-based rendering isolates visual-specific logic.

units.title: Cache last render params for partial re-render
units.detail: Store the value list, dot settings, max visible amount, and axis-label functions in member variables on every call. Then a separate function can re-render the graph with only a single parameter changed, e.g. swap visual type or nudge max-visible amount.

units.title: Single-parameter setters wrap cached render
units.detail: Expose small functions like SetGraphVisual(visualType) and IncreaseVisibleAmount() that call the main show function with cached values plus their one change. This keeps buttons trivial and the display logic centralized.

units.title: Swap axis label formatting per currency
units.detail: The Y-axis label is produced by a delegate-like function, so changing display just means passing a different formatter: dollar (value + '$', rounded) versus euro (value / 1.18f + '€', rounded). The label-setting function receives the formatter as a parameter.

units.title: Update one value via stored visual list
units.detail: With each data point wrapped in a visual object, updating a single index is just: access visuals[index] and call its set-info method with freshly computed position and label. No object creation or list rebuild needed.

units.title: Bar exceeds graph borders after value spike
units.detail: Updating a single value without recomputing the Y min/max lets bars escape the graph bounds. Fix: recalculate Y scale from the full value list on update and rescale every visual when the scale changes.

units.title: Return multiple values with out parameters
units.detail: Use out parameters (e.g. CalculateYScale(out float yMin, out float yMax)) to return both bounds from one function, keeping the calculation in a single place instead of duplicated member-variable bookkeeping.

units.title: Axis labels stale after rescale
units.detail: After the Y scale changes, existing axis labels kept old numbers because they were instantiated once and only stored in a generic cleanup list. Fix: keep a dedicated list of label RectTransforms and recompute each label's text during the rescale.

units.title: Only re-render all when scale changes
units.detail: Compare Y bounds before and after the value change; if unchanged, update only the single modified point. If changed, re-render everything and the labels. This avoids wasteful full refreshes when the scale is stable.

units.title: Auto-size tooltip from preferred text size
units.detail: Size a tooltip's background using Text.preferredWidth/preferredHeight plus a fixed padding, then apply that to the background RectTransform. The tooltip always exactly fits whatever text it shows.

units.title: UI draw order follows hierarchy, tooltip hidden
units.detail: UI sorting order is determined by hierarchy position, so bars created after the tooltip render on top of it. Fix: call SetAsLastSibling on the tooltip whenever it is shown so it always draws last (on top).

units.title: Static instance for global UI access
units.detail: Visual objects need to trigger the tooltip without holding a reference to the graph window. Pattern: keep a private static instance of the window, expose static ShowTooltip/HideTooltip wrappers, and call those from element mouse-over/out handlers.

units.title: Data log class decoupled from UI
units.detail: Keep the displayed data in a separate data-log class (list of values, one index per month) and fire events when data changes. The graph window subscribes to those events so the graph updates itself without the data source knowing about UI.

units.title: Full re-render on size change, single update otherwise
units.detail: When a data point's value changes, update just the last value via the visual wrapper; when the data list size changes (new month), call the full show-graph re-render since axis count has changed. Only re-render as much as necessary.

units.title: Prefab the graph for multi-window reuse
units.detail: Convert the graph's transform hierarchy into a prefab and drop it into multiple windows with different sizes. Making the tooltip non-static and graph functions public lets several windows each maintain their own independent graph instance.

units.title: Custom tilemap vs built-in Unity Tilemap
units.detail: Use Unity's built-in Tilemap when you need a simple sprite-in-grid; build a custom one on a generic grid when you want one data class powering both logic and visuals, or to learn how it works underneath.

units.title: Grid cells hold custom objects with sprite enum
units.detail: The grid stores a custom object (with a sprite-type enum: none/ground/path/dirt) instead of an int. A set-sprite function fires a value-changed event so the visual mesh regenerates on any change.

units.title: Skip drawing with zero-size quads
units.detail: For tile types with no sprite, set the quad size to Vector3.zero so the four vertices occupy no space and render nothing. This keeps mesh generation simple while avoiding wasted GPU draw work versus a full custom mesh.

units.title: Sprite atlas via pixel UV mapped to normalized
units.detail: Expose a serializable struct in the editor with a sprite-type and pixel coordinates (lower-left and upper-right corners), then at Awake convert pixels to normalized UV using the material's main texture width/height and store in a dictionary keyed by sprite type.

units.title: Nested objects need [Serializable] for JSON
units.detail: When the main save object contains an array of other save objects, the nested class must be marked [Serializable] or JSON serialization will produce empty data. The root save object doesn't need it.

units.title: Save grid as array of per-cell objects
units.detail: Iterate all grid cells, have each cell produce a save object (sprite type plus coordinates), collect them into an array (JSON-friendly), and wrap in a root save object. Load reverses it: read the root, apply each cell's saved sprite to the grid cell at its X/Y.

units.title: OnLoaded event refreshes the visual
units.detail: After loading, fire an OnLoaded event on the tilemap so the visual component subscribed to it regenerates its mesh. Reusing the same update method keeps the load path identical to the value-changed path.

units.title: Industry trend: big opportunities in small games
units.detail: Recent hits (Schedule One, Repo, Mega Bomb) plus 64% of small studios (10-49 employees) report shifting to smaller, more manageable projects. Small games are the one space AAA cannot compete on, leaving it to indie developers.

units.title: Solo dev timeline: short prototypes, small games
units.detail: For solo or very small teams: prototype in ~2 weeks and scrap it if the idea fails, then commit 6 months to 1 year on the one that works. Don't spend 1-3 months on prototypes the way larger studios report doing.

units.title: Use AI for back-end work, not player-facing
units.detail: Studios are using LLMs prudently: coding assistance, writing/planning, market research, NPC behavior. For solo devs the top use case is brainstorming — two heads (one AI) beat one. Only 5% of studios use no AI at all.

units.title: Genre success depends on team size
units.detail: Idle/clicker and building/automation rank low in broad-appeal surveys yet are excellent for 1-5 person teams; RPG and narrative games are extremely hard for solo devs but great for AAA. Pick genre based on your team size and platform, not the aggregate chart.

units.title: Diversify revenue with IP and partnerships
units.detail: 82% of studios diversify via collaborations and bundles (Vampire Survivors x Castlevania), and 32% reuse a successful IP across genres (SteamWorld Dig -> Heist -> Build). Even small indies can bundle with a similarly-sized game to lift both.

units.title: Steam Deck audience keeps growing
units.detail: Steam Deck sold 1 million units in Q1 2026 alone. If a game can reasonably support gamepad controls, test it on Steam Deck because that player base is now significant.

units.title: DOTS moved to preview, learn it now
units.detail: Unity 2022.2 graduates DOTS from experimental to preview with mostly fixed 1.0 syntax, plus DOTS physics and Netcode for Entities. Not yet for shipping projects, but stable enough to start learning so the syntax is ready when production lands in LTS.

units.title: Unity's full multiplayer tool stack
units.detail: Netcode for GameObjects (plus Netcode for Entities) handles multiplayer logic; Lobby and Relay connect players through firewalls; Game Server Hosting (formerly Multiplay) and Matchmaker provide dedicated servers. All integrate via SDKs and now need no manual Unity contact.

units.title: Fullscreen shader node for post-processing
units.detail: URP's fullscreen master node removes the nasty hacks previously needed for screen-space effects in Shader Graph and enables custom post-processing attached to a volume. HDRP also gained a water system, cloud layers, and volumetric clouds.

units.title: Per-object physics contact layers
units.detail: Collision filtering previously was controlled only via the per-layer Collision Matrix; 2022.2 adds specifying contact layers per object, giving much finer control over which objects collide without global layer configuration.

units.title: UI Toolkit recommended for editor tools
units.detail: UI Toolkit is now the officially recommended way to build editor windows and tools; all standard property drawers use it. Runtime UI still favors uGUI until UI Toolkit reaches parity next year.

units.title: DOTS complements GameObjects
units.detail: DOTS/ECS does not replace GameObjects; the hybrid workflow of attaching an entity to each GameObject and running ECS systems for hot paths yields the best results. Use GameObjects where they make sense and entities where they make sense.

units.title: Data-oriented state saves make replays easy
units.detail: Because ECS is data-oriented, the entire game state can be saved and played back easily. Record inputs during playtesting, then replay the exact demo file to reproduce and fix bugs.

units.title: Kinematic character controller for full control
units.detail: A kinematic character controller (not rigidbody physics) cleanly handles touching physics objects, hinges, moving platforms, rotating objects, slopes, steps, gears, and jump pads. Add contextual animations like leaning on steep slopes.

units.title: Reuse your own tools and assets
units.detail: The sample game was built by reusing a free third-person starter asset, a photon module, and a water shader from a previous demo. Reusing proven internal assets accelerates prototyping and validates your toolset in production.

units.title: Realistic real-time graphics on consumer hardware
units.detail: Impressive demos can run in real time (4K 30fps) on a high-end desktop (i7 + RTX class GPU), not a render farm. Even vanilla HDRP plus ray-traced/screen-space AO, shadows, and reflections can deliver CG-quality characters; hair is the hardest part.

units.title: Integer division silently truncates
units.detail: In C#, dividing one int by another gives an int: 3 / 10 equals 0, not 0.3. Always be aware of the data types involved and cast to float when you need fractional results.

units.title: Separate game logic from UI visuals
units.detail: Structure a level system so XP/level logic lives independently from the animated experience bar, then feed the UI from the logic. Separating logic from visuals keeps the animated moving bar clean and testable.

units.title: Pluggable damage popup effect
units.detail: Implement damage popups as a reusable effect with animated scale, movement, and alpha, plus a distinct visual variant for critical hits. Package it so it can be plugged into any game with minimal wiring.

units.title: Same input toggles throw and recall
units.detail: A projectile mechanic like a shield can use one input to both throw and recall: while in flight the same button returns it. Give the projectile physics so it bounces off walls and hits multiple targets.

units.title: DOTS is ECS plus Job System plus Burst
units.detail: Unity DOTS is composed of the Entity Component System, the Job System, and the Burst compiler, and was positioned as the main way to work in Unity in the future.

units.title: Level gating by equipment
units.detail: A complete level system uses different XP amounts per level, fires level-up events, and gates equipment on player level so the player unlocks better gear as they progress.

units.title: Function timer for delayed actions
units.detail: A small timer utility that triggers an action after a set time is invaluable for quickly testing things. It works by storing a callback and counting down over Update.

units.title: Scene manager with loading screen
units.detail: Wrap level loading in a simple clean class that shows a proper animated loading screen instead of a static image, keeping scene transitions polished and reusable.

units.title: Step away to solve hard bugs
units.detail: For bugs or design problems you can't crack, take a walk with no headphones and just think. Problems that seem impossible often become crystal clear after some movement and fresh context.

units.title: Reverse engineer finished code to learn
units.detail: Read through finished, well-structured projects (assets, tools, and books like Code Complete) to internalize clean code practices. This is an excellent way to take your skills to the next level.

units.title: Boxleiter method estimates sales from reviews
units.detail: Roughly estimate revenue by multiplying public review count by a factor of 20-70 (median ~30-40). A game with 500 reviews likely sold about 20,000 copies.

units.title: Wishlists before release drive launches
units.detail: Strong wishlist counts before release lead to strong launches. A beginner-friendly path includes a free demo, and non-obvious marketing levers like translating a cute game to Japanese, using festivals, and networking.

units.title: Learn by reverse engineering a toolkit
units.detail: Buy a finished tool/asset with source code and read through it to learn how it works, then repurpose it for your own projects. Most asset store items ship source, making this a powerful learning method.

units.title: Scope creep and bad estimates are standard
units.detail: Even experienced developers routinely double their estimated release dates. Plan for slippage instead of treating overruns as failure.

units.title: Cozy genre games can succeed on Steam
units.detail: Cozy games with lush, gorgeous art (heavy greenery, relaxing vibe) have a strong audience. A dev who went from complete beginner to a successful cozy game launch demonstrates the genre's potential.

units.title: New input methods fragment XR development
units.detail: When a major headset introduces a completely different input method (eye tracking, no controllers), existing interaction toolkits and abstraction layers break. Developers may have to build one version for all headsets and another for that platform.

units.title: Eye-tracking as cursor is a great input idea
units.detail: Using the eyes as a cursor (look, then tap to select, flick to scroll) is an intuitive concept that should spread to mixed reality and VR as cameras point at the eyes.

units.title: Voice-to-text fails with accents
units.detail: Voice dictation usually only works well with perfect English; non-native accents frequently get misheard. Don't rely on voice input as the primary text entry method.

units.title: Price point blocks mainstream XR adoption
units.detail: However impressive the tech, a $3500 headset cannot make XR mainstream. Excitement about the technology doesn't translate to adoption when the cost is that high.

units.title: Battery life vs content length
units.detail: A 2-hour battery cannot finish most movies (which exceed two hours), so hardware limits can outpace the product vision. Check whether the headline use case actually fits within hardware constraints.

units.title: External display enables personalization
units.detail: A headset's outward-facing screen showing eyes can be modded with custom sprites for personal expression (like Watch Dogs 2). Fun as a toy, but it won't change the product's core value much.

units.title: Engine licensing tiers compared
units.detail: Engine terms are very generous: Unity is free until $200k/year revenue, Godot is 100% free, Unreal is free until roughly $1M. A new entrant offers $20 flat with no royalties on exports.

units.title: A fork over an engine gives near-full access
units.detail: A user-friendly layer on top of an internal engine (e.g., S&box over Source 2) gives developers access to roughly 90%+ of the underlying engine without needing direct contact with the engine owners, plus standalone publishing on Steam royalty-free.

units.title: Free tools still need a revenue path
units.detail: When a well-funded dev opens their engine royalty-free, the key insight is giving newcomers a real path to build games without giving up revenue share. Evaluate any tool's license by what it costs you as you succeed.

units.title: First-game plan: scope, Steam page, demo
units.detail: A practical three-step plan for a first game: 1) build a small-scope project, 2) quickly set up a Steam coming-soon page, 3) publish a free demo during Steam Next Fest.

units.title: Keep demos live after festivals
units.detail: Leave your game demo up after the festival ends so YouTubers and reviewers have more time to find and play it, increasing your chances of coverage.

units.title: Game design lessons are universal
units.detail: Analyzing any single game's design reveals universal principles that transfer to your own games, so a public critique of one game is valuable to every developer, not just that game's maker.

units.title: Engines are just tools
units.detail: Visual quality comes from the developer, not the engine. Both Unity and Unreal can produce gorgeous or ugly games; the tool choice matters far less than how you use it.

units.title: Why Unity got a bad reputation
units.detail: Unity's 'bad games' reputation comes from the forced 'Made with Unity' splash screen on the free tier during the Steam Greenlight flood of beginner games, not from engine limits. The splash screen is now optional.

units.title: Lighting is the biggest visual lever
units.detail: Paying attention to lighting makes games look great: use adaptive probe volumes for near-baked but dynamic global illumination, ray tracing for top-end visuals, or screen-space global illumination for performance.

units.title: Bake lights with production-validated tools
units.detail: Light baking assets like Bakery produce gorgeous results and are validated in production (used by Call of Duty Mobile). Baking gives big visual gains on modest hardware.

units.title: Toon shaders for stylized games
units.detail: Anime/toon shaders (e.g., Arthoon) are great for stylized looks and are production-proven in the author's own game. Stylized shaders make a game stand out compared to flat default materials.

units.title: Pixel art favors hardcore genres
units.detail: Analysis of 6,400 pixel art games shows the big pixel-art winners are turn-based RPGs and difficult games, while cute/cozy games underperform. Pixel art suits a more serious, gamer-oriented audience.

units.title: Bad pixel art is easy to make, hard to avoid
units.detail: Marketing is visual and you must hook players in seconds; bad or inconsistent pixel art is a huge handicap. Good pixel art can be a real advantage (e.g., Cast and Chill's gorgeous pixel art drove its success).

units.title: Low poly assets mix well across packs
units.detail: For non-artists, a low-poly style with soft colors stays visually consistent even when you buy asset packs from different publishers, whereas 2D/pixel art from multiple sources rarely fits together.

units.title: What 500 reviews actually means
units.detail: Only ~5% of 6,400 pixel art games reached 500 reviews, but 500 reviews is a genuine hit: via the Boxleiter method (×30-40) that's roughly 20,000 copies sold, i.e., hundreds of thousands in revenue.

units.title: Avoid weak pixel-art genre combos
units.detail: Horror, visual novel, bullet hell, puzzle, and first-person are the worst performers in pixel art. Note that several (puzzle, bullet hell, visual novel) are already hard genres on Steam regardless of art style.

units.title: Players judge the final game, not the tools used
units.detail: Players care about whether a game is fun, not whether it was made with AI, purchased assets, or hand-built. A 93% positive review game with an AI disclosure shows disclosures don't scare players off.

units.title: Use AI for prototyping, replace before release
units.detail: AI-generated visuals, audio, and 3D are great for quickly prototyping a game that looks better than gray boxes, but hire proper artists or buy quality assets before the final release.

units.title: AI as a second head for solo devs
units.detail: Chat AI is excellent for brainstorming design problems: ask for 10 ideas, discard the 8 bad ones, and combine the 2 decent ones with your own thinking.

units.title: Bad AI art gets bad reviews regardless
units.detail: If AI art is visibly broken (e.g., characters with 10 fingers), players will dislike it—just as they would dislike badly drawn human art. Quality matters, not the tool's origin.

units.title: 'Launch broken, fix later' only works with a marketing budget
units.detail: Cyberpunk, No Man's Sky, and Cities Skylines recovered from bad launches only because everyone already knew the games and wanted them to succeed. Most indies get exactly one shot at impressing players.

units.title: Bad indie launch is nearly unrecoverable
units.detail: Without a massive marketing budget, launching broken or unfinished means no one will be waiting for your fixes. A Steam algorithm needs initial momentum you can only brute-force with big money.

units.title: Constant updates without an audience are screaming into the void
units.detail: One dev shipped a weekly update for 7 months of Early Access with zero sales impact because nobody knew or was waiting for the game. Updates only compound value if there are players following.

units.title: Make your launch the best it can be
units.detail: Don't count on recovering from a bad launch; polish before release. Still fix bugs and add feedback-driven updates afterward, but don't sink a year into one massive update if nobody can hear about it.

units.title: Early Access does not mean two launches
units.detail: If the Early Access launch does poorly, the full launch usually will too—an EA launch doesn't give you a second chance.

units.title: Use descriptive names, avoid diminutives
units.detail: Rename fields like 'text' to 'interactionStringTextMeshPro' and 'cam' to 'mainCamera'. Short names force your brain to decode meaning, wasting mental bandwidth. IDEs make rename refactoring trivial (Ctrl+R+R).

units.title: Always write explicit access modifiers
units.detail: Omitting an access modifier defaults to private in a class but public in an interface, forcing your brain to infer. Always write 'private'/'public' explicitly to keep code self-documenting.

units.title: Always add curly braces to if statements
units.detail: A one-line if without braces silently attaches only the first statement; a later 'Debug.Log' you think is inside the if is actually outside. Always use braces to make the block unambiguous.

units.title: Strings are brittle identifiers
units.detail: Using strings with GameObject.Find fails on invisible differences like a trailing space or lowercase L vs uppercase I that look identical. Never use strings as identifiers; use direct references.

units.title: Prefer direct references over Find by name
units.detail: Instead of GameObject.Find with a string name, expose a serialized field and drag the reference in the editor. It is immune to name typos and invisible whitespace.

units.title: Almost never use public fields
units.detail: Public fields allow any of a thousand classes to read/write them and corrupt state. Make fields private and expose to the editor only via [SerializeField], keeping them safe from the rest of the codebase.

units.title: Interaction target should be a typed object, not a string
units.detail: Model the thing you interact with as its own class (e.g., DoorObject) found via TryGetComponent instead of comparing tag strings. Put the interaction logic in an Interact() method on the object, and let the interaction system just call it.

units.title: Use null-conditional operator for optional components
units.detail: For components that may or may not exist (like animator or audioSource), use animator?.SetBool(...) and audioSource?.Play() instead of hard references, avoiding NullReferenceExceptions.

units.title: Const strings for unavoidable string APIs
units.detail: Unity APIs like Animator parameter names force you to use strings. Limit the damage by defining a private const string (e.g., 'open') and referencing the constant instead of scattering raw strings.

units.title: You are not your players
units.detail: After hundreds of hours of dev, the obvious-to-you is invisible to players. Never assume players share your familiarity; the average player misses mechanics you find trivial.

units.title: Playtest by watching real players
units.detail: The best playtesting is watching a player play—physically or via screen+face recordings—while staying silent. Coaching players mid-test hides problems, because 99.99% of real players won't have you there.

units.title: Tutorials must be almost too obvious
units.detail: If a mechanic is silently blocked (e.g., a machine stops because it's crowded), add bold messages and big warnings. Your tutorial needs to be nearly annoying in its obviousness to barely work.

units.title: Frustrated players cause refunds and negative reviews
units.detail: When mechanics are confusing or unexplained, players get frustrated, refund the game, and leave negative reviews. Smooth onboarding is a direct success lever, not a nice-to-have.

units.title: Test with hardcore and casual players alike
units.detail: Playtest with all kinds of players—from hardcore to casual—to tune the tutorial for the widest audience and maximize happy reviews.

units.title: Validate your game idea before production
units.detail: The biggest marketing mistake is building the game first and marketing second. Idea selection is where success is decided; a hook nobody wants makes marketing nearly impossible, while a wanted genre makes it easy.

units.title: The 5-second test for idea validation
units.detail: Post fake progress shots or GIFs of game ideas on social media; an idea that gets 10x the views/likes of your other 20-50 ideas is a strong signal to build. It's a compass, not a guarantee.

units.title: Pick a proven genre plus a unique twist
units.detail: Choose a genre with proven demand (incremental, clicker, job simulator) rather than crowded weak ones like 2D puzzle platformers. A pure clone fails—you need a readable twist.

units.title: Games must be readable in 3 seconds
units.detail: With attention spans at all-time lows, your game needs to hook players in a single GIF or screenshot instantly. The vision must sell itself before the player reads anything.

units.title: Int division truncates to int
units.detail: 25 / 100 with both as ints equals 0, not 0.25, because int/int yields an int. Cast at least one operand to float to get a real percentage, e.g. in health systems.

units.title: Cannot modify transform.position component directly
units.detail: transform.position is a property returning a copy, so transform.position.x = 5 won't compile. Construct a new Vector3 or read the position, modify, and reassign the whole value.

units.title: Input.mousePosition is screen space, not world space
units.detail: Instantiating at Input.mousePosition won't place an object under the cursor because it's pixel coordinates. In 2D use Camera.ScreenToWorldPoint; in 3D convert via a raycast against a floor.

units.title: Time.deltaTime makes movement frame-rate independent
units.detail: DeltaTime holds seconds since the last frame, so multiplying speed by it means the object moves a fixed distance per second regardless of FPS. Always use it in Update for consistent movement.

units.title: Action vs Func delegates
units.detail: Action<T> is a delegate returning void; Func<T,R> returns a value (Func<float> returns a float). Delegates let you store functions in variables for callbacks, weapon swapping, and async web responses.

units.title: PlayerPrefs lacks native bool support
units.detail: PlayerPrefs natively stores only string, int, and float—no bool. Store bools as an int/string 0 or 1 via a helper function. Use PlayerPrefs for preferences, not save files.

units.title: Nullable types make any type support null
units.detail: Structs can never be null, but appending ? (e.g., Color?) wraps them in a nullable with a HasValue flag. Use it to represent 'no value' instead of magic numbers like -1.

units.title: Ternary operator as if shorthand
units.detail: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse assigns different values from a condition (e.g., state = health > 0 ? "alive" : "dead"). Use sparingly—never sacrifice readability for compactness.

units.title: Cannot implicitly convert Transform to GameObject
units.detail: A Transform has a .gameObject property and a GameObject always has a .transform, but the types aren't interchangeable. Access target.gameObject explicitly instead of expecting implicit conversion.

units.title: Use Unix timestamps to dodge timezone pain
units.detail: Unix time is seconds since Jan 1 1970, a single value you can convert into any timezone. Use DateTimeOffset.Now.ToUnixTimeSeconds() for achievements, leaderboards, and mod creation times.

units.title: transform.forward setter for look-at rotation
units.detail: Calculating a direction to a target and assigning transform.forward rotates the object toward it—simpler than wrestling with quaternions. Works with .right and .up too (e.g., aligning to surface normals).

units.title: Value types are copied, reference types shared
units.detail: Color (and other structs) are value types: assigning to a SpriteRenderer copies it, so later changes to your variable don't affect the renderer. Understanding copy-vs-reference prevents infuriating bugs.

units.title: Namespaces organize code and avoid collisions
units.detail: Namespaces like UnityEngine.UI group related types and prevent name clashes (e.g., UnityEngine.Random vs System.Random). Use full type names to disambiguate, but don't create a namespace per class.

units.title: Modulo operator loops indices back to zero
units.detail: index = (index + 1) % list.Count wraps back to the start at the end, perfect for cycling lists and object pooling. Also useful for day/night cycles: time % dayLength loops the day.

units.title: MonoBehaviour is optional for non-component logic
units.detail: Only extend MonoBehaviour when the class must be attached to a GameObject or needs Start/Update called by Unity. Plain C# classes work for logic containers and allow constructors; manage their update calls manually.

units.title: ref vs out: modification vs assignment contract
units.detail: ref passes a reference you may modify but don't have to; out promises the parameter WILL be assigned before the function exits (compile error otherwise). Both return extra data from functions.

units.title: Structs can't be null unless made nullable
units.detail: Color, int, bool, Vector3 are value types and can never be null; append ? (Color?) to make them nullable, e.g., a nullable Vector3 target position that means 'no target'.

units.title: Normalize vectors for consistent movement
units.detail: Normalizing sets a vector's magnitude to 1 so an object moves at constant speed regardless of distance or direction. Skipping it makes diagonal movement faster and bullets/characters speed-vary.

units.title: A quad mesh needs 6 triangle indices
units.detail: A quad uses 4 vertices and 4 UVs, but the triangles array needs 6 values because each logical triangle requires 3 vertex indices. Mistaking 'two triangles' for an array size of 2 is a common error.

units.title: Orthographic size is half the vertical units
units.detail: Camera.orthographicSize equals half the visible vertical world units (a size of 70 shows -70 to +70). Horizontal span depends on aspect ratio; zoom by changing orthographic size.

units.title: Func<Vector3> for following moving targets
units.detail: Pass a delegate returning the target position instead of a fixed Vector3, so a camera or tutorial arrow follows moving objects (e.g., a moving dinky). Use lambdas like () => new Vector3(...).

units.title: Static variables survive scene loads
units.detail: Loading a scene does not reset static variables, so they're a simple way to pass data (score, coins, setup) between scenes. Note that disabling domain reload also persists statics between play sessions.

units.title: JSON for saving and loading
units.detail: Create a save object, serialize it to JSON, and write it to a text file—simple and human-editable. Don't fight players cheating single-player saves; for multiplayer never trust the client and keep authority on the server.

units.title: Profiler finds real performance bottlenecks
units.detail: Use the profiler (and deep profile) to see memory, garbage, and per-function timing instead of guessing what to optimize. Premature optimization is the root of all evil—measure first.

units.title: Input System equivalent of GetMouseButtonDown
units.detail: Mouse.current.leftButtonWasPressedThisFrame replaces Input.GetMouseButtonDown(0). The Input System is more complex but far more capable—e.g., gamepad support and virtual cursors.

units.title: Have as many classes as needed, no more
units.detail: There's no magic class count (one game had ~300 classes with a 1000-line player class). The goal is managing complexity: enough structure to find anything fast, but not so many tiny pieces it gets messy.

units.title: Unity is still heavily game-focused despite headlines
units.detail: Big splashy acquisitions (movies, ironSource ads) dominate news, but Unity constantly ships game-focused work: URP updates, DOTS, Netcode for GameObjects, UI Toolkit, free samples, and game dev courses.

units.title: Quiet package updates compound engine value
units.detail: Most engine improvements arrive as quiet package updates (2D animation burst boosts, sprite shape, DOTS progress) rather than headline features. Following package release notes reveals the real engine trajectory.

units.title: A good game does not sell itself
units.detail: High-quality games can still flop in the indie market without marketing. Quality is necessary but not sufficient; the same effort must go into building an audience before release.

units.title: Estimate sales from review count (Box Slider)
units.detail: Multiply the number of reviews by 20-70 depending on optimism to estimate copies sold (25 reviews x 40 = ~1000 sales). A quick heuristic for whether a game found an audience.

units.title: Gross revenue shrinks drastically before profit
units.detail: From gross revenue subtract ~10% refunds/chargebacks, Steam's 30% cut, then taxes (10-50%). A 25k gross can become ~11k net, and that is revenue, not profit, so costs still come out.

units.title: Put Steam page up ASAP to farm wishlists
units.detail: Wishlists are the #1 launch metric; aim for ~12 months of wishlist collection rather than 5. Post alpha/beta screenshots early, not only polished shots, to start gathering an audience.

units.title: Wishlists convert to ~20% first-week sales
units.detail: Game Discover Co data shows median first-week sales of about 0.2 x wishlists. A game launching with 1000 wishlists sells roughly 200 copies in week one, then the store algorithm buries it.

units.title: Steam visibility review buckets
units.detail: Below 10 reviews the score is invisible; 10-49 is weak; 50+ (ideally by day 1-3) is where you want to be; 500+ unlocks Overwhelmingly Positive. Actively encourage reviews to reach 50 ASAP.

units.title: Pre-make tons of GIFs and drip-post them
units.detail: If your game is visual, make GIFs in advance and release 3-5 per week on Twitter/Reddit/Imgur/TikTok. 12 months at 3/week = 156 chances at virality versus a handful of pre-launch posts.

units.title: Every game needs a strong hook
units.detail: A unique, compelling hook ('time moves when you move') makes people need to try the game. A merely well-made generic game won't stand out, no matter how polished it is.

units.title: Premium price requires a wishlist base
units.detail: $25 is a premium indie price; with few wishlists you only sell to impulse buyers, and $25 is far outside impulse range. Price lower or build awareness before charging premium.

units.title: Failed launches can still have a long tail
units.detail: A quality game can recover through regular Steam sales (weekly plus spring/summer/winter). As discounts hit 50%+ it can keep selling for months even after a poor launch.

units.title: Games need multi-domain expertise
units.detail: Making a good game requires programming, art, sound, music, game design, UI and UX simultaneously. Because games are complex across many domains, current AI can't replace developers; that would need near-AGI.

units.title: AI progress plateaus, it does not explode
units.detail: AI capability curves show massive gains followed by plateaus with minor improvements, not endless exponential growth. AGI may be much farther off than hype suggests; keep building skills regardless.

units.title: Interactive world state is AI's hard problem
units.detail: Generating text/images is easy to take for granted; keeping a consistent world state (objects persisting when you look away, actions affecting the world) is the next barrier for AI game generation.

units.title: Over-scoped projects end abandoned
units.detail: A solo dev spent 5 years on a huge survival game then quit for mental health. Overscoping is nearly universal: ambitious projects get restarted repeatedly and never reach a finished state.

units.title: Early Access pressure erodes mental health
units.detail: Players constantly ask for updates once a game is in Early Access. Daily update pressure plus years of weekly updates is stressful and compounds burnout the longer EA runs.

units.title: Always have a plan to the finish line
units.detail: Running in circles (changing maps/systems repeatedly) without a concrete path to release is a top failure mode. Know exactly what 'done' means and stick to the plan.

units.title: Beginners: build games in 3-6 months
units.detail: Make many small games instead of one giant one; you learn far more from each. Estimate what you could build in 6 months, then cut that scope in half twice.

units.title: Ship minimal complete state instead of quitting
units.detail: If a project stalls, don't discard the work: cut to a bare-minimum completion plan (one main quest, essential NPCs, no new systems) and finish in 1-2 months rather than abandoning it.

units.title: Perfectionism can kill your game
