units.detail: Waiting for a perfect masterpiece can cost years of development. Releasing a good-but-imperfect, fun experience beats releasing nothing; the 'perfect or nothing' mentality destroys projects.

units.title: Trim features to what supports the core
units.detail: When cutting scope, keep only what existing systems need: a single main quest, bare-minimum tutorial NPCs, no new mounts/pets/content. Scrap buggy multiplayer to make a solid single-player game.

units.title: Detect double-click via click time delta
units.detail: Record Time.time on each click; a second click arriving within a threshold (~0.2s) of the last counts as a double-click. Test currentTime - lastClickTime <= doubleClickTime.

units.title: Single vs double click = different actions
units.detail: Use one click for the primary action (move) and a double-click for a special action (dash), mapping one input source to two distinct behaviors.

units.title: Keep input code separate from player logic
units.detail: The input handler decides single vs double click, then calls the player's Move()/Dash() methods; the player never sees input details. This separation keeps both sides reusable and testable.

units.title: Download web data with request object + coroutine
units.detail: Create a web request for a URL, yield the async send call inside a coroutine, then check for network/HTTP errors before reading the returned text. Wrap in a using/dispose scope to avoid leaks.

units.title: Reusable static download wrapper with callbacks
units.detail: Wrap downloads in a static class exposing Get(url, onSuccess, onError) delegates. Since coroutines need a MonoBehaviour, keep a private static host object to run them from a static context.

units.title: External data keeps shipped content updatable
units.detail: By scraping a web page you control, a shipped game's content (e.g. workshop item lists) can change without publishing a new build — just edit the remote page.

units.title: Download textures and build sprites at runtime
units.detail: Use a texture-specific download function and construct a sprite from the returned Texture2D. The image never exists in the project files — it is fetched live from a URL.

units.title: ECS visibility needs RenderMesh and LocalToWorld
units.detail: In DOTS/ECS a visible sprite needs both a RenderMesh (mesh+material) and a LocalToWorld component; RenderMesh alone won't render. Translation/Rotation/Scale mirror the classic Transform.

units.title: ECS sprites don't auto-size like SpriteRenderer
units.detail: With ECS there is no automatic scaling from sprite bounds; the mesh must be created at the correct size or a scale component must be set per sprite.

units.title: GPU instancing breaks Sprite/Default shader
units.detail: Enabling GPU instancing on Unity's Sprite/Default shader makes sprites vanish; use Legacy Shaders/Transparent/Diffuse instead to get batching. Instanced sprites also go dark until ambient lighting is set to white.

units.title: Build a quad mesh through code
units.detail: A simple quad needs 4 vertices, 4 UVs and 6 triangle indices (two polygons). Define vertices/UVs in clockwise order and index triangles clockwise so the front face is visible.

units.title: Dynamic buffers store variable-size lists in ECS
units.detail: ECS components can only hold value types (no arrays/lists). Dynamic buffers hold a variable-size list of buffer elements, enabling things like one entity targeting many enemies.

units.title: Define buffer element struct and add buffer
units.detail: A buffer element implements IBufferElementData as a struct; EntityManager.AddBuffer returns a DynamicBuffer you add elements to. Access another entity's buffer via GetBufferFromEntity using the entity as an array index.

units.title: Set InternalBufferCapacity to avoid reallocations
units.detail: Growing a dynamic buffer past its capacity allocates new memory and copies elements — costly in DOTS. Declaring an InternalBufferCapacity reserves space so common sizes never reallocate.

units.title: Upgrade single-target to multi-target via buffer
units.detail: A system holding one target entity in a component can be extended to attack N enemies by swapping to a dynamic buffer of target entities and cycling the buffer in the attack system.

units.title: Auto-size tooltip background to text
units.detail: Set the background RectTransform sizeDelta from the text's rendered bounds (force a mesh update first), plus optional padding, so the box always matches the content exactly.

units.title: Mouse position vs canvas scale mismatch
units.detail: Input.mousePosition is in pixels but UI is scaled by the Canvas Scaler; divide the mouse position by the canvas RectTransform lossyScale, and anchor/pivot to lower-left so the origins match.

units.title: Clamp tooltip to stay on screen
units.detail: Before placing the tooltip, add its background width/height to the position; if it exceeds the canvas rect, push it back. This edge detection keeps the element fully visible at screen edges.

units.title: Delegate-driven dynamic tooltip content
units.detail: Show the tooltip with a Func<string> re-evaluated every frame so content such as skill cooldown timers or colored TMP text updates live without rebuilding the UI.

units.title: Unity handles every art style and genre
units.detail: E3 2021 shows Unity across realistic shooters (Escape from Tarkov), pixel-art 3D (Replaced), cartoony management sims (Two Point Campus), RTS, RPGs and more — the engine is not the limiter.

units.title: Realistic rendering is achievable in Unity
units.detail: Escape from Tarkov's realistic urban environments, dynamic lighting and firefights demonstrate Unity can reach high-end realistic visuals, not just stylized indie looks.

units.title: ECS + jobs run thousands of AI entities
units.detail: A full Marines-vs-zombies scene (spawning, targeting, animation, AI, combat) built in pure ECS runs hundreds of entities at 60-100 FPS with no per-unit MonoBehaviours.

units.title: Mesh-per-frame animation with precomputed cache
units.detail: Pre-calculate one mesh per animation frame (quads per body part) at startup and cache them; at runtime select the mesh for the current animation/frame/direction. This was the fastest tested approach.

units.title: Meshes can't be updated inside jobs
units.detail: Mesh is a reference type and the graphics API must run on the main thread, so mesh drawing and animation selection stays single-threaded and won't benefit from the job system.

units.title: Quadrant system limits target search
units.detail: Spatial partitioning buckets units by position into quadrants; a unit only searches nearby quadrants for targets instead of every entity. Essential when the map is huge, less so on small maps.

units.title: Action queue for ECS combat interactions
units.detail: Instead of entities mutating each other in parallel, the shooter enqueues an action into a native queue and a single main-thread system processes all damage afterward, avoiding race conditions.

units.title: Mix ECS and classic objects pragmatically
units.detail: Not everything needs ECS: visual effects such as blood, muzzle flashes and dead bodies can stay as normal game objects while units and AI run in ECS. Convert where the performance benefit matters.

units.title: Steam algorithms change; older marketing advice stale
units.detail: Game marketing meta changes quickly; strategies that worked in 2018-2020 won't necessarily work now. When consuming gamedev/marketing advice, always weigh the context and date it was created.

units.title: Start beginners with pre-designed clone projects
units.detail: Beginner gamedevs should remake games whose design is already done (Flappy Bird, Arkanoid, Snake) to focus purely on technical implementation, accumulating experience before designing unique games.

units.title: Players rarely recognize asset packs
units.detail: Players mostly don't care what assets a game uses, even recognizable ones like Synty packs; they just want fun games. Don't avoid asset packs fearing players will notice.

units.title: Building tools is a valid gamedev path
units.detail: Making tools for other developers can earn more than making games. Tool development is an equally viable career path as game development.

units.title: Rapid prototype genre hits in under a week
units.detail: Shop-simulator prototypes (shelves, pricing, checkout, customers) can be built in under a week using a reusable toolkit of utilities, useful for validating a hot genre quickly.

units.title: The Door Problem: game design complexity
units.detail: A seemingly trivial game design question (how does a door work) has a billion valid answers, illustrating how hard game design really is. Every design question hides enormous complexity.

units.title: Reusable base movement class enables fast expansion
units.detail: Clean reusable code (a base position/movement handler) lets you add new unit types like workers to a tiny RTS game by duplicating the base and adding role-specific state machines, rather than rewriting movement.

units.title: Finite state machine for worker AI
units.detail: Model worker behavior as states (idle, moving to resource, gathering, moving to storage) driven by a switch on state in Update; transitions trigger based on distance-to-target checks.

units.title: Data wrapper class decouples transforms
units.detail: Wrap resource nodes in a lightweight class holding a transform reference and exposing a GetPosition() accessor so logic code doesn't deal with Unity transforms directly, keeping logic separate and testable.

units.title: Distance threshold before acting on target
units.detail: When moving toward a target, check Vector3.Distance to the target and only switch to the gather/interact state once within a small threshold (e.g., 5 units); otherwise keep setting the movement target.

units.title: Spend-only-if-affordable resource pool
units.detail: Implement a resource pool with AddGold() and TrySpendGold(): the spend function only deducts and returns true if enough gold exists, otherwise returns false—prevents negative balances and lets UI react.

units.title: Build queue with tick-based construction
units.detail: Queue unit construction and progress a counter on a periodic tick event; when tick count exceeds max, spawn the unit. Expose normalized progress for UI bars and helper functions for queue state.

units.title: Perception distance filtering for units
units.detail: Filter which targets units acquire by max distance: friendly units search infinitely, while enemies only acquire opponents within a small radius—creates localized aggression and keeps units on their own side until approached.

units.title: DOTS = ECS + Job System + Burst
units.detail: Unity DOTS is composed of the Entity Component System (entities package), the Job System, and Burst; entity graphics rendering requires URP/HDRP with Forward+ rendering, not built-in pipeline.

units.title: ECS components hold data, systems act
units.detail: Components (IComponentData structs) are pure data containers; systems (ISystem structs for unmanaged, SystemBase classes for managed types) are what actually modify component data each update.

units.title: ECS speed comes from memory layout
units.detail: DOTS performance is mostly about memory management: structs stored contiguously and cache-friendly. Using structs vs classes is foundational knowledge for DOTS because copies vs references behave differently.

units.title: Authoring component + Baker pattern
units.detail: To attach an ECS component in-editor, create a MonoBehaviour authoring component exposing fields, plus a nested Baker class extending baker that reads authoring values and calls AddComponent with GetEntity using TransformUsageFlags.

units.title: Systems run on main thread unless you write jobs
units.detail: Making a system (ISystem or SystemBase) does NOT make it multithreaded; all systems run on the main thread. Actual parallelism requires writing proper jobs with Burst.

units.title: Disabling domain reload persists static data
units.detail: When you disable domain reload for DOTS (recommended for source-gen speed), static fields and events are not reset between play sessions—data persists across play mode runs. Be extra careful with statics in DOTS.

units.title: Explicit read/write refs enable job parallelism
units.detail: Mark query params explicitly as ref rw or ref ro (never omit): multiple jobs can run concurrently reading the same data, but only one job can write at a time. Omitting makes an implicit copy hurting performance.

units.title: Prefer ISystem, default to Burst jobs
units.detail: By default write ISystem (struct) over SystemBase since it supports Burst for unmanaged types; use SystemBase only when you specifically need managed types. Prefer DOTS for cases, don't go all-or-nothing.

units.title: Single-file ECS requires matching filename
units.detail: If you combine component, authoring, and baker in one file, the filename must match the MonoBehaviour authoring class name; Unity requires the script filename to match the MonoBehaviour class, not the component.

units.title: Cinemachine brain + virtual cameras
units.detail: Cinemachine works on top of normal cameras: a Brain component sits on the main camera and processes data from multiple Virtual Cameras (follow/look-at targets) to produce the final shot, with no code needed.

units.title: Dead zone and soft zone camera framing
units.detail: Virtual camera aim has a dead zone where the camera won't move at all, a soft zone where it eases to track, and an outer edge where tracking becomes instant—great for platformer/demo framing without code.

units.title: Priority-based camera switching with interpolation
units.detail: With multiple virtual cameras, the one with highest priority is active and the Brain smoothly interpolates position/FOV between cameras; lowering priority smoothly transitions back—useful for cutscenes and zooms.

units.title: Swap follow/look-at targets at runtime
units.detail: Even with no-code setup, you can programmatically swap a virtual camera's follow and look-at targets at runtime (e.g., point at a cube while still following the character) for dynamic framing.

units.title: Value types default, reference types null
units.detail: Value types (int, float, bool, structs) default to zero/false and can never be null, so uninitialized ints are 0—that's why F-cost math with an uninitialized H-cost doesn't error. Reference types default to null and throw NullReferenceException.

units.title: Suffix collection vars with type name
units.detail: Name list/array variables with the plural of their type appended (e.g., gridPositionList) so collections are instantly distinguishable from single values at a glance, avoiding subtle misreads during debugging.

units.title: Consistency beats any naming convention
units.detail: Naming rules are personal—yours aren't inherently better than another's as long as you are consistent. Choose rules that work for you and follow them consistently, refining over time.

units.title: Prefer explicit types over var
units.detail: Avoid var (especially on function return values) because it forces readers to hunt for the type, harming readability. Code is written once but read many times; keep it explicit. Acceptable when the type is visible on the right side.

units.title: JSON is human-readable by design
units.detail: JSON is intentionally not encrypted and easily editable—that's a feature. For single-player games don't fight player cheating in save files; for multiplayer never trust the client regardless of file format.

units.title: Matchmaker queues, pools, and rules
units.detail: Unity Matchmaker uses queues (ticket types like ranked/casual), pools (grouping tickets, with filters like platform=value), and rules for matching. Rules define match definition, teams, player count, and per-rule conditions.

units.title: Relaxation tiers for matchmaking patience
units.detail: Define range relaxations that loosen match criteria over time: e.g., start seeking 4 players, after 10s accept 3, after 15s accept 2, after 20s accept 1—keeps players from waiting forever and fills lobbies progressively.

units.title: Skill-based matching with difference rule
units.detail: Implement skill matchmaking as a rule comparing player skill data with a max difference (e.g., 200); add a relaxation that disables the rule after a timeout so matches still form when no close-skill opponent exists.

units.title: Poll ticket state, never trust initial create
units.detail: Creating a matchmaking ticket only registers it; you must poll ticket status (about once per second to avoid rate limits) and check for assigned/multiplay assignment states, then read IP/port and start the client.

units.title: Backfill needs a separate ticket flow
units.detail: Client-side matchmaking alone only creates new servers; to let late players join existing lobbies you must, on the server, create/approve a backfill ticket periodically, update it when player lists change, and delete it when the game stops accepting players.

units.title: Difficulty enum with spawn-count thresholds
units.detail: Drive difficulty progression by number of level parts spawned: map thresholds to an enum (easy/medium/hard/impossible), return difficulty from a dedicated function, and switch on it to pick the pool to spawn from.

units.title: Dedicated difficulty function over inline ifs
units.detail: Extract difficulty calculation into its own function returning an enum instead of stacking ifs in the spawn logic; keeps spawn code clean and thresholds centralized and tweakable.

units.title: Testing prefab override field
units.detail: Add a serialized 'testing platform' field: if set, the generator always spawns it (with a debug log) so you can rapidly iterate on a single level part in isolation before releasing it to the random pool.

units.title: Score combines coins and distance
units.detail: Compute final endless-runner score as coins collected plus level parts spawned (distance proxy), then write name/score to a persistent high-score table supporting save/load.

units.title: Endless runner: spawn at end-position marker
units.detail: Each level part prefab contains an 'end position' child transform marking where the next part connects; the generator instantiates a random part at the last end position and reads its end position for the next spawn.

units.title: Connect parts at end markers, not hardcoded offsets
units.detail: Avoid hardcoded spawn offsets in code; place an end-position marker inside each part in the editor so parts can vary in length/height and still stitch together infinitely—just apply changes to the prefab.

units.title: Spawn more when player nears map end
units.detail: In Update, measure distance from player to the last end position; when within a threshold, spawn another random part and preload several parts on start so the map always extends ahead of the player.

units.title: Reuse same parts with different difficulty
units.detail: The same hand-built level parts can be reused across difficulty tiers—swap which parts are in the active list per level or difficulty to create easy vs hard runs without new content.

units.title: Field-of-view detection: distance, angle, raycast
units.detail: Detect a player in a view cone by checking three conditions in order: distance within view distance, angle to player less than half the total FOV (Vector3.Angle vs aim direction), and a raycast with no obstruction between enemy and player.

units.title: Compare angle to HALF the FOV
units.detail: Vector3.Angle returns the angle from the center aim direction, so the player is 'inside' only when that angle is less than FOV/2, not the full FOV value—a classic off-by-2x detection bug.

units.title: Clean classes make effects reusable
units.detail: Because the FOV class had no references to the player, attaching it to enemies instead required only wiring origin and aim direction—clean, decoupled code makes effects trivially reusable across entities.

units.title: Serialize FOV per enemy for variety
units.detail: Expose FOV angle and view distance as serialized fields per enemy and feed them into the shared FOV component at instantiation, so different enemies have different detection stats from the same code.

units.title: Raycast check makes walls block sight
units.detail: Add a Physics2D raycast along the direction to the player; only count as detected if the ray hits the player object, so walls occlude vision and stealth gameplay works.

units.title: Steam's 30% covers massive audience access
units.detail: A game sold directly on an unknown site may move ~10 copies in a week vs ~1,000 on Steam. 30% buys access to a huge accumulated player base and ecosystem—compare percentage-of-big-number vs 100%-of-tiny-number.

units.title: Time/money tradeoff in game costs
units.detail: Creating anything costs either your time or your money; you must always spend one—decide consciously which one you invest in a given project.

units.title: Decouple systems with events
units.detail: Use C# events so one object decides when an action happens (guest added to queue) and another decides what to do (building reacts). No direct references between systems needed, keeping code clean and testable.

units.title: Invoke event only if subscribed
units.detail: Guard every event invocation with a null check for subscribers before raising it, passing EventArgs.Empty. This is the standard C# event invocation pattern.

units.title: Action callback on movement completion
units.detail: Pass an Action as a callback parameter to a move function so code runs exactly when the object arrives at its destination, instead of polling every frame for arrival.

units.title: Periodic timer helper for spawning
units.detail: Use a periodic utility function that triggers an action at a fixed interval to automate repeated behavior (adding guests every second), replacing manual button clicks.

units.title: List index maps to slot position
units.detail: Keep a guest list and position list with matching indices so list element zero always equals the front slot. Compare the arriving entity against the first list entry to detect 'reached front'.

units.title: Fire event only at queue front
units.detail: After repositioning all entities, trigger the 'arrived at front' event only when the entity that reached its position is the first in the list, so others don't fire it.

units.title: CPU vs GPU particle systems
units.detail: Unity has two particle systems: built-in (CPU) and VFX Graph (GPU). GPU can simulate millions of particles; CPU is better when particles must interact with dynamic physics.

units.title: CPU-to-GPU transfer is expensive
units.detail: Transferring data from CPU to GPU is computationally costly, so GPU particle systems handle physics-based particle interactions poorly. Use the CPU built-in particle system for dynamic physics instead.

units.title: VFX Graph needs compute shaders
units.detail: VFX Graph requires compute shader support. Most mobile devices support it, but very old/cheap devices may not, forcing you to fall back to the built-in CPU particle system.

units.title: VFX Graph structure: contexts and blocks
units.detail: VFX Graph is node-based with contexts (spawn, init, update, output) containing blocks (spawn rate, velocity, output). Data flows left to right; large graphs are understandable if read piece by piece.

units.title: Learn VFX from sample graphs
units.detail: Import official VFX Graph learning templates and samples, then open their graphs to inspect node logic. Graphs are effectively open source, making them excellent for learning by reverse-engineering.

units.title: Humanoid rig enables animation retargeting
units.detail: Unity's humanoid rig type allows any humanoid animation to be used on any humanoid character. This is what makes Mixamo animations compatible with custom characters.

units.title: Remote Config: tweak values without rebuild
units.detail: Unity Remote Config lets you define variables in-game and change them remotely without uploading a new build. Great for fast iteration on gameplay parameters.

units.title: Game overrides for segmented A/B testing
units.detail: Game Overrides targets specific player types with different values, enabling A/B tests to analyze which configuration performs best before rolling out.

units.title: Cloud Save for persistence and cross-platform
units.detail: Cloud Save stores player data (not just save files) in the cloud, and combined with an authentication system it becomes cross-platform across devices.

units.title: Relay connects players without port config
units.detail: Unity Relay lets players connect peer-to-peer without opening ports or dealing with firewalls/NAT. Use with Lobby to group players and Netcode for gameplay networking.

units.title: Old Unity projects break from renames
units.detail: Unity renames namespaces and pipelines over time (e.g. LWRP became URP). Old project files fail with errors like 'type or namespace not found' that require updating the package or namespace.

units.title: Ship complete projects for learners
units.detail: Delivering full project files with all packages and dependencies pre-installed lets beginners open, hit play, and see everything work, instead of hitting upgrade errors they can't fix.

units.title: Separate movement base from logic layer
units.detail: Split a car into a base script that handles spline following and a logic script that decides whether to call MoveForward. The logic layer listens to traffic rules and only moves when allowed.

units.title: Detect cars ahead with raycast
units.detail: Fire a raycast forward each frame; if it hits a vehicle, stop or slow down, otherwise keep moving. This simple check prevents rear-ending without complex physics.

units.title: Use boxcast not raycast for boxes
units.detail: A thin raycast misses vehicles offset to the side. For box-shaped cars, refactor to a box cast that sweeps the vehicle's full shape so corner cases are still detected.

units.title: Scale stopping distance with speed
units.detail: Compute stopping distance based on current velocity: slow cars need a tiny gap, fast cars need a large one. This makes traffic smoothly slow down without collisions.

units.title: Detect rules via collider and component
units.detail: Give stop signs and traffic lights a trigger collider and a script. Cars raycast forward, check for the component on what they hit, and react (stop timer, wait, resume).

units.title: Traffic light as a state machine
units.detail: Implement lights with a simple state machine (green/yellow/red) plus a state timer that counts down and transitions between states, rather than hard-coded timing logic.

units.title: Track intersection occupancy
units.detail: Have the intersection script track which car is currently inside and reject new entrants while occupied. Cars only enter when empty, preventing gridlock at intersections.

units.title: Stagger traffic lights with offsets
units.detail: Expose timing and offset fields on each traffic light and configure them per-light so only one direction is green at a time, keeping intersection flow conflict-free.

units.title: Keypad decoupled from door via functions
units.detail: Build a reusable access system where doors/chests expose simple open/close functions and a separate keypad script validates codes and calls them. Swap or combine keypads freely.

units.title: Learn by doing challenges
units.detail: Practice labs with objectives and self-built scenes teach better than passive tutorials. Attempt problems first, check solutions after, and treat partial progress as success.

units.title: VR mocap makes custom animations fast
units.detail: With a VR headset and a tool like Animotive, a solo developer can record high-quality custom mocap animations in about a minute, replacing the hunt through giant animation packs.

units.title: Record multi-character animations solo
units.detail: Place multiple characters in a scene, embody and record each one in sequence. The tool syncs them to the exact same timeline, producing perfectly timed multi-character animations alone.

units.title: VR mocap limits: upper body only
units.detail: Headset-only mocap controls the upper body, so you can't record backflips or kicks. Legs and elbow IK are still good enough for most custom animations in testing.

units.title: Export mocap as FBX to use anywhere
units.detail: Recorded mocap exports as a standard FBX that loads into Blender or Unity as a normal humanoid animation, usable with any humanoid character immediately.

units.title: Study engine vendor ebooks and samples
units.detail: Unity publishes free, highly detailed ebooks (100+ pages) and downloadable samples on URP, UI Toolkit, VFX, optimization, and more. Read them for depth that YouTube tutorials rarely cover.

units.title: Project Auditor flags improvement spots
units.detail: Unity's Project Auditor runs a checklist over your whole project and surfaces places where you could improve, paired with an ebook explaining profiling and optimization.

units.title: Input Manager being deprecated
units.detail: Unity 6.3 warns that the old Input Manager will be deprecated in the future. Plan to migrate to the new Input System for future-proof projects.

units.title: AI Navigation 2.0 major rewrite
units.detail: Unity's AI Navigation package jumped to 2.0, a massive difference from before. For simple pathfinding games, the built-in navmesh is usually all you need.

units.title: Learn compute shaders for GPU work
units.detail: Compute shaders look like magic initially but become understandable with practice. Use official tutorials and examples to get started for high-performance GPU computation.

units.title: Addressables control memory and load times
units.detail: Addressables give you fine control over when assets load and unload, keeping memory low and games feeling snappy. Addressables can also load remotely from your own or any server.

units.title: Cloud Content Delivery CDN distribution
units.detail: Unity's Cloud Content Delivery is an official CDN for shipping content updates (used with or without Addressables), letting you push assets without a full build.

units.title: Dynamic Resolution stabilizes frame rate
units.detail: Dynamically lower or raise rendering resolution as gameplay gets hectic, keeping frame rate stable during heavy scenes instead of letting it dip.

units.title: Build Size Report finds space hogs
units.detail: Unity's Build Size Report identifies which assets are consuming how much of your build's space, so you can easily find and fix bloat.

units.title: Unity Authentication unlocks gaming services
units.detail: Unity Authentication is the required starting point for interacting with Unity Gaming Services, enabling persistent player identity.

units.title: Localization boosts store algorithms
units.detail: Unity's Localization package makes localizing games easy and is strongly recommended, since localization massively increases your chances of success with store algorithms.

units.title: Decal projector projects onto geometry
units.detail: A decal projector projects a sprite onto any world geometry rather than a flat quad, making it ideal for blood splatter, bullet holes, graffiti, and dirt in levels.

units.title: Cloud Diagnostics auto-captures player bugs
units.detail: Enable cloud diagnostics so bug reports from players appear on your dashboard automatically, without relying on manual reports. It's a must-have for shipping bug-free games.

units.title: User reporting with screenshots and save data
units.detail: Add a manual player-reporting tool that includes a screenshot plus data like the player's save file, giving you the context needed to reproduce and fix issues.

units.title: TextMesh Pro fallback fonts for missing glyphs
units.detail: If the current font lacks a glyph for a character, TextMesh Pro falls back to a different font you designate. Configure fallback fonts so special characters never render as empty boxes.

units.title: Frame Debugger analyzes render pipeline
units.detail: The Frame Debugger steps through each render pass to show exactly how your game is being drawn, revealing what you can optimize about the rendering process.

units.title: Floating point precision loss with large coordinates
units.detail: When an object is very far from the world origin, float precision causes geometry to wobble and deform. The problem appears when a scene simultaneously needs super large and super tiny numbers (e.g. a planet and tiny people on it).

units.title: Floating origin point and its limit
units.detail: The floating origin technique teleports objects back toward the origin so nothing drifts too far, but it only works when the whole world moves together. It fails when two objects must be genuinely far apart, like a spaceship and distant planets.

units.title: Dynamic scaling fakes huge distances
units.detail: Keep the player locked at coordinate zero and move all other objects only a little, simulating growing distance by scaling the object smaller instead of moving it further away. From the player's view it looks identical, but no huge coordinates are ever created, avoiding precision loss.

units.title: Two solutions cover most floating point cases
units.detail: Use a floating origin for most problems, and when you need multiple objects genuinely far apart, combine small position changes with scale changes to fake the distance. This keeps both distance and scale in representable ranges.

units.title: Unity DOTS for extreme performance
units.detail: Unity DOTS (Data-Oriented Tech Stack) can yield over 200x faster code and was credited for the massive scale of Iion. It is an intermediate-to-advanced tool; beginners should stick with regular GameObjects.

units.title: Real-time hair physics as holy grail
units.detail: Real-time hair physics is extremely expensive, which is why characters usually have short or tied-up hair. Its imperfect look reveals the shot is running in real time rather than pre-rendered, and likely only a few characters get the expensive system.

units.title: Interior mapping fakes building interiors
units.detail: Interior mapping makes windows appear to show rooms using a shaded shader trick with no real geometry. It makes buildings feel lived in while staying cheap.

units.title: Blend shapes for unique NPC bodies
units.detail: Varying NPC body shapes come from blend shapes with sliders that modify body parts. Combining them across NPCs yields an illusion of uniqueness.

units.title: What makes water look realistic
units.detail: Good water combines layered foam, ripples, stacked noise maps, and refraction that changes underwater. These tiny details stack to make the water convincing.

units.title: Detecting ray-traced reflections via occlusion
units.detail: If an object reflected in a puddle is blocked from the camera by another object, screen-space reflections could not show it. Seeing the occluded object in the reflection implies real ray-traced reflections.

units.title: Volumetric lighting and fog
units.detail: Volumetric fog has actual volume and reacts to light differently per region, unlike a flat billboard. High-quality indirect lighting on interiors hints at baked GI or adaptive probe volumes rather than expensive Lumen-style GI given the frame budget.

units.title: Modding shares logic across features
units.detail: Car modding, weapon attachments, and character customization are the same underlying system: attach/replace parts and update visuals and stats. Build it once and reuse the pattern.

units.title: Simple destruction from sliced mesh
units.detail: Destruction is easy: pre-slice a mesh into parts and spawn a prefab of fragments when the object hits the floor or takes the breaking trigger. The drama comes from timing the break.

units.title: Depth of field guides player focus
units.detail: Keeping the subject sharp while blurring the background naturally pulls the eye to the important object. Some games even change focus dynamically as objects approach the camera.

units.title: Tiny details compound into quality
units.detail: Heat distortion on exhausts, leaves blowing when a car flips, subtle post effects — individually trivial, but together they make a scene feel excellent. Density of small details is the takeaway.

units.title: Design the game before building it
units.detail: Write out the full game design first — mechanics, goals, hazards, win condition — so you know exactly what to implement. Both course games started from a clear written design before any work began.

units.title: Visual scripting node graph concepts
units.detail: Visual scripting teaches the same concepts as code: super units (reusable sub-graphs), groups for organization, events for inter-script communication, and state machines for AI. These map directly onto functions, comments, messaging, and FSM design.

units.title: Reuse systems across projects
units.detail: Import the same options menu, sound/music scripts, and health system between games rather than rebuilding them. Reusing components speeds development and enforces consistency.

units.title: Build basics then polish stages
units.detail: Establish a complete feature set first (movement, combat, pickups, goals), then iterate polish: particles, shaders, trails, animations, camera shake. Separating core from polish keeps scope under control.

units.title: Early access sets a high bar
units.detail: Modern players expect early access games to be polished and feature-rich; a 30-hour playthrough with no bugs and smooth late-game performance is the competition. If you go early access, ship a complete experience.

units.title: Better inventory split UX
units.detail: Right-click and drag left/right to pick a split amount beats pop-up windows or spamming +/- buttons. Tiny input improvements disproportionately improve game feel; a slider would be better than repeat-button mashing.

units.title: Day/night cycle adds believability
units.detail: A simulated day/night cycle — even not astronomically accurate — makes a world feel much more believable for little effort. The star's sky position driving day and night reinforces the simulation.

units.title: Lock camera while queuing actions
units.detail: Holding shift to queue actions freezes the camera so the player can click precisely. If the camera keeps moving, actions become frustrating to target.

units.title: Show version/build info for bug reports
units.detail: Displaying the version and build in a corner lets you diagnose bugs shown in YouTube videos and know whether they are already fixed. Valuable for early access or always-in-development games.

units.title: Remind players of mechanics in the UI
units.detail: Rather than teaching commands once in a tutorial, quietly show action reminders in a screen corner. Players forget mechanics; subtle persistent reminders prevent frustration.

units.title: Nail the first minutes of the game
units.detail: Most players never finish games, so the start must be great or they'll never see the good content later. If a required window forces the player to stare at it constantly, that's a design problem.

units.title: Always give player action feedback
units.detail: If a building is out of range, the player should know before acting. Change a bounding box color or add a subtle indicator rather than silently failing, since silent failures feel broken.

units.title: Free demolish encourages experimentation
units.detail: Costly demolition pushes careful first-time building; free demolition encourages reworking and optimizing production lines. Choose based on which behavior you want: careful thinking vs experimentation.

units.title: Confirm permanent consequences
units.detail: Dismantling a building with items can lose items forever with no confirmation, and auto-zoom on build mode causes misclicks. For actions with serious permanent consequences, always ask for confirmation.

units.title: Detect and teach wrong input habits
units.detail: If testers intuitively try the wrong button (e.g. right mouse to rotate instead of middle), listen for the incorrect input and show a popup teaching the correct one. Adapt to players rather than fighting them.

units.title: More mechanics are not better
units.detail: Adding a subpar combat system to a great building game could pull players away from what they enjoy and make the game worse. Only add features that genuinely improve the game; prototype first.

units.title: Game feel comes from layered feedback
units.detail: Punchy combat is animation timing plus screen shake, punchy sound effects, and particle effects on hits. Even the first punch in a game can feel powerful if these layers are right.

units.title: Hook the player in the first minutes
units.detail: The very first actions should be instantly satisfying for a quick dopamine hit, because the first minutes determine whether the player stays. Polishing the opening is one of the highest-leverage design investments.

units.title: Sound design sells every action
units.detail: Powerful sound effects make actions feel impactful; swapping in weak sounds can make a game feel ~90% less satisfying. Sound is often undervalued but is central to game feel.

units.title: Avoid carpal tunnel input design
units.detail: Requiring a click per swing works for combat engagement but is tedious for gathering. Hold-to-repeat or hold-and-aim systems avoid repetitive-click strain while still feeling active.

units.title: Show progress while gathering
units.detail: If a tree needs ten hits with no visual feedback, players doubt they are doing it right. Add a health bar, progress bar, or visual change so the player always knows their input worked.

units.title: Think from the player's viewpoint
units.detail: When a pickup message shows only the amount gained and not the running total, players can't tell if they hit a crafting target. Guess what the player is thinking mid-game and add the missing info (e.g. total in parentheses).

units.title: Add physics to the world
units.detail: Felling a tree into real falling logs that can crush bushes or enemies makes gathering satisfying and grounded. Physics on interactions adds life with minimal cost.

units.title: Map tagging suits procedural worlds
units.detail: Letting players pin and label any map position with icons and text is cheap to add and pairs perfectly with procedurally generated worlds, where each player's world is unique and needs personal orientation.

units.title: Death penalty is a design slider
units.detail: Drop-items-on-death adds stakes, but the designer chooses intensity: keep items recoverable, grant a temporary buff after death, and cap skill loss to soften it. Balance stakes against frustration to fit your target audience.

units.title: Rest buff drives return-to-base
units.detail: A timed rest buff that gives large stamina/health regen when sheltered encourages players to periodically return to base. It builds attachment to home without punishment.

units.title: Bonuses feel better than punishments
units.detail: Frame mechanics positively: a buff while rested rather than a debuff while unrested. Presenting mechanics as rewards instead of penalties makes the game feel better.

units.title: Make near-death escapes satisfying
units.detail: A player who accidentally enters a high-level area and dies instantly feels cheated. Letting the enemy pull back or leave them at 1 HP on first encounter makes them feel they barely escaped — more satisfying than instant death.

units.title: Boxcast for forgiving grappling hook aim
units.detail: Instead of a projectile, fire a boxcast along the aim direction with a generous box size so players don't need perfect aim; attach to the closest valid edge. Edges are usually manually marked by level designers rather than auto-detected, then the hook animates to the target and the player pulls.

units.title: Swing rope control and auto-disconnect
units.detail: During a swing, let the player shorten/lengthen the rope to convert momentum into height. Disconnect automatically when the hook falls behind the player relative to their facing/velocity, plus momentum and swing progress, to make release feel seamless.

units.title: Takedowns are simple logic plus animation
units.detail: A spherecast around the player finds enemies in range and in front; a button prompt triggers a pre-made animation. All the complexity is in the animation, not the logic.

units.title: Sprite sheets fake complex effects
units.detail: Sandstorms and explosions are usually sprite sheet frames on large camera-facing quads, not real simulations. Interpolated frames on billboard quads look massive and complex at a fraction of the cost.

units.title: Vehicle drop uses cursor raycast and ghost
units.detail: Select the vehicle on a device UI, raycast to the cursor position for the drop point, show a ghost preview like a building system, then spawn and let it fall.

units.title: World space canvas for floating icons
units.detail: A world space canvas keeps UI elements pinned above positions in the world. For crowded 128-player scenes, only show names above squad mates and reveal other names when the player looks directly at them (via boxcast near the cursor).

units.title: Interactable via interface keeps code modular
units.detail: Implement an IInteractable interface instead of hardcoding object types; the player just detects anything within range that implements the interface and triggers its interact action. This makes interaction code work with any object.

units.title: Minimap areas via mask textures
units.detail: Build the map from a base texture plus mask textures; tint each masked region a color to show enemy/neutral/friendly control. This pixel-mask technique is reusable for any segmented map display.

units.title: Wingsuit activation via velocity threshold
units.detail: Monitor the downward Y velocity; once it passes a threshold, switch animation state and allow wingsuit/parachute deployment. Keep the weapon in normal pose until the velocity triggers the fall state.

units.title: Tornado pulls: power vs control
units.detail: Pulling players toward a tornado is just applying force to rigidbodies, but it must not remove player control. Use a hard cutoff: normal movement outside, complete loss of control only when deep inside.

units.title: Two ways to summon a mount
units.detail: Most games spawn the horse off-screen near the player and have it run over; Elden Ring just makes it appear because magic fits the theme. The approach depends on your game's theme and style — multiple valid solutions exist for the same problem.

units.title: Hold-attack with minimum charge time
units.detail: While the button is held, count up a timer with time.time; on release, if above a minimum charge threshold, trigger the attack. Simple and effective for charge attacks.

units.title: Hit detection: spherecast vs boxcast
units.detail: A spherecast around the player detects all damageable objects in an area (arcade feel); a boxcast shaped exactly like the sword gives extreme accuracy. Pick based on how realistic your combat is.

units.title: Knockback makes combat feel responsive
units.detail: A small knockback on a blocked or landed hit makes the game feel far more alive than a hit with no reaction. Tiny physical responses massively improve game feel.

units.title: Dodge invincibility frames (i-frames)
units.detail: Set an invulnerability timer on dodge; while active, ignore damage. This is more forgiving than real-time dodging, doesn't require perfect hitboxes, and lets players dodge through attacks — satisfying and better for player control.

units.title: Attack cancel with queued input window
units.detail: To keep heavy attacks meaningful yet allow perfect follow-ups, queue the dodge input during an attack but only execute if it was pressed within ~100ms of the window. This prevents both canned inputs and requiring gun-like reflexes.

units.title: Traversal as level design shortcut
units.detail: In open worlds, jump pads replace the shortcut network of linear Souls levels, letting players make large vertical/horizontal jumps once unlocked. Design traversal mechanics around the world's structure.

units.title: Sneak detection via FOV angle test
units.detail: Compute the angle between the enemy's facing and the player; if outside the enemy's FOV (e.g. -45 to +45), the player is not detected. Optionally add a hearing mechanic via spherecast radius around the enemy.

units.title: Ghost shader via fresnel glow
units.detail: Add a fresnel-based glow to mesh edges plus a blue tint to make summoned allies look ghostly. Cheap and looks convincing for phantoms.

units.title: Cinemachine map camera
units.detail: Set a fixed downward camera, a quad with the map texture, and make a Cinemachine body follow a cursor game object so the camera pans to the mouse. Simple way to build a scrollable 3D map.

units.title: Cursor magnet snapping
units.detail: Nudge the cursor onto nearby interactive icons when it approaches, making selection forgiving — especially valuable for controller play where precision is lower than a mouse.

units.title: Guiding wind as navigation
units.detail: Replace GPS arrows with a wind particle system that flows toward the objective, optionally following the pathfinding route so it never crosses walls. A shared wind vector also drives grass vertex shaders, making the world feel reactive to the navigation.

units.title: Spawn NPCs off-screen near the player
units.detail: For summoned entities that don't persist, pick a random position just outside the camera's view near the player and spawn there, then have it approach. This avoids pop-in for many open-world spawns.

units.title: Detection UI grows with fill masks
units.detail: Raycast to ensure the target isn't occluded, then increase a fill amount each frame; a shaped mask plus rotating white fill renders the expanding detection wedge. Reusable for health, timers, and meters.

units.title: Diegetic guidance instead of UI markers
units.detail: Guiding the player with in-world particles, a fox companion, or environmental cues feels immersive versus pinned UI markers. The fox uses simple logic: spawn near max distance from its shrine, move faster than the player, stop and wait if the player falls behind.

units.title: Perfect dodge reward: vignette, bloom, slow-mo
units.detail: On a well-timed dodge, increase vignette and bloom intensity via a volume post-processing profile and slow time by lowering Time.timeScale. Rewards layered on a simple timer make the dodge feel cinematic.

units.title: Simplify arc attacks to boxcasts
units.detail: Rather than simulating a perfect arc shape, use a boxcast covering the arc area so all enemies within take damage. The player sees the same result and development stays simple — games are about smoke and mirrors.

units.title: Fake thrown objects with particles
units.detail: Throw a particle that follows the visual trajectory, then spawn the actual noise object at the destination instead of simulating a physical throw. Same result, avoids expensive physics and mid-air activation bugs.

units.title: Zoom in by switching FOV
units.detail: Zooming the camera is just switching to a narrower field of view. With Cinemachine, use a second camera with a narrow FOV and raise its priority to smoothly interpolate the zoom.

units.title: Chain assassinations via second spherecast
units.detail: After the first assassination, spherecast around that target to find a second enemy; if found, auto-pan the camera (slow-mo + bloom + vignette) and offer a chain prompt. Keep limits so surrounded players can't one-shot everything.

units.title: Black-and-white post effect
units.detail: A black-and-white look is simply setting color saturation to zero. Combined with shallow depth of field, it creates dramatic state changes (e.g. smoke bomb / inventory) cheaply.

units.title: Fear mechanics make players feel powerful
units.detail: High reputation makes enemies flee or collapse in fear for an easy kill. Gate it with cooldowns (e.g. only every so often) so it feels great without trivializing the game.

units.title: 3D-feel UI via rotated world canvases
units.detail: Rotate world-space canvases slightly toward the screen center at each corner so bars tilt inward, giving the HUD a subtle 3D perspective while underlying elements stay rotation-free and easy to work with.

units.title: Context-sensitive actions via boxcast
units.detail: A boxcast around the player finds interactables and tests distance to swap the action prompt (e.g. web strike to takedown as you close in). Simple range checks drive UI prompts.

units.title: Perch targeting picks closest to screen center
units.detail: Boxcast from the camera through the screen center to find objects tagged as perchable, then pick the one closest to the screen center. A basic UI element marks the selected target.

units.title: Detection cone with vertical limit
units.detail: Flatten Y to zero, test horizontal angle against the enemy FOV, check distance, then verify the Y difference so players above or below aren't spotted. Prevents cheap exploits and enables vertical stealth approaches.

units.title: Games fake reality instead of simulating it
units.detail: An enemy noticing a downed ally is often faked with an invisible marker: the enemy's detection cone checks the marker and enters an alert state. It's far cheaper than simulating full awareness and yields the same experience — the goal is player experience, not simulation accuracy.

units.title: Gadget throw faked with particle trajectory
units.detail: Spawn a particle that follows the throw arc, then spawn the real gadget at the landing point. Avoids physics cost and mid-air activation bugs while looking identical.

units.title: Cinemachine priority camera animation
units.detail: Create a second virtual camera with an orbiting animation; raise its priority to trigger a special cinematic shot, then lower it when the animation ends and the brain interpolates back. Extremely easy scripted camera work.

units.title: Quicktime events are timed button checks
units.detail: A QTE is a countdown timer that listens for the correct input within a window; failing triggers a designed outcome (e.g. missing the web). Masks with scaling circles visualize the remaining time.

units.title: Spidey-sense delivers readable warnings
units.detail: Before an off-screen attack, a particle burst and a directional indicator pointing at the attacker plus a dodge button prompt give the player three easily readable cues in one moment. Compose multiple UI layers for clarity.

units.title: Hold-to-charge interactables add risk/reward
units.detail: Making environment interactions require holding a button adds a risk/reward timer and prevents accidental triggers. Stronger effects demand longer hold times.

units.title: Add difficulty via attack immunity
units.detail: Instead of inflating health, make bosses invulnerable to specific attack types to force new strategies. Players must change approach rather than grind numbers.

units.title: Enemy stamina gates attacks
units.detail: Give enemies a stamina bar that regenerates; heavy attacks drain it and hitting zero triggers a stun state where the player can freely attack. Creates combat windows.

units.title: Chase sequences are scripted rubber-banding
units.detail: Chases are scripted animations where the target can never be caught: speed adjusts to the player's speed, and you can slow it further if the player falls behind. The designer controls how many mistakes to allow; at the end, lock speed so the player can catch up.

units.title: Constrain boss arena to script the fight
units.detail: Locking the player to a few positions (via invisible walls) lets you play an animation sequence exactly as designed while keeping normal attack/dodge mechanics. Reduced player freedom enables scripted encounters.

units.title: Mash and joystick QTE variants
units.detail: Mash QTEs use a radial-fill ring mask that fills as you press; joystick QTEs add random noise to cursor position each frame so the player constantly corrects toward the target. Both are easy to build and up to the designer on failure stakes.

units.title: Interpolate between virtual cameras
units.detail: Place virtual cameras for each view (free camera, car camera, hacked camera) and switch the active one; Cinemachine automatically interpolates between them for smooth transitions.

units.title: World-space UI with parallax
units.detail: Build in-world UI like phone call elements using a world-space canvas or game objects; giving layers slightly different depths creates natural parallax as the camera moves.

units.title: 3D minimap from sprites to meshes
units.detail: Convert a 2D minimap to 3D by swapping the camera from orthographic to perspective and replacing sprite icons with basic meshes (e.g. a helicopter model). Faded edges can be done with a mask or shader.

units.title: Two-range interaction detection
units.detail: Use a large boxcast to show icons above objects and a smaller one to allow actual interaction. As the camera rotates, icons appear first, then interaction becomes possible when closer.

units.title: Spotlight aims at a target object
units.detail: Make a spotlight look at a target game object and move that target around the ground to sweep the light. Simple scripted spotlight behavior.

units.title: Search AI patrols last seen position
units.detail: Store the last position where the enemy saw the player, then send them to a random point within a radius of that spot. Simple and believable search behavior.

units.title: Occlusion makes entities untrackable
units.detail: The helicopter raycasts to detect the player; when the player drives under a tunnel the raycast hits the overpass and fails, so the helicopter loses them. Line-of-sight checks naturally create hiding gameplay.

units.title: Detection modifiers for hiding states
units.detail: Hidden states like car-off or being behind transparent fences apply negative modifiers to the enemy detection radius; combine all modifiers and compare to distance to decide detection. Flexible and tunable stealth math.

units.title: Hacking cameras via camera switching and overlays
units.detail: Interacting with a camera activates a second virtual camera to interpolate to its view, and a renderer feature applies an overlay to all materials during the hacked state. Return to normal when done.

units.title: NPC reactions via spherecast
units.detail: Spherecast around the player to find objects that can react, then choose behavior by action type (phone smashed vs gunshot produces different reactions). One generic system drives all bystander responses.

units.title: Emissive textures fake building lights
units.detail: Real per-window lighting needs thousands of lights, so instead use emissive textures; toggling emission or setting emissive colors to black flips buildings bright to dark in one pass.

units.title: Surrender vs shoot-to-kill boolean
units.detail: Track whether the player used deadly force; cops arrest if non-lethal, shoot to kill if lethal. Simple state stored as a boolean changes police behavior meaningfully.

units.title: Time.timeScale drives slow-motion
units.detail: Setting Time.timeScale to e.g. 0.1 runs everything using deltaTime at 10% speed, an easy universal slow-motion. Keep it at 1 for normal speed; anything using unscaled time won't be affected.

units.title: Companion app as alternate play mode
units.detail: A phone/tablet companion can join the same game session with its own UI and abilities (e.g. hacking a helicopter) to help the main player. Multi-device play adds novel cooperative depth.

units.title: Noise objects call listener interface
units.detail: A noise origin does a spherecast to find objects that implement a listen interface; those within range move to investigate the sound position. Decoupled, any object can react to any sound.

units.title: Game markets are big enough for many launches
units.detail: Steam has ~400M users and consoles ~200M more. Even a massive title takes millions of players, not everyone, so your game's potential audience still exists in the other genres and segments.

units.title: Only reschedule when genres overlap directly
units.detail: The one scenario worth moving your release date is when your game offers a very similar experience to the incoming hit (e.g. another Metroidvania vs Hollow Knight). For every other genre, audience overlap is so small it does not matter.

units.title: Launching next to a AAA can actually help
units.detail: Chill Aquarium launched the same day as Starfield and made ~$1.5M. Because most indies dodged that date, fewer games competed for the 'Popular Upcoming' slots, giving the survivor far more Steam visibility. Avoiding a big launch can cost you this.

units.title: Mega hits leave hundreds of millions untouched
units.detail: Hollow Knight sold 15M copies, yet ~585M players never played it and likely won't care about the sequel. Those non-overlapping millions are the audience your different-genre game can reach.

units.title: 150k wishlists is enough to succeed on Steam
units.detail: Roughly 150-160k wishlists is already more than big enough for Steam success. The chain is: get onto Popular Upcoming / New & Trending, let the algorithm find the non-overlapping players who want your game, and sales compound.

units.title: Hybrid DOTS: jobs only for hot paths
units.detail: Keep normal gameplay objects as MonoBehaviours and move only performance-critical operations (like pathfinding) into DOTS systems with Burst jobs. This gives speed where it matters without rewriting the whole game.

units.title: Trigger DOTS logic by adding components
units.detail: From a MonoBehaviour, add a component (e.g. a path-finding-params struct with start/end) to the linked entity; the DOTS system reacts, writes results to another component/buffer, and the game object reads them back with GetComponentData.

units.title: Write back mutated entity components
units.detail: When you read a component off an entity, modify it, and expect it to persist, you must call SetComponentData to write the new value back; otherwise the change is discarded.

units.title: Mix low-poly packs to build any game
units.detail: Asset packs in a consistent low-poly style (e.g. Quaternius packs) can be freely mixed across packs and used for nearly any genre: RTS, farming, racing, town sims, shooters. Buy a style family, not one game.

units.title: Visual assets speed up prototyping
units.detail: Having nice pre-made visual assets turns gray-box prototypes into presentable games quickly, which helps motivation and communication; asset quality is a force multiplier for programmer-led teams.

units.title: Build mini-games to learn game dev
units.detail: Using asset packs to build many small prototype mini-games is one of the fastest ways to learn; each mini-game applies familiar systems (attachment, driving, grid placement) to new contexts.

units.title: Prefer pre-made gesture and touch tools
units.detail: For swipes, drags, zoom, rotate, tap and gesture handling, use a mature ready-made asset rather than hand-rolling your own input code; it also usually includes shape/image recognition and on-screen touch buttons.

units.title: Resize textures at runtime for save files
units.detail: A texture resize tool can compress screenshots at runtime, so you can store a small compressed thumbnail in save files rather than a full-resolution image.

units.title: Ready-made systems for dialogs and quests
units.detail: Pre-built assets handle common mechanics: a dialogue system manages character communication, a quest machine tracks goals/rewards/logs, and a personality simulator models faction/mood reactions for RPGs.

units.title: ScriptableObjects define game data types
units.detail: Model building types, items, and quests as ScriptableObjects so one small system (grid placement, inventory, quest list) handles many content entries created in the editor without code changes.

units.title: Interface-based interaction system
units.detail: Raycast from the camera and look for objects implementing an IInteractable interface; show a prompt and start the interaction. The same system handles NPCs, statues, and pickups, and stays extensible.

units.title: Cheap semi-random AI for ambient life
units.detail: Give objects connected waypoints and let entities move to a random connected point repeatedly. It's a 'dumb' system but enough to make pedestrians and cars make a city feel alive without pathfinding.

units.title: Share one input method between player and AI
units.detail: A car controller exposes a function that receives inputs; both the player controller and AI controller call that same function. Movement logic lives in one place and AI reuse is trivial.

units.title: Simple core loops can be compelling
units.detail: A tight, simple loop (people park cars, you re-park them, deliver when they leave) is compelling enough to build a game around; nail the core loop before adding polish.

units.title: Data-oriented design: components vs systems
units.detail: ECS separates data from behavior: components only hold fields and implement IComponentData, systems act on that data, and an entity is just an instance of a component set. This differs from MonoBehaviour's data+behavior-in-one-object model.

units.title: Instantiate entities from an archetype
units.detail: Create an archetype (a fixed set of component types) and instantiate many entities at once by passing a NativeArray of entities to CreateEntity; dispose the NativeArray afterwards to avoid leaks.

units.title: Systems mutate matching entities via ForEach
units.detail: Extend ComponentSystem, implement OnUpdate, and use Entities.ForEach with ref parameters for components you want to modify. The lambda runs once per matching entity.

units.title: Sprite shader breaks with GPU instancing
units.detail: Unity's default sprite shader shows issues when GPU instancing is enabled, preventing batching of many entities. Using a legacy shader like transparent/diffuse lets thousands of entities batch and render.

units.title: Burst compiler gives massive ECS gains
units.detail: Enabling Burst on jobs can cut system time from ~50ms to ~3ms for 10k entities and keep 100k entities at 40fps. Combine ECS with Burst and the Job System for the full DOTS performance stack.

units.title: Entity rendering requires specific components
units.detail: To render an entity you need Translation, LocalToWorld, and a RenderMesh (a shared component holding mesh + material). Shared component data is set separately from regular component data.

units.title: HDRP vs URP target different hardware
units.detail: HDRP (high-definition render pipeline) targets high-end systems and consoles with maximum visuals; URP (universal) targets compatibility across every supported device. Choose based on your audience's hardware.

units.title: Physical cameras use real photography values
units.detail: HDRP cameras can simulate real-world physics: sensor type/size, ISO, shutter speed, lens focal length, and aperture shape. Great for realistic visuals and high-quality screenshots.

units.title: HDRP only supports 4x MSAA
units.detail: HDRP supports MSAA only in 4x mode and only for Forward rendering; you must enable it on the pipeline asset AND on the camera or global settings. Other AA (FXAA/TAA/SMAA) run as post-processing and can stack.

units.title: Volumes apply settings globally or locally
units.detail: Volumes can be global or local (collider-based) and carry post-processing plus non-post effects like fog, exposure, and ambient occlusion. Local volumes trigger effects only while inside the collider.

units.title: Dynamic resolution stabilizes framerate
units.detail: Set a min/max resolution percentage on the pipeline asset, enable dynamic resolution on the camera, and drive the scale from a script (e.g. target 60fps) to keep gameplay smooth on weaker devices.

units.title: Choose netcode by game scale
units.detail: Use Netcode for GameObjects for small-scale co-op games; use Netcode for Entities (DOTS-based) for very fast, complex multiplayer. Netcode for Entities can still be mixed into game-object-based games via linked entities.

units.title: Worlds exist but the connection does not
units.detail: Creating client/server worlds does not start a network connection. You must bootstrap it, e.g. subclass ClientServerBootstrap, override the world-name/initialize function, and set an AutoConnectPort.

units.title: Enable runInBackground for multiplayer
units.detail: If Application.runInBackground is false, the game freezes when the window loses focus, which makes multiplayer time out and disconnect. Always enable Run in Background for multiplayer games.

units.title: Send and consume RPCs
units.detail: Send an RPC by creating an entity with your custom RPC struct plus a SendRpcCommandRequest component. The receiver sees it with a ReceiveRpcCommandRequest and must destroy the entity after reading it (use an EntityCommandBuffer).

units.title: RPC direction and sender identification
units.detail: Clients send RPCs only to the server; the server can broadcast to all clients or target a specific one. The source connection (the entity holding NetworkId) identifies which client sent a message.

units.title: Multiplayer Play Mode beats slow builds
units.detail: Instead of iterating via client builds, install the Multiplayer Play Mode package to spawn multiple Unity editor instances and test multiplayer connections in seconds.

units.title: Server authority with client prediction
units.detail: Netcode for Entities is server-authoritative and syncs continuous data through ghosts; client-side prediction (enabled by default) keeps movement responsive even under simulated lag.

units.title: Unity AI assistant knows your project
units.detail: The Unity 6.2 assistant is trained on Unity docs and has full project context, so it answers project-specific questions (why a mechanic fails, what a script does) far better than generic chatbots.

units.title: Attach real errors when asking AI
units.detail: Paste the actual console error into the assistant as a reference; it can then correctly diagnose issues like a serialized field needing an inspector assignment instead of pointing at the code.

units.title: Assistant run commands edit your project
units.detail: The assistant can execute editor actions (place N lights, create a UI window) from natural-language prompts; it generates an IRunCommand you can inspect before running. Results depend heavily on prompt specificity.

units.title: Ask AI to write better image prompts
units.detail: For AI image generation, prompt an LLM to write a detailed prompt, or have it ask you clarifying questions first, then feed that prompt to the generator. A bare 'sword' prompt yields random results; a detailed one yields usable sprites.

units.title: Unity AI generators cover all asset types
units.detail: Unity 6.2 includes generators for sprites, textures, materials, sounds, and animations, each with selectable models (per style/task), prompt and negative prompt, option counts, and output dimensions.

units.title: Unity AI is a tool collection, not one tool
units.detail: Unity's AI is a broad set of tools (assistant plus generators for 3D models, animations, sprites, textures, audio) trained specifically on Unity gamedev. It can also be used purely for code/analysis with no AI-generated assets.

units.title: Assistant has three modes: Ask, Plan, Agent
units.detail: Ask returns text answers and makes zero project modifications. Plan generates a reviewable plan without executing. Agent actually executes changes on the project after you approve.

units.title: Feed the AI project context for better output
units.detail: Attach prefabs, scripts, assets, or your current selection to prompts so the AI has real context instead of guessing. Drag-and-drop beats copy-pasting code into a web window.

units.title: Annotate screenshots to pinpoint exact objects
units.detail: Capture a screenshot and highlight the specific object you want changed instead of describing it vaguely. The more explicit the pointer, the better the AI targets the right thing.

units.title: Screenshot capture may include your whole desktop
units.detail: The annotation screenshot grabs the entire desktop including the taskbar, so don't capture sensitive info like passwords. There is also an option to capture only the editor windows.

units.title: Project Overview gives whole-project context
units.detail: The assistant can analyze the entire project into a document it references for answers. Refresh this after major project changes so the AI's context stays current.

units.title: AI assistant is great for learning
units.detail: Ask mode gives digestible explanations with examples and code snippets, more approachable than dry docs. It also explains error messages by analyzing the console.

units.title: DOTS = ECS, Job System, Burst
units.detail: The Data-Oriented Technology Stack promises performance orders of magnitude better than GameObject workflows by combining the Entity Component System, job system, and Burst compiler.

units.title: Set up DOTS physics directly with components
units.detail: Instead of colliders use PhysicsShape (choose box/sphere/etc.) and instead of Rigidbody use PhysicsBody. Both workflows produce identical ECS components.

units.title: Restitution controls bounciness
units.detail: Setting restitution to 1 with max combine keeps all energy, making objects bounce forever. On classic colliders you use a PhysicsMaterial with bounciness=1 instead.

units.title: ECS only adds components that are needed
units.detail: Static bodies (like floors) omit the velocity component while dynamic ones include mass, velocity, damping. This keeps code fast by storing exactly what each entity needs.

units.title: Modify DOTS physics from a system
units.detail: Create a component system with Entities.ForEach over entities having PhysicsVelocity and modify its Linear field (e.g., to jump on input).

units.title: DOTS raycast through CollisionWorld
units.detail: Get BuildPhysicsWorld from the world, access its CollisionWorld, and call CastRay with a RaycastInput holding From, To, and a CollisionFilter (belongsTo/collidesWith/groupIndex). The hit carries an Entity reference.

units.title: Collision filter uses layer bitmasks
units.detail: ~0 (bitwise NOT of zero) sets all bits, meaning the ray belongs to and collides with all layers. Filtering overrides the bit masks.

units.title: Handle DOTS triggers with ITriggerEventsJob
units.detail: Implement ITriggerEventsJob; Execute receives a TriggerEvent with an EntityPair (A and B). Use ComponentDataFromEntity to check for and modify components like PhysicsVelocity, then schedule with Simulation and PhysicsWorld dependencies.

units.title: Unity Physics vs Havok share same components
units.detail: Both engines use identical components; you switch via a Simulation Type dropdown on the physics step component. Unity Physics is free, Havok is paid (currently free trial).

units.title: Gravity is configurable in physics step
units.detail: You can modify gravity direction/magnitude (e.g., invert it) on the physics step component to create floating or upside-down gameplay.

units.title: Job system makes multithreading easier
units.detail: The Job System handles thread creation and management; you only define structs implementing IJob with an Execute function, then schedule and complete them.

units.title: One job on one thread gives no speedup
units.detail: A single task takes the same time whether on main or worker thread. Real gains come from scheduling many jobs and then calling JobHandle.CompleteAll at the end.

units.title: IJobParallelFor runs one index at a time
units.detail: Execute receives an index so the job operates on array elements (NativeArray of positions etc.), letting multiple indices run concurrently across cores.

units.title: Jobs cannot touch main-thread data
units.detail: Jobs can't access transforms or Time.deltaTime; pass needed values in as job fields. Always dispose NativeArray/NativeList after use.

units.title: Burst compile attribute for massive speedup
units.detail: Adding [BurstCompile] above a job turns it into highly optimized native code. In the demo it dropped job time from 40ms to 4ms; combined 140ms to 4ms.

units.title: IJobParallelForTransform works on transforms
units.detail: A specialized parallel job receiving an index and TransformAccess; create a TransformAccessArray from your transforms, schedule with it, and positions update automatically after completion.

units.title: Schedule all jobs first, complete later
units.detail: Creating a job then completing before the next serializes work back to single-threaded. Batch all schedules into a list, then CompleteAll once.

units.title: Mix automation, colony building, and defense
units.detail: Dinky Guardians combines resource gathering, giving orders to workers, defense towers, a tech tree, and full automation leading to a rocket launch goal.

units.title: Ship a demo as an alpha vertical slice
units.detail: Get core mechanics working end-to-end first; accept less polish in a demo. It's a starting point for the full game rather than a finished product.

units.title: Gather community feedback on game design
units.detail: When systems are done but design isn't iterated, ask players targeted questions (difficulty, number of units/zombies/resources) and collect feedback via forms and comments.

units.title: Study official sample projects
units.detail: Unity's free sample projects show how the engine team uses their own tools and reveal features you may not know exist. Download and dissect them as case studies.

units.title: PSD importer splits character layers automatically
units.detail: Draw characters normally with separate layers and Unity auto-splits the PSB into a proper sprite sheet in the sprite editor, removing the need to pre-separate body parts.

units.title: Sprite Shapes make arbitrary shapes from textures
units.detail: Edit a spline over a base texture to create weird shapes (bridges, pillars) instead of authoring separate textures. Profiles control fill, edge sprites, offsets, and angle-based variants.

units.title: 2D bones and IK animate characters
units.detail: Bones with 2D IK target points auto-calculate the chain to reach a position; grabbing a pelvis moves the whole rig correctly. The skinning editor defines each bone's influence area.

units.title: Timeline drives cutscenes and cinematics
units.detail: Timeline sequences UI, camera, animation, audio, and object tracks; paired with Cinemachine virtual cameras it produces polished intros that trigger gameplay when finished.

units.title: 2D lights combine normal maps and render layers
units.detail: Freeform and spot 2D lights interact with sprite normal maps; targeting specific render layers lets some lights affect only characters while others only the background.

units.title: Shader Graph drives animated effects
units.detail: Simple shaders using the time node to shift offsets create moving smoke, waterfalls, and waving webs without particle systems. Effects are fully editable in the graph.

units.title: Simple UI tricks make polished bars
units.detail: Health bars are plain sliders, ability rings are images with radial 360 fill that you drive via fill amount, and a custom HDR material adds glow.

units.title: Turn-based grid combat core loop
