units.detail: Units sit on a grid with a move radius; each turn allows one movement and one attack, alternating between teams, with an option to skip the turn.

units.title: Validate move radius via pathfinding
units.detail: Compute the path from the unit to every position within a radius and mark positions valid only if path length stays within the max move distance. Recompute when the unit arrives.

units.title: Store units in grid objects for clicks
units.detail: Instead of colliders and raycasts (which need collider sizes to match grid cells), store the unit reference on the grid object under the mouse and check it directly.

units.title: State machine gates input per turn
units.detail: A simple enum state (Normal vs Waiting) blocks new input while the unit moves, resetting to Normal via the move callback before recomputing valid positions.

units.title: Track grid occupancy on every move
units.detail: When a unit moves, clear the unit from its old grid object and set it on the new one, or click-targeting and range logic go stale.

units.title: Validate attack range before attacking
units.detail: Check a distance function before allowing an attack and show feedback (popup) when out of range. Hit chance based on distance and flanking can add XCOM-like depth.

units.title: Reuse clean systems across projects
units.detail: The grid and pathfinding systems built in earlier videos were reused for combat, heatmaps, and building areas because they were written cleanly and generically.

units.title: Pan camera to active unit for polish
units.detail: Calling a camera-follow function whenever the turn changes keeps the player focused on the active character.

units.title: Grid map cuts world into addressable cells
units.detail: A simple class wrapping a 2D int array with width/height lets you read and write values per cell; foundations for heatmaps, pathfinding walkability, and building areas.

units.title: Convert between grid and world coordinates
units.detail: World position = (x, y) * cellSize + origin; grid coords = (world - origin) / cellSize. Store cellSize and origin in the constructor for flexible placement.

units.title: Ignore invalid grid values silently
units.detail: For out-of-range coordinates, return a default/ignore instead of throwing, which would crash gameplay. Invalid-value policy is a deliberate design decision.

units.title: Visualize grid with debug text and lines
units.detail: Create a world text object per cell showing its value (centered via half-cell offset) and Debug.DrawLine the quadrant edges; store text refs so they update on value changes.

units.title: Use out parameters to return multiple values
units.detail: getXY uses out int x, out int y to return a grid coordinate from a world position, avoiding struct/vector plumbing.

units.title: Fire an event when grid values change
units.detail: An OnGridValueChanged event lets reactive systems (like a heatmap mesh updating colors) listen instead of polling, keeping the base grid reusable.

units.title: Give each AI concern its own class
units.detail: Extracting guest queue logic into a dedicated AI class with one responsibility (existing only while the guest is in queue) made the code more robust and fixed bugs.

units.title: Assign queue positions on arrival, not join time
units.detail: Guests can arrive at the entrance out of order, so position must be assigned when they reach the entrance; otherwise a late arrival can claim a front spot.

units.title: Track state to know who to relocate
units.detail: States (going to entrance vs waiting in queue) let relocation logic move only guests already waiting, while guests still heading to the entrance keep going.

units.title: Swap queue positions on request
units.detail: When a guest requests a position, cycle the list and swap them ahead of anyone still moving to the entrance, then send them to their corrected index.

units.title: Named pipes link two app instances
units.detail: C# named pipes provide two-way communication between two running instances (e.g., a control window modifying a main game window), useful for moderation or debug data.

units.title: Server waits, client connects to a pipe
units.detail: Server: NamedPipeServerStream with WaitForConnection then read via StreamString. Client: NamedPipeClientStream connecting to '.' local, then writes and closes.

units.title: Use separate pipes for read and write
units.detail: A single bidirectional pipe can only read OR write at a time, so you need one pipe for reading and another for writing to stay ready for both.

units.title: Pipe calls block; run them on threads
units.detail: WaitForConnection and ReadString block execution until something arrives, so server/client logic must run on separate threads.

units.title: Thread safety with queues and locks
units.detail: Worker threads can't touch Unity objects; enqueue received messages into a queue guarded by locks and process them on the main thread.

units.title: NamedPipeServerStream missing in 64-bit builds
units.detail: Standalone 64-bit builds throw 'not implemented'; compiling the server as 32-bit (x86) with Mono fixes it. Client works fine as standard.

units.title: Encode pipe messages as JSON
units.detail: Wrap payloads in a command struct and serialize to JSON so structured commands pass cleanly between instances and decode reliably on the other side.

units.title: Unity cancels the runtime fee
units.detail: Unity completely dropped the per-install/sale runtime fee after last year's backlash, keeping two positives: no forced splash screen on free tier and revenue limit raised from $100k to $200k.

units.title: Unity moves to simpler per-seat pricing
units.detail: Instead of the complex runtime fee, Unity keeps the per-seat license model with standard price increases for Pro (devs over $200k) and Enterprise (over $25M).

units.title: Decide engine fit by analyzing the terms
units.detail: Read new license terms and judge against your actual revenue and user counts; for most indie games the thresholds would never apply, so nothing changes in practice.

units.title: Community backlash can force policy reversal
units.detail: A massive developer response and engine-switching trend forced Unity to reverse its runtime fee, showing that trust and terms matter as much as feature quality.

units.title: Developers are spoiled for engine choice
units.detail: Modern engines (Unity, Unreal, Godot, GameMaker) are all excellent with free tiers, so engines must actively earn your choice rather than winning by default.

units.title: No retroactive pricing changes
units.detail: Changing payment terms after release is scummy and burns trust. Scope new fees to future versions only (e.g. next LTS) so existing/published games are untouched.

units.title: Lock terms to a version
units.detail: Tie the Terms of Service to the specific engine version so developers can stay on an old LTS and keep the old terms indefinitely. Publishing TOS history on GitHub adds transparency.

units.title: Cap fees at % of revenue
units.detail: A revenue-percentage cap (e.g. 2.5%) bounds the worst case so the fee can never exceed what a game actually earned, unlike unbounded per-install charges.

units.title: Self-reported metrics build trust
units.detail: Let developers report their own usage numbers instead of a hidden vendor algorithm. Self-reporting means developers trust nothing from the vendor, which is a huge trust win.

units.title: Count engagements not installs
units.detail: Replace 'installs' with 'initial engagements': unique downloads for F2P, sales for premium. Exclude reinstalls, piracy copies, and refunds; one copy counts once.

units.title: Raise free tier threshold
units.detail: Doubling the free-tier revenue limit and removing the splash-screen upsell on the free plan are low-cost concessions that restore goodwill after a pricing backlash.

units.title: No telemetry by default
units.detail: Do not phone home unless a feature requires it (like cloud diagnostics/analytics). Opt-in data collection respects user privacy and avoids distrust.

units.title: Tint via white base + multiply
units.detail: Use a white texture as the base and multiply each pixel channel by a tint color. White areas take the exact tint while dark areas interpolate, giving natural shading.

units.title: Tint pixel array before merge
units.detail: When assembling a sprite from layered pixel arrays, apply the tint to the hair/beard color arrays before merging them onto the head texture so the final sprite is colored.

units.title: Randomize from color arrays
units.detail: Keep arrays of hair colors and pick one randomly at runtime, applying the same color to hair and beard, to cheaply multiply character variation.

units.title: Exclusive-perk sustainability model
units.detail: Keep educational content free and give supporters early access (one-week exclusive project files) instead of paywalling lessons, keeping value optional while staying sustainable.

units.title: Liquid from particles plus shader
units.detail: Simulate fluid as thousands of tiny spheres with a shader applied on top to make them read as liquid. Particles give cheap physics-driven fluid behavior.

units.title: One camera per liquid type
units.detail: When one shader must apply to all particles on screen, use a separate camera per liquid type and change a particle's layer to change its visual, enabling multiple fluids in one scene.

units.title: Scriptable object as type tag
units.detail: Store a scriptable object reference on each particle to identify its type, then handle reactions in collision listeners (e.g. lava + water converts both to stone).

units.title: Bubbling force improves reactions
units.detail: Add random upward force to lava so it churns and shifts, clearing space for more conversion reactions like turning stone — makes physics interactions more visually interesting.

units.title: Swap positions for density sorting
units.detail: On collision, if dense stone is above lighter lava, swap their positions so heavier material sinks — a simple way to fake density layering.

units.title: Pointer events need physics raycaster
units.detail: IPointerDownHandler/IPointerUpHandler are meant for UI. To use them on world objects, add a physics raycaster, otherwise clicks won't register on game objects.

units.title: Clamp drag along an axis
units.detail: Project the mouse position onto the pin's axis to get the closest point; clamp movement with a dot-product test at the minimum and a distance check at the maximum.

units.title: Procedural quad mesh for pipes
units.detail: Generate a custom mesh from four points to draw a quad connecting pipe entry to exit, giving an arbitrary-shape connector without authored art.

units.title: Player triggers for environment damage
units.detail: Make the player a trigger collider that listens for fluid collisions and applies damage (lava), plus a head-height collider counting water exposure for drowning.

units.title: Tired brain compounds errors
units.detail: Late-night debugging after a long workday fails repeatedly and destroys morale. Resting and returning fresh solves the same problem quickly.

units.title: Show failures in tutorials
units.detail: Leaving failed attempts in the final video is honest: polished tutorials hide hours of trial-and-error that is a normal, necessary part of the process.

units.title: Template-based UI list instantiation
units.detail: Keep a hidden template UI entry and a container; instantiate the template per item, set anchoredPosition to -height*index, then activate the copies.

units.title: Persist lists with PlayerPrefs + JSON
units.detail: Serialize data to a JSON string and store it under a PlayerPrefs key; on load, deserialize back. This is the simplest way to save a high-score table.

units.title: JsonUtility rejects bare lists
units.detail: JsonUtility serializes objects, not arrays/lists directly. Wrap the List in a [System.Serializable] container class so it serializes to JSON.

units.title: Sort on load, not on save
units.detail: Re-sort the list after loading (or after each insert) so displayed entries always appear highest-score-first regardless of insertion order.

units.title: Polish rank rows
units.detail: Format ranks as 1st/2nd/3rd then 'th' after, alternate row background with a modulo on the index, and show gold/silver/bronze trophies for the top three.

units.title: Entities.ForEach replaces job structs
units.detail: Simple DOTS jobs can be written as entities.ForEach which auto-creates and completes the job and uses Burst, cutting boilerplate versus manual job structs.

units.title: Author GameObjects, convert to entities
units.detail: Keep the familiar GameObject workflow and convert objects to entities at runtime; a conversion checkbox/attribute handles the boilerplate, and the inspector shows ECS component values.

units.title: Live-edit a running build
units.detail: Live link lets editor changes appear instantly in a build running elsewhere (another PC, console, mobile), ideal for tuning values and iterating on level design.

units.title: Node shader graph with previews
units.detail: Visual node-based shader editing with a live preview at every step removes the guesswork of debugging handwritten shaders — see results as you connect nodes.

units.title: Hide scene objects not disable them
units.detail: Hidden objects stay enabled at runtime, so you can tidy a cluttered scene without accidentally losing behavior that a disabled GameObject would lose at play.

units.title: Incremental garbage collection
units.detail: Spread GC work smoothly across frames instead of clearing all at once, avoiding massive frame-time spikes in long-running games.

units.title: Hold-time maps to launch force
units.detail: Store start time on mouse down; on release compute hold time, normalize by max hold time clamped to 0-1, then force = normalized * maxForce for charge mechanics.

units.title: Press vs held vs release input states
units.detail: GetMouseButtonDown fires once on the press frame, GetMouseButton stays true while held, GetMouseButtonUp fires on release — use all three for a charge-and-fire mechanic.

units.title: Screen-point raycast for placement
units.detail: Raycast from the camera through the cursor's screen point to get a world position for placement; works identically in first and third person with a centered cursor.

units.title: Auto grid level from aim height
units.detail: Compute the building level with Mathf.Round(worldY / gridHeight) from the raycast hit, so looking up or down automatically selects the grid floor to build on.

units.title: Limit build distance from player
units.detail: Reject placement when the raycast hit is farther than a max build distance from the player so players can't place objects unreachably far away.

units.title: Sky raycast returns origin zero
units.detail: A raycast that hits nothing defaults the position to (0,0,0), placing objects at the world origin. Fix with invisible boundary colliders around the world or an explicit collision test.

units.title: Grid snap needs invisible edge colliders
units.detail: Placement anchors to the lower-left corner point, so invisible trigger colliders on wall edges let floor tiles snap onto surfaces instead of floating unplaced.

units.title: Camera aims toward player aim
units.detail: Offset the camera slightly toward where the player is aiming, not straight down the middle, for a more dynamic feel and extra visibility in shooters.

units.title: Hitboxes smaller than visuals
units.detail: Make colliders roughly 20% smaller than the visible object so hits feel fair and satisfying instead of frustratingly large.

units.title: Animated trailing health bar
units.detail: On damage the red health drops immediately while a white segment trails down afterward, clearly showing how much health a single hit cost.

units.title: Teach mechanics in a safe tutorial
units.detail: Let players try each special mechanic in a low-stakes tutorial so they don't die from unknown mechanics in a real level — deaths from ignorance feel unfair.

units.title: Flash unused abilities
units.detail: If a player holds grenades but hasn't used them after a while, flash the icon so they remember the ability exists instead of struggling without it.

units.title: Interaction tied to character not cursor
units.detail: Pickups and interactions that trigger based on the character position instead of the mouse position are fiddly and easy to miss; prefer cursor-based interaction.

units.title: Show max weapon range
units.detail: Give a visual range indicator (or change the cursor) when aiming past a weapon's maximum range so players stop wasting shots from out of range.

units.title: Top-down shooters underperform on Steam
units.detail: Top-down shooters historically struggle on Steam regardless of polish, so viability depends on deep content, abilities, and differentiation from the crowded market.

units.title: Store page: capsule, blurb, GIFs
units.detail: A strong animated capsule, a short punchy one-line description, and animated GIFs are the highest-impact Steam store page elements for converting visits into wishlists.

units.title: Separate visual object from interaction collider
units.detail: Keep physics logic on a dedicated invisible child object with a collider and let the visual object simply follow its position. This decouples physics from visuals so rotating/circular objects remain easy to grab.

units.title: Dragging by raycasting the handle breaks on fast mouse movement
units.detail: If you raycast the handle collider every frame while dragging, a fast mouse can exit the collider between frames and the object stops following. Instead, raycast once to grab, then raycast onto a separate invisible 'grab plane' to get the drag position.

units.title: Mesh colliders/planes only raycast from one side
units.detail: A quad/plane mesh collider has a single visible face; raycasts from the back will miss. Rotate the grab plane so its collider points toward the player/camera before using it as a drag surface.

units.title: Constrain dragging along a spline track
units.detail: Instead of letting a grabbed object follow the mouse freely, find the nearest point on a spline to the drag position and move the object there. Reusing one spline-following system powers levers, infinitely rotating wheels (closed spline), and segmented wheels (snapped spline).

units.title: Spline functions mix local and world space
units.detail: Spline 'get nearest point' expects and returns local-space positions. Passing world positions sends objects to strange places. Convert input with InverseTransformPoint and output with TransformPoint using the spline container transform.

units.title: Grabbable component exposes MoveGrabbable(position)
units.detail: Keep the interaction system free of per-object details: it only finds what is grabbable via TryGetComponent and calls MoveGrabbable(target). Each handle owns its own movement, visual references, and spline, keeping responsibilities separated.

units.title: Spline T value is normalized game state
units.detail: The nearest-point function also outputs T, a 0-to-1 normalized position along the spline. Expose it as the handle's logical state so game logic (doors closed at 0, open at 1) stays decoupled from visuals.

units.title: Prefer SerializeField over public fields
units.detail: Exposing fields via private SerializeField keeps the public API clean while still letting the inspector assign references. It signals intent and improves encapsulation.

units.title: Tactile interaction + theme = distinct game
units.detail: A generic grab/drag/spline interaction system becomes many different games (Iron Nest war machine, Car Mechanic Simulator, Contraband Police) by layering a clever theme on top. The mechanics are the generic layer; the theme makes the game unique.

units.title: Automated playtesting: bots play your game in parallel
units.detail: Unity Game Simulation runs many cloud builds in parallel, each playing the game itself, to test parameter combinations instead of manually replaying levels. Games must be self-playing via a fixed command script, classic AI, or ML agents.

units.title: Combine multiple parameters into combinations
units.detail: The value of simulation comes from running multiple values per parameter and testing all combinations (e.g., 3 speeds x 2 wait timers = 6 combos), with several runs per combo to average out noise.

units.title: Gate gameplay until config download finishes
units.detail: Fetch simulation parameters asynchronously (on Start), apply them in the callback, then set an isReady flag. The Update loop early-returns until isReady so the game only runs once parameters are applied.

units.title: Simulation counters only accept whole numbers
units.detail: Output counters are stored as long (integer). Storing a float forces truncation, losing precision. Multiply by 1000 to store milliseconds so short runs keep meaningful precision.

units.title: Default parameter value must be valid
units.detail: The cloud validates the build using the default parameter values; an invalid default (e.g., moveSpeed 0 that never reaches the goal) makes validation fail. Always set defaults to values that actually work.

units.title: Quit game cleanly after setting result
units.detail: After writing results, quit the app to free the cloud instance for reuse. Guard with a platform check so the editor stops play instead of actually quitting during local testing.

units.title: Analyze raw vs aggregate simulation data
units.detail: Raw data gives every run's parameters and result; aggregate data groups runs per parameter combo with average, min, max, and standard deviation. Use logs to debug individual failures. Use results to tune toward target outcomes (e.g., finish in 1.8s).

units.title: Raycast-to-sky shadows fail because colliders differ from visuals
units.detail: Checking sunlight by raycasting up fails because physics colliders are simplified capsules, not the detailed mesh (and per-leaf mesh colliders tank performance). Detect light by line of sight to the sun instead.

units.title: Second camera with tiny render texture detects sun visibility
units.detail: Render a low-res (1-pixel) camera that always points at the sun onto a render texture with transparent background. Read back the pixel alpha: transparent alpha = seeing sky = in sun; opaque = blocked = in shade. Tiny resolution + tiny FOV keeps it cheap.

units.title: Directional lights ignore position, use rotation only
units.detail: Transform.LookAt(light position) fails because directional light position is meaningless. Point the detection camera using the inverted light's forward: cameraForward = -light.transform.forward.

units.title: Day/night cycle is just a modulo float
units.detail: Track a daytime float increased by deltaTime, wrap it with modulo (e.g., 24), and derive hours by flooring. Drive both logic and the animator from one multiplier so visual sun motion always matches logical time.

units.title: Never compare floats/colors with direct equality
units.detail: Float precision makes direct color comparison unreliable. Use a tolerance-based difference function that sums RGB+A channel deltas and compares against a max threshold.

units.title: Offset camera near clip so it looks outside the character
units.detail: With near clip at 0, the detection camera sees through the character's head instead of the sky. Set a small near-clip offset so it samples from outside the player model.

units.title: Scale damage intensity with exposure time
units.detail: Accumulate time spent in sun; activate increasingly intense particle/post-processing effects at thresholds (e.g., 15%, 50%) and only deal damage after max exposure. Reset the timer when safe. Overlay post-processing via a higher-priority volume toggled by weight.

units.title: Creators prioritize entertainment first, promotion last
units.detail: Content creators' order of goals is: entertain viewers, pay bills, then promote your game. Your coverage is an accidental side effect, so pitch games that will make a good video, not just games you want promoted.

units.title: Email pitch checklist for content creators
units.detail: A good pitch email has: parseable title (game name + genre), release date/embargo, genre/platform/price/summary, direct Steam link, a redeemable game key, trailer, screenshots/gifs, and press-kit assets. Keep it short; don't bury information.

units.title: Don't make creators jump through hoops for a key
units.detail: Include the Steam key directly in the email rather than forcing creators to request one through a form. Lower friction massively increases the chance they play and cover your game.

units.title: Press kit must enable great thumbnails
units.detail: Thumbnails drive clicks, and creators build them from your assets. Provide transparent PNGs, logos, key art, screenshots, and characters so they can make compelling thumbnails. A visually interesting game with a rich press kit gets covered more.

units.title: Marketing is a multiplier on a good game
units.detail: All outreach tips multiply success only if the game itself is compelling. A great game survives a simple email; a weak game won't be saved by perfect pitching.

units.title: Invest in Steam capsule art even if you can't art
units.detail: The Steam capsule/icon is the first impression and a top differentiator against low-effort games. Even programmers-only devs should hire an artist for at least the capsule; it matters enormously for festival/Next Fest visibility.

units.title: Rejection from creators isn't personal
units.detail: No coverage despite following every rule happens for many benign reasons: lost in thousands of emails, crowded release timing, wrong audience fit, or unclickable title. Don't take it personally; keep applying the guidelines to raise odds.

units.title: Creators find games via inbox, demos, festivals, Discord
units.detail: Most creators discover games through email, browsing Steam demos/new releases and Next Fest, audience suggestions on Discord, and Twitter for devs/publishers (not players). Community 'play this game' buzz is one of the strongest signals.

units.title: You can't identify an engine by how a game looks
units.detail: Cuphead, Genshin Impact, Rimworld, and Escape from Tarkov all use Unity yet look nothing alike. Visual identification only works on amateur games that keep defaults (default skybox, cubes, lighting, asset flips).

units.title: Identify engine from project file structure
units.detail: Unity builds contain an executable plus a Data folder full of Unity DLLs; Unreal builds typically show a Binaries/ThirdParty structure. Inspect shipped files to confirm the engine reliably.

units.title: SteamDB depot search reveals game files without buying
units.detail: On SteamDB, inspect a game's depot containing Windows files and search the file list (e.g., for Unity DLLs) to confirm the engine without installing anything. Only works for Steam games.

units.title: Verify engine via job postings, blogs, devs' Twitter
units.detail: When files aren't available (Epic-only, console, pre-release), check job listings requiring C#/Unity, developer blogs showing the editor, or the lead programmer's Twitter for engine mentions or hashtags.

units.title: Grid system stores per-cell game data
units.detail: Instantiate a data class at every grid position to store world state (moisture float, radiation float) independent of visuals. A visual layer (tilemap colors) renders what the grid contains. Grids generalize to soil, farming, building, and more.

units.title: Map normalized floats to enum categories
units.detail: Convert a 0-1 moisture float into discrete states (dried out/dry/moist/wet) with an enum plus simple thresholds, and radiation as boolean above a threshold. This keeps logic readable while storing continuous values.

units.title: Cloud rain simulation via texture-to-boolean-grid cache
units.detail: Define cloud shapes on a texture, convert each pixel to a cached boolean grid once, then periodically project cloud world position to grid and add moisture to covered cells. Caching avoids expensive per-pixel GetPixel calls every update.

units.title: Run large simulations on a tick interval, not every frame
units.detail: Updating every grid cell each frame is a serious perf hit on big worlds. Run logic every N seconds (timer-based ticks) instead; players won't notice, and it's far cheaper than optimizing the loop itself.

units.title: Water spreads by neighbor moisture transfer
units.detail: Each tick, compare a cell to its neighbors and transfer moisture from wetter to drier cells. Even one spawn cloud slowly wets the whole map, making the system feel realistic with simple logic.

units.title: Systems interact through the shared grid
units.detail: Plants/building systems just ask the soil grid for moisture and radiation at their position; moisture controls growth speed, radiation determines whether crops are clean or contaminated. Composition over coupling keeps each system simple.

units.title: GetPixel per frame per pixel is expensive
units.detail: Reading texture pixels individually is costly; convert the texture to a cached boolean/float array once and read from the array during simulation ticks.

units.title: Render textures show a camera feed in UI
units.detail: Assign a camera's output to a render texture, then display it in UI with RawImage (Image only accepts sprites, not textures). Render textures enable remote camera views, mirrors, and probe feeds.

units.title: Enable camera per snapshot for picture not video
units.detail: To capture stills instead of a live feed, keep the probe camera disabled and only enable it momentarily to render a frame onto the texture, then disable again. This matches 'take a photo' behavior.

units.title: Collisions need a Rigidbody on one side
units.detail: OnCollisionEnter never fires if neither object has a Rigidbody. When the landing trigger/separate piece had no rigidbody it silently failed; put the landing collider on the main object that owns the Rigidbody.

units.title: Rotate landing object to match surface normal
units.detail: On collision, use the collision normal to set the projectile's transform.up so it aligns with the surface it landed on, then freeze the rigidbody. Separate the landing collider from the physical-shape collider to listen only to the former.

units.title: Per-camera post-processing via layers and volumes
units.detail: Give the probe a different look by putting its post-processing volume on a dedicated layer, having the probe camera apply only that layer, and the main camera ignore it. Layer-masked volumes isolate effects per camera.

units.title: Fire projectile from camera position and velocity
units.detail: Spawn the projectile at the camera position and set its Rigidbody velocity from the camera's forward vector. This gives a clean first-person launcher with zero extra aiming math.

units.title: Clean-dirt mask shader from three textures
units.detail: Combine a clean texture, a dirty texture, and a single-channel dirt mask in a shader: show dirty where mask is 1, clean where 0. Progress is made by painting the mask's pixels to black as the player scrubs.

units.title: Map raycast UV hit to pixel coordinates
units.detail: A raycast hit exposes textureCoord, normalized 0-1 UVs (0,0 lower-left, 1,1 upper-right). Convert UVs to pixel coordinates by multiplying by texture dimensions, then edit pixels at that spot.

units.title: Brush texture + multiply for smooth painting
units.detail: Instead of cleaning a hard square, multiply the brush texture (black center, white edges = zeros and ones) with the dirt mask so strokes fade smoothly at the edges for natural-looking cleaning.

units.title: Percent clean = painted pixels / original dirt pixels
units.detail: Clone the original full-dirt mask before painting; count dirty pixels in each, then divide clone count by original to get percentage cleaned. Optionally add noise after cloning so objects don't start at exactly 100% dirty.

units.title: Rotating the object needs no extra code
units.detail: Because the whole minigame works on raycasts and UVs, simply rotating the object (e.g., to clean the back) keeps all click-to-pixel mapping working automatically with zero changes.

units.title: Raycast point + delayed action timer for artillery
units.detail: Aim by raycasting from the camera forward to get a world point, show a target indicator there, then spawn explosion VFX after a timed delay (action/delegate timer) instead of instantly. A two-state machine (normal/aiming) handles input flow.

units.title: Detect player inside gas with OverlapSphere
units.detail: Place a trigger sphere on the gas visual; each frame use a physics overlap sphere at the player position filtered by the gas layer. If colliders are found, the player is inside gas. Layer masks keep detection cheap and targeted.

units.title: Post-processing volume layer must be in camera volume mask
units.detail: A local post-processing volume only affects a camera if its layer is included in that camera's volume mask. Forgetting to add the gas layer to the camera makes the blur/green effect never appear.

units.title: Counter-item as full-screen UI with walk animation
units.detail: The gas mask is just a full-screen UI texture; an animator bool 'isWalking' scales it slightly while moving. Full-screen UI images are a cheap way to represent equipment states and vision effects.

units.title: Dynamic mesh as a UI element for drawn arrows
units.detail: Build a path as a dynamic mesh and assign it to a CanvasRenderer via SetMaterial/SetMesh so players can draw on the minimap. Append vertices from mouse screen-space converted to the transform's local space; skip frames where the mouse barely moved; place a rotated arrow texture at the last point.

units.title: Delegates unlock delayed callbacks and flexibility
units.detail: Using Action/delegate types lets a timer fire a callback (spawn explosion after 2s, deal damage over time) without hardcoding. Not knowing delegates blocks otherwise simple designs.

units.title: Define your own success metric and conversion math
units.detail: Success is personal: publish, learn, or sell a decent number of copies. A common rule of thumb is ~10k wishlists converts to ~1k sales; set a wishlist goal that matches your break-even point and dev cost.

units.title: Publish your Steam coming-soon page as early as possible
units.detail: Wishlists are extremely important in the Steam ecosystem. Get the store page live as soon as the core idea and some visuals exist; every extra day the page is visible accrues wishlists.

units.title: Devlog videos convert viewers to wishlists
units.detail: Regular devlog videos (announcement, progress, devlog) each drove ~10-15k views and roughly 10% of viewers added the game to wishlists. Steady content beats waiting for one big spike.

units.title: Next Fest is a major wishlist source
units.detail: A strong Steam Next Fest demo can earn up to ~10k wishlists; even a good-but-not-great showing may net ~1k, which compounds to 2-3k more by release. The demo is the deadline to prioritize before the festival.

units.title: Don't compare yourself to devs at other career stages
units.detail: Comparing a beginner's skills or income to a senior dev with 25 years of experience is a false premise. The only valid comparison is against your past self: are you better than a few months ago?

units.title: Income scales with volume of shipped games
units.detail: Earnings per hour climbed from ~2 cents to $5/hr across ~40 Flash games. Repeatedly finishing games builds skill and revenue; an upward trend, however tiny, is a strong motivator to continue.

units.title: Use others' success as proof, not discouragement
units.detail: Seeing others earn much more should be read as 'this is possible' rather than 'I'm failing'. Find hope in the uptrend of your own numbers instead of feeling crushed by someone else's.

units.title: Normalize comparisons to equal experience levels
units.detail: If you compare to a veteran, compare to them at your stage (e.g., their first week or first Flash game), not their current skill. This applies to any learned skill like lifting or programming.

units.title: Steam net revenue is under half of gross
units.detail: After Steam's cut, chargebacks, refunds and taxes, net is roughly 50% or less of gross revenue. A $120k gross game yielded ~$50k net; always do this math before judging a launch.

units.title: Keep a financial buffer for flops
units.detail: Long careers in indie dev survive because of careful risk management and savings that withstand a complete flop. Treat every single-game result as not telling the whole story.

units.title: Wishlists and followers are the key pre-launch metric
units.detail: Announce the game as soon as possible and gather wishlists/followers before release, because early sales in the first days decide whether you compete with great games or trash. ~6k wishlists and 4k followers were solid numbers.

units.title: Long dev cycles hurt profitability
units.detail: 17 months on one game is too long for an indie; the longer you spend the harder it is to profit. Aim for ~6-8 month solo dev cycles. Splitting time with a YouTube channel also tanked productivity.

units.title: Combine trending genre with proven genre and clear name
units.detail: Battle Royale Tycoon merged a hot game mode (battle royale) with the author's proven genre (tycoon/management). A generic-but-clear name that instantly communicates the game captures attention better than an obscure unique one.

units.title: Track all real costs: time, assets, services, ads
units.detail: Actual costs for a 7-month game: ~$10k in living expenses (time), ~$600 effective on assets, $360 music, $740 localization (7 languages), $150 logos, $2.6k ads. Direct cost ~€4k plus $10k time = ~$14k total.

units.title: Low costs are the real survival strategy
units.detail: Surviving 10+ years without a mega hit comes from extremely low monthly costs, high efficiency, and living in a low cost-of-living country. Expensive living in places like San Francisco makes indie profitability nearly impossible.

units.title: Paid ads rarely return for indies and can't be tracked
units.detail: Steam offers no attribution, so ad-generated wishlists/sales are unverifiable. If experimenting, set the lowest cost per click possible, let ads run for months as filler, and assume they had some impact while keeping spend small.

units.title: Asset costs are hard to track accurately
units.detail: Assets bought at 50-95% off, reused across many projects, or given free make exact costing impractical. Estimate effective cost (e.g., half of undiscounted total) rather than the listed price.

units.title: Set concrete goal scenarios before launch
units.detail: Define good/bare-minimum/great targets (e.g., 1k week-one copies, $20k gross, $2k/month dev income) so you can objectively score the result later. When timelines slip, revise the numbers rather than abandoning the goals.

units.title: Overly ambitious timelines fail even with experience
units.detail: Even 10-year veterans miss release dates badly (planned 4 months, took 7). Don't be too harsh on yourself when scope and schedules blow up; games always take longer than estimated.

units.title: 90% of solo dev time goes to coding when using assets
units.detail: Buying art assets shifts almost all project time to programming (importing assets + writing code), which is the fastest way for a programmer to ship. Choose engines/tools based on your language comfort.

units.title: Buy assets to solve problems, fill art, or save time
units.detail: Justified asset purchases are ones you can't build well yourself (e.g., super-fast multi-threaded pathfinding), art you can't make, or tools that save significant iteration time. All three are valid reasons.

units.title: Luck is a factor, but work shrinks it
units.detail: There is always luck in game success, but improving skills (marketing, game design, programming) increases your odds and 'gets luckier'. Focus on controllable factors, not external ones.

units.title: Feasibility of indie income depends on cost of living
units.detail: Living on game revenue is easy at $750/month costs and nearly impossible in $10k/month cities. 'Making a living' is defined relative to your expenses, not an absolute number.

units.title: Engine choice matters less than commitment
units.detail: All modern engines (Unity, Unreal, Godot, Game Maker) are excellent; pick one and stick with it. Choose by language familiarity (C# -> Unity, C++ -> Unreal, GDScript -> Godot) or a coin flip.

units.title: Write clean code; it enables reuse across projects
units.detail: Good code style kept complex systems (boss fights, health, spawning) maintainable and reusable. Clean-code principles are universal across engines and languages; Code Complete is a recommended reference.

units.title: Self-discipline is the #1 solo-dev skill
units.detail: With no supervisor, the hardest part is forcing yourself to work. Early on you may only manage 2 hours/day; deliberately train self-discipline, then 'just start' and make lots of games to gain experience.

units.title: Ship more, smaller games to learn faster
units.detail: Making four 6-month games teaches far more than one 2-year project. Work on portfolio games in tandem with job hunting so you progress on both fronts at once.

units.title: Sequels are risky and often underperform
units.detail: A direct sequel (Survivor Squad Gauntlet) got 80 reviews vs 500 for the original despite being better. Sequels aren't guaranteed success; prefer pursuing new ideas unless a sequel is clearly warranted.

units.title: Multiplayer cheating: never trust the client
units.detail: The only reliable anti-cheat is server-side authority so cheating isn't even possible. For co-op games don't spend time on it; for competitive games invest heavily, but full prevention is a losing battle even for AAA.

units.title: Forgetting your codebase after a break is normal
units.detail: Coming back to a project you feel lost in is expected; re-read the code and context returns quickly. Long breaks only cause real forgetting, and it's common to stop playing games once you make them.

units.title: Polish whatever the player spends most time doing
units.detail: Decide polish targets from your game's core activity: UI micro-interactions for management games, impactful attack feel for action games. Analyze the game, find the dominant activity, polish that hardest.

units.title: Smooth difficulty with spawn limits, variety, pickups
units.detail: Stable difficulty curves use max alive enemy caps, weighted randomization of enemy types (e.g., 15/50/35%), health pickups, and per-stage spawn rates that start slow and escalate.

units.title: The Steam algorithm is driven by money
units.detail: Everything the Steam visibility system rewards reduces to 'does the game sell'. Games proven to sell get promoted and sell more; games with no evidence of sales stay invisible.

units.title: Store page traffic is not a direct visibility factor
units.detail: Raw visits don't move the algorithm; only resulting sales and wishlists do. Buying cheap fake impressions won't trigger Steam and is a waste; genuine traffic that converts helps.

units.title: Under 10 reviews your game is invisible to Steam
units.detail: No score exists below 10 reviews, and hundreds of unreviewed games are algorithm-invisible. Desperately ask players for reviews to clear 10 (ideally 50); sub-40% 'mostly negative' also hurts visibility.

units.title: Review score isn't a factor above ~40% positive
units.detail: Officially, review score only matters when 'mostly negative' (<40%), though FIFA/NBA sell millions with negative reviews because brute-force marketing drives sales. Indies without big budgets still need positive reviews to convert players.

units.title: Wishlists matter before release, not after
units.detail: Wishlists are a strong pre-launch sales predictor and trigger email notifications at launch and on >20% discounts, driving launch sales. After release the number itself is irrelevant to visibility.

units.title: Wishlist count doesn't earn daily deal invites
units.detail: The daily-deal invite myth is false; the actual threshold is roughly $200k+ in revenue. Money, not wishlist count, is what Steam rewards after release.

units.title: Early Access has no visibility bonus
units.detail: Early Access games don't appear on New & Trending regardless of sales, and many players never buy EA titles. Choose EA based on game readiness and roadmap, never for visibility; two-launch benefits only apply to EA hits.

units.title: Localization is a real visibility factor
units.detail: English is only ~30% of Steam's audience, so single-language games never reach two-thirds of players. Minimum viable: English + Simplified Chinese, then add genre-appropriate languages (German/Polish for tycoons, Japanese for anime).

units.title: Controller support matters for Steam Deck
units.detail: Games without controller support aren't promoted to controller/Deck players. With an input system it's easy to add, making it a high-value inclusion for most genres.

units.title: Sales velocity is more important than volume
units.detail: Selling 1,000 copies in an hour boosts visibility far more than 1,000 copies in a month. Plan big events, updates, and healthy discounts to create velocity spikes.

units.title: Steam snowballs, but you start the ball rolling
units.detail: Launching on Steam with zero marketing yields nothing; Steam only amplifies existing momentum. You must supply the initial push through marketing, events and sales before the algorithm helps.

units.title: Overnight successes are actually years of work
units.detail: BattleBit looked like it came out of nowhere but was developed for 7+ years, with 8 years of prior modding. Apparent overnight hits are the result of a long build-up of work and audience.

units.title: Wishlists roughly equal 10x followers
units.detail: Using a ~10:1 wishlist-to-follower rule, 70k followers meant ~700k wishlists before launch, likely a top-10 all-time wishlist count. Growing slowly but consistently for years is how to get there.

units.title: Grow a community alongside development
units.detail: BattleBit developed with a Discord community, Patreon support and 700k playtesters, gathering feedback and audience year over year. This eliminates launch-day luck by guaranteeing demand.

units.title: Steam pays net-30, causing server cash crunches
units.detail: Steam pays 30+ days after month-end, so a hit multiplayer game can face huge server bills before revenue arrives; BattleBit had to take a loan despite millions in sales. Plan cash flow around net-30.

units.title: Gross to net: expect ~50% loss to taxes and costs
units.detail: After taxes and (for multiplayer) server costs, net from ~$36M gross was perhaps ~$10M. Regional pricing also drags effective price below list ($15 avg -> ~$12).

units.title: Success = great game + marketing + waiting audience
units.detail: BattleBit won by targeting a huge, underserved audience (players let down by the latest Battlefield), focusing on excellent core gameplay, and gathering that audience over years. Luck shrinks when demand is pre-built.

units.title: You don't need a mega hit to be a successful indie
units.detail: Aim to make a great game, market it, and build a community that wants it, not to sell millions. Monumental hits inspire, but a sustainable solo career needs far less.

units.title: Combine knowledge from multiple tutorials to innovate
units.detail: Powerful results come from mixing separate skills: desktop duplication + transparent Unity window + a shatter effect produced a breakable-desktop toy. Tutorials aren't standalone — learn the underlying mechanism and remix it.

units.title: Desktop duplication project shows desktop inside Unity
units.detail: A free GitHub project captures the desktop as a custom texture type inside Unity; combined with a transparent window it enables desktop-games where the player interacts with their real screen.

units.title: Use a camera render texture as the shatter input
units.detail: Convert the desktop-duplication texture into a Texture2D and feed it to a break-the-screen effect so the 'shattered' surface is your captured desktop rather than game world.

units.title: Shatter effect via pre-sliced mesh + physics
units.detail: Build a screen-shaped object, slice it into pieces with ProBuilder's slice tool, give each piece a Rigidbody + MeshCollider, then in Awake loop children calling AddExplosionForce for a nice shatter.

units.title: Aspect ratio must match the screen mesh
units.detail: For 16:9 (1080p/4K) use a flattened cube scaled 1.6 x 0.9 so the shatter mesh lines up with the camera view. Position a separate camera to frame it exactly.

units.title: Screenshot method freezes the game for shatter
units.detail: For a game-over/transition feel, take a screenshot into a Texture2D (ReadPixels after end of frame) and assign it to the shatter material so the scene appears frozen while it explodes. Render textures keep it live.

units.title: URP shader uses _BaseMap, not _MainTex
units.detail: Older materials expose the main texture as _MainTex, but URP lit materials name it _BaseMap. If SetTexture with _MainTex fails, switch the property name.

units.title: Overlay camera keeps game running under shatter
units.detail: For a 'special ability' variant, make the shatter camera an overlay with alpha 0 background and stack it on the main camera; the game continues playing beneath the shattering overlay.

units.title: Capture screenshot before enabling the explosion
units.detail: Take the screenshot while the normal scene is visible, then enable the explosion transform; otherwise you capture the sliced pieces instead of the real screen.

units.title: Camera positioning shortcut: Ctrl+Shift+F
units.detail: To quickly aim a camera at an object, select it, position the scene view, then press Ctrl+Shift+F to snap the camera to the current view.

units.title: Boss fight as a health-threshold state machine
units.detail: Define an enum of stages and advance on health thresholds (e.g., below 70% -> stage 2, below 30% -> stage 3, dead -> battle over). Each stage changes spawns, shields and difficulty.

units.title: Trigger start battle via event, then unsubscribe
units.detail: Use a physics trigger to fire a start event; the boss script subscribes, starts the battle, and unsubscribes immediately so the battle can't start twice.

units.title: Decouple systems with start/end battle events
units.detail: Doors, keys and trophies subscribe to boss-battle start/end events so the battle script knows nothing about them. This event-based wiring keeps each system single-purpose and reusable.

units.title: Random spawn from a container of positions
units.detail: Keep empty child objects as spawn markers under a container, read their transforms into a list in code, and pick a random one per spawn for varied encounters.

units.title: Weighted enemy randomization by difficulty
units.detail: Pick a random 0-100 value and branch thresholds to control enemy-type odds (e.g., 15% shooter, 50% charger, 35% archer), and cap the number of alive enemies for a stable difficulty.

units.title: Spawn-rate schedule creates difficulty curve
units.detail: Escalate spawns per stage (few slow spawns on stage 1, faster/more on later stages) plus health pickups so difficulty ramps smoothly instead of overwhelming the player instantly.

units.title: Learn boss-fight logic, not the exact template
units.detail: Boss fights are unique; the portable insight is how to structure multiple stages, events and actions in a state machine, then apply that logic to your own bosses.

units.title: Custom editor tools multiply productivity
units.detail: A custom inspector with click-to-select buttons and scene gizmos built a full scripted cutscene in ~60 seconds versus ~30 minutes manually. Investing in tools for your own workflow pays off massively.

units.title: Capture clicks in OnSceneGUI with Event.current
units.detail: Read Event.current.type (MouseUp/MouseDown) inside OnSceneGUI to intercept clicks, then raycast from the mouse to find the object the user is clicking on.

units.title: Object deselects before MouseUp fires
units.detail: OnSceneGUI only runs while the object is selected, and clicking elsewhere deselects it first, so MouseUp never fires. Block selection changes with HandleUtility.AddDefaultControl(GetDefaultControl()) and holding Ctrl.

units.title: Find clicked object via GUIPointToWorldRay + raycast
units.detail: Convert the mouse position with HandleUtility.GUIPointToWorldRay, raycast, then check hits for a target component (via TryGetComponent) to filter valid click targets. Requires colliders on objects.

units.title: Scene view only repaints on changes
units.detail: OnSceneGUI gizmos can lag because the scene view doesn't redraw on mouse move. Call SceneView.Repaint() (e.g., in OnSceneGUI or OnGUI) to force responsive updates.

units.title: Generic click-to-select helper for any type
units.detail: Wrap raycast + component lookup in a generic function (T) that outputs both component and collider, then reuse it across unit, door, and action selection in editor tools.

units.title: Post-processing volumes are a nested component system
units.detail: The volume itself only exposes weight, priority and profile; the actual effects (bloom, color adjustments) live in the profile as components. Access them via profile.TryGet<T>() rather than searching the volume directly.

units.title: Get and modify an effect via profile.TryGet
units.detail: volume.profile.TryGet<Bloom>(out Bloom bloom) then bloom.intensity.value = 10f. Requires using UnityEngine.Rendering.Universal for the Bloom type. Works identically in URP and HDRP, not the built-in pipeline.

units.title: Flash effects by lerping volume weight
units.detail: Add a second volume with higher priority and weight 0 containing only the effect; to flash the screen (e.g. player damage) simply animate the weight up and down instead of modifying effect parameters.

units.title: Volume inspector hides per-effect parameters
units.detail: Only weight/priority/profile are reachable from the Volume component; effect fields are not exposed. The volume system stores a components list on the profile, and the VolumeComponent.TryGet is the intended lookup API.

units.title: Read package source to learn unknown APIs
units.detail: Right-click a component and pick Edit Script, or search in the Project window Packages folder (unhide it with the 'I' icon toggle) and use the search bar to find any built-in class source. Read how a system stores data to know how to modify it.

units.title: Use an empty marker component instead of layers
units.detail: Detect interactables (like ladders) with a do-nothing component and TryGetComponent on the raycast hit instead of layer checks. More adaptable than layers when you have many object types.

units.title: Raycast from an elevated origin to avoid floor hits
units.detail: Fire the detection raycast from transform.position + Vector3.up * 0.1f and with a short max distance (0.4f) so you don't start climbing from far away and don't hit the floor or pebbles.

units.title: Climb by swapping movement Y and Z
units.detail: When climbing, set targetDirection.y = targetDirection.z and zero the Z (and optionally X to prevent sliding). Also set grounded = true and clear vertical velocity so gravity doesn't fight the climb.

units.title: Cache climb direction to prevent dropping when backing up
units.detail: If the release raycast uses the current input direction, moving backward on the ladder raycasts behind you, misses the ladder, and drops you. Store the grab direction once when first grabbing and raycast along that cached direction.

units.title: Distinguish climb up/down with Vector3.Dot
units.detail: dot = Vector3.Dot(currentTargetDirection, lastGrabDirection). Positive means climbing up, negative means climbing down, and it keeps working no matter which way the player faces.

units.title: Push forward when releasing ladder at the top
units.detail: Without it, grabbing/dropping jitters up and down at the top edge. On release at the top, apply a forward/up velocity to jump the gap so the character leaves smoothly.

units.title: Auto-climb vs button-press ladder interaction
units.detail: Approach-and-hold climbing feels like Half-Life; a button grab (press E when close) feels like Elden Ring. Both share the same core logic; the only change is gating the grab behind a button press instead of doing it automatically.

units.title: Override speed while climbing
units.detail: Speed calculated from input breaks when moving straight into a wall; when climbing, manually set the target speed so the climb is smooth and consistent.

units.title: Input Manager is deprecated in Unity 6.3
units.detail: Unity 6.3 LTS marks the old Input Manager for deprecation; projects using it get a warning. Install the Input System package and migrate, though it is still usable during the 6.3 upgrade cycle.

units.title: Input System shorthand equivalents for GetKey
units.detail: Keyboard.current[Key.W] with .isPressed (held), .wasPressedThisFrame (down), .wasReleasedThisFrame (up). Keyboard.current also supports indexing by a Key enum variable for rebindable keys.

units.title: Mouse input in the new Input System
units.detail: Mouse.current.position.value is a Vector2 control (use .ReadValue() to get it); Mouse.current.scroll.ReadValue().y for the wheel; Mouse.current.rightButton.wasPressedThisFrame / wasReleasedThisFrame for clicks.

units.title: OnMouseEnter stops working with Input System
units.detail: The legacy OnMouseEnter/Exit MonoBehaviour callbacks aren't supported by the Input System. Replace them with IPointerEnter etc., and add a PhysicsRaycaster (or 2D variant) to the camera plus an EventSystem in the scene or they still won't fire.

units.title: Replicate GetAxisRaw without actions
units.detail: For quick prototyping, approximate GetAxisRaw (W/S vertical, A/D horizontal) by polling individual Keyboard.current keys with isPressed; for real games use proper Input Actions so designers define bindings.

units.title: Scriptable Objects keep game data out of code
units.detail: Store item/recipe data (name, sprite, craft matrix) in ScriptableObjects so the code handles only logic. Adding new content becomes a pure editor task: create new assets, no code changes, no recompile.

units.title: Define an asset via CreateAssetMenu attribute
units.detail: Extend ScriptableObject instead of MonoBehaviour and add [CreateAssetMenu(menuName = "ScriptableObjects/ItemScriptableObject")] so designers can create items/recipes from the Assets > Create menu.

units.title: ScriptableObject type vs enum for item identity
units.detail: You can keep an enum type inside the SO to migrate an existing system, but building fresh you'd use the ScriptableObject asset itself as the type and drop the enum entirely.

units.title: Expose starting data through a serializable struct array
units.detail: Define a [Serializable] struct {ItemScriptableObject item; int amount;} and an array field; populate the starting inventory in the inspector instead of hard-coding it. On Start, iterate the array and add items.

units.title: Model recipes as SOs with a helper accessor
units.detail: A RecipeScriptableObject stores the output item plus a 3x3 ItemScriptableObject matrix, with a small function GetItem(x, y) so the crafting logic stays clean. Custom Inspectors can visualize the matrix beautifully.

units.title: Scriptable Objects can hold logic, not just data
units.detail: Besides fields, an SO can expose helper methods (like GetItem(x,y) on a recipe). Shader Graph and the Scriptable Render Pipeline use ScriptableObjects heavily for data management — a pattern worth copying.

units.title: Anchoring graph origin to transform corner
units.detail: Create the graph background and anchor it to the transform so the graph has a fixed origin at the lower-left corner, making it easy to place dots and lines for each data point.

units.title: Separate data from visualization interface
units.detail: Model each visualization (line graph, bar chart) as its own class behind a common interface so the same dataset can be rendered either way — and new custom visualizations can be plugged in without touching the data layer.

units.title: Update one graph point without rebuilding everything
units.detail: Provide a function to modify a single data point that only updates that point's visual instead of destroying and recreating all points; this avoids wasted allocations and keeps the graph performant on live data.

units.title: Feature checklist for a reusable graph widget
units.detail: A complete graph tool should offer: axis separators, axis labels, y then x scaling for arbitrary values, runtime controls (which values, how many visible), and tooltips showing exact point values — all working across visualization types.

units.title: Detect runtime errors via log callback
units.detail: Subscribe to Application.logMessageReceived; inspect the LogType and show an in-game window when type is Error or Exception. Display the condition (message) and stack trace so players/devs see exactly what broke.

units.title: Unsubscribe from static events or reload breaks the listener
units.detail: Application.logMessageReceived is a static event, so it isn't cleared when the scene's UI is destroyed. Always unsubscribe in OnDestroy (or use OnEnable/OnDisable), otherwise a reloaded scene fires the event on two copies of the detector.

units.title: Show each unique error only once
units.detail: An error firing every frame makes the window instantly hide-and-show. Keep a list of already-shown error strings and skip re-showing duplicates (hash the text to save memory if desired).

units.title: Add copy-to-clipboard to error windows
units.detail: Let players copy the error text with GUIUtility.systemCopyBuffer wrapped in try/catch (it can fail in edge cases). Combine with drag-to-move and a close button so the player can report the exact error without screenshots.

units.title: Cloud Diagnostics auto-reports player errors
units.detail: Unity's Cloud Diagnostics (one-button enable) notifies you whenever a player hits an error with the stack trace. It's a build-time complement to in-game error windows, and can pair with user-report features for automated bug reports.

units.title: Represent pixel art as a grid of color cells
units.detail: Reuse a generic grid system where every position holds data (here a single color) and clicking modifies the grid object; a tilemap-style visual rebuilds the mesh on changes. One pixel per grid cell.

units.title: Meshes can only display colors present in their material
units.detail: A mesh can't just print an arbitrary color — it must exist on the material texture. Store each pixel's color as a UV coordinate pointing into a color-palette texture (or a Color2 UV field), and paint by assigning those UVs to the quad.

units.title: Save a texture to PNG
units.detail: Build a Texture2D at grid size, loop cells calling SetPixel(x, y, color), call texture.Apply(), then EncodeToPNG() to get a byte array and File.WriteAllBytes to disk. Load back with LoadImage and set filterMode = Point for crisp pixels.

units.title: GetPixel requires read/write enabled texture
units.detail: Reading back pixel colors (Texture2D.GetPixel) fails unless the source texture's Import Settings have Read/Write enabled under Advanced. Tick it before sampling a palette texture.

units.title: Build reusable systems once, reuse everywhere
units.detail: The same grid system powers heatmaps, tilemaps, pixel art and more. Writing clean, generic systems pays off by being applicable to many future scenarios with minimal changes.

units.title: Color picker via raycast texture coordinate
units.detail: Place the color palette on a quad and raycast to get the hit texture coordinate (same technique as cleaning in a part-based simulator), then map that UV to a selectable color. Add brush-size controls to paint multiple cells.

units.title: Everything visible is a mesh you can generate in code
units.detail: Dynamic meshes let you build visuals that adapt at runtime. A mesh is just vertices, UVs and a triangle index array; generate one for a quad, assign it to a MeshFilter + MeshRenderer, and call MarkDynamic() if you'll mutate it often.

units.title: Stroke thickness from a 90-degree offset vector
units.detail: For a stroke, compute forward = mousePos - lastPos, then take the cross product of forward with the 2D normal (-1) to get a perpendicular vector; multiply by line thickness and offset two new vertices up/down from the current position.

units.title: Triangle winding must be clockwise to face camera
units.detail: When adding triangles to a dynamic mesh, keep the vertex indices in clockwise order or the quad faces away and is invisible. Each added quad needs 2 vertices and 6 triangle indices.

units.title: Throttle stroke points by minimum distance
units.detail: Adding a quad every frame spawns up to 1000 polygons/second. Only append a new segment when the distance from the last point exceeds a threshold (e.g. 0.1f) — lower values are smoother, higher values are cheaper.

units.title: Start the stroke as a single point
units.detail: Begin a stroke with one point instead of an initial quad; the line looks naturally tapered at the start rather than abruptly thick. Solid-color meshes also only need a single UV pair per vertex.

units.title: Drag UI windows with IDragHandler
units.detail: Implement IDragHandler and in OnDrag move the target rectTransform: dragRectTransform.anchoredPosition += eventData.delta. OnDrag only fires while the cursor moves, which is exactly the window-drag behavior you want.

units.title: Divide mouse delta by canvas scale factor
units.detail: Under a CanvasScaler with a reference resolution, the raw eventData.delta is in screen pixels, so the window won't follow the cursor exactly. Fix it by dividing the delta by canvas.scaleFactor before adding to anchoredPosition.

units.title: Send a UI window to the front with SetAsLastSibling
units.detail: UI render order follows hierarchy order, so on pointer down call dragRectTransform.SetAsLastSibling() to bring the dragged window above all others. Implement IPointerDownHandler to trigger it.

units.title: Auto-locate the Canvas by walking up parents
units.detail: Instead of requiring hand-assigned references, walk up the transform's parent chain until you find a Canvas (or reach the root), and default the drag rect transform to transform.parent. Keeps the script drop-in usable with zero setup.

units.title: Drag the title bar, move the parent window
units.detail: Put the drag handler on the title object and reference the parent window's rectTransform as the thing that moves; this also lets you run extra behavior on IBeginDragHandler/IEndDragHandler, e.g. making the window transparent while dragging.

units.title: Drop detection with IDropHandler
units.detail: Implement IDropHandler's OnDrop on equipment slots and read the currently dragged item from the drag system's static current item (e.g. UIItemDrag.instance.GetItem()). Fire an event with the dropped item so the equipment window reacts.

units.title: Validate item type against the slot before equipping
units.detail: Expose a TryEquip(EquipSlot, item) that checks item.GetEquipSlot() matches the target slot (weapon/helmet/armor). Without this, dragging a helmet onto the weapon slot wrongly equips it.

units.title: Keep UI separate from game logic via events
units.detail: Have a CharacterEquipment class own the equipped state and fire an OnChanged event; the UI subscribes and redraws. This decoupling means equipping from any code path still updates the visuals automatically.

units.title: Show equipped gear with a portrait camera
units.detail: Render a camera attached to the player into a Raw Image (RenderTexture) so the equipped item visually appears on the character in the UI, even when the main camera is far away. Clear the container and rebuild UI items when the loadout changes.

units.title: Visualize equipment by swapping textures
units.detail: Updating what the character wears on the mesh comes from swapping the character texture (e.g. a modular spritesheet sampling a specific texture region), which keeps equipment visuals decoupled from animations.

units.title: Boxleiter method estimates Steam sales from reviews
units.detail: Multiply the number of Steam reviews by a factor of 20 to 70 (pessimistic to optimistic) to estimate copies sold. 25 reviews x 40 = ~1,000 copies, which at $25 equals ~$25k gross revenue.

units.title: Gross revenue pipeline to developer net income
units.detail: After gross revenue, subtract refunds/chargebacks (~6-11% refunds, 1-2% chargebacks; assume 10%), then Steam's ~30% cut, then taxes (10-50% by country, assume ~30%). $25k gross ends up ~$11k net in the developer's pocket.

units.title: Revenue is not profit and not success
units.detail: Small gross revenue that survives deductions rarely covers developer costs, so a polished-looking game with tiny review counts is likely unprofitable regardless of how good it looks. Use estimates to spot flops before deep analysis.

units.title: Launching with tiny content turns hype into flop
units.detail: Releasing with only a single map / ~10 minutes of gameplay, even with 100k wishlists, produces a flood of negative reviews. Players cannot be satisfied by marketing alone; the base game needs a solid amount of content at launch.

units.title: Price relative to genre competitors
units.detail: Charge the amount typical for your genre: co-op/friend-slot games hover around $10, incremental games $3-5, complex simulation games ~$30. Pricing double the genre norm kills sales and invites negative reviews.

units.title: Always ship with a launch discount
units.detail: Even a 10% launch discount is infinitely better than none for indies; only AAA titles can skip it. A discount plus no day-one DLC/merch avoids the perception of greed that triggers review-bombs.

units.title: Over-monetized launch reads as greedy
units.detail: Shipping a $20 game with $10 of DLC and a $30 plushy at launch, while genre rivals charge $10 with none of it, angered players and produced negative reviews. Dropping the price after launch then infuriated early buyers further.

units.title: Estimate wishlists from Steam followers
units.detail: Steam follower counts are public; the follower-to-wishlist ratio is roughly 10:1. ~11k followers ≈ 110k wishlists, which would rank ~199th among ~4,400 upcoming Steam games.

units.title: Refund rates spike after disappointing launches
units.detail: Typical refund rate is 5-15%, but angry launches (The Day Before) can reach ~90% refunds. Review counts overstate sales success when massive refunds follow, so a 'decent' review count can still mean financial failure.

units.title: Workshop/UGC needs a solid base game first
units.detail: Games like RimWorld and Terraria thrive on workshop content, but only because their base game is already substantial. Don't ship a barebones game hoping players build the rest; add mod support after a decent base exists.

units.title: Animations imported inside FBX are read-only in Unity
units.detail: Animations embedded in an FBX file cannot be edited (delete/move keys) in Unity. Fix by duplicating the animation (Ctrl+D or Edit > Duplicate) so it becomes a standalone editable animation file outside the FBX.

units.title: Unity cannot natively edit humanoid animations
units.detail: Dragging humanoid bones in the scene view does not record keyframes; only editing body-part fields in the animation window works, which is unusable as a workflow. Edit humanoid animations in Blender or with the Umotion asset.

units.title: Input System jitter from FixedUpdate polling mismatch
units.detail: The Input System package defaults to processing events in FixedUpdate, which runs less often than Update. Reading ReadValue() every Update then returns stale 0,0 values and causes jerky camera/player movement even with constant mouse input.

units.title: Set Input System to process events in Dynamic Update
units.detail: In Edit > Project Settings > Input System Package > Update Mode, select 'Process Events in Dynamic Update' so input is refreshed every frame. This eliminates stuttering for movement and mouse-look code that polls each Update.

units.title: When stuck, identify exactly what you don't understand
units.detail: Comments like 'it doesn't work' or 'I didn't understand anything' are unanswerable. Pinpoint the specific object, line, error, or concept first; you learn faster by isolating what you don't know before asking for help.

units.title: Import only assets you actually use
units.detail: Importing huge asset bundles bloats a project and slows opening/compiling. In a throwaway test project, find the asset you need, then export just that asset (plus its textures/materials) as a single .unitypackage into your main project.

units.title: Assembly definitions speed up compilation
units.detail: Splitting code into multiple assemblies means Unity recompiles only changed assemblies instead of the whole codebase on every edit. Essential for large projects; covered via asmdef files.

units.title: Prefer a Timer class with delegates over coroutines
units.detail: Coroutines force a rigid pattern: IEnumerator return type, yield return, StartCoroutine, and a MonoBehaviour host. A simple Timer class taking a delegate and firing after N seconds is more flexible and reusable for one-shot delayed actions.

units.title: Use Animator Any State for interruptible animations
units.detail: Transitions from Any State fire regardless of the current state, so a shoot action can restart the shoot animation even while it's still playing. Any State makes animations responsive to player input (e.g., cancelable attacks).

units.title: Learn by remaking tiny classic games
units.detail: Remake lots of extremely simple games (Snake, Arkanoid, Pong, Flappy Bird, Pac-Man, Missile Command) to learn through quantity. Building ~40 small games teaches far more than one giant project for beginners.

units.title: LookAt is a simple alternative to quaternion rotation
units.detail: transform.LookAt(position) does the same as setting transform.forward, just taking a target position instead of a direction. It's a clean alternative to confusing quaternion math when rotating an object toward something.

units.title: Steam page should signal an experienced dev
units.detail: The store page's job is to create the illusion of a deep, complex, competent game made by an experienced developer, not an asset-flip or first project. Show gameplay, depth, and polish in every element.

units.title: Screenshots must show the gameplay loop and UI
units.detail: Show the core loop with visible UI: getting resources, crafting, tech trees, fighting bosses. UI reveals depth instantly (health, money, damage meters). Prefer ~5 excellent screenshots over many repetitive ones; the first 4 become the hover preview.

units.title: Capsule art doubles as streamer thumbnails
units.detail: Streamers reuse your capsule as their video thumbnail, so a strong capsule increases the odds they pick your game. Provide layered PSD/separated-frame assets so creators can easily build compelling thumbnails around your art.

units.title: Capsule art must follow genre conventions
units.detail: Don't be unique in capsule art; signal your genre. Spaceship games need a prominent ship with afterburners ('spaceship ass'), open-world games need a character viewing the world below. Study successful games in your genre and borrow their visual signals.

units.title: How Steam shoppers actually evaluate a game
units.detail: Observed shopping behavior: people rapidly click through screenshots or read the short description first; the trailer is only watched if they're already interested, then they scroll to the long description. Short description is scanned for keywords that signal the gameplay they want.

units.title: Steam visibility marketing is mostly free
units.detail: You don't need paid ads to get Steam visibility; most store-page work (screenshots, capsule, description, dev logs, YouTube) is free. Spend effort on page quality rather than assuming marketing requires budget.

units.title: NullReferenceException means accessing a null reference
units.detail: C# objects are reference types: a variable stores a reference (pointer) to memory, not the object. Accessing a member with '.' on a variable set to null throws NullReferenceException; errors only occur when you try to use the null object.

units.title: Four-step process to fix any NullReferenceException
units.detail: 1) Go to the offending line from the stack trace. 2) Analyze which objects on that line could be null. 3) Add Debug.Log/Console.WriteLine before the line to see stored values. 4) Decide the fix: null-check it, or trace backwards to where it should have been assigned.

units.title: Transform.Find is case-sensitive
units.detail: Transform.Find(name) returns null when the name doesn't match exactly, including case. A lowercase 'helmet' in code vs 'Helmet' in the hierarchy silently returns null and causes a NullReferenceException. Match names character-for-character.

units.title: Local variable shadows field, leaving field null
units.detail: Re-declaring a field's name with its type inside a method ('Transform circleVisualTransform = ...') creates a local variable that shadows the member field; the field is never set and stays null. In VS, Ctrl+Shift+Up/Down highlights all references to spot the shadowed one.

units.title: Unassigned serialized field causes runtime NRE
units.detail: A [SerializeField] reference that's never dragged into the inspector is null at runtime. If the design requires the reference, the fix is simply to drag it in the editor rather than add a null-check.

units.title: Use debugger breakpoints to inspect variable values
units.detail: Set a breakpoint in Visual Studio to pause execution; the debug windows show the exact value of each variable (e.g., confirming a reference is null). An advanced alternative to Debug.Log, useful for stepping through code line by line.

units.title: 3D item inspect view via RenderTexture + dedicated camera
units.detail: Render a spawned 3D prefab with a separate camera into a RenderTexture, then display it in UI. Spawn the object far away (1000,1000,1000), destroy the previous instance on selection, and set the raw image's texture to the render texture.

units.title: Raw Image required for RenderTexture display
units.detail: Unity's Image component only accepts Sprites, so a RenderTexture must go on a Raw Image component instead. This is why the inspect view uses Raw Image rather than Image.

units.title: Rotate inspected object with IDragHandler delta
units.detail: Implement IDragHandler to receive PointerEventData.delta (mouse movement this frame) and add it to the object's Euler angles. Map delta.x to Y rotation and delta.y to X rotation (with a minus to match drag direction) for natural drag-to-rotate.

units.title: Ctrl+Shift+F snaps camera to scene view
units.detail: Position the scene camera where you want the shot, select the camera object, press Ctrl+Shift+F to place the camera at the scene view's exact position/rotation. Copy the transform component and paste values after leaving Play Mode to keep the setup.

units.title: Entity field + GenerateAuthoringComponent converts prefabs
