units.detail: Create an IComponentData struct with an Entity field and add [GenerateAuthoringComponent]. The generated authoring component exposes a GameObject field in the inspector; a ConvertToEntity script automatically converts it to an entity at runtime.

units.title: IConvertGameObjectToEntity with conversion utility
units.detail: Implement IConvertGameObjectToEntity on a MonoBehaviour and call GameObjectConversionUtility.ConvertGameObjectHierarchy(root, settings) inside the Convert() method to manually produce an entity prefab, storing it in a static field for spawner systems.

units.title: IDeclareReferencedPrefabs registers converted prefabs
units.detail: Implement IDeclareReferencedPrefabs to add prefab GameObjects to a reference list, then in IConvertGameObjectToEntity use ConversionSystem.GetPrimaryEntity(prefabGO) to fetch the already-converted entity prefab.

units.title: Four ways to store a converted entity prefab
units.detail: Store the converted entity in an IComponentData component (requires querying it), a static field (accessible anywhere), a singleton via GetSingleton<T> (for the single-prefab case), or a blob asset for more complex data. DOTS is in preview so best practices aren't settled.

units.title: One hour daily beats seven hours on weekends
units.detail: Spending ~30-60 minutes every day is far more effective for retaining knowledge than cramming 7 hours into one weekend. Consistency and daily exposure make material stick; adapt the chunk to your schedule.

units.title: Experiment to find your productive schedule
units.detail: There's no universal best time to work. Try mornings before work (e.g., 6-8am), lunch breaks, or nights, and keep what fits your brain; one person's night-owl shift can be another's burnout. The author found morning work far outperformed evening work for them.

units.title: Learn by watching, then applying in an empty project
units.detail: For any new topic: watch tutorials/docs, then open an empty project and write code immediately. E.g., for voxels: make one cube, multiply it by a thousand, find performance issues, then add/remove voxels. You only learn by doing, not by passively watching.

units.title: Post Steam announcement at release
units.detail: Immediately after releasing, post a Steam announcement so followers get a client popup and wishlist owners get an email. Post it from your developer page to notify followers across all your games at once.

units.title: Publish trailer and launch posts
units.detail: Make the game trailer public on YouTube and post simple 'game is out' messages with the trailer link on Facebook and Twitter. Impact scales with your audience size, and pinning the post builds an archival record of releases.

units.title: Send keys via influencer platforms
units.detail: Use a service like Keymailer to send Steam keys to YouTubers and Twitch streamers, seeing their stats and deciding per-influencer instead of maintaining a manual list.

units.title: Key sellers abuse free key requests
units.detail: Many who request Steam keys just resell them on third-party sites. Set a minimum threshold (e.g. 10k+ subscribers) before sending keys to limit your keys ending up on gray markets.

units.title: Build a press list and pitch
units.detail: Create your own list of press covering your genre (e.g. Rock Paper Shotgun for PC) and email short descriptions with trailer links. Model your release on other indie press releases; coverage is rare but can broaden reach.

units.title: Email your mailing list at launch
units.detail: Send an email to your biggest fans (signups from a website form or in-game) with a call to action to buy at launch. Launch-day purchases increase store visibility, which drives more sales.

units.title: Curator Connect sends direct copies
units.detail: Steam's curator system delivers the game straight to a curator's account rather than as a key, so copies can't be resold on the black market. It's the safest way to reach reviewers.

units.title: Only 100 curator copies available
units.detail: You get only ~100 curator copies, so don't send to everyone. Target curators whose genre matches your game—wasting a copy on a mismatched reviewer (e.g. visual novel curator for an action game) loses the opportunity.

units.title: Read and reply to reviews
units.detail: Monitor early reviews for hidden game-breaking bugs, fix and ship updates fast (Steam updates are free). Reply professionally since your reply is an official developer statement, and mine negative reviews for improvement ideas.

units.title: Re-engage early-access reviewers
units.detail: At full release, reply to old early-access reviews letting people know the game is significantly improved and fully released. Some will retry and convert negative reviews to positive ones, improving your score.

units.title: Monitor cloud diagnostics post-launch
units.detail: Use a crash/error reporting dashboard to see what failures players hit even when they don't send logs. Deduce the cause from error stacks and player feedback, or add safeguards so the error can't break the game.

units.title: Showcase player workshop items
units.detail: If you implemented a workshop highlight widget that rotates items from a collection, keep updating that collection as players create items so new creations appear in-game automatically.

units.title: Sell on multiple stores
units.detail: Beyond Steam, submit to Humble (easy approval, good dashboard for weekly sales, embeddable widget) and GOG (curated, requires DRM-free—keep Steam integration easily removable). Add other stores to maximize reach.

units.title: Write store text as player benefits
units.detail: Write short, punchy sentences from the player's perspective. Instead of '10 weapons', say 'destroy your enemies with 10 different weapons'. Add animated GIFs to grab attention.

units.title: Keep trailer 60-90 seconds
units.detail: Make the trailer brief, getting to action and hooking viewers in the first 10 seconds—never open with 30 seconds of studio branding. Fast-paced music should match the game's feel (fast for action, complexity for tycoon).

units.title: Use 5-6 clean gameplay screenshots
units.detail: Keep screenshots few but varied, hide the UI, and show pure gameplay only—Steam requires screenshots to feature just gameplay without added elements.

units.title: Choose niche Steam tags
units.detail: Tags drive store placement and recommendations, and devs get extra weight in their own tags. Avoid hyper-competitive ones like 'indie' and pick accurate niche tags where your game can rank on the tag's new-release page.

units.title: Implement all feasible Steam features
units.detail: Add achievements (a must for some players), stats, leaderboards, and Steam Cloud for saves/options. Trading cards help a long sales tail but may require reaching a sales threshold before you can add them.

units.title: Trading cards gated by threshold
units.detail: New games may not be allowed trading cards until they reach a certain sales/engagement threshold. Plan to add them later when eligible since card collectors contribute to a long tail.

units.title: Pre-populate the Workshop
units.detail: Add your own workshop items before release so players have content to play with at launch, and create an official guide with instructions for complex modding (e.g. Lua scripting for custom quests).

units.title: Design for localization from the start
units.detail: Always fetch strings from a central class/method instead of hard-coding, so adding languages is just adding translations. Supporting more languages can double or triple sales.

units.title: Make gameplay framerate-independent
units.detail: Use Application.targetFrameRate and verify the game is still fully playable at ~10 FPS so players on weak machines aren't broken. Game logic must never depend on framerate.

units.title: Test all resolutions and anchor UI
units.detail: Test at multiple aspect ratios (e.g. 16:9 and 5:4). Anchor UI to the correct corners; centering everything breaks layouts on more square resolutions.

units.title: Use a first-frame loading safety message
units.detail: Show an error/contact message on the very first frame and hide it only after successful load completes. If loading fails, the message stays visible so players know something went wrong and how to reach you.

units.title: Automate localization testing
units.detail: Write a script that switches the language every second while playing so you can see all text change correctly, and verify special-character fonts (Chinese, Korean) render properly.

units.title: Ship a changelog file
units.detail: Store a changelog (version, date, changes) inside the game folder and mirror it on a pinned forum thread so players can see what changed each update.

units.title: Launch with a 10-20% discount
units.detail: Launch with a 10-20% discount. Launching at full price is hard to succeed at unless you're AAA, and the discount can help launch-week visibility.

units.title: Dash as instant teleport
units.detail: Implement a dash as an instant position change toward the last move direction by a fixed distance, triggered on a key press, rather than continuous movement.

units.title: Instant teleports pass through walls
units.detail: A plain transform.position jump ignores colliders, so the player dashes through walls. Fix by raycasting from the position toward the dash direction and only moving if the path is clear.

units.title: Separate CanMove from TryMove
units.detail: Refactor movement into a CanMove(direction, distance) raycast check and a TryMove(direction, distance) helper that handles diagonal/horizontal/vertical component movement. Reusing TryMove lets the dash inherit wall-checking automatically.

units.title: Spawn effect at pre-dash position
units.detail: Store the position before dashing, and if the dash move succeeds, instantiate a one-shot sprite-animation effect there, rotating it toward the move direction and scaling it to the dash distance divided by sprite width.

units.title: Short dash into wall doesn't move
units.detail: When dash distance exceeds wall proximity, the player doesn't move forward at all. Improve by raycasting to the wall, measuring distance, and reducing the dash travel to stop right next to it.

units.title: Dash vs dodge roll difference
units.detail: A dash is an instant teleport while a dodge roll is a slide—movement animated over several frames. Choose the approach based on the intended feel and animation needs.

units.title: State machine for character abilities
units.detail: Use an enum state (Normal, DodgeRollSliding) switched in Update: normal state runs normal movement, sliding state runs the roll and returns to Normal when speed decays to near zero.

units.title: Slide toward mouse world position
units.detail: Set the slide direction as mouse world position minus player position when starting the roll, then move the transform toward it each frame using Time.deltaTime so it is framerate-independent.

units.title: Decay slide speed for natural stop
units.detail: Start with a slide speed and reduce it by itself times a factor and deltaTime each frame; when it drops below a threshold, transition back to the normal state so the roll ends smoothly.

units.title: Reuse TryMove for sliding collision
units.detail: Route the dodge-roll movement through the same TryMove function used by movement/dash so the slide also respects walls, sliding along them rather than through them.

units.title: Play roll animation on state entry
units.detail: Trigger the dodge roll animation once when entering the sliding state, driven by the slide direction, so the visual matches the actual movement.

units.title: RTS unit selection via OverlapBox
units.detail: For drag-box selection, compute the lower-left and upper-right corners from the click and call a physics OverlapBox to return every collider (unit) inside. Simple and fast.

units.title: Flow field pathfinding for thousands of units
units.detail: A* computes a path per unit and gets expensive with many units. Flow fields compute directions to a single endpoint once, then every unit just follows the field—ideal when you have thousands of entities (e.g. zombie hordes).

units.title: Fog of war with camera + render texture
units.detail: Point a camera down at the world, draw circle sprites per unit/building the camera only sees, and render to a texture drawn over the world. Set the camera to 'don't clear' so explored areas persist and the texture grows over time.

units.title: Grid-based vs freeform building placement
units.detail: Place buildings by spawning a prefab at the mouse position; the key design decision is whether placement snaps to a grid or is freeform—both are valid, so decide based on your game's feel.

units.title: Scriptable objects define building data
units.detail: Represent building types (cost, build time, stats) as ScriptableObjects instead of per-instance data. They're great for any structured data like crafting recipes or weapon parts.

units.title: Resource manager with dictionary
units.detail: Store resource amounts in a dictionary keyed by resource type. On building placement, ask the manager if resources suffice, and only spend them if affordable. Dumb-but-simple and extensible.

units.title: Two resource generation models
units.detail: Resources can be gathered manually by villager units (Age of Empires style) or generated automatically by buildings on a timer. Both are valid; pick based on your design intent and AI complexity.

units.title: C# Queue for unit spawn queue
units.detail: When a building queues unit production, store pending units in a C# Queue (FIFO). A simple timer ticks the queue: when the current unit's time elapses, spawn the prefab and dequeue the next.

units.title: Timed event hordes
units.detail: A horde attack is just spawning many enemies at preset positions at preset times. Level designers define which day spawns which horde (composition via ScriptableObject: slow/fast/big counts); a simple day/time float triggers it via a C# event.

units.title: Simple zombie AI as design shortcut
units.detail: Zombie AI is trivially simple: follow a path toward a target, and while moving, physics-query for nearby targets to stop and attack. If compelling enemy AI is hard, swap human enemies for zombies—it simplifies AI requirements drastically.

units.title: Villager gatherer AI loop
units.detail: A gatherer just needs to know the selected point, then alternate between a resource point and a drop-off point, gathering and depositing. The core loop is moving between two points with state.

units.title: Procedural map generation options
units.detail: Maps can be hand-placed (preferred for campaigns) or procedurally generated via stacking noise textures or wave-function-collapse-style random point placement. Choose based on whether you need authored missions or skirmish variety.

units.title: Performance is the RTS core challenge
units.detail: RTS means hundreds/thousands of units, so performance is always on your mind: learn the profiler, use for-loops over foreach, avoid per-frame garbage, prefer structs over classes, and consider DOTS for data-oriented performance.

units.title: Parkour = hold points + closest match
units.detail: Climbing/ledge-grabbing is logically simple: define hold points (markers with a ScriptableObject of data), physics-query for nearby ones matching player input, pick the closest, and pick the matching animation. The real cost is content—hundreds of animations and edge cases.

units.title: Inverse kinematics for dynamic animation
units.detail: Static animation libraries can't cover every hand/ledge position, so layer IK on top to make grabs land exactly. Unity's built-in Animation Rigging package does this and is great for making animations dynamic.

units.title: Highlight system via interfaces or events
units.detail: Two ways to build an eagle-vision highlight: (1) physics-query around the player and toggle highlight on objects implementing an interface, or (2) player fires an event and nearby listeners highlight themselves. Interfaces let you treat chests, enemies, and objects uniformly.

units.title: Post-processing desaturation for vision mode
units.detail: For a 'detect' vision mode, desaturate the whole scene with a post-processing volume and render highlighted objects with a distinct shader/outline (e.g. switch an outline color from black to white when interactive).

units.title: Eagle-eye cursor via raycast + spherecast
units.detail: Find the 3D point under the cursor with a raycast to terrain, then spherecast around that point to find anything interactable within an area and tag it. Great for bird/remote-view targeting.

units.title: Show tagged markers through walls
units.detail: World-space UI markers get occluded. Fix by using a material/shader that doesn't write depth, or an overlay/stencil camera that renders only the UI layer on top of the main camera.

units.title: Map reveal via mask blend
units.detail: Keep locked and unlocked map textures and blend them with a mask texture that you update per synchronized tower. Animate the reveal with a grayscale-driven shader transition.

units.title: Interaction system with interface
units.detail: Give every interactable a collider and an interactable interface. The player does an overlap sphere, filters implementers, picks the closest, shows the input prompt, and triggers its interaction—covering assassination, looting, talking, and more.

units.title: Stealth enemy state machine
units.detail: Enemy AI is a simple state machine: Idle (patrol) → Investigate → Attack. Detect via spherecast (more forgiving than exact raycast) plus a Vector3.Dot angle check so the player behind isn't detected. Track the last known position; if not found after a timeout, return to Idle.

units.title: Alert other enemies via spherecast
units.detail: When one enemy spots the player, spherecast around its position to find nearby allies and tell them to attack the same position, creating coordinated enemy behavior cheaply.

units.title: Virtual cursor with input system
units.detail: Gamepad menu navigation works well with a virtual cursor that moves over and identifies objects, using the input system. Feels more intuitive than button-to-button navigation.

units.title: Play video previews via Video Player
units.detail: Show 'what this skill does' clips in menus by rendering a video onto a texture/material with the Unity Video Player—'show, don't tell' improves tutorial and skill UI.

units.title: Store UI text as localized ScriptableObjects
units.detail: Loading-screen hints, codex, and database entries are just text/images: store them as ScriptableObjects and use localized strings so the same content auto-translates across languages.

units.title: Link accounts to identify users
units.detail: For a live-stream viewer overlay, require users to link their YouTube account to your website account so you can map chat users to custom characters during the stream.

units.title: Character customization via tinting pixels
units.detail: Implement simple customization (skin/hair/beard) by tinting pixels of specific colors and copy-pasting parts between sprite sheets, instead of authoring every combination.

units.title: User-drawn texture template
units.detail: Let users draw onto a downloaded base texture with fixed squares per sprite (head down/right/up, hands, feet). Validating sprites manually in an admin page prevents inappropriate content from appearing on stream.

units.title: Fetch live chat data via HTTP from Unity
units.detail: The overlay polls chat data from Unity with HTTP requests to a server/YouTube API, driving mesh-based character animations and transparent UI (e.g. transparent TextMeshPro windows).

units.title: Minimal playable game loop
units.detail: A first game only needs a jumpable player, an obstacle moving across the screen, and collision-based game-over that reloads the scene. Even a basic loop like this counts as a real game and a valid learning milestone.

units.title: Impulse force for jump
units.detail: Add jump by applying an upward impulse force to a Rigidbody on input (e.g. ForceMode.Impulse with Vector3.up) rather than manually setting velocity, so physics handles the arc.

units.title: Trigger-based score zones
units.detail: Score by placing invisible trigger colliders between obstacles; on trigger enter, increment a score exposed through a simple singleton. This avoids destroying anything and keeps scoring decoupled.

units.title: Prefab and duplicate obstacles
units.detail: Turn obstacles and score zones into prefabs, then duplicate and position them to build the level. Prefabs make tuning and iterating on the obstacle design instant.

units.title: Avoid evergreen comps from less competitive eras
units.detail: Never benchmark against old evergreen hits: Terraria (2011, 1M+ reviews) came from an era of far less competition and still gets updates. Indie market moves fast, so advice/data from 5 years ago may no longer apply; use recent releases within roughly the last year.

units.title: Risk profiles differ for publishers vs self-funded devs
units.detail: Publishers diversify a portfolio so a few flops are fine if some are hits, while a solo dev betting years on one game needs a much more conservative estimate plus a plan B (contract work). When pitching publishers, be optimistically framed but not delusionally so.

units.title: Get Steam page up as early as possible
units.detail: Time is the most impactful marketing lever: the earlier your public Steam page is live, the more time you have to accumulate wishlists, which build up over time. Most impactful thing in marketing is simply time.

units.title: Steam Next Fest and free prologues for wishlists
units.detail: Participating in Steam festivals can gather huge wishlist volume (though it converts worse than organic wishlists). A well-designed free prologue/demo that leaves players wanting more reliably converts to wishlists.

units.title: Diversify marketing channels by game type
units.detail: Use YouTube devlogs or entertaining clips (match style to your personality and game), subreddits targeting your specific audience (mind self-promo rules), TikTok/Instagram shorts, and gifs for Twitter/Imgur even if results are limited. The goal is attention.

units.title: Build an email mailing list
units.detail: Keep a signup form on your website and mention it whenever you mention the game. Subscribers are already pre-interested, so the list is hard to grow but very powerful for launch.

units.title: Paid marketing needs higher price to make sense
units.detail: Paid ads depend on funds and game price: a $5 game can barely justify paid marketing, but at $15-20 it becomes much more viable. The alternative to doing marketing is getting no sales.

units.title: Five price tiers for indie games
units.detail: Tiers: free, $3-5, $10-15, $20+, and free-with-microtransactions. Free = learning/feedback for first game. $3-5 = impulse-buy experimentation. $10-15 = solo/small-team sweet spot competing with Terraria/FTL. $20+ = top-tier team games with IGN-level polish. MTX = extremely hard, mostly mobile-only.

units.title: Price according to content and genre saturation
units.detail: At $10-15 players expect ~10 hours of quality, polished, bug-free content plus a clear marketing strategy. At $3-5 the game still must be unique (cheap doesn't excuse boring). A unique niche can charge more; crowded genres like platformers cannot.

units.title: Physics pickup/drop via camera raycast
units.detail: Fire a Physics.Raycast from the camera's position and forward (not the player's transform, whose origin sits at the feet), within a pickup distance, using a layer mask that excludes the player layer so you don't have to tag every object.

units.title: Grab point child of camera vs player
units.detail: Design choice: child the hold transform to the camera (object rotates with your view, feels glued) vs child to the player controller (object stays put while looking around; controller must rotate to face look direction). Pick per game feel.

units.title: Smooth rigidbody carry with Lerp + MovePosition
units.detail: In FixedUpdate, move the carried rigidbody toward the target with Vector3.Lerp(current, target, Time.deltaTime * ~10) and set useGravity=false while held. Set rigidbody Interpolate = yes for extra smoothness.

units.title: Jitter when pushing a carried object
units.detail: A carried rigidbody trembles when it collides with the player because it still has velocity fighting the script's movement. Fix by raising rigidbody drag (~5) or lerping velocity toward zero; alternatively use isKinematic while held, but then physics forces won't apply (object passes through colliders).

units.title: Toggle grab/drop with null state check
units.detail: Use TryGetComponent<ObjectGrabbable> on raycast hit to identify grab targets; store a currentObject field. In the input handler, if currentObject is null attempt to grab, else call Drop() and clear the field. Refactorable into an interface for varied pickup behaviors.

units.title: Refactor tiny pieces with constant testing
units.detail: Refactoring must not change behavior. Instead of reworking 1,000 lines at once, change one small piece at a time and test continuously so any breakage is immediately found (just undo to the last working state).

units.title: Refactor vs complete restructuring
units.detail: Small refactors = reorganizing one system without behavior change. Complete restructuring/rewrite = ignoring old code and rebuilding; only then keep old files or commented-out code until the new version fully works, then delete it. Most refactors are the small kind.

units.title: Refactor continuously to avoid technical debt
units.detail: Technical debt accumulates as you add features on top of messy code until adding anything new breaks everything else. Constantly ask 'can I write this better?' and clean up before moving forward, or productivity collapses on complex projects.

units.title: Quantity of sufficient quality over one masterpiece
units.detail: Long-term indie viability comes from shipping many small games of sufficient quality (Cliff Harris, Jeff Vogel model) rather than gambling 5 years on one Stardew Valley-tier hit. Lower the risk so you can keep doing it for a decade.

units.title: Keep burn rate as low as possible
units.detail: A 6-month game costs $24k at $4k/month but only $6k at $1k/month - the difference between needing ~5,000 vs ~500 sales to break even. Low living costs and small budgets make profitability dramatically more achievable; a $350+10-month game can easily profit.

units.title: Small polished scope over 40 hours of mediocrity
units.detail: Players prefer a tight 2-hour quality experience that leaves them wanting more over a huge buggy mess. Keep at least ~2 hours of excellent content so refund-window players stay happy, but don't undershoot to a single hour.

units.title: Early Access is for feedback, not funding
units.detail: Expect only a few hundred to ~1,000 copies in Early Access with no funding; don't bet on it financing completion. Players now demand final-game polish even in EA. The Steam review score is your most valuable asset - a single negative review stays forever, even if the bug is fixed in 30 minutes.

units.title: Harvest the long tail, discount slowly
units.detail: Old games keep selling a little each month; over 10 years a catalog adds up meaningfully. Discount slowly (25% first 6 months, 50% year two, 75% later) and avoid $1 bundles that pay ~10 cents/copy and permanently devalue the game.

units.title: Spend as much time marketing as developing
units.detail: If you only develop, nobody will see your game. Aim to match dev time with marketing (devlogs, tutorials, TikTok/Instagram shorts, general social media) - the advice is even more critical now than in 2017, and even non-social devs must do it.

units.title: A better sequel can sell far worse
units.detail: Survivor Squad's sequel was better in every way and took more time/art money, yet sold ~1/10th as much - the first benefited from early Greenlight-era timing. Expect a flop after a hit and keep a safety strategy; don't reinvest everything into the next game.

units.title: Swap character mesh: renderer, bones, avatar
units.detail: To retarget a new character onto an existing controller, change the SkinnedMeshRenderer, swap in the new character's bones, and assign the new mesh's avatar. Only these three steps are needed.

units.title: Duplicate breaking avatar bone mapping
units.detail: Duplicating a character renames the bone hierarchy (e.g., 'root' becomes 'root (1)'), and avatars map by exact GameObject name, so animations stop and the character T-poses. Fix: rename the bones to match the avatar's expected names and verify the SkinnedMeshRenderer's root bone reference.

units.title: Mixamo import checklist for retargeting
units.detail: For Mixamo characters, set the FBX rig Animation Type to Humanoid and click Apply before dragging into the scene, then follow the swap checklist: humanoid rig, correct skin mesh root-bone reference, exact bone names, and the new avatar assigned.

units.title: Pack JSON data + PNG screenshot into one save file
units.detail: Convert the JSON save string to bytes with Encoding.Unicode.GetBytes and append the PNG bytes into a single byte array written as one file. On load, ReadAllBytes and reconstruct - but you need byte boundaries to split them.

units.title: Header-based save file format with byte sizes
units.detail: Store a serialized header (containing JSON byte size) and make the first 2 bytes a ushort (BitConverter.GetBytes) holding the header size. On load, read the ushort, parse the header JSON, slice the JSON bytes, and treat the remainder as the image.

units.title: Screenshot capture differs between render pipelines
units.detail: OnPostRender works only on the built-in pipeline; on URP/scriptable pipelines you must hook a RenderPipelineManager callback instead. The rest (RenderTexture, ReadPixels, EncodeToPNG) is identical.

units.title: Screenshot can come from any camera
units.detail: The captured image doesn't have to be the player's view: use a second camera for a character/equipment shot, an overhead city view, or anything else. Keep the header class extensible so you can add fields like save date later.

units.title: Call Unity from JS via SendMessage
units.detail: Use unityInstance.SendMessage('objectName', 'methodName', value) in HTML/JavaScript. The target object must have a matching script, and the optional value can be a number or string - enough to pass any data, since strings can hold JSON.

units.title: Pass structured data into WebGL via JSON strings
units.detail: Stringify a JS object with JSON.stringify and pass it to a Unity method that parses with JsonUtility.FromJson, then use it to drive visuals. PHP can feed this too via json_encode + echo, enabling a Unity WebGL build to visualize live external data.

units.title: ML-Agents beats classic AI for evolving games
units.detail: Machine learning beats hand-coded bots when games change often: adding a mechanic (e.g., 4-match explosion) requires no AI code changes, just retraining. In a fixed game classic AI is simpler, but ML shines for continuously updated games and for giving stuck players hints.

units.title: Bridge custom game to ML-Agents via abstract Board
units.detail: Implement the match-3 extension's abstract Board class (rows, columns, cell types, special types) with GetCellType, GetSpecialType, IsMoveValid, and MakeMove, mapping your game types to ints. The built-in sensor and actuator then work with any match-3 game that exposes simple events and functions.

units.title: Handle invalid moves requested during training
units.detail: The ML trainer may request a move that is invalid; your MakeMove implementation must tolerate that without crashing. Also watch for the weird action-mask initialization error - loading another scene and returning fixes it.

units.title: Design rewards to match game goals
units.detail: Give rewards aligned with actual scoring (e.g., per gem destroyed; per glass destroyed on glass levels) and add a negative per-move reward when speed matters so the AI minimizes turns. End episodes on running out of moves or winning, reloading the scene to replay.

units.title: Test heuristics, then train in parallel builds
units.detail: Verify the setup by forcing heuristics (built into the actuator) before training. For speed, build a server build (no rendering) and run multiple environments in parallel; reuse a previous model via initializeFrom to make the AI learn a new mechanic quickly.

units.title: Detect nearby interactables with physics overlap query
units.detail: Instead of keeping a list of transform references to every NPC and checking distances (which doesn't scale to hundreds of objects), query the physics world once with an overlap sphere around the player and filter results by component. Objects without colliders are invisible to physics queries, so interactables must have colliders.

units.title: Prefer component filtering over layer masks
units.detail: Layer masks work but the engine caps you at 32 layers, which you can exhaust with many object types. Query all objects and filter the returned colliders by checking for an interactable component instead, so new object types don't consume layers.

units.title: Interfaces decouple player from interactable types
units.detail: A chain of if/type checks in the player (NPC, door, button) tightly couples the player script to every interactable type and breaks on reuse. Define a common IInteractable interface (Interact(transform), GetInteractText, GetTransform) and have all objects implement it so the player code stays one generic check.

units.title: Prioritize the closest of multiple interactables
units.detail: Overlap results depend on physics-world order, not proximity, so with two NPCs in range the wrong one can win. Collect all matching interactables, then loop and track whichever has the shortest distance to the player and return that one.

units.title: Tightly-coupled interaction code needs rewriting per new type
units.detail: Adding door and button support via explicit component checks works but forces you to edit the player script every time you add an interactable, and the script breaks if reused in a game without doors/buttons. This is the exact scenario where a shared interface pays off.

units.title: Point-in-hex test combines bounds and dot products
units.detail: First test horizontal bounds (x between the side corners), then vertical bounds (z between top/bottom corners), then for each diagonal take the corner-to-corner direction, rotate it 90 degrees to get the perpendicular, and dot-product it with the direction from the corner to the test point; positive on all sides means inside.

units.title: Dot product classifies a point against a line
units.detail: The dot product of the perpendicular of a line direction and the direction toward a test point is positive on one side of the line and negative on the other (near +1/-1 when aligned). This is the same primitive used to detect if an object is behind another.

units.title: Perpendicular rotation sign depends on axis convention
units.detail: When computing the 90-degree perpendicular vectors for each hex diagonal, the sign of the rotation angle must be flipped per corner because the rotation direction (clockwise vs counter-clockwise) differs per side; getting a sign wrong inverts which side registers as inside.

units.title: Hex geometry derives corners from half-size
units.detail: Store only half-size and center, then derive corners: top/bottom are center offset by half-size; side corners are center offset by half-size horizontally and a quarter-size (half the half-size) vertically. Reusing derived values keeps corner definitions consistent.

units.title: Serialize object to JSON to debug many fields at once
units.detail: Instead of a Debug.Log per field, convert the whole data structure to JSON and log it once to quickly verify computed values like hex corners. Same pattern works for any debugging of nested data.

units.title: Throttle path tracking with timer and distance gate
units.detail: Recording a position every frame floods the list with redundant points (60/sec). Sample on a fixed interval (e.g. 0.2s) and only add the new point when it's farther than a minimum distance from the last recorded one so standing still adds nothing.

units.title: Guard against empty-list on first path sample
units.detail: Reading the last element of the path list before any point was added throws an error. Initialize the list with the starting position in Start() before Update() begins sampling.

units.title: Raise LineRenderer above the floor for minimap visibility
units.detail: A path drawn flat on the floor is invisible to a top-down minimap camera. Apply a constant Y offset to every recorded position before feeding the LineRenderer so the line renders cleanly above the geometry.

units.title: Dashed path texture needs repeat mode and tile mode
units.detail: For dot/dash path visuals the texture's wrap mode must be Repeat (Clamp breaks it) and the LineRenderer texture mode must be Tile rather than Stretch, otherwise the texture is stretched once across the whole path. Tune the texture scale for dash density.

units.title: Edit-mode tweaks are lost when leaving play mode
units.detail: Component changes made during play revert on stop. To keep line/path visual settings, right-click the component, Copy Component, stop, then right-click Paste Component Values.

units.title: Short-term and long-term path via capped list
units.detail: Maintain two lists: a complete path and a short path capped at N points by removing the oldest element (RemoveAt(0)) when it exceeds the cap. The short path naturally fades as the player moves, giving both recent and whole-playthrough views from one recording loop.

units.title: Persist path with JSON and PlayerPrefs
units.detail: Serialize a save object holding the tracker position and both path lists to JSON and store it under a named PlayerPrefs key (use a constant, not a raw string). On load, restore lists, teleport the player via its controller's teleport method (not transform directly) and refresh the visual.

units.title: Central tick system instead of per-object timers
units.detail: Run one periodic timer on a single object and fire a static event on each tick; other objects subscribe and act on it. This keeps timed logic (construction, resource generation) out of hundreds of Updates, improving performance, and even works for non-MonoBehaviour objects.

units.title: Event carries tick value via EventArgs subclass
units.detail: Publish events as EventHandler with a custom EventArgs subclass holding the current tick, letting subscribers read the count without touching the source. Fire only when there are subscribers.

units.title: Derive slower tick rates with modulo
units.detail: For actions needed less often than the base tick, fire a second event when tick % N == 0 (e.g. every 5th tick), giving you multiple periodicities from a single clock instead of more timers.

units.title: Clean code means easy to understand and modify
units.detail: Define clean code as code that is easy to understand and easy to modify; everything else (performance, style) is a separate concern. You spend roughly 10x more time reading code than writing it, so readability is the highest-value investment.

units.title: Naming is the highest-impact clean code practice
units.detail: Good names are architecture: a variable named 'dsc' is unreadable a month later when context is gone, while 'health', 'Damage()', 'Heal()' read instantly. Naming clearly is the cheapest change that most improves code quality.

units.title: Write for future-you and the maintainer
units.detail: Even solo, you're always at least two people: present-you with full context and future-you without it. Write code as if the person maintaining it knows where you live, so it stays sensible without today's mental context.

units.title: Apply decoupling, single responsibility, information hiding
units.detail: Keep systems as separated as possible so you can focus on one thing at a time; each class/function does one thing; expose as little as possible to reduce mental load. These guidelines make debugging and expanding large projects dramatically easier.

units.title: Keep one source of truth for each piece of data
units.detail: Each piece of game data should live in exactly one place rather than being copied around; duplicated state is a major debugging pain because copies drift out of sync.

units.title: Replace magic numbers and string identifiers
units.detail: Named constants/constants for magic numbers and enums instead of string identifiers prevent typos silently breaking logic and make intent obvious. Prefer composition over overused inheritance, and treat refactoring as a constant iterative process.

units.title: Clean code is a guideline, not a rulebook
units.detail: Clean code is not about performance, impressing others, or a specific book; it's practical guidance. Break a guideline when doing so genuinely makes the code easier to understand and modify.

units.title: General steps for adding modding to any game
units.detail: Players drop files into a mod folder inside the build; the game dynamically loads those files by type; a UI lets players compose mods; the selection is saved to a file; optionally upload it to Steam Workshop or a UGC service. Every game's implementation differs but the pipeline is universal.

units.title: Load mesh/texture/sprite at runtime for mods
units.detail: OBJ meshes are runtime-loadable where FBX is not (Unity has no built-in runtime FBX loader); a free OBJ loader returns a GameObject whose MeshFilter exposes the mesh. Textures load via File.ReadAllBytes into a Texture2D then LoadImage, and a Sprite derives from the texture via Sprite.Create.

units.title: Package mod data into a single byte file
units.detail: Store mesh data (vertices/triangles/uvs) as JSON and combine it with texture, icon, and name bytes into one file with a header describing sizes. Bytes are the universal mod currency, so the same data can save locally or upload to UGC/Workshop.

units.title: Integrate mods through ScriptableObjects
units.detail: Loading mods as runtime-created ScriptableObject instances (e.g. a KitchenObjectSO holding name, icon, prefab) means the rest of the game consumes them like any built-in asset, so all existing systems work with player-made content without changes.

units.title: A mesh is vertices, triangles, and UVs
units.detail: Vertices are positions, triangles connect them into faces, and UVs map texture coordinates per vertex. To display a mesh you assign these arrays to a Mesh and hook it into a MeshFilter plus a MeshRenderer with a material.

units.title: Triangle winding order must be clockwise to face camera
units.detail: Triangle index order determines facing: counter-clockwise triangles are culled (invisible from the front). A quad needs two triangles = six indices sharing the diagonal, ordered clockwise.

units.title: Cinemachine shake via noise profile amplitude
units.detail: Add a Basic Multi-Channel Perlin noise field to the virtual camera and assign a noise profile preset; frequency controls shake speed and amplitude controls how far the camera moves. A script sets amplitude high then decays it back to zero.

units.title: Expose shake via static instance for easy calls
units.detail: Make the shake controller a static instance set in Awake so gameplay scripts call CinemachineShake.Instance.ShakeCamera(intensity, time) from anywhere, keeping the Cinemachine wiring encapsulated.

units.title: Choose hard-stop vs smooth-decay shake by feel
units.detail: Counting the shake timer down then snapping amplitude to zero gives a punchy stop; Mathf.Lerp from starting intensity to zero over the timer gives a smooth falloff. Smooth decay fits explosions/impacts, hard stop fits rapid-fire shots.

units.title: Four methods for character customization
units.detail: From simplest to complex: (1) swap material/texture for reskins, (2) swap the visual mesh to change shape, (3) add parts with regular MeshRenderers parented to bones, (4) add parts with SkinnedMeshRenderers that deform with bones. Which one works depends heavily on how the asset is set up.

units.title: Multi-material characters need every skinned mesh changed
units.detail: Characters made of multiple SkinnedMeshRenderers (one per body part) require swapping the material on every part; changing only one leaves the face and hands visibly different colors.

units.title: Add parts by parenting MeshRenderers to bones
units.detail: Attach a mesh-render part as a child of the target bone (or a pre-made attachment point) and it follows the animation automatically. For misaligned assets, parent an offset object inside a zeroed parent on the bone and prefab the offset wrapper.

units.title: SkinnedMeshRenderer needs exact root bone and bones array
units.detail: Instantiated skinned parts are invisible unless the bones array (invisible in the inspector) and root bone are copied exactly from the source character; even the bone order must match or the visual is missing/mispositioned. Assign both arrays from the base renderer in code.

units.title: MeshRenderer parts don't deform with bones
units.detail: Regular mesh-render parts rigidly follow bones and won't squash/stretch, which looks fine for normal animations but odd for heavy squash-and-stretch; use skinned parts when deformation matters.

units.title: Destroy unused customization parts after selection
units.detail: If the character prefab contains every variant as disabled objects, only show them in the customization screen, then recursively destroy all unselected parts once the player finalizes to cut memory and draw calls.

units.title: Detect behind-target with Vector3.Dot
units.detail: Dot(enemy.forward, directionFromEnemyToPlayer) returns +1 directly in front, 0 at the side, -1 directly behind. Accept a threshold (e.g. within -0.9) to make the backstab check forgiving instead of requiring a perfect 180 degrees.

units.title: Combine direction check with a distance check
units.detail: The dot product alone is direction-only, so a player behind the enemy at any distance triggers a backstab; gate the special attack on the distance being within backstab range as well.

units.title: Align attacker and victim for matched animations
units.detail: For a convincing backstab, rotate the player to face the enemy, rotate the enemy to the same forward, and place the enemy at a fixed distance in front of the player (position + direction * tuned distance) so both animations line up perfectly.

units.title: Teleport enemy instead of smoothing when controllers conflict
units.detail: If another system (AI) also moves the enemy, smooth movement to the victim position can conflict; a fast snap-teleport to the target position is invisible in Souls-style games because the sequence is so quick.

units.title: Sell impact with attacker+victim animation plus effects
units.detail: A backstab feels powerful when both characters play matched animations simultaneously, reinforced by screen shake, blood particles, and damage feedback on the victim rather than just playing the attacker's animation.

units.title: Mouse position is screen pixels, not world
units.detail: Mouse/input position returns pixel coordinates relative to the game window (0,0 at bottom-left), not world space; it must be converted before use, and 2D vs 3D need different conversions.

units.title: 2D: convert screen point to world
units.detail: Use Camera.ScreenToWorldPoint(Input.mousePosition) with an orthographic camera, then zero out the z since the resulting z equals the camera's z, not the world plane.

units.title: 2D method returns camera position in 3D
units.detail: ScreenToWorldPoint on a perspective camera lacks depth info and returns the camera's own position, so the object never follows the mouse; the most common 2D-in-3D bug.

units.title: 3D: raycast from camera through mouse
units.detail: Cast a ray from the camera through the mouse screen point and raycast against the scene; the hit point is the true world position where the mouse points.

units.title: Filter raycasts with layer masks
units.detail: Expose a layer mask so the pick ray only hits the ground layer, letting cursor placement ignore objects standing in front (essential for RTS and city builders).

units.title: Jobs copy struct data, not references
units.detail: The job system hands each job a copy of the struct, so writes inside Execute never mutate the original instance; results must go through shared native containers.

units.title: Plain fields give stale job results
units.detail: Reading a plain int field after scheduling shows its default value because the job only modified its copy; you must route output through shared memory.

units.title: NativeArray as job output buffer
units.detail: Pass a length-1 NativeArray so the job writes to index 0; after JobHandle.Complete() the main thread reads that slot. Native collections are the shared-memory channel between job and main thread.

units.title: Dispose native collections after use
units.detail: Native collections are unmanaged memory, so always call Dispose() (with an appropriate allocator like TempJob) when finished to avoid leaks.

units.title: Bridging object events into ECS
units.detail: C# events are object-oriented while DOTS is data-oriented, so fire OO events from ECS either by draining a native queue after a job or by spawning event entities.

units.title: NativeQueue for system events
units.detail: Persist a NativeQueue in the system, enqueue events inside jobs via NativeQueue.ParallelWriter, then force Complete(), dequeue, and invoke a regular C# event listeners can subscribe to.

units.title: Queue unreadable before job completes
units.detail: The job system refuses reads on a native container still being written by a scheduled job; call Complete() first, but know that this creates a sync point that stalls the whole game.

units.title: Defer completion to frame end
units.detail: Store the job handle and drain the queue from a separate system marked to run at the end of the frame, moving the sync point to a cheaper moment at the cost of added complexity.

units.title: Event entities via command buffer
units.detail: On an event, queue an EntityCommandBuffer.Concurrent action to create an entity with an event IComponentData; later query those entities, invoke events, and destroy them. Avoids direct EntityManager use which forces sync points.

units.title: Same-frame versus next-frame events
units.detail: System-managed command buffers run at the end of simulation (delivering next frame); create and Playback your own buffer to deliver events on the exact frame, trading a bigger sync cost.

units.title: One hooky mechanic can sell a game
units.detail: MECCHA CHAMELEON made ~$50M on a single instantly understandable mechanic (paint-to-camouflage hide-and-seek) that is technically simple; recognizable, unique mechanics drive viral success.

units.title: Raycast UV drives texture painting
units.detail: The raycast hit provides UV texture coordinates (normalized 0..1); multiply by texture pixel dimensions to get the exact pixel to paint at the click point.

units.title: Texture must be Read/Write enabled
units.detail: SetPixel fails with 'texture memory cannot be accessed from scripts' unless Read/Write is enabled in the texture import settings.

units.title: Compressed textures reject SetPixel
units.detail: Compressed formats throw 'unsupported graphics format for SetPixel'; set Compression to None in the import settings to make the texture writable.

units.title: Brush painting with SetPixels
units.detail: Paint continuously while the mouse is held (isPressed), write a block of pixels sized width*height using a color array, offset x/y by half the brush so it centers on the cursor, then Apply() to commit.

units.title: Clamp brush to texture bounds
units.detail: Painting near an edge throws out-of-range exceptions; validate x>=0, y>=0, x+brushWidth<=width, y+brushHeight<=height before writing pixels.

units.title: Skinned mesh is in bind pose
units.detail: A SkinnedMeshRenderer's mesh doesn't follow animation so you can't raycast it while posing; BakeMesh the current pose onto a plain mesh on a child with a MeshCollider and raycast that.

units.title: MeshCollider must not be convex
units.detail: A convex MeshCollider on a baked character mesh produces wrong hit positions/UVs; leave Convex unticked for painting raycasts.

units.title: Swap to baked mesh in paint mode
units.detail: Place the baked-mesh object at the exact transform of the character, hide the skinned mesh and show the baked one while painting (or vice versa) to snap a pose and paint it in place.

units.title: Custom render pass for post FX
units.detail: Extend ScriptableRendererFeature + ScriptableRenderPass, inject at the 'Before Post Processing' render event, and Blit the camera color target with a material/shader to apply the effect.

units.title: Cannot blit a texture into itself
units.detail: Copying a source texture directly into itself fails; allocate a temporary render texture and blit source -> temp -> source instead.

units.title: Shader Graph effects as post FX
units.detail: Any shader graph sampling the scene texture can be dropped on a material and used in a custom render pass; swap materials to swap effects without new code.

units.title: Stretched quad for beams and tracers
units.detail: Spawn a textured quad mesh at the midpoint between origin and target, rotated to the direction angle, with height set to the distance; this renders any beam/line effect between two points.

units.title: Tile material by distance
units.detail: Scale the material texture-tiling Y by distance/textureHeight so short and long tracers both show the fade correctly instead of stretching; clone the material first so the asset isn't modified.

units.title: UV cycling for sprite-sheet fades
units.detail: Animate UV coordinates to step through frames of a sprite sheet (frame width * current frame) so effects like tracer fades play out smoothly instead of vanishing instantly.

units.title: Juice: muzzle flash and screen shake
units.detail: Spawn a short-lived flash sprite at the gun endpoint plus a small screen shake to sell weapon feel; combine the stretched tracer for a complete impact effect.

units.title: Clone materials before runtime edits
units.detail: Modify a duplicated material instance rather than the original asset so runtime changes to texture scale or UVs don't affect other objects sharing it.

units.title: Clamp stats via encapsulated API
units.detail: Keep stat values private and expose set/increase/decrease functions that clamp between min/max constants instead of public fields any class could corrupt out of valid range.

units.title: Event-driven UI updates
units.detail: Fire an OnStatsChange event from the single function that mutates stats and let UI subscribe, avoiding wasteful per-frame updates that redraw when nothing changed.

units.title: Nested class per stat type
units.detail: Wrap single-stat logic in a nested class keyed by a StatType enum so attack/defense/etc. reuse one implementation instead of duplicating functions per stat.

units.title: Normalize stats for UI display
units.detail: Expose a value/max (0..1) accessor so bars and radar charts scale uniformly regardless of stat range, and UI never needs to know the absolute values.

units.title: Dynamic UI mesh via CanvasRenderer
units.detail: Build a Mesh from vertices, UVs, and triangles and hand it to a CanvasRenderer (SetMesh + SetMaterial) to draw custom shapes like radar charts directly on a canvas.

units.title: Radar vertices from angles and values
units.detail: Place each stat vertex at center + size * normalizedValue * direction(angle), one angle per stat per full circle; connect every vertex back to the origin to fill the polygon.

units.title: Multiplayer is data synchronization
units.detail: Multiplayer game dev is fundamentally about synchronizing data (positions, turns, scores, spawning) between clients; mastering it for a simple game transfers to every genre.

units.title: Network topologies explained
units.detail: Dedicated server, client-hosted listen server (host = server + local client), and distributed authority are the main options; host + clients is simplest for co-op style games.

units.title: Server is the source of truth
units.detail: Only the server may spawn objects and make authoritative state changes; clients request actions (e.g. via RPC) and the server validates and applies them.

units.title: RPCs, network variables, transforms
units.detail: Use RPCs for one-off client-to-server commands, NetworkVariable for small continuously synced data (scores, current player), and a NetworkTransform component to auto-sync object position.

units.title: Separate game logic from visuals
units.detail: Keep the game manager (logic/state) and visual manager (presentation) decoupled, using a singleton for single-instance managers; this keeps multiplayer logic clean and testable.

units.title: Typewriter via substring and timer
units.detail: Advance a character index on a per-character timer and set the text to substring(0, index), resetting the timer by timePerChar each step; display text is always a prefix of the full string.

units.title: Low framerate breaks per-frame typing
units.detail: A single if with a huge deltaTime only prints one character per frame and falls behind the wall-clock speed; use a while loop to print as many characters as the accumulated timer allows.

units.title: Invisible filler keeps text position
units.detail: Append the unwritten remainder wrapped in an alpha-0 color tag so every character sits in its final spot while typing, instead of centered text jumping as it grows.

units.title: Singleton manager of writer instances
units.detail: One manager MonoBehaviour holds a list of nested writer instances so many concurrent text effects run without spawning GameObjects; expose static API so callers never pass references.

units.title: Remove finished writers from list
units.detail: Have each writer's update return true when complete so the manager removes it from the list, preventing zombie instances from accumulating over time.

units.title: Skip-on-click typewriter behavior
units.detail: If a writer is active, clicking writes the full text instantly and destroys the writer; otherwise clicking starts a new message; check active via remaining character count.

units.title: onComplete callback stops sounds
units.detail: Pass an Action invoked when writing finishes or is skipped, so a looping talking sound starts on begin and stops reliably on both normal completion and skip.

units.title: Bloom needs a full settings chain
units.detail: Glow only works when every link is set: material emission enabled, a Volume with the Bloom override added, HDR enabled on the render pipeline asset, Post Processing enabled on the camera, and the scene view 'Effects' toggle on. Missing any one silently produces no glow.

units.title: Emission never works with black
units.detail: An emission color of black produces no glow. Use any non-black color combined with an intensity value greater than 1 so the value exceeds the bloom threshold.

units.title: Bloom threshold vs intensity
units.detail: The bloom threshold is the minimum color intensity that triggers glow; raise it above your emission intensity and nothing glows, lower it (e.g. 0.1) and the whole scene glows. Intensity is a global multiplier that scales scene-wide glow without editing materials.

units.title: Bloom works on sprites too
units.detail: Bloom isn't limited to 3D materials: any surface whose final output carries emission above the threshold, including sprite/UI shaders, receives the same glow effect.

units.title: Zoom lens shader via scene color
units.detail: Sample the Scene Color node behind an object and feed it to Base Color to make a 'see-through' lens. Apply Tiling (scale) with Screen Position as the UV input to zoom the sampled background in or out.

units.title: Scene color needs transparent surface
units.detail: Sampling Scene Color with an Opaque surface renders a stale/buggy image that doesn't update. Switching the shader's surface type to Transparent fixes it and produces a correct live see-through effect.

units.title: Per-pixel zoom shifts to corner
units.detail: Connecting Screen Position to Tiling's offset zooms but pivots from the corner because every pixel uses its own screen coordinate. The fix is to compute the object's screen position once in C# (WorldToScreenPoint normalized by screen width) and pass it as a Vector2 material property for the offset, so all pixels share the object-center logic.

units.title: Follow target as a Func getter
units.detail: Instead of a fixed position, give the camera a Func<Vector3> that returns the follow target each frame. This decouples the camera from any specific object, letting it pan to NPCs or cutscene points and back to the player by swapping the delegate.

units.title: Smooth exponential camera follow
units.detail: Move toward the target using direction * distance * moveSpeed * deltaTime. This speeds up when far and slows near the target, giving natural smoothing, but must be clamped to avoid overshoot.

units.title: DeltaTime follow overshoots at low FPS
units.detail: Exponential movement with deltaTime can overshoot and oscillate around the target at very low framerates (e.g. 5 FPS). Fix by comparing distance before/after the move and snapping to the target position when the new distance is greater, and skip the move entirely when distance is zero.

units.title: Smooth orthographic camera zoom
units.detail: Store a target zoom value and each frame increase orthographicSize by (target - current) * zoomSpeed * deltaTime. Clamp overshoot in both directions so zoom never passes the target at low framerates.

units.title: Camera system independent of gameplay
units.detail: A camera that accepts a target position function plus a target zoom (either as delegates or fixed values for cutscenes) is fully decoupled from the player. Any gameplay object can redirect it for cutscenes, then return control to the player target.

units.title: Map a value range to a needle angle
units.detail: Convert a 0-to-max value to a gauge angle by normalizing (value/max) then interpolating across the angle span: angle = startAngle - normalized * totalSpan. This same mapping is reusable for any analog dial.

units.title: Unity Euler angles rotate counterclockwise
units.detail: Positive Z rotation in Unity goes counterclockwise, so a clockwise speedometer needle must use negative angles (e.g. 220 down to -20), computed by subtracting the normalized span from the start angle rather than adding it.

units.title: Generate gauge labels from a hidden template
units.detail: Duplicate a hidden label template, rotate each copy to its corresponding angle, set its text to the matching value, then counter-rotate just the text child back to zero so numbers stay readable instead of rotating with the dial.

units.title: Control UI render order via siblings
units.detail: In Unity UI, render order follows hierarchy: later siblings draw on top. Call SetAsLastSibling on the needle after generating the labels so it renders above them.

units.title: Buildings as data-driven scriptable objects
units.detail: Store each building's prefab, sprite, name, and stats in a ScriptableObject asset so designers add new buildings without touching code. Building logic lives in scripts attached to the prefab.

units.title: Find nearby objects with physics queries
units.detail: Use an OverlapSphere (physics query) to find all colliders in an area, then filter results by tag or component to keep only the relevant type (e.g. trees). This is the general pattern for buildings sensing nearby resources or units.

units.title: Node-based pathfinding for road networks
units.detail: For road/connection games, place nodes only at intersections and branch points instead of a full world grid, then run the same A* logic over them. This is far more memory and CPU efficient on large maps (author measured ~100x faster).

units.title: Road connection points as child transforms
units.detail: Represent a building's road/entry attach points as empty child GameObjects in its prefab. Designers can place them freely, and the game positions/connects roads at those transforms.

units.title: Supply chains are crafting chains
units.detail: A supply chain is objects converting from one type to another. Model recipes as data (inputs/outputs) in scriptable objects; the building reads its recipe, requests the input, and crafts the output.

units.title: Time control via timescale or custom updater
units.detail: Speed up game time with Time.timeScale for simplicity, but that can glitch particles/button animations. A robust alternative is a custom updater that owns a list of entities and calls their update with a modifiable deltaTime parameter, letting you run different systems at different rates.

units.title: Run expensive logic on timers, not every frame
units.detail: Systems like finding nearby trees or retrying pathfinding don't need per-frame updates. Add a timer to run them 1-5 times per second, massively improving performance on simulations with many units and buildings.

units.title: Task-list system for building jobs
units.detail: When the player places a building, push concrete tasks onto a shared list (gather wood, carry it, build). Units of different jobs scan the list for tasks they can satisfy, check prerequisites (resources available), and execute them. This cleanly models dig/build chains.

units.title: Many-simulated-units games fit ECS/DOTS
units.detail: Games where thousands of units each move, carry tasks, and render (like a large city sim at ~2000 population) are the ideal use case for an ECS/data-oriented design: each unit and resource becomes an entity instead of a MonoBehaviour.

units.title: Clock hands from normalized day time
units.detail: Keep game day as a float (optionally 0-1 via modulo), advance it with deltaTime/secondsPerDay, then rotate each hand by normalizedTime * 360 * revolutionsPerDay, negating the angle for clockwise movement.

units.title: Hours text rounds, not floors
units.detail: Converting hour = dayNormalized * 24 to string rounds up, so 1.8 displays as 2. Apply floor before formatting. For minutes, take the fractional part (mod 1) of hours and multiply by 60, then floor again.

units.title: Health bar from a stretchable white pixel
units.detail: Build a bar from a 1x1 white pixel sprite with pixels-per-unit=1: a dark background, an inner bar whose pivot is at the left (shift the sprite right by half its width inside an anchor parent), tinted red, plus an optional black border. Set fill by scaling the anchor's X to a normalized 0-1 value.

units.title: Flash a bar at low health via modulo
units.detail: Flash the bar white when health is low by checking (health*100) % 3 == 0 to pick white vs red on a periodic timer. A cheap way to signal danger without an animation system.

units.title: Static factory builds UI hierarchy from code
units.detail: A static Create(position, size, ...) function on the bar class constructs the parent, background, bar, and sprite entirely in code. This makes the component portable across projects with just one script, no prefab or editor setup, and supports options like border thickness/color and bar/background colors.

units.title: Health as a plain non-MonoBehaviour class
units.detail: Implement HealthSystem as a regular class with a constructor (max health), methods Damage/Heal, and GetHealth/GetHealthPercent accessors, clamping values between 0 and max. Keeping logic out of MonoBehaviour makes it reusable and unit-testable.

units.title: Int division breaks health percent
units.detail: health / maxHealth with two ints returns a truncated int (0.9 becomes 0). Cast at least one operand to float before dividing to get the correct 0-1 percentage.

units.title: Event-driven UI updates over per-frame polling
units.detail: Instead of syncing a health bar every Update, raise an OnHealthChanged event from the health system and update the bar only when subscribed. Identical visuals with far better performance when many bars exist, since nothing runs on frames where health didn't change.

units.title: Split heart into fragments and per-heart objects
units.detail: Each heart is 4 fragments; model a single heart as its own class (fragment count, take damage, heal) and keep a list of hearts instead of one bare integer. This mirrors the 4-fragment heart UI and makes per-heart logic clean.

units.title: Separate logic class from visual class
units.detail: Keep health logic (pure class, no MonoBehaviour) fully separate from the UI visual class. The logic class stores state and fires events; the visual subscribes and renders. This keeps code clean and lets you reuse logic without UI.

units.title: Damage hearts from last to first
units.detail: Iterate hearts from the end of the list toward the start when applying damage: if damage exceeds a heart's fragments, empty it, subtract absorbed damage, continue; otherwise take the remainder and break. Makes multi-heart damage feel like draining from the tail.

units.title: Heal hearts from first to last with clamping
units.detail: Iterate hearts from index 0 forward. Compute missing = maxFragments - current; if healAmount exceeds missing, fill the heart and carry over; else heal by healAmount and break. Clamp so heal never exceeds the per-heart max.

units.title: isDead when first heart is empty
units.detail: Death can be determined simply: if the first heart in the list has zero fragments the system is dead. Fire an onDead event when damage is applied so visuals can react (e.g. popup).

units.title: Animate heal over time, keep damage instant
units.detail: Run a timer (e.g. every 50 ms), compare visual fragments to logic fragments, and add one fragment at a time to animate healing. Skip the loop entirely when not healing using an isHealing flag, and only refresh visuals instantly on damage.

units.title: Use events to decouple logic from visuals
units.detail: Expose onDamage, onHeal, onDead events from the health logic class instead of the logic knowing about UI. The visual subscribes on setup and refreshes all hearts on any event. Keeps systems independent and reusable.

units.title: Hex grid = square grid with odd-row offsets
units.detail: A hex grid is a square grid with each odd row offset on X by half the cell size, and the row spacing on the vertical axis is 0.75 of the cell size (half + quarter), not a full cell size. Get these offsets right for perfect hex alignment.

units.title: Hex world-to-grid: round then check 6 neighbors
units.detail: Plain rounding fails on hex grids near edges. Instead round to get a rough grid position, gather its six neighbors (offsets differ by odd/even row), then pick the neighbor whose world position is closest to the tested point.

units.title: Neighbor offsets depend on odd/even row
units.detail: For hex neighbors above/below, the X offset is -1 on odd rows but 0 on even rows (and vice versa). Left/right neighbors are always X±1. Getting these wrong silently selects the wrong cells, so verify neighbor lists for both row parities.

units.title: Detect odd/even row with modulo 2
units.detail: Use the modulo operator (value % 2 == 1) to detect an odd row and conditionally apply the X offset or neighbor offsets. Works identically for XZ (3D) and XY (2D) planes.

units.title: Name magic numbers with constants
units.detail: Values like the 0.75 vertical offset multiplier appear in several places; define a named constant (e.g. HexVerticalOffsetMultiplier) instead of scattering raw numbers so the code stays understandable.

units.title: Divide rough Z by vertical offset multiplier
units.detail: When computing the rough grid Z from a world position, also divide by the 0.75 vertical multiplier. Skipping this makes the rough estimate drift on larger grids, breaking the neighbor-closest approach.

units.title: Avoid per-hex objects and raycasts for scale
units.detail: Instantiating a mesh+physics object per hex with raycast tests does not scale to huge grids. Prefer pure math coordinate conversion plus one dynamically generated mesh for the whole grid to stay performant.

units.title: Hit counter driven only by events
units.detail: The hit counter subscribes to player events (onEnemyHit, onEnemyKilled, onDamage) and never touches player internals. This keeps the counter decoupled so it can be dropped onto any game. Reset counter and hide it on damage.

units.title: Kill bonus: killing blow counts twice
units.detail: When an enemy is killed, increment the hit count again on top of the hit event, giving a small satisfying bonus for the finishing blow (e.g. 3 hits shown as 4).

units.title: Threshold-based color changes for intensity
units.detail: As the counter rises, change the text color at specific hit thresholds (white, blue, green, yellow, orange, red) to communicate escalating intensity. Helps with parsing a hex color string directly in code.

units.title: Continuous size growth clamped to a max
units.detail: Grow the counter font size by a small per-hit amount (e.g. 0.07 per hit) rather than discrete thresholds, then clamp with min/max so the text never becomes unreadably large.

units.title: Shake intensity scales with counter and decays
units.detail: Store shake intensity; each update, if intensity > 0, subtract intensityDrop * Time.deltaTime. Set intensity = base + perHit * hitCount on every hit and clamp it, so shaking grows with the combo and eases back to zero.

units.title: Hide counter until first hit via mesh renderer
units.detail: Disable the text's mesh renderer in Awake so the default text isn't shown; re-enable it whenever the counter is set. A clean way to make UI appear only when relevant.

units.title: Thin walls via edge slots instead of tiny grid
units.detail: Making the grid tiny to get thin walls causes performance problems at scale. Instead place floor cells on a normal grid and add four edge slots (up/down/left/right) where thin wall/stair edge objects snap, giving thin walls with a normal-sized grid.

units.title: Multiple levels by moving the grid origin on Y
units.detail: Each grid system has an origin vector; placing multiple grid systems (one per floor) and activating one at a time gives you multi-level buildings. All objects are positioned relative to their grid origin, so moving origin moves everything placed.

units.title: Object types as scriptable objects
units.detail: Represent each placeable object type as a ScriptableObject holding a prefab and a visual (ghost). Reusing one building system across wall/floor/door types is just adding new data objects, and adding variations (glass walls, window walls) only needs new prefabs.

units.title: See-through walls with depth-based rendering
units.detail: To see the player inside buildings, render the character with a different material when occluded: one render feature renders the character with a behind-material only when depth is greater (occluded), another renders the normal material when depth is less (visible). Requires putting characters on their own layer.

units.title: Save system stores object type plus grid position
units.detail: Persist each placed object as a save entry of (objectType, gridPosition). On load, instantiate the same object at the same grid position. Simple and covers both grid-locked and loose general objects.

units.title: Two placement modes: grid-locked and free
units.detail: Separate objects into grid-snapped objects (walls, floors, stairs, doors) and general objects placed freely anywhere (trees, crates, rocks). Both work with the same save system, letting you dress up a village around structured buildings.

units.title: Reuse tooltip code for complex variants
units.detail: Duplicate the base tooltip class to make an item-stats tooltip, reusing the mouse-following and keep-on-screen logic. The main change is anchoring: lower-left anchor positions with a plus offset, upper-left with a minus offset.

units.title: Static wrapper functions for tooltip access
units.detail: Expose public static Show/Hide functions that forward to a private static instance set in Awake, so any class can show a tooltip anywhere without holding a reference.

units.title: Data component per button for tooltip info
units.detail: Attach a small item-info component (sprite, name, description, stats) to each UI button. On setup, iterate buttons, read that component, and add the tooltip trigger with that item's data, keeping tooltips data-driven.

units.title: Level system as pure logic class with events
units.detail: Model leveling with three fields: current level, current XP, and XP needed for next level. AddExperience increases XP, fires onExperienceChange, and on level-up fires onLevelChange. UI and player subscribe independently to keep logic decoupled.

units.title: Use a while loop to allow multi level-ups
units.detail: A single if that levels up once fails when a large XP drop spans several levels. Loop while current XP exceeds XP-to-next so one big reward can raise multiple levels correctly.

units.title: XP bar via image fillAmount
units.detail: Represent the XP bar with a UI Image and just set its fillAmount to the normalized XP (experience / experienceToNextLevel), remembering to cast to float to avoid integer division truncation.

units.title: Animated wrapper class around logic
units.detail: Don't animate inside the logic class (it must add XP instantly). Create a separate wrapper class that holds its own level/xp values, subscribes to the real system's events, and eases one unit per update toward the target so bars visibly fill.

units.title: Display logic level as level + 1
units.detail: The logic class uses 0-based levels internally; add one when showing in UI (getLevelNumber + 1) so the player reads natural 1-based levels.

units.title: Trigger non-MonoBehaviour updates via a function updater
units.detail: To run per-frame logic in a plain class, use a utility that invokes a callback every Update (e.g. FunctionUpdater) instead of forcing MonoBehaviour. Avoids attaching to a GameObject and keeps classes reusable.

units.title: Separate resource logic from UI bar
units.detail: Keep mana/resource logic (current, regen, spend, normalized getter) in its own plain class updated separately, and let the bar class only read a normalized value. The bar knows nothing about the resource rules, and vice versa.

units.title: Clamp regenerating resource to max
units.detail: If regen is not clamped to the max value, mana overflows past full, so spending never visibly drops the bar. Always clamp the amount after regen so spend actions show an effect.

units.title: Animated texture by shifting raw image UV rect
units.detail: Use a RawImage instead of Image to animate a bar texture: shift the UV rect.x over time to scroll the texture, and set the texture's wrap mode to Repeat so it tiles seamlessly instead of stretching.

units.title: Mask width to show partial fill without fillAmount
units.detail: RawImage has no fillAmount, so drive a Mask's width (from anchored left) multiplied by the normalized resource amount to reveal/cut the bar, while the texture inside keeps animating.

units.title: Edge glow positioned at the bar fill boundary
