units.detail: Add a glow sprite whose anchored X equals the mask width so it rides the leading edge of the fill. Hide it when the resource is full (normalized == 1), and optionally animate its alpha/position for extra polish.

units.title: 9-slice sprite for stretchable UI borders
units.detail: Define slices in the Sprite Editor and set the border image to sliced (not simple) so it stretches cleanly to any size, keeping corners crisp while the middle stretches.

units.title: Rendering requires mesh filter, renderer, and material
units.detail: To draw anything you need a MeshFilter (shape), a MeshRenderer, and a Material with the texture. A sprite renderer is just a quad with two triangles plus a material under the hood.

units.title: Mesh needs vertices, UVs, and triangles
units.detail: Build a mesh from three parallel arrays: vertices (Vector3), UVs (Vector2, same size as vertices, normalized 0-1), and triangles (int indices, three per polygon). Assign all three to the Mesh to complete it.

units.title: Use clockwise triangle winding for front face
units.detail: The front/back face of a polygon is defined by index order; counter-clockwise triangles face away and won't render with backface-culling shaders. Always list triangle indices in clockwise order.

units.title: A quad is two triangles: 4 verts, 4 UVs, 6 indices
units.detail: To make a square, add a fourth vertex and a second triangle (0,2,3 clockwise). Vertices and UVs stay equal in count; triangle count is 3 per polygon.

units.title: Select texture region with normalized UV math
units.detail: To show a sub-rectangle of a texture on a quad, compute normalized UVs by dividing the pixel position and size by the texture's pixel width/height. Enables sprite-sheet animation and tile rendering.

units.title: Modify local array then re-upload to animate meshes
units.detail: To animate a dynamic mesh, edit values in a local vertices array and then reassign it to the mesh. Uploading per-frame from a local copy (with extra vertices for body parts) is the basis of custom 2D animation systems.

units.title: Minimap via a second camera and culling masks
units.detail: Easiest minimap: a second camera rendering only a dedicated layer. Put icon sprites (player, enemies, buildings) on that layer and deselect it from the main camera's culling mask so icons never appear in the main view.

units.title: Render minimap into a render texture shown as RawImage
units.detail: Assign the minimap camera a RenderTexture and display it on the UI with a RawImage (Image takes sprites, not textures). Set the camera's background to a solid dark color so the minimap isn't transparent.

units.title: Circular minimap with a mask and border
units.detail: Wrap the RawImage in a container with a Mask component using a circle sprite (hide mask graphic) to clip the minimap into a circle, then layer a border sprite on top for polish.

units.title: Scale icons relative to orthographic zoom
units.detail: Increasing the minimap camera's orthographic size shows more area but shrinks icons, so icon sprite sizes must be scaled relative to the zoom level. Otherwise icons become tiny or misleading.

units.title: Auto-size tooltip background to text
units.detail: Size the tooltip background using the text's preferredWidth and preferredHeight plus padding on each side (padding * 2), applied to the rect's sizeDelta. Works for arbitrary and multi-line text.

units.title: Convert mouse position to UI space
units.detail: Input.mousePosition is screen space; use RectTransformUtility.ScreenPointToLocalPointInRectangle with the parent rect and UI camera to get a local UI position. A Screen Space Camera canvas needs the UI camera reference; Screen Space Overlay does not.

units.title: Show tooltip via mouse-over-once and mouse-out-once
units.detail: Expose static Show/Hide tooltip functions, then hook a mouse-over-once callback to Show with the button's description and mouse-out-once to Hide. This gives per-element help text without coupling tooltip to the window.

units.title: Separate warning tooltip class
units.detail: Duplicate the normal tooltip into its own warning class rather than overloading the base tooltip with warning behavior. This keeps both classes simple and avoids issues when multiple warnings need to display.

units.title: Auto-hide UI element with countdown
units.detail: Give a showTimer float, decrement it by deltaTime in Update, and hide the element once it drops below zero. Recharge the timer to its max value every time the element is shown.

units.title: Optional parameter with default duration
units.detail: Make the show function accept an optional float (e.g. showTimerMax defaulting to 2 seconds) so callers can override duration while most calls stay short.

units.title: Flashing animation via odd/even states
units.detail: Increment a flashTimer by deltaTime; when it exceeds flashTimerMax, advance a flashState counter. Use a switch on state: odd states show one color scheme, even states the reverse, producing a blink. Reset timer and state to zero each time the element is shown.

units.title: Alternating text/background colors
units.detail: Make a warning pop, e.g. red background with white text on odd frames and white background with red text on even frames, so the message is highly visible.

units.title: Tooltip as reusable UI element
units.detail: A tooltip is a UI element that shows extra info on hover, follows the mouse, and auto-sizes its background to fit whatever text it is given. It is essential for UI-heavy games.

units.title: Keep tooltip always on screen
units.detail: Calculate the tooltip's background size and reposition it if it would leave the screen, so it is always readable.

units.title: Real-time updating tooltip text
units.detail: Support tooltips whose text changes every frame, such as a live cooldown or cost display, instead of only static strings.

units.title: Expose helpers and extension methods
units.detail: Wrap tooltip setup in static helper functions and extension methods so callers write one short line instead of repeating boilerplate.

units.title: Write adaptable, readable code
units.detail: Code that is easy to read and understand lets you quickly adapt a system (e.g. a tooltip) into something different like a complex item-stats window by reusing the mouse-follow and stay-on-screen logic.

units.title: Correct position after placement
units.detail: Instead of validating/clamping the raw mouse position before converting to canvas space, place the tooltip at the computed position and then correct the anchored position afterwards. This avoids screen-space conversion complications and is easier to follow.

units.title: Clamp tooltip inside canvas
units.detail: Compute mouse X plus the background rect width; if that exceeds the canvas width, reset the anchored X to canvas width minus background width so the tooltip hugs the screen edge. Apply the same logic to Y with heights.

units.title: Anchor left for simple bounds math
units.detail: If the tooltip is anchored to the middle, bounds math needs rect width divided by two. Anchor to the left side so coordinates run 0 to canvas width and the clamp calculation stays trivial.

units.title: UI sorting order is hierarchy based
units.detail: In Unity UI, render order follows hierarchy: any window instantiated at runtime becomes the last sibling and will cover the tooltip. Fix by calling SetAsLastSibling() on the tooltip inside its Show function so it is always on top.

units.title: Func<string> for live tooltip text
units.detail: Accept a Func<string> instead of a static string and re-evaluate it every frame in Update so text reflects changing state like a cooldown. This is slightly slower than a static string but fine when only one tooltip exists.

units.title: Static string version delegates to func
units.detail: Keep the simple overload that takes a plain string and have it internally call the Func overload returning a fixed lambda, so there is one code path for setting text and sizing the background.

units.title: Extension method for tooltip setup
units.detail: Create an extension method on Transform (e.g. transform.AddTooltip(...)) so callers can attach and configure a tooltip with one readable line, supporting either the static-helper or extension-method pattern.

units.title: Keep hover hooks separate from button logic
units.detail: Put mouse-over and mouse-out tooltip actions on a dedicated button UI class so they do not overwrite the button's normal behavior or existing event listeners.

units.title: Grid system as genre core
units.detail: Turn-based strategy is fundamentally grid-based: split the world into discrete grid positions and apply gameplay logic per position. Grids simplify design rules and give designers control, and are reusable for hex maps, city builders, inventories, and factory games.

units.title: Action point economy
units.detail: Characters spend action points per action like each move. To show move range, find the max move distance, then run pathfinding from each candidate grid point to verify it is actually reachable given costs.

units.title: ScriptableObjects for data-driven content
units.detail: Store all data for abilities, weapons, equipment, and enemy types in scriptable objects so designers can author content without touching code.

units.title: Vision cone via forward vector + raycasts
units.detail: Define an enemy's view cone using transform.forward, then raycast or use math to find grid positions inside the cone and which of those are behind cover. It is line-of-sight detection projected onto a grid.

units.title: Overwatch system
units.detail: Let the player pick a covered area; compute the guarded grid positions once, then during the enemy turn auto-fire at any unit entering those positions. Reuses the same position-detection logic as vision cones.

units.title: Cover modifies hit chance
units.detail: No/low/high cover simply applies 0, slight, or big accuracy penalties when attacking a target. Mark cover via a small script holding a cover-type enum; during grid init, raycast each position for cover objects and during movement check neighbor positions for the best cover.

units.title: Flanking removes cover bonus
units.detail: A unit is flanked when the cover point next to it does not sit between attacker and defender. Raycast or scan grid positions between the two units; if no cover blocks the line, apply a negative accuracy penalty, making the unit easier to hit.

units.title: Spray zones and friendly fire
units.detail: Shooting can hit units between attacker and target: scan grid positions along the shot line and apply the same accuracy roll to every unit present, friendly or not. Weapons with an arc (shotgun/SMG) extend the check across all positions in the arc.

units.title: Morale as second health bar
units.detail: Morale is mechanically identical to health: a number that always takes damage even when a shot misses. Below half morale, the unit has fewer action points and lower accuracy next turn; at zero it is broken and cannot act. This reduces the frustration of pure RNG like XCOM's 98% miss.

units.title: Map prefab with designer markers
units.detail: Author each map as a single prefab containing empty game objects or markers for spawns, patrol routes, and trigger positions. Enemy scripts reference the patrol points and walk through them in order, letting level designers place everything visually.

units.title: Level scripting via trigger positions
units.detail: Attach a map-specific logic class to the map prefab. Check each time a unit moves whether it reaches a marker position, then trigger cutscenes, dialogue, or enemy spawns. Keeping logic and position references on the prefab makes each level self-contained.

units.title: Overall world map with colored regions
units.detail: Slice the world map into texture regions you can color dynamically to show conquered/available missions. Detect clicks with rough-shaped colliders per region plus a simple mouse raycast.

units.title: Skill trees with requirements
units.detail: Skills are unlocked via cost, prerequisite previous skills, and requirements. Build them as data objects (scriptable objects rather than enums) so new skills are content, not code.

units.title: Custom shaders make games stand out
units.detail: The same object looks massively different under a stylized/cell-shaded shader with outlines, which is one of the biggest ways to differentiate a game's look. Apply the shader to every material on the character.

units.title: Start from asset pack demo scenes
units.detail: Level design is hard; use the demo scenes shipped with modular asset packs as starting levels, then drop in your own working character. This is faster than building an environment from scratch.

units.title: Interaction via simple interface
units.detail: Implement an IInteractable interface with the functions the interaction system needs (interact/on-interact hooks) on doors and NPCs, plus a collider so the system can find the object. New interactables are just new scripts implementing the interface.

units.title: Avatar masks for layered animation
units.detail: Use an avatar mask so an upper-body layer plays a spell-charge animation while the base layer still handles walking. Drive it by setting the layer weight to 1 while charging and 0 otherwise, so arms and legs animate independently.

units.title: Sandbox scene for fast iteration
units.detail: Play-test mechanics in a tiny bare-bones scene instead of the massive final level, since loading a giant level every Play press destroys iteration speed. Build features in the sandbox, then apply them back to the real level.

units.title: Camera-based targeting sphere cast
units.detail: Sphere-cast forward from the camera with a radius and max distance, pick the first enemy object found, and show a target indicator. Attacks then auto-aim at the marked target.

units.title: Homing projectile lifecycle
units.detail: Give a projectile a target reference, move toward it each frame, and when close enough spawn an explosion and destroy itself. On impact, read the target's health component and apply damage.

units.title: Volumetric light shafts sell the scene
units.detail: Volumetric/god-ray lights (one volumetric light cast through several windows) dramatically improve scene quality; viewers may not notice their absence but their brain registers it. The light bends around obstacles rather than passing through walls.

units.title: Minimal quest system
units.detail: A quest only needs a title and an isComplete flag plus a list of objectives. Keep it intentionally simple; complexity can be added later via data objects.

units.title: Juicy XP popups from 3D objects
units.detail: Turn a plain textured cube into an animated XP popup using a shader with vertex shake and a glow/hit effect, then animate it fading out. Listen for an enemy-death event to spawn it.

units.title: Full game without writing code
units.detail: Unity visual scripting can build a complete FPS with multiple weapons, shields, hookshots, pickups, keys, doors, enemies, and a boss fight with zero hand-written code.

units.title: Modularity enables cheap content scaling
units.detail: Build every mechanic pre-modularly so adding new weapons, enemy types, or pickups is a small configuration task rather than a rewrite.

units.title: UV coordinates explained
units.detail: UVs are the position in the texture applied to each vertex, stored as a 0-to-1 percentage: lower-left of the texture is (0,0), upper-right is (1,1).

units.title: Convert pixels to UV
units.detail: Convert sprite-sheet pixel coordinates to UVs by dividing X by texture width and Y by texture height, casting to float so the division is not truncated to an int.

units.title: Keep UV/vertex/triangle order consistent
units.detail: Vertices, UVs, and triangles must all follow the same winding pattern (e.g. left-top, right-top, left-bottom, right-bottom). Mismatched ordering produces garbled or missing mesh faces.

units.title: Mirror a sprite region via negative width
units.detail: When a sprite sheet only has one facing, mirror a body part by passing a negative width and a shifted X (e.g. 256 + negative width) so you reuse the same texture region without extra sheet space.

units.title: Validate inputs in dev, strip in production
units.detail: Add input validation (null/length checks throwing exceptions) while developing, then remove it once the system is tested and you are confident inputs are always valid. Performance is about making safe assumptions on your data.

units.title: Apply UVs by assigning mesh.uv
units.detail: Editing a UV array alone does nothing visible: you must assign mesh.uv so it is uploaded to the graphics card. This enables real-time sprite-frame switching for animations.

units.title: Transforms always pivot at origin
units.detail: A game object always transforms from its own origin, regardless of the sprite it renders or collider attached. To change the pivot, reposition child objects relative to the parent.

units.title: Scale from an edge via child offset
units.detail: To make a health bar shrink right-to-left, put the bar sprite in a child object shifted by half its width inside an empty container, then scale the container. The shift relocates the effective pivot.

units.title: Rotate around a custom pivot
units.detail: For a clock hand, nest the sprite inside a container and offset the sprite so the pivot sits at one end, then rotate the container on the Z axis. The same trick drives rotation-based mechanics.

units.title: Stretch texture toward a target
units.detail: To draw a texture from 0,0 to a far point, put the container at the origin, offset the sprite so the pivot is at the origin end, then rotate to aim and compute the needed scale. Avoids midpoint math.

units.title: Sprite pivot setting vs code pivot
units.detail: For 2D sprites you can set the pivot directly in the texture import settings, but this does not work for 3D objects or the common white-pixel trick, so understanding the parent/child offset technique matters.

units.title: Inspector shows local not world transforms
units.detail: The Inspector displays a child's local values relative to its parent, so moving/scaling the parent leaves the child's displayed local values unchanged. Understanding local vs world space is essential for transform math.

units.title: Render camera to render texture for screenshots
units.detail: To capture a camera at arbitrary resolutions, set camera.targetTexture to a new RenderTexture with the desired width/height/depth, then read the pixels back into a Texture2D via ReadPixels and encode to PNG.

units.title: Screenshot must be taken after rendering
units.detail: Reading pixels before the frame renders yields empty/black output. Use a bool flag set by the request call, then capture inside OnPostRender (built-in pipeline) once per frame and clear the flag.

units.title: Static instance for triggering screenshots
units.detail: Keep a private static instance of the handler and expose a public static TakeScreenshot(width, height) so any script can request a capture through a static call without a direct reference.

units.title: Secondary camera for off-screen views
units.detail: Attach the capture script to a secondary camera to render views different from the main camera (e.g. portrait view, separate layer content) without affecting what the player sees, and preserve alpha for transparency in the PNG.

units.title: One-line screenshot with ScreenCapture.CaptureScreenshot
units.detail: Call ScreenCapture.CaptureScreenshot(fileName) with the file path to save the entire game window (including UI) instantly. An optional supersize parameter multiplies resolution, useful for print-quality images.

units.title: Coroutine screenshot with ReadPixels
units.detail: Yield WaitForEndOfFrame so the frame is fully rendered, then ReadPixels from a screen-sized rectangle into a Texture2D (ARGB32, no mipmaps), Apply(), and EncodeToPNG to a byte array to write to disk.

units.title: OnPostRender not called in URP/HDRP
units.detail: OnPostRender only fires in the built-in render pipeline. On URP/HDRP subscribe to RenderPipelineManager.endCameraRendering (unsubscribe in OnDisable/OnDestroy); this callback runs after the camera but before UI, so UI is excluded.

units.title: Gray screenshot means wrong texture format
units.detail: If a screenshot comes out gray, the Texture2D format is wrong. Use RGBA/ARGB32 to preserve color and transparency rather than a luminance-only format.

units.title: Capture only part of the screen
units.detail: Instead of a full-screen rectangle, pass a custom x/y/width/height to ReadPixels to grab just a corner or region, giving you control over exactly which part of the camera view is captured.

units.title: Disable canvas to exclude UI from screenshot
units.detail: ScreenCapture.CaptureScreenshot and the WaitForEndOfFrame method both include UI. If UI should not appear, disable the canvas (or its GameObject) just before capturing and re-enable it afterward.

units.title: Build multiplayer from the start
units.detail: Converting an existing single-player game to multiplayer requires refactoring nearly every system to decide client vs server ownership, causing extensive debugging. Designing for multiplayer from the outset is drastically easier.

units.title: Server authority vs client visual systems
units.detail: Mark systems with WorldSystemFilter attributes: movement/combat logic runs only on the server (source of truth), while visuals like selection highlights run only on the client since the server has no rendering.

units.title: DefaultGameObjectInjectionWorld points to server on host
units.detail: World.DefaultGameObjectInjectionWorld resolves to the server world when running as host, so client-side MonoBehaviour logic silently runs against the wrong world. Access the client/server world explicitly from the bootstrap instead.

units.title: RPCs cannot contain nested native containers
units.detail: NativeList/NativeArray fields inside an RPC throw 'nested native containers are illegal in jobs', and dynamic buffers cannot implement both IRpcCommand and IBufferElementData. Workaround: send one individual RPC per command (e.g. per selected unit).

units.title: Dynamic physics entities must be ghosts
units.detail: In Netcode for Entities, dynamic objects with physics need the GhostAuthoring component to be synchronized across server and client; otherwise physics queries break with 'not supported' errors.

units.title: Netcode + DOTS physics needs config object
units.detail: Combining Netcode for Entities with DOTS physics requires an entity with a NetCodePhysicsConfig component set to 'Any Physics Entities' mode, or physics queries for selection/damage silently fail.

units.title: Addressables load assets on demand
units.detail: Anything referenced in a scene is loaded when the scene loads, wasting memory and startup time. Marking assets as Addressable defers loading until requested, drastically cutting load time and footprint.

units.title: Addressables is fully asynchronous
units.detail: All Addressables APIs are async (sync variants are deprecated) and never block the main thread. LoadAssetAsync returns an AsyncOperationHandle; subscribe to its Completed event, check Status == Succeeded, then use .Result.

units.title: String asset keys are brittle
units.detail: Path strings are case-sensitive and easy to mistype, causing silent load failures. Prefer AssetReference fields (assignable in the editor) or AssetLabelReference instead of hand-written strings.

units.title: Typed asset references enforce asset type
units.detail: Generic AssetReference accepts any asset, causing runtime type errors. Built-in typed variants (AssetReferenceGameObject, AssetReferenceTexture2D) restrict the editor picker; for missing types subclass AssetReferenceT<T> with a serializable class.

units.title: Cannot load an addressable folder directly
units.detail: Folders inside an addressables group are only organizational; loading them by path or asset reference fails. Mark the contained objects with a shared label and load by that label instead.

units.title: Separate addressables groups into bundles
units.detail: Each addressables group builds into its own asset bundle, so grouping assets by usage enables downloading/loading them independently and keeps initial download size small.

units.title: Serverless leaderboard with Azure Functions
units.detail: Create a Function App with an HTTP trigger per endpoint: GET returns stored scores, POST appends a new score. Use consumption (serverless) plan and a storage account for persistence; free tier usually costs pennies per month.

units.title: Newtonsoft serializes properties not fields by default
units.detail: JsonConvert.SerializeObject can return empty JSON when the class uses public fields, because the default settings only convert properties. Convert fields to properties (get/set) or change serializer settings.

units.title: Newtonsoft breaks on Unity Vector3
units.detail: JsonConvert on Unity's Vector3 throws a self-referencing loop on the 'normalized' property, and System.Numerics.Vector3 differs in field naming. Use Unity's JsonUtility for Unity types and a custom Vector3 in the function.

units.title: Server is source of truth for scores
units.detail: Do not trust client-sent scores: run validation logic server-side in the function before writing to storage so players cannot submit fake data.

units.title: Async multiplayer for turn-based games
units.detail: Store game state in cloud storage and mutate it via cloud functions; players poll for updates instead of holding a live connection. Supports play-anytime multiplayer (like Civilization), but requires server-side validation since clients send state.

units.title: Custom mod workshop with cloud storage
units.detail: Replicate Steam Workshop on any platform by storing a mod list JSON plus each mod's files (sprites/scripts) in blob storage with upload/download functions, letting players share custom content without a Steam dependency.

units.title: Player messages and shared worlds
units.detail: Elden Ring-style messages, score histograms, and persistent player-built structures all use the same pattern: one function reads the blob, one writes it, and the game polls or re-renders on response.

units.title: CinemachineConfiner bounds camera view
units.detail: Add a CinemachineConfiner extension to a virtual camera, assign a bounding shape made from an empty GameObject with a PolygonCollider2D, and edit points (Ctrl+click a segment to delete) to keep the camera inside the play area.

units.title: Confiner collider breaks physics raycasts
units.detail: The bounding shape is a physics object that blocks raycasts/collisions. Mark it isTrigger and put it on the Ignore Raycast layer (or configure the layer collision matrix) so it only constrains the camera.

units.title: Confine screen edges vs camera center
units.detail: The 'Confine Screen Edges' toggle accounts for the camera's visible size so the viewport never leaves the bounds even when zooming; disabling it only constrains the camera's center point.

units.title: Camera sensor feeds visual input to agent
units.detail: Add a CameraSensor to an ML-Agents agent pointing at a camera with a restricted culling mask; the rendered image becomes the agent's observation. A RenderTextureSensor works equivalently using a render texture target.

units.title: Vision observations explode training cost
units.detail: A 50x50 grayscale image is 2500 observations (color triples it to 7500) versus ~6-50 for hand-crafted observations, so vision-based training needs far more compute and time.

units.title: Simplify visual input for fast training
units.detail: Use grayscale, tiny resolutions (e.g. 20x20), and culling-mask-restricted simplified scenes so the signal-to-noise ratio improves and training finishes in reasonable time on a standard machine.

units.title: Observation stacks infer motion from frames
units.detail: Stacking multiple frames feeds the network temporal info (e.g. direction of a moving target) at a training cost; with a single frame the agent cannot infer velocity.

units.title: Mix classic AI movement with ML perception
units.detail: Let a simple classic AI script handle movement/navigation while ML-Agents performs only perception (identifying a pig vs sheep), triggered manually via RequestDecision instead of every frame. Avoids needing to train motion too.

units.title: Prefer world state over vision when possible
units.detail: In a game engine you have the full world state, so raycasts/direct component access are simpler and train far faster than vision. Reserve vision for when the signal genuinely can't be extracted another way.

units.title: Give the AI a 'do nothing' action
units.detail: If discrete action branches always force a shoot, an agent with no visible target shoots randomly. Add an explicit shoot/don't-shoot action branch so the model can choose not to act.

units.title: ML-Agents is three cooperating parts
units.detail: The ML-Agents Python package runs the learning algorithm, the Unity scene is the learning environment, and the C# package defines observations/actions and uses the resulting brain.

units.title: Reinforcement learning is an observe-decide-act loop
units.detail: The agent gathers observations, the algorithm picks an action, the action executes, and correct behavior earns a reward; over many episodes the agent learns which actions maximize reward. Subclass Agent and override CollectObservations and OnActionReceived.

units.title: Discrete vs continuous actions
units.detail: Discrete actions are integers with a branch size (e.g. size 5 yields 0-4), used for choices; continuous actions are floats from -1 to +1, used for analog control like steering. You decide what each number means.

units.title: Vector observation space size counts floats
units.detail: A Vector3 position counts as three observations. Passing two positions means a space size of 6, and the space size must match the total float count your CollectObservations adds.

units.title: Retraining with same ID overwrites or errors
units.detail: Running mlagents-learn twice with the same run id fails; pass --force to overwrite prior data or use --run-id with a new name to keep runs separate.

units.title: Use Python virtual environments for ML
units.detail: Create a per-project venv (python -m venv venv) and activate it before installing pytorch and mlagents, keeping package versions isolated between projects and avoiding compatibility conflicts like numpy version mismatches.

units.title: Input actions asset structure
units.detail: The new Input System organizes input as Action Maps (contexts like player/vehicle/UI) containing Actions (move, jump) with Bindings to physical inputs. Action types: value (analog), button (press/release), and pass-through.

units.title: Input has started, performed, canceled phases
units.detail: Every action fires multiple times per press: started (pressed), performed (held), canceled (released). For a button you usually only act on the performed phase, checked via context.performed.

units.title: Three ways to consume player input
units.detail: PlayerInput component offers Send Messages / Broadcast Messages, serialized UnityEvents wired in the inspector, or C# events subscribed in code. UnityEvents are easiest; C# events fire for all actions via onActionTriggered.

units.title: 2D vector composite for WASD movement
units.detail: Add a 2D Vector Composite binding to a value action to combine up/down/left/right keys (e.g. WASD) into a Vector2, then read it with context.ReadValue<Vector2>() to drive movement.

units.title: Interactions and processors modify action behavior
units.detail: Interactions (hold, tap, multi-tap) change when an action triggers, while processors (invert, dead zone) transform the value sent. Useful for complex inputs like requiring a hold before firing.

units.title: Animation curves are just X/Y graphs
units.detail: Animation curves are really just a graph of points you can use to map any two values. Pick any meaning for X and Y (level, time, wave index, health, speed) and sample with Evaluate(x).

units.title: Health-per-level from a curve
units.detail: Map player level (X) to max health (Y) and call curve.Evaluate(playerLevel) on level-up. Designers reshape difficulty visually in the editor without touching code.

units.title: Curve-driven ability speed
units.detail: For a dodge roll, evaluate the curve at 0 to set the starting speed, accumulate a timer each frame, and evaluate at that time to set current speed. Exit when below a minimum threshold.

units.title: Animation curves only hold floats
units.detail: Curves sample to floats, so cast with Mathf.RoundToInt (or similar) when the result feeds an int field like health or enemy count.

units.title: Curve is constant past last keyframe
units.detail: Evaluating beyond the last key returns the last key's value forever. Waves past the curve's end keep the same enemy count rather than extrapolating.

units.title: Particle systems are built on curves
units.detail: Fields like Size over Lifetime and Velocity over Lifetime are animation curves. Right-click keys for exact time/value and choose free/linear/constant/weighted tangents to shape behavior.

units.title: Author weird balance with curves, not formulas
units.detail: Shapes like 'fast health gain, then a dip, then a spike' are trivial to draw as a curve but painful as a manual value table or a math function.

units.title: Curves drive wave difficulty
units.detail: Use one curve for enemies-per-wave and another for enemy health-per-wave, both keyed on wave index, to create escalating or scripted difficulty like boss waves.

units.title: NavMesh is a baked pathfinding mesh
units.detail: The navigation mesh is baked from the scene geometry and agents use it to plan paths. Bake from Window > AI > Navigation.

units.title: Agent radius and height shape walkability
units.detail: Baking with a larger radius removes narrow gaps the agent can't fit through; taller agents can't pass under low overhangs. Re-bake after changing to see the walkable area shrink.

units.title: Max slope and step height limit traversal
units.detail: The baked mesh only lets agents climb slopes under the max angle and steps under the step height; tune them for ramps and stairs.

units.title: Off-mesh links bridge disconnected areas
units.detail: Drop height and jump distance settings generate links so agents can drop off ledges or jump between separate mesh regions that aren't directly connected.

units.title: Area masks restrict which agents walk where
units.detail: Mark terrain as a named area (e.g. water) and toggle it in each agent's area mask so only chosen agents traverse that region.

units.title: Move agents by setting a destination
units.detail: Give the pathfinding agent a destination transform and it plans a route, automatically routing around obstacles instead of ramming into them.

units.title: Relay bypasses firewalls and port forwarding
units.detail: A hosted relay lets players connect across different networks without opening ports or sharing IPs; the host gets a join code friends paste to connect.

units.title: Init services and auth before networking
units.detail: Await UnityServices.InitializeAsync and anonymous sign-in before touching the relay; both are awaitable so the game keeps running instead of freezing.

units.title: Await network calls so games don't freeze
units.detail: Internet requests take time; using async/await pauses only that function while the rest of the game runs. Forgetting await/async freezes the frame waiting for a reply.

units.title: Create allocation then request a join code
units.detail: Call CreateAllocationAsync(maxConnections) where the count excludes the host, then GetJoinCodeAsync(allocationId) to get the shareable string.

units.title: Open the connection right after allocating
units.detail: A relay allocation is not held if no connection follows; a client that joins later gets 'join code not found'. Start the transport immediately after allocating.

units.title: Wrap relay calls in try/catch
units.detail: Awaitable service calls can throw (e.g. service disabled or network down) and crash the game. Catch RelayServiceException and log the details.

units.title: Distribute the join code via Lobby data
units.detail: Store the relay join code as Lobby member data (not public data) when the host starts the game; clients poll and auto-join, skipping manual code sharing.

units.title: Choose when to start the realtime connection
units.detail: Allocate the relay and start netcode only when the host presses Start Game, or start the host immediately on lobby join if you need live data transfer inside the lobby.

units.title: Distance field vs smooth render modes
units.detail: Distance field (16/32) stays crisp at any size; 'Smooth' produces a clearer bitmap that's ideal when you plan to hand-edit the atlas texture with effects.

units.title: Padding must contain effect overflow
units.detail: When adding outlines, shadows or strokes to glyphs, increase atlas padding (e.g. to 10) so effects stay inside their cell and don't bleed onto neighboring characters.

units.title: Fonts must actually contain each glyph
units.detail: The character set limits what renders, and if the chosen font family lacks a character you won't see it no matter what text you type.

units.title: VirtualMouseInput makes a gamepad-driven cursor
units.detail: The Input System's built-in VirtualMouseInput component moves a virtual cursor from the gamepad stick and fakes clicks from a button, so controller players can use mouse-driven UI.

units.title: Game view and canvas scaler must match
units.detail: If the Game view aspect (e.g. 16:9) differs from the canvas reference (1080p), the canvas scales and the cursor no longer maps onto buttons. Keep both Full HD/1080p.

units.title: Clamp the virtual cursor to the screen
units.detail: In LateUpdate, clamp the virtual mouse position to Screen.width/height with Mathf.Clamp and push the clamped value back via InputState.Change so the cursor never leaves the screen.

units.title: Navigation for simple menus, cursor for complex
units.detail: Button navigation is fine for vertical main menus, but complex interfaces like automation-game UIs work far better with a virtual cursor controlled by the gamepad.

units.title: Webhook-to-LLM-to-auto-post pipeline
units.detail: A comment webhook triggers a server call to the LLM, the async run is polled until complete, the final message is fetched, and the reply gets posted back automatically.

units.title: Platforms may lack a comment-posting API
units.detail: When the teaching platform exposes no API for posting comments, automate the browser UI (e.g. Selenium) to type and submit the generated reply.

units.title: Action vs Func delegates
units.detail: Action is a void-returning delegate (optionally with parameters); Func returns a value. Delegates make clean callbacks, e.g. so a game doesn't freeze while waiting on an HTTP response.

units.title: Rotate toward a target via transform.forward
units.detail: Compute the direction to a target and assign it to transform.forward to point at it; the same trick works with transform.up to align with a collision normal.

units.title: Cost of living is indie's biggest lever
units.detail: Sustaining $2k/month means a 6-month game only needs to earn $12k to be a success, while a $10k/month lifestyle needs $60k for the same game. Lower expenses massively improve viability.

units.title: Success needs dev skill AND marketing
units.detail: A great game with no marketing, or good marketing of a bad game, both fail. Both halves must reach a sufficient level before revenue becomes reliable.

units.title: Steam marketing meta changes over time
units.detail: Wishlists, demos and Steam festivals didn't exist in 2013; following an old success roadmap won't transfer to today's ecosystem, so strategies must be re-evaluated each year.

units.title: Review-to-sales multiplier shrinks over time
units.detail: Older games sold ~70-100x their review count because few reviewed then; now the multiplier is closer to 40. Use a current multiplier when estimating sales from reviews.

units.title: Experience compounds in game dev
units.detail: In six months a beginner produces a flappy-bird-scale game, while a 10-year veteran can ship a 40,000-line automation game in ~7 months. Skills drastically change what the same time yields.

units.title: Reverse-engineer revenue targets from costs
units.detail: Work backward from living expenses: with a $2k/month target and a 6-month dev cycle, a game needs only ~$12k to break even, which sets a realistic success bar.

units.title: Reusable systems make new games fast
units.detail: Starting from a grid-building system built for a previous project got placement, nodes, buildings and belts working in about an hour. Clean, reusable code pays off across projects.

units.title: Sketch the design on paper first
units.detail: Define the base resources, processed resources, final items and needed buildings before coding so implementation stays focused instead of spinning in circles.

units.title: Move conveyor items back-to-front
units.detail: Process belts from the last position in the path backwards; otherwise a single empty spot between items stalls everything because each belt checks a still-occupied neighbor.

units.title: Guard against loops when tracing belt paths
units.detail: Finding a path's start by walking backwards never terminates if the belts form a loop, causing infinite loops and crashes. Detect cycles explicitly.

units.title: Run logic on a fixed tick, not every frame
units.detail: Driving belt movement on a 200ms tick instead of Update keeps all items synchronized and saves performance; the same tick pattern is used across production games.

units.title: Program to interfaces for versatility
units.detail: Make grabbers operate against storage/item-slot interfaces so they work with any building that implements them, instead of hard-coding specific item types.

units.title: Data-drive items and recipes with ScriptableObjects
units.detail: Define each item type and recipe (inputs, outputs, amounts, craft effort) as scriptable objects so content lives in the project files and is trivially swappable.

units.title: Build an asset library over years
units.detail: Reusing icons and art drawn for a five-year-old game filled the new game's visual gaps instantly; code and assets both compound across projects.

units.title: OBJ and SVG are editable text formats
units.detail: Satire video: OBJ files list vertices/UVs/normals and SVG lists vector points in plain text, so models and textures can in principle be edited by hand in any text editor.

units.title: Reviews matter for store visibility
units.detail: Store algorithms treat having ~10 reviews as a threshold: going from no score to some score gives a big visibility boost. Early review velocity matters for new asset/game releases.

units.title: Buy assets to fill skill gaps
units.detail: You don't need to master every skill (e.g., 3D modeling); buy quality assets from specialists so you can focus your energy on programming and design.

units.title: Tutorials hide the struggle
units.detail: A tutorial's final video is the polished result after all research, trial and error, and mistakes. Encountering bugs is normal and part of the learning process for everyone.

units.title: DOTS stack traces may misreport the error line
units.detail: Unity DOTS does source generation, so the stack trace line can differ from the actual line throwing the error. If logs placed before the reported line don't run, examine surrounding lines.

units.title: Disabling GameObject leaves singleton null
units.detail: A singleton initialized in Awake is never set if the GameObject is disabled, so later access throws NullReference even though the code looks correct. The reported stack line isn't always the root cause.

units.title: Entity Command Buffers defer structural changes
units.detail: ECBs queued for end of frame apply component adds only after systems run; a system executing in between sees stale state and includes entities that should be excluded. Fix: create and play the ECB manually right after the query instead of deferring.

units.title: Treat bugs as learning opportunities
units.detail: Each bug you solve teaches you what to check next time (e.g., check order of operations). Don't get frustrated; catalog the lesson from every strange bug.

units.title: Desktop Duplication for live desktop capture
units.detail: The free Desktop Duplication Unity asset (by hecomi) streams the desktop as a real-time Texture2D using the Windows 8.1+ Desktop Duplication API, with multi-monitor support and editor options.

units.title: Screenshots via transparent window come out black
units.detail: Capturing the screen with a transparent Unity window gives a black background, not the content behind it. Use the Desktop Duplication API instead to get the real desktop image as a texture.

units.title: Old open-source projects can power new ideas
units.detail: An 8-year-old GitHub project from a dev on another continent solved a modern automation need. Open-source tooling and comments on old videos can still be highly useful later.

units.title: Experience builds game-building confidence
units.detail: After years of writing code and shipping many game genres, you gain confidence you can build any game you imagine. The path is writing lots of code and making lots of games, not innate talent.

units.title: Match game scope to current skill
units.detail: When skill level couldn't handle complex SWAT breaching AI, the dev pivoted to dumb zombie AI and manual unit control. Remap your vision to what you can actually build, then grow into the harder version later.

units.title: Technical feasibility vs excellent design
units.detail: Building a game technically is different from nailing the game design, which is more art than science. Consider scope and design quality separately from technical ability.

units.title: Remake simple games to learn fast
units.detail: Flappy Bird, Pong, Pac-Man, or a basic platformer teach core mechanics quickly. Make a dozen 'crappy' games fast to accumulate the experience that unlocks bigger ambitions.

units.title: Remake an existing game into a new genre
units.detail: Taking an official open project (Unity Open Projects) and converting it from action-adventure into an RTS was a fun hobby project: reuse the art assets and mechanics you know, but design them for a new genre.

units.title: Design on paper before coding
units.detail: Write down ideas and open questions on paper to get a clear overview of direction before touching code. Pre-production thinking made the build flow smoothly.

units.title: Hobby projects scale to available time
units.detail: A complete RTS with gathering, building, combat, and minimap was built in ~20 hours spread over two months, fitting around a day job. Small-scope projects are achievable with limited weekly time.

units.title: TextMeshPro rich text is exploitable in user content
units.detail: TextMeshPro enables rich text by default, so user-posted chat strings can inject size/color tags and wreck UI. Sanitize or strip rich-text tags when displaying untrusted input.

units.title: Scriptable objects define resource types
units.detail: Define each resource type and its data as a scriptable object stored on the node, read through a resource manager singleton that fires UI-update events on change.

units.title: Minimap via camera + render texture
units.detail: Add a second camera above the map rendering only a dedicated layer, place quads on that layer on objects, and render to a render texture displayed in the UI. Simple and effective.

units.title: Learn together with live chat
units.detail: Finding the right class to drive depth of field through code was done collaboratively with live stream chat. Live coding sessions convert unknown APIs into shared knowledge.

units.title: Old-school FPS aiming locks vertical axis
units.detail: Recreate Doom-style aiming by reading only horizontal mouse movement and leaving the Y axis at zero so the player rotates left/right but never looks up or down.

units.title: Weapon wobble and camera bob via animations
units.detail: The weapon is a UI image with an animator (idle/walk/shoot states) and the camera bob is a separate animator on the camera; simple animations sell the movement feel.

units.title: Billboard sprites toward the camera
units.detail: Keep a sprite always facing the player by grabbing the main camera position, computing the angle from the sprite transform, and rotating it each frame.

units.title: Box cast instead of ray when aiming is locked
units.detail: With no vertical aiming, a direct raycast misses because Doom hits objects above/below the crosshair. Use a virtual box cast from the player that damages every target inside.

units.title: Reuse clean code across years and projects
units.detail: The health system built on the channel's first video was dropped into this game two years later unchanged. Writing clean, reusable, decoupled systems pays off repeatedly.

units.title: Generic interactable interface for doors and buttons
units.detail: Implement a simple interactable interface plus a trigger collider; the player presses a key to interact with all colliders near them. The same system opens doors, presses buttons, and drives elevators.

units.title: Remake one game instead of all games
units.detail: Instead of recreating every Squid Game challenge, managing scope meant focusing on a single game (Red Light Green Light) and polishing it as much as possible.

units.title: Scope zoom with second camera and render texture
units.detail: A second camera rendering to a render texture gives the best-visuals rifle scope zoom; combine with depth of field and a bring-up animation for a convincing scope effect.

units.title: Recolor existing assets instead of modeling
units.detail: Find a similar character model in your asset library, recolor the texture, and use ProBuilder to tweak geometry (e.g., dragging helmet edges). You can create custom-looking content without modeling skill.

units.title: Unity's built-in Ragdoll Wizard
units.detail: The Ragdoll Wizard (Tools menu) auto-generates rigidbodies, colliders, and joints: drag in each body part, select them correctly, click a button, and you get working ragdolls.

units.title: Cinemachine impulse for screen shake
units.detail: Add an impulse listener to the virtual camera and an impulse source component, then manually generate the impulse on shoot for easy, controlled screen shake.

units.title: Search assets before building from scratch
units.detail: Instead of writing an outline/highlight shader, search purchased asset bundles and import an existing highlight asset—it worked in minutes. Don't reinvent the wheel when a tool already exists.

units.title: State machine for AI variety
units.detail: Players in a mini-game got distinct behaviors (stop on time, stop too late, run back, attack the door) from one manager state machine for the round and per-player states for movement.

units.title: Decouple UI from logic with events
units.detail: Heavy use of C# events kept UI completely decoupled from logic scripts (health, ammo, stats), making the code clean and systems independently testable.

units.title: Model every game action as a shared interface
units.detail: Movement, shooting, abilities, and even spinning are all 'actions'. A common action interface/base class holding the owning unit and on-complete callback lets you add new action types easily.

units.title: Pre-production design pays off in dev time
units.detail: Dedicated days to outline systems and interactions meant the two-hour build was fast. Pre-production plus reusable code plus experience each massively cut build time.

units.title: Turn blocker prevents action overlap
units.detail: A simple flag that blocks any action input while the current action is running prevents spam-click bugs in turn-based or real-time action systems.

units.title: Each action returns valid positions
units.detail: Expanding each action to return a list of valid grid positions enforces rules like max move distance or shoot range, keeping action validation clean and per-action unique.

units.title: Grid-based half/full cover system
units.detail: Add a cover script to every solid object, then scan all grid positions once to mark each as half or full cover based on what occupies it, mirroring how pathfinding walkability is computed.

units.title: Hit percentage from distance and cover
units.detail: A simple accuracy formula factoring target distance and cover state, plus a per-unit accuracy roll, gives XCOM-style hit chances. No complex math needed for a prototype.

units.title: Overwatch via position-change events
units.detail: Subscribe to every unit's grid-position-change event and fire on the enemy if it enters the overwatch range, reusing the hit-percentage calculation with a penalty.

units.title: Fog of war by grid line of sight
units.detail: From each unit, raycast/check grid positions in all directions and stop beyond grid cells marked as full cover; hide enemy visuals (but keep logic active) when not seen.

units.title: Simple scoring AI: shoot if you can, else move
units.detail: Enemy AI rules: if a player is in range, shoot; otherwise evaluate candidate positions by number of targets in range from there and move to the best. Prioritize weakest units.

units.title: Action camera via secondary virtual camera
units.detail: A second Cinemachine virtual camera positioned behind the shooter looking at the target, enabled during an action and disabled when done, gives dramatic action cuts.

units.title: Animation curve for grenade arc
units.detail: Drive the grenade's vertical position from an animation curve (placed points define the arc) while moving horizontally in code; curves aren't just for animations.

units.title: Animation curves as gear ratio tables
units.detail: Define each gear's acceleration curve (y=accel, x=car speed). Curves peak at slightly higher speed per gear, so evaluating them tells you the optimal shift point—simple, not physically accurate, but works for arcade feel.

units.title: 3D UI via overlay cameras and render textures
units.detail: Place 3D models (cars, gauges) offset in the world, render each with its own camera to a render texture shown in UI, or stack an overlay camera on the base camera. Keeps 3D UI unaffected by speed effects on the main camera.

units.title: Delegates let player and AI share one controller
units.detail: Expose throttle, brake, gear, and NOS as delegate fields on the car script; a player script wires them to input and an AI script wires them to its own logic, so one controller drives both.

units.title: Separate visuals from logic scripts
units.detail: One compact script handles only car logic (speed, gears, state) and another only visuals (wheel rotation, brake lights, exhaust). Each stays small and independently modifiable.

units.title: Sell speed with FOV, camera, and shake
units.detail: As normalized car speed rises, interpolate camera FOV up (40→100), move the transposer offset from the side to behind the car, and scale Cinemachine noise amplitude for screen shake. Small effects combine into a strong sense of speed.

units.title: Quaternions fix wheel rotation that Euler fails
units.detail: Euler-angle wheel rotation would randomly stop working; switching to quaternion rotation fixed it. Prefer quaternion-based rotation for continuous spinning objects.

units.title: Record your own play to tune AI difficulty
units.detail: Play badly, record which speed triggers each gear change, and store those values in scriptable objects per difficulty (easy/normal/hard). The AI just matches the recorded thresholds.

units.title: Research genre games before building
units.detail: Before prototyping, watch gameplay of similar flash games to study what works and what doesn't, then apply your own twist. Research-first de-risks the design.

units.title: Modify asset-pack models for your needs
units.detail: Take an asset from a pack (e.g., a boost gauge) and tweak it with ProBuilder—add dashes, thin lines, elongate the needle—to get exactly what you want without modeling from scratch.

units.title: Toy maker vs artist mindset for game devs
units.detail: Instead of chasing one 'dream game' masterpiece, some devs see themselves as toy makers who enjoy building many small games focused on systems and mechanics rather than stories and characters. This reframes a large portfolio of interesting games as a valid goal rather than a compromise.

units.title: Dream game videos suffer survivorship bias
units.detail: People making videos about 'building my dream game' get more clicks and views, so you mostly see that narrative online. If you don't have one single dream game, you're not weird - it may just be that 'dream game' is a more compelling title than the reality.

units.title: Sales decay curve makes month-one revenue a trap
units.detail: Games sell a lot at launch then sales dwindle over time with small bumps from sales/updates; Project Zomboid-style year-over-year growth is the rare exception. Expanding your team based on first-month sales will outpace revenue as the curve decays, bleeding money.

units.title: Employee cost is ~2x salary
units.detail: A developer salary of ~30-40k in Europe roughly doubles to ~60k when accounting for taxes and company expenses. 20 employees means ~$1.2M/year just to keep them paid, which quickly eats even a $4M hit.

units.title: Never negotiate from a position of desperation
units.detail: The Rise of Industry dev, desperate to save his house, sold his IP for 5K (+45K advance) after it had generated $4M, and the publisher exploited bundles and a sequel without him. Desperation destroys leverage in any business deal.

units.title: Build years of runway before going full-time
units.detail: The dev only moved out of his parents' house once he had ~20k in the bank (about 3 years of runway), and only started YouTube after comfortable savings, accepting 20 months with zero income. Risk-averse indie dev means minimizing fixed costs and keeping a cash buffer.

units.title: Sustained stress causes burnout and panic attacks
units.detail: Working non-stop under financial pressure led to constant panic attacks and hospital visits for the dev. The personal cost can outweigh the financial cost, so build habits (working out, runs, rest) to sustain a 50+ year career.

units.title: Revenue paid as wages isn't 'lost' money
units.detail: A tragic $4M-to-broke story is softened because the money paid out as developer wages funded jobs rather than being wasted. Selling your IP to a studio that then makes a passionless sequel (mixed reviews) shows what happens when the original vision is removed.

units.title: SSAO instantly grounds a scene
units.detail: Screen-space ambient occlusion adds soft shadows at geometry contacts (corners, car interiors), giving flat lit scenes much more depth and making objects feel grounded. It improves almost every scene except deliberately cel-shaded looks.

units.title: URP SSAO lives in the renderer, not the volume
units.detail: With URP 10+ (Unity 2020 LTS) ambient occlusion is NOT a volume override - it's a renderer feature on the URP asset's render object. Add it under 'Add Renderer Feature > Screen Space Ambient Occlusion'. Being a renderer feature means it ignores volume weights/bounds, which is fine since intensity usually shouldn't vary by area.

units.title: Baked AO only affects static objects
units.detail: Lightmapped/baked ambient occlusion (under Lighting settings) only works on static objects, so it fails for moving players or cars. Screen-space AO is camera-based and covers dynamic objects, which is why it's preferred for interactive scenes.

units.title: Tune SSAO for low-end devices
units.detail: For performance, downsample the SSAO effect, use depth-only source, and drop sample count to low. This lets even low-end mobile targets include ambient occlusion as a quality setting.

units.title: Free Steam companion app as content hub
units.detail: Package all your tutorial game builds and interactive lessons into a single free, continuously-updated Steam app. Wishlists on the free app drive Steam visibility, and the platform opens future options like multiplayer tutorials, live-stream minigames, and a central place to distribute new projects.

units.title: It's never too late to start game dev
units.detail: Age (30, 40, 50+) or current skill level doesn't gate learning game dev; the barrier is much lower now. Free engines (Unity, Unreal, Godot, Game Maker), free educational content, and visual scripting make a first game achievable for anyone this year.

units.title: Tutorials require active application
units.detail: Tutorials are guides, not the whole path - passively watching or copy-pasting doesn't transfer knowledge. Pause, write/modify code, and observe what changes so you understand why it works; the learning happens through application.

units.title: Buy assets to cover missing art skills
units.detail: A programmer with zero art skills can ship gorgeous games by leveraging the Asset Store for models, animation, and tools instead of learning 3D art - exactly how Dinky Guardians was built. Similarly, visual scripting lets designers build games without code.

units.title: Making games just for fun is a valid goal
units.detail: Crowded markets only matter if you're chasing financial success; if your goal is enjoying the process or playing with friends, the competition is irrelevant and you're doing it right as long as you have fun.

units.title: Indie success is meritocracy, but game quality is minor
units.detail: A good game is only a small part of modern success - you also need strong marketing. Saying 'it's all luck' is wrong, but expecting a good game alone to sell is equally wrong; both strategy and quality are required.

units.title: Wishlists predict launch sales
units.detail: Wishlists are the best sales predictor - a common rule of thumb is wishlists ≈ 10x Steam followers, and you want at least ~5,000 (ideally 10,000+) wishlists at launch to have a real shot. Under 1,000 wishlists predicts a couple dozen to a couple hundred copies.

units.title: Effort spent doesn't equal player value
units.detail: Players only judge the final product, not how long it took - a weekend game can beat a multi-year project. Equity around effort is a fallacy that leads devs to misjudge why their game failed.

units.title: Success is a spectrum, not only mega hits
units.detail: Between $5k games and $100M games lies a huge range; for a low-cost dev, $1k/month in Portugal can count as success. Don't benchmark only against Vampire Survivors or Stray - define success relative to your costs.

units.title: Visuals and hook decide 3-second first impression
units.detail: With crowded Steam releases, subpar visuals or a missing unique hook means players move on within seconds. Games like Undertale succeed with simple art only when the concept is truly special; also avoid overpricing at $20 without standout presentation.

units.title: Game dev is a marathon, flops are one game
units.detail: A single flop (e.g., 100 copies sold) shouldn't define you; take time off, study what went wrong, and apply it to the next game - the same dev's next title can become their biggest success. Never gamble your whole life on one game.

units.title: Solo dev means one driving person, not zero help
units.detail: A useful definition of 'solo dev' is: one person whose departure means game over, even if they direct a small army of contractors for art, music, and sound. Manor Lords fits this as a 'solo director' despite 250+ credited names and an orchestra.

units.title: 'Just make it multiplayer' ignores real complexity
units.detail: The 'solo dev did it' narrative gives players ammunition for unrealistic demands like converting single-player games to multiplayer or expecting small studios to ship as fast as a supposed solo dev - multiplayer is not a one-button feature.

units.title: Solo dev has no strict definition
units.detail: 'Solo dev' is a fuzzy spectrum, not binary - buying art/sound, using an engine (built by thousands), or hiring composers all blur the line, and taking the argument to the extreme would require building your own CPU. Labeling is marketing/by feel, not objective fact.

units.title: Stylized graphics are not bad graphics
units.detail: Realistic ≠ good and stylized ≠ low effort; consistent intentional styles (Minecraft, Theme Hospital, Schedule I) look great within their own art direction. Judging a game's quality by realism is a misconception.

units.title: Polish the interactions players repeat most
units.detail: Games can be janky in peripheral systems yet feel extremely polished where it counts - the actions a player does over and over must be satisfying. No voice acting beats bad voice acting, so omit rather than half-implement.

units.title: A great Steam page signals effort
units.detail: An effective Steam page has a nice capsule, a punchy short description of the progression fantasy ('small time to kingpin'), and rich long description with animated gifs showing gameplay. A text-only page reads as low effort and kills first impressions.

units.title: Low effort makes success harder, not impossible
units.detail: A low-effort game can still find success (e.g., Pokémon Arceus) but only with a captive audience that buys regardless; without that, polish and presentation are worth pursuing to avoid looking low effort.

units.title: Tutorial code is a starting point, not production
units.detail: Tutorials teach one goal and aren't perfect production code, but that usually doesn't matter. Premature optimization is the root of evil - a 5x gain on a 0.5ms system isn't worth the time; profile first and only optimize genuine hotspots.

units.title: Clean code looks needlessly complex to beginners
units.detail: Patterns like SerializeField + private fields, or updating UI via events, look convoluted to novices but prevent coupling bugs at scale. If an instructor does something that seems 'wrong', suspect inexperience rather than error - the pain of tech debt teaches this best.

units.title: Learn fast: leverage prior experience
units.detail: There's no secret to fast learning, only accumulated experience - new topics are usually mostly familiar patterns (grids→hex grids, multiplayer concepts→Netcode). Building 10 games across 10 genres beats 10 similar games because diverse systems transfer.

units.title: Speed-watch, then hands-on, then teach
units.detail: To learn a new topic quickly: read docs, watch video tutorials at 2x-3x speed, then actively experiment in a project. Teaching the topic to others (or making a tutorial) forces real understanding and cements the knowledge.

units.title: Low cost of living is the indie cheat code
units.detail: Living cheaply (e.g., ~$700-800/month in Portugal, cheap rent) dramatically lowers the sales needed to survive and survive flops. Careful cost control is what lets a dev absorb a game making only 10% of its predecessor.

units.title: TikTok reach beats conversion ratio
units.detail: TikTok gives massive reach (millions of views) but low wishlist conversion. Since the base number is so huge, even a below-average conversion still yields a large absolute number of wishlists, so it remains a strong marketing channel.

units.title: Marketing advice has a shelf life
units.detail: Marketing/sales advice typically stays valid only 1-2 years because platforms and player behavior change fast (e.g. demos went from net-loss to a requirement after Steam Next Fest). Only trust advice under ~2 years old.

units.title: Publish demo ASAP, but only when presentable
units.detail: Launch your demo as early as possible to build community, but 'as soon as possible' means when the game already looks good and sells the vision — never a gray-box prototype. Ideally time the launch to coincide with a Steam festival so the demo launch doubles as a marketing beat.

units.title: Next Fest is must but oversaturated
units.detail: Steam Next Fest is mandatory for success and also oversaturated; big wishlist counts grow more (100k->200k) than small ones (5k->3k). Join anyway — even non-major games gain thousands of wishlists.

units.title: Publishers want a following first
units.detail: Publishers differ: some want a large existing following, some want a blank slate. Most (especially for first-time devs) want proof of interest before investing — Manor Lords landed a publisher only after ~700k wishlists.

units.title: Kickstarter now requires an audience
units.detail: Kickstarter success without a community was possible 10-15 years ago (Double Fine raised 3.3M), but today the platform is oversaturated and burned backers make it near-impossible without a pre-existing following that comes to pledge.

units.title: Publisher quality varies wildly
units.detail: Some publishers are invaluable partners (Hooded Horse) and others take 30-40% and deliver nothing. Vet the specific publisher rather than treating 'publisher' as one category; a good publisher can be a win-win.

units.title: Integer division truncates to zero
units.detail: Dividing two ints in C# returns an int, so 30/100 yields 0 instead of 0.3, silently breaking math like health percentages. Cast one operand to float before dividing so the result is a float.

units.title: Health percentage via float cast
units.detail: For a health bar you need a 0..1 ratio: keep health as ints but return (float)current / max. A single float cast on one operand makes the division float-based and yields 0.3 for 30/100.

units.title: Know implicit type limitations
units.detail: Every data type has implicit limitations (int can't hold fractions). Being aware of them prevents silent bugs like truncated division results when doing math with integers.

units.title: Structure scripts for expandability
units.detail: On complex projects, how you organize and structure scripts and write clean, understandable code determines how easily the project can grow. Prioritize maintainability from the start of a large codebase.

units.title: Learn by doing, not watching
units.detail: Passively watching tutorials doesn't build real skill; you must actively apply what you learn. Hands-on challenges with objectives and starting files, then comparing your solution, is far more effective.

units.title: Refactor dirty code into clean code
units.detail: A useful practice challenge: take working but messy code and refactor it to still function while being well-structured. Reviewing others' solutions exposes many valid ways to solve the same problem.

units.title: Single Responsibility Principle
units.detail: A class should have only one reason to change. Refactor one monolithic Player class handling input, movement, audio and collisions into a component system of small single-purpose classes — behavior stays identical but maintenance improves dramatically.

units.title: Interface Segregation Principle
units.detail: Don't force clients to depend on interfaces they don't use. Split one monolithic interface (take damage + explode + trigger effect) into small focused interfaces so objects only implement what they actually need.

units.title: Open/Closed Principle
units.detail: Classes should be open for extension but closed for modification. Instead of an area calculator that switches per shape type, use a base class with subclasses so adding new shapes never requires editing the original calculator.

units.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
units.detail: High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not low-level modules. Making an interaction system (interact with NPC, push button, open door) work through interfaces instead of concrete types keeps it flexible.

units.title: Singleton pattern for single instances
units.detail: A Singleton stores a single instance of a type with easy global access — ideal for managers like audio where only one should exist. Typical implementation: a base class that returns the existing object or creates one if absent.

units.title: Command pattern for undo/redo
units.detail: Encapsulate an action as an object with Execute and Undo methods, then push commands onto a stack to implement undo/redo systems (e.g. moving a character through a maze then stepping backward/forward).

units.title: Dirty flag pattern avoids recomputation
units.detail: When expensive logic (like world-streaming sector loads) may run repeatedly, gate it behind a simple dirty flag test; only run the complex logic when the flag is set, keeping most frames to a cheap check.

units.title: Structured courses beat self-study for 3D
units.detail: For learning Blender modeling from zero, structured courses with video lectures, quizzes, challenges and the ability to jump between lectures make the basics much easier to absorb than random tutorials.

units.title: Cloud = rented online servers
units.detail: The cloud is just online servers you rent so you don't buy hardware, manage data centers or do maintenance — you only write logic. Billing is pay-per-use, so small indie usage often costs cents to under $10/month.

units.title: Azure hierarchy: account/subscription/resource group
units.detail: Azure is organized as: Azure account > subscriptions (billing/invoicing) > resource groups (logical grouping, e.g. all leaderboard services) > resources (the actual services like a web API or database). Everything you create selects a subscription and resource group.

units.title: Web API as a game backend
units.detail: Expose REST endpoints (GET/POST) from an Azure web API and call them from Unity via HTTP. This enables cloud mechanics like leaderboards and persistent in-world player messages (Dark Souls / Elden Ring style).

units.title: Web app vs web API
units.detail: A web app is a page meant for human users (images/text); a web API is meant for programs to interact with via requests. Games talk to APIs, so build an API endpoint your game can call rather than a browsable page.

units.title: .NET Framework vs Core vs .NET
units.detail: The .NET Framework ran only on Windows; .NET Core made C# cross-platform (Linux/Mac); they later merged into a single product just called .NET (e.g. .NET 6). Pick the plain .NET runtime for new cloud services.

units.title: Persist messages through a cloud API
units.detail: A simple in-memory list on the server stores messages; Unity POSTs new messages (position/rotation/text as JSON) and GETs all nearby ones to spawn them. Real persistence needs storage, but the pattern proves the cloud mechanic.

units.title: Reflection dynamically inspects code
units.detail: Reflection lets you inspect and invoke types at runtime using their names via strings (typeof + GetMethod/GetType + Invoke) without compile-time references. Essential for validation systems that test code which may not exist yet.

units.title: Extension methods extend types externally
units.detail: Extension methods add functions to a type without modifying it, which is especially useful when you don't have source access to the type. Define them as static methods taking the extended type as the first argument.

units.title: async/await keeps programs responsive
units.detail: Async/await with Task lets slow operations (like contacting a web server) run without blocking the program. It's critical for UI that stays responsive during network calls, but must be understood to be used correctly.

units.title: Multi-threading gives speed, easy mistakes
units.detail: Multi-threading uses all CPU cores for parallel work and can give massive performance wins, but it's very easy to introduce subtle bugs. Only use it when you know exactly what you're doing.

units.title: Boxing wraps value types as objects
units.detail: Because everything in C# derives from object, value types (int, bool) get wrapped in a box when used as objects. This costs allocations, so be aware of implicit boxing in performance-sensitive code.

units.title: Span is a zero-allocation array view
units.detail: Span lets you work on arrays or slices of arrays without creating new data or objects — it's basically a pointer. Using it is extremely performant for logic over array slices.

units.title: default keyword beats hardcoded values
units.detail: Use default(T) instead of hardcoding: default of int is 0, bool is false, objects are null. This makes code robust to type changes and avoids magic default values.

units.title: Tuples and anonymous types organize data
units.detail: Both tuples and anonymous types let you group data without first defining a class. Anonymous types create a generated type via new { ... }; tuples are similar and are compared differently — choose based on whether you need a named reusable type.

units.title: Take your time on the learning journey
units.detail: There's no rush and no competition — the only goal is that you actually learn. It doesn't matter how long it takes or that someone else learns faster; this applies to any skill acquisition.

units.title: Nullable types handle absent values
units.detail: Nullable types (int?, bool?) allow value types to represent 'no value' with null instead of predefining a sentinel like -1. This is cleaner than magic values for optional data.

units.title: Enum flags turn enums into bit masks
units.detail: Using [Flags], an enum becomes a bit mask so you can combine multiple options into one value (bitwise OR) and test membership (bitwise AND). Useful for combinations of toggle-like settings.

units.title: Unsafe code is powerful but dangerous
units.detail: Unsafe C# with pointers can do impressive things but bypasses the safety checks C# provides. Use it only wisely and rarely — the safety exists for a reason.

units.title: Console apps with command-line args
units.detail: Many useful programs need no UI: a simple console app controlled via command-line arguments is an excellent option. The Main function receives the args array you can parse for configuration.

units.title: LINQ queries any collection
units.detail: LINQ gives query operations (filter, select, sort, union) over any data — lists, arrays, XML, databases. If you know SQL, LINQ will feel familiar, and it replaces loops with declarative queries.

units.title: IDisposable guarantees cleanup
units.detail: The using statement + IDisposable interface makes sure you never forget cleanup code (file handles, connections). It scopes the resource lifetime so disposal happens automatically at block exit.

units.title: Operator overloading defines custom math
units.detail: You can define what +, * and == mean for your own classes, e.g. how two Player objects add together or compare. Only add overloads that match the natural meaning of the operation.

units.title: Declare a variable: type name = value
units.detail: Variables are containers of data. Write the type first (int, float, string, etc.), then the name, then optionally initialize with a value, e.g. int i = 56.

units.title: Core C# data types
units.detail: Basic types are int for whole numbers, float/double for decimals (double has more precision), bool for true/false, char for a single character, and string for text.

units.title: Calling non-static function from static
units.detail: Main is static, so calling a normal (instance) function from it produces an error. Fix it by making the called functions static too.

units.title: Conditions evaluate to a boolean
