units.detail: An if takes any condition that evaluates to true or false using comparisons like <, >, ==, <=, >=, !=. The exclamation point inverts a boolean; combine conditions with && (and) or || (or), and group with parentheses.

units.title: Switch statement with cases and break
units.detail: Switch on a value and write a case per possible value, ending each with break. A special default case runs when no case matches.

units.title: Arrays must be initialized or they are null
units.detail: Declaring int[] arr only makes a null reference; you must initialize it with new int[size] (defaults to zeroes) or with an inline element list.

units.title: Arrays are fixed size, Lists grow
units.detail: Arrays have a fixed size once created, while Lists can expand and contract with methods like Add and Remove. Lists are declared as List<T> and must be created with new.

units.title: Four loop types in C#
units.detail: foreach iterates every element of any collection; for splits into init/condition/increment sections separated by semicolons; while runs while a condition is true; do-while tests the condition only at the end.

units.title: Enums define a set of named values
units.detail: An enum (enum) declares a specific list of allowed values. They are very useful for switching over a small set of states.

units.title: Classes group fields and functions
units.detail: C# is object-oriented: write class + name, then instantiate with new. Classes can have custom constructors and hold any fields and methods.

units.title: public vs private access, default is private
units.detail: private members are only accessible inside the class; public members are accessible anywhere. If you omit the access modifier, the default is private.

units.title: Local variables only exist inside their function
units.detail: A variable declared inside a function has scope limited to that function (or code block). To share data across functions, declare it as a member field of the class.

units.title: Console.ReadKey keeps the console open
units.detail: A console app exits immediately after running. Adding Console.ReadKey() at the end pauses it until a key is pressed so you can verify output.

units.title: Comments for intent, not to explain bad names
units.detail: Use single-line // and block /* */ comments for extra text, but clean code should be understood without comments. If it isn't, rename variables to clarify intent instead of commenting.

units.title: Type safety catches errors at compile time
units.detail: C# is strongly/type-safe: writing code with the wrong type produces a compile-time error instead of an error that suddenly appears while running. This makes it a good first language.

units.title: C# is a versatile multi-purpose language
units.detail: Created by Microsoft in 2000, C# is an object-oriented, multi-purpose language used for Unity games, ASP.NET/Blazor websites, Xamarin mobile apps, Azure cloud, IoT, and desktop apps, and it runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux.

units.title: Add logs to visualize what code does
units.detail: When code doesn't behave as expected, beginners often misunderstand what the code is doing. Sprinkle logs at various points to see exactly what happens line by line.

units.title: Ask specific debugging questions
units.detail: Never post just 'it's not working'. Include the exact compile error, the line throwing it, what result you expected, and what you actually got, so others can help you.

units.title: Take your time; learning is not a race
units.detail: You are not in competition with anyone but yourself. Do not expect to finish a course in a day, week, or month; knowledge that took an expert 10 years to gather needs slow, focused study.

units.title: Refactoring keeps code readable
units.detail: Refactoring means rewriting your code to make it as readable and understandable as possible. Intermediates must treat it as a natural part of the coding process, not a skipped extra step.

units.title: Value vs reference types cause copy bugs
units.detail: Value types (like int) are passed as copies; modifying them inside a function doesn't affect the original. Reference types are passed as references and do change outside. Not knowing this leads to confusing bugs.

units.title: Float literals need an F suffix
units.detail: Writing 3.5 creates a double, not a float, so assigning it to a float fails. Append F (e.g. 3.5F) to make a float literal; forgetting the F is a classic beginner error, especially in Unity.

units.title: Three decimal types: float, double, decimal
units.detail: float is 4 bytes, double is 8 bytes, decimal is 16 bytes, with increasing precision. Use decimal when precision is paramount such as money; float/double otherwise. Doubles are the C# default for plain decimals.

units.title: Int is a 32-bit signed integer
units.detail: int is a signed 32-bit type storing roughly -2.1 to +2.1 billion. Use long/ulong for larger numbers or byte/short when memory-limited; you'll mostly use int in practice.

units.title: Integer overflow wraps to the minimum
units.detail: Incrementing an int past its maximum causes an overflow that loops back to the absolute minimum value. Always pick a type big enough to store the values you need.

units.title: Strings use double quotes, char uses single
units.detail: A string is written with double quotation marks; a char is a single character in single quotes. Mixing them (or putting the semicolon inside the quotes) causes errors.

units.title: String interpolation embeds variables cleanly
units.detail: Prefix a string with $ and wrap variables in curly braces ({name}) to inject values, avoiding messy plus-sign concatenation: $"My name is {name}". Escape literal quotes with a backslash.

units.title: var lets the compiler infer the type
units.detail: Writing var infers the type from the assigned value (10 -> int, 10.2 -> double, false -> bool, "false" -> string). It's valid and personal preference; Code Monkey prefers explicit types for clarity.

units.title: String plus number concatenation is left-to-right
units.detail: 'number' + 5 + 6 yields 'number56' (all concatenated), while 5 + 6 + 'number' yields '11number' (math first, then concatenation). Code evaluates left to right, and a string plus anything becomes a string.

units.title: Implicit vs explicit numeric conversions
units.detail: Larger types implicitly accept smaller ones (int into long, float into double) because no data is lost, but the reverse requires an explicit cast in parentheses, which may lose data.

units.title: Casting to int truncates, it does not round
units.detail: Forcing 35.9 into an int yields 35; everything after the decimal point is ignored, not rounded. This matters when converting floating-point values.

units.title: Integer division silently truncates
units.detail: 1 / 10 where both operands are int returns 0, because an int cannot store 0.1. Cast one operand to float first to get 0.1. Weird math results usually mean you're losing data to an integer division.

units.title: Convert class parses strings to numbers
units.detail: Use Convert.ToInt32/ToInt64 (for int/long) to turn a numeric string into a number; the alias int maps to System.Int32, long to System.Int64, and so on. This only works if the string actually contains a number.

units.title: Reflection inspects code dynamically
units.detail: Reflection lets you inspect and work with your code at runtime without directly calling functions or reading fields. Useful for tools and dynamically driven systems.

units.title: Extension methods extend types you don't own
units.detail: Extension methods add functions to a type without modifying it, which is essential when you lack source-code access to the type itself.

units.title: Static constructors run once per class
units.detail: A static constructor runs a single time for the entire class (unlike a normal constructor), useful for one-time class-level setup.

units.title: nameof avoids hardcoded strings
units.detail: nameof(SomeType) gives you the string name of a type or member at compile time, letting you avoid fragile magic strings in your code.

units.title: sizeof reveals type memory footprint
units.detail: sizeof(T) returns the byte size of a type (int is 4 bytes, short is 2, byte is 1), helping you understand and manage memory usage.

units.title: default returns a type's default value
units.detail: default(int) is 0, default(bool) is false, default(object) is null. Using the default keyword is better than hardcoding default values.

units.title: Records create immutable data types
units.detail: Records are a compact way to define immutable types for organizing data, reducing boilerplate compared to writing full classes.

units.title: Null-safe operators handle nulls cleanly
units.detail: The null-conditional operator (?. ) only proceeds if a value isn't null (e.g. before firing an event), and the null-coalescing operator (??) returns a default when a value is null.

units.title: Span is a zero-allocation view over arrays
units.detail: Span lets you run logic on arrays or slices without creating new objects or allocating memory; it's essentially a pointer, making it insanely performant.

units.title: Command-line args control console apps
units.detail: A console app's Main function can accept command-line arguments, enabling useful programs that need no UI and are controlled entirely from the terminal.

units.title: Functions organize code and kill copy-paste
units.detail: Grouping logic into named functions keeps a program readable and lets you change behavior in one place that automatically updates every call site, instead of editing duplicated code everywhere.

units.title: Defining a function does not run it
units.detail: Code executes top to bottom from Main; merely declaring a function does nothing. You must call it by name with parentheses and a semicolon, and the name must match case-exactly.

units.title: Function syntax: return type, name, params
units.detail: Define a function as return type + name + parentheses. Use void when returning nothing. Parameters are declared as type + name, separated by commas, and are essentially local variables.

units.title: Non-void functions must return on every path
units.detail: If a function declares a return type, every code path must hit a return statement or you get 'not all code paths return a value'. Return the condition itself to shorten simple boolean functions.

units.title: Overload functions with same name, different params
units.detail: Multiple functions can share a name as long as their parameter lists differ in count or types. The IntelliSense dropdown shows every overload when you type the call.

units.title: Chain functions by passing return values
units.detail: A function's return value can be passed directly as an argument to another function as long as the types match, or stored into a variable for later use.

units.title: Value types are passed by copy
units.detail: Passing an int into a function copies the value; incrementing it inside only changes the copy, so the original outside remains unchanged (36 inside, 35 outside).

units.title: Name functions meaningfully, not X
units.detail: Give functions names that describe what they do (like SayHello) instead of meaningless letters. Good names make the program self-explanatory.

units.title: return; in a void function stops execution
units.detail: In a void function you can call bare return; to halt execution at that point. Lines after it are flagged as unreachable code, which means they will never run.

units.title: Single equals assigns, double equals compares
units.detail: = assigns a value; == tests equality. Using one equals in a condition either errors or silently assigns, a very common beginner mistake.

units.title: if/else controls which code block runs
units.detail: Write if (condition) { code } optionally followed by else { code }. The if block runs when the condition is true; the else block runs when it is false, avoiding paired if/not-if checks.

units.title: Logical AND, OR, and NOT with truth tables
units.detail: && is true only if both operands are true; || is true if either is true; ! inverts a boolean. You can chain as many conditions as you want and group them with parentheses.

units.title: Conditions evaluate strictly left to right
units.detail: Combined conditions are evaluated from left to right, two at a time, so the final result depends on the order you write them. Use parentheses to force a specific grouping.

units.title: Short-circuit evaluation skips work
units.detail: With ||, once an operand is true the compiler stops evaluating the rest; with &&, once an operand is false it stops. This matters when later operands are expensive function calls.

units.title: If without braces captures only one line
units.detail: Omitting the code block makes only the immediately following statement part of the if; later lines run unconditionally because C# indentation is ignored. Always add braces.

units.title: Indentation doesn't matter, blocks and semicolons do
units.detail: C# ignores whitespace entirely; only code blocks (curly braces) and semicolons define structure. Indent properly anyway for your own sanity.

units.title: Chain else-if to handle ranges
units.detail: Write else followed immediately by if to test successive conditions (age under 20, else if under 30, else ...). This runs exactly one branch and is clearer than many standalone ifs.

units.title: Single & or | is bitwise, not logical
units.detail: Logical AND/OR require two characters (&& and ||). A single & or | is a completely different bitwise operation, so don't typo it.

units.title: Ctrl+arrow and Home/End speed up editing
units.detail: Hold Ctrl while pressing arrows to move word-by-word instead of letter-by-letter; Home/End jump to line start/end. Combine with Shift to select fast without touching the mouse.

units.title: Ctrl+Shift+Up/Down cycles symbol references
units.detail: Place the cursor on any symbol and press Ctrl+Shift+Up/Down to jump to its next or previous reference across the file, making it easy to find every use of a function, event, or variable.

units.title: Ctrl+, searches any class or symbol
units.detail: Pressing Ctrl+, opens a search window to find any class, method, or file by name. Icons distinguish classes, fields, and events. This avoids hunting through the solution manually.

units.title: Ctrl+Home/Ctrl+End jump to file extremes
units.detail: Use Ctrl+Home and Ctrl+End to jump straight to the beginning or end of a file, which is much faster than scrolling through large classes.

units.title: Refactoring for readability is essential
units.detail: Refactoring is rewriting code to be as readable and understandable as possible. Intermediates must treat it as a natural, unskippable part of the coding process.

units.title: Value vs reference explains sticky bugs
units.detail: If a change 'doesn't stick', you are usually working with a value type copy rather than a reference. Understanding value vs reference types is crucial for intermediates.

units.title: Build the project before watching the walkthrough
units.detail: Watch only the goal lecture describing what to build, then attempt it yourself. Watch the solution lecture only after you complete it or get seriously stuck, to genuinely validate your knowledge.

units.title: Practice projects prove you learned
units.detail: Building small practical projects (like FizzBuzz or Hangman) forces you to apply everything from the beginner section; if you can build them unaided, you actually gained the knowledge.

units.title: Classic beginner exercises: FizzBuzz and Hangman
units.detail: FizzBuzz (print numbers, replacing multiples of 3/5 with Fizz/Buzz) and Hangman are simple, doable projects that exercise variables, conditions, loops, and functions end to end.

units.title: Declare and assign a variable
units.detail: Write the data type (e.g. int), a name (can't start with a number), then = value. The value must match the declared type; int cannot hold decimals like 35.2.

units.title: Increment shorthand: ++, +=, -=, *=, /=
units.detail: age = age + 1, age += 1, and age++ all increment by one; ++/-- only change by one, while +=, -=, *=, /= accept any value.

units.title: // is a comment, not division shorthand
units.detail: Trying to write {slash}{slash} as a shorthand division doesn't work: the two forward slashes start a comment instead. Only ++ and -- have special increment/decrement shorthands.

units.title: Unassigned local variable error
units.detail: You may declare a variable without a value, but you must assign it before using it or you get 'use of unassigned local variable'.

units.title: age + health prints 125, not both values
units.detail: Adding two numeric variables does math, so printing age + health outputs the sum. Convert them to a string (e.g. concatenate a quoted string) to print both values separately.

units.title: Green squiggles are suggestions, not errors
units.detail: Faded text with a green underline is a code suggestion (like 'value never used'), not an error. It disappears once the variable is actually used, so don't worry about it.

units.title: Declare multiple variables on one line
units.detail: Write one type followed by comma-separated variable names (int age, health, power;), optionally initializing each (int x = 1, y = 2;).

units.title: Learn by doing, not passively watching
units.detail: Watching tons of tutorials without writing code is 'tutorial hell' and never graduates you to building your own projects. Do exercises that force you to actually write and run code to truly learn.

units.title: Exercise checkers are exact and case-sensitive
units.detail: An automated exercise verifies your code matches exactly: the correct type spelling, exact variable names, and exact values. Any deviation (like a capital S) fails, reinforcing that code must be precise.

units.title: Custom error messages give contextual hints
units.detail: Instead of raw compiler output, a companion window listens to errors while knowing which exercise is active and shows human-written explanations for common beginner mistakes, plus hint, solution, and apply-solution buttons.

units.title: Exercise flow: goal, hint, solution, apply
units.detail: Each exercise presents a clear goal, offers a lecture-derived hint when stuck, shows the full solution, and can auto-apply the solution so you see the final working code before ending.

units.title: FAQs and quizzes reinforce each lecture
units.detail: After each lecture, revisiting frequently-asked questions and taking a multiple-choice quiz with detailed explanations refreshes and deepens the topic, not just correct/incorrect answers.

units.title: Play finished game, then read source
units.detail: A powerful learning loop: play a fully playable game, then open its complete project files and study the source code to see how every element actually works.

units.title: Map each game element to a tutorial
units.detail: For every game feature, link to the specific step-by-step tutorial that shows how that element was built. Concrete element-to-resource mapping accelerates understanding.

units.title: Multiplayer is just synchronizing data
units.detail: Multiplayer games are fundamentally about synchronizing data. Once you can synchronize a simple game like tic-tac-toe, you can synchronize far more complex data for shooters, horror, or strategy games.

units.title: Choose netcode stack by game scale
units.detail: Use Netcode for GameObjects for small-scale co-op games (Among Us, Valheim). Use Netcode for Entities, built on the DOTS ECS stack, for fast-paced complex multiplayer like CoD or Apex. Pick based on scale and performance needs.

units.title: Dedicated server vs listen server
units.detail: Client-server topology uses a dedicated server with normal clients; client-hosted (listen server) makes one client both server and player (host). Client-hosted is the simplest, needs no cloud, and can later be swapped for a dedicated server because server/client code is decoupled.

units.title: RPCs vs ghosts vs ghost fields
units.detail: RPCs are simple one-off messages. Ghosts are objects automatically synchronized across the network (spawn on server, clients see them). Ghost fields let you continuously sync custom data just like transform data is synced automatically.

units.title: Domain reload off leaves statics stale
units.detail: Disabling domain reload speeds up play mode, but static fields and static event handlers will no longer reset between play sessions. Keep this in mind when using statics or you'll get stale-state bugs.

units.title: DOTS events replace C# events
units.detail: DOTS is data-oriented, so normal C# events (which use objects/delegates) don't fit. Build a custom DOTS-compatible event system using components and entity queries instead.

units.title: Keep UI as game objects in DOTS
units.detail: Even in DOTS games, UI is usually better made with normal game objects and updated via DOTS events and queries. Don't force ECS onto UI.

units.title: Server validates all player actions
units.detail: The server validates player actions: non-current players cannot act, and win logic is checked server-side. Never trust clients; the server is the authority for game rules.

units.title: Lobby groups players, relay bypasses firewalls
units.detail: Lobby lets players create and join groups; relay lets them connect over the internet without firewall or port-forwarding issues. Together they make worldwide peer connections just work.

units.title: DOTS 2D game uses 3D template
units.detail: DOTS doesn't yet support 2D natively, so a 2D DOTS game uses flat 2D meshes inside the 3D URP template.

units.title: Design problems vs technical problems
units.detail: Design problems are how to take an idea (e.g., 'make a health system') and figure out an implementation. Technical problems are fixing bugs where something behaves wrong. Each has its own solving framework.

units.title: Design framework: 4 steps
units.detail: 1) Identify the problem precisely. 2) Break it into its smallest core components, splitting until you can't split further. 3) Plan each component at a high level (pseudo-code). 4) Write concrete implementation details.

units.title: Technical framework: 3 steps
units.detail: 1) Identify the problem (e.g., bullet heals instead of damaging). 2) Locate it — find the exact line of code responsible, usually via debugging. 3) Fix it.

units.title: No one writes bug-free code first try
units.detail: You will never write a 100% bug-free system on the first pass. Expect and embrace fixing issues; debugging is itself a core skill.

units.title: Tutorials hide the real work
units.detail: A 20-minute tutorial may represent hours of research and failed iterations; you only see the final polished code. Beginners misread this as 'code is written perfectly once.' Understand the hidden problem-solving process.

units.title: Problem solving is learned, not innate
units.detail: It's a skill with levels: the same problem that took days at the start takes minutes with experience. It's gained only by solving many problems, not by watching.

units.title: Health system component breakdown
units.detail: Example decomposition: store HP value, damage function, heal function, min/max clamping, death when HP hits zero. Build tiny components and combine them to construct the high-level system.

units.title: Refactoring separates beginners from pros
units.detail: Beginners believe code is written once and must be right the first time. Intermediates treat code as a living thing that constantly changes; rewriting/reorganizing it is a normal part of the process.

units.title: Get it working, then get it right
units.detail: First goal: make the system work. Second (often missed): review the working code and refactor — better variable names, split functions doing too many things, group scattered data into custom classes. Dirty code first is OK; leaving it dirty is not.

units.title: Constantly look for improvements
units.detail: After any system works, ask: could names be clearer? Is any function doing too much? Does a set of data belong in its own class? Keep the code you'll reuse clean, since projects grow in complexity.

units.title: Separate logic from visuals
units.detail: Keep gameplay logic in its own script and presentation (e.g., thruster visuals) in a separate script that only reads the logic state. Decoupling makes systems reusable and testable.

units.title: Never use strings to identify objects
units.detail: Avoid identifying objects by name or tag strings. Use a stronger method (component references, enums, types) so renames or refactors don't silently break references.

units.title: Landing detection: slow AND upright
units.detail: A safe landing requires checking both that the vehicle descends slowly enough (velocity threshold) and at the right angle (alignment with the pad), using math on the physics state.

units.title: Singleton pattern for game manager
units.detail: Use the singleton pattern to give easy global access to a single instance such as a game manager; combined with events it simplifies wiring across scripts.

units.title: Decouple UI code from logic
units.detail: UI classes should only observe logic (via events) and not own gameplay state, so windows can be rebuilt or restyled without touching game code.

units.title: Abstract input behind actions
units.detail: Instead of listening to key presses directly, map inputs to named actions through an abstraction layer. Adding gamepad or touch support then becomes trivial — just bind new devices to the same actions.

units.title: State machine for game flow
units.detail: Model game states (waiting for input, playing, game over, restart) with a state machine to keep transitions explicit and manageable.

units.title: Add levels via prefab data
units.detail: Structure levels so adding a new one is just adding another prefab/config, and design that data so levels can be arbitrarily complex.

units.title: Polish separates good from great
units.detail: A polish pass of small tweaks and effects is a mandatory stage; polish is what distinguishes good games from great ones.

units.title: Post-processing for instant visual boost
units.detail: A few post-processing settings, set up early before building the game, make scenes look dramatically better with minimal effort.

units.title: Agree on naming rules first
units.detail: Before writing game code, establish coding style and naming conventions (at professional Steam-game quality) so the whole project stays consistent.

units.title: ScriptableObjects as data definitions
units.detail: Define types and recipes as ScriptableObject assets (e.g., a cutting recipe mapping ingredient to slices) so designers can create content without touching code.

units.title: C# interfaces for interactions
units.detail: Model interaction capability with a C# interface (e.g., Interact/AlternateInteract), letting different objects each implement different behavior behind a common contract.

units.title: Events for input and state changes
units.detail: Use C# events to notify systems of input and state changes so producers and consumers stay decoupled.

units.title: State machine + timer for cooking
units.detail: A cooking stove uses a small state machine (idle, cooking, burned) with timers; recipes define cooking and burning durations.

units.title: World-space canvas for progress UI
units.detail: Attach a world-space UI canvas to an object to display a real-time progress bar (e.g., cutting progress) positioned in the 3D world.

units.title: Rebindable controls architecture
units.detail: Expose a controls screen where keys and gamepad inputs are rebindable and support any gamepad (Xbox/PS/Switch). Designing input as data from the start makes this easy.

units.title: Pick a design that shows many skills
units.detail: Choose a game design (character + interactions, like a kitchen) that naturally exercises many engine/language features — interfaces, events, data assets, state machines, shaders, input system.

units.title: Dynamic buffers store lists in components
units.detail: Dynamic buffers let you store a list or queue of data inside an ECS component — e.g., a unit spawn queue for a barracks building.

units.title: Custom baking systems create entities
units.detail: Write a custom baking system when you need to generate additional entities beyond what authoring provides, e.g., to make a DOTS animation system work correctly.

units.title: DOTS runs code 200x faster
units.detail: DOTS (ECS + job system + Burst) can make some code run over 200x faster, enabling far more complex games or making 60 FPS and low battery consumption easier to hit.

units.title: DOTS = ECS + jobs + Burst
units.detail: DOTS is Unity's high-performance stack: data-oriented ECS instead of object-oriented, plus the job system for multithreading and the Burst compiler for fast machine code. It requires a different way of thinking.

units.title: Not every system must be DOTS
units.detail: Mix normal MonoBehaviour scripts and DOTS systems in one project (e.g., a MonoBehaviour reading mouse position to feed DOTS units). Use each where it fits.

units.title: Write simple system, then Burst it
units.detail: First get behavior working in a simple, readable system, then refactor it into a fast Burst-compiled parallel job. Working first, optimize second — the speedup is often ~100x.

units.title: Structural changes are expensive
units.detail: Entity spawning creates structural changes in ECS, which have performance implications. Be deliberate about when and how entities are created or destroyed.

units.title: Blob assets for large read-only data
units.detail: Blob assets are the main way to store large amounts of data (e.g., animation clip data) in a structured, easily readable form inside ECS.

units.title: Flow field beats A* for many units
units.detail: Flow field pathfinding is preferred over A* when you have tons of units: compute one flow field and every unit follows it, instead of pathing per unit.

units.title: Burst-compatible random is different
units.detail: Unity's usual random API is not Burst-compatible; the DOTS random class works differently (typically seeded per call), so migrate random usage when writing jobs.

units.title: DOTS events need data-oriented design
units.detail: Events normally require objects and delegates, which clash with ECS. Build an event system using components and queries to keep it data-oriented.

units.title: Reuse components to build features fast
units.detail: The defensive tower was built quickly by reusing previously made components and systems (targeting, firing, health). Good component design makes new gameplay cheap.

units.title: RTS is ideal for learning DOTS
units.detail: An RTS — many units, many systems, tons of simultaneous logic — is the natural genre for learning a performance stack like DOTS, since it stresses exactly what ECS optimizes.

units.title: Server authoritative vs client authoritative
units.detail: Decide who owns game state. Server-authoritative (server validates actions, syncs to clients) is safer but more work; client-authoritative is simpler but trusts the client. Choose per feature.

units.title: Multiplayer has no single player object
units.detail: In multiplayer there is no single player object, and many single-player assumptions break. Things like a 'selected counter visual' must be rethought per-client.

units.title: Decide what to sync per system
units.detail: For each system, decide what must be synchronized versus what can stay local (e.g., cutting counter visuals local, stove state network-synced). Don't blindly sync everything.

units.title: RPCs vs network variables
units.detail: Use RPCs for one-off events and messages; use network variables when the server owns a continuously changing state that must stay synced (like a cooking timer).

units.title: Handle disconnects and late joins
units.detail: Multiplayer games must clean up objects when a player disconnects mid-game so nothing crashes, and define a policy for players joining after the game started — allow or reject.

units.title: Scene flow for connection
units.detail: A clean connection flow: main menu, lobby list/create, connection, character select (all players ready), then load the game scene together. Load scenes only when everyone is ready.

units.title: Support offline single player too
units.detail: Architect so all multiplayer connections can be bypassed for offline single player — broadens the audience and makes testing easier; netcode design often makes this cheap.

units.title: Host can kick; server enforces rules
units.detail: The host gets extra controls like kicking players, and the server enforces shared-choice rules (e.g., preventing two players from picking the same character color).

units.title: Wait for all players ready to start
units.detail: The game only starts when every player has confirmed ready (and passed the tutorial), with a synchronized countdown so all clients begin in sync.

units.title: Only server spawns/destroys network objects
units.detail: Only the server spawns shared objects (recipes, pickups) and destroys them (e.g., trash counter), so all clients see identical state. Clients request, the server acts.

units.title: Teach what you actually use
units.detail: Teach using exactly the same practices and technology you use in your own shipped games — practical advice grounded in real production beats detached theory.

units.title: Build varied mini-games to learn
units.detail: Building small complete games across different genres (factory, top-down shooter, spaceship constructor) is an effective way to broaden skills and learn by doing.

units.title: Unity LTS vs tech release versions
units.detail: Unity provides long-term support (LTS) versions that are extremely stable and tech releases for testing new features. For most projects, use the LTS version (e.g., 2019.4).

units.title: HDRP vs URP render pipelines
units.detail: The High Definition Render Pipeline is optimized for the absolute best visuals, while the Universal Render Pipeline focuses on running on anything. Indie devs usually work in URP unless pushing visual limits.

units.title: Game objects are composed of components
units.detail: A game object is the base building block in Unity; behavior emerges by composing it with components. Each component has a single purpose, and adding more components adds more logic and visuals.

units.title: Every game object has a Transform
units.detail: All game objects have a Transform component by default, which stores position, rotation, and scale. It is the one component every object always has.

units.title: Mesh filter stores, mesh renderer draws
units.detail: Rendering a mesh requires two components: the Mesh Filter stores the mesh data and the Mesh Renderer renders it using materials. Each has a single narrow purpose.

units.title: Rigidbody plus collider enables physics
units.detail: Adding a Rigidbody puts an object into the physics world so it falls with gravity; adding a collider gives it a physical shape. Together they enable interactions like bouncing and rolling.

units.title: MonoBehaviour Start and Update lifecycle
units.detail: Scripts used as components must extend MonoBehaviour. Start runs once before the first frame and Update runs once per frame. Debug.Log writes messages to the console.

units.title: 2D sprites and orthographic camera
units.detail: For 2D visuals use a SpriteRenderer instead of mesh components, and switch the camera projection from perspective to orthographic to get a flat 2D look.

units.title: Scenes organize separate game worlds
units.detail: Scenes are the main way to organize parts of a game, e.g., main menu, gameplay, and different areas. Each scene is a completely separate world with its own objects.

units.title: Learning programming patterns improves code
units.detail: Studying programming patterns helps you spot bad practices and refactor messy code into clean code, covering patterns like Observer, Singleton, Factories, Delegates, and Strategy, which leads to making better games faster.

units.title: Curate learning bundles across skill areas
units.detail: Structured courses provide a different learning path than free tutorials and can be curated into bundles (e.g., Unity, Blender, and programming patterns) that take a beginner through all areas of game development.

units.title: Visual scripting basics and demos
units.detail: Visual scripting lets you build game logic without writing code and can be learned through live sessions that cover basics, more complex scripts, and demo projects.

units.title: Break big games into core components
units.detail: You can't build a project by thinking of the final massive result. Break it into core components (player controller, world, combat, inventory, quests) and work on each one individually.

units.title: Cut scope in half, repeatedly
units.detail: If you tend to think in massive terms like an MMORPG, lower your scope: cut the vision in half, then cut it in half again until you have something you can actually build.

units.title: 2D bool array for L-shaped buildings
units.detail: Instead of storing a building's width and height, define a 2D bool array marking occupied positions true and empty positions false. When placing, loop the array and only require empty grid cells where the array is true.

units.title: C# multi-dimensional arrays syntax
units.detail: In C#, adding a comma inside the square brackets of an array declaration defines extra dimensions, e.g., a 2D bool array for grid shapes, and you can have as many dimensions as needed.

units.title: Minimap via second camera and layers
units.detail: A minimap works by adding small sprite icons on a dedicated layer invisible to the main camera, placing a second camera above looking down, and rendering that camera's view to a texture displayed in the UI.

units.title: EventHandler vs Action for events
units.detail: EventHandler is the C# standard for events and works with any delegate type, and the sender parameter helps other programmers understand your code. Working solo you may prefer the simpler Action delegate.

units.title: event keyword restricts external control
units.detail: Without the event keyword, any class can call or reset a delegate field. Adding event limits outside classes to only subscribing and unsubscribing, so only the defining class can invoke or clear it.

units.title: Events decouple logic from UI visuals
units.detail: C# events let logic code notify others without caring if a UI element exists, keeping logic and visual code nicely separated and decoupled.

units.title: A strong hook makes marketing easier
units.detail: Marketing becomes much easier when your game idea has a good hook; a generic hook (e.g., 'another pixel platformer') makes selling far more difficult, so study how profitable indie games are analyzed.

units.title: Steam page is the marketing baseline
units.detail: The most basic prerequisite for marketing an indie game is simply having a public Steam page, which is where players discover and wishlist the game.

units.title: Indie marketing learning resources
units.detail: Study sources that analyze why games succeed: the Clark Tank show (steam chart analysis), the GameDiscoverCo newsletter, and Chris Zukowski's articles and store-page analyses.

units.title: Problem solving is the core skill
units.detail: Problem solving is the one skill required to build anything—any game, any system—and it's what top-company engineers are expected to have. It can be taught with courses full of practice problems.

units.title: Server-authoritative vs client-authoritative
units.detail: In multiplayer games you must decide whether the server or the client is authoritative over state. The decision affects sync logic and is one of the most important multiplayer design considerations.

units.title: Only server spawns network objects
units.detail: When synchronizing spawns in multiplayer, only the server should spawn objects so all clients see the same list; clients never spawn gameplay objects directly.

units.title: Choose RPCs vs network variables
units.detail: For synchronized state, use RPCs for one-shot events and network variables when the server should keep track of a state and sync it to clients (e.g., a stove's cooking state).

units.title: Refactoring improves code quality
units.detail: Refactoring, e.g., migrating from the legacy input manager to the new Input System, is a highly valuable skill that massively improves the quality and maintainability of your code.

units.title: Scriptable Objects define data types
units.detail: Use Scriptable Objects to define types of data such as ingredients, plates, and recipes. This keeps definitions data-driven instead of hardcoded in logic.

units.title: State machines and timers for complex logic
units.detail: Complex behaviors like a cooking counter with cook/burn recipes can be modeled with a basic state machine plus timers, keeping each state's logic explicit and manageable.

units.title: Establish naming and coding style early
units.detail: Having proper naming rules and good code standards is paramount when writing a full game; they keep a codebase clean and maintainable over many files.

units.title: Polish separates good games from great
units.detail: The polish stage—small tweaks and effects—is what separates good games from great games and should be a planned phase of development.

units.title: Multiplayer requires different thinking
units.detail: Multiplayer changes design decisions: there is no longer a single player object, and you must sync game state, handle disconnects, late joins, pausing, and lobby/relay/connection flows.

units.title: Design levels by painting a texture
units.detail: You can design a level by drawing pixels in a texture, then reading each pixel at startup and spawning objects based on its color (e.g., a blue pixel marks the player spawn).

units.title: Texture import settings for pixel reading
units.detail: To read pixels reliably, enable Read/Write, disable mipmaps, and set the filter mode to Point. Also save the source as a bitmap, since compression can corrupt the colors.

units.title: GetPixels is faster than GetPixel
units.detail: GetPixels returns a flattened array (width times height) and is much more performant than calling GetPixel per coordinate, but GetPixel is easier to follow when prototyping. Refactor to GetPixels later.

units.title: Switch on hex color string
units.detail: Convert each pixel color to a hex string and use a switch statement on it to decide what to spawn, with constants defining each object's color for clarity.

units.title: Scale pixels to world with units-per-pixel
units.detail: Define a constant for units per pixel and multiply pixel coordinates by it (e.g., pixel 2,2 with 20 units/pixel becomes world position 40,40), making level scale easy to tune.

units.title: Multiple object types via color switch
units.detail: Extend a texture-based level system by adding a color constant and switch case per object type (wall, health, ammo, enemy), each spawning the matching object at the pixel position.

units.title: Auto-spawn boundary walls from texture size
units.detail: Loop the texture width and height to automatically spawn walls on all four outer edges, keeping the player inside level bounds without hardcoding them in the texture.

units.title: Pure colors keep level code simple
units.detail: Using pure colors (like pure red for enemies) keeps pixel-matching code simple and readable; any unique hex value works, but pure colors make the mapping obvious.

units.title: Sekiro-style dual health and posture bars
units.detail: A combat system can use two bars: a normal health bar that decreases with damage and increases with healing, plus a posture bar that fills when the player parries, breaks when full, and glows to signal the break.

units.title: Separate logic from visuals
units.detail: Writing systems like health bars with logic and visuals kept separate makes code much cleaner and easier to reuse and modify later.

units.title: Use enums for state handling
units.detail: State handling with strings causes real bugs; using enums for state handling is safer and more maintainable.

units.title: Adjust console lines per log entry
units.detail: Unity lets you change how many lines are displayed per console log entry, making the console more compact or expanded to see more information or the log trace.

units.title: GameObject constructor overloads
units.detail: Create game objects with the default constructor or use optional constructors to pass a name and pre-add components, producing clearer, more compact, and more performant code.

units.title: Transform pivots and parent-child tricks
units.detail: By default a pivot sits at an object's center, which makes things like a health bar scaling from one edge seem impossible. Managing transform parents and children lets you place the pivot exactly where needed.

units.title: Sound manager keyed by enum
units.detail: A clean sound manager can use an enum to reference audio clips, play 2D or 3D sounds via a single AudioSource, and be extended easily with more sounds and features.

units.title: Game design documents scale with team
units.detail: Whether to write a game design document depends on team size: AAA studios have very different requirements than one- or two-person teams, so tailor detail to your scale.

units.title: Battle royale shrinking damage circle
units.detail: A shrinking damage circle needs a current size and position, a white preview circle showing the next randomly generated size and position, and a customizable shrink timer and speed.

units.title: Reusable code library enables rapid prototyping
units.detail: Building a library of clean, generic, reusable scripts and assets lets you assemble a complex prototype (an RTS) in 15 minutes by composing existing systems like camera follow, health, and utilities. Invest in reusable code so future work is faster.

units.title: State machine for simple unit AI
units.detail: A two-state machine (normal/busy) keeps unit logic simple: normal state handles movement and combat, busy state does nothing while an animation plays. Blocking logic during animation prevents conflicting actions.

units.title: Static list registry for closest-enemy search
units.detail: Keep all units in a static List registered on spawn, then search it for the closest unit of the opposing team. This avoids expensive scene queries and works for both teams with one flag.

units.title: Skip dead units during target acquisition
units.detail: When scanning the registry for the closest enemy, you must skip dead units with a 'continue', otherwise you target corpses and hit null references. This bug surfaced right after adding damage/kill logic.

units.title: Health-changed event drives health bar
units.detail: Instead of polling health every frame, subscribe to a health-changed event and update the world-space health bar size from the event callback. Event-driven UI is decoupled and efficient.

units.title: Death polish: flying body plus camera shake
units.detail: On death, spawn a ragdoll-like prefab launched along the attack direction and add a small camera shake. These reusable effect systems make minimal mechanics feel satisfying.

units.title: Anti-cheat breaks when patching executables
units.detail: Tamper-proof and anti-cheat solutions detect modifications to the executable, so a binary patch can break them. If your game uses anti-cheat, you must rebuild from the updated editor instead of using the patch tool.

units.title: Hotfix-only editor upgrades are low risk
units.detail: Updating only the patch/hotfix version of your Unity editor (same minor version) is essentially bug fixes and rarely breaks anything, but always keep a backup before upgrading regardless.

units.title: Security vulnerability patching workflow
units.detail: For shipped apps, either update the editor, recompile and republish, or use the vendor's standalone patch tool on existing executables when you lack source code. Platform-level mitigations (e.g. Steam, Windows Defender) can also block exploits on the backend.

units.title: 2D lights require URP plus Sprite Lit material
units.detail: 2D lights only appear with URP, a 2D renderer, and the 2D packages installed, and sprites must use a Sprite Lit shader or they won't be affected by 2D lights. Misconfigured projects silently get no lighting.

units.title: Target sorting layers limit what a light affects
units.detail: Each 2D light has target sorting layers controlling which layers it lights. Configure this per light so backgrounds and characters respond to different lights.

units.title: Sprite secondary textures enable rim lighting
units.detail: Sprites can carry secondary normal maps (fake 3D surface lighting) and mask maps (control which areas receive light). A mask map used as a rim-light channel greatly improves readability.

units.title: Fake directional light via rotating spotlight
units.detail: 2D has no directional light, so use a spotlight with a 360-degree angle and rotate its parent to simulate a day/night sun. Multiple rotated day/night lights plus color gradients create convincing cycles.

units.title: Fake shadows using lights tinted black
units.detail: Create soft, controllable shadows by tinting a freeform or sprite light black; interpolating between frame points makes the shadow morph smoothly. These look better in daylight than realtime shadows.

units.title: Blob shadows under characters
units.detail: For characters, prefer a simple soft blob-sprite shadow over hard Shadow Casters, which look harsh and suit night scenes. Blob shadows are the standard, good-looking daytime approach.

units.title: Rule tiles automate tile placement decisions
units.detail: Rule tiles define neighbor-based rules that select the correct sprite automatically while painting, making round/corner tilemaps fast to lay out and always visually correct.

units.title: Tilemap API can drive gameplay logic
units.detail: Tilemaps aren't just visuals: scripts (e.g. a terrain manager) use the tilemap API to read and write tiles, enabling dig/plant/watering mechanics. Consider your own generic grid system if you need more flexibility.

units.title: GameObject brush paints objects with own sorting order
units.detail: The GameObject brush paints regular objects instead of tiles, giving each placed object (trees, props) an independent sorting order so overlapping objects render correctly. Useful for anything not painted on the floor.

units.title: PSD importer auto-splits layered character art
units.detail: Drawing a character on separate Photoshop layers/folders lets the PSD importer slice each body part into its own tight sprite automatically, replacing painful manual sprite-sheet drawing.

units.title: 2D lighting performance checklist
units.detail: Use the Frame Debugger to find GPU bottlenecks, keep render scale low, minimize shadow-casting lights on screen, minimize blend styles, and cap max light count — critical for mobile 2D games.

units.title: Animation Rigging creates new animations without being an animator
units.detail: Take a generic idle animation and apply a Two Bone IK constraint so the hand dynamically reaches any target. This method yields animations tailored to exact positions without using Blender/Maya.

units.title: Animate constraint weight to reach code-set targets
units.detail: Record an animation that only ramps the IK constraint weight from 0 to 1; set the IK target position in code. The system smoothly moves the hand to whatever item, even if it's slightly off the recorded spot.

units.title: Two animations needed to stop animating a rig
units.detail: You cannot stop animating one part once its animation starts, so use two separate animations and constraints: one that dynamically sets the grab target, and a second that animates the arm pulling the item back.

units.title: Animation Events sync pickup timing
units.detail: Fire Animation Events (e.g. OnGrabItem, OnStoredItem) from keyframes: parent the item to the hand bone on grab, then destroy it once stored. Events decouple animation timing from gameplay logic.

units.title: Rigging override order follows hierarchy
units.detail: Animation Rigging applies constraints in hierarchy order, so child/later constraints override earlier ones. Order constraints deliberately (the pull-back constraint below the grab constraint) for the intended result.

units.title: Vertex-displacement shaders bend visuals, not logic
units.detail: Curved-world effects use a vertex transformation shader keyed off distance to camera: colliders, navmesh, and transforms stay flat up top while only the rendered visuals curve. Game logic stays normal and simple.

units.title: Clicking curved visuals misses the collider
units.detail: With visuals-only bending, raycasts fail because colliders sit at the flat logical positions. If interaction matters, use a companion script that also moves transforms/colliders along the curve.

units.title: Choose bending granularity per object
units.detail: Mix how objects bend: shader-only visuals, transforms moved by script (fixes distortion on tall objects), or a shader-bent visual with a script-moved child collider. This gives per-object control over interaction and distortion.

units.title: Batch-swap materials to a new shader
units.detail: Instead of swapping each material to the curved-world shader manually, use a renderer-overview tool to list all scene renderers/materials and apply the swap in one click, then tune via a controller script.

units.title: Render textures redirect camera output
units.detail: A render texture is a texture you can render onto: assign it as a camera's output texture and that camera renders to the texture instead of the screen. This enables TVs, minimaps, and custom post-processing.

units.title: Raw Image needed for RenderTextures in UI
units.detail: The UI Image component expects a Sprite and silently rejects a texture/render texture. Swap to a Raw Image component to display RenderTextures on the canvas.

units.title: Minimap: orthographic camera plus culling mask
units.detail: Point an orthographic camera straight down, create a dedicated minimap layer, set the camera's culling mask to only that layer, and exclude the layer from the main camera. Display via a UI Raw Image, optionally masked into a circle.

units.title: Capture main camera as a screenshot
units.detail: Set the camera's targetTexture to a render texture, call Render(), then set it back to null so the camera returns to the screen. This captures one frame into the texture for screenshots or processing.

units.title: Shader Graph requires an SRP
units.detail: Shader Graph does not work on the built-in render pipeline; you must install URP or HDRP, create a render pipeline asset, and assign it in project settings before shaders will function.

units.title: Property reference name must match code exactly
units.detail: Shader properties have a display name and a reference name (conventionally underscore-prefixed). Material.SetColor/SetFloat must use the exact, case-sensitive reference string or the change silently does nothing.

units.title: Shader Graph node inputs are typed
units.detail: Node ports declare types (t2 = 2D texture, rgb = color). To use a texture's color you must pass it through a Sample Texture 2D node; connecting the raw texture to albedo fails. Effects are just colors and math per pixel.

units.title: Drive shaders from code via property setters
units.detail: Expose shader properties (colors, slider floats) and modify them at runtime with material.SetColor("_Color", value) or SetFloat, letting gameplay manipulate effects freely.

units.title: GPU vs CPU particle systems coexist
units.detail: VFX Graph runs on the GPU, rendering millions of particles but with limited direct physics interaction; the built-in system runs on the CPU with thousands of particles but can read physics and per-particle state. Choose by workload.

units.title: Spawn rate needs matching capacity and culling bounds
units.detail: Raising spawn rate alone spawns few particles; you must also increase the particle capacity, and the culling bounds box must be visible to the camera or the system won't render.

units.title: Expose properties to reuse one VFX graph
units.detail: Expose parameters on a VFX graph and use per-instance override checkboxes on the effect component. One graph can then produce many visually distinct effects (colors, sizes) without duplicating graphs.

units.title: You can't use tools you don't know exist
units.detail: Deliberately survey the engine's feature set (video player, render textures, navmesh, etc.) because unknown tools expand your solution space — e.g. knowing about the video player enables in-game tutorial videos you'd never consider otherwise.

units.title: Visual scripting teaches programming logic without code
units.detail: Node-based visual scripting builds working games while teaching how logic, objects, and scripts interact, making it both a non-coding game-dev path and a stepping stone into real programming.

units.title: Learn by building games of different genres
units.detail: Learning a tool by completing multiple small games (e.g. a simple platformer then a feature-rich RPG) builds transferable skills with a smooth difficulty curve, instead of one long monotone project.

units.title: Visual scripting teaches logic without code
units.detail: Visual scripting visualizes the logic and flow that programming is built on; once you grasp the logic, learning the syntax of a real language is much easier. It opens game dev to people scared of code.

units.title: ECS: components, entities, systems
units.detail: In ECS, components hold data, entities hold instances of components, and systems run logic over entities with matching components. Querying entities by required components is the core pattern.

units.title: DOTS-based scripting auto-benefits from Burst and Job System
units.detail: Unity's visual scripting graphs are built on DOTS, so generated scripts automatically get the performance of the Burst compiler and Job System. This also makes it a learning tool for understanding ECS.

units.title: DOTS lacks Sprite Renderer support
units.detail: The DOTS implementation doesn't support the Sprite Renderer; entities built from GameObjects need a Mesh Filter and Mesh Renderer instead to be visible.

units.title: Convert GameObject to entity component
units.detail: Adding a 'Convert to Entity' component turns a GameObject into an entity at runtime and destroys the GameObject. The Entity Debugger then shows the resulting entity and its components.

units.title: Dragging an object auto-builds a query
units.detail: Dragging a GameObject onto a visual scripting graph auto-creates a query listing every component it has; prune the query down to only the components you modify so logic only runs on the relevant entities.

units.title: Per-frame add vs absolute set translate
units.detail: To move an entity continuously, use a translate node in 'add' mode rather than 'set' mode; setting an absolute value once would not accumulate motion each frame.

units.title: Multiply movement by delta time
units.detail: Making movement frame-rate independent requires multiplying speed by delta time; the demo ran at 800 FPS and moved correctly only because of this.

units.title: Store direction and speed as data components
units.detail: Instead of hardcoding motion, store a direction (+1/-1) and a move speed in small data components; logic reads these values and multiplies direction x speed x delta time.

units.title: Code viewer exposes generated C#
units.detail: Visual scripting includes a code viewer that shows the C# equivalent of the graph, which is an excellent way for programmers to learn how ECS queries and systems work.

units.title: Animation rigging layers dynamic motion over animation
units.detail: The animation rigging package computes bone positions/rotations in real time (IK, aim, chain) on top of static animations, so characters can look at moving targets without baking it into the clip.

units.title: Rig Builder + rig GameObject with constraints
units.detail: Rig setup adds a Rig Builder component that references a child rig GameObject; all constraints are placed as components on objects inside the rig.

units.title: Multi-aim constraint points a bone at a target
units.detail: The Multi-Aim constraint takes a constraint object (the bone to rotate) and a source object (the target to look at), so a head or turret always faces a moving object.

units.title: Bone render setup visualizer selects bones
units.detail: Bone Render Setup adds a clickable visualizer for every bone, making it easy to select specific bones and see which one you are constraining instead of accidentally selecting the skin mesh.

units.title: Aim axes must be read in local space
units.detail: To configure aim/up axes correctly, select the bone and switch the transform handle to local space; parent rotation can make the world-space forward axis different from the bone's local forward.

units.title: Rig settings apply only on play or preview
units.detail: Because rigging runs through jobs, changing constraint settings while playing or previewing has no effect; exit and re-enter play/preview mode to apply new values.

units.title: Animation preview window iterates without play
units.detail: Enabling preview in the Animation window runs animation rigging in edit mode, letting you adjust targets and constraints without pressing Play.

units.title: Effectors are visual gizmos for targets
units.detail: The effector window adds visible gizmos (box, ball, locator, square) to target/hint objects, making rigging setup much clearer to work with in the scene view.

units.title: Blend rigs via weight
units.detail: Rig and constraint weight define how much they affect the final pose; lerping weight from 1 to 0 smoothly blends from looking at a target back to the normal idle animation (e.g. based on distance).

units.title: Smooth weight transitions with Mathf.Lerp
units.detail: Drive constraint weight toward a target value each frame using Mathf.Lerp so gaze shifts are smooth rather than snapping between states, triggered by events like a key press.

units.title: Find package class namespace via Edit Script
units.detail: Right-clicking a package component and choosing Edit Script reveals its namespace and class name (e.g. UnityEngine.Animation.Rigging), which you add as a using directive to code against it.

units.title: Two Bone IK auto-setup from tip
units.detail: For a two-bone chain (hip/knee/foot or shoulder/elbow/hand), assign the tip bone and use Auto Setup From Tip Transform to fill root/mid bones and create a target plus an optional hint.

units.title: IK hint steers middle-joint bend
units.detail: The hint is a soft target for the middle joint; place it in front for knees/elbows since human joints generally don't bend backwards. If unassigned, the system guesses the bend direction.

units.title: Rotation limits keep poses humanlike
units.detail: Set min/max rotation limits on aim constraints so heads stop around 90 degrees instead of over-rotating, and disable individual constraint axes to allow only yaw or only pitch.

units.title: Write down your goals
units.detail: Studies suggest simply writing goals down massively increases the chance of achieving them; a clear goal is like a race track versus driving blind in a desert.

units.title: Use SMART goals
units.detail: SMART = Specific (clear numbers/actions), Measurable (trackable progress), Achievable (doable solo with your skill set), Relevant (what you actually want), and Time-bound (a deadline).

units.title: Seven-step path to game development
units.detail: Build tiny games, follow beginner/intermediate tutorials, ship a complete simple game, study Clean Code, make and publish a 3-month game, study Code Complete, then make and publish a 6-month game.

units.title: Rely on discipline, not motivation
units.detail: Motivation is random and out of your control; self-discipline is the ability to make yourself do what you know you need to do whether you feel like it or not.

units.title: Don't punish yourself for missing goals
units.detail: Missing an ambitious goal still leaves you better off than never defining one; take a breath and keep working the plan instead of being harsh on yourself.

units.title: Scale plan detail to experience
units.detail: An expert launching a game may only need a list of mechanics and a belief in the timeline, while a beginner needs step-by-step guidance; match planning detail to your skill level.

units.title: Track concretely to achieve fitness goals
units.detail: The author's fitness breakthrough came from writing down a specific plan (calories, macros, training splits) and tracking every food and workout; concrete tracking makes vague desires achievable.

units.title: Protect health to sustain long game-dev careers
units.detail: Fitness, regular breaks, walks and hydration prevent burnout when working 8-10 hours daily without weekends; find any activity you enjoy and do it.

units.title: Keep code free of magic numbers
units.detail: Every number in code should be self-explanatory; replace raw constants with named local variables or fields so intent is clear.

units.title: SerializeField for private editable fields
units.detail: Variables used in only one script should be private; add [SerializeField] when they need editing in the Inspector instead of making them public, keeping code clean.

units.title: Test at limited frame rates
units.detail: Manually cap the frame rate during testing because bugs can appear on low frame rates that never occur at high ones; always test across hardware scenarios.

units.title: Script Execution Order window
units.detail: The Script Execution Order window lets you force one script's Start to run before another's, which matters when initialization has dependencies.

units.title: Write adaptable reusable code
units.detail: Reworking a tooltip system into an item stats window quickly worked because the code was clear and reusable; clean, adaptable code lets you create new features fast.

units.title: Clock UI from basic rotation math
units.detail: Display in-game time by rotating clock hands based on time values (hours/minutes or minutes/seconds); once you understand the math you can show any time format.

units.title: Tint pixels while masking parts
units.detail: Tint sprite pixels by color but use a mask to preserve regions like eyes; this enables modular sprite customization (e.g. skin color tinting).

units.title: Enable Unity Analytics in Services window
units.detail: Window > General > Services, create a project ID, then enable Analytics; basic stats (DAU, MAU, sessions per user) start sending immediately with a single button press.

units.title: Analytics data takes up to a day
units.detail: Events can take a few hours to about a day to appear on the dashboard, so a fresh setup may show empty even after playing the game.

units.title: Send custom analytics events via code
units.detail: Call Analytics.CustomEvent(name) or Analytics.CustomEvent(name, Dictionary<string,object>) and check the returned AnalyticsResult equals AnalyticsResult.Ok to confirm the event was sent.

units.title: No-code analytics via Event Tracker
units.detail: The Analytics Event Tracker component fires events on lifecycle/UI/timer triggers with parameters, letting designers send events without touching code (e.g. instantiate a prefab on game start).

units.title: Custom event parameter limit
units.detail: Custom events support a maximum of roughly 10 parameters; choose them wisely and use quantized values rather than raw data.

units.title: Store analyzable data, not raw values
units.detail: Instead of logging a raw Vector3 death position (which needs custom tooling to analyze), split the level into sections by rounding position/20; deaths then map to a few buckets that are easy to aggregate.

units.title: Funnel analyzer finds drop-off
units.detail: Funnels chain events (win level 1, win level 2...) to show what percentage of players reach each stage, revealing where players abandon your game and whether the drop-off is natural or excessive.

units.title: Use death data to rebalance difficulty
units.detail: Counting deaths per level showed level 1 had far more deaths than levels 2-3, indicating the difficulty curve was too steep; analytics directly guided rebalancing.

units.title: Don't ignore low-resolution users
units.detail: Market insights show a significant portion of players use small resolutions and modest hardware; ensure UI and text remain readable and adaptable on low-end devices.

units.title: URP vs HDRP vs built-in render pipeline
units.detail: The built-in pipeline was a black box hard to extend; URP runs on every Unity platform with good performance and looks, while HDRP pushes high-end PC/console visual limits.

units.title: Prefer linear color space
units.detail: Unity previously defaulted to gamma color space, which is more performant but looks worse; use linear color space unless targeting the absolute lowest-end mobile devices.

units.title: Render Pipeline Converter upgrades imported assets
units.detail: Window > Rendering > Render Pipeline Converter upgrades store assets using legacy Standard shaders to URP; enable the material converter and run it whenever importing asset packs.

units.title: Per-quality render pipeline assets
units.detail: Each quality setting can reference a different URP asset with its own settings; the editor uses whichever quality level is selected, so use max quality in-editor.

units.title: Match shadow resolution to style and platform
units.detail: Shadow resolution ranges from 256 (mobile) to 4k; low values are too blurry and 4k too crisp for stylized scenes, so pick intentionally (e.g. 512 for a cartoony look).

units.title: Oversized shadow distance blurs shadows
units.detail: All shadows within the max distance must fit in one shadow texture, so a huge max distance makes every shadow a blurry mess; set it only as large as your scene needs (or use cascades).

units.title: Shadow cascades allocate resolution by distance
units.detail: Cascades (1-4) dedicate more shadow resolution to objects near the camera and less to far ones; essential for scenes with long shadow distances.

units.title: Baked lighting is static; probes add dynamics
units.detail: Light baking produces high-quality but static lighting; light probes store baked values at points in space so dynamic objects moving through the scene pick up the right light.

units.title: Reflection probes with box projection
units.detail: Reflective materials only reflect the sky by default; place reflection probes inside vs outside and use box projection so reflections track distance-based movement.

units.title: Shader Graph and VFX Graph need no code
units.detail: Shader Graph builds shaders with a visual node editor (great for non-shader programmers) and VFX Graph creates GPU particle systems supporting thousands to millions of particles.

units.title: Render Objects feature for occluded outlines
units.detail: Adding the Render Objects render feature to a URP renderer draws selected layers through occlusion, e.g. showing a player outline while behind walls, without writing render code.

units.title: Local volumes scope post-processing to areas
units.detail: A local post-processing volume only applies when the camera is inside its trigger area, enabling effects like gas zones confined to specific regions.

units.title: Simple Lit fits stylized art
units.detail: For stylized/low-poly looks, the Simple Lit shader gives great results versus the physically based Lit shader, which suits realistic scenes.

units.title: URP 2D renderer enables 2D lighting
units.detail: URP's dedicated 2D renderer adds 2D lights and effects impossible in the built-in pipeline, a major reason 2D game workflows have improved.

units.title: Custom cursors are high-value polish
units.detail: Custom animated cursors (per context: move, attack, grab) make a game feel noticeably more special and professional; a tiny detail that costs little to add.

units.title: Authoring a custom cursor texture
units.detail: Draw a small (e.g. 32x32) texture, set its Texture Type to Cursor, enable Read/Write, and set an offset hotspot to define the exact clickable point; the editor shows the active area.

units.title: One-line API to switch cursor type
units.detail: Changing cursors collapses to a single call that sets an active cursor from a ScriptableObject asset, decoupled from gameplay systems so it can be layered on at the end of a project.

units.title: Priority logic chooses cursor state
units.detail: Each update default to the normal cursor, then override it through checks: unit selected -> move cursor, unit under mouse (raycast) -> target cursor; last check wins.

units.title: Keep polish systems decoupled
units.detail: Cursor/Polish systems intentionally have no coupling to gameplay; they add an extra bit of quality without risking interference with existing mechanics.

units.title: Throw object toward mouse with AddForce
units.detail: Compute throw direction as mouse world position minus the player position, then AddForce(direction * force, ImpulseMode.Impulse) on the object's Rigidbody2D.

units.title: State enum drives weapon behavior
units.detail: A throwing weapon uses states (WithPlayer, Thrown, Recalling) with different update logic per state: physics while thrown, homing velocity while recalling, parent-follow while with the player.

units.title: Physics in FixedUpdate, visuals in LateUpdate
units.detail: Apply physics motion in FixedUpdate and do visual/sorting follow-up in LateUpdate so rendering stays in sync with the final state.

units.title: Push thrown object beyond grab radius
units.detail: On throw, position the object at least one grab-distance away from the player, otherwise it is instantly re-grabbed on the same frame.

units.title: Auto-grab and manual recall with same button
units.detail: One button both throws and recalls based on a query (is with player); grabbing is also automatic when within grab distance, while recall works from any distance.

units.title: Bouncy physics via physics material
units.detail: Create a physics material with friction 0 and bounciness 1 and assign it to the Rigidbody so the projectile bounces off walls instead of sliding.

units.title: Physics-based recall can't pass walls
units.detail: Recall via physics velocity stops at walls, which is a deliberate design choice; make recall kinematic and move the transform directly if you want it to pass through.

units.title: Auto-target nearest enemy on hit
units.detail: On hitting an enemy, preserve velocity magnitude but retarget the direction toward the closest nearby enemy so a thrown weapon chains between enemies.

units.title: Damage only when moving fast enough
units.detail: Gate damage on a velocity-magnitude threshold so a stationary thrown weapon acts as a harmless mine instead of killing enemies that step on it.

units.title: Trail toggled by weapon state
units.detail: Enable the Trail Renderer only while the weapon is flying and disable it once grabbed or idle, avoiding a lingering trail on a resting object.

units.title: Melee attack as input + animation + area damage
units.detail: A melee swing is: on click, play the attack animation toward the target position, damage all enemies within a radius of the player, and add screen shake for feedback.

units.title: Reuse a damage-enemies-in-range function
units.detail: Extract enemy area damage into a shared function taking a position and blast radius; grenades and melee swings both call it, and it returns a kill count for effects.

units.title: Static stat class for per-kill bonuses
units.detail: Model a stackable bonus with a per-kill constant, a static counter, reset and get methods; add speed bonus on kill and reset on taking damage.

units.title: Cap stacking stats to sane values
units.detail: An uncapped per-kill move-speed bonus quickly becomes absurd; cap the counter at a max and keep the effect meaningful but bounded.

units.title: Lose temporary bonuses on hit
units.detail: Subscribe to the player on-hit event to reset the bonus and reapply it through the same interface methods, keeping the risk/reward loop consistent.

units.title: Game feel: shake and popups on events
units.detail: Screen shake on kills and text pop-ups on hits communicate state clearly and make combat feel satisfying; small feedback elements are high-value game feel.

units.title: Static factory creates and sets up prefab
units.detail: A static Create(spawnPos, targetPos, prefab) method instantiates a projectile prefab and immediately calls a setup function (set velocity toward target, aim rotation).

units.title: Bouncy projectile setup
units.detail: A bouncy grenade uses a capsule collider slightly larger than the visual, a physics material with friction 0 and bounciness 1, and linear drag to control travel.

units.title: Callback from projectile to spawner
units.detail: Pass an Action<Vector3> into the spawned projectile so it can notify the spawner (explode animation, area damage, screen shake) exactly at its death position.

units.title: Dummy component tags explode-on-contact objects
units.detail: An empty marker component used as a tag lets projectiles detect which colliders should trigger an explosion via TryGetComponent, avoiding string or layer checks.

units.title: Self-destruct via timer
units.detail: Subtract delta time in Update and destroy the game object when the timer passes zero, so grenades explode after a fixed lifetime even if they never hit anything.

units.title: Blast radius damage on explosion
units.detail: On explosion, iterate a copy of the enemy list, damage every enemy within the blast radius, and remove dead ones from the live list during iteration.

units.title: Flying-body and shake death effects
units.detail: Spawn a reusable flying dead-body prefab launched along the direction away from the explosion and add camera shake to sell impact and keep the screen readable.

units.title: Centralize all player input in one class
units.detail: Move firing and other input logic out of the player/movement class into a single game-handler class so all input lives in one place. Keep the movement class responsible only for animation and movement.

units.title: Expose animation functions behind an interface
units.detail: Have the character class implement an interface exposing can-play/shoot/reload and the gun-end position, so the input handler can trigger animations and spawn projectiles without knowing implementation details.

units.title: Per-weapon static ammo counters
units.detail: Store current ammo as a static int on each weapon class so all instances share one ammo pool; expose static has-ammo, can-reload and reload functions used by the input handler.

units.title: Refill ammo only when reload animation finishes
units.detail: Pass an Action callback that fires when the reload animation completes; if the animation is interrupted, ammo is never restored. This prevents animation cancelation from cheating the reload.

units.title: Firing past max destroys the oldest projectile
units.detail: When a sticky-bomb launcher fires while the max (e.g. 8) active bombs exist, explode and remove the oldest instead of allowing more. Gives the weapon a soft cap and interesting trade-offs.

units.title: Freeze a projectile by destroying its physics components
