units.detail: When a projectile should stop dead on contact, destroy its Rigidbody2D and Collider inside the trigger handler so it stops in place and no longer fires collision events.

units.title: Scale projectile speed by click distance
units.detail: Set projectile move speed proportional to distance from shooter to target, clamped between min and max. Short clicks lob weakly, far clicks fire fast, giving the player aim control.

units.title: Track all projectiles in a static list
units.detail: Keep a static list of every live grenade; instantiate the list lazily and add on spawn. A static explode-all function iterates the list, explodes each, then clears it, enabling one-button detonation.

units.title: Fake vertical arc on a 2D projectile
units.detail: Simulate depth by tracking a fake bomb-state/height value that interpolates a vertical offset over the projectile's lifetime, so a top-down game looks like it has an arc.

units.title: Orthographic camera size is half visible height
units.detail: Camera orthographic size equals half the vertical space shown, so size 15 shows 100 total units (minus 50 to plus 50). Knowing this makes placing world objects predictable.

units.title: Singleton asset-reference object for code spawning
units.detail: Create a GameAssets singleton with public sprite/prefab fields, a static instance set in Awake, and force it to run first via Script Execution Order so other scripts can safely reference assets at startup.

units.title: Set rigidbody velocity for repeatable jumps
units.detail: Assign jump velocity directly each frame instead of adding force, giving an identical jump height every time so the game is skill-based and fair. Freeze the X axis so the bird only moves vertically.

units.title: Resize pipes with sprite slicing
units.detail: Set sprites to Sliced draw mode with the pivot on the bottom and resize the SpriteRenderer size (width/height) rather than scaling the transform, so stretched bodies keep crisp edges.

units.title: Escalating difficulty over score
units.detail: As more pipes spawn, shrink the gap between them and spawn them more frequently, so the game naturally gets harder and rewards skilled play.

units.title: Pick netcode tier by player count
units.detail: Netcode for GameObjects suits small co-op games (like Overcooked), while Netcode for Entities (DOTS) handles hundreds of players, is server-authoritative, and includes client-side prediction for fast competitive games.

units.title: Relay beats firewalls and NAT
units.detail: A relay server acts as a middleman on the internet that players initiate connections to, so even players behind strict firewalls/NAT can connect, avoiding peer-to-peer connection failures.

units.title: Treat multiplayer as modular tools
units.detail: Combine separate services (netcode, relay, matchmaker, lobby, voice chat, auth, leaderboards, hosting) as needed per use case rather than one monolithic stack; co-op can use player-hosted relay, competitive can use auto-scaled dedicated servers.

units.title: Use analytics on tutorial completion
units.detail: Track tutorial completion and funnel data to find where players get stuck, then target fixes there; even basic event tracking meaningfully improves the game.

units.title: Event-driven grid updates visuals
units.detail: Grid cells fire an on-changed event; a visual controller subscribes and rebuilds/updates the prefab per cell on any change. This cleanly separates simulation data from presentation.

units.title: BFS flood-fill to reveal connected empty cells
units.detail: When revealing an empty Minesweeper cell, run a queue-based search (with a visited set to avoid infinite recursion) revealing all connected empty cells and stopping at number cells and mines.

units.title: Random placement can overwrite cells
units.detail: Placing mines at fully random coordinates can hit an already-mined cell, yielding fewer mines than requested. Guard with an if-not-already-a-mine check and retry.

units.title: Count neighbors to build mine indicators
units.detail: For each empty cell, gather the up-to-8 valid neighbors and count mines, mapping the count to an indicator number. Validate bounds so corner cells only check existing neighbors.

units.title: Flags are visual markers only
units.detail: Right-click flags store a boolean on the cell and swap the icon sprite; they do not affect game logic. Keep pure-visual mechanics decoupled from simulation.

units.title: Win condition: all non-mine cells revealed
units.detail: After each reveal, scan the grid; if every non-mine cell is revealed the player wins. Only unrevealed non-mine cells keep the game going.

units.title: Scrolling liquid via texture offset
units.detail: Animate a falling-liquid effect by continuously increasing the material texture offset with wrap mode set to Repeat; changing a material offset is far cheaper than swapping sprites or animating particles.

units.title: Replace Instantiate/Destroy particles with one dynamic mesh
units.detail: Confetti particles that constantly instantiate/destroy caused ~100ms freezes and 90fps. Rendering every part as a quad on a single dynamic mesh looks identical but hit 400fps with no stutter.

units.title: Merge many static objects into one mesh
units.detail: Replacing ~500 separate ground-tile game objects with a single combined mesh eliminated 400+ draw calls/batch objects while looking identical. Batch static scenery aggressively.

units.title: Grid-based overlays visualize game state
units.detail: Split the map into segments holding values and render overlays (environment, crowd, needs) as grid-based or dynamic-mesh views so players quickly grasp spatial game state like happiness or traffic.

units.title: Trash can absorbs trash until full
units.detail: When spawning trash, prefer a nearby trash can: add to it until full, only then spawn on the floor. Gives buildings a purpose in a maintenance/cleanliness simulation.

units.title: Self-collision by comparing head to body cells
units.detail: After each snake move, iterate every body part's grid position and compare to the head's position; a match means the snake ran into itself and the game is over.

units.title: State machine halts updates after death
units.detail: Store an alive/dead state and switch on it in Update so the snake stops moving once dead, preventing input or movement from continuing after game over.

units.title: Wrap world edges by validating grid coords
units.detail: After moving, validate the new grid position: x below 0 becomes width-1, x above width-1 becomes 0, and same for y. Wrapping grid coordinates keeps the snake inside the level seamlessly.

units.title: Pass dependencies via setup functions
units.detail: Instead of global statics, give objects a Setup(reference) function and call it from the game handler after construction. This makes object references explicit and easier to reason about.

units.title: Constructor runs before references are wired
units.detail: Spawning food in the level constructor crashed because the snake reference was only assigned afterward. Defer any logic that needs injected references until the Setup call.

units.title: Re-roll random spawns until valid
units.detail: Loop randomizing the food position while it equals the snake's position, guaranteeing food never spawns on the snake. Repeat-until-valid is a cheap guard for random placement.

units.title: Static show() on a UI window instance
units.detail: Store a private static instance of the game-over window and expose a static Show() that calls the instance's show method, so any game code can open the window without direct references.

units.title: Keep game-over window hidden until death
units.detail: Set the window inactive in Awake and only activate it on the death event; its retry button just reloads the game scene. Clean event wiring keeps UI state in sync with gameplay.

units.title: Static fields persist across scene reloads
units.detail: A static score variable kept its old value after reloading the scene because statics survive scene destruction. Reset all static state inside an initialize function called from Awake.

units.title: Loading scene that waits one frame
units.detail: Loading the loading scene then immediately the target scene never refreshes the screen, so the old frame hangs. Load the loading scene, wait one frame via a callback script, then load the target so players see the loading screen.

units.title: Duplicate game scene to build menu scene
units.detail: Instead of creating a menu scene from scratch, duplicate the playable scene and delete all gameplay objects, keeping only the camera and UI. This preserves all your UI setup and configuration work.

units.title: Show/hide UI submenus via containers and enum
units.detail: Group UI into container GameObjects per submenu and track them with an enum. A single ShowSubMenu function hides all containers then switches on the target enum to reveal only the desired one.

units.title: Application.quit does nothing in the editor
units.detail: Application.Quit() silently does nothing in the Unity editor, so a quit button appears broken during testing. It only works in a built executable.

units.title: Reposition UI to center via code on Awake
units.detail: Position UI elements off to the side in the editor for easy editing, then on Awake reset their anchoredPosition (and sizeDelta) to zero so they appear centered at runtime.

units.title: Pause game by scaling time to zero
units.detail: Set Time.timeScale to 0 to freeze all deltaTime-based logic (snake movement stops), and back to 1 to resume. Guard logic that must ignore the pause by using unscaled time.

units.title: Escape key toggles pause by checking timeScale
units.detail: On Update, read Escape and branch: if Time.timeScale equals 0 the game is paused so resume, otherwise pause. This turns Escape into a pause toggle instead of a one-way pause.

units.title: Add scenes to Build Settings before loading
units.detail: A new scene must be dragged into File > Build Settings before SceneManager.LoadScene can find it by name. Missing this step throws a runtime load error.

units.title: Store direction with each body history point
units.detail: A plain position list is insufficient for rotating body segments; store an enum direction alongside each recorded grid position so every segment knows which way the snake was heading when it passed that point.

units.title: Corners need previous and current direction
units.detail: To pick the correct corner sprite/rotation, a segment must know both its own direction and the direction of the previous segment. Store a reference to the previous move position in each entry.

units.title: Guard null previous direction for first segment
units.detail: When computing the previous direction, check whether the previous move position exists (e.g. the snake head). If null, return a default direction instead of throwing.

units.title: Rotate 2D sprites via Z Euler angle
units.detail: In 2D only the Z component of transform.eulerAngles matters. Convert the movement direction into an angle (e.g. switch over direction enum, or Mathf.Atan2) and assign Euler(0,0,angle) to point the sprite correctly.

units.title: Create body visuals once and reuse
units.detail: Don't instantiate/destroy sprites every frame while the snake moves; create one GameObject per body segment when it grows and reuse it across frames, updating only its position.

units.title: Set sprite sorting order by index
units.detail: Give each body segment a SpriteRenderer sortingOrder of -index so newer segments render behind earlier ones and the head stays on top, preventing weird z-fighting between segments.

units.title: Dedicated class per snake body segment
units.detail: Extract each body segment's visuals, transform and grid position into its own class with a constructor and an update method. This keeps the main snake class readable as the game grows.

units.title: History list with insert-at-front and trim
units.detail: Record snake history by inserting the current position at index 0 each move, then trimming the list to bodySize+1 by removing the last element. Body parts are then placed at history[0..bodySize].

units.title: Respawn food away from entire snake body
units.detail: When choosing a random food spawn, loop generating positions while the chosen spot is contained in the full snake position list (head plus body history) so food never appears on any segment.

units.title: Return bool from try-eat function
units.detail: Rename the eat handler to TryEatFood and return a bool so the snake knows whether it ate. Only when true does it grow its body size before trimming the history list.

units.title: Rename symbols with refactor shortcuts
units.detail: Use the IDE's rename refactoring (Ctrl+R,R in Visual Studio) instead of manual find/replace so all references update automatically and names stay consistent.

units.title: Grid-based movement with integer coordinates
units.detail: Model a grid game's positions with integer vector types (Vector2Int in Unity) so each unit is exactly one grid cell and transform position maps 1:1 to grid position.

units.title: Timer-based automatic movement
units.detail: Accumulate deltaTime into a timer; when it exceeds the move interval, apply the current direction to the position and subtract the interval. This makes movement happen on a fixed cadence rather than per key press.

units.title: Prevent 180-degree direction reversal
units.detail: Allow a direction change only if the new direction is not the exact opposite of the current one; otherwise the snake instantly collides with itself. This is a classic snake movement bug.

units.title: Separate input, movement and render functions
units.detail: Split Update into small named functions (HandleInput, HandleGridMovement, then set transform) so each concern is testable and readable instead of one monolithic Update.

units.title: GetKeyDown fires only on the press frame
units.detail: Input.GetKeyDown triggers once per press frame while GetKey triggers every held frame. For continuous direction steering use GetKey; reserve GetKeyDown for one-shot actions like attacks.

units.title: Static manager with factory for one-shot audio
units.detail: A static sound manager can create a temporary GameObject with an AudioSource and call PlayOneShot, freeing callers from owning any audio objects. Encapsulate all sound playback in one class.

units.title: Enum plus serializable clip pairing for sounds
units.detail: Define a sound enum and a serializable class bundling a sound enum value with an AudioClip. A manager array of these is configured in the editor, and a lookup maps enum to clip. Adding sounds means adding an enum value plus an array entry.

units.title: Extension methods to extend classes without editing
units.detail: Attach new behavior to an existing class without modifying its source by using extension methods (this keyword on the first parameter). Ideal for adding sounds to buttons you don't control.

units.title: PlayerPrefs for simple persistent data
units.detail: Store a high score with PlayerPrefs.SetInt(key, value) and read it back with GetInt(key, defaultValue) where the default handles a missing key. Use a static Score class to keep this logic out of UI scripts.

units.title: C# event to push data changes to UI
units.detail: Instead of polling, expose a static event (e.g. OnHighScoreChange) fired whenever saved data updates. UI subscribes on Awake and refreshes itself, so screens update the moment a new high score is set.

units.title: Conditional game-over messages and hidden score
units.detail: Pass an isNewHighScore bool to the game-over window: show a congratulations message only on a record, always show run score and saved high score, and hide the corner score display behind the window for a clean look.

units.title: ChipTone and SFXR for simple sound effects
units.detail: Create small retro game sound effects for free using chip-tune tools like ChipTone (an expanded SFXR). Good for low-effort audio in indie projects.

units.title: Screen Space Camera with dedicated UI camera
units.detail: Set canvas render mode to Screen Space Camera with a separate orthographic UI camera whose clear flags are 'Don't Clear', so the UI renders over the main camera view. This is required for 2D UIs to show correctly.

units.title: Scale UI by matching height to reference resolution
units.detail: Use Canvas Scaler with Scale With Screen Size, a 1280x720 reference resolution and Match Height. UI then scales on the vertical axis and you only manage horizontal placement.

units.title: Park UI containers off-scene while editing
units.detail: Move UI container GameObjects to a far offset (e.g. 1000,1000) so they don't block the scene view, then rely on code to reposition them. Keeps the scene clean during development.

units.title: Static game handler instance for cross-script access
units.detail: Store the GameHandler in a private static instance set on Awake, plus static score fields and static getter/add functions. UI windows can then read game state without finding the object or using GetComponent chains.

units.title: Expose animation triggers from a base class
units.detail: Wrap your animation system behind a base script exposing functions like PlayPunch(dir, onHit, onComplete), IsPlayingPunch() and PlayIdle(). Game logic then drives animations without depending on a specific animation tool.

units.title: Normalized WASD movement scaled by deltaTime
units.detail: Build a movement vector from WASD keys, normalize it so diagonals aren't faster, and translate by direction*speed*deltaTime for framerate-independent motion.

units.title: State enum gates which update logic runs
units.detail: Track a state enum (Normal/Attacking). While Normal, run movement and attack checks; while Attacking, allow re-attacking (for combos) but not movement. This prevents animations from being cancelled each frame by movement/idle logic.

units.title: Combo by chaining punch then kick
units.detail: In the attack handler, check whether the punch animation is currently playing; if so play kick, otherwise play punch. Rapid clicks produce punch-kick combos while waiting lets the full animation finish.

units.title: Point attacks toward the mouse position
units.detail: Aim attacks by computing a normalized direction from the player transform to the mouse world position, then pass it to the attack animation so hits face the cursor.

units.title: Camera follows player with mouse offset
units.detail: Instead of centering the camera on the player, shift it slightly toward the mouse: return player position plus (mousePosition - playerPosition) scaled by a small factor, so the player stays on screen while aiming ahead.

units.title: Central GameAssets holder for prefab references
units.detail: Create a singleton GameAssets MonoBehaviour with public prefab fields wired in the editor. Factory functions like Enemy.Create(position) instantiate via GameAssets.Instance, avoiding scene/asset lookups scattered through code.

units.title: Track all instances in a static list
units.detail: Have each spawned enemy add itself to a private static list on Awake. Target-finding code iterates this list; a helper computes the closest enemy within a max range.

units.title: Get closest enemy within max range
units.detail: Iterate all enemies, skip any outside max range, and keep the nearest by comparing Vector3.Distance. Return null when nothing qualifies so the caller can distinguish 'no target' from a hit.

units.title: Target nearest to mouse, not nearest to player
units.detail: If you pick targets by proximity to the player, clicks far away still hit the same enemy and feel wrong. Choose the enemy closest to the mouse position so the player can deliberately switch between nearby targets.

units.title: Attack position should be offset toward the mouse
units.detail: Using the raw mouse world position as the attack point makes hits register across the whole screen. Instead compute attack position as player position plus normalized direction-to-mouse times a fixed offset, so only enemies near that reachable point get hit.

units.title: Simple int health, die at zero, skip dead in targeting
units.detail: Track health as an int, decrement per hit, destroy the GameObject when it drops to zero, and have the closest-enemy search skip (continue) any enemy flagged dead to avoid hitting corpses.

units.title: Flying-body death effect
units.detail: On death, spawn a reusable effect prefab that moves outward in the direction the enemy was knocked, scales up, rotates, and self-destroys after ~1 second. A cheap but satisfying death flourish.

units.title: Knockback pushes target away from attacker
units.detail: On a non-lethal hit, move the enemy away from the attacker by a fixed knockback distance. Keep the player at a constant distance from the enemy afterward so attack animations always connect regardless of prior spacing.

units.title: Spawn hit particles and shake only on real hits
units.detail: Gate impact effects and screen shake behind an 'hit enemy' bool so punching air produces nothing. Also scale screen shake intensity higher on kills than on normal hits so important moments read clearly.

units.title: Static instance singleton for global reference
units.detail: Give a core entity (e.g. the player) a public static self-reference assigned in Awake so other scripts can access it anywhere without wiring references manually. Simple to set up, works in any engine, but be aware of lifetime issues with scene reloads.

units.title: Move toward a target with normalized direction
units.detail: Compute the direction to move as (target.position - my.position).normalized, then add direction * speed * deltaTime to the transform each frame. Optionally scale by a constant speed so movement is uniform regardless of distance.

units.title: Stop-moving distance prevents target overlap
units.detail: Use Vector3.Distance between the mover and its target and only move while the distance is above a configured 'stop moving distance'. Below it the mover holds still, which also triggers the idle animation instead of walking in place.

units.title: Hit animation cancelled by idle next frame
units.detail: If the update loop plays the idle/move animation every frame, an attack/hit animation started on the same frame is overridden immediately. Fix: add a state machine (normal vs busy) — while busy the movement/idle code is skipped, and the busy state is cleared when the animation completes.

units.title: Switch on current state each update
units.detail: Drive behavior with an enum state: in Update, switch on the current state — 'normal' runs movement logic, 'busy' does nothing. Helper methods (SetStateNormal, SetStateBusy) encapsulate transitions, and the state resets to normal in the animation-complete callback.

units.title: Kinematic rigidbody projectile moved by transform
units.detail: For a projectile, add a collider plus a kinematic rigidbody and drive movement by directly modifying transform.position each frame rather than AddForce. This gives precise, controllable motion while still firing physics collision callbacks.

units.title: Trigger-based collision destroys projectile
units.detail: Make the projectile's collider a trigger and implement OnTriggerEnter2D to react when it touches another physics object — here destroying the projectile on impact. Triggers detect overlaps without physically pushing objects.

units.title: Static create method with shared prefab registry
units.detail: Expose a public static factory (e.g. WebProjectile.Create(position, direction)) that instantiates a prefab referenced from a GameAssets singleton, sets it up, and returns it. Centralizes prefab references in one scene object so any script can spawn the projectile with one line.

units.title: Max travel distance lifetime for projectiles
units.detail: Track distance traveled each frame (speed * deltaTime) and destroy the projectile once it exceeds a max-travel constant. Prevents unbounded objects from flying forever and cluttering the scene hierarchy when they miss all walls.

units.title: Aim projectile at mouse position
units.detail: Aim at the cursor by setting direction = (mouseWorldPosition - owner.position).normalized and passing it to the projectile factory. Converts a screen-space cursor into an in-world aim vector.

units.title: Static events decouple effects from gameplay logic
units.detail: Fire public static events (OnWebReachedMaxDistance, OnWebHitObject) at the moment of destruction/impact so other systems can subscribe and spawn visual effects without the projectile knowing about them. Keeps core logic clean and separate from polish effects; null-check the event before invoking.

units.title: Shooting state allows repeats but blocks movement
units.detail: Add an explicit 'shooting' state: while shooting you cannot move, but you can fire more projectiles (handle-shoot still runs in that state). Restores to normal when the shoot animation completes.

units.title: Web zip: slide toward clicked point
units.detail: Store a target position and direction on input, then move the transform by direction * speed * deltaTime while the 'web zipping' state is active. End the state when within a small distance of the target.

units.title: Decelerate for a smooth stop instead of abrupt
units.detail: Instead of stopping exactly at the target, add a 'sliding' state that reduces speed each frame (speed -= speed * deltaTime * factor) and only returns to normal once speed is very low. Begin the slide early, before actually reaching the target, for a natural ease-out feel.

units.title: Animate growing line with tiled sprite
units.detail: Render a web/beam with a sprite renderer in Tiled draw mode, pivot at one end, and grow it by changing the width (size.x). Animate over time (lerp between start and end size) and re-position/re-rotate it each frame so it stays attached to the moving character's hand.

units.title: Keep visual reference as member for per-frame updates
units.detail: Store the instantiated web/beam as a member variable (not a local) so the update loop can reposition it, re-rotate it toward the target, and resize it to the exact current distance every frame, then destroy it when the slide begins.

units.title: Validate idea with questions before coding
units.detail: Before writing any code, write down lots of design questions (movement, world shape, antagonist, win/lose conditions) and answer them, then describe gameplay step by step. This validates the core idea cheaply and guides implementation.

units.title: Prototype validates code architecture, not just gameplay
units.detail: When a prototype is the seed of a real product, don't write throwaway dirty code — build it with clean abstractions (interfaces like IInteractable, ICarryObjectParent) so you can prove the architecture scales to all planned features. Dirty prototypes suit game jams, not serious projects.

units.title: Compose idea from audience favorites plus a twist
units.detail: Build a marketable game idea by combining familiar genres your target audience already loves (automation/building like Factorio) with a fresh hook (co-op action like Overcooked). The combination gives a unique twist while staying within a known audience.

units.title: Trailer before announcement boosts wishlists
units.detail: Launching a Steam page without a trailer is a mistake; games with trailers wishlist at a much higher rate. If you can't animate a trailer, build the actual systems and record gameplay footage instead.

units.title: Use dioramas for Steam page screenshots pre-prototype
units.detail: To create a Steam 'coming soon' page before any prototype exists, assemble asset-pack art into staged dioramas in a Unity scene and capture screenshots, using tools like Umotion for posed character animations.

units.title: Reuse prior architecture across projects
units.detail: Cut prototype build time dramatically by reusing interaction and carry-object architecture you already built and taught before (IInteractable, carry-object parent). Experience and existing patterns let you build systems that took months in hours.

units.title: Use AI for ideation, not code
units.detail: Let an LLM brainstorm names and creative options (e.g. generated 'dinky' creature names) while you write all the code yourself. AI is a brainstorming shortcut, not a code author.

units.title: Wrap every async service call in try-catch
units.detail: All lobby/network API calls can throw (server errors, connection failure) and will break the game if uncaught. Always wrap them in try-catch handling a LobbyServiceException and log the error.

units.title: Lobbies expire after 30s without heartbeat
units.detail: A lobby becomes inactive (invisible to searches) if it receives no data for 30 seconds. Hosts must periodically send a heartbeat — e.g. every 15s from a timer — to keep the lobby alive until all players have joined.

units.title: Public vs private lobbies and lobby codes
units.detail: Public lobbies are searchable by anyone; private lobbies are only joinable by ID or a short human-readable lobby code. Share the code (not the long ID) with friends to let them join a private lobby directly.

units.title: Query lobbies with filters and ordering
units.detail: Build a QueryLobbiesOptions with a count, a list of QueryFilter (field, value, operation like greater-than on available slots or custom S/N data) and QueryOrder for sorting. Leave options empty to return all lobbies.

units.title: Await async calls to avoid freezing
units.detail: Network service calls must be awaited (and their containing method marked async) or the game freezes waiting for a server reply. Awaiting pauses only that function and lets the rest of the game keep running.

units.title: Standard UI mask can only have one shape
units.detail: A UI Mask component masks children by the parent's rendered image, so you can only have a single mask shape. Multiple separate areas can't be masked by multiple parents — you must combine them into one mesh or one texture.

units.title: Custom MaskableGraphic mesh mask
units.detail: Extend MaskableGraphic and override PopulateMesh(VertexHelper) — clear the helper, then add multiple UIVertex quads to build an arbitrary mask shape out of several pieces. Add a Mask component and it masks children across all the quads at once.

units.title: UI vertices need a color or they don't render
units.detail: VertexHelper quads in a custom mask won't render/work if added with an empty color — always supply a color to each UIVertex (e.g. a random/placeholder color). This is required for the mesh to draw.

units.title: PopulateMesh not called every frame
units.detail: The UI system only calls PopulateMesh when it deems a redraw necessary, so per-frame animation of a custom mask does nothing by default. Call SetVerticesDirty() in Update to force regeneration each frame.

units.title: Animate mask reveal per text line
units.detail: Drive reveal animations with a container of lines each carrying startTime/totalTime fields; a single custom mesh mask reads those values and grows its quads over time so multiple text lines reveal smoothly in sequence with one mask.

units.title: Visual scripting teaches programming concepts
units.detail: Learning visual scripting exposes you to logic flow, variables, and programming concepts, making it a valid stepping stone into actual programming. Naming nodes with normal C# terminology makes translation to code straightforward later.

units.title: Incremental course games build difficulty
units.detail: Structure learning around building complete games of increasing complexity (simple platformer first, then an action RPG reusing the same concepts) so fundamentals are learned simply and then applied to a feature-rich project.

units.title: Physics-based movement keeps sliding during attack
units.detail: If movement is applied via rigidbody velocity each FixedUpdate, an attack state still slides because the last move direction persists. Fix: reset the move direction vector to zero when entering the attack state.

units.title: Snappy attacks: allow re-input mid-animation
units.detail: To make attacks responsive, keep handling attack input during the attacking state (not just the normal state) so players can chain attacks without waiting for the previous animation to finish. Trade-off: some games want attacks to fully commit.

units.title: Target nearest enemy near the aim point
units.detail: Aim combat by computing an attack position offset from the player toward the mouse cursor, then run a closest-enemy search against that point (not the player position). This lets players pick which surrounding enemy to hit while clicking near it.

units.title: Static enemy registry with add-on-spawn remove-on-death
units.detail: Keep a static list of all live enemies: add each enemy to it in the spawn/create method, and remove it in the death/die method. Guards against targeting dead enemies and enables global queries like 'closest enemy'.

units.title: Simple closest-point search algorithm
units.detail: Iterate the enemy list, skip any outside a valid range, and track the best candidate: first in-range enemy becomes the closest, later ones only replace it if strictly nearer. Return null if none found, and null-check before using the result.

units.title: Knockback from attacker position
units.detail: Push a hit enemy away by computing direction = (enemy.position - attacker.position).normalized and adding direction * knockbackDistance to the enemy transform. Pass the attacker's position into the damage call and reuse the same direction for directional particles.

units.title: Snap attack direction onto the actual target
units.detail: Don't use the raw mouse direction for animations/dash once a target is found — build an 'attack direction' that equals the direction to the real enemy (defaulting to the mouse direction when no target exists) so the character faces and lunges at who they actually hit.

units.title: Model crafting grid as 2D item array
units.detail: Represent the crafting area with a multi-dimensional array of Item references. Provide helper functions: IsEmpty, GetItem, SetItem, Increase/DecreaseAmount, RemoveItem, and TryAddItem (accepts only if empty or same item type, else stacks the amount).

units.title: Recipe matching by comparing grids
units.detail: Define each recipe as a grid of item types. To find the output, iterate the grid and fail if any cell that should contain an item is empty or holds a different item; return the recipe output if all cells match.

units.title: Recipe dictionary keyed by output item
units.detail: Support multiple recipes by storing them in a dictionary keyed by the output item type, then iterate all recipes to find a grid match. Returns none if nothing matches, making it trivial to add new recipes.

units.title: Crafting output must consume ingredients
units.detail: Producing an output that doesn't consume its recipe is a bug — players craft for free. When the output is removed/taken, loop the grid and remove one amount from every recipe position so ingredients are actually spent.

units.title: Rebuild UI from state on change events
units.detail: Keep the crafting logic and its visual fully separated: the logic fires an OnGridChanged event whenever items change, and the UI clears and rebuilds all visible items from the grid data on that event. Avoids tracking individual item updates.

units.title: Item holder interface enables containers
units.detail: Implement a common item-holder interface (RemoveItem/AddItem/CanAddItem) on inventory, crafting grid, and equipment so moving an item between containers automatically removes it from its old holder. This lets inventory→craft→equip chains work cleanly.

units.title: Entrance position follows direction of last two points
units.detail: Place a queue entrance by taking the vector between the last two queue positions (un-normalized to keep spacing) and adding it to the final position, so the entrance extends the path in the same direction instead of always going one fixed way.

units.title: Guard index-out-of-range on short lists
units.detail: Code that computes a direction from the 'last two' list entries crashes with index-out-of-range when the list has fewer than two items. Guard: if the list has fewer than two positions, fall back to a default (e.g. offset from the single last position).

units.title: Recompute derived positions in one function
units.detail: Encapsulate entrance-position calculation in a dedicated function and call it after every queue mutation (add/remove position). Keeps derived data consistent whenever the source list changes.

units.title: Only remove a queue position when it's empty
units.detail: Removing the last queue position while a guest still occupies it corrupts the queue. Before removing, verify the guest count is below the position count, and only then drop the final position and recompute the entrance.

units.title: Modular character via interchangeable scripts + interfaces
units.detail: Build a character as many single-purpose modules (movement, attacks, AI, animation). Interactions go through interfaces (IMoveVelocity, IMovePosition, IAttack) instead of concrete classes, so you swap a component in the editor and behavior changes without touching other code.

units.title: GetComponent with concrete type breaks when swapping modules
units.detail: Requesting GetComponent<MoveVelocity> throws NullReferenceException once you swap in MoveTransformVelocity. Fix: get the component by the shared interface type (GetComponent<IMoveVelocity>), so the caller works with any implementation.

units.title: Rigidbody velocity vs direct transform movement
units.detail: Movement module moving the Transform directly ignores collisions (passes through walls), while a module setting Rigidbody.velocity respects physics. Same interface, two behaviors; pick per character type (e.g. ghost vs solid player).

units.title: Move-to-position via interface for direct vs pathfinding
units.detail: A MovePositionDirect module sets velocity straight toward a target; MovePositionPathfinding computes an A* path and follows waypoints, idle at path end. Both implement IMovePosition with SetMovePosition, so the input module is agnostic.

units.title: AI modules reuse player movement modules
units.detail: NPCs use the same IMoveVelocity/IMovePosition modules as the player but add a behavior module (MoveRoam picks random nearby positions, MoveWaypoint walks a waypoint list). Player input modules are just one more swappable layer.

units.title: Compose sprite sheet in code with GetPixels/SetPixels
units.detail: Create a new Texture2D at sheet resolution, copy base texture pixels into it with GetPixels/SetPixels, then overlay body/head regions copied from separate body-part sheets at fixed coordinates. Call Apply() to push the result to the GPU.

units.title: Textures need Read/Write enabled for GetPixels
units.detail: GetPixels/SetPixels throw unless the import settings have Read/Write Enabled turned on for every source texture (base, head, body). Enable it in the Texture Import Settings.

units.title: Texture coordinate origin is bottom-left
units.detail: When placing body parts with SetPixels, the origin is the lower-left corner of the texture. Compute offsets from that corner (e.g. head at X=0, Y=384 on a 512x512 sheet) rather than assuming top-left.

units.title: Randomize variation by selecting part index
units.detail: With body parts laid out on a fixed grid in the sheet (e.g. 4 heads, 4 bodies at 128px steps), pick a random index and copy from X = index * partWidth. Four parts each yield 4x4=16 variations with no extra art.

units.title: Alpha-aware pixel overlay merge function
units.detail: To layer hair/beard over a head, write a MergeColorArrays(base, overlay): skip where overlay alpha is 0; if overlay alpha == 1 fully replace; otherwise lerp each channel by the overlay alpha. Use merge, not SetPixels, so the base isn't wiped.

units.title: Layer randomization order and bald chance
units.detail: Compose head = base head, then overlay random hair, then overlay random beard (on top of already-merged pixels). Add a 70%-chance flag per feature and use index -1 to represent 'none' for extra variety.

units.title: Tint pixels by multiplying color
units.detail: Tint a white texture to any color by multiplying each pixel's channels by the target color. For skin, use a base-white face texture and multiply by a randomly chosen skin color.

units.title: Mask-limited tinting to protect detail areas
units.detail: A blanket tint also recolors eyes. Fix: use a mask texture where protected regions (eyes) have alpha 0; only interpolate the tint where mask alpha > 0, lerping toward tintColor * baseColor by mask alpha.

units.title: Reuse same skin color across body regions
units.detail: Apply the same picked skin color to the face (masked) and to bare hands, so a white hand texture gets the matching tint. One random color drives multiple tinted parts for cohesion.

units.title: Modular sprite sheet series strategy
units.detail: Build one final sheet by layering base, body, head, then composited hair/beard, then tints for hair/skin/primary+secondary body colors; save the parameter set (indexes + colors) as JSON to reproduce the exact character.

units.title: Color-coded mask for primary/secondary areas
units.detail: Encode two tint regions on one mask texture: pure green marks primary areas, pure blue marks secondary. Tint a pixel only when its mask alpha > 0 AND the mask color matches the target color, enabling two-color bodies from one mask.

units.title: Parameterize tint function with mask color
units.detail: Extend TintColorArrayInsideMask with a maskColor parameter and an equality check (maskColor == targetMaskColor). Call it twice on the same pixels with different target colors to apply primary then secondary tints.

units.title: Pre-colored parts stay as-is, white parts get tinted
units.detail: Design the base body so already-colored sections are left untouched and only white sections receive the primary/secondary tints. Mask applies the tints exactly where white parts are, keeping the preset design intact.

units.title: Data class holds sprite parameters for save/load
units.detail: Put all generation parameters (hair/beard/body indexes, hair/skin/primary/secondary colors) in a plain class, plus static GenerateRandom() and Load() factories and instance Save(). The texture builder takes the data object instead of randomizing internally.

units.title: JSON + PlayerPrefs for simple persistent save
units.detail: JsonUtility.ToJson(data) into a string, store with PlayerPrefs.SetString(key, json); load with PlayerPrefs.GetString + JsonUtility.FromJson<T>. Reproduces the exact sprite sheet every load. PlayerPrefs is the simplest persistence for quick prototypes.

units.title: Sentinel index -1 encodes 'has no feature'
units.detail: Use a hair/beard index of -1 to mean 'bald/clean-shaven' in the serialized data, and skip overlay logic for negative indexes. Keep the -1 convention consistent between random generation and rendering.

units.title: Merge nearby tasks so workers carry multiple items
units.detail: Before assigning an order, loop tasks and merge ones whose pickup and dropoff positions are within a max distance, producing a combined task (grab A, grab B, drop A, drop B). One transporter moves multiple items, roughly doubling throughput without extra hires.

units.title: Minimal maintenance-state class
units.detail: A lane/object needs a small float state (default 1): repair() resets to 1, NeedsRepair() when < 1, IsUsable() when above a low threshold, SpendMaintenance() to decay it. A visual subscribes to the on-change event to show a broken icon.

units.title: Guest money + limited ATM keeps economy stable
units.detail: Spawn guests with randomized money; they leave when broke. Counter that with ATM/coffee buildings that refill money/energy, but cap withdrawal (max ATM/coffee visits per guest) so guests never stay in the park forever.

units.title: Compose complex building from simple sub-buildings
units.detail: The restaurant works by chaining small buildings: stove cooks, counter passes orders between waiter and cook, table where guests sit. Workers and guests flow through each step; simpler sub-parts reused make complex features easier to build and debug.

units.title: Unity Multiplayer Play Mode for fast iteration
units.detail: Install the Multiplayer Play Mode package, then spawn up to three extra client windows from the Multiplayer menu. Each is a full Unity editor window with its own hierarchy, scene, and console log, cutting test iterations from multi-minute builds to ~10 seconds.

units.title: Play Mode scenario tags for per-client config
units.detail: Configure play-mode scenarios and assign tags per local instance; read the tag in code to branch behavior, e.g. make one window join the red team and another blue. Speeds up testing team-specific logic.

units.title: Generic task system decoupled from task types
units.detail: Rename the monolithic task to TaskBase and make TaskSystem<TTask> where TTask : TaskBase. Move concrete task definitions (TakeWeaponToSlot, TakeWeaponFromSlotToPosition) into game classes. The system handles queueing/requesting; it never knows task internals.

units.title: Multiple task systems with different task types
units.detail: Instantiate TaskSystem<Task> for workers and TaskSystem<TransporterTask> for transporters; each worker listens to its own typed system and only executes tasks it understands. The systems are completely ignorant of each other, keeping code cleanly separated.

units.title: Worker AI executes typed tasks via actions
units.detail: Task carries data (slot/target positions) plus Action<WorkerAI> callbacks for grab/drop. The worker's TaskAI moves to the slot position, invokes the grab action, moves to target, invokes drop, then requests the next task.

units.title: Add a task type without touching the task system
units.detail: Because the system is generic and decoupled, adding a second worker type (transporter) required only: new subclass of TaskBase, a typed system instance, and a duplicated worker TaskAI — no edits to the shared task system class.

units.title: You only truly learn by doing
units.detail: Interactive, handcrafted exercises beat passively watching videos; tutorials should require practice to escape 'tutorial hell'. Exercises with hints, solutions, and video walkthroughs push learning past consumption.

units.title: Ad games need millions of plays
units.detail: Free games with ads are nearly unprofitable (6M plays earned ~$1000 total) because you need millions of players, whereas a paid niche game can profit from a few hundred copies. A unique theme for a specific niche beats chasing mass scale.

units.title: Simplify ambition to match skill
units.detail: A complex SWAT AI concept failed because of multi-step AI and aiming limitations, so the same top-down game was reworked into a zombie game with simpler AI. Match your game's systems to your current skill level rather than forcing a design you can't execute.

units.title: Long ambitious games can fail harder
units.detail: An 18-month, higher-quality sequel sold ~10% of its predecessor, proving effort and quality don't guarantee sales. A 3-month cheap remake of a proven flash game became far more profitable — timeboxed, proven-concept games de-risk an indie career.

units.title: Save profits to survive failures
units.detail: An indie hit can fund a few failures only if you keep spending low; one 18-month flop nearly ended the career. Overspending on a success removes the safety net needed for the next inevitable failure.

units.title: Marketing drives discovery, not quality
units.detail: Games with excellent reviews and low prices can still fail without marketing, and 'no-marketing' experiments fail even with minimal cost. A compelling, instantly-understood concept is the biggest part of marketing.

units.title: Stick to proven profitable genres
units.detail: After tycoon games succeeded, the developer kept choosing tycoon-like concepts instead of risky genre switches, since marketing is easier with a unique theme in a familiar genre. Reuse what works; only innovate where you can afford it.

units.title: Don't reinvent the wheel
units.detail: Use an existing engine/tool rather than building your own engine, because you can't realistically make both an engine and a game. Picking proven tools (Unity, Visual Studio) over writing everything from scratch is the pragmatic path.

units.title: Done beats perfect
units.detail: You don't need the best or most complete setup — 'something that just works' is fine, even for basic HTML/PHP/JS web dev. Getting something done is better than getting it done perfectly.

units.title: Back up in three places
units.detail: Keep game backups locally on multiple drives, on external drives, and in cloud storage (Azure/AWS/GCS) at various stages of progress. Any single cloud provider or local drive is fine for basic versioned backups.

units.title: Use AI as brainstorming partner
units.detail: Use AI to generate 10 thumbnail or mechanic ideas, then discard the bad half and combine the good ones with your own judgment — never let it write tutorials or scripts. AI thumbnails supplement, not replace, hired artists for custom game art.

units.title: Unity can't edit humanoid bones
units.detail: Unity does not allow modifying humanoid animation bones directly in the editor; use an asset like UMotion or Blender to tweak the 1% of a bought animation that's almost right. Buy assets that are ~99% what you need and tweak the rest.

units.title: Ask players for Steam reviews
units.detail: Reviews matter enormously to the Steam algorithm, so explicitly request reviews in the game and in the announcement video. Post-launch, spend the first week reading feedback and fixing bugs before returning to tutorials.

units.title: Multitasking dev and content is heavy
units.detail: Developing a full game alongside regular videos was far more work than expected, requiring a huge final sprint. If content is part of your plan, budget time for both or stagger them.

units.title: First-week sales predict first year
units.detail: First-week Steam sales multiplied by a ratio of 2–6 (≈5 if you keep updating) estimates first-year gross. $13k first week ≈ $50k year one, placing a game in the top 15% of Steam games.

units.title: Steam earnings are heavily skewed
units.detail: Most games never make $5k while the top ~3% of ~50k games earn millions; ~1,200 games release monthly. Making a living on Steam is extremely difficult but not impossible.

units.title: Low cost of living is an indie edge
units.detail: Surviving on ~$750/month in a low-cost country means a 6-month solo game can turn a profit even on the bottom tier of the revenue chart. Your personal burn rate defines how easy or hard 'making a living' from games is.

units.title: Capture player emails in-game
units.detail: Add a widget that lets players sign up with their email so you can notify them when your next game launches. Reusing an audience list from previous games gives a huge head start.

units.title: Cross-promote games via website feed
units.detail: A widget that downloads your game list from your own website lets old games show your newest titles automatically, and updates retroactively. Data-driven promotion keeps every release visible inside all your previous games.

units.title: Don't hardcode years or dates
units.detail: The monthly report and award ceremony hardcoded '2015', so playing years later shows a permanently stale in-game year. Read dates from the system clock instead of baking them into the game.

units.title: Reveal tutorial UI contextually
units.detail: The early tutorial was confusing with all buttons visible; hiding options until the tutorial actually teaches them fixed it. Show controls contextually instead of all at once.

units.title: Sales simulation math needs iteration
units.detail: The hardest part was tuning sales algorithms so revenue relates to game quality, studio fans, and marketing without spiraling to extremes. Such systems require many rounds of iteration and real number tuning.

units.title: Reuse assets across all games
units.detail: A generic talking sound effect made 10 years ago still appears in new releases — proven assets are portable and save time. Build a small library of reusable SFX/art for future games.

units.title: Difficulty: fail but always recover
units.detail: A casual management game should let every project eventually turn a profit and include a load/borrow system so players always recover from a bad launch. Tune difficulty through constant iteration and number tweaking.

units.title: First games are for learning
units.detail: Treat early projects as learning exercises, not money-makers, and don't obsess over review scores. Read player feedback to improve, but accept that everyone starts bad and skills grow over time.

units.title: Read company economics before outrage
units.detail: Judge company moves using basic economics and stock market knowledge: a 4% layoff when the company holds $1.7B in cash saves a drop in the bucket, and stock-mergers spend $0 cash. Separate hype headlines from the actual deal structure.

units.title: Check if flagged tech was deprecated
units.detail: Malware/adware accusations about an acquired SDK were real historically but based on 2015–2016 usage; the tool was discontinued in 2020. Verify the age and deprecation status of a claim before assuming it still applies.

units.title: An engine is just a tool
units.detail: All you want from a game-making tool is the ability to make the games you want; use whatever engine enables that, regardless of company drama. Engine choice should be about fit, not vibes.

units.title: Failure is part of learning
units.detail: Pen spinning (like programming or any skill) involves failing and dropping the pen constantly before it clicks; failure is part of the process, so don't get annoyed — just keep trying. Practice makes it automatic, and a physical fidget can keep your brain focused.

units.title: Ring and core needs system
units.detail: A Red Dead-style need has an outer ring that drains first, then an inner core that drains only when the ring is empty; regeneration speed scales with how full the core is. Spend from the ring, fall back to the core, and clamp everything between 0 and the total.

units.title: Tick-based regen simulates heartbeats
units.detail: Instead of smooth regen, regenerate in discrete ticks whose frequency depends on core fill (full core = 1 tick/sec, empty = 1 per 2 sec) and add a small delay after last use before regen starts. This sells the illusion of heartbeats and prevents regen while actively spending.

units.title: Event-driven UI updates
units.detail: Fire an OnValuesChanged event whenever a need's values change so the UI can subscribe and re-render, keeping logic (needs system) decoupled from visuals (UI script). Use normalized-value getters so fill amounts can be set directly on UI Image components.

units.title: Nested class per need, dictionary of needs
units.detail: Model a single need (ring, core, total) as a nested class, then hold Health/Stamina/Deadeye instances in a dictionary keyed by an enum and look them up by type. One prefab visualizes any need by swapping the core icon, and Update() iterates all needs for regen.

units.title: UI Image fill modes for rings and cores
units.detail: Use the Unity UI Image 'Filled' type with Radial360 (origin top) for the outer ring and vertical fill (origin bottom) for the core; stack a black total-image behind the current image. Set fillAmount via normalized values so deplete and regen just work.

units.title: TryUse pattern gates sprint
units.detail: Expose TryUseNeed(amount) returning a bool (ring first, then core; false if both insufficient) and call it in Update with amount × deltaTime; keep sprinting only while it returns true. This makes resource-gated movement trivial and robust.

units.title: Natural language is not exact enough to be a programming language
units.detail: English is full of nuance and ambiguity, so asking an AI in plain language cannot reliably produce code that does exactly what you intended. The need to keep refining via dialogue means you are effectively programming in a very inefficient language.

units.title: The door problem: technical implementation vs design questions
units.detail: Making a door technically (a hinge) is trivial, but building a feature is 90% answering design questions: can all doors open, how does the player distinguish openable vs decorative doors, what unlocks them, etc. The same applies to programming — defining exact requirements is the real work.

units.title: Programming is problem solving, not syntax
units.detail: Core computer science skill is general problem solving, which transfers to any new language in about a week. The value of learning to program persists even if AI can write boilerplate code, because the thinking skill remains.

units.title: Future is programmers plus AI, not AI replacing them
units.detail: AI is a great accelerator for domain experts without coding skills: they can prototype ideas in natural language, validate them, then hand off to professional developers to productize. The best use is closing the technology divide, not removing the programmer.

units.title: Enable scene management on NetworkManager for auto scene sync
units.detail: When scene management is enabled on the Netcode NetworkManager, only the host loads scenes and all clients automatically unload/load the target scene. If disabled you must handle scene transitions manually; scene loads should always go through the network manager once a connection exists.

units.title: Leave NetworkManager player prefab empty to control spawning
units.detail: Galactic Kittens sets no player prefab on the NetworkManager so nothing spawns on join; instead players are spawned manually when entering the character select and gameplay scenes. Do this when you want custom spawn timing rather than automatic prefab spawn.

units.title: NetworkObjectReference passes references through RPCs
units.detail: Client RPCs only accept value types, not references, so you cannot pass a player object directly. Pass a NetworkObjectReference instead and reconstruct the object on the receiving side with TryGet, then GetComponent for the type you need.

units.title: Server-authoritative state synced via RPCs
units.detail: Only the server mutates shared state (player connection states, selected characters); it then broadcasts to clients with a ClientRpc so all clients update their local copy. Clients request changes through ServerRpc and the server applies and re-syncs them.

units.title: Immediately update local UI after sending ServerRpc
units.detail: After a client sends a ServerRpc to change its character, update the local UI right away. Otherwise the change must round-trip to the server and propagate back, adding perceptible delay.

units.title: Kick clients with targeted ClientRpc
units.detail: To remove an over-limit client, build a ClientRpcParams whose target is only that client ID and have it call NetworkManager.Shutdown. Alternative: connection approval on the NetworkManager rejects during the handshake before the client fully connects.

units.title: Bootstrap scene holds persistent singletons
units.detail: A dedicated bootstrap scene creates globally needed objects like the NetworkManager and a persistent scene-loading manager marked DontDestroyOnLoad, so exactly one instance survives all scene transitions. Always start play from the bootstrap scene or you get errors.

units.title: Learn by tutorial plus final project files
units.detail: Following a step-by-step tutorial then downloading and reading the finished project code is one of the best ways to learn. Recreating mechanics from games you play and asking what systems/purpose each element serves builds game design skill.

units.title: ECS is another tool, not the only way
units.detail: ECS/Data-Oriented design offers excellent performance and a different way of thinking about problems, but it is one option in the toolkit. A good skill is knowing when to use GameObjects vs ECS based on the game.

units.title: A game is many systems working together
units.detail: Beyond mechanics, a complete game needs support systems: saving/loading, scene management, sound, UI. Players never notice them but they are essential and are where finishing a game gets hard.

units.title: Only 32% of Steam games earned $500 in 2024
units.detail: Of ~18,000 Steam releases, just over 5,000 made at least $500. For professionals this is actually encouraging: your real competition is the smaller indie tier, not every hobbyist release.

units.title: Steam revenue is extremely top-heavy
units.detail: The top 10% of games make 85% of all revenue; the rest split the remaining 15%. Always look at median revenue (indie median ~$20k, hobbyist ~$1.3k) instead of the flattering averages when evaluating the market.

units.title: Choose your genre with revenue data
units.detail: Puzzle platformers and party games are massively oversupplied with tiny median revenue, while casual, simulation and shop/management games sell far better. Unless you make literally the best puzzle platformer ever, a simulation genre is the safer bet for earning money.

units.title: Don't price your indie game under $10
units.detail: Indies often price at $5, which forces tens of thousands of sales just to break even. General rule: never go under $10, scale to $15–20 with quality, and above $20 only for very special games.

units.title: Publishers raise median revenue but cost money
units.detail: Self-published median is ~$3k vs ~$16k with a publisher, but the publisher takes a cut and bad ones exploit developers. Read the contract carefully before signing; also indie games average higher review scores (83%) than AAA (79%).

units.title: Shop simulators are low-complexity, high-demand
units.detail: Shop/management sim games resonate with the Steam audience and are technically straightforward (walk around, look at objects, interact with that specific object). Making them well still takes skill, but the programming logic is simple iteration-heavy work.

units.title: Multi-Aim Constraint rotates bones toward a target
units.detail: Use a Multi-Aim Constraint (Animation Rigging package) to make a character's weapon/hand aim at any world-space target. Configure the aim and up axes in local space — check the gizmo vectors (e.g. aim on X, up on -Z) so rotation is correct.

units.title: Constraint order in hierarchy breaks aim
units.detail: If the hand constraint is evaluated before the body constraint, rotating the body afterwards knocks the hand off-target. Put the body aim constraint above the hand aim constraint in the hierarchy so body rotation happens first, then the hand refines the aim.

units.title: Lower body constraint weight for natural rotation
units.detail: Rotating the whole spine 100% to face the target looks robotic; dropping the body Multi-Aim weight to ~0.7 makes the torso rotate less while the hands still aim perfectly, giving a more natural posture.

units.title: Two Bone IK places the second hand on the weapon
units.detail: Add a Two Bone IK constraint with the left hand as the tip, auto-setup from the tip to pick shoulder and elbow, then child the target to the right hand and position it on the weapon. Adjust the elbow hint so the arm bends the natural way.

units.title: Drive rig weight with interpolation for aiming on/off
units.detail: Store the Animation Rig reference and smoothly lerp its weight between 0 and 1 in Update when aiming starts/stops. This lets the character stay in normal animation while idle and only activate IK while aiming, instead of an instant snap.

units.title: Use an empty target object and paste component values
units.detail: Aim constraints reference a target object, so drive it from your mouse-picking object rather than a hand-placed sphere. Since transforms changed in play mode are lost on exit, use Copy Component / Paste Component Values to keep tuned positions.

units.title: Static factory method for spawning prefabs
units.detail: Create a public static Create(position, damage, isCritical) method on the popup class that instantiates the prefab and calls Setup internally. This contains all spawn logic in one class, so callers just call DamagePopup.Create() with no prefab references.

units.title: GameAssets singleton for global prefab references
units.detail: Keep a single persistent object (static instance attached to a scene object) holding references to all assets. Access it anywhere as GameAssets.instance, avoiding drag-drop wiring scattered across scripts.

units.title: Damage popup lifecycle: rise, scale, fade, destroy
units.detail: Give popups a timer: count down from a max, scale up during the first half of the lifetime and down during the second, fade the TextMeshPro alpha after the timer, and Destroy once alpha reaches zero. Move via a damped vector so it starts fast then slows.

units.title: Differentiate critical hits visually
units.detail: For critical hits use a larger font size and a different color (e.g. red) versus normal hits (smaller, yellow). Color can be parsed from hex using a helper like UtilsClass.GetColorFromString.

units.title: Popups must render on top of everything
units.detail: Put the popup TextMeshPro on a dedicated sorting layer above the default render layer, and increment a static sorting order per popup so newer popups always draw over older ones instead of flickering under them.

units.title: Finishing games is a skill you must practice
units.detail: Starting prototypes is easy; taking a project to the finish line teaches the real skills — polish, options menus, save systems, localization, Steam backend, endings. Complete many small games (like the Flash-era workflow of ~40 finished games) to build this muscle.

units.title: Pick a game you can finish in 1.5 months
units.detail: Always underestimate your timeline, so a 1.5-month scope becomes roughly 3 months. Target something slightly more complex than Flappy Bird but not much, for your first complete game.

units.title: Launch a Steam 'coming soon' page early
units.detail: Prepare the Steam page and set it to coming soon within the first month, then start experimenting with devlogs, shorts and marketing to gather wishlists. The goal is learning the Steam backend and marketing, not revenue.

units.title: Publish a demo for Steam Nextfest and iterate on feedback
units.detail: Get a playable demo out for the festival window, listen to feedback and analytics, watch actual playthroughs on YouTube, then polish and finish for a November/December release. The first game's only goal is learning; money is a bonus.

units.title: Beginners: start even simpler than the plan
units.detail: Absolute beginners should first finish a free 10-hour course and a few very simple games (Flappy Bird, Space Invaders clones) to get familiar with the engine before attempting the festival demo plan.

units.title: Courses vs tutorials serve different purposes
units.detail: A course is a guided multi-hour path building a complete thing and teaches how systems connect together; a tutorial answers one specific question. Beginners benefit from courses because they don't know which questions to ask; experienced devs grab tutorials on demand.

units.title: Courses cover the glue between systems
units.detail: Tutorials teach isolated systems but not how to wire them together (e.g. resource manager to building manager). A complete course explicitly shows those connections, plus tiny but valuable tips (like [System.Serializable] to show custom classes in the inspector) that are too small for their own video.

units.title: Paying improves follow-through
units.detail: Psychological sunk-cost means people are much more likely to finish a course they paid for than a free tutorial series. If you struggle with self-discipline, that alone can justify paying for a course.

units.title: Parallax moves each layer by a camera fraction
units.detail: In LateUpdate (after the camera moves), compute the camera's frame delta and add it to each background multiplied by a per-layer effect multiplier (e.g. 0.4 for trees, 0.6 for mountains). Use a Vector2 multiplier to control horizontal and vertical parallax independently.

units.title: Infinite scroll teleports using texture unit size
units.detail: Set sprite draw mode to Tiled and size it to at least 3 screens. Each frame, if the absolute difference between the layer position and camera position exceeds the texture unit size (sprite width / pixels per unit), relocate the layer to the camera plus the modulo offset. Use Mathf.Abs so both left and right snapping work.

units.title: Independent horizontal and vertical infinite booleans
units.detail: Expose separate toggles for infinite horizontal and vertical scrolling per layer so a mountains layer can tile left-right while clouds tile both axes and a fixed background (parented to the camera) doesn't move at all.

units.title: A* core: G cost, H cost, F = G + H
units.detail: G is walking cost from the start node, H is a heuristic estimate to the goal (assume no obstacles), F = G + H. Always expand the open node with lowest F, stop when the current node is the goal, and trace the path back through each node's previous-node link.

units.title: Use integers for A* costs (10 and 14)
units.detail: Multiply straight move cost by 10 and diagonal by 14 (sqrt2 scaled) so the algorithm works with ints instead of floats, avoiding floating point comparisons. Use max-int as the initial G cost sentinel.

units.title: Data-oriented A*: structs, indexes, flat arrays
units.detail: Convert the object-oriented version by storing path nodes as structs with int index fields, linking the previous node as an index rather than a reference, and storing open/closed lists as int index lists into a flat NativeArray grid.

units.title: Structs are copied; write back after modification
units.detail: Because path nodes are value types, reading a node and mutating its costs only changes a local copy. You must write the modified struct back into the array, and remember to Dispose every NativeArray/NativeList you create.

units.title: Burst + Jobs give massive pathfinding speedup
units.detail: With the algorithm written using only value types, mark the job with [BurstCompile] and Schedule multiple jobs, then Complete them all. Unoptimized object A* took 700ms on a 20x20 grid; the Burst-compiled job system ran it in ~0.05ms.

units.title: Burst rejects managed arrays
units.detail: A plain int2 array for neighbor offsets is not supported inside a Burst-compiled job. Store the neighbor offsets as a struct with fixed array values or use NativeArray so the job compiles cleanly with [BurstCompile].

units.title: Request-response via component add/remove
units.detail: To request a path, add a request component to an entity; a system queries entities with that component, runs the job, writes the result to a buffer, then removes the component so the work runs only once per request. This add-trigger-remove pattern cleanly decouples requesters from processors.

units.title: Batch schedule jobs then complete all
units.detail: To parallelize per-entity work across worker threads, schedule every job into a list first, then complete them all at once. Scheduling one job and immediately running/ completing it forces sequential execution on the main thread, leaving worker threads idle.

units.title: Dynamic buffer for variable-length per-entity data
units.detail: Store a list of values (like path positions) on an entity using a dynamic buffer, added at conversion time via an authoring component. Buffers let each entity hold its own arbitrary-length collection without per-element components.

units.title: Path stored reversed, decrement index
units.detail: The generated path was stored reversed in the buffer, so the follower must decrement its index (walking backward) instead of incrementing to advance toward the destination. Keep track of the current index in a small follow component initialized to -1 (invalid) until a path exists.

units.title: Mix DOTS with plain GameObjects
units.detail: Use DOTS/ECS only where absolute performance is needed (e.g., pathfinding for thousands of units) and keep GameObjects for non-critical visuals and inputs. You do not have to choose all-or-nothing; a native array snapshot of the GameObject-managed grid map is shared into the job.

units.title: Burst pathfinding cost is tiny vs rendering
units.detail: With 10,000 units, A* pathfinding runs in a few milliseconds across parallel burst jobs while the majority of frame time goes to rendering. Optimize the renderer before assuming pathfinding is the bottleneck.

units.title: One dynamic mesh renders thousands of particles
units.detail: Build a custom mesh out of quads (4 vertices + 6 triangles each), add/update quads by rewriting vertex/UV/triangle arrays and reapplying them to the mesh. Thousands of persistent particles render as a single mesh instead of thousands of objects, so particles stop moving and simply stay in the mesh forever.

units.title: 65k vertex limit requires mesh chunking
units.detail: Unity meshes cap at 65,000 vertices, so a quad-based mesh holds roughly 15k quads before needing a second mesh. Track a quad index, and once you exceed the max, spawn another mesh rather than overflowing.

units.title: Pixel coords struct plus normalized UV struct
units.detail: Expose a user-friendly serialized struct with pixel coordinates (lower-left, upper-right) and convert it internally into a normalized UV struct by dividing by texture width/height. Keep editor-facing data in pixels and runtime data normalized to avoid duplicate math everywhere.

units.title: Decouple particle system via events
units.detail: The mesh particle system only needs an 'on shoot' event with a position/direction; it never references the player or weapon code. Subscribe to the event from a separate handler so systems stay reusable and testable.

units.title: Persistent vs vanishing particles
units.detail: Persistent particles (blood, footprints, shells) move, slow down, stop, and remain on the map forever; transient ones (dirt kicked while walking) must be destroyed. Track each particle in a per-system class list and remove entries once movement completes.

units.title: Singleton handler with single spawn call
units.detail: Wrap particle logic in a singleton handler exposing one call like SpawnShell(position, direction) that instantiates an internal per-particle class. Callers stay clean while the handler owns updates, slowdown, randomization, and cleanup.

units.title: Pixelate by quantizing UV coordinates
units.detail: To pixelate a sprite, multiply the UV by a pixelated amount, apply floor to discard decimals, then divide back to 0-1. This snaps UVs to discrete segments so the texture samples blocky cells, with higher amounts producing bigger pixels.

units.title: Zero pixelation still shows pixels without branch
units.detail: Even with the slider at 0 the constant multiplier still quantizes to ~200 segments, so some pixelation remains. Fix it by comparing the amount to 0 and branching (compare + select/branch nodes) to pass the original unmodified UV when no pixelation is requested.

units.title: Animate shader properties from scripts
units.detail: Expose the effect amount as a material/ shader property and lerp a target value in code, calling SetFloat with the property reference each frame. A ~30-line script can animate pixelation in and out smoothly.

units.title: World space canvas places UI in the world
units.detail: Switch a Canvas render mode to World Space to position UI elements physically in your 3D/2D scene, rendered by the main camera and occluded by other objects like normal geometry. Works identically in 2D and 3D and supports input fields, scroll views, and sliders in the world.

units.title: UI Image Filled type for health bars
units.detail: Set a UI Image type to 'Filled' (horizontal or radial) and drive the fill amount for health bars and radial timers. This is far simpler and more flexible than building bars from scaled sprite renderers.

units.title: Each world canvas adds a draw call
units.detail: Every separate canvas is drawn as its own batch, so hundreds of active world-space canvases hurt performance. Disable canvases when not needed and remove the GraphicRaycaster component when you don't need input on them.

units.title: CanvasGroup fades many elements at once
units.detail: Put multiple UI elements in a container with a CanvasGroup to adjust alpha/visibility of the whole set at once. Separate static elements from constantly updating ones into different canvases so one changing element doesn't force repainting everything.

units.title: Decouple clicks from logic via events
units.detail: A ButtonSprite component fires a static event when a node is clicked; the game handler subscribes and casts the sender to the node type to route the order. This keeps the clickable object unaware of the game's higher-level logic.

units.title: Auto-continue from nearest valid node
units.detail: After depleting an ordered node, the AI asks the manager for the nearest node within a max distance that still has resources, filters invalid candidates from the list, and continues mining there; otherwise it returns to idle and waits for a new order.

units.title: Visualize AI state with a text mesh
units.detail: Attach a TextMesh above the unit that shows the carried amount when greater than zero and hides (empty text) otherwise, updated on awake and whenever the inventory changes. Cheap, useful debug/player feedback.

units.title: Pin legacy asset dependency versions
units.detail: An old Unity package that still works mostly can break after upgrade because its dependencies changed: this photo mode requires Cinemachine 2.6.5, and 3.x is not a drop-in upgrade and produces errors. Download the full project/zip so you get the exact pinned versions it was built against.

units.title: Deprecated render target APIs after upgrade
units.detail: When upgrading to modern Unity, obsolete render APIs surface errors: RenderTargetHandle becomes RTHandle, RenderTargetIdentifier becomes ShaderPropertyToID lookups, and init/release calls and blit functions are renamed. Follow an upgrade guide (e.g., an official discussion thread) to refactor each occurrence, though some effects may still silently fail after compiling.

units.title: Photo mode as drag-and-drop feature
units.detail: A free photo mode package adds view roll, view distance, focus, aperture, exposure, contrast, saturation, vignette, frames, and stickers, plus hiding the UI for screenshots. It is a high-value-to-effort feature for players and can be wired up by dropping in a prefab and assigning a player object reference.

units.title: Animated custom cursors add cheap polish
units.detail: Custom animated cursors make games stand out with minimal effort: ship a set of pre-made cursors, swap them automatically on mouse-over or via a single function call. Package polish like this is a low-cost way to elevate perceived quality.

units.title: Generic grid class accepts any cell type
units.detail: Convert a grid from storing ints to Grid<T> so the same class holds booleans, ints, enums, or custom objects. This unlocks tilemaps, minesweeper, pathfinding walkability, and cell objects holding their own logic without per-use-case grid code.
