units.title: Reference-type cells default to null
units.detail: default(T) is 0 for value types but null for classes, so a generic grid of a custom class crashes on access until cells are initialized. Null-check every access or pass a factory to construct real cell objects up front.

units.title: Func factory creates default cell objects
units.detail: Give the grid constructor a Func<T> that creates a default cell (e.g., () => new HeatMapGridObject()). The grid stays generic while callers decide which concrete cell type and initial state each position starts with.

units.title: Cells own logic and notify grid of change
units.detail: Move domain logic into the cell object (min/max clamping, normalized value) and have it call back into the grid to trigger the changed event when its internals mutate. The grid becomes completely generic and decoupled from any specific use case like heatmaps.

units.title: Override ToString for debug visualization
units.detail: Overriding ToString() on cell types makes debug drawing and inspector text show meaningful values automatically (e.g., current value, letters + numbers). It converts a generic grid into readable output with zero extra code per use case.

units.title: Write code for the problem at hand
units.detail: Solve only the requirements you currently have, not imaginary future ones; over-abstraction and premature optimization waste time when requirements never change. You can always refactor later when new requirements actually arrive.

units.title: Refactoring is a normal part of the process
units.detail: Code is a living thing: write it once for the current design, then go back and refactor/expand it each time requirements change. The grid system evolved from a simple grid to generics to a city-builder over years because refactoring happened at each new requirement, not ahead of time.

units.title: Detours, not coding ability, kill finished games
units.detail: Most people can start a project but few finish; premature optimization and endless 'nice-to-have' modularity are major detours that cost time and never pay off. Focus limited time on the actual goal, whether it is code, art polish, or mechanics.

units.title: Leave a tiny task undone for a quick win
units.detail: At the end of a work session, deliberately leave a 1-5 minute task unfinished (e.g., one missing click handler) so your next session starts with a fast, easy win that overcomes the hardest part: starting. The task must be tiny; a big unfinished task has the opposite effect.

units.title: Self-discipline beats motivation
units.detail: Motivation is uncontrollable and comes and goes, so serious projects should run on self-discipline: do the work during work hours regardless of how you feel. Relying on motivation leads to 10-hour days followed by days of nothing.

units.title: Experiment to find your own workflow
units.detail: Productivity advice is highly individual: leaving tasks unfinished stresses some people, so their in-between strategy is finishing tasks but preparing a small to-do list for the next session. Test different approaches (docs style, work hours, alone vs with others) and keep what works for you.

units.title: Code executes top to bottom
units.detail: Programs run instructions sequentially from top to bottom, one after another. Function calls temporarily jump execution but ultimately return to sequential flow, so treat execution order as linear.

units.title: Semicolons end each instruction
units.detail: In C# every instruction must end with a semicolon; without it the compiler assumes the instruction continues. Newlines and indentation are ignored by the compiler (unlike Python), so the semicolon is the only real statement terminator.

units.title: Code is case-sensitive
units.detail: Identifiers must match exactly, including capitalization (WriteLine with lowercase L does not exist). Beginners assume English-equivalent casing works, but the compiler requires 100% exact spelling; when something won't compile, check capitalization first.

units.title: Curly braces define code blocks
units.detail: Curly braces group code into blocks (namespace, class, function) and determine what code is valid where. Executable instructions belong inside a function like Main, not directly in class or namespace scope where only fields and functions are allowed.

units.title: Matching opening and closing symbols
units.detail: Every opening curly brace and parenthesis needs a matching closing one; an imbalance causes compile errors. Editors highlight the matching pair when the cursor sits on a bracket, making mismatches easy to spot.

units.title: Use IDE error tooltips
units.detail: Red squiggly underlines reveal error details when hovered (e.g., 'expected semicolon'). Some messages are self-explanatory while others are confusing, so use them as a starting point rather than the final answer.

units.title: Quadrant system for neighbor search
units.detail: Spatial hashing groups nearby entities into quadrant buckets so neighbor-finding algorithms only test entities in the same (or adjacent) bucket instead of every entity. This cut 10,000x10,000 unit-target matching from ~56ms to ~14ms per frame.

units.title: Hash position to integer key
units.detail: Floor X and Y by the quadrant cell size, then multiply the Y term by a large multiplier to produce a unique integer key per grid cell (0,0)->0, (60,0)->1, etc. This maps any position to its bucket cheaply.

units.title: Multiple values per key with NativeMultiHashMap
units.detail: Use a NativeMultiHashMap (key -> many values) to store all entities that fall in each quadrant. Iterate values by TryGetFirstValue followed by repeated TryGetNextValue until it returns false.

units.title: Convert quadrant placement into jobs
units.detail: Rewrite the per-entity insertion loop as an IJobForEach over entities, passing the multi-hash-map as .AsParallel for concurrent writes, to gain multithreading. Placement of 1000+ units then runs in about 1ms.

units.title: Store data, not just entity
units.detail: Rather than storing bare entities in quadrants, store a small struct (entity + position + type) so downstream systems avoid expensive EntityManager lookups to fetch component data. This makes the system more robust and faster.

units.title: Opt-in entities with tag component
units.detail: Add a marker component (e.g., QuadrantEntity with a type enum) to only place entities intended for the quadrant system. Querying only translation would wastefully bucket unrelated entities like particle effects.

units.title: Containers can't grow inside jobs
units.detail: Native containers cannot grow dynamically inside a job, so an undersized hash map throws 'hash map is full'. Allocate with sufficient capacity, expand via SetCapacity on the main thread, and clear persistent containers before rebuilding each frame.

units.title: Search neighboring quadrants
units.detail: For accurate targeting, search the entity's own bucket plus the 8 adjacent keys (+/-1 on X and +/- the Y multiplier). Quadrant size directly limits effective search range, so tune it to the game's targeting radius.

units.title: Queue tasks that validate before running
units.detail: A QueuedTask wraps a func that returns the real task only when its condition is met, otherwise null. While null, the task stays queued; when the func finally returns a task, it is moved to the executable task list.

units.title: Func vs Action delegates
units.detail: An Action returns void while a Func returns a value. Use Func<T> when the callback must produce a result, as here where the validation callback returns the task to execute or null.

units.title: Validate on a timer, not every frame
units.detail: Poll queued-task conditions every ~200ms instead of every frame, since a task invalid this frame is unlikely to be valid the next. Use a periodic-timer utility to avoid wasted per-frame checks.

units.title: Enqueue helper wraps validation func
units.detail: Provide an EnqueueTask overload that accepts either a QueuedTask object or directly the validation func, auto-wrapping the latter. This keeps the call site simple while preserving the conditional-execution behavior.

units.title: Reuse systems from prior projects
units.detail: A shipped game's lobby logic was lifted almost unchanged from a previous course/project. Reusing and re-purposing systems you already built massively speeds up development of new, more complex games.

units.title: High-quality code eases post-release iteration
units.detail: Keeping roughly 95% of code well-structured makes a game easy to expand and modify, enabling near-daily post-release updates driven by player feedback. Structure pays off when you iterate fast.

units.title: Steam reviews affect store visibility
units.detail: Crossing review-count thresholds (e.g., 50 reviews) moves a game into a new Steam review bucket that can boost visibility, so explicitly ask players for reviews early. First-week sales also strongly predict first-month performance.

units.title: Clone in-editor template transforms
units.detail: For UI repeated only within a single window, keep a template object in the editor instead of making prefabs (which clutter the project). Deactivate the template, Instantiate it, re-activate the copy, then set position and fields.

units.title: Helper function clones and positions lists
units.detail: Wrap clone-and-position logic in one helper and drive it with a loop to fill lists or duplicate buttons from a single editor-defined prototype. Editing the template retroactively updates everything generated from it.

units.title: Collapse console stack traces
units.detail: Set the console's Log Entry line count to 1 so each message shows compactly without its stack trace. Highlight any message to reveal its full stack trace on demand, keeping the console readable.

units.title: Visualize state with Debug.DrawLine
units.detail: Draw debug lines between two points (with optional color and duration) to see what the code is doing in the scene instead of reading console text. Great for showing paths, ranges, and spatial relationships.

units.title: Debug lines need Gizmos enabled
units.detail: Debug.DrawLine is invisible until the Gizmos toggle is enabled in the Game view. Without a duration the line is visible for only one frame, which is ideal for drawing fresh lines every frame from Update.

units.title: Draw pathfinding paths and grids
units.detail: Render a path by drawing lines between consecutive points, and draw grid or quadrant boundaries with four lines each, refreshed per frame. This gives an instant visual check that the algorithm behaves correctly.

units.title: Limit framerate to test low-end hardware
units.detail: Set Application.targetFrameRate (e.g., 10fps) to simulate a slow machine and expose frame-rate-sensitive bugs, then set it to -1 for unlimited when done. Always test across multiple framerates before shipping.

units.title: DeltaTime overshoot at low framerates
units.detail: Movement computed as speed * deltaTime works fine at high fps but overshoots and oscillates around the target at low fps because deltaTime becomes huge. Fix by clamping the move amount to the remaining distance to the target.

units.title: Name your magic numbers
units.detail: Replace unexplained literals (movement speed 20f, attack range 5f) with named variables so the code reads as intent. When the same number is used in multiple places, make it a shared member variable so values can't drift out of sync.

units.title: Name created GameObjects
units.detail: Pass a name to the GameObject constructor so dynamically spawned objects are identifiable in the hierarchy. Ten objects all named 'GameObject' make runtime debugging nearly impossible.

units.title: Attach components via constructor
units.detail: Use the GameObject constructor overload that accepts component types to spawn an object with components (e.g., SpriteRenderer, Unit) already attached, instead of separate new + AddComponent calls.

units.title: Static singleton prefab for asset references
units.detail: Put all commonly used asset references on one MonoBehaviour prefab (e.g., GameAssets) exposed through a static property. On first access, if the internal instance is null, Resources.Load and instantiate the prefab so any code — even non-MonoBehaviour — can reach assets without dragging references into every component.

units.title: Null ref from unguaranteed Awake order
units.detail: Calling another script's field in Awake can throw a NullReferenceException if that script's Awake hasn't run yet, since Unity's default execution order between scripts is undefined. Fix by forcing the initializer script to run first.

units.title: Force script execution order in editor
units.detail: In Project Settings > Script Execution Order, drag scripts above or below 'Default Time'; scripts run top-to-bottom, so place scripts that initialize first (like setting a static instance) before scripts that depend on them.

units.title: SerializeField keeps fields private but editable
units.detail: Marking a private field with [SerializeField] keeps it inaccessible to other classes while still showing it in the Inspector for dragging references or tuning values — avoids polluting the public API just for editor convenience.

units.title: Sort top-down sprites by Y position
units.detail: In a front/top-down 2D game (like Pokémon), lower Y world position should draw in front of higher Y. Use a sorting-order base minus position.y, and subtract an offset so sorting is based on the character's feet rather than the object origin.

units.title: Efficient sprite sorting implementation
units.detail: Implement Y-sorting using Renderer.sortingOrder so it works for both SpriteRenderer and MeshRenderer, recomputed in LateUpdate so it runs after the transform moves. Optimize with a run-once toggle (destroy self) for static sprites and a timer that only recomputes every ~100ms.

units.title: White pixel texture for tintable rectangles
units.detail: Instead of authoring a texture for every rectangle (health bars, backgrounds), use a single white 1x1 texture on a SpriteRenderer: scale it to any size and tint it any color. One asset covers every use case.

units.title: Ignore clicks when mouse is over UI
units.detail: Use EventSystem.current.IsPointerOverGameObject() to detect when the pointer is over UI, so gameplay actions like RTS move orders are blocked while interacting with UI windows or buttons.

units.title: Click-through UI elements via raycast filter
units.detail: To let specific transparent UI panels pass clicks through: raycastAll from the pointer, remove results that carry a dummy marker component (e.g., MouseUIClickThrough), then treat remaining hits as UI. Cleaner than testing names, tags, or layers.

units.title: Enums over strings for state handling
units.detail: Represent states and item types with enums instead of strings. The compiler catches typos and rejects invalid values at compile time, eliminating silent runtime bugs where a mistyped or miscapitalized string simply doesn't match.

units.title: Serialize custom classes to show in Inspector
units.detail: When several arrays hold connected data (spawn position, sprite, speed), group the fields into one custom class marked [Serializable]. The Inspector then shows a clean array of grouped objects instead of parallel arrays that are error-prone when sizes or indexes mismatch.

units.title: Steam build review can delay launch
units.detail: Even with a fully prepared build and store page, Steam's manual build review has no ETA and repeated support requests just return 'wait'. Budget review latency into announced launch timelines.

units.title: Adopt consistent naming conventions
units.detail: Pick a naming scheme — PascalCase functions (matching Unity/C#), camelCase fields and parameters, PascalCase properties, UPPER_SNAKE constants — and follow it consistently; consistency matters more than the specific style. Avoid single-letter names and cryptic abbreviations.

units.title: Replace magic numbers with named variables
units.detail: Inline numbers with hidden meaning (like '10') are obvious while writing but mysterious later. Assign them to well-named local or member variables so the code is self-documenting when you return to it.

units.title: Minimize public access to fields
units.detail: Public fields are readable and writable from anywhere, multiplying the places bugs can hide. Prefer private fields for encapsulation; only expose what other classes truly need, and keep editor-tunable values private via serialization.

units.title: Never identify objects by tags or strings
units.detail: String/tag-based identification breaks silently at runtime on the smallest typo or an invisible space, and the compiler won't catch it. Prefer direct object references, marker components, or singletons so mistakes surface as compile errors.

units.title: Decouple gameplay logic from UI via events
units.detail: Instead of logic classes referencing and driving UI directly, fire events (e.g., OnPlayerDied) and let UI listen and update itself. Logic stays independent — removing the UI class won't break the game code and systems stay separately testable.

units.title: Use TextMeshPro over legacy Text
units.detail: Unity's legacy UI Text component is outdated; TextMeshPro is better in every way. Switching only changes the using directive (TMPro) and class names for UI vs world text.

units.title: New Input System for released projects
units.detail: Legacy Input Manager is faster to set up, fine for demos and prototypes, but the new Input System has far better features and should be used when refactoring for a real release.

units.title: Choose URP render pipeline for new games
units.detail: The built-in render pipeline is aging; HDRP is for pushing visuals to the limit; URP is the best default for most new games, offering features like 2D lighting and shadow graphs.

units.title: Use Unity LTS versions for stability
units.detail: LTS (long-term support) versions are the stable choice for shipping games; the newest non-LTS release trades stability for the latest features. Unity's default-installed version is typically the right one to use.

units.title: Prefer diegetic in-world UI over popup menus
units.detail: Before building a separate UI window for an interaction, consider placing the UI directly in the world (world-space canvas with button images). Interacting with buttons physically in the world keeps players immersed and is simple to implement with a world-space canvas plus raycast.

units.title: Implement in-world UI via canvas raycast
units.detail: Put a world-space canvas in front of an object (vending machine), lay out buttons as normal UI images, then raycast from the mouse position each frame to detect what's under the cursor. Use an interface or component lookup to identify hovered objects, and trigger pointer-down events per button.

units.title: Build a scanning vision mode with layered cameras and render features
units.detail: A scanning mode combines: a post-processing volume that tints the whole screen (color adjustment + grain), a camera renderer that overrides scannable-object materials with an animated outline shader, a second camera rendering only the scanning layer as a dark silhouette, and a third renderer adding an extra outline on the selected object. Objects are identified by layer masks.

units.title: Highlight scan objects with a vertex-noise flat-color shader
units.detail: A very simple Shader Graph shader can make scannable objects stand out: move vertices with noise for a subtle animated glitch and output a flat color. Combined with black silhouettes and an extra after-rendering outline, it clearly separates scan mode from normal mode.

units.title: Switch renderers per-camera for scan effects
units.detail: In URP you can swap which renderer a camera uses (e.g., main camera) and give each renderer custom render features that apply to specific layer masks. This allows different rendering treatments (override material, add outlines) without touching the original materials.

units.title: Keep scan-mode logic in one small script firing events
units.detail: Centralize scanning in a sub-100-line script holding references to all cameras and the post-processing object. Enable/disable everything in one function, and on update raycast to find the hovered scannable object, firing a C# event when the active scan target changes so separate UI scripts can subscribe.

units.title: Force a valid solution when generating hack minigame boards
units.detail: For a hacking minigame (buffer, timer, hex grid, horizontal/vertical alternation), pure random board generation often produces an unwinnable sequence. Instead, force a solution by construction: pick a random value from the first horizontal row, then from the following vertical line, alternating until the whole sequence exists. This guarantees winnability.

units.title: Hacking minigame rule set: alternate horizontal/vertical selection
units.detail: The Cyberpunk hack minigame: start on the topmost horizontal line, then alternate between horizontal and vertical selection per step; you have a buffer (attempt count), a timer starting on first selection, and must match a target sequence. This simple ruleset gives the right complexity for a bonus minigame.

units.title: AAA systems are often simple under the hood
units.detail: Complex-looking AAA mechanics usually decompose into simple building blocks: world canvas + raycast for diegetic UI, layered cameras and simple shaders for scanning, and a small script with forced generation for the hack minigame. Dig into systems before assuming they are hard to replicate.

units.title: Wrap transforms in a domain object to avoid direct coupling
units.detail: Create a small plain C# class (e.g., ResourceNode) that holds a reference to a Transform and exposes clean methods like GetPosition(), GrabResource(), and HasResources(). The AI works with domain objects instead of raw transforms, which keeps code cleaner and lets you add data/behavior (resource amount, depletion sprite) without touching call sites.

units.title: Filter resource selection to only valid nodes
units.detail: When picking a resource node for an AI to gather from, clone the candidate list, remove invalid nodes (depleted, too far), then return a random valid one. Guard with a count check and return null when nothing is available so the AI knows to keep waiting instead of assuming success.

units.title: AI must null-check when no valid node exists
units.detail: Once a lookup function can return null (no resources left), any AI state machine that previously assumed a node is always found will break. Only switch states when the returned node is not null, otherwise stay in the waiting state.

units.title: Swap sprite via renderer reference when state changes
units.detail: When a resource node depletes, grab the Transform's SpriteRenderer component and swap in a 'depleted' sprite from a central assets reference class. Centralizing prefab/sprite references in a static assets class keeps components decoupled from scene wiring.

units.title: Let the gatherer carry multiple resource units
units.detail: Extend the AI to carry more than one resource: only go to storage when the carried amount reaches the capacity (e.g., 3 units), mining the node repeatedly until depleted or inventory full. This makes gather loops efficient instead of one-trip-per-resource.

units.title: Gatherers should respect the ordered resource type
units.detail: When a gatherer finishes one node, it should only pick up a nearby node of the same resource type it was ordered to mine, not switch to whatever is nearest. Add a filter comparing the candidate node's type to the current gather type so behavior matches player intent.

units.title: Regenerate nodes via timed full reset
units.detail: Implement node regeneration by storing a max amount, and when a node depletes start a timer (e.g., 5 seconds) that resets the resource amount to full and restores the sprite. A helper timer object that fires an action after a delay keeps the logic simple.

units.title: Regenerate nodes via constant per-second drip
units.detail: Alternative to full reset: call a function periodically (e.g., every 2 seconds) that adds exactly one resource and updates visuals, clamping so the amount never exceeds the max. Constant drip suits nodes meant to be steadily farmed.

units.title: AI can mine into negative inventory without a capacity check
units.detail: If a gatherer always mines a fixed amount (e.g., 3) regardless of remaining node resources, the amount goes negative when a node is nearly depleted. Fix by also going to storage when the node runs out mid-mine: return to storage if inventory is full OR the node has no resources left.

units.title: Centralize sprite updates in one function
units.detail: Instead of swapping sprites inline everywhere, write a single UpdateSprite() method that inspects the current amount and picks the correct sprite. Call it after every state change (depletion, reset, regeneration) so visuals always match the data.

units.title: Use a static resource bank class with events
units.detail: Model the player's total resources as a static class (GameResources) holding amounts, Add/Get functions, and a C# event fired whenever an amount changes. Static means any system can access it, and the change event lets UI update reactively without polling.

units.title: Subscribe UI text to a resource-changed event
units.detail: Have a UI window subscribe to the resource bank's amount-changed event in Awake and update its Text component in the handler. Firing the event inside the Add function notifies all subscribers automatically, keeping the display in sync with the source of truth.

units.title: AI deposits resources into the bank at storage
units.detail: When the gatherer reaches the storage position, call the resource bank's Add function with the carried amount before resetting its inventory and going idle. Centralizing where deposits happen keeps the flow explicit and easy to reason about.

units.title: Use enums plus dictionaries for multiple resource types
units.detail: Replace hard-coded per-resource int fields with a ResourceType enum and a Dictionary<ResourceType, int>. Initialize the dictionary by iterating Enum.GetValues and setting each key to zero, so adding a new resource type requires no other code changes.

units.title: Keep the same public API while changing internals
units.detail: Refactor a resource bank to use a dictionary internally while preserving the existing external functions/events. Callers and UI keep working unchanged during migration, letting you verify nothing broke before renaming or changing signatures.

units.title: Compute total inventory by iterating all resource types
units.detail: For capacity checks ('inventory full'), calculate the total carried by looping over every resource type and summing the dictionary values instead of tracking a single int. Isolate this in small helper functions (GetTotalInventoryAmount, IsInventoryFull, DropInventoryToBank).

units.title: Let resource nodes declare their own type
units.detail: Have each resource node store its resource type (passed in its constructor), return it from GrabResource, and pick its depleted sprite via a switch on that type. The gatherer then increases the matching dictionary entry and plays the right animation (mine vs. chop) per type.

units.title: Initialize static state before anything uses it
units.detail: A static resource bank backed by a dictionary must be initialized (Init) before first use. Call the init function at the start of the game handler's setup so keys exist before any Add/Get runs.

units.title: Return multiple values using the out keyword
units.detail: To return several pieces of data from one function without creating a class/struct, add out parameters to the signature. The function must assign every out variable before exiting; callers declare locals, pass them with 'out', and read them afterward.

units.title: Struct return object as alternative to out params
units.detail: When a function needs to return multiple values, you can define a small struct (e.g., ZombieHitInfo with hit, damage amount, knockback) and return an instance. This is the alternative to out parameters; both work, out avoids defining a new type.

units.title: Compiler requires out variables to be assigned before exit
units.detail: With the out keyword you must assign values to those parameters on every code path before the function returns; the compiler enforces this (the original error disappears once set). Use this to guarantee all outputs are initialized.

units.title: Scale damage by distance to explosion
units.detail: Make damage falloff by computing damage from the distance between target and explosion center (e.g., 50 damage right on top, 1 at the edge), plus a random chance to cause knockback. Return hit bool, damage amount, and knockback together from one function.

units.title: Master basics before advancing
units.detail: Beginners should build a solid foundation of Unity/C# basics before tackling intermediate topics. Attempting advanced systems without basics leads to messy, hard-to-fix code. Roughly 70% of core game dev knowledge transfers across any game type, so don't skip learning because your target game is different.

units.title: Learn by building slightly-beyond-your-skill games
units.detail: At the intermediate stage, improve by analyzing your weak points and building things just a bit more complex than your current skill (e.g., Flappy Bird then Pac-Man). Constantly working at the edge of your abilities is how you grow; no guide needed.

units.title: Don't memorize code, learn logic and Google the syntax
units.detail: You are not supposed to memorize code; train logical thinking so you can figure out solution steps, then Google the syntax for the specific language (e.g., how to make an array in PHP). Using Google is a normal, permanent part of the development process at every skill level.

units.title: Take your time; courses need months, not hours
units.detail: A 10-12 hour course contains a decade of knowledge and should take at least one month to a few months, not its raw duration. Don't rush or compare yourself to others; the only goal is that you're learning, and knowledge is just a matter of time.

units.title: Build individual systems instead of full games to practice
units.detail: To train a specific weak area, build single focused systems (weapon attachment, house building, Tetris inventory) either alone or by combining self-attempts with tutorials. Every system can be built a million ways, so a different approach isn't wrong.

units.title: Automate dedicated server setup with a compile-time symbol
units.detail: Define a custom scripting define symbol (e.g., DEDICATED_SERVER) and wrap server-only logic in #if blocks. A dedicated server build can then skip menus automatically: load the lobby scene immediately on the main menu script, avoiding any player-driven flow.

units.title: Netcode server must listen on 0.0.0.0 to be reachable
units.detail: When setting up the NetworkTransport for a hosted server with Unity Game Server Hosting, you must pass the listen address 0.0.0.0 (not null) or clients cannot connect; the server will be unreachable. The listen port must match the port provided by the multiplay allocation (not the query port).

units.title: Drive servers from allocation config and report readiness
units.detail: A server build should: wait for the multiplay allocation event, read its config, set the transport port, start the server (not host), load the game scene, then call a 'server ready' API so the service knows it can accept players. Later set it unready (e.g., when the game starts) if joins should close.

units.title: Send periodic server-alive checks to the hosting backend
units.detail: Call the server query/update API every frame or update to tell the backend the server is still alive, and optionally set concurrent users. The SQP server query handler must be started after services init; the per-update check keeps the server from being considered dead.

units.title: Server list requires web API and basic auth, not the SDK
units.detail: The Game Server Hosting package can't list servers; that data lives in a separate web API endpoint. Create a service account with the 'Multiplay API Viewer' permission, concatenate key ID + secret, base64 encode, and send it as an Authorization header. The returned JSON may be malformed for Unity's built-in JsonUtility, so wrap it in a list field.

units.title: Create allocations via token exchange, not direct auth
units.detail: Creating regular server allocations uses a different web API than the server list and requires OAuth-style token exchange: POST the base64 key to the token exchange endpoint with your desired scopes to receive a JWT, then send that as a Bearer token. This flow should live in a trusted backend, not client code, since players shouldn't allocate servers you pay for.

units.title: Disable camera to stop dedicated-server log spam
units.detail: Headless server builds emit noisy warning spam from the camera. Setting camera.main.enabled to false on the dedicated server build silences those log warnings. Also pass -nographics in the fleet's launch parameters to run without rendering.

units.title: Idea duplication is not a real threat
units.detail: A game is far more than an idea: turning it into a game requires thousands of unique decisions, so two people starting from the same idea still make vastly different games. Game jams (same theme, wildly different results) prove this; idea theft basically only happens after you're already hugely successful.

units.title: Wishlists don't expire or decay
units.detail: Data shows wishlist conversion stays roughly flat over time (~20%), even for lists years old, so keeping a Steam Coming Soon page up long before launch has no penalty. Old wishlists convert as well as fresh ones, so gather them early.

units.title: You don't need a following; you need content creators and Steam's algorithm
units.detail: Success comes from having content creators with audiences play/promote your game, or from a game that fits the Steam algorithm so Steam itself promotes it, not from your own dev channel followers. Game makers and game players are different audiences; devlogs for developers rarely convert to game sales.

units.title: Contact content creators early with a solid, playable build
units.detail: Don't save your 'one shot' for launch: creators who genuinely like a game play it multiple times over development, each time adding more wishlists (which don't decay). Reach out as soon as you have something solid and playable, then again near release; never pitch alpha screenshots.

units.title: There is no permanent Steam algorithm black mark
units.detail: The belief that low launch wishlists permanently doom a game from the algorithm is a myth. The algorithm reacts daily to performance; a weak launch just means less visibility, but if you later push traffic and people like the game, visibility grows again. A bad page/trailer can be recovered from if the game is good.

units.title: Big AAA launches rarely bury other games
units.detail: Even a massive release (e.g., 500k concurrent players) is only ~5% of Steam's audience, so it can't cannibalize everything. Launching near a huge game is fine as long as you're not the exact same genre; avoidances by other indies can even give your game more visibility.

units.title: Mesh boolean operations with ProBuilder
units.detail: ProBuilder supports mesh boolean operations (intersection, union, subtraction) for cutting holes/doors/windows or merging objects. Workflow: convert the mesh via 'ProBuilderize', build a cube as the cutter, enable the experimental features toggle in preferences, then use the experimental Boolean tool to pick two meshes and an operation. Apply creates a brand new object without modifying originals.

units.title: Use subtraction to carve door and window holes
units.detail: Position a ProBuilder cube where you want an opening, run a subtraction boolean, and the wall comes out with a perfect hole for a door or window. Union can merge objects into fewer game objects to simplify a scene.

units.title: Buy assets outside your skill set
units.detail: Use the asset store for 3D models, textures, animations, effects, UI, and sounds when art is not your strength. Even skilled artists save time buying instead of building everything from scratch.

units.title: Genre game-builder tools speed up prototyping
units.detail: Complete genre frameworks (RPG builder, top-down engine, colony sim, RTS, platformer, visual novel) ship with quests, inventory, combat, and documented systems so you can stand up a full game quickly instead of building every system.

units.title: Buy a mature character controller
units.detail: A basic controller is easy but a proper one that handles every scenario is complex and time-consuming. A tested controller asset (player, car, ship) saves massive time.

units.title: World-building tools compress months of level work
units.detail: Terrain generators, prefab painters, and city generators place trees, buildings, roads, and sidewalks in hours or days instead of manually placing objects over weeks or months.

units.title: Terrain edits must update the nav mesh
units.detail: When real-time terrain digging changes geometry, the nav mesh must update too, otherwise players and AI cannot navigate the new caves.

units.title: Don't build universal systems from scratch
units.detail: Save systems, pathfinding, and debug consoles are needed by almost every game; mature solutions with serialization, encryption, and multithreading beat hand-rolling them.

units.title: Polish separates good games from great games
units.detail: Tiny feedback like screen shake, zooms, and color changes on every player action massively improves game feel; text animation and custom cursors also add professional polish with little effort.

units.title: Add an in-game debug console
units.detail: A command console invoked with a single attribute lets you set ammo or trigger states by typing commands during testing, replacing custom debug keys and debug code.

units.title: Sale daily deals give deeper discounts
units.detail: Store sales have flat 50% discounts plus daily deals at 70%; check the daily deal calendar before buying so you can grab the deeper discount when your target asset hits it.

units.title: Watch asset reviews before buying
units.detail: Asset review videos show how a tool works, its workflow, and whether it fits your project before you spend money, reducing bad purchases.

units.title: Billboard sprite effects for 3D
units.detail: 2D sprite effects (explosions, slashes, projectiles) can be used in 3D games by making the sprite always face the camera.

units.title: Customizable character packs cover many roles
units.detail: A single asset with head/face/body/armor/weapon/height customization plus an inventory system can produce every character in your game, from medieval melee to sci-fi soldiers.

units.title: VR interaction kits use physics-driven bodies
units.detail: Non-kinematic rigid bodies give VR objects a real sense of weight with accurate collisions, enabling grabbing, stabbing, and weapon interactions that feel solid.

units.title: Learn by doing, not just watching
units.detail: Tutorials are only the first and smallest step of learning; you must open a project and write code yourself to solidify knowledge and escape tutorial hell.

units.title: Increase participation levels to learn
units.detail: Progress from passively watching, to reading FAQ, to answering quizzes, to writing real code; more active participation forces knowledge retrieval and retention.

units.title: Don't skip ahead in courses
units.detail: If you don't understand a topic, stay there, research it, and experiment until it clicks before moving forward; skipping just compounds confusion.

units.title: Active application needed at any skill level
units.detail: Even advanced developers research new tech by watching videos and reading docs, then loading a fresh project and writing code to truly internalize it.

units.title: Define 'small game' by skill level
units.detail: Small is relative: beginners should make one-weekend games, then scale to two-week, one-month, two-month, and six-month projects only as skills improve.

units.title: Make many tiny games when learning
units.detail: Making 10-20 really small focused games teaches more than spending 6-12 months on one big game as a beginner.

units.title: Validate your idea before long development
units.detail: Don't exceed 12 months of development unless your idea is validated with hard data like 50k wishlists; 1k wishlists signals weak hype and extra time won't change the numbers.

units.title: Small timeframes don't equal slop
units.detail: Quality within a fixed time frame depends on skill, not time spent; notable hits shipped in weeks. Invest in skills so the same 6 months yields more complex games.

units.title: Pick a sustainable release cadence
units.detail: An experienced solo dev can ship roughly two games per year at six months each, increasing complexity over time as skill grows rather than extending dev time.

units.title: Search before grinding on a stuck problem
units.detail: When stuck for hours, Google, YouTube, or Reddit for someone with a similar problem; knowing how to ask the right question is a skill you develop over time.

units.title: Take a break to solve hard problems
units.detail: When stuck, take a shower, walk the dog, or step away from the computer; answers often surface with fresh eyes after a break.

units.title: Getting stuck is a normal learning phase
units.detail: Being stuck often as a beginner is natural, not a failure; accept it as part of the process and don't let it demotivate you.

units.title: Tutorials hide the struggle behind them
units.detail: You only see the polished final version; behind each 10-20 minute video are roughly 8-10 hours of research and trial-and-error, so don't expect to learn it in the video's runtime.

units.title: Experience turns hard tasks into typing exercises
units.detail: A player controller takes about a week the first time but minutes after writing hundreds; accumulated experience is the most powerful force in development.

units.title: No tutorial replaces active practice
units.detail: Watching a video covers only 10-20% of learning; writing the code yourself is the remaining 80% where knowledge is actually internalized.

units.title: Rebuild an image as a particle scatter
units.detail: Bake a texture into a point cache (position + color per pixel), spawn one particle per point, then apply turbulence or vector field forces to scatter the image into particles.

units.title: Spawn all particles once with a single burst
units.detail: Use a single burst whose count equals the point count so the full image appears instantly at activation, instead of particles trickling in at a constant spawn rate.

units.title: Use periodic burst while iterating an effect
units.detail: Add a periodic burst with a delay so the effect auto-refreshes for testing; disable it and keep only the single burst for the final effect.

units.title: Vector fields give flowy, less random motion
units.detail: A vector field is a 3D voxel grid with a vector per position; scattering with it looks smoother and less random than turbulence, and you can author custom fields for exact flow.

units.title: Sequence image fade with effect activation
units.detail: Use a timeline to animate the source image alpha from 1 to 0 exactly when the particle effect activates, so the image hides as it turns into particles.

units.title: Centralize scene loading in a static loader
units.detail: Make a static Loader class with an enum of scene names and a load function, so code deals with typed scene values instead of strings scattered everywhere.

units.title: Loading screen never renders if target loads same frame
units.detail: Loading the target scene immediately after the loading scene means the screen never refreshes (it only updates on Update), so the player sees a hang; defer the target load by one frame.

units.title: Defer scene load with a static Action
units.detail: Store the target scene load in a static Action, have a script call it after the loading scene's first Update, invoke it, then set it to null.

units.title: Show real progress with LoadSceneAsync
units.detail: Use SceneManager.LoadSceneAsync and poll the returned AsyncOperation.progress (yielding each frame until done) to drive a loading bar; progress bar fill via an image fill amount.

units.title: Loading bar may jump 0 to 90%
units.detail: Small or simple scenes can't be broken into chunks by Unity, so the bar jumps from empty to nearly full; smooth progress depends on how the target scene is composed.

units.title: Dual health/posture system adds two win conditions
units.detail: Sekiro-style vitality plus posture lets you defeat enemies two ways (chip health or break posture) and makes defensive play meaningful; the UI is also visually distinctive.

units.title: Separate game logic from UI visuals
units.detail: Keep a plain class for state and events, and a separate UI class that subscribes to those events to update bars; this keeps logic clean and reusable.

units.title: Sliced sprite expands from center
units.detail: Configure a sprite's borders in the Sprite Editor and use Image type Sliced so the bar stretches from center to both sides while edges stay correct, perfect for a posture bar.

units.title: Integer division returns 0 in C#
units.detail: Dividing an int by another int truncates (e.g., 80/100 = 0), so cast to float before dividing to compute normalized values like 0.8.

units.title: Notify UI via events
units.detail: Define public events (e.g., OnHealthChange) using EventHandler, null-check before invoking, and pass EventArgs.Empty; UI subscribes to update bars whenever state changes.

units.title: Clamp values before firing state events
units.detail: Cap health at 0 and posture at max before firing death/posture-broken events so bars never overflow into negatives or past the maximum.

units.title: Color a bar from yellow to red as it fills
units.detail: Map normalized fill 0→1 to green 1→0 while red stays 1, giving yellow → orange → red; lerp is unnecessary when you just decrease the green channel.

units.title: Show last-hit damage with a ghost bar
units.detail: Keep a secondary damage bar at the pre-hit value, wait a short timer after being hit, then shrink it down to the current health to visualize the last hit's damage.

units.title: fillAmount vs width for bar types
units.detail: Use Image.fillAmount for left-to-right bars and RectTransform width with a sliced sprite for center-expanding bars; each matches a different UI presentation.

units.title: Alpha became a separate shader input in SG 10
units.detail: Feeding an RGBA color into Base Color no longer applies alpha in Shader Graph 10; use a Split node and connect the A channel to the separate Alpha input.

units.title: Old shader graphs still load in new versions
units.detail: Shader graphs made in much older Unity versions load fine in Shader Graph 10; you only need small conversions like reconnecting alpha.

units.title: Master nodes replaced by a single Master Stack
units.detail: In Shader Graph 10 you can no longer add or delete master nodes; change the shader target type and surface settings through the Graph Inspector instead.

units.title: One graph targeting multiple render pipelines
units.detail: The + icon in the master stack lets a single shader graph compile for both URP and HDRP, avoiding duplicate graphs and easing asset store compatibility.

units.title: Animate a scrolling shield texture
units.detail: Tile a hexagon texture and feed Time (combined into a Vector2) into a Tiling and Offset node's offset to scroll the pattern upward over time.

units.title: Textures won't repeat until wrap mode is Repeat
units.detail: A tiled/scrolling shader looks clamped and wrong if the texture import wrap mode is Clamp; switch it to Repeat on all used textures.

units.title: Combine node labels use colors not vectors
units.detail: In Shader Graph the Combine node labels channels as R/G/B which map to X/Y/Z; easy to misread when building Vector2 offsets and tiling.

units.title: Negate time to flip scroll direction
units.detail: Multiplying the time value by -1 (Negate node) before the offset reverses whether a texture scrolls up or down.

units.title: Layer gradients for richer effects
units.detail: Add a gradient texture tiled more times and scrolling faster than the base hexagon texture to give a force field depth; multiply by an extra color for intensity.

units.title: HDR emission color times texture for glow
units.detail: Multiply an HDR color property by the emission texture and feed it into the Emission slot so the shield glows and reacts to bloom.

units.title: Port a shader to 2D via Sprite-Lit
units.detail: Duplicate the graph and switch the master to Sprite-Lit: emission is baked into color, so multiply emission by base color into the Color input and add an alpha multiply.

units.title: Content creators can make or break a game
units.detail: A single YouTube/Twitch coverage can turn an unknown game into a hit (e.g. Splattercat's Vampire Survivors video preceded its explosion). Creator coverage is extremely valuable to the indie ecosystem even though the creator earns very little from it.

units.title: Coverage economics for indie YouTubers are terrible
units.detail: Indie game videos have ad rates around $2 RPM, so 10K views is roughly $30 (not $180). Making a video takes many hours for tiny pay, so sponsorships become necessary to sustain the channel.

units.title: Sponsored coverage feels less genuine than organic
units.detail: Viewers take 'sponsored' content less seriously than organic coverage. This tension means devs dislike paying (feels icky/selling out) while creators increasingly need sponsorships to survive. Both positions are reasonable.

units.title: Devs value coverage but sharing revenue feels tone-deaf
units.detail: Backlash came from a dev bragging about millions in sales while refusing to pay creators. Expectation shifts: 10 years ago paying for coverage was seen as selling out; today it's a normal part of the creator economy.

units.title: Buy vs build is a time-versus-money equation
units.detail: When you need an asset you always pay: in time if you build it, in money if you buy it. Compute how many hours it takes you to build it; if your hourly worth exceeds the cost, buy it.

units.title: Buying is usually 10x faster than building
units.detail: A $30 text-animation asset might take 50 hours to build even with 25 years of experience, and the store asset is better (thousands of dev hours behind it). Spending 20-50 bucks usually beats spending 50-100 hours.

units.title: Third-party tools have learning curves and opinionated code
units.detail: Tools worth using always have a learning curve (docs, custom inspectors) and integration quality varies: some are opinionated and hard to wire into your code. Factor in learning/integration time, but it's still usually faster than building.

units.title: Can't build what you lack skills for
units.detail: If you don't have the skill (e.g. no 3D modeling ability), building takes ~1000 hours of practice first. Spend those hours on your core skill instead and buy the asset pack.

units.title: Accumulate personal utilities across projects
units.detail: Build reusable utilities while making games; over a decade of projects you end up with a powerful personal toolkit. This is what many asset packs are: polished versions of utilities one dev wrote for themselves.

units.title: Engine is just a tool, game is the goal
units.detail: The goal is to make a game; the engine choice is secondary. Choose whatever engine you want but base it on valid arguments rather than misconceptions or non-issues.

units.title: Many engine features are a positive, not bloat
units.detail: An engine supporting tons of use cases (2D, 3D, ML, terrain, AR/VR) doesn't hurt your game; just use the tools relevant to you. Bloat complaints usually confuse feature count with quality.

units.title: Pick render pipeline by target quality
units.detail: Unity has three render pipelines: use HDRP for AAA/console/high-end PC, URP (universal) for everything else, and built-in legacy only for specific legacy needs. The decision is a 30-second question.

units.title: Use the latest LTS Unity version
units.detail: Unity versions are LTS (long-term support, stable, 2yr support), Tech, and Preview. For game making just use the latest LTS; you don't need to track the monthly hotfix versions unless you're about to release.

units.title: Text Mesh Pro is built-in, not third party
units.detail: TMP was acquired and integrated into Unity long ago; it's a default built-in package, not a downloadable third-party fix. The legacy text renderer remains only for backwards compatibility.

units.title: Unity crashes usually come from experimental packages
units.detail: In the author's ~10,000 hours, crashes mostly involved ML Agents or experimental packages (marked as such). Stable LTS releases rarely crash; keep experimental features out of real projects.

units.title: GDD detail level depends on team scale
units.detail: A 300-person AAA team needs an excruciatingly detailed design document so everything comes together. Solo/small-team devs should keep it loose and iterate, since detailed docs make you uneasy about changing broken design.

units.title: Use design pillars to stay loose but focused
units.detail: Define a few pillars (e.g. 'player is weak, direct confrontation discouraged') instead of a rigid doc. When iterating, check design changes against pillars so combined mechanics don't silently break your core vision.

units.title: Separate abilities can combine to break a pillar
units.detail: A smoke bomb meant for escape plus a takedown ability turns the grenade into an offensive tool, breaking a stealth pillar. Strict design docs prevent catching such emergent breaks; iterating against pillars fixes them (e.g. blind only when player is far).

units.title: Iterate on prototypes to discover the real game
units.detail: Blueprint Tycoon started as a mercenary-supplier game; iterating revealed crafting/supply-chain was the fun part and the theme was changed to support it. Design 'as you go' beats predicting everything in pre-production.

units.title: Calibrate GDD detail with a one-month project
units.detail: To find your ideal level, make a small one-month game with a design doc first. If you over-constrained yourself, go looser next time; if you were too blind, add more upfront design.

units.title: Using assets is not cheating
units.detail: Players judge the final game, not how it was made. Successful Steam games built on recognizable asset packs get great reviews with zero mention of assets. There are no bonus points for building everything yourself.

units.title: Asset flip = uploading a template unchanged
units.detail: Buying a game template and uploading it without changes is an asset flip (bad). Using a template or assets as a starting point and adding your own mechanics/content makes it your original game.

units.title: Build your own scenes, don't ship demo scenes
units.detail: Games using the asset pack's included demo scene straight up are 'on the edge of acceptable' even if players don't mind. Customize the scene and combine packs rather than shipping the template scene verbatim.

units.title: Without assets some games would not exist
units.detail: If the dev has no modeling skills, the choice is use assets or cancel the game. Assets enabled timely, fun games (e.g. a Battlefield 2042 parody) that couldn't exist if built from scratch. Use every tool to bring your idea to life.

units.title: Unity has three UI systems
units.detail: Unity UI (UGUI, game-object based), UI Toolkit (web-inspired: UXML + USS + C#), and IMGUI (legacy code-driven). All are valid; choice is mainly personal preference.

units.title: Runtime UI in UGUI, editor tools in UI Toolkit
units.detail: Match Unity's own guidance: use Unity UI for runtime game UI and UI Toolkit for editor tooling (huge upgrade over the IMGUI 'nightmare'). UI Toolkit is already stable enough for production runtime if you prefer it.

units.title: UI Toolkit still lacks some features
units.detail: UI Toolkit is near feature parity but lacks serialized events, visual scripting support, custom materials/shaders, and mesh clipping. Fine for most games but check these if you need them.

units.title: UI Toolkit's separation suits teams, not solo devs
units.detail: Splitting structure (UXML), styling (USS) and logic (C#) lets three people work in parallel, but a solo dev gains little. Web devs may find UI Toolkit more familiar; both UGUI and UI Toolkit work fine on mobile.

units.title: One difficulty setting can't fit every player
units.detail: With a single fixed difficulty, some players find it perfect, others unplayably hard — the exact designer-intended experience reaches almost no one. It's the core problem of the Souls approach.

units.title: Two types of players: challenge seekers vs frustration avoiders
units.detail: One player type gets an endorphin rush from finally beating a hard boss; the other just feels prolonged frustration with no payoff. Knowing this explains why hard games polarize audiences.

units.title: Indie games should offer difficulty settings
units.detail: Souls-likes can have one difficulty because they have massive loyal audiences; an indie with a single too-hard setting will get negative reviews. Cater to everyone with easy/normal modes plus hardcore or new-game-plus for challenge players.

units.title: Difficulty is accessibility
units.detail: Some players are physically incapable of beating a reflex-based boss no matter how they practice — for them the game is literally unplayable without an easy mode. Difficulty settings make the game accessible to more players.

units.title: Camera orthographic size = half the vertical view
units.detail: In Unity 2D the camera's orthographic size is half the visible vertical units (size 5 shows -5 to +5). To get 100 units of vertical play space, set size to 50.

units.title: Stretch a 1x1 white pixel for UI/background rects
units.detail: Import a 1x1 white texture with pixels-per-unit = 1 and stretch it on a sprite renderer to draw arbitrary rectangles (backgrounds, hit boxes). Reuse one white pixel instead of generating textures.

units.title: Centralize asset references in a static class
units.detail: Keep all asset references in one GameAssets class with a static instance (set in Awake) and access like GameAssets.instance.snakeHeadSprite. Force its Awake to run first via Script Execution Order so fields are set before use.

units.title: Use sorting layers to control render order
units.detail: Create sorting layers like 'background' that render before 'default' so objects draw in the intended order. Keep an extra layer above default for popups/overlays.

units.title: State machine via enum + switch in Update
units.detail: Model simple AI with an enum of states (idle, moving to resource, gathering, moving to storage) and a switch in Update executing logic per state. Transition states when actions/animations complete.

units.title: Decouple AI from direct object references
units.detail: Instead of the AI holding node/storage transforms, have it ask the game handler for the nearest resource or storage position when needed. This makes the AI adaptable and the game centralizes world knowledge.

units.title: Drive units through an interface
units.detail: Define a unit interface with MoveTo, PlayAnimation and IsIdle so AI code depends on behavior, not a concrete class. Check IsIdle before issuing movement so commands don't interrupt a unit mid-animation.

units.title: Gatherer AI loop: find node, mine, return, drop
units.detail: Core loop: idle → find resource node → move to node → play mining animation → carry resource → move to storage → deposit → back to idle. Simple state machine can be extended to any resource type.

units.title: Decouple logic from visuals with data classes
units.detail: Represent resources with a ResourceNode class tracking amounts and a GameResources class for adding/removing amounts, rather than hanging logic off transforms. Logic stays engine-agnostic and visuals can swap freely.

units.title: Design a self-expanding gameplay ecosystem
units.detail: Design loops that compound: gather gold+wood → construct tower → tower spawns a new controllable gatherer → it gathers more and builds another tower. This turns a simple mechanic into a complete mini-game.

units.title: Start battle via trigger collider + event
units.detail: Place a trigger collider at the arena entrance; on enter, fire an event the battle system subscribes to. Keeping the trigger script free of any battle-system reference keeps the classes decoupled.

units.title: State machine prevents double battle start
units.detail: Track an enum state (Idle/Active). Only start the battle when state == Idle, then set it to Active so the trigger can't fire twice.

units.title: Unsubscribe event after it fires once
units.detail: After a one-shot event fires (e.g. player entered trigger), unsubscribe to avoid wasted CPU cycles on future invocations.

units.title: Enemy waves as serializable class array
units.detail: Wrap enemy spawn references in a Wave class marked [Serializable] so the inspector shows the field. Each wave holds an enemy array plus a spawn timer that counts down in Update.

units.title: Wave over only when spawned and all dead
units.detail: A wave is finished only if its timer has elapsed AND every enemy in it is dead. The whole battle is over when every wave reports finished; checking this each frame is wasteful.

units.title: Test win condition on enemy death, not per-frame
units.detail: Polling 'is battle over' every frame wastes CPU since most frames nothing changes. Better: fire an event on enemy death and re-evaluate only then.

units.title: Battle events connect to doors cleanly
units.detail: Expose OnBattleStart/OnBattleOver events from the battle system; a separate connection script closes the entry door on start and opens the exit door on end, keeping the battle system ignorant of other systems.

units.title: Place object at mouse world position
units.detail: Convert Input.mousePosition to a world point with Camera.ScreenToWorldPoint to spawn buildings exactly where the cursor is.

units.title: ScriptableObject defines building types
units.detail: Extend ScriptableObject and add [CreateAssetMenu] to generate assets that hold per-type data (prefab, sprite). Swapping the active type changes what you spawn without touching code.

units.title: Build UI buttons dynamically from a template
units.detail: Hide a button template, instantiate copies under the parent, position them via anchoredPosition, set their sprite from data, and attach onClick listeners via lambdas.

units.title: Clicks pass through UI to world
units.detail: Raw mouse-button checks spawn objects even when clicking UI buttons. Fix: guard with EventSystem.current.IsPointerOverGameObject() and only place when the pointer is NOT over a UI element.

units.title: OverlapBox tests building footprint clear
units.detail: Instead of testing a single point, use the building's BoxCollider size+offset with Physics2D.OverlapBox so the full footprint blocks placement, preventing overlap.

units.title: Expanding build radius via proximity rule
units.detail: Require an existing building within a max radius before placing (OverlapCircleAll + tag component). Seed the world with a starter HQ so the first building has a valid anchor, enabling RTS-style area expansion.

units.title: Empty script used as a tag component
units.detail: Attach a component with no code to game objects and test GetComponent<T>() != null to identify types cheaply, avoiding string tags or layer setup.

units.title: AI drives any car controller via inputs
units.detail: The driver AI only needs the car controller to expose accelerate/brake/turn functions, so the same AI works with player control or ML drivers on top of any controller.

units.title: Dot product decides forward vs reverse
units.detail: Dot(forward, directionToTarget) > 0 means the target is ahead (accelerate), < 0 means behind (reverse). Signed angle about the up axis decides left/right turn amount.

units.title: Stopping distance + pre-brake prevents overshoot
units.detail: Compare distance to target against a reach distance to stop; if distance is under a larger stopping distance and speed is too high, apply brakes BEFORE reaching the target so fast cars stop cleanly.

units.title: Do a 180 instead of reversing long distances
units.detail: If the target is behind AND far away, go forward and turn around rather than reversing the whole way; reserve reversing for short distances. Small distance = reverse onto target.

units.title: Decouple logic from visuals via base class
units.detail: Have movement logic call animation functions on a base class (PlayWalk(dir), PlayIdle(dir)); the animation system can be swapped as long as the function contract stays the same.

units.title: time.deltaTime makes movement frame-rate independent
units.detail: Multiply movement by time.deltaTime (seconds since last frame) so speed stays constant regardless of FPS.

units.title: Normalize diagonal movement or you move faster
units.detail: Combining X=1,Y=1 gives a vector of magnitude ~1.41, moving diagonally faster. Normalize the move direction so magnitude is always 1.

units.title: Idle animation uses last move direction
units.detail: Store the last nonzero move direction while moving and pass it to the idle animation so the character faces where it last moved instead of resetting to a default.

units.title: Raycast before moving to respect walls
units.detail: Cast a ray from current position toward the intended move direction for the frame's move distance; only update position if nothing is hit.

units.title: Slide along walls by testing axes separately
units.detail: When a combined diagonal move is blocked, retry horizontal-only movement, then vertical-only movement. This lets the character slide along walls instead of getting stuck.

units.title: Skip raycast when test direction is zero
units.detail: Raycasting a zero-length direction (e.g. only pressing W while checking horizontal) makes start==end and misbehaves. Guard each axis test with direction != 0 before casting.

units.title: World-space chat bubble as character child
units.detail: Parent the bubble (background sprite + icon + TextMeshPro) to the NPC/player in world space so it moves with them automatically, avoiding UI-space coordinate conversion.

units.title: Size bubble to text via rendered bounds
units.detail: Call ForceMeshUpdate before GetRenderedValues so text metrics are ready; then size the background sprite with padding to match the text width.

units.title: Sprite draws corners stretched unless sliced
units.detail: Scaling a normal sprite stretches corners badly. Set the SpriteRenderer to Sliced mode and define borders in the Sprite Editor so corners stay clean at any size.

units.title: Static factory + asset reference spawns bubbles
units.detail: Expose ChatBubble.Create(parent, offset, icon, text) that instantiates a prefab via a GameAssets singleton reference, so any script spawns a bubble with one call.

units.title: Auto-destroy bubbles with delayed Destroy
units.detail: Call Destroy(gameObject, seconds) so chat bubbles vanish after a set lifetime, and layer a fade-in animation + text writer for polish.

units.title: Next-checkpoint-index tracks correct path
units.detail: Keep the index of the next valid checkpoint; compare the passed checkpoint's index against it. Match = correct (advance index), mismatch = wrong checkpoint.

units.title: Register checkpoints from parent transform children
units.detail: Place all checkpoints as children of one container and enumerate transform children in order, avoiding manually filling a serialized list. Order matches hierarchy top-to-bottom.

units.title: Modulo index loops checkpoints for laps
units.detail: After the last checkpoint, advance with (index + 1) % count so the sequence wraps back to the first, enabling multiple laps.

units.title: Per-object index list supports many racers
units.detail: Store a next-checkpoint index per car (list of ints keyed by car transform) instead of a single index, so multiple objects on the track are tracked independently.

units.title: Prefer TryGetComponent over GetComponent
units.detail: Use collider.TryGetComponent<T>(out t) instead of GetComponent + null check for slightly better performance in frequent collision callbacks.

units.title: Int jump counter beats boolean for upgrades
units.detail: Track airJumpCount vs airJumpCountMax as ints so adding a triple jump (or more) is just raising the max, enabling runtime upgrade systems instead of a hardcoded double jump.

units.title: Held jump re-presses before landing get dropped
units.detail: Using GetKeyDown means pressing jump right before landing won't jump on touch. Split: use GetKey for grounded auto-jump while holding, GetKeyDown for air jumps so buffering feels responsive.

units.title: Jump orbs reset air jumps mid-air
units.detail: Trigger colliders that reset the air-jump counter and auto-jump the player let them cross huge gaps (Metroidvania style); add a cooldown timer + alpha feedback so the orb can't be spammed.

units.title: UI icons show remaining air jumps
units.detail: Instantiate one icon per max jump and hide them one-by-one as air jumps are spent, resetting visibility on landing, giving clear player feedback on remaining jumps.

units.title: UI drag/drop needs three interfaces
units.detail: IPointerDownHandler, IBeginDragHandler, IDragHandler (plus IEndDragHandler, IDropHandler) drive drag events. Drag events only fire if IDragHandler is also implemented.

units.title: Scale canvas breaks drag-follow precision
units.detail: Adding the raw mouse delta mis-tracks the object because the canvas scale != 1. Divide the movement delta by the canvas scaleFactor so the dragged object follows the cursor exactly.

units.title: Dragged item steals raycasts from drop target
units.detail: The dragged object's image blocks the raycast so the slot below never receives the drop. Toggle CanvasGroup.blocksRaycasts off while dragging (and on when done) so the slot gets the event.

units.title: Snap dropped item to slot position
units.detail: In the slot's OnDrop, read eventData.pointerDrag (the dragged object) and set its RectTransform anchoredPosition to the slot's, snapping items into place.

units.title: Enum state machine for simple enemy AI
units.detail: An enum (Roaming, ChaseTarget, ShootingTarget, GoingBackToStart) plus a switch in Update drives behavior. Each state runs only its own logic, and is the base pattern for expanding any AI.

units.title: Random roam around a stored start position
units.detail: Store the spawn position; pick random offset positions near it, move there, and re-pick when close, so enemies patrol a local area instead of wandering off.

units.title: Distance thresholds trigger chase, attack, abandon
units.detail: Check distance against a target-range to start chasing, an attack-range to fire, and a much larger range to give up, revert to start position, then roam again.

units.title: Fire-rate timer stops machine-gun shooting
units.detail: Checking attack range every frame makes the enemy fire every frame. Gate shots with nextShootTime = Time.time + fireRate so shots happen at a fixed cadence.

units.title: Locking state while animation plays
units.detail: Enter a 'Shooting' state when firing and return to Chase only via the shoot-complete callback, so the attack animation fully plays instead of being cancelled next frame.

units.title: Separate movement, aiming, and AI concerns
units.detail: Keep pathfinding/movement in one script and aiming/shooting in another; the AI only calls their functions. Each system works independently and can be swapped or reused.

units.title: Inventory as list of type+amount pairs
units.detail: Model an inventory as a simple list of entries, each holding an item type enum and an int amount. Store/use/stack/drop all reduce to manipulating this list, and the same class can be attached to players, NPCs, or enemies.

units.title: Stackable item add logic
units.detail: When adding an item, check if it is stackable; if so, check if that item type already exists in the inventory and increment its amount instead of adding a new entry. Non-stackable items are always added as separate entries.

units.title: Reference aliasing when dropping item
units.detail: If item entries are class references, decrementing the amount of a 'drop' copy also modifies the entry still in the inventory because both point to the same object. Fix by duplicating the item into a new instance before removing it from the list; using a struct instead of a class also avoids this.

units.title: Event-driven UI refresh on data change
units.detail: Expose an OnItemListChanged event from the inventory and fire it whenever an item is added/removed. The UI subscribes and re-renders from scratch, first destroying all instantiated children except the template to avoid duplicates.

units.title: Singleton asset provider for sprites
units.detail: Keep all item sprites in one scene script exposed through a static instance, and let the item class return its sprite via a switch on its type. This centralizes asset references so prefabs and UI never store sprites directly.

units.title: Decouple item use with delegate
units.detail: Pass an Action<Item> 'use item' callback into the inventory constructor instead of referencing the player directly. The player supplies a lambda/switch that implements per-type effects (heal, mana), keeping inventory logic reusable.

units.title: Struct vs class for value-like data
units.detail: Small data holders like an inventory item behave like values; a struct copies by value and avoids the aliasing bug where mutating one reference changes another. Choose struct when mutation-through-shared-reference is a hazard in your game.

units.title: Serialize data class for inspector
units.detail: Mark a plain data class with [System.Serializable] so its public fields (item type + amount) appear as an editable asset in the Unity inspector, letting designers place world spawners with configured items.

units.title: Jump by setting velocity directly
units.detail: Set the rigidbody's velocity directly (e.g. velocity = Vector2.up * jumpVelocity) rather than applying AddForce, because velocity assignment gives an immediate, controlled jump while forces are gradual. Tune gravity scale up to reduce floatiness.

units.title: Unlimited jumps without grounded check
units.detail: If the jump input always applies velocity, spamming the key makes the character fly. Gate the jump behind a grounded test so it only triggers while touching the ground.

units.title: BoxCast for ground detection
units.detail: A single raycast from the center misses when the character stands on an edge. Instead, cast a small box (collider bounds center, same size, pointing down, offset by ~0.1) so grounded detection covers the full body width.

units.title: Grounded cast hits own collider
units.detail: A downward ground check can collide with the player's own hitbox, so the character is always 'grounded'. Filter the cast with a layer mask that only includes platform layers.

units.title: Three midair movement modes
units.detail: Air control is a design decision: full control (movement code always runs), no control (movement only when grounded), or partial control (shift horizontal velocity by acceleration*deltaTime, clamp to max speed, keep vertical velocity) giving a controllable-but-sluggish feel.

units.title: Wall friction keeps player stuck midair
units.detail: Holding toward a wall while jumping causes friction that pins the character against it until keys are released. Applying a zero-friction physics material to the rigidbody lets the player slide up and off the wall.

units.title: Key-door matching by enum type
units.detail: Give each key and each door a shared enum value (Red/Green/Blue). A door opens only when the key holder contains the matching enum, which makes adding new key types a matter of extending the enum.

units.title: Key holder list with query methods
units.detail: Implement a key holder as a list of key types with AddKey, RemoveKey, and a Contains(query) function. Trigger entry handlers capture keys by GetComponent; the holder just manages the collection.

units.title: Door with two colliders
units.detail: Use one big trigger collider to detect when the player is near enough to open, plus a second solid collider matching the door that actually blocks movement. The solid collider lives on a child object.

units.title: Consume or keep keys on use
units.detail: Decide per game design whether opening a door consumes the key (remove from holder) or just requires holding it. Both are a one-line change in the open flow.

units.title: Collision event requirements
units.detail: Trigger events fire when both objects have colliders and at least one has a rigidbody. On entry, GetComponent to identify the key, add it to the holder, then destroy the key object.

units.title: UI update via change event
units.detail: Drive the key-holder UI by an OnKeysChanged event invoked on add/remove. The UI rebuilds the container each time, destroying old key images except the template, then instantiating one per held key.

units.title: Simplest fluid sim = many particles
units.detail: Represent a fluid as hundreds of tiny rigidbody particles and let the physics engine handle collision and flow. Accuracy and looks scale with particle count, but every particle is a physics object, so performance degrades fast.

units.title: Merge particles with blur + threshold shader
units.detail: Render only the particle layer to a low-resolution render texture (auto-blurs clusters), then apply a shader that samples the texture and runs a step/threshold node on its alpha to convert blurry masses into a solid, clean shape.

units.title: Layered cameras to isolate a layer
units.detail: The main camera culls out the fluid layer while a second camera renders only that layer into a render texture, which is then displayed on a quad. Both cameras use layer-based culling masks.

units.title: Transparent quad background setup
units.detail: For the fluid overlay, the render texture's background must be solid color with alpha 0 and the display material must be transparent (surface=transparent, alpha blend), or the overlay shows a solid black block. Size the quad to 2x the orthographic camera size and place it in front of the camera on +z.

units.title: Faded sprites improve merging
units.detail: Use a faded circle sprite scaled larger than a small collider, so overlapping particles visually blend into one continuous body before the threshold shader snaps it into a solid shape.

units.title: Tune material feel per liquid
units.detail: Zero friction and zero angular drag with higher gravity scale gives slippery water; increasing friction makes slimy goo. Changing gravity scale to a negative value turns the same system into a floating gas (steam, toxic cloud).

units.title: Foam edge via shifted texture sample
