units.detail: Create surface foam by sampling the fluid texture at a tiny vertical offset, subtracting it from the normal sample, stepping the result, and multiplying by a foam color. This is the same shifted-sample trick used for outline shaders.

units.title: Minimap built from layer camera
units.detail: A minimap is a camera rendering a dedicated icon layer into a render texture that is masked and displayed in the UI. Control it with scripts rather than inspector wiring.

units.title: Static singleton subsystem classes
units.detail: Give each minimap subsystem (window, camera) a static instance set on Awake, plus public static Show/Hide/SetZoom wrappers so any script can control them without scene references.

units.title: Facade class as single entry point
units.detail: Wrap all subsystem functions and events in one main static class (e.g. MiniMap.ShowWindow, MiniMap.SetZoom) so external code only ever touches that class, keeping the system clean and replaceable.

units.title: Minimap zoom via orthographic size
units.detail: Zoom the minimap by adjusting the camera's orthographic size (larger = sees more). Add min/max clamping and a fixed zoom-change amount, and expose GetZoom for other systems.

units.title: Event setup needs script execution order
units.detail: Because the facade re-fires events from subsystems, subsystems must initialize before the main class calls Init. Fix by setting script execution order in Project Settings (camera, then window, then icons, then the game handler that calls Init).

units.title: Icons scale to zoom via event
units.detail: Icons subscribe to an OnZoomChanged event and rescale from a base scale based on current zoom, so they stay a constant world size instead of covering the map when zoomed out.

units.title: Dialog with Action callbacks
units.detail: Build a question dialog whose ShowQuestion(text, yesAction, noAction) takes System.Action delegates. Convert them to UnityEngine.Events.UnityAction with new UnityAction(action) for Button.onClick listeners, since they have identical void/no-arg signatures.

units.title: Hide dialog before firing callback
units.detail: Hide the dialog and deactivate its object BEFORE invoking the yes/no action. If you hide afterward, a callback that opens a second question will immediately be hidden again by the first dialog's hide.

units.title: Singleton for global dialog access
units.detail: Expose the dialog through a public static instance property (get public, set private) assigned on Awake, so any script anywhere can ask a question with one line, including chaining questions inside callbacks.

units.title: Reusable dialog prefab
units.detail: Make the fully-styled question dialog a prefab so it drops into any scene; edit visuals inside the prefab once and every instance updates. This generalizes to tooltips and other reusable UI.

units.title: Grab UI refs with Find+GetComponent
units.detail: Instead of serialized drag-and-drop, find child objects by name (transform.Find) and GetComponent for TextMeshPro and Button references on Awake, which survives prefab reuse.

units.title: Write/read text files for saving
units.detail: Save data with File.WriteAllText(path, contents) and load with File.ReadAllText(path) using System.IO, storing files under Application.dataPath. It's the most basic persistent storage beyond PlayerPrefs.

units.title: Custom file format with separator
units.detail: Store multiple values by joining a string array (gold, x, y) with a unique separator string via String.Join, then Split on the same separator and parse each index back to its type on load.

units.title: Separator must never appear in data
units.detail: A separator-based format breaks if the separator string can occur inside the data itself. Pick a unique sentinel string, and define it as a single shared constant on both save and load paths so it can't drift.

units.title: JSON serialization via JsonUtility
units.detail: Use Unity's JsonUtility.ToJson(obj) and JsonUtility.FromJson<T>(json) to serialize an entire save object. JSON lets you store structured data like Vector3 directly instead of hand-managing separators.

units.title: Static SaveSystem with Init
units.detail: Isolate saving into a static class with Init (ensure the saves directory exists via Directory.Exists + Directory.CreateDirectory), Save(string), and Load() that returns the save string or null when no file exists. The caller converts to/from its save object.

units.title: dataPath can't be a const
units.detail: Application.dataPath is only available at runtime, so it cannot be a compile-time const. Use a static readonly field to keep the 'constant-like' path while staying valid.

units.title: Auto-incrementing save slots
units.detail: Generate unique save files by looping while File.Exists(saveNumber + ".txt") and incrementing the number, so each save creates a new slot instead of overwriting.

units.title: Load the most recent save
units.detail: Use DirectoryInfo.GetFiles to list save files and track the one with the highest LastWriteTime; if none exists, return null to signal 'no save' to the caller.

units.title: PlayerPrefs as key-value store
units.detail: PlayerPrefs is Unity's cross-platform persistent key-value store; on Windows it lives in the registry (HKCU/Software/Company/Product), on macOS in Library/Preferences, on Linux in config. Keys are strings mapping to float/int/string.

units.title: Store Vector3 as separate keys
units.detail: PlayerPrefs has no Vector3 function, so split it into discrete keys (PlayerPositionX/PlayerPositionY) saved as floats and rebuilt into a Vector3 on load.

units.title: PlayerPrefs only auto-saves on exit
units.detail: PlayerPrefs writes to disk automatically when the app exits, but to support saving/loading during gameplay you must call PlayerPrefs.Save() manually right after setting values.

units.title: Detect missing save with HasKey
units.detail: Before reading floats, check PlayerPrefs.HasKey for a known key to decide whether a save exists; otherwise you'd load garbage defaults when there is no save.

units.title: Defaults keep old saves valid
units.detail: GetInt/GetFloat accept a default value used when the key is missing. This keeps saves from previous game versions loadable when you add new saved fields, by falling back to a sensible default.

units.title: Interface decouples shop from player
units.detail: Define an IShopCustomer interface (BuyItem, TrySpendGold) instead of referencing the player class, so the shop works with any actor that implements it. The shop only depends on the contract, not the concrete player.

units.title: TrySpendGold pattern
units.detail: Make spending a method that returns bool: TrySpendGold(amount) checks affordability, deducts if possible and fires a gold-changed event, else returns false. The caller only buys after a successful spend, and can show a 'cannot afford' warning on failure.

units.title: Shop opens via trigger area
units.detail: Place a large trigger collider over the shop zone; OnTriggerEnter2D looks up IShopCustomer on the entering collider and shows the shop UI with that customer, OnTriggerExit hides it.

units.title: Dynamically populate UI from template
units.detail: Generate each shop row by instantiating an item template into a container, positioning it by index * rowHeight, and wiring name/cost text, sprite, and a click handler bound to the item type via the button script's callback.

units.title: Feedback when purchase fails
units.detail: Silently ignoring clicks when the player can't afford an item is confusing. Surface a tooltip warning ('cannot afford') on failed TrySpendGold so the failure reads as intentional feedback.

units.title: Singleton GameAssets for sprites
units.detail: A single scene object holds references to every game asset and is reached through a static instance; item classes return their sprite from it via a switch on item type, avoiding scattered sprite references.

units.title: Separate player skills into own class
units.detail: Instead of having the player class directly track/unlock skills, create a dedicated PlayerSkills class with a single responsibility. The player holds an instance, and the UI receives and interacts with that PlayerSkills reference, keeping UI logic decoupled from gameplay.

units.title: Enum-driven skill definition
units.detail: Define all possible skills as an enum (MovementSpeed, HealthMax, Whirlwind, EarthShatter). Store unlocked skills in a list of that enum type and check membership with a 'contains' call. This makes adding new skills a small localized change.

units.title: Prerequisite skills via requirement lookup
units.detail: Give each skill a GetRequirement function returning the prerequisite skill type, using a dedicated None enum value (instead of null) to represent 'no requirement'. A TryUnlock function checks the requirement is unlocked and has enough points before unlocking, returning a bool so the UI can show a warning.

units.title: Event on skill unlocked for passive effects
units.detail: Fire an OnSkillUnlocked event (with event args carrying the skill type) whenever a skill is unlocked. Listeners subscribe and apply immediate effects like movement speed or max health via a switch on the skill type, while active skills are only gated at use-time.

units.title: Guard against double-unlocking
units.detail: Before adding a skill to the unlocked list, check it is not already unlocked, so accidentally triggering unlock twice doesn't duplicate entries or double-apply effects.

units.title: Three visual skill states via material swap
units.detail: Show locked skills black-and-white with low alpha, unlockable skills black-and-white at full alpha, and unlocked skills in full color. Use a desaturated shader/material; swap materials or set material to null (default) based on the locked/unlockable/unlocked state, refreshed on unlock events.

units.title: Refactor repeated UI logic into skill button class
units.detail: Instead of copy-pasting update-visuals logic for each button, create a serializable SkillButton class holding references and an UpdateVisual method. Iterate over a list of them to keep the code clean while keeping behavior identical.

units.title: Draw unlock path lines between skills
units.detail: For each unlock path, hold the target skill type plus an array of connection images. On visual update, darken all links first, then highlight (gold + glow texture) the links for skills that are unlocked or currently unlockable, making the progression path obvious.

units.title: Skill points economy tied to leveling
units.detail: Gain a skill point on every level-up event, store the count in the PlayerSkills class, and require points > 0 in TryUnlock. Deduct points on successful unlock and fire an event so the UI indicator refreshes when points are added or spent.

units.title: Static SoundManager with enum-indexed clips
units.detail: Make the sound manager a static class. Define a Sound enum and a serializable SoundAudioClip pair (sound + clip) stored in an array; a lookup function finds the clip matching the requested enum value, with an error log if nothing matches.

units.title: Playing sound every frame is the naive bug
units.detail: Calling PlaySound inside movement code fires it every frame (thousands of times/sec). Fix: maintain a dictionary of sound->lastPlayedTime and gate 'move' sounds behind a cooldown interval (e.g. 50ms), returning whether the sound may play before invoking.

units.title: Positional 3D audio by spawning temp object
units.detail: For sounds placed in world space, spawn a GameObject at the given position with an AudioSource set to its clip, then Destroy it after audioClip.length so it cleans up when playback finishes.

units.title: Extension methods to add sounds to existing class
units.detail: Add functionality (e.g. button hover/click sounds) to an already-written class via an extension method (this ButtonUI param) instead of modifying that class. It reads as a method on the target class but lives in the sound manager.

units.title: Reuse one-shot audio object for performance
units.detail: PlayOneShot can reuse a single persistent GameObject/audio source created once (lazy init) since no positioning is needed, avoiding per-call allocation. Positional sounds still need per-spawn objects; a further optimization is an object pool instead of create/destroy.

units.title: Sprite sheet animation via shader UV offset
units.detail: Render every unit as one quad mesh sharing a single material; display a single frame by passing a normalized UV rect (width, height, xOffset, yOffset) to the shader through a material property block. Frame = width 1/frameCount; advancing the frame shifts the x offset.

units.title: Component holds animation state, system animates it
units.detail: In ECS, store currentFrame, frameCount, frameTimer, and frameTimeMax in a component. A job-based system increments the timer by deltaTime, wraps the current frame modulo frameCount, and (optionally) precomputes UV and matrix so the main-thread renderer just draws.

units.title: Compute per-unit values off the main thread
units.detail: Move UV calculation and matrix computation into the Burst-compiled job running with the animation update instead of per-unit foreach on the main thread, so rendering does almost nothing except issuing draw calls.

units.title: Sprite sorting via Y-based z-offset
units.detail: To get automatic sprite sorting, offset the z position by position.y * smallFactor when computing the render matrix, so sprites lower on screen draw in front of higher ones.

units.title: Reuse MaterialPropertyBlock and arrays
units.detail: Create the material property block and the UV value array once outside the render loop and mutate/reuse them rather than allocating per entity per frame. This cut frame time from 50ms to 30ms at 10,000 animated units.

units.title: Bottleneck is per-entity draw calls
units.detail: Graphics.DrawMesh is called once per entity, so 10,000 units = 10,000 calls, the main bottleneck. The fix is Graphics.DrawMeshInstanced (renders many meshes in one call) but it comes with limitations and setup covered in a follow-up.

units.title: Input window API via action callbacks
units.detail: Show(title, defaultText, validChars, charLimit, onCancel, onOk) receives actions (delegates) as callbacks; OK invokes onOk with the current input field text, Cancel invokes onCancel, and both hide the window. This keeps the window reusable anywhere in the game.

units.title: Whitelist character validation
units.detail: Use the input field's validate callback: a ValidateChar(validChars, addedChar) returns the character if validChars.IndexOf(addedChar) != -1, else returns an empty char (rejected). This lets you restrict input to numbers, uppercase letters, etc. Plus an int characterLimit cap.

units.title: Singleton static access for UI windows
units.detail: Make the input window a singleton with static Show functions wrapping private instance methods, so any code can open the window without passing references around. A companion int-typed Show variant auto-restricts to digits and parses the string to int on OK.

units.title: UI blocker for modal windows
units.detail: Add a fullscreen transparent image behind the window that blocks clicks on buttons beneath it. Ensure both the blocker and window call SetAsLastSibling on show so they render on top and receive input in the correct order.

units.title: Keyboard enter/escape support
units.detail: In Update, map Return/KeypadEnter to trigger the OK button's click and Escape to trigger Cancel, giving players keyboard flow for submitting input instead of only mouse.

units.title: GetClosestEnemy within range
units.detail: Keep a static list of all alive enemies (populated on awake/spawn). A GetClosestEnemy(position, maxRange) helper cycles the list, skips dead entries, and returns the nearest within range; towers call it to find their target each update.

units.title: Fire-on-every-frame requires a shoot timer
units.detail: If the tower spawns a projectile whenever an enemy is in range, it fires one arrow every frame. Add a countdown shoot timer reset on each shot so fire rate is manageable.

units.title: Projectile carries enemy reference and damage
units.detail: Pass the target enemy reference (not just a position) plus damage amount to the projectile's setup. It moves toward the enemy's position and, on arrival, calls enemy.Damage(damage) and destroys itself - keeping hit logic inside the projectile.

units.title: Tower upgrade overlay on mouse-over
units.detail: Attach a collider to the tower; on mouse enter show an overlay UI (range + damage upgrade buttons) positioned at the tower's transform. Buttons call tower methods that simply modify range/damage fields used by targeting and projectile spawning.

units.title: Grid-snapped tower placement
units.detail: Right-click to instantiate a tower prefab at the mouse position validated/snapped through a reusable grid system, so placement aligns cleanly instead of floating anywhere.

units.title: Manual projectile movement with arrival check
units.detail: Simplest projectile: in Update compute direction to target, translate by moveSpeed, and when within a small distance of the target, trigger impact and destroy. Optionally set Euler angles to face the movement direction.

units.title: Turn-based battle as a state machine
units.detail: BattleHandler tracks a state (WaitingForPlayer / Busy) and an active character. Input is only read when waiting for the player; after an action completes, chooseNextActiveCharacter swaps the active unit and grants that unit its turn.

units.title: Attack sequence via nested callbacks
units.detail: Chained callbacks drive the attack: slide-to-target -> onSlideComplete plays attack animation -> onHit deals damage -> onComplete slides back -> onReturnToIdle fires onAttackComplete to end the turn. Lambdas keep the sequence readable and self-contained.

units.title: Non-normalized sliding gives ease-out motion
units.detail: Move toward a slide target using direction * speed * deltaTime WITHOUT normalizing, so the character moves quickly then slows as it approaches - a cheap natural ease-out. Trigger an onSlideComplete action within a small distance threshold.

units.title: Constructors replaced by Setup for prefabs
units.detail: MonoBehaviour prefab instances can't use constructors, so add a public Setup(isPlayerTeam) called right after Instantiate to assign textures, animations, and starting health. Expose config through a static instance singleton on the battle handler.

units.title: Visual active-unit indicator
units.detail: Give each character a selection circle rendered beneath it. SetActive(false) to hide and SetActive(true) to show; the handler hides the previously active unit's circle and shows the new one whenever active character changes.

units.title: Facing direction based on team side
units.detail: Store whether a character is on the player team and play left/right idle animations accordingly so both characters always face each other during battle.

units.title: Screen-space camera canvas rendering
units.detail: Use the Screen Space Camera render mode with a dedicated orthographic UI camera (clear flags = depth only) instead of screen-space overlay, which keeps the scene view clean and enables perspective/UI-shader effects later.

units.title: Scale with screen size, match height
units.detail: Set canvas to Scale With Screen Size with a 1280x720 reference and match mode on Height: UI only rescales when the vertical resolution changes, so you only worry about horizontal anchoring, and it stays correct across aspect ratios.

units.title: Corner-anchored persistent UI (e.g. version)
units.detail: For always-visible UI like a version label, stretch a container across the canvas, anchor the text to the bottom-left corner, and set offset+overflow (size 0) so it stays glued to the corner at any resolution.

units.title: Organize hierarchy with container GameObjects
units.detail: Keep the scene hierarchy organized by nesting the main camera under a GameHamlet container and placing UI off to the side (e.g. at 1000,1000) so it can be viewed next to the game scene without blocking the origin.

units.title: ScriptableObjects as data-driven part definitions
units.detail: Model each weapon part as a ScriptableObject holding a part-type enum and prefab reference (extensible with any stats later). A generic SetPart destroys the current part and spawns the new one at the matching attach point - one function handles barrels, stocks, mags, etc.

units.title: Dictionaries don't serialize in the editor
units.detail: A serialized Dictionary field shows nothing in the Inspector. Fix: expose a serializable list of key/value pairs in the editor, then build the actual dictionary from that list in Awake.

units.title: Subclass ScriptableObjects for extra data
units.detail: Only barrels need a muzzle offset, so make BarrelPart extend WeaponPart and add the extra field there, instead of burdening every part type with unused data. ScriptableObjects can be extended like any C# class.

units.title: Restrict parts per weapon body
units.detail: Define body-type ScriptableObjects that hold the allowed parts list, the body prefab, and a corresponding UI prefab, so each body (pistol vs rifle) only offers compatible modular parts.

units.title: Randomize via repeated part changes
units.detail: Randomizing a loadout is trivially easy: get the list of applicable part types, loop 0-50 times calling the same ChangePart function with a random part. Clean code made this feature nearly free.

units.title: Mouse-delta jump when refocusing window
units.detail: Clicking outside the game and back produced a huge mouse delta (weapon flipping 180°). Fix: clamp the mouse delta to a sane maximum so out-of-window jumps are ignored.

units.title: JsonUtility serializes ScriptableObjects
units.detail: Save loadouts by creating a plain save object (body reference + list of part references), converting to JSON with JsonUtility, and reversing on load - Json serializes ScriptableObject references automatically.

units.title: Pack screenshot bytes with save data
units.detail: For save files with previews: write Json bytes + PNG screenshot bytes, prepend a header containing the Json byte size, and concatenate. Load reverses it - read header size, read Json, read screenshot. Capture the image from a dedicated camera at end-of-frame.

units.title: Wind effect via vertex displacement
units.detail: A grass sway effect is made by displacing mesh vertices in the shader (modifying the vertex position output of the master node) rather than moving the whole object - anchored at the bottom, swaying more near the top.

units.title: Sway needs a detailed mesh
units.detail: Vertex-based effects only work if the sprite has vertices to move. Tight mesh type generates the complex silhouette mesh with many vertices, while Full Rect just makes a 4-vertex quad - so ensure the import mesh type is Tight for a sway effect.

units.title: Sway only on X using position split
units.detail: Drive sway with gradient noise sampled at a time-scrolled position. Split the position into components and apply the noise displacement only to the X, recombining with the original Y and Z so vertices don't bob up-down or forward-back.

units.title: Subtract 0.5 for bidirectional sway
units.detail: Noise outputs 0..1, so displacement only goes one direction. Subtract 0.5 to shift the range to -0.5..+0.5 so vertices sway left and right around their resting position.

units.title: Anchor bottom via UV Y mask
units.detail: Multiply the sway displacement by the UV's Y value (0 at bottom, 1 at top) so the sprite stays planted at the ground and moves most at the top.

units.title: Identical adjacent sprites sway in sync
units.detail: Using object-space position makes every identical sprite sway with the exact same phase - unnatural. Switch to world-space position (optionally scaled) when sampling noise so each object sways slightly differently.

units.title: Expose wind intensity and speed properties
units.detail: Expose the wind intensity (a multiplier on displacement) and wind speed (the noise scale driving the scroll) as editor properties so artists can tune them and code can drive dynamic wind per area.

units.title: Simulate multiplayer by separating logic from inputs
units.detail: Instead of writing separate player and AI scripts, have one core player script that requests input through delegates (getInputVector, etc.). A player-input controller feeds real input; a bot controller feeds AI-generated input. Both characters share the same core logic, so new mechanics benefit both instantly.

units.title: Delegate-based input injection
units.detail: The core player component holds delegate fields for movement/interact inputs and a SetInputDelegates function. Controllers assign implementations on Start, so the player never knows whether input comes from keyboard, gamepad, or AI.

units.title: AI driven by scripted action lists
units.detail: Define a serializable bot action struct (moveTo, interact, wait) and an array of them in the inspector. The bot controller computes movement direction toward the current target (feeding the shared input delegates), counts down wait timers, and advances to the next action when reached/interacted.

units.title: Clean interactions make AI features free
units.detail: Because all actions funnel through one shared interaction system, the same bot logic does construction, resource gathering, and defense automatically - no per-feature AI code needed. Keep gameplay entry points decoupled from input sources.

units.title: Cinemachine blending for slow camera shots
units.detail: For trailer camera moves, set the Cinemachine Brain's blend time to a large value (e.g. 10s) and toggle between two virtual cameras with different priorities during runtime. The brain smoothly interpolates between them for a slow cinematic pan - no hand-authored camera animation.

units.title: Playtesting sources ordered from close to broad
units.detail: Find playtesters in this order: friends/family first (expect biased positive feedback), then itch.io demos (players are forgiving of jank), then Reddit/Twitter/Discords (harsher honest feedback), then a Steam demo without Next Fest, and finally Next Fest itself. If you can't get playtesters early on, it's a warning sign the idea isn't appealing.

units.title: Using store assets doesn't scare players away
units.detail: Players only care that a game is fun, not whether it uses recognizable asset packs. Proof: Soulstone Survivors, No Plan B, Motor Town, Clown Field 2042, and Perfect Heist 2 all use Synty assets and are commercial hits with positive reviews. For programmers with no art skill, buying assets is a valid path.

units.title: Making a game is free now
units.detail: Unity, Unreal, and Godot are all free, plus there are free tutorials/courses and thousands of free assets and tools on storefronts. There is no cost barrier left to start making games.

units.title: Good games do not sell themselves
units.detail: Marketing is essential; only a literally perfect 10/10 game might launch on zero wishlists. A dev who launched with only 200-300 wishlists was essentially guaranteed to be buried. Success = development effort + equal marketing effort.

units.title: Idea thieves are not a real threat
units.detail: Ideas are just a starting point; every decision diverges the result, so two devs with the same idea make completely different games (as game jams prove). The real threat for indies is obscurity, not theft, so talk about your game constantly.

units.title: Building a Lunar Lander step by step
units.detail: Core recipe: rigid body + gravity, input-driven force/torque, sprite shape terrain, Cinemachine follow camera, landing detection via velocity dot product against the landing pad normal, thruster particles, trigger-collider pickups, HUD, crash/restart UI, levels, mobile touch input, and polish.

units.title: Escape tutorial hell by building things
units.detail: Blindly following tutorials never teaches you to make your own game. You must actively write code and apply knowledge (e.g., rebuild Flappy Bird or a health system from scratch). Interactive exercises force the application that makes knowledge stick.

units.title: Sorting layers define 2D render order
units.detail: In 2D there's no depth, so sprite render order is set by sorting layers and sorting order on the Sprite Renderer instead of distance to camera. Define layers, set their order (top layer renders last = on top), then assign each object to a layer.

units.title: Same layer+order causes nondeterministic rendering
units.detail: If multiple sprites share both the same sorting layer and sorting order, which shows on top is undefined and can flicker/change. Always assign distinct sorting orders (e.g., 0, 10, -10) to make behavior deterministic.

units.title: Global Light 2D only affects default layer
units.detail: With URP 2D renderer, the Global Light 2D by default targets only the Default sorting layer, so sprites moved to other sorting layers render completely black. Fix: set the light's target sorting layers to all layers.

units.title: Sorting order range is -32000 to 32000
units.detail: Sorting order is stored as a short: integers only, no decimals, clamped to ±32,000 (65,000 total values per layer). Sorting order only sorts within the same layer; any object on a higher layer always beats max order on a lower layer.

units.title: UI sorting uses hierarchy order, not layers
units.detail: Canvas UI elements have no sorting layer/order; their render order is their position in the hierarchy (first child renders first, later children on top). World-space canvases do expose a sorting layer/order field.

units.title: Sorting layers vs physics/camera layers differ
units.detail: Sorting layers (sprite render order) and the game object Layer field (used by cameras, physics, collisions) are completely separate systems with similar-sounding names. Changing one never affects the other.

units.title: Bezier splines from repeated lerps
units.detail: A smooth spline is built by nesting linear interpolations: lerp between a-b and b-c, then lerp between those two results for quadratic; one more level gives cubic (bezier) curves. Cubic uses 4 points (2 anchors + 2 handles) per segment; longer splines are just more segments.

units.title: Bezier curve helper functions
units.detail: Refactor nested lerps into reusable functions: QuadraticPoint(a,b,c,t) = Lerp(Lerp(a,b,t), Lerp(b,c,t), t) and CubicPoint(a,b,c,d,t) = Lerp(QuadraticPoint(a,b,c,t), QuadraticPoint(b,c,d,t), t). The math makes splines fully runtime-editable.

units.title: Spline use cases: roads, orbits, terrain
units.detail: Splines generate smooth paths through world points, useful for roads, terrain, orbits, or anything needing a smooth shape. Extensions: a spline follower with position+rotation, closed loops, and procedurally generating a mesh along the spline points (two vertices per point connected to previous two).

units.title: Sprite blur via multi-sample offset average
units.detail: Blur a sprite by sampling the texture multiple times with small UV offsets (left/right, then up/down, optionally diagonals), adding all samples, and dividing by the sample count to normalize color. A single float 'blur amount' property drives offsets via a combine vector2, with one negated copy for the opposite direction.

units.title: Animating shader float from C#
units.detail: Control a shader property from code with material.SetFloat("_BlurAmount", value), using the exact reference name defined in the shader graph. Clamp the value and change it in Update based on input/toggle state.

units.title: Main texture reference must be _MainTex
units.detail: The primary texture property reference in a sprite shader graph must be named exactly _MainTex so the Sprite Renderer applies the sprite automatically. Sample it with Sample Texture 2D and feed RGBA into the Sprite Lit Master node.

units.title: Dissolve effect with noise + step
units.detail: Dissolve by multiplying sprite alpha with noise, then passing through a Step node with a threshold (0-1) as the dissolve amount. Animate the threshold over time (1 - value so 0 = visible) to dissolve in/out. An outline glow comes from a second step slightly ahead of the first, subtracted to isolate the edge, multiplied by an HDR color.

units.title: Dissolve control script and teleporter
units.detail: Drive dissolve with material.SetFloat and SetColor. Public StartDissolve(speed)/StopDissolve() methods set a bool updated in Update (amount += speed * Time.deltaTime, clamped). Teleporters call start/stop on trigger enter and set per-teleporter colors.

units.title: Sprite outline by shifted alpha subtraction
units.detail: Outline = sample texture shifted by thickness in each direction (left/right/up/down), sum the shifted alphas, clamp 0-1, subtract the original alpha to isolate the rim, then multiply by an outline color and add on top. Scale-based approaches break (they scale from corner), so use UV offsets. Very large thicknesses need diagonal samples too.

units.title: Animated two-color outline via noise
units.detail: Extend the outline with a gradient animation: offset scrolling noise by time, multiply by the base outline color and by an inverted copy times a secondary color, add both, then multiply the whole thing by the outline mask.

units.title: Shifting texture scales from lower-left corner
units.detail: Scaling a sprite texture with tiling/offset to fake an outline scales from the texture's lower-left corner, not each body part's center, breaking the effect for multi-part sprites. Use per-direction UV offsets instead so each part grows outward from itself.

units.title: Additive sprite tint for hit/heal flashes
units.detail: Additive tint: multiply tint RGB (alpha stripped) by tint alpha, add to the texture color, and keep sprite transparency separate by multiplying texture alpha by base color alpha in the final combine. Set tint via material.SetColor with fade-down alpha in Update for damage (red) or heal (green) flashes.

units.title: Solid-color tint with a blend node
units.detail: For a flat solid tint, blend the texture with the tint color using a Blend node set to Over, using tint alpha as opacity. This swaps out the add/multiply chain of the additive version for a single overlay blend.

units.title: Tint alpha must not affect sprite transparency
units.detail: If you multiply the tint color directly by the texture, lowering tint alpha fades the sprite out. Split the tint, apply alpha only to the RGB, and route texture-alpha x base-alpha separately to the output so the sprite stays opaque while the tint fades.

units.title: Steam page must present the hook fast
units.detail: Shoppers spend ~30 seconds on a page, so the genre and hook must be obvious immediately. Short description should be simple (genre up front, not crammed with mechanics); complexity goes in the About section. The first four screenshots are the most important since they appear on hover.

units.title: Lead screenshots with the core concept
units.detail: Show the game's core hook in the first 3-4 screenshots, not late-game content. A dev showing only advanced machines hid his actual hook (the cute characters), making the game read as generic. Build a level specifically covered in the hook element for those first shots.

units.title: Trailer slot 1 must be gameplay, not cinematic
units.detail: Valve uses the first trailer for hover previews, so a black-screen cinematic with 'in a world...' text looks awful on hover. Always put the gameplay trailer first, go straight into gameplay (first 5 seconds), keep it ~45s max, and show the basic gameplay loop.

units.title: Use all 20 Steam tags and refresh them
units.detail: Tags drive Steam's recommendation algorithm. Use all 20 tags (blank space in the list means you're under-tagging), avoid irrelevant ones like free-to-play for paid games, and re-tag monthly/quarterly. Tags put your game in front of the right audiences.

units.title: Screenshots must signal quality and erase jank
units.detail: With ~170k games released per year, screenshots must prove you're a high-quality game and hide any roughness. Show variety, and include UI where appropriate (even Manor Lords missed UI). GIFs in the About section help skimmers understand the game faster than trailers.

units.title: The game itself drives success
units.detail: A great Steam page only supports an already-great game; even a perfect page won't sell a mediocre one (Manor Lords succeeded because it's a great game in a Steam-perfect genre). Don't over-attribute success to page tricks.

units.title: Bundle games and post updates
units.detail: Bundling your games (or with same-genre devs) is nearly free money that most indies ignore. Regular updates also make a page look alive and active, which helps conversion.

units.title: Primary Steam visibility: festivals + streamers
units.detail: Tweeting into the void doesn't market a game; the two real visibility channels are online festivals (Steam features them on the front page) and streamers/YouTubers who generate wishlists. Streamer traffic converts ~20% of wishlists into sales on the next discount.

units.title: Get streamers with a pro thumbnail and demo
units.detail: Streamers live or die by thumbnails, so hire an artist for a great thumbnail and have a fun demo live. Email: 'I'm making this game, you play this type, here's my thumbnail, demo's live now.' No reply usually means your pitch/graphics aren't exciting enough, not spam.

units.title: Release the demo early, not at launch
units.detail: Get a demo out as early as possible so streamers play it before launch, building wishlist influx and festival eligibility. Demos need to exist well before launch, not at launch.

units.title: 7,000 wishlists minimum before release
units.detail: ~7,000 wishlists (sometimes as low as 5-6k depending on competition) qualifies you for 'Popular Upcoming' the week before release, which generates ~1,000 wishlists/day. Converting enough sales (~$8,000 gross within a short window) leads to 'New and Trending'. Publishers push 30-50k for a conversion buffer (conversion rates range 1-30%).

units.title: Start marketing when four things are ready
units.detail: Put the Steam page live (as a big marketing beat, not just 'it's Thursday') when: genre is locked, art style decided, four distinct environments/biomes staged (even mockups) for screenshots, and an 'announce trailer' exists to shop to press and streamers.

units.title: Make more, smaller games to learn
units.detail: Prefer four small games in two years over one massive one: repeating release and marketing cycles teaches intangible skills faster. This experience builds the confidence to know when a demo or trailer is 'good enough'.

units.title: New demo launch rules: don't waste the wishlist email
units.detail: Steam now legitimizes demos: the first time you launch a demo you can email all prior wishlisters, and ~90 concurrent demo players can get you onto 'New and Trending Free' (10 slots). It's a one-time-only launch boost, so don't launch the page and demo together, and don't launch weeks before Next Fest (that's when everyone else does, crowding the 10 slots).

units.title: Launch demo months before Next Fest
units.detail: Launch the demo months/years before Next Fest, keep it up gathering wishlists, run playtests (free, don't count against the one-time boost) to perfect it, and arrive at Next Fest with the best demo. Two weeks before Next Fest is the worst time to launch a demo.

units.title: Steam page readiness: trailer, capsule, 3 environments
units.detail: A coming-soon page needs: a locked genre, a paid professional capsule (never make it yourself), 30 seconds of gameplay in a trailer (can be faked/staged with fast cuts), and three distinct biomes/environments so you don't look like one asset pack. Get the page up early but meeting this bar.

units.title: Launching a Steam page gives no free visibility
units.detail: There is no Steam widget granting free wishlists when you publish a coming-soon page. All the visibility comes from the outside marketing event you make around it (announce trailer, press, festivals).

units.title: Next Fest ML algorithm = guaranteed baseline only
units.detail: Valve's first-two-days machine learning gives every game a guaranteed baseline of Next Fest visibility (hobbyist games get some views now instead of zero), but NOT equal visibility. Games entering with 2,000+ wishlists still do better, and 50k-100k wishlist games dominate trending charts, so build wishlists before the last Next Fest before launch.

units.title: Wishlist benchmarks are deflating, not inflating
units.detail: Contrary to fear of wishlist inflation, required wishlist numbers have been deflating. Genre choice is the biggest marketing decision you make. Blood/horror-themed simple games are among the easiest entry-level genres for indies.

units.title: Make many games to learn launch instincts
units.detail: Releasing many games builds the tacit skill of knowing what a good demo feels like (John Romero: 'We just knew. We made a bunch of games.'). These intangible skills can't be learned from blog posts.

units.title: Co-op 'friend slop' genre still growing
units.detail: Aggregate concurrent players across all friend-slop co-op games is higher than ever, and each new hit (Mecha Chameleon, Lethal Company) converts new players into the genre. A 3-6 month co-op game is still a reasonable bet, especially since small fast games teach the most.

units.title: Publish your Steam page early
units.detail: Don't delay your store page waiting for the game to be 'done' — people can find and wishlist it early. The real 'too early' is only when the game sucks: never ship AI placeholder art, since Steam players detect it and it kills trust.

units.title: Indie games sell the human-made promise
units.detail: There is an implicit agreement: dev brings handcrafted quality, player pays. Players won't pay for AI art and can't be talked out of it — any disclosure sounds like hiding. AI for code is tolerated, AI for visible art is not.

units.title: Steam page must be cohesive, not a score
units.detail: Ranking: capsule first, then screenshots, trailer, description — but the whole page must tell one coherent 'competent dev' story. One great asset reused from three angles reads as asset-store slop; a bad screenshot undermines a great capsule.

units.title: One codebase for game and demo
units.detail: Architect the demo to slice off the full game from a single source so you never maintain two codebases. Demo updates then become free marketing beats (e.g., refresh it for NextFest and invite content creators).

units.title: Keep demo up after launch to boost reviews
units.detail: Games that keep their demo downloadable after release have review scores ~5 percentage points higher because haters refund/leave on the demo instead of the full game. No sales difference was measured — it's a review-hygiene play.

units.title: Set release date ~2 months out for calendar
units.detail: Steam's personal calendar replaces popular upcoming and gives ~2 months of pre-launch visibility that grows toward launch, plus a 'launch this month' slot — roughly 3 months of exposure vs 1 day before. Set a locked, realistic release date early to claim the slot.

units.title: ~7K wishlists still the calendar threshold
units.detail: Surveying personal calendars shows the minimum bar is about 2-3K followers (~2-7K wishlists), lower than the old 7K rule. Check your own calendar and find the lowest-follower game to gauge the real cutoff.

units.title: Horror trailers can go viral
units.detail: Horror trailers have a magic ability to spread hugely — some games got 100K wishlists off a single trailer. Horror devs should invest heavily in testing and studying how horror trailers are built.

units.title: Wholesome genre needs community networking
units.detail: Wholesome games succeed via the Wholesome Games community — devs must spend time on social media so the curators notice and invite them to exclusive festivals and features.

units.title: Steam 30% buys the whole platform
units.detail: The 30% cut covers access to a massive audience plus backend tools, self-service features, and the Workshop. It's a tiny slice of a massive pie: 50 copies self-hosted became 500 on day one of Steam.

units.title: NextFest now levels the field
units.detail: The old meta was pumping wishlist velocity the week before NextFest. Now the first ~2 days give every game equal impressions regardless of prior wishlists, so a genuinely good game can break out without a marketing budget.

units.title: Join every themed mini-festival
units.detail: Games can enter only one NextFest but unlimited themed festivals (RTS, idle, couch co-op, visual novels). These are extra discoverability slots — register for every eligible one via the self-service backend calendar.

units.title: Make multiple games, cross-promote
units.detail: Making several games is the closest thing to a cheat code: each release is easier and markets better, and the 'More from' store section lets your catalog cross-promote each other. One game then quitting is a common mistake.

units.title: Demos now get dedicated store pages
units.detail: July 2024 gave demos separate store pages linked to the full game, replacing the tiny corner button. Demos are extremely important for wishlists, and the dedicated page strengthens the demo-to-full-game funnel.

units.title: Localize beyond English
units.detail: English is only ~23-50% of the Steam audience while Simplified Chinese is ~50%. Not localizing leaves a huge playerbase untapped; Chinese is one of the highest-value languages to support.

units.title: First-time purchasers buy more than one game
units.detail: Steam tracked 1.7M new users who played 141M hours and spent $94M across multiple games, not just their first one. New players spread into indies, so the ecosystem benefits every developer.

units.title: Steam's AI stance is about IP rights
units.detail: Steam doesn't ban AI itself — it enforces that devs own all rights to input data. Big studios (The Finals, High on Life) convince Valve they licensed the training data; small indies have little voice to do the same.

units.title: If using AI, pick data-licensed tools
units.detail: Unity AI and Adobe Firefly train on owned/licensed data, reducing copyright issues. Avoid tools that don't disclose input sources, since AI legality is still a gray area.

units.title: Separate AI assets for easy replacement
units.detail: Organize project files to clearly split AI vs non-AI content so that if Steam rejects the game, AI assets can be swapped out quickly. Replacing is easier than convincing Valve you own the rights.

units.title: Steam tags signal trending genres
units.detail: Steam tags carry huge algorithmic weight in discovery queue, genre listings, and 'more like this'. When Steam adds a tag (bullet heaven, desktop companion, organizing, cleaning), it's a signal that genre is trending with enough players and games.

units.title: Desktop companion games are a hot genre
units.detail: Games that live in a small window on the desktop (Rusty Retirement, Desktop Defender) blew up; Desktop Defender made ~$250K on a game creatable in roughly a month. Watch trending tags to pick next game ideas.

units.title: Cleaning/organizing genres keep growing
units.detail: Cleaning games grew from Viscera Cleanup Detail to PowerWash Simulator ($43M); organizing games got a name only now (Unpacking, A Little to the Left). Established genres like incremental also remain strong — new tags mean rising, not that old hits are dead.

units.title: Apply the matching official tag
units.detail: If your game matches a new official tag like 'bullet heaven' (formerly Vampire Survivors-like), apply it immediately — an official tag means Steam now routes discovery traffic for that genre to you.

units.title: Popular upcoming now favors huge wishlist counts
units.detail: Steam's refreshed homepage weights popular upcoming toward wishlist totals (games shown had ~80K-500K wishlists) rather than upcoming release date. The old 7K wishlist target no longer grants front-page visibility — that bar is effectively out of indie reach.

units.title: Personal calendar is the new targeted discovery
units.detail: The personal calendar recommends upcoming games based on what you play, replacing popular upcoming's mass-market slot. It's far less traffic but higher-intent: fewer wishlists, but those that come are likely buyers.

units.title: Steam optimizes for sales, not wishlists
units.detail: The old popular-upcoming boost (thousands of wishlists pre-launch) is largely gone. If the smaller, higher-intent wishlists convert better on day one, the change may still help — but there's now no specific wishlist number that triggers a positive outcome; it's 'the more the better'.

units.title: External marketing rules are unchanged
units.detail: Demos, NextFest, community building, short-form content, and newsletters remain essential regardless of the homepage change. Only the final pre-launch boost changed; the strategy of building wishlists off-Steam first still holds.

units.title: Devs keep only ~40% of gross revenue
units.detail: A $10 game nets about $4: VAT/consumption tax (0-25% by buyer's country) comes out first, then refunds/chargebacks (5-25%), then Steam's 30%, then US withholding (0-30% without a tax treaty), then your own income tax. Budget on net, never gross.

units.title: Clickbait marketing inflates refunds
units.detail: Misleading marketing that oversells the game drives refund rates to 25%+ — The Day Before hit 46-50%. Make the store page clearly communicate what the game actually is to keep refunds low.

units.title: Use ~40% of gross for revenue estimates
units.detail: When doing market research on how much a game might make, estimate net as roughly 40% of gross (or ~30% in high-tax countries). Don't run a business on gross figures.

units.title: Stop Killing Games: keep games playable
units.detail: The EU initiative asks publishers to leave discontinued games in a functional state — either patch out online checks for the single-player portion or release server binaries so players can host. It doesn't demand IP transfer, resources, or converting multiplayer games to single-player.

units.title: A 3-sentence initiative starts a conversation
units.detail: The proposal is deliberately a bare-bones prototype (like a game's first design) that gets iterated through consultations before becoming law — it's not meant to be the final legislation itself. Laws of this kind are typically not retroactive.

units.title: Build games with a shutdown plan
units.detail: Designing a game with an eventual shutdown in mind from pre-production (e.g., shipping map data locally instead of streaming from cloud servers) makes end-of-life support trivial, whereas retroactive changes mean re-architecting the whole game.

units.title: Server binaries keep old games alive
units.detail: Early multiplayer games (CS 1.6, Quake, Battlefield) remain playable today because Valve shipped dedicated server binaries and players hosted their own. That's the model the initiative wants to enshrine: no dependency on the developer after support ends.

units.title: Expiring licenses shouldn't kill owned games
units.detail: When car/music licenses expire, publishers can stop selling but shouldn't take the game from existing owners (GTA SA still plays its original radio songs on old copies). Removing playability from buyers is the actual harm.

units.title: Tutorial hell is passive learning
units.detail: The real problem isn't tutorials — it's watching without doing. Tutorials are step one; step two is actively building something yourself. Stopping tutorials entirely is the wrong advice.

units.title: Watch, then rebuild with small changes
units.detail: After a tutorial, rebuild the project and modify one small requirement — e.g., turn a key-door system into a locked chest. Making your own decisions forces real understanding and exposes what the tutorial pre-planned for you.

units.title: Getting stuck is normal and necessary
units.detail: Tutorials hide the potholes (a 1-hour mistake-filled build is edited down to a 20-minute video), creating the illusion that getting stuck means failure. Stuck = debugging = using your brain = learning.

units.title: Messy first code is fine, refactor after
units.detail: First pass should just solve the problem; with more context afterward you can rewrite the solution at higher quality. Iterate: build, get stuck, solve, compare against professional code, improve.

units.title: ECS + job system for massive performance
units.detail: Unity's ECS with the job system gives clean, safe multi-threaded code that can yield ~10x speedups, enabling thousands of entities (e.g., marines vs endless zombie waves). The main constraint is how memory is shared between jobs and the main thread.

units.title: Spatial partition for nearest-target search
units.detail: A simple loop that finds each unit's closest target works for small counts, but a quadrant/spatial-partitioning system is what scales to thousands of units finding targets among thousands of targets.

units.title: Infinite levels from pooled parts
units.detail: Create a pool of interesting level sections and procedurally instantiate them as the player approaches the end. This gives infinite variation and easy expansion of themes or difficulty.

units.title: Hit counter juice scales with combo
units.detail: A satisfying hit counter animates bigger and shakes harder per hit, like in Hyper Knights. Tiny escalating details turn a plain counter into a rewarding effect.

units.title: Zelda-style hearts as quarter segments
units.detail: Split each heart into 4 segments so damage and healing can affect a quarter heart or a whole heart independently. Keep logic and visuals separated so it's easy to add heal-over-time animations.

units.title: Bolt super units = reusable visual functions
units.detail: Super units wrap visual scripting logic into modules with custom control/value inputs and outputs that can be reused across graphs — the visual-scripting equivalent of a function, the main tool for managing complexity and avoiding spaghetti graphs.

units.title: Nest private logic, separate macro for reuse
units.detail: Use a nested super unit for behavior used only inside one graph, and a standalone flow macro for general behavior you want to reuse (e.g., a 'get mouse world position' unit).

units.title: Rotate toward mouse via Atan2
units.detail: Screen-to-world-point converts mouse position, then direction = normalized(target - transform position), angle from Atan2(x, y) converted to degrees applied as euler Z rotation. Good reusable math pattern for top-down shooters.

units.title: Free education as industry investment
units.detail: Publishing high-quality educational content for free, without monetization, can be a deliberate investment to raise the quality bar of an entire industry. Ad costs are production spend, not necessarily a revenue strategy.

units.title: Marketing is a multiplier, not the product
units.detail: Marketing amplifies the base game: 100 * 0 = 0. Even brilliant marketing cannot save an unmarketable idea, so game quality and idea appeal are the real lever.

units.title: Validate marketable idea before marketing spend
units.detail: A dev spent $500 on Reddit ads and got only 16 wishlists, then blamed the ads. Rule one of game marketing is 'have a marketable game'; diagnose the game before tweaking ad targeting.

units.title: Dying genres resist any marketing
units.detail: Breakout and Flappy Bird clones are not marketable no matter how many features or mechanics they add, because Steam's quality bar is extremely high. Genre choice itself gates discoverability.

units.title: Wishlist loss-leader math for Steam
units.detail: A ~$1-per-wishlist target at a 5% conservative conversion can justify a loss-leader spend to kickstart Steam's snowball algorithm. When the real cost balloons to ~$700 per customer, the strategy (and the game) is broken.

units.title: Order-of-magnitude gaps mean bad game
units.detail: If ad results are ~1000% off your model (e.g., $700 vs $20 per customer), the problem is the product, not the marketing. Tweaks won't fix an order-of-magnitude gap.

units.title: Players' scarcest resource is time
units.detail: Players have hundreds of high-quality games to play, so their limiting factor is time, not money. Even a free game that isn't enticing struggles to attract players.

units.title: Make games for fun have no rules
units.detail: Commercial intent demands a marketable idea and marketing, but hobbyist games have no rules. Separate your goals before judging a game's success.

units.title: Function timer for one-line delayed logic
units.detail: A reusable function timer class executes an action after a delay with a single line of code. It's the highest-leverage utility, reused in nearly every project for 10+ years.

units.title: Drag-and-drop reusable toolkit components
units.detail: Encapsulating systems (timers, tooltips, error popups, health, grid, chat bubbles) into drop-in components with tutorial links speeds up prototyping and final games alike.

units.title: Game hook beats feature count
units.detail: The initial genre and hook determine marketability far more than piling on features. Adding more content to a weak concept doesn't attract interest.

units.title: Limit scope; cut rather than run long
units.detail: It's very hard to make up sales after long development. Keep the first game tiny, make mistakes cheaply, and save the dream game for your fifth, sixth, or seventh project.

units.title: Visuals are a marketing signal
units.detail: Players extrapolate from programmer art to assume bugs and shallow design, and won't spend time on your game. Presentation quality is one of the most important marketing aspects.

units.title: Kit-bash asset packs to stand out
units.detail: Using the most popular asset packs as-is makes games look identical. Tweak colors and textures (kit-bashing) and mix multiple art styles so your game doesn't look like everyone else's.

units.title: Ideas are cheap; implementation matters
units.detail: Nobody will steal your first-time dev idea; two devs given the same prompt build different games. Identical-game rivals like Peglin and Roundguard even bundled together and both sold well.

units.title: Show floors produce bad playtest data
units.detail: Conference booths are loud and chaotic, and passers-by aren't your audience, so you get ephemeral, sloppy feedback that can drive drastic design decisions. Don't treat show-floor sampling as playtesting.

units.title: One-on-one playtesting with genre fans
units.detail: Recruit genre-targeted players from subreddits/Discord, run a survey, then watch them quietly play a build one-on-one. This surfaces UX flaws, bugs, and unclear text that self-testing misses.

units.title: Playtest quotes become marketing copy
units.detail: Listener reactions during playtests (e.g., 'best graphics of any zombie shooter') are ready-made store-page and tweet copy, since fans naturally describe the game's selling points.

units.title: Popular Steam genres to study
units.detail: Horror, open-world survival-craft, deckbuilders, roguelikes, management, and simulation genres consistently do well on Steam. Study and play the top games in a genre before committing to an idea.

units.title: Task queue with validation gate
units.detail: A task stays queued until a validate function returns true, then it executes. This lets you add tasks anytime while guaranteeing they only run when prerequisites (e.g., free storage slot) are met.

units.title: Action delegates customize task execution
units.detail: Store delegate/action fields in task data (grab, drop) so the worker logic is generic and callers inject the actual behavior, including who executed it via a parameterized action.

units.title: Reserve target slots before arrival
units.detail: Mark a slot as 'weapon incoming' as soon as the task is queued so two workers don't claim the same empty slot. This prevents duplicate assignments while the worker is en route.

units.title: Parent carried object to the carrier
units.detail: To make a worker carry a weapon, parent the weapon transform to the worker transform on grab and reparent to null on drop. The carried object then follows all carrier movement automatically.

units.title: Slot state tracked and visualized
units.detail: A slot class holding its transform plus current/claimed item, exposing IsEmpty() and color feedback (gray empty, red occupied), makes validation logic and debugging easy to reason about.

units.title: Never make fields public
units.detail: Exposing fields publicly couples code and invites misuse; instead expose properties or methods. This is framed as one of the most important lectures for clean, expandable code.

units.title: C# events decouple systems from UI
units.detail: Units and actions fire events the UI subscribes to, so the game runs perfectly with or without UI. Decoupling via events keeps presentation code from leaking into gameplay logic.

units.title: Singleton pattern for shared services
units.detail: A single global instance provides convenient access to shared systems (like the game manager). Use it deliberately since it trades testability and decoupling for convenience.

units.title: Generics reuse one class for grid and pathfinding
units.detail: Refactoring the grid system to use C# generics lets the exact same class serve both grid logic and A* pathfinding data, removing duplication before implementing the algorithm.

units.title: Interfaces enable a generic interact action
units.detail: Modeling interactables behind a C# interface lets one 'interact' action open doors, destroy crates, or do anything else, making the action infinitely extensible.

units.title: Cinemachine simplifies camera control
units.detail: Using Unity's Cinemachine makes camera movement, rotation, zoom, and cutscene-style action cameras dramatically easier than hand-rolling camera code.

units.title: ProBuilder slices destructibles for explosion
units.detail: Use Unity's built-in ProBuilder to slice crates into parts and explode them for satisfying destruction, then update pathfinding when destructible objects are destroyed.

units.title: Action-point turn systems are extensible
units.detail: Giving each unit action points spent on move/shoot/grenade/interact actions, with generic action handling, makes adding new enemy types, actions, and maps easy. The pattern generalizes to Civ/Tactics-style games.

units.title: Prefab variants and animation retargeting
units.detail: Using prefab variants and animation retargeting lets you reuse a base unit and skeleton animations across many unit types, an efficient way to expand enemy variety.

units.title: Task object is a data holder
units.detail: A task class contains all info the worker needs (e.g., target position). Workers request the next task from the queue; request returns the first task and removes it from the list.

units.title: Poll for tasks on a timer, not every frame
units.detail: Workers request a task every ~200ms rather than every update, avoiding wasted lookups. If no task exists, they simply wait and retry on the next tick.

units.title: Worker-task split scales to many workers
units.detail: Separating worker state machines from the central task queue means multiple workers can share one system with no extra effort; tasks are handed out and executed sequentially.

units.title: Modular task types with varied parameters
units.detail: Different task types can hold different fields (position vs animation vs action) and different execution logic, composing simple tasks (move, then animate, then act) into complex cleanup behaviors.

units.title: Multiple task systems working in tandem
units.detail: Two independent task systems (one drops weapons into slots, another picks them up) with one worker each can coordinate complex behavior, showing how to combine systems to build emergent gameplay.

units.title: Model task types as subclasses of a base task class
units.detail: Create one subclass per task type (e.g., MoveToPosition) extending a common base Task class. Each subclass carries its own parameters; the task queue stores them all as the base type. This lets you add new behaviors without touching the queue or dispatcher.

units.title: Mark base task class abstract
units.detail: Make the base Task class abstract so it can never be instantiated directly; it exists only as a base for the concrete task types. You get compile errors if you ever try to create a raw base task, which prevents misuse.

units.title: Unity C# lacks switch-on-type; use if/else type checks
units.detail: When dispatching a task, test its type with `if (task is MoveToPosition) {...} else {...}` and cast to the concrete subtype, then return after handling. Older Unity C# versions do not support `switch` on type; when C# 7 lands, prefer a type switch. Keep each handler in its own function.

units.title: Worker loop: request, execute, reset
units.detail: A worker repeatedly requests a task from the system; if none is returned it waits (e.g., 200ms) and asks again. If a task arrives it executes it, then an on-completion action resets the worker to waiting. Multiple tasks queue up and run sequentially in FIFO order.

units.title: Imitation learning vs reinforcement learning
units.detail: Reinforcement learning has the agent try random actions until it stumbles into rewards; for multi-step sequential tasks (move to button, press, reach food) the odds of pure-luck success are near zero. Imitation learning instead records a human demonstration and has the agent copy it, making complex tasks tractable.

units.title: GAIL: adversarial imitation learning
units.detail: GAIL (Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning) runs a second algorithm, a discriminator, that tries to guess whether an action came from the agent or the recorded demo. The agent improves by learning to behave like the demo well enough to fool the discriminator.

units.title: Behavioral cloning can't beat its demos
units.detail: BC (Behavioral Cloning) simply copies the exact actions from the demonstration, so it can never perform better than the demos you give it. GAIL generalizes to the goal, and extrinsic rewards push beyond the demo. Combine all three for superhuman performance.

units.title: Layer BC, GAIL, and rewards for superhuman AI
units.detail: Use all three signals: BC first teaches the agent to act exactly like you, GAIL teaches it to achieve the same goal, and extrinsic rewards let it improve beyond the demo. Start with high `strength` on the demos so it learns the basics, then lower to ~0.1 so extrinsic rewards dominate.

units.title: Demos teach bad habits too
units.detail: The agent learns exactly what you recorded; ram into walls during a demo and it will learn to slam into walls. Record clean, goal-completing demonstrations and make them as numerous as possible - more and better data yields a better agent.

units.title: Add negative step reward only after success
units.detail: Train the agent to complete the task with positive rewards first, then add a small negative reward per action to encourage speed and efficiency. Starting with the penalty makes learning much harder, so introduce optimization pressure only once the agent already succeeds.

units.title: Record demos, then switch mode to train
units.detail: Attach a Demonstration Recorder, enable recording, run the scene with the heuristic behavior, and play the task correctly many times. Copy the saved .demo file into Assets, then disable recording and set behavior type back to training before running ML training with a config that points `demo_path` at it.

units.title: Build many small games, not one big one
units.detail: Making 5-20 mini projects teaches far more than spending the same time on a single large project. Code Monkey made ~40 flash games in five years and credits that breadth with his fast skill growth; variety across genres is the goal.

units.title: Build every game twice: quick then proper
units.detail: Each project has two challenges: first build the game so it works (even in one giant class), then rebuild it properly with separate classes per responsibility - a Bird class, a collision handler, a score manager, a game state manager. Even intermediate devs learn from the 'proper' pass.

units.title: Simple games force real design decisions
units.detail: Even Flappy Bird forces implementation choices such as moving the bird left-to-right versus moving the environment around a stationary bird - both valid with different trade-offs. Building both ways teaches you which approach works better for your design.

units.title: Clone classics to learn specific skills
units.detail: Each classic teaches distinct skills: Snake and Asteroids teach teleportation and momentum physics, Breakout teaches one-axis input and physics, Space Invaders and Pac-Man teach simple-to-complex AI, Angry Birds teaches environment physics and level design. Pick the clone that targets the skill you lack.

units.title: Success is a personal, defined goal
units.detail: Success means different things to different people - from releasing any game, to making $10k, to being a full-time dev, to building a cultural phenomenon. No level is wrong; you must explicitly define which one you are aiming for, otherwise you can never know if you achieved it.

units.title: Set quantifiable goals to stay motivated
units.detail: A vague goal like 'be a successful game dev' is unmeasurable. Use concrete, ideally mathematical goals - e.g., 'make enough money to stay a full-time dev' computed from your burn rate - so you always know exactly how close you are to the finish line.

units.title: Learn by cloning, then go original
units.detail: Learn C#/Unity basics, clone classic games to build technical skill, and only then build a small original game. Having already finished a clone gives you the confidence to take an original project to release. Level zero to one is the hardest jump but is very achievable.

units.title: Localize games - English is only ~23% of Steam
units.detail: Per the Steam Hardware Survey, English is just 23% of the Steam audience, so an English-only game misses ~80% of potential players. Localization is a high-ROI way to find success, especially with strong growth in Latin America and Southeast Asia.

units.title: Make small 6-month games to cut risk
units.detail: Prefer 6-month projects over 2-3 year ones; long projects are risky and tricky. Solo or tiny teams can still find massive success (Balatro made ~$28M as a solo game; a supermarket simulator prototype took ~4 months). Small games still learn into polished, interesting results.

units.title: Efficiency tools make games cheaper
units.detail: The right tool can make you work ~5x faster, and working 5x faster means your game costs ~5x less to make. Studios ranked efficiency tooling as the main way they mitigate risk, ahead of live ops, publisher support, and avoiding over-hiring.

units.title: Stay in the same genre to reuse knowledge
units.detail: Making successive games in the same genre lets you reuse code and domain knowledge, speeding up production and improving quality. Code Monkey makes mostly management/tycoon games for exactly this reason, though the 2025 Unity report shows most studios prefer new ideas in a different genre (spin-offs reusing an IP).

units.title: Stagger platform releases as an indie
units.detail: For solo devs or 1-5 person teams, a staggered release across platforms is usually smarter than a simultaneous multi-platform launch - unless a deal forces simultaneous. Managing one release at a time is far easier and less risky than coordinating several at once.

units.title: Decide networking architecture early
units.detail: Choose peer-to-peer versus dedicated server early in development. Retro-fitting a dedicated server onto a peer-to-peer game is a significant re-architecture cost, so lock in the networking architecture before you build deeply on it.

units.title: Multiplayer is winner-takes-all
units.detail: Multiplayer games have a far higher revenue ceiling (Lethal Company, Fortnite) but suffer a cold-start problem: few players scare off more players, spiraling to a dead game. It is high-risk, high-reward, and multiplayer revenue and MAU keep rising in Unity's reports.

units.title: Add UGC to extend game life
units.detail: User-generated content - even something as simple as a level editor or Steam Workshop support with custom characters/levels - can give a game a second life and raise its ceiling. 52% of surveyed US gamers say the ability to generate content makes them play longer.

units.title: Find the fun in the core loop fast
units.detail: Multiplayer games live or die on the core gameplay loop, so prototype it quickly and iterate. Also plan live-ops and update strategy from the start, and treat players as a community (managed feedback) rather than dashboard numbers if you want longevity.

units.title: Singleton and Observer are the essential patterns
units.detail: In every game and every genre, the two must-know patterns are the Singleton and the Observer (events). Code Monkey has never shipped a game without at least one singleton and at least one event, and says those two alone cover most game problems.

units.title: Object pooling to kill spawn/destroy stutters
units.detail: Spawning and destroying objects (bullets, spells) constantly causes stutters and poor performance. Pre-create a pool of objects, then enable and reuse them instead of instantiating/destroying; disable and return them to the pool when done. Modern engines often ship a built-in pool class.

units.title: Command pattern for undo/redo
units.detail: Wrap each action in a command that exposes both execute and undo functions. Keep a list of commands so you can replay them in order to execute, or walk the same list calling undo to reverse everything - the clean basis for undo/redo systems.

units.title: Patterns are guidelines, not mandates
units.detail: Design patterns are a cheat-code library of solved problems, but they are also personal preference. Use one when it helps, and skip it when it hurts - e.g., Code Monkey has never found a use for the Factory pattern despite its popularity. Match pattern complexity to your game's complexity.

units.title: Strategy pattern via interfaces for modularity
units.detail: The Strategy pattern is mostly just interfaces: implement one algorithm multiple ways and swap implementations freely. Example: a character controller that moves with physics or without physics by implementing the same movement interface, so you can switch engines at runtime.

units.title: Beginner systems: health, XP, enemy AI, inventory
units.detail: Good entry-level systems to build: a health system (damage/heal functions), an experience system (add XP, level thresholds), simple enemy AI (which at its simplest is just a state machine), and a basic inventory system. All are achievable by complete beginners.

units.title: Grid-based building system (like Valheim)
units.detail: A house/building system built on a grid: store parts in grid cells and validate placement (can this part go on this tile type?). The beginner version is simple; a Valheim-style version adds supports where over-accumulation collapses the structure - a much more complex, impressive challenge.

units.title: Modding = dynamically loading external files
units.detail: Modding support is simple in theory: watch a special folder, load the files it contains at runtime, and expose hooks. Modding sprites/textures is easy; the impressive version adds loading custom interpreted code (e.g., Lua) or assemblies so players can add real logic, massively multiplying mod depth.

units.title: Custom inspectors massively improve data editing
units.detail: A good custom inspector turns opaque fields into usable tools: previews for icons, waveforms for audio clips, sliders/progress bars for numeric ranges, enum toggle buttons, tabs to organize a big manager script, and validation. With hundreds of weapons/items this efficiency is huge.

units.title: Conditionally show fields by C# expression
units.detail: Make inspector fields appear only when relevant using a condition expression, e.g., show range, ammo, and projectile fields only when weapon type is not melee (`@category != WeaponType.Melee`). This hides irrelevant data and prevents mistakes, and can also be driven by a bool-returning method in code.

units.title: Keep inspector customization out of source code
units.detail: Prefer visual/declarative inspector design stored in separate data files over scattering attributes through code. Source stays 100% clean, non-programmers (designers, artists) can build inspectors, and the design files sync normally with version control as plain text.

units.title: Validate fields so bad data fails visibly
units.detail: Add validation rules that raise errors in the inspector, e.g., a color field must satisfy `color.a >= 1` with message 'Color alpha is not one'. This catches invisible-bug data like a color with alpha 0 that renders nothing and leaves you wondering why nothing shows on screen.

units.title: Learn by applying, not watching
units.detail: You only truly gain knowledge by putting what you watch into practice. Watch a tutorial, then write and apply the code yourself rather than blindly copy-pasting.

units.title: Making games for fun is valid
units.detail: If you want to make games for money that's one valid path, but making them just for fun, to build something you enjoy, is equally legitimate. You don't have to monetize everything you do.

units.title: Power of accumulated experience
units.detail: After decades of programming and building games, experience gives you the ability to build any game genre you can think of. Genre-specific skills generalize; the longer you build, the more genres open up.

units.title: Reverse-engineer metrics for revenue goals
units.detail: To reach a specific sales/revenue target, reverse engineer the numbers backwards from the goal to figure out what wishlist, follower, and marketing inputs are actually required at each step.

units.title: Unity Student Plan free assets
units.detail: Unity offers a Student Plan giving free tools and assets to anyone enrolled at almost any university. You can grab it and build real games from those free assets.

units.title: Finishing projects is a key skill
units.detail: Rather than abandoning a game after years of work, find a way to take it to the finish line. The skill of completing projects is extremely valuable and often more important than the project itself.

units.title: Self-imposed crunch in game dev
units.detail: Crunch means working beyond ~40 hours/week (60-100 hours). Surveys show about 74% of devs who work 40+ hours cite self-imposed pressure, not management or peers, as the main cause.

units.title: Never sacrifice sleep
units.detail: No matter how many projects or deadlines you have, always sleep at least 8 hours. Consistent sleep (plus physical fitness) is cited as the main reason the author avoided burnout despite constant overwork.

units.title: Estimate wishlists from Steam followers
units.detail: Steam wishlists are private but followers are public (via steamdb charts). Wishlists are roughly 10-15x the follower count, so ~1,000 followers implies about 10,000-15,000 wishlists.
