units.title: Event appearances generate wishlist spikes
units.detail: Showing a game at a major event (e.g., The Game Awards, ~20M+ views) generates measurable wishlist bumps. Even a pre-show slot earned ~9,000 wishlists, while top announcements got 90,000-400,000.

units.title: Existing audience carries to sequels
units.detail: Sequels and games by a studio with an established fanbase (e.g., Long Dark 2, Split Fiction) instantly attract large wishlist counts because the audience from prior games is already waiting.

units.title: Say yes to free major-event slots
units.detail: Some event slots are given free to smaller indie studios. If you get offered a slot at a huge show, take it immediately since even the lowest-performing showcased games gained ~9,000 wishlists.

units.title: The door problem in game design
units.detail: Even a trivial feature like 'a door' hides a million design decisions: can the player open it, how, which doors open, locked vs never-open, enemy spawn doors, co-op sizing. This is the classic example of how complex game design is.

units.title: Game design is its own discipline
units.detail: Game design is separate from programming, art, and story. A designer's job is answering all the tiny questions a feature creates, and there is no objective right or wrong answer, only what fits your game.

units.title: Visually communicate usable vs decorative
units.detail: If some doors can be opened and others can't but they look identical, players get confused. Use cues like police tape, color coding (green=open, red=closed), piled trash, or removed door knobs to communicate usability.

units.title: Distinguish locked, never-open, and openable
units.detail: Players need to know if a door is locked (will open eventually) versus one that will never open. Pick from many valid locked-door implementations: key, hackable console, puzzle, story moment, etc.

units.title: Multiplayer multiplies design complexity
units.detail: Every single-player design question becomes doubly complex in multiplayer: does a door lock after both players pass, what if one player lags behind, does a player in a doorway block another, teleport vs wait for the straggler.

units.title: Tiny decisions define final game quality
units.detail: Over a 6-month to 2-year development cycle you make a thousand (or a million) small decisions. The quality of the final game is the sum of all those tiny decisions, many of which the player never even notices.

units.title: Stick to one genre to compound success
units.detail: If maximizing long-term revenue, repeatedly making games in a genre you know and are good at is the best strategy: you build on your own knowledge and can market new games directly to your previous games' audience.

units.title: Same genre, new theme each game
units.detail: Two Point Studios intentionally makes the same management-genre game with a different theme each time (Hospital, Campus, Museum), keeping the humor/style/audience while making each a completely different game.

units.title: Genre consistency builds a baseline
units.detail: Publishing similar-genre games means each launch starts from a higher baseline instead of marketing from scratch, and you can even command a large wishlist count before the game is near release.

units.title: Prototype to find passion + market overlap
units.detail: The best scenario is an idea you want to work on that also has market potential. Prototype tons of ideas until you find one matching both, since prototyping is cheap and iteration speed is key.

units.title: Decide revenue-first vs passion-first
units.detail: Developers must consciously choose between the strategy with the best odds of financial success (staying in one genre) and exploring many different ideas. Both are valid; just make the decision deliberately.

units.title: Build the project before seeing the solution
units.detail: Watch the project overview, pause, and actively build it yourself before watching the walkthrough. You only learn by doing; watching the solution first defeats the purpose.

units.title: Normalize case for case-insensitive matching
units.detail: When matching guessed letters against a hidden word, convert both sides to lowercase before comparing (e.g., ToLower on input and word). Keep the original string only for display so the printed word preserves its original casing.

units.title: Track guesses to prevent duplicates
units.detail: Keep a list of all guesses and reject a letter the player already entered, skipping the rest of the game logic for that input so repeated guesses don't waste lives.

units.title: Iterate string characters with foreach
units.detail: In C#, 'foreach (char c in word)' cycles through every character of a string, letting you check each letter against the guessed list and build up a masked display string (show guessed letters, underscore the rest).

units.title: Skip non-guessable characters in puzzles
units.detail: Spaces (and other non-letter characters) in a hidden word should be displayed directly rather than as blanks, and the game logic should skip them with 'continue' so they are never guessed.

units.title: Test divisibility with the modulo operator
units.detail: A number is divisible by another when 'n % divisor == 0' (remainder is zero). This is the standard way to implement FizzBuzz-style conditional output.

units.title: Order if-chains from most specific to least
units.detail: In FizzBuzz, checking 'divisible by 3' before 'divisible by 3 AND 5' breaks the AND case because the else branch guarantees the number is not divisible by 3. Always test the most specific condition first.

units.title: Avoid impossible nested else conditions
units.detail: Inside an else block, the outer if's condition is already known to be false, so inner conditions contradicting it can never trigger. Be careful chaining nested ifs so inner checks aren't impossible.

units.title: Multiple valid solutions, tests as truth
units.detail: Any programming problem has many correct solutions (different loop types, booleans + continue, etc.). If your code passes all the tests, it's correct regardless of approach.

units.title: Inclusive loop bounds need <=
units.detail: Looping from 1 to 100 inclusive requires 'i <= 100'. Using only 'i < 100' silently skips 100, a classic off-by-one error.

units.title: DOTS uses a hybrid workflow
units.detail: Production DOTS games combine Entities with GameObjects instead of going 100% ECS, meaning the GameObject workflows you already know remain applicable when working with Entities.

units.title: Pick netcode by game scale
units.detail: Netcode for Game Objects targets small-scale co-op games; Netcode for Entities targets super-fast competitive games or games with lots of data. Both reach 1.0 alongside the 22 LTS release.

units.title: Unity Gaming Services are engine-agnostic
units.detail: UGS tools (Lobby, Relay, Matchmaker, Game Server Hosting, Friends, Leaderboards, UGC) can be used in non-Unity games too, e.g., Apex Legends uses Unity's Game Server Hosting despite not being made with Unity.

units.title: Choose Unity version by release timeline
units.detail: Pick the Unity version that will be LTS by the time you release: if launching within ~6 months use the current one, if a year+ out consider the newer version. Upgrading is much easier nowadays than it used to be.

units.title: WebGL lacks WebSocket in Unity Transport 1.0
units.detail: Unity Transport 1.0 does not work on WebGL because it has no WebSocket support; Transport 2.0 (experimental) adds it. Expect the web build of a NGO game to fail until then.

units.title: Unity answers: engine improves via feedback
units.detail: Unity prioritizes the highest-impact work: bugs are marked 'won't fix' when a workaround exists, a better tool is recommended, or the affected user count is tiny relative to the refactor cost.

units.title: Unity 6 release naming stages
units.detail: Unity 6 ships as: beta (bleeding edge, experimentation only), then preview in May (all features, no breaking changes, production-usable), then full release (~end of year) as an LTS with a longer support cycle.

units.title: Free one-click GPU performance features
units.detail: Unity 6 adds GPU Resident Drawer, GPU Occlusion Culling, and a spatial-temporal post-processing upscaler that deliver massive performance gains (e.g., 60 to 300 FPS) by simply enabling a checkbox, no graphics expertise needed.

units.title: SRP pipelines become the default
units.detail: From Unity 6, URP/HDRP become the defaults for new projects (they already power ~90% of 2023 PC/console releases). The built-in pipeline remains supported through Unity 6 for existing shader/tool investment.

units.title: AI tools supercharge prototyping speed
units.detail: AI asset tools (sprite, texture, behavior tree, animation, sound generation) let you quickly test any game idea at the prototype stage; swap in professional assets once the project goes into production.

units.title: Distributed authority scales multiplayer
units.detail: Instead of one host or dedicated server holding all authority, distributed authority splits the multiplayer synchronization workload across multiple clients, enabling more complex games and larger worlds without heavy server resources.

units.title: Automated moderation for small teams
units.detail: Automatic voice/text moderation tools (safe voice, safe text) identify and stop toxic players, a huge help for small teams that can't staff a dedicated moderation team.

units.title: Bake GI scenarios for day/night cycles
units.detail: Adaptive Probe Volumes automatically place hundreds/thousands of light probes and can bake multiple lighting scenarios, then swap between them so a day/night cycle interpolates perfectly.

units.title: LTS vs tech stream versions
units.detail: Unity ships two tracks: LTS (latest stable, use it in real projects) and tech/beta stream (cutting-edge tools being developed, for experimentation). Pick LTS for production work.

units.title: Always use the latest LTS in projects
units.detail: For maximum stability, use the latest LTS Unity version in your projects rather than tech/beta versions. The author sticks with LTS and only upgrades deliberately.

units.title: Visual scripting for designer-programmer workflow
units.detail: Making visual scripting a built-in engine tool (from Bolt) lets hardcore programmers and designers work together flawlessly and is a core pillar of Unity's workflow improvements.

units.title: Unity incremental release cadence 6.x
units.detail: Unity moved to incremental versioning (6.0 LTS, 6.1, 6.2, 6.3 LTS...) instead of yearly-major versions, delivering features continuously without breaking changes. Understand release timing when adopting engine features.

units.title: Production verification by Unity
units.detail: Unity validates engine changes against real shipped titles (Pokemon Sleep, Second Dinner, Phasmophobia, Dredge) to keep every release stable. Real-world validation beats demo testing.

units.title: WebGPU and mobile web support
units.detail: WebGPU gives browsers direct GPU access enabling compute shaders and heavier games in the browser; mobile web support lets Unity games run without a native app install, lowering the barrier to play.

units.title: Vulkan and graphics jobs on Android
units.detail: Enabling graphics jobs with Vulkan on Android yields large performance boosts, similar to what's already possible on desktop. Test rendering backend settings by default on mobile for free gains.

units.title: Foveated rendering for XR
units.detail: Foveated rendering tracks where the eyes look, rendering full resolution only in a small circle and dropping resolution outward, producing massive performance gains on XR devices.

units.title: Project Auditor project health scan
units.detail: Run Project Auditor to automatically scan an entire project for potential improvements, mistakes, and hidden issues, then fix them in one window. A fast way to audit a large codebase.

units.title: Sentis precomputed simulation model
units.detail: Train an on-device ML model offline on expensive deformations (e.g., cloth), then run inference in real time instead of computing them at runtime. Precompute hard math into a model whenever runtime cost is prohibitive.

units.title: Automatic LOD generation for meshes
units.detail: New mesh LOD systems auto-generate all LOD levels from a high-poly source, including skinned meshes, collapsing 81M to 4.5M polygons with little visual loss (Nanite-like).

units.title: ECS for all merging objects and entities
units.detail: Unity plans to merge GameObjects and entities into a single native model so devs don't choose between DOTS and GameObject workflows. Keep an eye on unification of data-oriented and object-oriented code.

units.title: Core CLR engine upgrade
units.detail: Moving the engine to a modern .NET runtime (Core CLR) brings faster reload, faster compilation, and access to the latest C#/.NET versions. Runtime upgrades are a big lever for iteration speed.

units.title: Streaming content import pipeline
units.detail: Rewriting the content pipeline to import assets iteratively (low-res first, high-res async) removes the long black-screen waits when importing large batches of assets, making the editor feel responsive.

units.title: Adaptive probe volumes lighting
units.detail: Adaptive probe volumes auto-place light probes across a scene, bake high-quality GI, and interpolate between lighting scenarios, giving near-raytraced looks at a fraction of the cost.

units.title: One-click rendering performance features
units.detail: GPU Resident Drawer (instance drawing), GPU occlusion culling, and spatial-temporal upscaling each provide large frame-rate boosts with a single checkbox, ideal for non-graphics programmers.

units.title: AI tools for prototyping, not shipping
units.detail: AI-generated sprites/models/sfx are great for making prototypes visually interesting, but replace them with professional art before launch. Their value is highest for beginners and jams.

units.title: UI Toolkit for editors, Unity UI for runtime
units.detail: UI Toolkit is far better for building editor windows and tools, while Unity UI remains preferable for in-game runtime UI. Pick per context rather than forcing one system.

units.title: Multiplayer Center streamlines services
units.detail: A Multiplayer Center lets you pick a game genre and parameters, then suggests and one-click installs the relevant Unity Gaming Services tools. Preset-driven tooling reduces onboarding friction.

units.title: Multiplayer play mode in-editor testing
units.detail: Multiplayer Play Mode runs multiple Unity instances in the editor so you can test multiplayer without making full builds, drastically speeding up iteration on netcode.

units.title: Distributed authority networking
units.detail: Distributed authority lets multiple players own authority over different parts of the world instead of a single host, potentially enabling large-scale MMO-style games on Netcode for GameObjects.

units.title: Shader Graph heatmap performance mode
units.detail: A heatmap color mode tints shader graph nodes by performance cost, helping you spot expensive nodes while authoring shaders.

units.title: Licensed-data AI avoids copyright issues
units.detail: Unity licenses training data to keep AI output copyright-safe, which is slower and yields lower quality than competitors, but protects developers. Weigh legal safety versus generation quality.

units.title: Be early on new platforms
units.detail: Supporting the Apple Vision Pro SDK right at announcement lets you prepare content before launch when competition is low. Being first on a new device can pay off.

units.title: Incremental upgrades over breaking majors
units.detail: Unity abandoned Unity 7-style breaking releases in favor of small incremental 6.x updates, delivering the same features (core CLR, ECS for all, pipeline merge) without breaking projects. Prefer non-breaking evolution for long-lived products.

units.title: Merging URP up to HDRP level
units.detail: Unity plans one render pipeline by building URP up to HDRP parity (adding screen-space reflections, dynamic GI) rather than dumbing HDRP down, then merging them on a shared render graph.

units.title: Unified netcode stack
units.detail: Netcode for GameObjects and Netcode for Entities will be merged into one stack after ECS-for-all, giving a single networking solution. Consolidation of duplicated stacks reduces long-term maintenance.

units.title: Unity UI reversal avoids breaking projects
units.detail: Unity reversed plans to deprecate Unity UI; games like Hearthstone still depend on it. Before deprecating a widely-used API, consider the breakage cost across existing products.

units.title: Platform Toolkit one code path to consoles
units.detail: A single API abstracts Xbox, Steam, Switch, and other console SDKs so you write code once and publish everywhere, plus pre-certification validation before contacting platform holders.

units.title: AI agents analyze profiler data
units.detail: AI agents can attach to the profiler, answer 'why is my game slow', point out slow render passes, and suggest settings changes. LLMs are strongest at reading diagnostic data and giving targeted fixes.

units.title: Render 3D models as 2D
units.detail: Toggle a checkbox to render a real 3D model inside a 2D game, with sorting, 2D lights, and effects applied, removing the pre-processed 3D-to-2D sprite workflow.

units.title: Fewer, more stable releases
units.detail: Reducing preview packages and doing two tech releases plus an LTS per year produced more stable Unity versions validated on real productions. Fewer experimental features equals better stability.

units.title: GPU lightmapping bakes ~100x faster
units.detail: GPU lightmapper bakes lighting about 100 times faster than CPU baking, dramatically cutting lighting iteration time. Use GPU baking when available.

units.title: Hybrid renderer and Burst gains
units.detail: Hybrid renderer with Burst took 100k dynamic entities from 37ms to 6.9ms (5x) by moving rendering to data-oriented, burst-compiled code. Data-oriented rendering is dramatically faster.

units.title: Camera stacking in URP
units.detail: Universal Render Pipeline added camera stacking for layered rendering effects, working toward parity with the built-in pipeline. Understand feature parity gaps when adopting a new renderer.

units.title: Separate UI logic, hierarchy, and style
units.detail: UI Toolkit separates hierarchy and styling (CSS-like) from logic, making UI scale to any resolution/aspect ratio. Separation of concerns improves UI maintainability.

units.title: Launch many small games to compound experience
units.detail: Most devs release one game then quit, losing the compounding experience of multiple launches. Making small games fast gives more learning and better odds of long-term success (Rovio made 50+ games before Angry Birds).

units.title: Scope management after first game
units.detail: You can't estimate build time until you finish a real game; features always take longer than you think. Use past project time/complexity as a baseline for future estimates and pad aggressively.

units.title: Validate game ideas with feedback ASAP
units.detail: If selling commercially, validate that players want your idea before spending years on it; 50%+ of Steam games earn under $1k because there was never an audience.

units.title: Avoid saturated genres like 2D platformers
units.detail: Saturated genres (2D platformers/metroidvanias) are very hard to succeed in commercially even when well-made, because supply vastly exceeds demand. Pick genres with more demand per unit of effort.

units.title: Success is not linear with effort
units.detail: A 'better' sequel can sell far worse than the original (100K then 20K). With multiple games you can absorb hits and misses instead of betting everything on one.

units.title: Don't overengineer game code
units.detail: Clever modular systems (interfaces, generics) are fun but often unused by the final game, adding complexity for nothing. Match architecture complexity to actual needs and refactor when requirements grow.

units.title: Early access needs polish now
units.detail: Players no longer forgive unpolished early access or demos; a bad launch is nearly impossible to recover from. Release short-but-perfect content (Thronefall demo) rather than wide-but-broken.

units.title: Spend half your effort on marketing
units.detail: Technical completion alone won't sell a game; by game two you must dedicate roughly as much effort to marketing as development. Marketing is a learnable skill, not luck.

units.title: Marketing is the #1 skill
units.detail: In an attention economy, marketing is the most important skill for a professional indie dev; a good game is the bare minimum and does not sell itself. Marketing is the study of getting attention.

units.title: Estimate Steam sales via Boxleiter method
units.detail: Estimate units sold by multiplying review count by 20-70 (roughly 40 average). e.g., 50 reviews ≈ 2,000 copies. Use it to sanity-check whether a game actually made money.

units.title: Gate launch on wishlist/follower thresholds
units.detail: Aim for at least ~1,500 followers and ~5,000 wishlists before launch; if under that after years of work, delay and market harder. You only get one launch.

units.title: Steam algorithm rewards early sales
units.detail: Steam only promotes games that already sell; an initial day-one push (via wishlist notifications and marketing) signals the algorithm to boost visibility, compounding sales.

units.title: Devlog audience is not a player audience
units.detail: Code Monkey's tutorial channel gathered 20M views but sold only ~500 copies of his game: game-dev fans don't buy games like players do. Match your marketing audience to your buyers.

units.title: Free prologue to build wishlists
units.detail: A free prologue/demo designed to leave players wanting more plus Steam Next Fest participation gather large wishlist counts, even if they convert at a lower rate than organic traffic.

units.title: Put up the Steam page early
units.detail: Time is the most impactful marketing factor: the earlier your store page is live, the longer wishlists accumulate, and wishlists drive the Steam promotion loop at launch.

units.title: Optional splash screen on free Unity
units.detail: Unity 6 made the splash screen optional even on the free tier, letting builds jump straight to gameplay. Players rarely review-gate on engine splash screens anyway.

units.title: GPU Resident Drawer instance rendering
units.detail: Enable GPU instanced drawing (GPU Resident Drawer) to merge draw calls; in a dense demo scene it jumped 70 FPS to 200+ FPS with just settings changes (URP asset to instance drawing, forward+), no scene edits.

units.title: GPU occlusion culling results vary by scene
units.detail: GPU occlusion culling can lower FPS (triangles drop 8M to 1M but batches rise and FPS falls 190 to 120) depending on scene. Always profile it in your actual game before enabling.

units.title: Combine GPU and baked occlusion culling
units.detail: GPU occlusion culling and the classic baked CPU occlusion culling are independent and can run together; bake static occluders (marked static) and combine for better culling in dense scenes.

units.title: STP upscaling low-res rendering
units.detail: Spatial-temporal post-processing upscales a lower render resolution back to full res with little visual loss, boosting FPS most when the game is GPU-bound. Test at 0.3-0.6 render scale.

units.title: STP requires TAA on, MSAA off
units.detail: Spatial-temporal upscaling auto-enables TAA and requires MSAA disabled on the render pipeline asset; leaving MSAA on breaks it. Check both settings when enabling the upscaler.

units.title: Editor overhead hides upscaler gains
units.detail: Upscaler and draw-call gains barely show in the editor because of editor overhead; FPS gains only materialize in real builds. Always measure performance changes in built players.

units.title: Marketing is a multiplier on game idea
units.detail: Marketing multiplies the quality of the game; zero times anything is zero, so a generic game won't be saved by marketing, and a great game with no marketing relies on luck.

units.title: Hook first: spend time on ideation
units.detail: The most important pre-marketing decision is what the game is: its theme/hook/unique angle. A clear hook (e.g., vampire blood-harvesting bar tycoon) makes every later marketing step easier.

units.title: Simulator genre succeeds via theme swap
units.detail: Simulator/tycoon games succeed largely by swapping a fresh theme onto familiar mechanics (card shop, power wash, gunsmith simulators). Pick a novel subject in an established, in-demand genre.

units.title: Descriptive game name and store capsule
units.detail: A name like 'Blood Bar Tycoon' plus a clean capsule (character, readable title, not-too-busy background) makes the game instantly understandable in search results and feeds.

units.title: Trailer: action fast, add SFX
units.detail: Start trailers with gameplay immediately (no logos), keep them skimmable since players preview them small and muted, and add sound effects so they stand out when unmuted. Show the endgame goal.

units.title: Localize text-light games cheaply
units.detail: If a game isn't text-heavy, adding localization is inexpensive and unlocks huge markets; use the engine's localization package with a lecture-ready workflow.

units.title: Track tutorial dropoff with analytics
units.detail: Implement analytics events at every tutorial stage so you can see where players bounce; a great demo requires an easy, well-telegraphed tutorial.

units.title: Wishlist CTA in menu, end, and quit
units.detail: Add wishlist call-to-action buttons in the main menu, at the end of the game, and on the quit prompt to capture intent at every natural moment.

units.title: Polish makes simple actions satisfying
units.detail: Animated transitions and small bounces (walls lifting, placement effects, good SFX) turn mundane interactions into satisfying juice that significantly improves perceived quality.

units.title: Tooltips with question-mark help
units.detail: Pair contextual tutorial tips with always-available question-mark help and a dynamic tooltip system, since players get lost even right after a tutorial prompt.

units.title: Multithreaded pathfinding scales to hundreds of units
units.detail: The A* Pathfinding Project runs searches on background threads so hundreds of units pathfind nearly free; hand-rolling multithreaded pathfinding is a huge time sink better bought off the shelf.

units.title: Tune re-path rate to map dynamism
units.detail: Lower the AI re-path rate (default 0.2s) when the map changes constantly; raise it on static maps to cut pathfinding cost. Match recalculation frequency to how often obstacles move.

units.title: Funnel modifier smooths raw paths
units.detail: Raw polygon-node paths are jagged (center-of-cell hops); a funnel modifier converts them into smooth direct paths. Post-process search output before following it.

units.title: Choose graph type for gameplay
units.detail: Navmesh for free movement, grid graph for tile logic, point graph when units may only traverse specified points (adventure routes), layered grid for elevation/overpasses. Match representation to the game's movement rules.

units.title: Two ways to update dynamic obstacles
units.detail: Update pathfinding dynamically via tag swaps (units avoid closed doors, apply penalties) or by cutting/re-baking the navmesh itself. Tags are cheaper; mesh cuts handle geometry changes.

units.title: Cache flood paths for zero-cost lookup
units.detail: Precompute/cache all-pairs or flood paths once and look them up at runtime (multi-target paths drop from ~2ms to 0ms). Caching path results gives near-free pathfinding for repeated queries.

units.title: Path penalties shape AI preference
units.detail: Assign penalty costs to restricted zones so AI strongly prefers avoiding them but can still pass through when needed, versus hard traversal bans. Soft constraints enable graceful degradation.

units.title: Destroy defers, object still a child
units.detail: Unity's Destroy() doesn't remove an object until end of frame, so child lists still contain 'destroyed' children and break logic that checks immediately. Unparent manually before destroying, or don't assume the list updated.

units.title: Experience lets you recognize issues fast
units.detail: Having hit a bug years ago lets you recognize and fix it in seconds (deferred Destroy breaking parent lists). Debugging skill compounds; remember gotchas so future-you fixes them instantly.

units.title: Two gamedev career paths: games or assets
units.detail: Game devs can earn money either by making games or by becoming a full-time tools/assets developer. Both are viable, and which is easier depends on your skill set. Tools built to help you build a game can end up more valuable than the game itself.

units.title: Game market ≠ asset market for customers
units.detail: Even though the gaming market is larger than the asset market, players are much harder to acquire than developers buying assets. Games require marketing, lots of testing, and balancing conflicting feedback, and take much more time and skill.

units.title: Sell on multiple platforms and stores
units.detail: Don't sell only on Steam: also use Humble Store, GOG, Epic, and consoles (Xbox, PlayStation, Switch). Similarly, don't sell assets only on the Unity Asset Store; also use Fab, TurboSquid, and Envato.

units.title: Asset stores are extremely crowded
units.detail: About 70 new assets launch on the asset store every day. Making yet another generic low-poly pack will sell zero copies, just like a generic platformer on Steam. The same marketing rules that apply to Steam games (validate idea, analyze audience, find reach) apply to assets.

units.title: Use review counts to gauge asset sales
units.detail: Asset store sales numbers aren't public, but most assets have 0-5 reviews, so a pack with hundreds of reviews (e.g., A* Pathfinding Project with ~800) implies massive sales. Use review volume as a success proxy when evaluating an asset market.

units.title: Horizon Worlds vs Horizon OS are different
units.detail: Horizon Worlds is Meta's Roblox-like UGC social platform moving to mobile, while Horizon OS is the operating system powering Quest devices and VR games. When Horizon Worlds moved to mobile, it was not a sign Meta was abandoning VR.

units.title: VR tools now use drag-and-drop building blocks
units.detail: The Meta SDK inside Unity provides building blocks (camera rig, hand tracking, passthrough, teleport) that add all required game objects and components via simple drag and drop, making VR prototyping far easier than the manual setup required years ago.

units.title: Design VR games for sitting and hand tracking
units.detail: Meta predicts the fastest-growing VR audience is mainstream adults who use headsets as virtual TVs: sitting, no controllers, hand tracking only. If this audience grows as expected, being an early developer of hand-tracked, seated VR games could be a big advantage.

units.title: VR market: solid, niche, slowly growing
units.detail: Quest saw record usage in 2025 with no new hardware launches; 100+ titles crossed $1M gross revenue. VR is not dying or exploding, but has less competition than Steam and a much smaller install base, making its net viability for indies unclear.

units.title: Market VR games outside the store
units.detail: Quest store users arrive with the intent to buy something they saw on social media (TikTok, Instagram, YouTube) and do not browse the store, unlike Steam's organic audience. Marketing outside the store matters more than store optimization.

units.title: Estimate VR revenue via review multipliers
units.detail: On Steam you estimate sales by multiplying review count (~85x for VR titles like Gun Club VR). Applying the same multiplier to Quest store review counts gives a rough sense of relative revenue, but Quest numbers remain a guess because Meta hides data.

units.title: Subscription services as secondary income
units.detail: Meta Horizon Plus is a Netflix-for-games subscription (1M+ subscribers, $20M paid to devs last year) built around usage payouts plus minimum guarantees and designed to be sustainable for developers, unlike games-pass-style models. Games must be ~1 year old with strong revenue to qualify, so treat it as a secondary income stream.

units.title: Steam requires typing phrase to release
units.detail: Releasing on Steam means clicking 'release my app' and then typing the exact phrase 'I want to release my app', making the moment intentional and memorable. Once within 2 weeks of the release date you can no longer change it, so you commit to launching.

units.title: Releasing games is a muscle
units.detail: The first game release is the hardest; after learning the Steam backend, every subsequent release is mostly copy-paste from previous games. Publish a small game (even a Flappy Bird clone) just to experience the full process end-to-end.

units.title: Demos double as playtesting
units.detail: Because modern marketing requires a demo, players playtest your game before launch, which catches game-breaking bugs that would otherwise surface at release. A solid demo means release day is far less buggy.

units.title: Release day bugs must be fixed fast
units.detail: If a game-breaking bug is found at launch, fix and post a patch within minutes, because overnight sales will hit a large player base with the bug. Devs often skip sleeping right after release to monitor forums and error diagnostics.

units.title: Walk away from the screen to solve problems
units.detail: Stepping away from the computer (walking the dog, warm shower) often makes stubborn problems suddenly clear. It's a free, universally recommended tip for stress and stuck game-dev problems.

units.title: Create a personal release ritual
units.detail: Mark release day with something special (e.g., ordering a giant pizza) to turn a stressful event into a motivating milestone. Rituals make the important day memorable and give you something to look forward to with each launch.

units.title: Genie 2 generates playable worlds from images
units.detail: Google's Genie 2 turns a single static image into an interactive, frame-by-frame generated world that responds to player input (move, look, interact) with physics, NPCs, and lighting. It is image generation, not a real 3D mesh world.

units.title: AI world generation degrades over time
units.detail: Genie 2 only generates up to about a minute of coherent gameplay; movement accumulates noise until the output becomes a pixelated mess. It also has long-term memory, so out-of-view geometry remains consistent when you look back.

units.title: Use AI worldgen for concept validation
units.detail: Have an artist draw concept art, feed it to a world-generating AI, and walk around the result to see your game idea in action before building. Brainstorming and idea validation is one of the strongest current use cases for this kind of AI.

units.title: Mine AI glitches for game mechanics
units.detail: The outtakes where AI generation goes wrong (ghosts appearing, spells that never stop) would be game-breaking bugs, but can inspire mechanics for your game, such as a spell that destroys the caster if held too long.

units.title: AI augments developers, not replaces them
units.detail: AI is a tool to work with you: it generates raw ideas and mess, and the human developer shapes them into a cohesive experience. It remains far from creating a creative game on its own, so game devs shouldn't quit learning.

units.title: Extract sub-meshes from combined asset meshes
units.detail: The Mesh Extractor tool lets you split a single combined mesh (e.g., a bed with mattress) into separate parts by selecting polygons manually or with 'select linked'. It exports only the needed textures/materials as a prefab.

units.title: Asset packs are one giant mesh per object
units.detail: Many asset packs ship objects as a single mesh that can't be split in-editor without 3D art skills. A mesh extractor acts as a multiplier on all assets you already own, letting non-artists get exactly the part they want.

units.title: Recolor parts without touching shared textures
units.detail: Low-poly packs often share one texture across many objects via UVs, so recoloring the original texture would recolor everything. Extract a part as its own mesh, export only its texture, then recolor just that isolated texture.

units.title: Extractor works on skinned meshes
units.detail: You can select parts of skinned meshes (e.g., a character's hat) and swap/cut them between characters for customization and variation, not just static geometry.

units.title: Export extracted meshes to FBX for Blender
units.detail: Extracted parts are saved as Unity assets, but Unity's FBX exporter package can convert them to FBX for use in Blender or other 3D modeling software.

units.title: Escape tutorial hell by building on courses
units.detail: Don't blindly copy-paste tutorials; use them to learn then modify and expand the result into something unique. A student took a course game and overhauled it (new map, art, mechanics, clients, levels), which is the strongest way to actually learn gamedev.

units.title: Small design change can transform gameplay
units.detail: Changing where recipes are delivered (from a fixed counter to a client-chosen table each time) completely changes how the game plays. Similarly, requiring dish washing adds meaningful new work loops. Small mechanical additions can drastically alter game feel.

units.title: Finish and publish your first project
units.detail: Taking a prototype to the finish line (polish, level progression, upgrades) and publishing to Steam teaches a massive amount even if it sells nothing. Publishing is an essential part of becoming a game developer.

units.title: Tactile micro-interactions drive satisfaction
units.detail: Supermarket Simulator's success comes from forcing the player through many tiny tactile actions: scanning each item, taking money, giving exact change. Automating those steps into one click would remove the satisfaction, proving more required actions can mean better gameplay.

units.title: Polish the actions players repeat most
units.detail: The game looks janky in places but is very well polished where it counts: the moment-to-moment interactions players do constantly, plus a satisfying meta progression of incremental upgrades. Spend limited time/resources polishing the repeated loop, not unused details.

units.title: Demo/prologue can unlock wishlist growth
units.detail: Supermarket Simulator had only ~2,000 wishlists until it launched a prologue (demo); a month and a half later it had ~70,000. A great demo showing the core loop can drive massive wishlist growth even when visuals are weak.

units.title: Players don't care about assets or AI art
units.detail: Players only want a fun game; they don't care whether assets were handmade, bought, or that the capsule image was AI-generated. This genre proves you can succeed with simple visuals and an interesting theme.

units.title: Steam's scale means a market for every genre
units.detail: With ~300 million monthly active users and varied preferences, there's demand for almost any kind of game. Comments saying 'I'd never play this' actually highlight how a genre can still be huge for other audiences.

units.title: Genre choice is the biggest success factor
units.detail: Supermarket Simulator (interaction/simulator genre) made ~$28M while the far more polished Bionic Bay (platformer) made ~$250k. If your goal is to make a living, genre selection matters more than visuals or polish; games that look stunning still fail in crowded genres.

units.title: Estimate revenue from review counts
units.detail: Apply a multiplier of 20-70 (roughly 40 as a middle ground) to review count to estimate units sold. Example: 65,000 reviews x 40 = ~2.6M copies of Supermarket Simulator, though discounts and price point mean revenue is lower than units x full price.

units.title: Gross revenue hides the real picture
units.detail: $250k gross on a 4-year, 3-person project nets to roughly $8k per developer per year after Steam's 30% cut, refunds/chargebacks (5-10%), and ~40% income tax. Always evaluate revenue against costs, team size, and dev time.

units.title: Pick genres with high success odds
units.detail: Analysis of Steam tags shows craft/build/sim genres (RTS, city builder, farming, management, survival, building) have ~20% of titles reaching 500 reviews, versus ~4-5% for puzzle platformers and shmups. 500 reviews (~20k copies) puts a game in the top 2-3% of indies.

units.title: Interaction games: simple core, themed skin
units.detail: Most successful simulator games are built on the same simple core: a character controller, movable objects, and an interaction system (look + interact). The theme on top (supermarket, crime scene cleanup, card shop, contraband checking) is what differentiates them.

units.title: 'Mistake' only matters if profit is the goal
units.detail: Choosing a hard genre is only a mistake from the viewpoint of maximizing money. Making games for fun or passion is perfectly valid; just don't expect a puzzle platformer you made for fun to sell a million copies.

units.title: Weak visuals hurt wishlists, not gameplay
units.detail: Supermarket Simulator sat at ~2,000 wishlists for months because its subpar visuals failed to attract interest; the game only blew up to 70,000 wishlists after a demo proved the gameplay. Don't conclude visuals don't matter - they hurt at first, and a great demo overcame them.

units.title: Create reusable Unity Hub project templates
units.detail: Unity Hub's Templates tab lets you turn any existing project into a custom, reusable template with name, description, version, and icon, so new projects start with your preferred structure and pre-installed packages instead of duplicating folders by hand.

units.title: Template checkbox must include project settings
units.detail: If you don't enable the 'project settings' checkbox when creating a template, spawned projects will use the built-in render pipeline instead of URP and the legacy input manager instead of the input system, breaking your intended setup.

units.title: Templates version via source control
units.detail: Custom templates support a versioning system that can integrate with source-control providers, letting you update a template from version to version. Sharing templates with others is not yet a first-class feature.

units.title: Arduino vs Raspberry Pi
units.detail: Arduino is a microcontroller with pins you control via simple code, best for simple control, servos, and sensors; Raspberry Pi is a full computer with an OS, USB, HDMI, and audio ports, best for complex logic.

units.title: Fitness as an RPG leveling loop
units.detail: Weightlifting works like an RPG: each rep earns experience, and consistent grinding raises your level, then you pick up heavier weight and keep leveling. There is no level cap, so the loop continues for life.

units.title: Project Auditor sanity checks whole project
units.detail: A Unity static-analysis suite that audits scripts, assets, settings, and build reports, producing a prioritized list of potential issues and recommendations. It's built into Unity 6.4 (Window > Analysis) and installable via Package Manager on older versions.

units.title: Treat tool suggestions as judgment calls
units.detail: Static-analysis findings are suggestions, not bugs. Group by severity, review each with context, and only apply the changes that genuinely fit your code path before blanket-applying them.

units.title: LoadImage keeps CPU-readable texture copy
units.detail: ImageConversion.LoadImage defaults to keeping a CPU-accessible copy of the image, wasting memory. Pass markNonReadable:true when the CPU won't read the texture back; it still renders correctly and is cheaper.

units.title: Avoid AddComponent in frequently-updated code
units.detail: Adding/removing components every frame is costly; prefer instantiating prefabs with components pre-attached. It's only a real problem in per-frame paths, not one-time setup.

units.title: Object pool frequently spawned objects
units.detail: Object.Instantiate is expensive (CPU time + managed allocation). For spawn/destroy loops like bullet-hell shooters, use an object pool instead; for rare spawns a plain Instantiate is fine.

units.title: Raycast allocates; use NonAlloc overload
units.detail: Physics.Raycast allocates managed memory each call. For frequent casts, use the RaycastNonAlloc variant that fills a preallocated buffer. Sparse casts can keep the normal version.

units.title: Read/write mesh flag duplicates mesh data
units.detail: Marking a model/mesh read/write enabled duplicates its data in memory for CPU access. Disable the flag once your runtime mesh modifications are done; inline Unity-generated meshes may be .asset files you can't change.

units.title: Resources folder tradeoffs
units.detail: The Resources folder is convenient but ships all contents regardless of use, bloating builds. Prefer AssetBundles or Addressables; an intentional Resources usage is still fine, you just should know why.

units.title: Enable SRP batcher on custom shaders
units.detail: Shaders not compatible with the SRP batcher skip a cheap draw-call optimization. Enable it on your custom shaders; built-in assets like TextMeshPro shaders may still show as incompatible.

units.title: Prune layer collision matrix
units.detail: Leaving every layer-collision box ticked increases CPU work for collision detection. Disable pairs you never collide (e.g., all 2D physics if unused) to save performance.

units.title: Use build report to shrink builds
units.detail: The build report lists what's bloating your build size. Disable splash screen, use managed stripping, optimize mesh data, and pre-bake collision meshes to reduce footprint.

units.title: Underserved Audience Method for game ideas
units.detail: Instead of 'what game do I want to make', ask 'what audience is served badly?'. Find a game with lots of reviews but negative ratings: demand is proven, execution was bad, so beating them on execution captures that audience.

units.title: SteamDB search for underserved games
units.detail: On SteamDB filter by a game tag (job simulator, management, base building, life sim, colony sim), games only, min ~100 reviews, min ~5% rating, then sort by worst rating. This surfaces popular-but-disappointing titles worth one-upping.

units.title: Estimate sales from review count
units.detail: The 'box art method' estimates copies sold as reviews × ~30-100 (use 40-50). ~100 reviews ≈ 4-5k copies; at $10 that's ~$50k gross, already top 10% of Steam.

units.title: Mine reviews for fixable pain points
units.detail: Read reviews of the target game: repeated complaints tell you what not to do, positives tell you what players loved. Only act on problems a small team can fix (e.g., bad controls, UI, bugs, progression) not scale complaints like 'isn't GTA'.

units.title: Make games in the demand/passion Venn
units.detail: Validate demand first, then build the overlap of 'you want to play it', 'you want to make it', and 'it has players'. Never make genres you dislike just for money—you can't execute well on them.

units.title: Inflated review counts are traps
units.detail: Reviews can be inflated by deep-discount pricing, one-time streamer anomalies, or impossible player expectations. Check pricing history on SteamDB and be wary of genres where players compare to AAA titles.

units.title: Prototype visually before building
units.detail: After filtering, validate the audience with GIFs and short-form video prototypes before full development. Since demand is already proven, you mainly need to execute well to capture it.

units.title: Tilemap needs 2D packages installed
units.detail: The built-in Tilemap requires the 2D Sprite and 2D Tilemap Editor packages. 2D template projects include them; otherwise install via Package Manager (Unity Registry) first.

units.title: Slice sprite sheet before paletting
units.detail: Set sprite mode to Multiple, correct pixels-per-unit, open Sprite Editor, slice by grid cell size (or automatic if evenly spaced), apply, then drag the texture into the Tile Palette to generate per-tile assets.

units.title: Tile gaps fixed by sprite atlas
units.detail: Misaligned tiles show seam lines. Create a Sprite Atlas, add the texture, and gaps disappear at build/runtime—the atlas only packs when the game runs, so seams remain visible in the editor play view.

units.title: Stack tilemaps with sorting order
units.detail: Duplicate the tilemap for foreground layers (e.g., background/over/details) and raise the sorting order (e.g., 10). Pick the active tilemap from the dropdown to paint on the right layer.

units.title: Offset tile placement between cells
units.detail: To place tiles straddling grid corners, either move the tilemap object by half a cell or change the tile anchor (0.5 = center, 0,0 = bottom). Both give sub-cell positioning control.

units.title: Add rotated tiles in palette edit mode
units.detail: Enter Tile Palette edit mode, ctrl-click to copy tiles, make duplicates, then rotate each by 90/180/270 with the select tool. Save and exit to paint the rotated variants. Adjust each sprite's pivot in the Sprite Editor to change placement.

units.title: Tile scale doesn't shrink grid cell
units.detail: Scaling a palette tile only scales the sprite, not the grid occupancy, so scaled tiles can't sit flush. For small details, create a second grid with a smaller cell size (e.g., 0.5) instead.

units.title: Tilemap Collider adds world collisions
units.detail: Duplicate a tilemap, add the Tilemap Collider component, erase tiles you want non-solid, and every remaining tile gets a collider. This makes platformers trivial: draw the world, add one component.

units.title: Static system with nested MonoBehaviour
units.detail: Make the main class static (no MonoBehaviour) and nest a private MonoBehaviour subclass holding Awake/Update. A public static Create() instantiates a GameObject with the nested component if none exists, so no scene setup is needed.

units.title: Expose only needed static API
units.detail: After the static refactor the class exposes only the essentials—Create() and a GetTick() accessor—while the tick timer and GameObject lifecycle stay hidden inside. Callers no longer manage objects or subscribe to implementation details.

units.title: Scenarios as progression with objectives
units.detail: Structure progression as scenarios: each has different visuals, build area, guest preferences, and research, completed via objectives (reach a rating, guest count). A degree-of-completion option lets players advance early or chase bonus objectives.

units.title: Guest preference systems add depth
units.detail: Spawn guests with preference profiles (favorite arena type/layout/size); they visit everything but prioritize matches and pay more when all preferences match. Give players a window to see current preferences so they can plan the park.

units.title: Advertising as late-game worker sink
units.detail: Once all research in a scenario is done, keep the lab/workers busy with an advertising system (flyers, newspaper, TV) that adds a guest bonus multiplied by park rating. This keeps a system engaging past its original purpose.

units.title: Longer months smooth per-month stats
units.detail: When buildings take a long time to complete, a short month makes monthly aggregates inconsistent. Extend the month (e.g., 1000 ticks to 1700) so each monthly value is smoother and easier to read as good/bad.

units.title: Overlap state phases to cut wait time
units.detail: Instead of strictly sequential arena phases (fight → leave → clean → setup), run the phases concurrently—guests leave while workers clean while they set up. Removes dead time and keeps stats smoother.

units.title: Batch mesh data before GPU upload
units.detail: Updating a dynamic mesh per-quad (add vertex/uv/triangle + upload each) is very slow. Fill plain arrays for all quads first, then set the mesh once at the end. Cut a 500ms hang to ~20ms by uploading once.

units.title: Monthly tip window teaches systems
units.detail: Ship a small end-of-month stats window with an assistant tip. Tutorials can't teach everything, so periodic tips explain one system at a time—cheap ongoing onboarding that also surfaces what guests complain about.

units.title: Transparent Unity window via DWM margins
units.detail: Call DwmExtendFrameIntoClientArea (DWM API) with MARGINS = -1 to get a sheet-of-glass effect making the Unity window background transparent. Requires a real build, not the editor.

units.title: DllImport to call Win32 API
units.detail: Use [DllImport("user32.dll")] from System.Runtime.InteropServices to call external Win32 functions (e.g., MessageBox). pinvoke.net documents signatures with C# examples for nearly every Win32 function.

units.title: Transparency needs specific build settings
units.detail: The effect requires: 'Use Flip Mode on Swap Chain' disabled, full screen windowed mode, built-in render pipeline, and camera background black with 0 alpha. Missing any of these breaks the transparency.

units.title: Guard Win32 hacks from the editor
units.detail: Running SetWindowLong click-through inside the Unity editor breaks the editor (clicks go through it). Wrap window-style code in #if !UNITY_EDITOR and restart Unity if it already ran.

units.title: Click-through + always-on-top windows
units.detail: SetWindowLong with WS_EX_LAYERED | WS_EX_TRANSPARENT makes the window click-through; SetWindowPos with HWND_TOPMOST keeps it above everything. Enable Run in Background (or Application.runInBackground) so it keeps running when unfocused.

units.title: Pixel click-through breaks alpha fades
units.detail: Per-pixel chroma-key click-through forces each pixel fully transparent or opaque, mangling alpha fades. A physics-based approach (raycast for colliders under the mouse, toggle WS_EX_TRANSPARENT) preserves fades and lets you define exact clickable regions.

units.title: Damageable interface unifies object types
units.detail: Define an IDamageable interface with one Damage() method and implement it on trees, logs, stumps, players, and parts. Combat and collision code then work against the interface, not concrete types, reusing one system across ~5 object kinds.

units.title: Tree chops into physics-driven prefabs
units.detail: When a tree's health hits zero, spawn a log + stump prefab with a Rigidbody and collider, offset slightly up and with random rotation so it actually topples. Smoke particles hide the swap. Deeper health events spawn smaller pieces.

units.title: Velocity-gated collision damage
units.detail: On collision enter, only deal damage if the other object implements IDamageable AND relative velocity exceeds a threshold, so light taps don't hurt. Randomize the damage amount and show a popup.

units.title: Falling logs stick without bounciness
units.detail: A log with bounciness 1 physics material gets a natural bounce on landing; removing it makes falls stiff and unsatisfying. Also spawn with slight random rotation or the log won't topple at all.

units.title: Satisfying small actions sell games
units.detail: Valheim's success comes partly from mundane actions being satisfying: chop a tree, it splits, falls with real physics, can knock down other trees, and hurts you if you stand under it. Simple systems can dramatically improve feel and believability.

units.title: Cinemachine impulse for screen shake
units.detail: Add a Cinemachine ImpulseSource on the player, fire GenerateImpulse() on hits, and attach an ImpulseListener to the camera (set up as a FreeLook orbiting camera) for easy, low-code screen shake.

units.title: FunctionTimer: fire action after delay
units.detail: A simple class holds an Action and a float timer; Update() counts down with Time.deltaTime and invokes the Action once it hits zero. A destroyed-flag guards against re-triggering every frame.

units.title: Static factory hides MonoBehaviour plumbing
units.detail: Keep the timer a plain class and nest a static MonoBehaviour hook that forwards Update(). A static Create(action, time) factory builds the timer + GameObject, wires the hook, and destroys them after firing—so callers just do FunctionTimer.Create(action, 3f).

units.title: Timers leave garbage GameObjects
units.detail: If the timer GameObject isn't destroyed after firing, dead timers accumulate as garbage. Pass the GameObject into the timer and Destroy it in the destroy-self step; also re-init the active-timer list when the scene reloads (null sentinel GameObject).

units.title: Cancel timers by name from a static list
units.detail: Track all active timers in a static list; give each an optional string name and StopTimer(name) iterates and destroy-selfs matching timers. Extra features like unscaled delta time and stop-all-with-name exist in the utilities version.

units.title: Cutscenes as chained timed actions
units.detail: Script cutscenes as a sequence of FunctionTimer calls (move character, wait, zoom, show bars, hide bars). Each timed action is one line, producing complex sequencing with no coroutine state machines.

units.title: Unity UGC adds modding to any game
units.detail: Unity's User Generated Content service lets developers define what content is (levels, weapons, quests—content is just bytes), lets creators build/upload mods (in-game tools, web Creator Center, or future Unity Bridge), and players browse/install. It's engine-agnostic and in open beta.

units.title: UGC package hidden until preview enabled
units.detail: The com.unity.services.ugc package is marked pre-release during open beta, so enable pre-release packages in Package Manager Project Settings (or add by name) before it appears. Link the project ID and enable UGC in the LiveOps dashboard first.

units.title: Anonymous auth limits creator web access
units.detail: Anonymous sign-in lets players download content but creators can't manage their mods in the web portal with it. Use a persistent auth method (e.g., username/email) if creators should manage mods outside the game.

units.title: FileStream with using to avoid leaks
units.detail: Open the mod file as a FileStream for the content upload, and always wrap it in a using block (or manually Dispose) so the stream is released—forgetting leaks memory. Do the same for the thumbnail stream.

units.title: Upload and download UGC content
units.detail: CreateContentAsync with CreateContentArgs(name, description, stream) uploads a mod; GetContentsAsync returns paginated results; GetContentAsync(id) fetches a Content, then DownloadContentDataAsync fills a byte[] you can decode however you like.

units.title: UGC tags use IDs, not display names
units.detail: When passing a tags list to CreateContentArgs you must use each label's unique internal ID (defined in dashboard Service Settings > Labels), not the display name. Content names/descriptions are plain strings.

units.title: Subscriptions track kept mods
units.detail: Downloading works without subscribing, but subscribing (CreateSubscriptionAsync by content ID) is how players track mods they want kept/updated. GetSubscriptionsAsync returns page results; the subscription carries its Content so you can download it.

units.title: UGS APIs share one pattern
units.detail: All Unity Gaming Services tools (Lobby, Relay, Matchmaker, Game Server Hosting, UGC) follow the same init → authenticate → call-async pattern, so learning one makes the rest easy to pick up.

units.title: Clean code makes big refactors tiny
units.detail: Because the course code has minimal dependencies, converting a full turn-based strategy game from square to hex grid touched only two classes—the grid system and pathfinding—while AI, actions, and visuals worked unchanged.

units.title: Encapsulate systems to enable expansion
units.detail: Writing systems with as few dependencies as possible means future expansions (new mechanics, different grid layouts) are low-risk additions rather than rewrites. Good architecture is an investment in extensibility.

units.title: Lock an Inspector to inspect another object
units.detail: Right-click an Inspector window and lock it; it keeps showing the current object while you select others elsewhere. Lets you edit/inspect one object while working on a different selection.

units.title: Drag objects into a locked Inspector list
units.detail: With an Inspector locked, select multiple objects in the hierarchy and drag them onto a list field (e.g. a Sprite array) in the locked inspector to fill the whole list in one drag.

units.title: Normal and Debug inspectors side by side
units.detail: Set one inspector to Debug mode and keep another in Normal to view the same object's public and hidden internal fields at once, useful for debugging.

units.title: Move a pivot object, not the camera
units.detail: Keep the actual camera static and move a separate pivot/target object that the camera follows and looks at. Movement, rotation and follow logic stay trivial and reusable.

units.title: World-space movement ignores object rotation
units.detail: Adding an input vector straight to transform.position moves in world space, so after rotating the object the W key strays instead of moving forward. Build direction from the object's local forward/right axes and scale by the input components instead.

units.title: Rotate around Y, not X/Z, in 3D
units.detail: For a 3D camera, only modify the Y euler angle for rotation; changing X or Z tips the camera into unusable angles. Verify the desired axis in the scene view.

units.title: Camera smoothing lags the target
units.detail: Default damping on a virtual camera makes it lag behind the moved target. Set the body X/Y/Z damping and the aim horizontal/vertical damping to zero for a snappy 1:1 camera.

units.title: Edge scrolling from mouse position
units.detail: Derive a pan direction from the mouse pixel position: if it is within a threshold of the left/right/top/bottom screen edge, move the camera that way. Gate it behind a boolean so players can toggle it.

units.title: Drag-to-pan by tracking mouse delta
units.detail: Store the last mouse position, compute the per-frame delta while the button is held, then translate the camera by the delta scaled by a pan speed. Convert the 2D delta into the 3D movement plane.

units.title: Two ways to zoom a camera
units.detail: Zoom can be achieved either by moving the camera closer to the target or by changing the field of view. The two feel different, so choose based on the desired effect.

units.title: Mouse scroll wheel is a Vector2
units.detail: Scroll input is a Vector2 because some mice scroll horizontally; read the Y component for zoom, not the raw value.

units.title: Toggle optional camera features
units.detail: Refactor each input method (edge scrolling, drag pan) into its own handler function gated by a bool, so features can be enabled or disabled from the inspector without editing logic.

units.title: Null-conditional operator for events
units.detail: Use ?. to invoke events or access members only when the target is non-null, removing verbose null checks, e.g. event?.Invoke(...). This is especially handy for event invocation.

units.title: Continuous collision detection stops tunneling
units.detail: Discrete CCD only checks at fixed time steps, so fast objects can pass through thin walls. Continuous CCD sweeps the object along its whole path to catch those collisions.

units.title: HelpURL attribute for custom scripts
units.detail: Decorate custom components with HelpURL so the inspector's help button opens your own documentation URL, useful for custom tools and shared code.

units.title: Mark assets dirty to surface unsaved changes
units.detail: Call EditorUtility.SetDirty on modified objects or scripts so Unity shows the unsaved-change indicator, preventing data loss when building editor tools.

units.title: URP ebook covers rendering and optimization
units.detail: Unity's free 120-page URP ebook moves from basics through lighting, shadows, reflections, custom shaders and performance optimization, and is a good self-study resource.

units.title: A satisfying core loop sells a simple game
units.detail: Power Wash Simulator's appeal is the satisfying act of transforming a dirty environment into a clean one; a deceptively simple mechanic done well can outperform complex ones.

units.title: Public-company disclosure explains silence
units.detail: A company under a pending merger must file disclosures and cannot speak freely, which explains sparse public communication during the deal period.

units.title: Hybrid DOTS workflow
units.detail: Don't go all-in on DOTS: use plain GameObjects where they make sense and entities where performance demands, mixing both approaches in one project.

units.title: UI Toolkit separates structure/style/logic
units.detail: Building UI with decoupled structure, stylesheet and logic lets you swap entire visual themes (e.g. per team) without recompiling code, and works for both editor and runtime UI.

units.title: Swap render pipelines per platform
units.detail: Unity planned support for URP and HDRP in one project so you can ship HDRP on console and URP on mobile from the same content, easing pipeline switching.

units.title: Update live games without new builds
units.detail: Cloud Content Delivery built on addressables lets you push content updates to a shipped game without uploading a whole new build.

units.title: Test multiplayer without separate builds
units.detail: Multiplayer Play Mode runs multiple game instances inside the same editor, and network simulation tools can test latency spikes, jitter and random disconnects.

units.title: XRI abstracts VR and AR devices
units.detail: The XR Interaction Toolkit handles interactions across VR and AR devices uniformly, avoiding per-device if-chains for input and logic.

units.title: Movie-grade VFX tools come to Unity
units.detail: Unity's Weta acquisition brings path-traced lighting, physics-based fluid/fire/hair simulation and puppet rigging into the engine for hyper-realistic visuals.

units.title: Scan asset libraries for realism
units.detail: Acquired libraries of scanned real-world objects, like Weta's, parallel Quixel Megascans and give hyper-realistic games a big head start on art assets.

units.title: Engine skills transfer across industries
units.detail: An engine used for movies, VFX, architecture and automotive means the skills you learn apply beyond games, strengthening the case for investing in a widely-adopted engine.

units.title: Incremental GC avoids frame spikes
units.detail: Instead of one giant stop-the-world collection, incremental garbage collection spreads the work over many frames, removing huge single-frame frametime spikes.

units.title: Instant play mode needs manual static reset
units.detail: Entering Play Mode without domain reload skips recompilation so static fields persist between plays; you must reset them yourself to avoid stale state.

units.title: LRP renamed to Universal Render Pipeline
units.detail: The lightweight render pipeline was renamed URP and became production-ready, with built-in post-processing replacing the separate v2 package and official 2D shader graph support.

units.title: Release cadence: tech vs LTS
units.detail: New features ship in tech releases while LTS gets bug-fix-only updates, so pick the newest LTS for stability. With a 2-tech + 1-LTS yearly cadence, features also arrive continuously via packages.

units.title: One-click GPU-driven rendering wins
units.detail: GPU Resident Drawer, GPU occlusion culling and STP upscaling are checkbox-level features that need no asset prep and make games run substantially faster.

units.title: GPU occlusion culling without baking
units.detail: GPU-based culling skips the CPU and needs no pre-baked occlusion map; anything hidden behind other objects is culled automatically and dynamically.

units.title: Upscale to render cheaper
units.detail: Render at a lower resolution and upscale (STP/DLSS/FSR-style) for much higher frame rates with little visible cost, and it works on mobile compute devices too.

units.title: Adaptive Probe Volumes automate lighting
units.detail: Automatic light-probe placement plus baked, interpolatable GI bakes gives Lumen-like global illumination and easy day/night cycles without hand-placing probes.

units.title: Decouple version names from years
units.detail: Using a non-year version number (Unity 6) avoids beginners grabbing an unstable tech release just because the year number looks more current.

units.title: AI generation needs owned training data
units.detail: To legally own AI-generated outputs, all training inputs must be owned and licensed; the platform also commits to defending against copyright challenges on outputs.

units.title: Run ML models locally at runtime
units.detail: A runtime inference engine runs trained ML models in-engine on any supported platform without network access, enabling complex models even on phones.

units.title: WebGPU gives browsers GPU access
units.detail: WebGPU lets web games access the GPU directly for much higher performance, potentially reviving the browser-game era.

units.title: Price AI tools for beginners
units.detail: A paid-only subscription with no free tier and nothing included for existing Pro users excludes students; a small monthly free credit tier lets people try before buying.

units.title: Choose engine release tier by timeline
units.detail: If shipping within about six months, stay on the LTS you already use; otherwise preview or beta lets you explore new features. Beta is unstable, preview is mostly stable and feature-complete.

units.title: Unity 6 is the new stable long-term release
units.detail: Unity renamed its LTS line to just 'Unity 6'. Unity 7 is not expected until 2026, so Unity 6 is the main version developers should target for a long time.

units.title: Enable GPU rendering optimizations for free perf
units.detail: GPU Resident Drawer, GPU occlusion culling, and spatial-temporal post-processing are three features that are simple to enable (roughly a single checkbox each) and can substantially improve performance even if you are not a graphics programmer.

units.title: Adaptive probe volumes auto-place light probes
units.detail: Adaptive probe volumes automatically distribute light probes in the world instead of manual placement, enabling high-quality baked direct and indirect lighting. Bake multiple lighting scenarios and blend between them for gorgeous day/night cycles.

units.title: Multiplayer Play Mode tests netcode fast
units.detail: Multiplayer Play Mode spawns several connected editor instances instead of requiring slow full builds, so you can quickly verify multiplayer code across clients and read all consoles at once.

units.title: Server/Shared authority splits ownership across clients
units.detail: Shared authority lets ownership of objects be split across multiple clients (each owning part of the world) rather than one host owning everything, making larger multiplayer games easier to build while keeping a host-to-client connection.

units.title: Study free official sample projects
units.detail: Unity publishes complete free sample projects (Fantasy Kingdom, Time Ghost, Mega City Metro) showcasing engine features; inspecting them is a fast way to learn how systems like large-scale multiplayer or high-end rendering actually work. Note sample assets are usually non-commercial.

units.title: Support versions are as stable as LTS
units.detail: Unity now labels releases as Preview, Support, or Long-Term Support. Support versions are as stable as LTS and are the recommended choice for new projects unless you are very close to release.

units.title: uGUI for runtime UI, UI Toolkit for editor tools
units.detail: Both Unity UI (uGUI) and UI Toolkit are viable for runtime UI in Unity 6, so pick by preference. However, UI Toolkit is far superior for building editor tools; for runtime UI, legacy uGUI remains a valid, well-loved choice.

units.title: Mesh LODs generated automatically at import
units.detail: Unity 6.2 generates LOD levels automatically at import time for high-poly models, saving you from authoring LODs by hand, which is especially valuable for realistic high-poly assets.

units.title: Developer data framework gives data control
units.detail: The developer data framework provides checkboxes controlling exactly what data Unity collects from your project, down to zero data if desired (though some tools may then stop working).

units.title: Unity AI free during beta
units.detail: Unity AI is free and unlimited during its beta period, so it is a good time to experiment with generation and assistant features before pricing is set.

units.title: Use the latest LTS or support version
units.detail: Unity's versioning model (pre-release/support/LTS) means you should generally use the newest LTS or support release for new projects. Older LTS versions stay supported ~2 years, so you can remain on them if you have a reason.

units.title: Platform toolkit abstracts console APIs
units.detail: The Platform Toolkit is a single API that abstracts Xbox/PlayStation/Switch/Steam differences, so you implement one layer to compile a game for all those platforms, making console porting much easier.

units.title: URP and HDRP share a common render graph
units.detail: Unity is working toward unifying its render pipelines; both URP and HDRP now use a common render graph, an early step toward a single pipeline in the future.

units.title: Render 3D meshes inside 2D scenes
units.detail: Unity 6.3 lets 3D meshes exist in 2D scenes and be affected by 2D lights, sprite masks, and sorting layers/groups, so you can drop 3D characters into 2D games without pre-processing them.

units.title: Remove physics backend to shrink builds
units.detail: If your project (e.g., a WebGL app) doesn't use physics at all, you can disable/remove the physics backend entirely to reduce final build size.

units.title: Custom UI shaders and post-processing in UI Toolkit
units.detail: Unity 6.3 adds customizable UI shaders and post-processing filters to UI Toolkit: create a UI shader graph, assign it via a material on visual elements, or apply pre-built filters like tint/opacity/invert/grayscale/blur through filter function definitions.

units.title: Host migration keeps player-hosted games alive
units.detail: Netcode for Entities adds automatic host migration: when the host disconnects, another client takes over and the game continues. It is currently only for Netcode for Entities, not Netcode for Game Objects.

units.title: Don't use betas for production projects
units.detail: Unity explicitly recommends not using beta releases for projects in production; use them to evaluate upcoming features before they reach LTS.

units.title: Single API for screen readers across platforms
units.detail: Native desktop screen reader support extends the screen reader API beyond Android/iOS to all major desktop platforms, letting one set of APIs make games and apps accessible (Narrator, VoiceOver, TalkBack, etc.).

units.title: Project Auditor ships built-in for project health
units.detail: The Project Auditor analyzes your whole project (code, assets, settings, build reports) for potential issues and offers one-click fixes; now a core package so even beginners discover it by accident.

units.title: Runtime sprite atlases enable modding
units.detail: Creating sprite atlases at runtime (Unity 6.4) means player-imported textures added after build can be combined into atlases, keeping draw calls low while supporting mods or user-generated sprites.

units.title: ECS becomes a core engine package
units.detail: Entities (DOTS) becomes a core package in Unity 6.4, pre-installed with the editor, as a step toward eventually merging game objects and ECS into one unified workflow.

units.title: Multi-threaded Burst works on web builds
units.detail: Unity 6.4 enables multi-threading for Burst-compiled jobs on the Web platform, which was previously thought impossible; worth benchmarking how close web performance gets to native.

units.title: Render sprites without GameObject overhead
units.detail: The Render Sprite API renders sprites without instantiating GameObjects, great for bullet-heaven games or huge unit counts where thousands of objects would otherwise tank performance.

units.title: Unity UI (uGUI) is officially staying
units.detail: After earlier plans to phase out Unity UI, Unity reversed course and uGUI will be supported for many years, so continuing to use it for runtime UI is safe.

units.title: Instance ID replaced by entity ID
units.detail: Unity 6.5 replaces instance IDs with entity IDs as the unique identifier for Unity objects (both game objects and entities), a foundational step toward unifying the object model and building tools on DOTS.

units.title: AI assistant explains profiler captures
units.detail: Unity's AI assistant can analyze profiler frame captures and translate the data into plain explanations, invaluable for beginners trying to figure out why a project is slow.

units.title: Core CLR massively speeds up iteration
units.detail: Core CLR (C# and ILR) only recompiles code that actually changed instead of reloading everything, killing the long domain-reload wait and enabling hot-edit-apply even on a running device; .NET 10 and C# 14 support.

units.title: Fast Enter Play Mode doesn't reset static fields
units.detail: Disabling domain reload (Fast Enter Play Mode, which will become default) skips static field reset, so code relying on static state can break; enable it now to prepare for the change.

units.title: URP becomes the main render pipeline
units.detail: Unity's direction: HDRP remains supported but gets no new active features while URP is brought up to match it (surface cache GI, screen space reflections, physical light units, volumetric fog), so you can use one pipeline on any device.

units.title: Netcode stacks merge into one package
units.detail: Netcode for GameObjects and Netcode for Entities will merge into a single Unity Netcode package with NGO usability but an ECS backend, plus NGO compatibility via a ghost API so existing NGO games can transition and gain features like client prediction.

units.title: GameObjects get DOTS power transparently
units.detail: The end goal of Unity's unification is working with normal GameObjects while everything runs on DOTS under the hood, giving you ECS performance without directly using entities.

units.title: Ask AI for tools with tuning parameters
units.detail: Have the AI build parametric editor tools with many exposed sliders instead of one-shot output: the AI gets you ~90% there and you fine-tune the rest manually, saving far more time than raw generation.

units.title: Ask AI for options, not a single answer
units.detail: For 'how should I implement X?' questions, prompt the AI for several possible approaches and pick yourself; it is also a great research tool for systems you have never built.

units.title: Break tasks down for AI assistants
units.detail: Don't ask for an entire game; ask for one tiny specific task at a time. Small, well-scoped prompts produce much better results than huge ones.

units.title: More detail reduces AI hallucinations
