units.detail: Hallucinations come from the AI guessing your intent, so give prompts as much detail and context (including dragging in related prefabs/assets) as possible to reduce them.

units.title: Prepare generated assets for reuse
units.detail: Generate characters in T-pose to make them easier to animate and ask for sprites on a solid-colored background so they are easy to cut out later.

units.title: AI analyzes profiler captures and screenshots
units.detail: Unity AI can read profiler captures to diagnose performance (e.g., it found huge triangles from ProBuilder grey-boxing hurting frustum culling) and has vision, taking screenshots to iteratively verify its own placement work.

units.title: Unity Authentication gives players a unique ID
units.detail: Unity Authentication provides a unique identifier per player so other Unity Gaming Services (cloud save, multiplayer, etc.) know which data belongs to whom.

units.title: Anonymous login makes onboarding seamless
units.detail: Anonymous sign-in is fully automatic and invisible to the user, giving instant player IDs; you can later upgrade an anonymous account to a linked account with external providers (Google, Apple, Facebook, Steam).

units.title: Parse hex string with Convert.ToInt32
units.detail: Convert a hexadecimal string to a decimal int with Convert.ToInt32(hex, 16); the inverse uses value.ToString("x2") to get a zero-padded two-digit hex string.

units.title: Color values are normalized 0-1, not 0-255
units.detail: Unity Color uses normalized floats (0-1), so when converting to/from hex (0-255) multiply by 255 and round when going to hex, and divide by 255f when going back to a normalized value.

units.title: Split hex colors by substring offsets
units.detail: For a RRGGBB(A) string, take substrings: red at index 0, green at 2, blue at 4 (each length 2), and alpha at 6 when the string is 8 characters; then convert each pair to a normalized float.

units.title: Make hex-to-color helper with optional alpha
units.detail: Expose Color-from-hex and hex-from-Color helpers, treating an 8-character string as having alpha and making alpha an optional parameter on output so callers control whether alpha is included.

units.title: DOTS focus shifted to conversion workflow
units.detail: Instead of a separate DOTS-only editor, Unity focused on automatically converting normal GameObjects into entities at runtime, so the familiar editor workflow still works.

units.title: Entities.ForEach lambda replaces job struct boilerplate
units.detail: Instead of defining a job struct, initializing it, and scheduling it, an Entities.ForEach lambda in OnUpdate runs the logic directly; add 'ref' for read/write access and 'in' for read-only access. Capture values like deltaTime outside the lambda.

units.title: Use visual scripting to learn ECS
units.detail: Visual scripting tools built on DOTS expose a code viewer, so you can build a visual graph and read the generated queries and Entities.ForEach to learn the underlying data-oriented logic.

units.title: ECS components are structs implementing IComponentData
units.detail: Entity data components must be structs (not classes) and implement IComponentData from the Unity.Entities namespace; fields like a public float hold the data.

units.title: Baker class links MonoBehaviour to entity component
units.detail: Because an IComponentData struct can't attach to a GameObject, you create an authoring MonoBehaviour with matching fields plus a Baker<Authoring> class whose Bake method calls AddComponent to copy the authoring values into the runtime component.

units.title: SystemBase vs ISystem
units.detail: SystemBase is a managed class (requires 'partial' due to codegen) and cannot use Burst; ISystem is an unmanaged struct that can be Burst-compiled for maximum performance. Use SystemBase for simple main-thread logic, ISystem for hot paths.

units.title: Aspects group components behind a logical API
units.detail: An aspect bundles several components into one object (e.g. TransformAspect wraps position/rotation/scale plus methods like Translate), simplifying system code by hiding multi-component logic behind a clean interface.

units.title: Idiomatic foreach with SystemAPI.Query
units.detail: ECS 1.0 favors 'foreach (ref TransformAspect t in SystemAPI.Query<TransformAspect>())' which runs on the main thread; use 'ref' vs 'ro' to declare read/write vs read-only access per component.

units.title: Entities.ForEach returns a job needing scheduling
units.detail: Entities.ForEach is a job; after the lambda you must call .Run() (main thread), .Schedule() (one worker thread), or .ScheduleParallel() (multiple threads), whereas the idiomatic foreach runs immediately on the main thread.

units.title: Use SystemAPI.Time not Time.deltaTime in ECS
units.detail: Inside systems use SystemAPI.Time.DeltaTime (captured appropriately) rather than UnityEngine.Time.deltaTime so timing is correct and Burst-compatible.

units.title: Hybrid architecture: game objects for game logic, DOTS for hot paths
units.detail: DOTS does not replace game objects; keep building the game mostly with GameObjects/MonoBehaviours and use DOTS only for performance-heavy parts like masses of units, combining both for the best workflow and speed.

units.title: Learn ECS only at intermediate level
units.detail: DOTS is an advanced topic; complete beginners should stick with GameObjects and transition once they're intermediate, since the entity/component/system mindset builds on basic Unity knowledge.

units.title: DOTS is three layers: Job System, ECS, Burst
units.detail: The Data Oriented Technology Stack is C# Job System (multi-core parallel jobs with race-condition safety), Entity Component System (data-oriented code layout), and Burst compiler (turns jobs into optimized machine code).

units.title: ECS separates logic from data
units.detail: Entities are identifiers, components hold pure data, and systems process that data. Contrast with MonoBehaviours where data and functions are coupled on the same object.

units.title: Cache-friendly memory layout boosts ECS performance
units.detail: MonoBehaviour objects scatter across memory causing CPU cache misses, while ECS packs component data contiguously in groups so the CPU streams through it linearly instead of jumping around.

units.title: Prefer production-ready DOTS only after 1.0
units.detail: DOTS 1.0 released as production-ready with Unity 2022 LTS, making it safe for real projects; before that, ECS was preview/experimental and unsuitable for shipping games.

units.title: Netcode for Entities targets fast-paced multiplayer
units.detail: Netcode for Entities supports highly optimized, fast-paced games with many networked objects (e.g. shooters) compared to Netcode for GameObjects which suits small co-op games; both layer on Unity's lobby/relay/matchmaking tools.

units.title: ECS complements rather than replaces GameObjects
units.detail: GameObjects are not deprecated; ECS is extra technology for scenarios like RTS games with thousands of units, massive world streaming, large-scale simulation, and high-connection multiplayer. Rebuild only the bottleneck in ECS.

units.title: ECS fits specific high-density scenarios
units.detail: Data-oriented ECS shines for games with tons of units/effects/NPCs on low-end devices, huge streaming worlds (e.g. Elden Ring scale on mobile), and massive-scale simulations; it's a targeted tool, not a default.

units.title: Unity and Unreal target different audiences
units.detail: Unreal 5 focuses on AAA studios and film with high-fidelity tools (Nanite, Lumen, Quixel), while Unity focuses on indie developers and broad platform reach; pick your engine based on team size and visual-fidelity goals.

units.title: Emulate modular gameplay features with ScriptableObjects
units.detail: Unreal's Game Feature Plugins (decoupled modular features loaded at runtime) can be approximated in Unity using a ScriptableObject-based data architecture combined with Addressables to swap content in and out.

units.title: Nanite and Lumen tradeoff: automatic LODs vs memory cost
units.detail: Virtualized geometry generates seamless LODs automatically and real-time GI removes light baking, but consider the memory/storage cost and whether your game needs photorealistic real-time lighting.

units.title: GameObjects + attached components define behavior
units.detail: In Unity, everything is a GameObject; what you attach as components (transform, mesh filter/renderer, rigidbody, custom MonoBehaviours) defines its behavior. Add components to change what an object does.

units.title: MonoBehaviour Start/Update lifecycle
units.detail: Custom logic extends MonoBehaviour; Start() runs once when the object is created and Update() runs every frame, which is where per-frame input and physics manipulation goes.

units.title: HDRP is maintenance-only; no new features
units.detail: Unity stopped feature development on HDRP (only porting to Nintendo Switch 2 for stability); it still works but expect no future features, so don't start new projects on it.

units.title: Use URP for new Unity projects
units.detail: Unity is merging render pipelines by advancing URP up to HDRP's level (real-time GI, screen-space reflections, physical light units); use URP by default to avoid being stuck on a dead-end pipeline.

units.title: Built-in render pipeline being deprecated
units.detail: Unity is starting the official built-in render pipeline deprecation in 6.5, with availability through 6.7 LTS (roughly until 2028) for live games; existing projects can stay but new work should target URP.

units.title: Store fees and alternative payment processors
units.detail: App stores take a massive ~30% cut on in-app purchases. Unity's payment solution (via Stripe) charges roughly 5%, and avoids the store cut entirely by not using the store's payment services. Useful lever for pricing decisions on any platform.

units.title: Distribution platforms solve discoverability
units.detail: Discoverability is the biggest challenge for game devs. Publishing inside a huge ecosystem (Fortnite's 500M registered accounts / 100M MAU, Roblox's 380M MAU) gives a new massive audience without relying on store algorithms. Platform owners court creators partly to beat competitors.

units.title: Layers organize rendering and physics
units.detail: Game objects assigned to layers affect camera rendering (culling mask) and physics interactions (layer collision matrix). A camera can ignore layers (hide HUD/background objects) and a layer matrix lets you define exactly which layer pairs collide.

units.title: Raycast hits floor debris without mask
units.detail: A raycast hits every collider in its path, so ground debris gets destroyed like a solid object. Filter by layer mask so bullets only collide with the layers you choose (e.g. objects, not ground debris).

units.title: Layer masks are int bitmasks
units.detail: An int is 32 bits and Unity has exactly 32 layers, so each layer is one bit. A mask is an int where selected layers have their bit set to 1; raycast physics functions consume this int. Understanding this explains how layer masks really work.

units.title: Build masks with bitwise operators
units.detail: Collide with one layer via `1 << layerNumber`. Combine layers with bitwise OR (`(1<<9) | (1<<10)`). Hit everything except a layer by inverting with `~`. Combine exclusions using bitwise AND of two inverted masks.

units.title: Raycast hit result carries collider info
units.detail: A raycast returns a hit struct containing the collider that was struck and the exact point on it. Set the target position to the hit point so projectiles stop at obstacles and appear to collide correctly.

units.title: VFX Graph handles millions of particles
units.detail: GPU-simulated particles in VFX Graph scale to hundreds of thousands of individually simulated particles at solid framerates, something the legacy CPU particle system cannot do.

units.title: Vector fields attract particles to shapes
units.detail: A vector field is a 3D texture of voxels, each storing a direction vector (like a wind map). Pointing vectors toward a shape makes particles flow into that shape. Stored as a 3D texture or .vf file; exposed property lets you swap the field at runtime.

units.title: Bind VFX properties to scene transforms
units.detail: Instead of animating VFX graph nodes directly, link an exposed transform property to a regular scene game object via a property binder. Animate that plain object (even with a timeline) and the effect follows — an easy way to animate effects.

units.title: Noise node drives randomized values
units.detail: Sample a noise node using ever-increasing time as the coordinate to get a smooth stream of pseudo-random values between 0 and 1, then lerp between min/max exposed properties to create effects like size pulsation.

units.title: Sine on a vector is per-component
units.detail: Applying sine to a vector does not compute the sine of the vector's angle; it computes sine of each component individually, treating the input as three floats. Radians (0..2pi), not degrees (0..360), are used in wave math.

units.title: Animate effects with sine/cosine waves
units.detail: Feed increasing time into sine and cosine waves, multiply by amplitude, and use the outputs as a position. Speed scales the wave frequency; amplitude scales travel distance. Combine waves for circular/orbital motion.

units.title: Complex VFX are simple systems combined
units.detail: Impressive effects decompose into few pieces: a moving spawn position, a force field (logo shape), a noise field, plus color/size randomization. Each subsystem is simple; layering them creates the polished result.

units.title: Color blend by lifetime and distance
units.detail: Blend particle color using a lifetime gradient, then tint based on proximity to a moving sphere: compute distance from particle to sphere center, subtract radius, sample a curve so on-sphere particles return to their original color.

units.title: Runtime fee needs BOTH thresholds
units.detail: Unity's per-install fee only applies when a game is ABOVE the revenue threshold (last 12 months) AND ABOVE the lifetime install threshold. Meeting only one does not trigger the fee — people commonly misread the chart as OR.

units.title: Fee is per install above threshold
units.detail: The 20c-per-install rate applies only to installs ABOVE the threshold, not retroactively to all installs. It's also a one-time charge per user (even if they play for years), not a monthly per-user fee — 'monthly' just describes the invoicing cadence.

units.title: Fees apply per game, not per studio
units.detail: Runtime fees are assessed per game, so a flop after a hit doesn't inherit the hit's revenue/install numbers. A game only qualifies while it individually exceeds both thresholds.

units.title: Separate demo project avoids counting installs
units.detail: Free demos count as installs but never trigger the fee (zero revenue). To be safe, make the demo a separate Unity dashboard project from the final game so demo downloads never accumulate against the paid game's install count.

units.title: Install tracking uses anonymous player ID
units.detail: Installs are tracked via a randomly hashed player ID stored in the registry, with no personally identifiable data. If the connection to Unity servers fails the game still runs — the online check is non-blocking.

units.title: Install-based fees are gameable
units.detail: Piracy and scripts that repeatedly uninstall/reinstall can inflate install counts, which could matter if a game is above the revenue threshold. Trust that the provider's fraud-prevention algorithm catches this; it's an unresolved risk.

units.title: Evaluate fees against your realistic scale
units.detail: For premium PC/console indies, install thresholds (200k) are huge compared to typical Steam sales, so fee changes rarely apply. Pick an engine based on realistic expected scale; the same math does not hold for free-to-play mobile.

units.title: Generational versioning minimizes churn
units.detail: Adopting longer release cycles (a major version every 2+ years, with .1/.2 in between) reduces upgrade disruption and keeps tutorials/documentation relevant longer. Benefits learners and content creators.

units.title: Offline baking + ML inference for real-time effects
units.detail: Compute super high-quality, expensive simulations offline, use the results as training data for a model, then run the small trained model for real-time inference (e.g. cloth deformation: 1.5GB precomputed → 50MB model, 1 hour training, 8ms runtime).

units.title: GPU-resident rendering offloads work
units.detail: Keeping draw submission/occlusion on the GPU (GPU resident drawer, GPU occlusion culling) makes rendering dramatically faster, especially with massive object counts. Combined with entity-based rendering and billboards, huge scenes render in real time on consumer GPUs.

units.title: Unified pipeline: author once, target later
units.detail: Authoring shaders/cameras once and choosing the renderer tier via dropdown removes an early, hard project decision. Deprecating old pipelines gradually (marked deprecated, removed a version later) gives users years of runway. Risk: feature-set differences across tiers.

units.title: Faster iteration: recompile less, import less
units.detail: Core CLR keeps long-lived engine code from recompiling on tiny code edits and keeps the runtime on the latest .NET. A content pipeline that imports only what changed, in the background, removes blocking progress-bar waits. Both directly speed up the edit→test loop.

units.title: Wizard tools remove architecture decisions
units.detail: A questionnaire-driven tool (multiplayer center) that recommends and installs the right netcode, hosting, and services for your game genre/features removes a common early dead-end for beginners.

units.title: Host migration belongs in the engine
units.detail: In client-hosted multiplayer, the game dies when the host disconnects unless you hand-roll migration. Engine-level host migration removes a highly-requested source of custom, buggy code.

units.title: Mid-level networking abstraction
units.detail: A mid-level netcode library abstracts packets, sockets, and connections so you focus on game logic, while still supporting scene management, animation, physics sync, and diagnostics. Trade-off: less control than raw sockets, less work than rolling your own.

units.title: Small-coop netcode, not massive-scale
units.detail: Object-based netcode is designed for small-scale co-op (Overcooked/Stardew-scale), not hundreds of players. For large networked simulations you need a different stack (entity-based/ECS netcode or a third-party solution).

units.title: WebGL blocked from raw sockets
units.detail: Browser builds can't freely access IP sockets, so WebGL lacks first-class netcode support (a workaround exists). Verify platform support before committing a networked game to web export.

units.title: Modular multiplayer services
units.detail: Netcode solves game logic; separate services handle the rest — lobby (public/private rooms to find players), relay (connect through firewalls/NAT without punch-through), dedicated servers, and matchmaking. Pick the pieces you need; they slot together.

units.title: Learn from full game samples
units.detail: Downloadable, fully-featured multiplayer game samples (co-op, 2D, 200-player battleground) are excellent study material — inspect how boss fights, spawning, and animation sync are coded rather than starting from scratch.

units.title: A* ported by swapping the neighbor function
units.detail: A* pathfinding is grid-agnostic. Converting square to hex takes two changes: use the hex grid's coordinate system and change which neighbors a node returns. The open/closed list algorithm stays identical.

units.title: Hex neighbors depend on even/odd row
units.detail: A hex cell has six neighbors, but the two 'above/below' neighbors shift depending on whether the row is even or odd. Testing the wrong offsets silently breaks pathfinding — compute offsets conditionally on `row % 2`.

units.title: Rough world-distance heuristic is fine
units.detail: When an exact heuristic (hex Manhattan distance) is hard to compute, use the actual world distance between grid positions as a rough guess. Heuristics only need to be a guess, so approximate is acceptable — but G cost must stay exact (straight-move cost).

units.title: Sync playback with remote teammates
units.detail: Real-time collaboration tools let a team load any media (images, video, 360, 3D models), sync playback, pause on a frame, and annotate. Working in-browser with no lag and no dropped frames beats ad-hoc video-conference review.

units.title: Draw notes inside the engine for team review
units.detail: A high-value collaboration use case: annotate directly inside the editor (e.g. draw notes on the game view) so the whole team sees them live. Most useful for artists and teams, less so for solo programmers.

units.title: Scriptable Objects define part types
units.detail: Model each buildable part (thruster, shield, cannon, laser) as a ScriptableObject definition. Adding a new part becomes creating a new definition + prefabs, with zero changes to core logic — a flexible data-driven design.

units.title: Interfaces generalize per-type logic
units.detail: Use interfaces so save/load and activation logic work uniformly across any part type regardless of its internal behavior. This enables supporting an arbitrary number of part types cleanly.

units.title: Destroy doesn't update hierarchy instantly
units.detail: Destroy() defers the actual removal, so checking child counts or parents in the same frame still returns stale data. Fix by deferring the child check, or restructure code to not depend on immediate hierarchy state after Destroy.

units.title: String-based find breaks silently
units.detail: Locating objects by string name is brittle — a single invisible trailing space in a button's name breaks Find and yields a confusing null reference. Avoid string lookups wherever possible; prefer direct references or events.

units.title: Particle Play/Stop can't be replayed
units.detail: After calling Stop() on a particle system, calling Play() again doesn't restart emission reliably. Toggle only the emission module (enable/disable emission) instead of the whole system play state.

units.title: IDragHandler needs IBeginDragHandler too
units.detail: Implementing only IDragHandler doesn't fire drag events; you must also implement IBeginDragHandler (even unused) for the events to trigger. Small interface dependencies in Unity's event system are easy to miss.

units.title: Separate edit and play mode logic
units.detail: During editing, parts are purely visual with colliders and no logic; in play mode the ship gains a rigidbody, gravity, and per-part behavior. A save/load system converts between the two states, enabling live iteration on your build.

units.title: Cinemachine camera setup is instant
units.detail: A virtual camera with follow/look-at targets handles smooth camera tracking with good defaults out of the box. Prefer it over hand-rolling camera movement for most projects.

units.title: World-space health bars with fill amount
units.detail: Attach a UI image with a Fill Amount to a world-space canvas to get a health bar that follows the object. Connect it to health-change events to update the fill — no custom drawing needed.

units.title: Minimap via dedicated camera + render texture
units.detail: A minimap is a second camera that only renders the minimap layer into a render texture, displayed on a UI raw image. Tagging objects with the right layer controls what appears.

units.title: World drag needs a physics raycaster
units.detail: The UI event system ignores world-space colliders by default. Add a physics raycaster to the EventSystem so drag/drop and pointer events work on world objects, not just UI elements.

units.title: Reusable health system saves years of work
units.detail: A small, generic health/damage class (created once) plugs into enemies, ships, and any damageable entity across many projects. Investing in clean, reusable core systems pays off repeatedly.

units.title: Trail renderer makes instant effects
units.detail: Adding a trail renderer component with a few settings gives projectile/bullet trails in seconds. Small built-in tools like this are fast wins for visual polish.

units.title: Static factory for spawning UI windows
units.detail: Make a static method that instantiates a window prefab into the canvas, initializes it with a follow target, and sets a random position so windows don't stack. A static entry point centralizes window creation.

units.title: Shared render texture shows one view
units.detail: Multiple windows using the same render texture all display the identical camera view. Create a new render texture per window instance, assign it to that window's camera as target texture, and to the raw image as display.

units.title: Dictionary dedupes windows per target
units.detail: Track spawned windows in a dictionary keyed by the followed transform. If the key exists, a window already follows that object, so skip spawning. This enforces 'one window per target' with minimal logic.

units.title: Destroy windows instead of hiding
units.detail: When windows are spawned dynamically, Destroy() them on close rather than SetActive(false). This avoids lingering inactive instances and keeps the canvas clean, and pairs naturally with the dedupe dictionary.

units.title: Pass domain object, not Transform, to UI
units.detail: Instead of passing a Transform to a UI window, pass the game character object so the window can read name, level, stats, and subscribe to its events. This decouples the UI from raw transforms and gives it all the data it needs.

units.title: Cache component references in Awake
units.detail: Grab Text/component references once in Awake and store them in member variables instead of calling Find/GetComponent every Update frame. This avoids per-frame allocations and keeps UI updates performant.

units.title: Update UI on events, not every frame
units.detail: Instead of refreshing the UI every frame, subscribe to the data source's events (e.g., experience gained, level up) and update only the affected widgets when they fire. Set immutable values (name) once at show time, mutable ones on events.

units.title: Split static vs dynamic UI updates
units.detail: Assign values that never change (like a character name) only once when the window is shown, while values that change (level, stats, bars) are updated on events. This reduces redundant work and keeps the UI responsive.

units.title: Generate UI bars through code for portability
units.detail: Create UI elements (cinematic bars) programmatically in Awake instead of hand-placing game objects in the scene. This makes the script drag-and-drop portable across projects without manual UI setup.

units.title: Anchor min/max define UI positioning
units.detail: UI anchors use two normalized vectors: anchorMin is the lower-left corner and anchorMax the upper-right. Setting both to the same Y (1 = top, 0 = bottom) locks a bar to an edge while sizeDelta controls its thickness.

units.title: Animation runs forever without clamp
units.detail: Animating sizeDelta toward a target each frame with no stop condition makes the bar keep growing past its target. Fix by clamping size to the target once passed and using an isActive flag to skip work when idle.

units.title: Calculate per-second change amount from target
units.detail: To animate a value over a duration, compute changeAmount = (target - current) / time and add changeAmount * deltaTime each frame. Reuse the same math for both show (target > 0) and hide (target = 0).

units.title: Randomize size, speed, rotation, color for life
units.detail: Spawned effects feel natural when given variation: random size multipliers, random fall speeds, random rotation speed with random clockwise/counter-clockwise direction, and a random tint from a color array.

units.title: Cannot modify a list while foreach iterating
units.detail: Removing elements from a list inside a foreach throws an error. Iterate over a clone of the list (new list) while removing destroyed items from the original.

units.title: Spawn timer with random batch counts
units.detail: Accumulate deltaTime into a spawnTimer; when it passes a threshold, reset by adding the max and spawn a random amount (1-4) of items per tick. Gives a continuous but varied stream of objects.

units.title: Destroy spawned objects past a boundary
units.detail: Return a boolean from each object's update indicating whether it was destroyed; remove it from the active list when true. This prevents unbounded object growth and leaked instantiated objects.

units.title: Graph positions via value normalization
units.detail: Map a data value to a graph position with Y = (value / yMax) * graphHeight and X = index * xSpacing. A value equal to yMax lands exactly at the top of the graph; zero lands at the bottom.

units.title: Draw line between points with rotated rectangle
units.detail: A line segment is a thin rectangle: sizeDelta length = distance, width = thickness; position at the midpoint (a + direction * distance * 0.5); rotate Z to the direction's angle (angle-from-vector utility). Set slight transparency so lines differ from dots.

units.title: Anchor UI elements at lower-left corner
units.detail: Setting anchorMin and anchorMax to (0,0) pins a UI object to the lower-left corner, then anchoredPosition and sizeDelta place it precisely. This makes programmatic UI layout predictable.

units.title: Func delegates for customizable formatting
units.detail: Accept Func<int,string> and Func<float,string> parameters to let callers customize axis label text (e.g., 'Day 1' or '$12'). Default them to null and substitute default delegates so existing callers keep working.

units.title: Disabled template objects for UI duplication
units.detail: Create one disabled template UI element per label/dash type and Instantiate copies of it, setting the copy active and re-parenting into the container. Templates give visual control while staying hidden and reusable.

units.title: Separator placement from normalized index
units.detail: For axis separators, compute normalized = i / separatorCount (cast int to float), then Y position = normalized * graphHeight and label value = normalized * yMax. This distributes labels evenly across the axis scale.

units.title: UI scales from center unless pivot changed
units.detail: A bar scaled via sizeDelta grows from its pivot (center by default), causing wrong positioning. Setting the pivot to (0.5, 0) makes the bar scale upward from its base, so a height of 'value' originates at the bottom.

units.title: Image without sprite renders solid color
units.detail: Leaving the sprite null on a UI Image component renders a solid colored rectangle, which is the simplest way to draw bars, lines, and fills in Unity UI.

units.title: Rename refactor for consistent naming
units.detail: Rename symbols project-wide (Visual Studio Ctrl+R,R) so related objects share one vocabulary (e.g., all 'circle' references become 'dot') instead of mixing names like 'circle' and 'dotConnection'. Keeps code clean and consistent.

units.title: Bar width multiplier creates gaps
units.detail: Pass the graph-position width into the bar renderer and multiply it (e.g., 0.9) so bars are slightly narrower than their slot, producing visible gaps between adjacent bars.

units.title: Negative start index with small data lists
units.detail: Starting an iteration at list.Count - maxVisible goes negative when the list has fewer items than the window, throwing an out-of-range error. Clamp the start index with Math.Max(start, 0).

units.title: Zero difference breaks buffer math
units.detail: If all visible values are equal, max-min = 0 and adding 20% of zero gives no buffer, so the single point hugs the top. Enforce a minimum range (e.g., 5f) so scaling always has headroom.

units.title: Dynamic X spacing from graph width
units.detail: Instead of a fixed xSpacing, compute it as graphWidth / maxVisibleValueAmount (with maxVisible+1 for a right-side buffer). This keeps every value inside the graph regardless of how many are shown.

units.title: Dynamic axis range from data with buffer
units.detail: Scan the value list for min and max, then extend the axis by ~20% of the range (max - min) rather than 20% of the max. Basing the buffer on the range keeps it visually consistent even for large magnitudes.

units.title: Normalize with min offset, not zero
units.detail: When the graph doesn't start at zero, normalize positions as (value - yMin) / (yMax - yMin), and label values as yMin + normalized * (yMax - yMin). Ignoring the min offset shifts the whole graph.

units.title: Destroy previous graph before redraw
units.detail: Keep every spawned graph object in a list and destroy all entries at the start of each redraw, then clear the list. Without cleanup, re-showing the graph stacks duplicate dots and distorts the scale.

units.title: Stress-test scaling with random data
units.detail: Verify dynamic axis scaling by periodically clearing the value list, filling it with random values, and redrawing. If the graph stays within bounds across many random inputs, the scaling is robust.

units.title: Interface for swappable chart visuals
units.detail: Define an IGraphVisual interface with a common AddGraphVisual(position, width) method, implemented by BarChartVisual and LineGraphVisual classes. The graph accepts the interface, so callers swap chart types without changing graph logic.

units.title: Constructor injection of renderer dependencies
units.detail: Give each visual class a constructor that receives its dependencies (graph container, dot sprite, colors, width multiplier) and stores them as members. This keeps each visual self-contained and easily configurable at construction.

units.title: Return spawn list for unified cleanup
units.detail: Have the visual's AddGraphVisual return a list of created game objects (a line graph needs both dot and connection) so the graph can add them all to its cleanup list with AddRange.

units.title: Verify swaps with periodic visual toggle
units.detail: During development, swap the graph visual every half-second via a periodic timer to confirm both bar and line implementations render correctly. Easy visual verification that the interface abstraction works.

units.title: UI arrow pointing at off-screen world targets
units.detail: For quest markers, render an arrow in UI showing the direction to a world target while it is off-screen, then switch to a marker (cross) placed on the target when it enters the screen. This avoids a floating arrow confusing the player when the target is visible.

units.title: Convert world position to screen point to test visibility
units.detail: Use the camera's WorldToScreenPoint on the target world position. The target is off-screen if screenX<0, screenX>Screen.width, screenY<0, or screenY>Screen.height. This single conversion powers both on/off-screen detection and arrow placement.

units.title: Point a UI arrow at an off-screen target
units.detail: Direction = (targetPos - cameraPos) normalized, then convert the direction vector to an angle and apply it as the arrow's rotation (EulerAngles z). The arrow stays rotated only while the target is off-screen.

units.title: Clamp off-screen marker inside screen edges
units.detail: Cap the target's screen position to the screen bounds (optionally with a border offset) so the arrow rides the edge instead of going off-screen. A dedicated UI camera converts the capped screen position back into UI world space via ScreenToWorldPoint for correct placement.

units.title: Swap sprite and rotation between off-screen and on-screen states
units.detail: Off-screen: show arrow sprite and rotate it toward the target. On-screen: show a cross sprite and reset rotation to zero. Keeping rotation logic in a separate method called only when off-screen prevents a rotating marker over the actual target.

units.title: Show/hide API instead of fixed target setup
units.detail: Expose public Show(targetPosition) and Hide() methods so the pointer can be reused for arbitrary targets over time. The window hides by default and only becomes visible with an active target, decoupling it from any single quest.

units.title: Pass colors as constructor parameters
units.detail: Thread arrow color and cross color through the pointer factory function into the pointer constructor, then apply each color when the corresponding sprite is active. This lets each pointer instance have its own color scheme.

units.title: Use hex strings to define colors
units.detail: A helper (GetColorFromString) parses hex strings like FF0000 into color objects, and can take an alpha value. Alpha 0 produces a fully transparent marker, useful when you only want to indicate an area rather than a precise position.

units.title: Optional sprite parameters with default fallback
units.detail: Sprite parameters default to null; inside the create function, if a parameter is null, substitute the default arrow/cross sprite. Callers get sensible defaults unless they explicitly want custom sprites.

units.title: Mathf.Clamp replaces manual bounds checks
units.detail: Replace repeated if X<0 set to 0 style checks with Mathf.Clamp(screenPos.x, border, Screen.width - border), clamping X and Y in a couple of lines. Cleaner and less error-prone than hand-rolled branches.

units.title: Object per pointer instead of member variables
units.detail: Refactor so each pointer is a QuestPointer object holding its own target position, game object, and sprites, updated via its own Update. The window keeps a List of pointers and iterates them, enabling multiple simultaneous arrows.

units.title: Template game object duplicated per instance
units.detail: Keep a hidden 'pointer template' object in the UI and instantiate duplicates of it for each active pointer, setting active true on creation. Destroy removes the instance from the list and destroys its game object when a target is reached.

units.title: Hide the template object or it leaks into gameplay
units.detail: After converting to a template that gets duplicated, the original template object remains visible in-game unless you deactivate it and explicitly set the duplicates active. Forgetting this leaves a ghost arrow on screen.

units.title: Create factory returns handle for later destruction
units.detail: Have the create-pointer function return the QuestPointer instance so the caller can store it and later destroy it (e.g., when the player reaches the target). This is the standard create/return handle pattern for dynamic objects.

units.title: Use editor rename shortcut to refactor method names
units.detail: Renaming a method that is used in multiple places is error-prone by hand; use the IDE's rename refactor (Ctrl+R, Ctrl+R in Visual Studio) to update all references consistently.

units.title: Set up sprite sheet for frame animation
units.detail: Change the texture import Sprite Mode to Multiple, open the Sprite Editor, and slice by cell size (the pixel dimensions of one frame). This produces an array of individual frame sprites from a single image.

units.title: Cycle frames safely with modulo
units.detail: Advance currentFrame = (currentFrame + 1) % frameArray.Length instead of a bare increment. Without the modulo the index overflows the array at the last frame and throws an index-out-of-range error.

units.title: Timer-driven frame advance
units.detail: Accumulate Time.deltaTime in a timer; when it exceeds the frame rate interval, subtract the interval and advance the frame. A frame rate of 0.1s equals 10 frames per second.

units.title: Cache component references instead of GetComponent each frame
units.detail: Store the SpriteRenderer reference in Awake and reuse it in Update rather than calling GetComponent on every frame. This avoids expensive per-frame lookups and improves performance.

units.title: Make inspector fields serializable for setup
units.detail: Mark the frame array as [SerializeField] so the sprite frames can be dragged in from the editor. Unlocking the inspector lets you select multiple sprites and assign them in one drag.

units.title: Loop flag controls whether animation restarts
units.detail: Add a 'loop' bool and an 'isPlaying' flag. When the frame wraps back to 0 and looping is disabled, set isPlaying=false and return early from Update, freezing the animation on the last frame.

units.title: Fire events when animation loops
units.detail: Expose C# events (EventHandler) fired each time the animation wraps back to frame 0, letting other systems react. An OnAnimationLoopedFirstTime event triggered once via a loop counter is useful for one-shot gameplay hooks.

units.title: Subscribe to events from a separate handler
units.detail: A separate script subscribes to the animator's loop events (e.g., spawning a debug popup) to verify they fire correctly. This keeps the animator reusable and decouples gameplay reactions from the animation logic.

units.title: PlayAnimation swaps frames and frame rate at runtime
units.detail: PlayAnimation(frameArray, frameRate) reassigns the frame array, resets the current frame to 0, and updates the interval, so you can switch between walk/idle animations on the fly. Per-animation frame rates let a 2-frame idle animate slower than a walk cycle.

units.title: Replaying the same animation every frame resets it
units.detail: If the input-driven code calls PlayAnimation every frame even when the animation is unchanged, the animation keeps resetting to frame 0 and appears frozen. Guard with 'only play if the requested type differs from the current active type'.

units.title: Enum + switch drives animation selection
units.detail: Define an AnimationType enum (Idle, Walk) and an active-type field. On input, switch on the requested type and call the matching PlayAnimation, then store the active type. Simple, readable way to map input to animation state.

units.title: Orthographic camera size defines visible vertical units
units.detail: With an orthographic camera, the Size value is the number of world units visible vertically (half above, half below center). Horizontal extent depends on resolution, so 16:9 shows a wider view than 4:3 at the same size.

units.title: White 1x1 texture with color tint for solid-color sprites
units.detail: A single 1x1 white PNG (pixels per unit = 1) can be tinted any color via the sprite renderer's color parameter, which acts as a multiply. One texture asset serves as the basis for many colored placeholders.

units.title: Sorting layers control 2D render order
units.detail: Render order follows the sorting layer list top to bottom; objects on a later layer draw on top of earlier ones. Putting the background on its own layer and game objects on a higher layer guarantees correct draw order regardless of position.

units.title: Use icon-flagged helper object to locate positions
units.detail: A scene helper object with an icon assigned shows up clearly in the Scene and Game views (with gizmos enabled), making it easy to read and mark positions, especially while paused. Great for placing test targets.

units.title: Organize scene with a game handler container
units.detail: Parent scene objects under a single 'GameHandler' empty object and keep scripts/scenes in clearly named folders. Structure like this makes projects far easier to navigate as they grow.

units.title: Verify a library installs with a timed debug popup
units.detail: After importing a utility library, run FunctionPeriodic to spawn a text popup at the mouse position every half second. Confirming the helper fires proves the library is correctly imported and wired into the scene.

units.title: In-game level editor via runtime transform gizmos
units.detail: Runtime transform gizmos let players manipulate objects while the game is running, which turns a game into a modding platform—players build and share their own levels. A powerful way to extend engagement beyond the core game.

units.title: Embedded scripting compiles player C# at runtime
units.detail: The Roslyn C# compiler package compiles code written by players while the game runs, letting them modify the game live. Useful for modding or creative tools where players write real code against the running game.

units.title: Add polish through destruction and post-processing
units.detail: Two reliable polish levers: destruction (slicing sprites/meshes into breakable pieces) and post-processing (pixelation, noir filters). Depth-based pixelation that scales with camera distance looks notably better than uniform pixelation.

units.title: First-time-sale assets beat re-sold bestsellers
units.detail: Asset store sales repeatedly discount the same top sellers. A curated bundle of assets that have never been on sale offers more value because buyers likely own none of them—a useful lens for both buying and selecting sale bundles.

units.title: Unity is a rendering engine, not just a game engine
units.detail: Unity renders 2D/3D and runs C# logic, so it can build any interactive program—stream overlays, launchers, dashboards, companion apps. Game dev skills transfer directly to non-game software.

units.title: Reuse game code for non-game apps
units.detail: A graph component built for a game was reused in a weight-tracking app to plot CSV data. Code built for gameplay (charts, animations, UI) often transfers wholesale to non-game tools, multiplying the value of game work.

units.title: Compose UI program from transparent window plus HTTP
units.detail: A live-stream overlay was built from a transparent Unity window layered over the desktop, a named-pipe connection to a control window, and HTTP requests to a chat API. Cross-window/inter-process composition (named pipes) is a clean pattern for tool UIs.

units.title: Simulate robots before building physical hardware
units.detail: Unity's physics and rendering make it ideal for training/validating robot IK path planners in simulation, then replaying real data back. Simulate-then-build workflows reduce risk and cost for physical systems.

units.title: Unity powers industrial and AR/VR training applications
units.detail: Unity is used across architecture/engineering/construction, automotive, retail, and manufacturing—AR experiences, in-car dashboards, virtual stores, and GPS-synced building previews. Non-game markets are a major Unity use case.

units.title: URP vs HDRP target audiences
units.detail: HDRP targets consoles and PCs for the absolute best visuals; URP targets any device including mobile. Pick HDRP only when maximum graphics matter and the target platforms are high-end.

units.title: HDRP uses real-world physical values
units.detail: Set lights by temperature and intensity and cameras by sensor size, ISO, and shutter speed using real-world values. Photography knowledge transfers directly and gives realistic results.

units.title: Decals add realism to scenes
units.detail: Place many decals throughout a level to break up perfectly clean surfaces and make scenes feel natural and alive. Disabling them makes a scene look too clean and artificial.

units.title: Spread light and reflection probes across levels
units.detail: Place light probes throughout the level for baked indirect light and separate reflection probes for different areas (outside vs inside) so objects receive correct ambient and reflection info.

units.title: Local volumes override post-processing per area
units.detail: Use local volumes with a blend distance to change exposure and other post-processing as the camera moves between areas (bright exterior to dark corridor). A global volume holds base settings like bloom, screen-space reflections, grain, and motion blur.

units.title: VFX Graph for ambient particles
units.detail: Ambient particles like butterflies, falling leaves, and dust are built with the VFX Graph using spawn/initialize/update/output blocks and can be reused by copy-pasting into your own projects.

units.title: Light Explorer audits all scene lights
units.detail: Unity's Light Explorer window (Window > Rendering > Lighting) lists every light with temperature, intensity, and range in one place, handy for auditing and tweaking a whole scene's lighting.

units.title: HDRP can be performant on modest hardware
units.detail: A detailed HDRP showcase scene ran at 80-100 FPS on a five-year-old GPU, so photoreal graphics in HDRP don't necessarily require top-end hardware if the scene is well built.

units.title: Evaluate pricing changes against your own use case
units.detail: License/pricing changes affect each developer differently based on scale and monetization. Instead of reacting emotionally, analyze how the change impacts your specific games and act accordingly.

units.title: Voice feedback respectfully, don't harass
units.detail: Companies read community feedback, so make your voice heard on official forums, but don't harass public-facing indie/community people who have no power to change policy.

units.title: Retroactive term changes destroy trust
units.detail: Changing pricing terms after developers have committed is hard or impossible to fully recover from; clarifying edge cases is not enough once developer trust is lost.

units.title: Engine tech and company decisions are separate
units.detail: Even amid vendor controversies, the engine itself remains capable. Developers can keep using a tool that fits their workflow while disagreeing with the vendor's business decisions.

units.title: Vendors send creators hardware and swag
units.detail: Engine and platform vendors send creators boxes of merch, notebooks, and dev kits as community outreach. It is marketing and goodwill, not a signal about product quality.

units.title: Unity consolidating on URP, HDRP stable
units.detail: Unity is moving all development effort to URP, keeping HDRP stable with no new features, and deprecating the built-in render pipeline. Eventually one render pipeline will serve mobile through high-end.

units.title: Real-time GI without lightmaps in URP
units.detail: URP is adding real-time global illumination with light bounces and no lightmap setup, fully scalable so it works on mobile as well as high-end, giving nice indirect lighting with zero baking workflow.

units.title: Use checkpoints when letting AI edit projects
units.detail: AI editing tools are not 100% reliable and can break a project. Snapshot/checkpoint before each AI action so you can roll back and retry without fear when it does something unwanted.

units.title: AI tools augment developers, not replace them
units.detail: Presented AI use cases (building levels from existing assets, profiler analysis, UI from sketches, scene annotations) speed up prototyping and tedious work but still need a developer. They are optional and can be disabled.

units.title: Use AI to analyze profiler bottlenecks
units.detail: Profiler output is overwhelming for beginners. Asking an AI to find hotspots and suggest fixes from captured frame data turns raw performance data into actionable optimization steps.

units.title: CoreCLR brings hot reload and modern .NET
units.detail: Moving Unity from Mono to CoreCLR gives hot reload by default, cuts compile-and-wait iteration time, and jumps Unity to the latest .NET/C# versions.

units.title: Unity pushing hard on web capabilities
units.detail: Unity is adding Burst/compiled C# jobs and compute shaders on web via WebGPU, plus higher memory limits, enabling multi-threaded and VFX-heavy games to run in the browser.

units.title: AI can prototype casual games today
units.detail: AI is already good at generating simple casual games like Flappy Bird or Subway Surfers-style clones. Complex, cohesive, polished games are still far beyond current AI.

units.title: Good AI output requires domain knowledge
units.detail: Impressive AI demos work because creators ask many follow-up questions. Someone with no game dev knowledge gets weak results, so you must understand the tool and the craft to get good output.

units.title: AI is a tool, not a replacement
units.detail: Like a hammer helping a carpenter, AI makes you more efficient but doesn't replace you. Competitive advantage remains humans plus tools versus other humans plus tools.

units.title: Use AI to validate many game ideas cheaply
units.detail: With idea selection critical, use AI to build quick prototypes of many concepts, test which have potential, then rebuild the winners from scratch with a proper codebase for polish.

units.title: Prototypes communicate vision across roles
units.detail: Non-coders can AI-vibe-code rough prototypes to show coders what they want, just as programmers sketch for artists. A rough prototype is a communication tool, not a final product.

units.title: Features can be must-have for some, useless for others
units.detail: A mechanic can be an absolute must-have for one player segment and completely ignorable for another (e.g., inventory automation for hardcore players). Features appeal to niches; pick what your audience values.

units.title: Inventory quality-of-life features
units.detail: Shift-click moving, bulk transfer between inventories, item comparison, and storage lookup are cheap additions that hardcore players in loot-heavy games deeply value.

units.title: Cutscenes must be pausable and skippable
units.detail: Never force players through long cutscenes with no pause or skip. Use hold-to-skip so a single button press doesn't accidentally skip, and a press should never skip by default.

units.title: Make intro studio logos skippable
units.detail: Long intro logo sequences before a game annoy players, especially with many involved studios. If you show them, always provide a way to skip them.

units.title: Switch input glyphs based on last input device
units.detail: Automatically detect the last touched input (keyboard vs gamepad) and swap UI glyphs accordingly, so players seamlessly switch devices without digging through options menus.

units.title: Detect last input with Unity Input System
units.detail: Unity's new Input System lets you listen for which device last provided input and swap active glyphs via an event, making keyboard/gamepad auto-switching easy.

units.title: Movable and scriptable UI for hardcore players
units.detail: Hardcore players (MMO raiders) expect movable HUD windows and even scripting to build custom UI. Fixed UI will drive away players who would otherwise play thousands of hours.

units.title: Add a petting interaction for animals
units.detail: A simple pet-the-dog/cat interaction (one animation plus one interaction) delights players. The 'can you pet the dog' community has hundreds of thousands of followers, so it's cheap goodwill.

units.title: Allow left/right shoulder aim in third-person
units.detail: Let players pick the default aim shoulder via a simple horizontal camera offset. It fixes cover blind spots and is mechanically useful, but few games offer it.

units.title: Every feature costs time; prioritize
units.detail: Even 'simple' features cost days of implementation. With limited time, build a priority list of player-pleasing features and implement the ones your audience most values, going down the list as far as you can.

units.title: Vibe coding means accepting AI output blindly
units.detail: Vibe coding is prompting an AI, accepting whatever it outputs without reading it, and re-prompting on errors. It works for throwaway weekend projects but not for code you must maintain.

units.title: Code is deterministic, AI output is random
units.detail: The same code always produces the same result, so you can reason about and fix it. Vibe coding instead relies on the randomness of AI generation, making debugging guesswork.

units.title: AI is terrible at debugging
units.detail: Surveyed founders say AI coding tools fail at debugging, which is most of the programming work. You must understand the code to instruct the AI precisely, so you may as well have written it.

units.title: AI speedups apply to prototypes, not production
units.detail: AI makes you a 10x engineer at prototyping, but production code needs someone who understands the codebase. Rolling the dice on AI for a real business feature is an insane way to operate.

units.title: Programs must be 100% correct, images 99%
units.detail: An image with small artifacts still works, but a program with one wrong line out of a thousand may fail entirely. You can't 'roll again' like image generation when code must be exact.

units.title: Fix one bug, don't rewrite the program
units.detail: If you understand the code, a one-line bug (e.g., score += 2 instead of += 1) is a tiny fix. AI workflows rewrite thousands of lines for one bug, creating thousands of new lines you must re-understand.

units.title: Parallel AI windows don't speed you up
units.detail: Running two AI coding windows on two features at once is multitasking; studies show the brain can't focus on two things well, so it's slower than sequential focused work.

units.title: Less attachment to AI code enables refactors
units.detail: Not writing code reduces attachment, making it easier to scrap and refactor. But the fix for over-attachment is knowing when a prototype is throwaway, not outsourcing the writing to AI.

units.title: Let audience vote on content priorities
units.detail: Community voting with weighted votes (3/1/-1) on a public suggestions list lets your audience steer what content gets made, sorted by votes, with completed items moved to a done section.

units.title: Scope is never accurate; halve your estimates
units.detail: Even experienced devs overshoot scope (a 6-month project becomes 8). A joke that's accurate: cut a project's scope in half twice and it's still as big as the original. Budget generously.

units.title: A feature costs its full lifecycle, not just code
units.detail: Adding a mechanic means code plus polish, testing, balancing, marketing materials, tutorial teaching, and player support. Writing the code is a tiny fraction of a feature's real cost.

units.title: New features ripple through connected systems
units.detail: Rarely does a mechanic exist in isolation; a health system touches weapons, trading, animation, and more. One 'tiny' feature forces you to modify many scripts across the game.

units.title: Keep the game explainable in one sentence
units.detail: If a game requires a paragraph to explain, it's hard to sell. Simple, focused games market better; hard-to-explain mechanics multiply marketing difficulty.

units.title: Fewer polished mechanics beat many rough ones
units.detail: Five mechanics at 90% polish beat fifty rough ones. Polish is what separates good games from great games; every added feature must also be polished to count.

units.title: More features means more bugs and coupling
units.detail: Each added feature brings more code, more bug surface, and more unavoidable coupling between systems. Even careful architecture can't fully prevent coupling as scope grows.

units.title: Gate features on 'can I make this excellent?'
units.detail: Before adding a feature ask: can I build it, integrate it with every system, polish it, and support it with UI/art/audio? If it can't be excellent, cut it — most features fail this test.

units.title: Simple NPC queue with position and guest lists
units.detail: A waiting queue is a list of queue positions plus a parallel list of guests. New guests first move to an entrance position, then to their own slot by list index.

units.title: Relocate all guests after dequeueing front
units.detail: When the front guest is removed, loop the remaining guests and move each to the position at their new index. Without this, guests leave a gap at the front.

units.title: Buildings request guests from the queue
units.detail: Keep queue and building as separate objects with a public 'get first in queue' call returning null when empty, and have the queue notify the building when a guest arrives later.

units.title: Entrance staging position before queue slot
units.detail: Route guests to a shared entrance position first and, on arrival, move them to their individual queue slot. It creates orderly, natural-looking queue entry.

units.title: Capacity check before adding to queue
units.detail: Expose a CanAdd() that returns whether the guest count is below the position count, so callers only enqueue when an available slot exists.

units.title: Visualize positions with debug sprites
units.detail: While building a system, spawn colored debug sprites at each computed position to verify placement before the real visuals exist.

units.title: Model waiting queue as a series of positions
units.detail: A queue is a list of positions; guests enter when space exists and each moves forward one slot when the front guest leaves. This makes queue logic simple and reusable beyond the demo.

units.title: Queue class with events to decouple building
units.detail: A WaitingQueue class holds positions and guest references with AddGuest and GetGuestInFront functions. Use events (guest added / reached front) so the connected building is notified without tight coupling, keeping code clean.

units.title: Runtime-editable queue positions for custom shapes
units.detail: Expose functions to add/modify queue positions at runtime so designers can create custom queue shapes. Each guest in the queue is driven by its own simple AI class that handles removal and extra in-queue behavior.

units.title: Chain of notifications moves guests forward
units.detail: When a guest reaches the front the building requests it; after the guest leaves the building, the next one waiting in front is notified and the chain continues. This is the core flow of the queue.

units.title: Gaming market is huge, avoid only same-genre launches
units.detail: With hundreds of millions of players, a massive game launch only threatens games in the exact same genre. Different genres draw from different player pools, so other games can launch alongside a megahit successfully.

units.title: Boxleiter method estimates copies sold from reviews
units.detail: Multiply the number of Steam reviews by a multiplier between 20 and 70 (about 40 is a good guestimate) to estimate total copies sold. Use this with wishlist data to check if a game met expectations.

units.title: Week-one sales are ~15-20% of wishlists
units.detail: A game with 100k wishlists typically sells roughly 15-20k copies in week one. Compare this expected value against Boxleiter-style review estimates to judge whether a launch underperformed or matched forecasts.

units.title: Verify your own advice with launch-window data
units.detail: When giving marketing advice, test it by researching Steam new releases and sales estimates around a major launch, including year-over-year comparisons for annualized franchises. Data backs or refutes claims about player-pool competition.

units.title: Delay release only when a megahit shares your genre
units.detail: Same-genre games launching near a megahit showed strong wishlists but very few reviews/copies sold, indicating real harm. If you compete in the exact same genre, delaying is justified; otherwise keep your date.

units.title: Find all AI-disclosure games via SteamDB search
units.detail: SteamDB supports an app-key search for AI content disclosure (AI content type equals 1) and lists every game carrying the AI disclosure. This gives a large, sortable sample for research instead of manual hunting.

units.title: AI disclosure does not tank review scores
units.detail: The review-score distribution for the 6,400+ games with the AI content disclosure matches Steam overall. Players judge games on fun and quality rather than on the presence of an AI disclosure.

units.title: Players rarely mention in-game generative AI
units.detail: Browsing hundreds of reviews for games using AI-generated voices, portraits, and art, AI is almost never mentioned. Occasional negative mentions (e.g., low-quality AI voices) appear but are not dealbreakers when the game is good.

units.title: Silent AI-avoiding buyers are unfalsifiable
units.detail: People who refuse to buy a game over AI leave no review, so their impact cannot be proven or disproven. Treat this critique as a judgement call rather than a measurable factor.

units.title: Treat AI tools like assets
units.detail: Players overwhelmingly care about having fun, not which tools built the game. Just as with asset packs, use any tool that is useful as long as it does not hurt the product quality players experience.

units.title: Steam Festivals are must-do indie marketing
units.detail: Participating requires a working demo, a coming soon page, and you can only join a single Steam Festival before release. They offer major exposure and wishlist gathering, but involve heavy competition (1200+ demos).

units.title: Subpar launch demo may kill organic visibility
units.detail: Launching with a weak early build (under ~9 minute median playtime) may cause the Steam festival algorithm to ignore the demo for the rest of the event, so later improvements never get organic traffic. Test thoroughly before the festival opens.

units.title: Festival wishlist benchmarks (median ~1100)
units.detail: Research by Chris Zukowski shows the median game gains roughly 1,100 wishlists per Steam Festival, an uptrending figure. Falling well below it indicates subpar performance; use it to calibrate expectations.

units.title: Feedback from your audience is positively biased
units.detail: Subscribers, friends, and family give flattering feedback unlike regular Steam players who don't know you. Never assume positive beta feedback represents the broader market; actively discount that bias.

units.title: Launch with enough wishlists or delay
units.detail: Releasing with very few wishlists (e.g., ~3,000) makes success unlikely regardless of game quality. For non-first games seeking financial success, keep building wishlists before launch instead of rushing.

units.title: First game: launch now; later games: build momentum
units.detail: For a first game, just ship it because the learning outweighs financial hopes. For later games chasing revenue, prioritize wishlist accumulation and promotion over speed.

units.title: Use devlogs and shorts to gather wishlists
units.detail: Posting regular devlogs plus many short-form clips (TikTok/Instagram) over several months can compound into meaningful wishlist totals before launch, roughly ~10/day in this case study.

units.title: Reuse existing systems to build fast
units.detail: The complex mini-game was built quickly because movement, grid, camera, pathfinding, character, and interaction systems were all reused from previous projects with tiny tweaks. Clean, generic systems compound into fast prototyping.

units.title: Generic grid system swapped XY to XZ for 3D
units.detail: A grid class written with generics works for any object; going from 2D to 3D is a one-line swap from an XY grid to an XZ grid. Generics pay off across projects.

units.title: Keep camera FOV small to avoid sprite distortion
units.detail: In a 2D-characters-in-3D-world setup, a wide FOV (60) heavily stretches sprites near screen edges. Lowering the FOV dramatically reduces that distortion and keeps the flat characters looking correct.

units.title: Drive particle emission rate from grid values
units.detail: Each grid cell holds a virus amount value; a per-cell particle system sets its emission rate over time from that value. Zero value = no particles, high value = dense particles, giving instant visual feedback on numeric state.

units.title: Modular character with swappable pathfinding modules
units.detail: A modular character system lets you swap movement modules: custom grid pathfinding or Unity NavMesh MovePosition both fit the same interface. Keep logic modules separate from movement so they can be exchanged freely.

units.title: Interaction-point handler for designer-friendly AI
units.detail: Manually placed and rotated interaction points (desks, misc, sinks) with a type enum are registered in a handler. AI requests the nearest point of a type, so level design is driven by placement, not code.

units.title: High NavMesh area cost blocks shortcut paths
units.detail: Giving the toilet NavMesh area a very high move cost prevents workers from cutting through it as a shortcut. Area-based movement cost is a lightweight way to steer AI routes.

units.title: Raycast from camera for 3D mouse position
units.detail: In 3D, convert screen mouse position into a world ray cast against the floor layer to get the world-space cursor. A visual indicator over the hit point clarifies where inputs will land.

units.title: Cone spray reduces grid values in an arc
units.detail: The spray computes a cone of world positions around a base direction, converts each to a grid position, and reduces the stored virus value there. Simple rules combined with the grid produce emergent, complex-feeling mechanics.

units.title: Simple state machine for worker behavior
units.detail: Workers use a handful of states (waiting, moving, going to toilet, washing hands, busy). Timers pick random move targets, and sick workers run a periodic update (every ~0.1s) that both spreads virus to the map and catches it from the map.

units.title: Cinematic via dedicated virtual camera
units.detail: Washing-hands cinematic is a Cinemachine virtual camera that zooms in while the worker plays an animation, then returns. Simple camera-based cinematics add polish without custom timeline complexity.

units.title: Never ship a game without post-processing
units.detail: Bloom, subtle vignette, and color adjustment (contrast/saturation) transform a flat scene into a polished look using identical assets. Post-processing is the cheapest, biggest visual upgrade available.

units.title: Shader looks make common asset packs stand out
units.detail: Screen-space cavity/curvature with thick outlines plus slightly non-flat colors hits a stylized-but-not-too-cartoony look; quibli, flat kit toon, and pixelate were alternatives. Spend time picking a shader identity so stock assets look intentional.

units.title: Search inside all Unity packages without importing
units.detail: The Asset Inventory tool searches every owned Unity package on disk (including Humble Bundle purchases) and previews audio before importing. Great for finding assets and sounds across a large library quickly.

units.title: Low-poly style mixes packs from different publishers
units.detail: Because low-poly art is style-consistent, props from different publishers (Synty, PolyPerfect, IMPIX) combine seamlessly. A non-artist can assemble a coherent-looking game purely from purchased packs.

units.title: Reuse your own previous projects' assets
units.detail: Icons, particles, and VFX from earlier videos and games were reused in the new title to prototype fast. Your past work is a free asset library; reuse it instead of starting from scratch.

units.title: Edit humanoid animations directly in Unity
units.detail: Umotion edits humanoid animation clips in-editor, ideal for small fixes like removing root-motion sliding feet that break a gameplay setup. Avoids needing a full DCC tool for minor adjustments.

units.title: Pick pathfinding by unit count and turn structure
units.detail: The A* Pathfinding Project handles thousands of units (used for 2,000-unit battles), while a turn-based game can use a custom DOTS implementation since it needs far less speed. Match the pathfinding strategy to the game's scale.

units.title: Volumetric lights and dissolve effects add polish
units.detail: Volumetric Lights 2 adds volume and particle fireflies to existing lights; a dissolve/materialize shader animates construction bottom-up. Directional effects (lights at night, building placement) make scenes feel alive and readable.

units.title: Quantum console calls any function in-game
units.detail: Adding a runtime console (Quantum) lets you invoke any method from inside the game, enabling fast testing like spawning items or granting action points. Indispensable for debugging systems without UI.

units.title: Make small games to learn 10x faster
units.detail: Ten small games teach more than one massive game in the same timeframe because each iteration exercises the full dev loop. Beginners reach experienced-dev level in months rather than years.

units.title: Execution multiplies the game idea
units.detail: A clone idea with flawless execution is still a clone; a clever idea plus good execution yields hits like Balatro. Because ideas drive success, testing more ideas (via small games) improves your odds.

units.title: Five years of work can yield twelve sales
units.detail: A real post-mortem: 5 years of dev produced $1.2k revenue (~12 cents/hour). Niche genre-mixes (JRPG + visual novel) plus a weak hook collapse the addressable market; hard marketing is a warning sign to pivot early.

units.title: Define success and stop lying to yourself
units.detail: If making games for fun, no rules apply - but don't secretly hope for a million sales while claiming it's just for fun. Clarify your success metric (learning, fun, or revenue) and act accordingly.

units.title: Beware survivorship bias in dev stories
units.detail: Stardew Valley-style multi-year success stories are extreme outliers; hundreds of similar efforts end with disappointing results. A rare success does not make five-year development a sound strategy.

units.title: Treat weak marketing interest as a pivot signal
units.detail: If the game is a slow crawl to build interest, continuing for years rarely changes that. Failure hurts less when scoped to six months instead of five years, so launch quickly and move to the next idea.

units.title: Analyze failures and learn the real lesson
units.detail: After a failed game, do a genuine post-mortem of what went wrong (genre, hook, marketing). The deepest lesson is often not the game design but the timeline - don't spend years on the next game either.

units.title: Classes vs structs decided fog-of-war performance
units.detail: A persistent fog-of-war made of tens of thousands of grid quads was unusable with reference-type classes due to scattered memory access; switching to structs made it fast. Match type choice to access patterns and volume.

units.title: Bake animations to sprite sheets for thousands of units
units.detail: Characters made of many separate body-part objects capped the game at 10-20 infected. Baking animations into sprite sheets and using one quad per enemy enabled hundreds of animated units on screen.

units.title: Persistent particles rendered on one mesh
units.detail: Bullet splatters that must stay on the floor were generated into a single growing mesh, allowing ~20,000 blood decals with one draw call. Batched geometry keeps persistent particle effects performant.

units.title: Procedural generation from handcrafted parts
units.detail: Levels were randomly assembled from handcrafted blocks, placing cities on circles of varying radius and then connecting them while guaranteeing all nodes are reachable. Connect-then-verify keeps generated levels playable.

units.title: Experience compounds: 30k lines in a year became 16k in two weeks
units.detail: The first game took a year to write 30k lower-quality lines; a decade later a demo needed 16k better lines in two weeks. Skill growth multiplies both speed and code quality dramatically.

units.title: Buy battle-tested assets when skills are missing
units.detail: Using the A* Pathfinding Project free version enabled a vision the developer couldn't build solo at the time. Buying proven systems is a legitimate way to unblock a project while learning.

units.title: Practice skills with mini-challenges to truly learn
units.detail: Watching tutorials alone teaches little; building a small project with the new skill (e.g., a traffic sim with self-made 3D models) is where real learning happens. Apply skills soon after learning them.

units.title: Blender default cube is 2x2 meters, not 1x1
units.detail: Scaling the default cube by 30x35 produced a house double the intended size because the base cube is two units across. Verify asset scale assumptions and correct transform sizes to fix it.

units.title: Use reference images and mirroring when modeling
units.detail: Modeling without reference images produced a windowless house; a side-view reference and the mirror modifier made the car cleaner and cut work in half. Both speed up beginners and improve quality.

units.title: Speed gaps come from experience, not talent
units.detail: A beginner needed two hours per car model while an expert makes ten in ten minutes. Difficulty seeming easy for others is years of accumulated experience, not innate ability - keep practicing.

units.title: Learn enough 3D to modify purchased assets
units.detail: The goal of learning Blender basics was to tweak bought models and create bespoke parts (grabbers, conveyor belts) that don't exist in any pack. Basic modeling complements asset store purchasing.

units.title: Wishlists are the make-or-break metric for Steam launches
units.detail: Steam notifies wishlisters on release, converting them into initial sales; Steam's algorithm then promotes games that are selling to more people. A game launching with ~600 wishlists gets essentially no organic push, while one with ~20,000 can snowball into a hit. Set a minimum goal of ~5,000 wishlists, ideally 10,000+, before launching.

units.title: Launching with no marketing means no one finds your game
units.detail: Without accumulated wishlists or audience, a release gets no notifications, no initial sales, and the algorithm ignores it entirely — the game effectively doesn't exist. Treat marketing as part of development, gathering wishlists from day one, not as an afterthought at launch.

units.title: The Steam flywheel: sales beget more sales
units.detail: Initial wishlist-driven sales trigger Steam's algorithm to surface the game to more players, which produces more sales and further promotion. A strong launch also leads to sustained sales and invitations to daily/summer/winter deals.

units.title: A marketable idea is half of marketing
units.detail: Beyond wishlists, a game needs a strong, marketable hook; a generic, simple game won't stand out even with visibility. Validate your concept's marketability before investing years of development — a good hook makes all marketing easier.

units.title: Define success against your own goals
units.detail: Success is subjective: a small game launched purely as a course companion can be 'successful' even with near-zero sales if that was the intent. Judge your launch against your stated goals rather than raw numbers.

units.title: Devlogs are a full marketing funnel
units.detail: An entertaining devlog series converts YouTube views into followers, followers into wishlists, wishlists into launch sales, and sales into algorithmic promotion. High-quality, story-driven devlogs over a long development arc are a proven indie marketing strategy.

units.title: Boxleiter method estimates sales from Steam reviews
units.detail: Estimate copies sold by multiplying review count by a multiplier that typically ranges from 20 to 70. For a game whose audience is heavily drawn from its own fans (higher review rates), use a lower multiplier, e.g. ~30.

units.title: Gross revenue is far from what you actually keep
units.detail: Roughly 200k gross from ~13,500 sales at $15 is not net profit. After chargebacks, sales tax, Steam's cut, and income tax, the final net number is usually less than half of gross.

units.title: A unique twist beats a niche genre's reputation
