units.detail: Fighting games rarely succeed on Steam, yet Punch A Bunch succeeded via distinctive physics-based controls, gorgeous visuals, and strong storytelling. Great visuals + unique idea + effective marketing can overcome a genre's poor odds.

units.title: Longer dev time means more wishlist runway
units.detail: A three-year development arc (with regular devlogs) gives a game years to accumulate followers and wishlists, whereas a rushed 2-week coming-soon page yields almost none. Treat the pre-launch window as a compounding marketing asset.

units.title: Pick a marketing channel that matches your skills
units.detail: Devlogs require personality and editing skill (extreme case: Warlock Dan). If that's not you, use your other strengths — e.g. tutorials that funnel viewers to your game — plus TikTok, Twitter/Reddit gifs, and Tiktok virality for thousands of wishlists.

units.title: Blob assets: immutable shared data for parallel reads
units.detail: A blob asset is a container of immutable data referenced by entities, safe to read from multiple jobs/threads simultaneously with no safety issues. Ideal for animation data, physics shapes, unit stats, pathfinding maps, and other constant data.

units.title: Build a blob asset with a BlobBuilder
units.detail: Construct a root struct via BlobBuilder.ConstructRoot, allocate space for BlobArrays, fill the data, then CreateBlobAssetReference with a persistent allocator to get a reference you can store in an entity component.

units.title: Forgetting ref on blob root silently copies data
units.detail: You must use the `ref` keyword on both the ConstructRoot call and the variable declaration for the blob root; otherwise you operate on a copy and your blob asset is wrong. This is an easy-to-miss footgun.

units.title: Blob string can't be created inside a using block
units.detail: BlobString construction doesn't work inside a `using` BlobBuilder block — you must create the BlobBuilder manually and dispose of it yourself.

units.title: GameObject conversion has two EntityManagers
units.detail: Inside a GameObjectConversionSystem there are two entity managers: the conversion world's (where the object is being converted) and the destination world's (where already-converted entities live). Use the destination manager to query already-converted entities like the player.

units.title: Share a blob asset via static field for spawned entities
units.detail: Instead of writing the blob asset reference onto every entity, store it in a static field (or authoring component) that entity spawners copy into each new entity's component at instantiation.

units.title: Delegates let you store behavior in a field
units.detail: A delegate is a function signature stored as a variable: assign any matching method to it and invoke it like a normal call. Swapping the assigned function changes behavior without changing call sites.

units.title: Multicast delegates chain multiple handlers
units.detail: Use `+=` to attach several functions to one delegate and `-=` to remove them; invoking the delegate calls all of them in order. This underpins how event publishers notify multiple subscribers.

units.title: Use Action and Func instead of hand-rolled delegates
units.detail: Action is a built-in delegate returning void with up to 16 typed parameters; Func's last generic type is the return value with preceding types as parameters. Prefer these over custom delegate declarations in most cases.

units.title: Anonymous lambdas can't be unsubscribed
units.detail: You can only remove a method from a delegate/event if you hold a reference to it; two identical lambda expressions are different references, so to add-then-remove, use a named method instead.

units.title: Swap behavior via a delegate instead of booleans
units.detail: Instead of an isUsingSword flag plus if/else per attack, store an attackFunction delegate initialized to punch and reassign it when upgrading. Input and attack code stay unconditional and new behaviors slot in cleanly.

units.title: Events decouple publisher from subscribers
units.detail: A publisher fires an event without knowing or caring who (if anyone) listens; subscribers attach/detach freely. This lets logic work standalone while visuals subscribe — reuse the same logic class with entirely different visual frontends.

units.title: Null-reference when firing an event with no subscribers
units.detail: Invoking an event with zero subscribers throws a NullReferenceException because the backing delegate is null. Guard with `if (OnSpacePressed != null)` or use the C# 6 null-conditional `OnSpacePressed?.Invoke(...)`.

units.title: Pass event data with EventArgs subclasses
units.detail: The standard EventHandler uses (object sender, EventArgs); to carry data, subclass EventArgs with fields and use EventHandler<TEventArgs> so subscribers receive typed, meaningful payloads.

units.title: UnityEvent exposes callbacks to the inspector
units.detail: Unlike C# events, UnityEvent fields appear in the inspector so designers can wire up method calls without code. Good for designer-friendly tools, though it lacks the `event` keyword's encapsulation.

units.title: Generics: one function, any type
units.detail: Declaring `void CreateArray<T>(...)` lets one implementation work with ints, strings, floats, or custom types, replacing duplicated hard-typed versions. The compiler also infers the type argument from call-site usage.

units.title: Generic classes hold any data per position
units.detail: Make a class generic (e.g. a grid or event-capture class) so each instance is customized to the data type it stores while sharing all logic. This is how a grid system can hold arbitrary cell data.

units.title: Constrain generics with where clauses
units.detail: `where T : struct` forces value types, `: class` reference types, `: new()` a parameterless constructor, and `: IEnemy` an interface implementation — enabling you to call interface methods on T safely. Combine multiple constraints as needed.

units.title: Generics work on interfaces and delegates too
units.detail: Action<T1,T2> and Func<TResult> show generics in delegates; interfaces like IEnemy<T> let implementations supply the type. Generic types follow T, T1, T2 naming by convention.

units.title: Interfaces are contracts without implementation
units.detail: An interface declares methods, properties, and events but no bodies; any implementing class must provide them. A class using an interface reference is guaranteed those members exist regardless of what else the class does.

units.title: Interfaces can't contain fields
units.detail: You may declare methods, events, and properties (get/set) in an interface, but fields are not allowed. Implement fields in the classes that implement the interface.

units.title: IDamageable pattern kills per-type bullet logic
units.detail: Instead of GetComponent<Enemy>() then GetComponent<Crate>() chains, define an IDamageable interface with a Damage() method; the bullet grabs one IDamageable and calls Damage(). Adding new damageable objects (tower, building) requires only implementing the interface — no bullet changes.

units.title: Interfaces bypass single inheritance limits
units.detail: C# classes inherit one base class but can implement many interfaces; structs can't inherit but can implement interfaces, and an interface can extend another interface, compounding required members.

units.title: while vs do-while: when the condition is tested
units.detail: while tests its condition before each run (may execute zero times); do-while tests after the block, guaranteeing at least one execution. Choose do-while when the body must run once regardless.

units.title: while/do-while risk infinite loops
units.detail: If the condition never becomes false (e.g. forgot to increment the iterator), the game hangs. The for loop mitigates this by forcing the iterator-update block in the signature.

units.title: foreach can't modify the collection being iterated
units.detail: Removing or adding elements inside a foreach throws an exception. To filter a list while iterating, use a regular for loop and decrement the index after removal — otherwise relocated elements get skipped.

units.title: continue skips, break exits, and break only breaks the innermost loop
units.detail: `continue` jumps to the next iteration, `break` exits the current loop. In nested loops, break only exits the loop it's inside, not outer ones. Custom classes support foreach by implementing IEnumerable/IEnumerator.

units.title: Scriptable objects store data as project assets
units.detail: ScriptableObjects (created via the CreateAssetMenu attribute) are serialized data containers in the project folder, separate from code and scenes. Fields are set per-asset instance in the inspector, making game data designer-friendly — ideal for items, recipes, weapons, and grid configs.

units.title: Scriptable objects are references, saving memory
units.detail: Assigning a scriptable object stores a reference to the shared asset, not a copy. Instantiating many enemies that share weapon data creates no duplicate data, delivering large memory savings in entity-heavy games.

units.title: Runtime SO edits don't persist in builds
units.detail: In the editor, changes made in play mode are reverted on exiting play mode; in a build, any runtime mutation is gone once the app closes and always starts from the values baked at build time. Don't use scriptable objects as runtime save state.

units.title: SOs make games designer-friendly
units.detail: Because data lives in inspector-editable assets, non-programmers can tune game content without touching code. Unity itself uses this pattern for the URP asset and post-processing profiles.

units.title: Subscenes stream world chunks for massive levels
units.detail: A subscene wraps a group of GameObjects that are converted to entities and cached in a binary file for near-instant load. Loading/unloading subscenes by player distance keeps CPU and memory low, enabling huge or infinite worlds (used in Unity's MegaCity demo).

units.title: Load/unload subscenes via SceneSystem
units.detail: Grab the SceneSystem from the world, then call LoadSceneAsync(subScene.SceneGUID) to stream in a subscene and UnloadScene to remove it. Wrap this in a distance check per subscene to stream the world around the player.

units.title: Cloud Save stores per-player and global data
units.detail: Unity Cloud Save persists JSON data in the cloud, loadable on any platform the player logs into. Data scopes: private player data (only owner reads/writes), public player data (others can read), and global data (shared across all players).

units.title: Cloud Code runs trusted server-side logic
units.detail: Cloud Code executes logic in the backend and returns results to the player, e.g. incrementing a global score shared by all players. Use it for operations that must be validated or shared server-side rather than trusted to the client.

units.title: Building block achievements are custom, not platform
units.detail: The achievements building block combines authentication, cloud save, cloud code (to validate unlock calls), and remote config (to define achievements). It is a completely custom system, distinct from Steam/Xbox achievements.

units.title: Value types store data, reference types store references
units.detail: Value types (ints, floats, bools, structs) directly contain their data; reference types (classes, objects, strings, arrays) hold a reference to data elsewhere. Assignment copies value-type data but copies only the reference for reference types.

units.title: Mutating through one reference changes all references
units.detail: Multiple variables referencing the same class instance all observe changes because they point to one shared object. With value types each assignment creates an independent copy, so modifying one variable never affects another.

units.title: Struct copies in NativeArray are not updated in place
units.detail: In Unity jobs, reading a struct from a NativeArray gives you a copy, so modifying it has no effect on the stored value. You must write the modified struct back to the array at the same index after changing it.

units.title: Jobs only support value types
units.detail: Unity's job system and Burst require blittable value types; classes are not allowed in jobs. This is why DOTS code works with structs and NativeArrays (a special job-compatible array) rather than class-based arrays.

units.title: ref keyword mutates value types in place
units.detail: Passing a value type with the ref keyword (on both parameter definition and call site) passes a reference to the original variable, so a function can modify the caller's value instead of a copy.

units.title: Value types cannot be null unless made nullable
units.detail: Value types can't hold null (e.g. int i = null is an error). Append a question mark (int?) which is shorthand for Nullable<T>, enabling null for value types like a weapon slot that the player may not have.

units.title: Engine choice matters less than developer skill
units.detail: Unity, Unreal, and Godot are all capable; game quality depends more on developer skill than engine choice. Don't waste energy on engine wars, just use what you started with until a game idea actually requires switching.

units.title: Flashy features need a real use case
units.detail: Nanite and Metahuman are impressive but useless to a solo dev making low-poly 2D games without an artist team. Before demanding shiny engine features, ask whether your game actually has a use case for them.

units.title: Unity announces only near-release features
units.detail: Unity stopped announcing far-future features after DOTS (announced 2018, 1.0 in 2023) drew years of complaints; now they showcase only shipped or months-away tools. Fewer flashy roadmaps but fewer permanently-in-preview features.

units.title: Minimum engine bar is draw + logic
units.detail: When choosing an engine, the minimum requirements are: can I draw something on screen and can I apply logic to it. If both work, you can build anything on top of them.

units.title: Unity Muse generates art, animations, and behavior
units.detail: Unity's Muse capabilities inside the editor generate textures, sprites, animations from text prompts, behavior trees for enemy AI, and a project-aware chat for debugging and brainstorming.

units.title: Make smaller projects instead of a 3-4 year first game
units.detail: Multiple successful indie games (colony sim, cozy management game) were built in ~6 months with teams of 3-4 people. Prefer smaller projects and fast launches over multi-year epics for your first games.

units.title: Unique visuals and hook win on storefronts
units.detail: Nowadays visuals are extremely important; a game with visually interesting art and a unique concept can get pushed to the top of storefronts and blow up during Steam Next Fest even before release.

units.title: Niche platforms reduce indie competition
units.detail: Tiny niche devices like the Playdate have few developers and less competition, which can help indies stand out, though getting on the platform requires networking. Devs there have collectively earned over $500k.

units.title: Rusty's Retirement: idle game at desktop bottom
units.detail: An idle farming game played at the very bottom of your desktop while you work elsewhere is a genius genre twist; it hit 6,500 followers (~70k wishlists) pre-release on premise alone.

units.title: Indie marketing budgets are high risk
units.detail: A $50k marketing spend is a very high-risk strategy for indies since games are cheap and advertising ROI is hard to achieve unless you have a huge budget. Approach paid marketing carefully.

units.title: Reuse knowledge by staying in one genre
units.detail: Making multiple games in a similar genre compounds your knowledge; complexity in later games (e.g. an interconnected Tycoon game after simpler ones) becomes feasible. You don't need exact sequels, just genre continuity.

units.title: Pick a clear, compelling game hook first
units.detail: Dungeon Clawler got 30k wishlists in two weeks because its claw-machine-with-skills hook is instantly interesting. Spend time choosing a hook that immediately sounds interesting before production.

units.title: Steam Daily Deal needs ~250k gross revenue
units.detail: A Steam Daily Deal sold more in 48 hours than the prior 6 months combined, but Valve manually curates it; the rough threshold to even be considered is ~$250k in gross revenue.

units.title: Rounding 1.5 and 2.5 both give 2
units.detail: C# (and many languages) use banker's/even rounding: 0.5 always rounds to the nearest even number for numerical stability, so 1.5 and 2.5 both round to 2. Surprising even to experienced programmers.

units.title: Post-launch PSN requirement caused review bombing
units.detail: Hell Divers 2 forced PlayStation accounts months after release, flipping tons of positive reviews to negative and removing the game from non-PSN countries. Never add a mandatory account barrier months post-launch.

units.title: Co-locate DVD data to reduce seek time
units.detail: GTA3 physically grouped related data together on the DVD so the read head moved less, squeezing out performance on limited hardware. Laying out data to exploit sequential reads is a classic optimization.

units.title: VR adoption needs software, not just hardware
units.detail: The Vision Pro cut production on weak demand; even excellent hardware (screen, passthrough, anchoring) fails without an installed base of software and developers. Hardware investment alone doesn't grow VR.

units.title: Floats trade large magnitude for precision
units.detail: A float stores 4 bytes and can represent huge or tiny magnitudes, but precision depends on decimal point placement: large numbers lose decimal digits. Floats cannot store very large numbers and tiny precision simultaneously.

units.title: Far positions jitter from vertex precision loss
units.detail: When an object moves to huge coordinates, each vertex's float position loses precision, so vertices clamp/round to the nearest representable value and the mesh visibly jitters or breaks. Unity warns to keep world coordinates small.

units.title: Floating origin teleports world back to zero
units.detail: For giant open-world or space games, periodically teleport the entire world (player and all objects) back near the origin, keeping relative positions identical, so floats never accumulate huge coordinates.

units.title: Use doubles for very large world positions
units.detail: Alternative to floating origin: store positions as doubles (8 bytes) to get a much wider precision range. Unreal uses doubles for positions to support massive open worlds; Unity uses floats so must shift or use doubles manually.

units.title: JSON is a lightweight structured text format
units.detail: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) uses curly-brace objects, name:value fields, commas between fields, and values that can be strings, numbers, objects, arrays, booleans, or null. It is easy for both humans and machines to parse.

units.title: JsonUtility ToJson/FromJson round-trips classes
units.detail: Unity's JsonUtility.ToJson(object) converts a class (e.g. player data with position and health) into a JSON string, and JsonUtility.FromJson<T>(json) parses it back into an object. Use plain classes to represent saveable game state.

units.title: Minimal save system: serialize, write, read, parse
units.detail: Build a save system by serializing a state class to JSON, writing it with File.WriteAllText to Application.dataPath, then on load reading with File.ReadAllText and parsing back into the class with JsonUtility.FromJson.

units.title: Announce only proven products, not demos
units.detail: Unity learned from DOTS that showing early prototypes breeds years of complaints; it now keeps AI vague until it's a production-ready tool. A research proof of concept is very different from a usable product.

units.title: Barracuda runs ML models on any platform
units.detail: Unity's Barracuda is a lightweight cross-platform inference engine (in development since 2018) that runs neural networks on all supported platforms; ML-Agents and Barracuda show Unity worked on AI for years before any announcement.

units.title: AI data consent has legal consequences
units.detail: Training on scraped internet data risks copyright lawsuits and studios banning AI tools to avoid liability. Collect training data with consent or build your own dataset; never expose developers to legal risk over provenance.

units.title: AI guiding principles: be unbiased, accountable, fair
units.detail: Unity's publicly-posted AI guiding principles (since 2018) are: be unbiased, accountable, fair, responsible, honest, and trustworthy. Focus AI on augmenting developers, not eliminating jobs or scraping data without consent.

units.title: Unity AI opts out and protects your data
units.detail: All Unity AI features are optional to install. Data you feed into the AI (prompts, source images) is used only to provide the service for your benefit and is not used for model training, protecting studio IP.

units.title: Generate textures, PBR maps, and audio in-editor
units.detail: Unity AI generators create sprites (with background removal, upscale, recolor, inpaint), materials that auto-generate all PBR maps (base, height, occlusion, smoothness), and short sound effects within seconds for prototypes.

units.title: Video-to-motion replaces mocap with a webcam
units.detail: The animation generator supports text-to-motion and video-to-motion: film yourself with a cheap webcam and the tool converts that motion into a game animation. This drastically lowers the barrier for custom animations on zero budget.

units.title: Audit AI-generated assets before shipping
units.detail: Right-click in the project window and choose 'search generated assets' to list everything with the Uni AI label. Review it before publishing so you know exactly what AI content is in your final game.

units.title: Project-aware AI assistant explains code and runs commands
units.detail: Uni's assistant is trained on Unity data, knows the asset store, and accepts attached references (scripts, prefabs, console errors). It explains code, generates comments, answers why an object is pink, and executes editor commands like placing prefabs.

units.title: Sentis inference engine runs models locally
units.detail: The inference engine runs machine learning models directly in the engine on-device, no cloud or servers. Download models from the Hugging Face page (e.g. text-to-speech) and run them with a script on a camera and an audio source.

units.title: Unity Studio is a browser-based 3D editor
units.detail: Unity Studio is a web-based editor aimed at Unity Industry users for building and sharing 3D (e.g. training apps) from a browser. It offers scene controls, a hierarchy, an inspector, and cloud-based asset import.

units.title: Unity Studio uses Scratch-like visual scripting
units.detail: Custom logic in Unity Studio is built with a visual scripting window (event listeners, key-press triggers, move-by-value actions, variables, debug log) similar to Scratch, rather than reusing Unity's existing visual scripting.

units.title: One-click web publishing from the browser editor
units.detail: Unity Studio lets you press a publish button, get a shareable link, and anyone can immediately view your built project in a browser — no local install or build step. Great for quick prototyping and sharing.

units.title: Two browser editors target different audiences
units.detail: Unity Studio is geared toward industry (training apps, assets in the cloud, teams) while play.unity.com (Struckt Studio) is geared toward making games. Pick per audience; browser editors are more limited than the desktop editor.

units.title: GameObjects are containers of components
units.detail: In component-based engines a GameObject is an empty container that composes behavior from any number of attached components. Create custom behavior by writing a component script and attaching it.

units.title: Component lifecycle: Awake, Start, Update
units.detail: Start runs once when the object first becomes active and before the first Update; Update runs once per frame. Awake runs before all Start calls, as soon as the component is initialized.

units.title: Awake runs even when script is disabled
units.detail: Awake executes regardless of whether the script is enabled, but Start only runs when enabled. Don't rely on Start for initialization that must happen while disabled.

units.title: Update, LateUpdate, and FixedUpdate timing
units.detail: Update fires every frame, LateUpdate fires every frame after all Updates, and FixedUpdate fires at a fixed time step (default 20ms). Use FixedUpdate for anything affecting physics since physics runs on that fixed rate.

units.title: OnEnable/OnDisable for setup and cleanup
units.detail: OnEnable and OnDisable fire whenever the component or its GameObject is enabled/disabled. Use them to build state on activation and tear it down on deactivation (e.g. generate a grid on enable, clean it up on disable).

units.title: Script execution order only reorders per callback
units.detail: Configured execution order changes the sequence only within each callback type: all Awakes run first, then all Starts, then all Updates. It does not run one script's full lifecycle before another's.

units.title: GameObject is the base entity with Transform
units.detail: Every GameObject is an entity that always carries a Transform and can hold any number of additional components. Disabling a GameObject disables all of its components at once.

units.title: Name dynamically created GameObjects
units.detail: When spawning objects at runtime, pass a name to the constructor (new GameObject("MyObject")) so it is easy to find and identify in the scene hierarchy during debugging.

units.title: Keep a 1x1 white pixel texture
units.detail: A single white pixel sprite can be tinted any color and scaled to any size, giving you instant rectangles for UI elements like health bars without dedicated art assets.

units.title: SpriteRenderer color field tints the texture
units.detail: The color field multiplies the sprite's texture colors, letting you tint a sprite any color (e.g. make a red sprite blue, or add transparency by lowering alpha).

units.title: Sorting layers and Order in Layer control draw order
units.detail: Sprites render on top based on sorting layer first, then Order in Layer within that layer. A sprite on a higher sorting layer always draws above sprites on lower layers regardless of order number.

units.title: Set sprite, color, and sorting order at runtime
units.detail: Grab a reference with GetComponent<SpriteRenderer>() then assign .sprite, .color, .sortingOrder, and .sortingLayerName. Sorting layers must already exist in the project for the string name to work.

units.title: Transform stores position, rotation, scale
units.detail: Every object has a Transform defining its position, rotation, and scale as Vector3 values (X, Y, Z). It is the main mechanism for moving, rotating, and scaling objects.

units.title: Child transforms inherit parent's transform
units.detail: Parenting a transform to another makes it move, rotate, and scale together with the parent. The inspector shows local values relative to the parent, not world values.

units.title: Inspector shows local not world transform values
units.detail: A child object at local (1,0,0) under a parent at (2,0,0) shows (1,0,0) in the inspector but its world position is (3,0,0). Confusing local and world space causes positioning bugs.

units.title: In 2D only rotate the Z axis
units.detail: For 2D scenes leave the transform Z position at 0 and rotate only around Z. X and Y rotation applies perspective distortion that only makes sense in 3D.

units.title: Pivot defines the rotation center
units.detail: The sprite's pivot point (center by default) determines what point an object rotates around. Change the pivot in the sprite import settings to rotate around a different anchor.

units.title: Manage parent world position and child local position
units.detail: In nested hierarchies only change the parent's world position and each child's local position; never change the parent's local position or the child's world position. This keeps math simple and predictable.

units.title: Rotated parents make world-space placement messy
units.detail: Setting a child's world position under a rotated parent produces weird local offset values (e.g. local -90 to reach global 0). Spawn and move units from the parent object, not children.

units.title: Create, parent, and iterate children in code
units.detail: Spawn a child with new GameObject(), then assign transform.SetParent(target). Iterate children with foreach on the transform or GetChild(index) with transform.childCount. Find children by name with transform.Find(name).

units.title: Hierarchy order defines UI draw order
units.detail: In UI and sprite hierarchies, objects lower in the hierarchy render on top of those above. Reorder at runtime with SetAsLastSibling and SetAsFirstSibling to control layering.

units.title: PostProcessingVolume only works on legacy pipeline
units.detail: The Post Processing Volume component only functions with the built-in legacy render pipeline. On URP/HDRP use the Volume component instead — no package install needed.

units.title: DOTS is three technologies, mostly production ready
units.detail: DOTS (Data-Oriented Technology Stack) = Entities (ECS) + Job System + Burst compiler. Job System and Burst have been production ready for years; only Entities remains in preview.

units.title: Use hybrid GameObject/Entity approach
units.detail: The intended direction is hybrid: use GameObjects where they make sense and Entities where they make sense, rather than pure ECS everywhere. Entities shine for massive-scale simulations and large synchronized multiplayer.

units.title: Visual consistency beats raw fidelity
units.detail: A game looks good when all assets look like they belong together, even at modest quality. Mixing mismatched art styles looks messy no matter how good individual pieces are.

units.title: No voice acting is better than bad voice acting
units.detail: Bad voice acting drags the whole game down a notch. If you can't get good actors, cut the voice work entirely — or use a neutral gibberish-style voice sound like the original GTA.

units.title: Play test with many people, not just yourself
units.detail: Testing alone on one machine misses bugs that appear with other setups and play styles. Get friends, family, and strangers to play so the first-screen experience is bug free.

units.title: Tight packed spaces beat vast empty worlds
units.detail: Players want interesting things to do, not huge empty terrain. Small, dense, well-designed spaces feel better than enormous worlds that are mostly nothing.

units.title: Remove bad content ruthlessly
units.detail: One weak level, weapon, or character drags down everything around it. A shorter game where everything is compelling beats a long game players quit after 5 hours.

units.title: Polish separates good games from great games
units.detail: Lack of polish looks low effort: no button animations, no sound effects, no VFX, things just appear and vanish. Animations and feedback on every interaction elevate a functional game into a professional-feeling one.

units.title: Show, don't tell — avoid wall-of-text tutorials
units.detail: Explaining the whole game in one giant text block screams beginner dev. Teach through contextual clues and clever level design (like Super Mario's first level), showing small hints only when the player acts.

units.title: Invest in a professional store page
units.detail: A good capsule image, five high-quality screenshots (no debug/prototype visuals), correct tags, a benefit-focused description, and a 1-2 minute trailer are essential for standing out on storefronts like Steam.

units.title: Unity offers strong ML, VR, and AR tools for indies
units.detail: Unity ships capable machine learning, VR, and AR tooling with enormous potential for small studios to make distinctive games. These areas are worth researching when picking a project direction.

units.title: LTS vs tech stream releases
units.detail: Unity has tech stream (new features, less stable) and LTS (long-term support, bug fixes only) releases. Use LTS for production projects and treat tech stream as a preview of what's coming.

units.title: Debug rendering stats with rendering debugger
units.detail: Window > Analysis > Rendering Debugger shows frame time, framerate, CPU/GPU stats. In-game, Ctrl+Backspace toggles the overlay and lets you inspect render modes like albedo/wireframe.

units.title: Resources.Load still valid for simple cases
units.detail: Unity docs dropped the 'not recommended' note on Resources.Load; it still works fine for simple things and Addressables adds complexity. Pick the simpler tool unless you need Addressables features.

units.title: UI Toolkit for editor and runtime UI
units.detail: UI Toolkit is a single tool for building both editor tools and runtime game UI, using style sheets. Learning it now carries over to future versions.

units.title: Use Span types to reduce GC pressure
units.detail: System.Span and ReadOnlySpan are zero/low-garbage C# types now usable inside Burst jobs. Prefer them when garbage collection is a bottleneck in hot paths.

units.title: Spline tool as native package
units.detail: Unity's splines package lets you author curved paths in-scene, place knots, and comes with samples like mesh extrusion and objects following a spline.

units.title: Default to the latest LTS version
units.detail: For 99% of projects use the latest LTS because it's maximally stable and doesn't require bleeding-edge features. Only use tech/preview when your project absolutely needs a preview feature (e.g. DOTS).

units.title: Pick LTS if launching soon
units.detail: If you're about a month from release, stay on LTS to avoid last-minute churn; if release is further out, the current support version is safe to use since it's equally stable.

units.title: Game jams teach the skill of finishing
units.detail: The main value of a game jam is learning to finish games: managing scope, completing an experience on a fixed schedule, and pushing through the unfun parts. Most beginners never finish their first projects.

units.title: Reusing code conflicts with jam rules
units.detail: Many jams require all code written during the event, which blocks reusing your existing systems. That rule is fine for beginners (rewriting improves skill) but wastes time for experienced devs with reusable libraries.

units.title: Game jams can encourage unhealthy crunch
units.detail: The 48-hour format pushes people into 14-16 hour days and skipped sleep, reinforcing the industry's crunch problem. Weigh the stress cost against what skills you actually gain.

units.title: Use jams when new, skip when experienced
units.detail: If you haven't yet mastered finishing games, scope management, or idea generation, game jams are excellent training. If you already have those skills, the added stress and fixed theme/time yield little benefit.

units.title: Game jam benefits beyond finishing
units.detail: Jams force quick idea generation, teach scope management, give peer feedback on your games, let you test team collaboration, and can refresh your perspective after a long project.

units.title: Invisible characters break string lookups
units.detail: String-based lookups like Find() silently fail on typos or invisible/whitespace characters that are hard to see, producing confusing runtime errors instead of compile-time ones.

units.title: Prefer direct references over string lookups
units.detail: Avoid magic-string lookups for objects/components; use serialized direct references or constants so errors are caught at compile/editor time instead of runtime.

units.title: Master one tool rather than learn many
units.detail: Being an expert in a single engine/tool yields far more productivity than being merely decent at several. Pick one tool and go deep on it.

units.title: Sample engines first, then commit to one
units.detail: Do surface-level research across engines to understand their strengths, then choose one and master it. That mastery is what lets you build complex features in hours instead of weeks.

units.title: Experience compounds across features
units.detail: After years with one tool, almost every new feature relates to something you already built, making new work dramatically faster. That compounding is the real payoff of mastering a tool.

units.title: Underestimating task effort is universal
units.detail: Even experienced developers routinely underestimate how long complex work takes. Estimating effort is a hard skill that improves with practice, so don't be too hard on yourself when estimates slip.

units.title: Prioritize high-value work when time is scarce
units.detail: When time is limited, choose work that delivers the most value (views, wishlists, momentum) and drop time-consuming, low-return tasks. Explicitly rank projects against each other.

units.title: Wishlist count predicts launch success
units.detail: Before launch, gather as many wishlists as possible (targeting thousands) because they convert into sales and are the key marketing metric pre-release.

units.title: Python as a gateway into game dev
units.detail: Many learn Python first and try games with it (e.g. pygame), making it a common entry point. For ML-Agents work you can run preset commands without writing Python yourself.

units.title: Horror games: small hook, huge audience
units.detail: Horror is quick to make and only needs a small unique hook to stand out, while having a large hungry audience. Even devs who dislike horror can succeed in it by following the formula.

units.title: Case study: fast game beats polished flop
units.detail: A studio spent 4 years on a well-reviewed game that peaked at 87 players and netted ~$50k, then a quick co-op horror game made in under a year peaked at 1,700 players. Speed plus genre fit can matter more than polish.

units.title: Horror success is not guaranteed
units.detail: Horror is not a cheat code; many horror games fail. It works because the genre is fast to build and has a big audience, but you still need a hook worth watching/playing.

units.title: Steam rejects games with unverifiable AI assets
units.detail: Valve rejects games whose AI-generated assets could infringe third-party IP, requiring developers to prove they own the full training data. If you can't, the game won't ship.

units.title: AI training data copyright is unresolved
units.detail: Legally, the ownership of AI training inputs is still unlitigated, so platforms take a cautious stance: no proof of rights, no publishing. This applies to art, text, and music.

units.title: Keep AI use to brainstorming, not shipped content
units.detail: Using AI for brainstorming (names, ideas) is low-risk, but shipping AI-generated assets is risky. If you ship AI content, ensure the tool guarantees rights over training data.

units.title: Prefer AI tools with IP indemnity
units.detail: Choose AI tools whose vendors indemnify customers over training-data IP (e.g. Adobe Firefly's clause defending users in lawsuits). This is the safest path for legally using AI output in commercial work.

units.title: Keep fields private, use [SerializeField] to expose
units.detail: To expose a field in the Unity editor, keep it private and add the [SerializeField] attribute instead of making it public. The field shows in the inspector while remaining inaccessible to other classes.

units.title: Minimize access to manage complexity
units.detail: Every field, variable, or class should be as limited as possible while still achieving its purpose. This reduces how much of the codebase you must keep in your head and is one of the best ways to manage complexity as code grows.

units.title: Public fields create untraceable spaghetti bugs
units.detail: If everything is public, any class can read and modify any field, so a buggy value could originate anywhere in the codebase and is very hard to trace. Example: a public speed field modified by UI, upgrade, and enemy classes makes it near-impossible to find who set a wrong value.

units.title: Expose behavior via public methods, not fields
units.detail: If other classes must change a value, expose a public method instead of a public field. Methods let you log callers, validate input, and fire change events (e.g., a speed-changed event the UI listens to) instead of polling the field every frame.

units.title: Private fields guarantee errors are local
units.detail: A private field proves no other class can touch it, so any error involving it must live inside that class. This lets you ignore the rest of the codebase while debugging a single bug.

units.title: Unity tutorials use public only for beginners
units.detail: Official Unity tutorials make fields public for simplicity when teaching complete beginners, not because it is best practice. Beginners can prioritize simplicity; more experienced devs should prefer private + [SerializeField].

units.title: Programming is problem solving, not writing code
units.detail: AI produces good output only if you ask the right questions and can review the result. Knowing what to ask and spotting flaws in generated code is exactly what separates good programmers from beginners, so AI won't replace those skills.

units.title: AI is confidently wrong on best practices
units.detail: AI gives confident answers that may be incorrect. Example: it correctly says don't make everything public, but also recommends using tags for object identification even though tag searching scans every GameObject and is inefficient. Always verify claims.

units.title: AI code mirrors beginner tutorial bad habits
units.detail: Because most training data is beginner tutorials, AI-generated Unity code reproduces their bad practices: public fields, missing access modifiers, tag/string identification instead of references, and non-layer-mask physics checks. Treat output as a draft to refactor.

units.title: Never blindly copy-paste AI code
units.detail: Use AI-generated code as a starting point or for quick reference, then review and improve it. It is an excellent tool for beginner-level questions, but pasting output directly into a game leads to quick-and-dirty implementations.

units.title: Prefer capsule/boxcast over raycast for ground checks
units.detail: When checking if a character is grounded, use a boxcast or capsule cast instead of a thin raycast for a more robust contact area. Keep the field private and [SerializeField] it rather than making it public.

units.title: Understand business incentives to predict behavior
units.detail: Unity needed revenue (engine side was unprofitable, ads-driven) and only earns from the top ~10% of big developers, so a reversal was unlikely despite indie backlash. Analyzing who actually pays can explain why companies keep unpopular changes.

units.title: Per-install fees break low-monetization games
units.detail: A per-install fee can exceed revenue for hyper-casual or low-monetizing games, forcing bankruptcy. A fairer model caps the fee as a percentage of revenue (e.g., 3-5%), so the company only profits when developers profit.

units.title: Decide engine use from your own use case
units.detail: Read and calmly analyze new terms against your specific situation (platform, revenue expectations) rather than following the crowd. E.g., Steam-PC indie games never crossed Unity's threshold, while free-to-play mobile with low per-user revenue was genuinely risky.

units.title: Treat platforms as tools, adapt to current reality
units.detail: Don't panic about hypothetical future term changes; assess current reality and adapt when things actually change. Treating an engine as a tool with capabilities and cost, not as a partner to trust, keeps decisions rational.

units.title: Real-time 3D configurators for product marketing
units.detail: Product configurators let customers interact with a 3D model (change colors, open doors, swap materials) and can be published to the web browser. This is a viable use of a game engine beyond game development.

units.title: Configurator rules constrain option combos
units.detail: Rules let you disable options when others are selected (e.g., selecting the red pack makes the white bumper unavailable), preventing invalid or conflicting configurations.

units.title: Wishlists matter before release, not after
units.detail: The purpose of wishlists is to trigger launch-day emails and seed visibility; building a large wishlist count must happen before release. After release, wishlists barely matter and only sales do, so don't plan to 'gather wishlists post-launch'.

units.title: Influencer coverage after release underperforms
units.detail: Millions of views from influencers that arrive after launch (like this game's 2M-view videos) won't fix a weak launch. Coverage timing matters more than volume; pre-release coverage feeds the wishlist launch engine.

units.title: Early Access suits systems games, not story games
units.detail: Early Access works for systems-based games but usually doesn't help story/horror games. Only use it if you have at least a year of development planned; launching EA a few months before 1.0 just splits and weakens a single launch.

units.title: A flopped Early Access rarely recovers at 1.0
units.detail: You essentially get one launch (normal or EA), and if it fumbles, the 1.0 release typically sells only a small fraction more, not a multiple. Revamping a failed EA game for 1.0 rarely turns it around.

units.title: Entity-backed GameObjects will merge DOTS and Mono
units.detail: Upcoming 'ECS for all' gives every GameObject an underlying entity, letting you mix fast ECS code and standard GameObject code in one project. This is expected to enable high performance without committing fully to DOTS.

units.title: Get real people to playtest your game
units.detail: Testers play differently than the developer, who already knows the rules. Playtesting surfaced a game-breaking bug (dying while held) that never occurred during development, plus confusions like which machines are needed to spawn crystals. Always have other people play.

units.title: Cloud diagnostics catch bugs without reports
units.detail: Unity Cloud Diagnostics lets you inspect errors and their stack traces from real players, so you can fix bugs or add safety checks without waiting for bug reports. Pair it with rapid feedback-driven updates to improve the game continuously.

units.title: Games need both a hook and an anchor
units.detail: The hook is the unique selling point that grabs attention; the anchor is the familiar part that gets players to try it. A great pitch combines both, like 'Pokemon with guns' — 80% familiar core loop, 20% unique twist.

units.title: Balance uniqueness with familiarity
units.detail: Too-unique games confuse players and get skipped even if great; too-familiar clones have no hook. Aim for a familiar genre core with one clear unique twist rather than a game that is unique in every dimension.

units.title: Leverage anchors: friends, influencers, brand, genre
units.detail: Anchors include word-of-mouth, trusted influencers, sequels/spin-offs, studio brand, awards, genre, and IP. Building a strong brand anchor (e.g., Spiderweb Software serving a core audience for 20+ years) reduces risk and creates repeat buyers.

units.title: Genre choice is the most important indie decision
units.detail: For financial success, pick your genre deliberately: crowded genres like platformers stack the deck against you, while currently hot genres like factory automation give an easier path. Choose the genre before writing any code.

units.title: Prefer small ~6-month games to build a brand
units.detail: Multi-year projects are extremely risky: if the game flops you lose years of work. Making smaller games frequently builds a brand anchor where players trust and buy whatever you make next.

units.title: Polish separates good games from great games
units.detail: Polish is the tiny animations, sounds, and flashes that make every action feel satisfying (Valheim resource gathering, Hearthstone card play, Marvel Snap). Removing polish from a great game reveals it is otherwise ordinary.

units.title: Polish playable demos, not just final releases
units.detail: Polish the start of any public demo — Steam Festival, Kickstarter, publisher pitches, or conventions — even while core mechanics are unfinished. If players quit in the first minutes you get no feedback; a polished first impression yields more data and funding.

units.title: Polish the player's first minutes and menus
units.detail: When running a live demo, spend 1-2 weeks polishing the main menu, buttons (hover animations + sounds), scene transitions, and tutorial onboarding instead of building missing late-game mechanics. Small presentational touches keep players playing longer.

units.title: Deconstruct satisfying games to learn polish
units.detail: A powerful exercise: pick a game or gif that feels great and list every small element making it satisfying — screen shake, layered particle effects, smoke puffs, bloom, color contrast, freeze frames. Identifying these trains polish as a learnable skill.

units.title: Layer multiple effects for impact
units.detail: A single explosion effect feels weak; combine a main blast plus a ground ring, forward-flying debris/meteors, and smoke puffs on impact. Layered effects sell momentum and make destruction feel powerful.

units.title: Sell speed with fixed objects and trails
units.detail: When everything moves along one axis, speed is invisible; add fixed barricades with clear details at the edges of the level and speed trails behind the player's car so relative motion reads clearly.

units.title: Use shake, bloom, and freeze frames sparingly
units.detail: Screen shake on any impactful action, subtle bloom, and brief freeze frames (like fighting games on hits) all increase impact. Avoid over-bloom that obscures the scene (e.g., Oblivion) — subtle amounts read best.

units.title: High-contrast color design guides the eye
units.detail: Keep NPCs and background muted (gray) while the player and effects are vivid (red, bright orange) so player actions pop. Strong color contrast makes the player's impact feel more significant.

units.title: Send JSON data via Unity WebRequest POST
units.detail: Create a UnityWebRequest with the URL and 'POST', set an UploadHandlerRaw with the JSON string converted to UTF8 bytes, and set the Content-Type request header to application/json. Use a DownloadHandlerBuffer to read the text response.

units.title: Read raw POST body in PHP
units.detail: In PHP use file_get_contents('php://input') to read the raw request body sent by a client, then json_decode it into an object to access fields like the message.

units.title: Never trust client input
units.detail: Escape all data received from users (e.g. with mysqli escape string) and use prepared statements with bound parameters to prevent SQL injection. Hardcoded DB credentials in source are only OK for simple learning demos.

units.title: SQL prepared statements for inserts
units.detail: Insert data by preparing a query with '?' placeholders, binding parameters with explicit types (string/int), then executing. This is the safe way to write user data to a database.

units.title: Simple 1-to-1 chat table schema
units.detail: For a one-student-to-one-admin chat, a table with auto-increment ID, message text, an is_admin boolean (instead of sender/receiver IDs), and a timestamp is sufficient. Extend fields only when adding multiple users.

units.title: UI Toolkit requires string identifiers
units.detail: UI Toolkit queries elements by string names (rootVisualElement.Q<Button>("name")), which are brittle and easy to mistype. The Unity author dislikes this but it's currently how element lookup works.

units.title: Field of view cone via raycast mesh
units.detail: Fire rays from an origin spread across the FOV angle; each ray becomes a mesh vertex (at the hit point if the raycast hits something, else at max view distance). Connect origin-to-previous-to-current vertices into triangles to form the cone.

units.title: Mesh winding order controls visibility
units.detail: Triangle winding (clockwise vs counterclockwise) determines whether a face is visible. When building meshes incrementing an angle, account for Unity's coordinate direction or triangles will be inverted.

units.title: Manual mesh bounds prevent culling
units.detail: A procedural mesh whose origin is far from its vertices gets culled (disappears) once the player moves away. Set very large mesh.bounds explicitly when assigning the mesh so it always renders.

units.title: Layer masks filter raycast targets
units.detail: Use a LayerMask on raycasts so only specific layers (walls) block the view cone while enemies pass through and remain visible inside it.

units.title: Stencil buffer masks visibility
units.detail: In a custom render pipeline, render the FOV mesh writing to the stencil buffer, then only render 'behind' objects where that stencil value was written. An inverted pass renders a black layer everywhere else for a stealth/horror look.

units.title: Split Update and LateUpdate for dependent systems
units.detail: When one component depends on another each frame (player sets origin/aim direction in Update, FOV rebuilds mesh in LateUpdate), order the work across two lifecycle methods so data is ready before consumption.

units.title: Tag entities with empty marker components
units.detail: Give entity types an empty marker component (e.g. UnitTag, TargetTag) so ECS can distinguish them and systems can filter which archetypes they run on.

units.title: Separate targeting state into own component
units.detail: Keep the unit tag empty and store targeting data (the target entity) in a separate HasTarget component that gets added/removed. This keeps the tag clean and makes filtering 'units with no target' trivial.

units.title: Defer structural changes via command buffer
units.detail: Use an entity command buffer (post-update commands) to add/remove components, so the updates execute after the main simulation finishes.

units.title: Check entity exists before acting on it
units.detail: When multiple units target the same entity and one destroys it first, other units error on a destroyed entity. Guard movement/destruction with an entity.Exists() check and remove the stale targeting component.

units.title: Job system and Burst order-of-magnitude gains
units.detail: Converting a single-threaded ECS loop to a JobComponentSystem dropped 1000x1000 target search from 270ms to 70ms; enabling Burst Compile dropped it to ~2ms. Profiling confirms each step's payoff.

units.title: Burst can't use entity command buffers
units.detail: Burst compiles only a limited C# subset, so EntityCommandBuffer use inside a job throws errors. Work around it by splitting the work.

units.title: Split burst job from unsupported-logic job
units.detail: Run the expensive closest-target math in a Burst job writing results to a native array, then schedule a separate non-Burst job (with a job dependency on the first) that adds the component via the command buffer.

units.title: ReadOnly and deallocate flags on native arrays
units.detail: Mark native arrays read-only where jobs don't write them, and use deallocate-on-job-completion so the job system frees the array. Remember to dispose any arrays you create outside the job.

units.title: Success on one game doesn't transfer
units.detail: A mega-hit first game can be followed by a flop (140k units to 1.2k; $1M to $1k). Every game stands alone, even sequels, because genre popularity and market timing shift.

units.title: Marketability is the #1 factor
units.detail: No matter how well executed a game is, it fails without a marketable idea. Social-deduction was hot during the Among Us era and arcade games are rarely hits on Steam; pick ideas that are currently marketable.

units.title: Track genre trends on Steam
units.detail: Genres rise and fall (Vampire-Survivor-likes, incremental games now). Regularly scan Steam's new release lists to see which genres are hot, saturated, or dropping off before committing to an idea.

units.title: Failure teaches more than success
units.detail: After a flop, write down and analyze what went wrong instead of moving on. Learning from failures improves your odds of future hits.

units.title: Define requirements before producing
units.detail: Decide what the game actually needs before making art or writing code. Unspecified production leads to tons of unused assets and throwaway systems.

units.title: Strong contrast is your hook
units.detail: A unique contrasting element makes a game or trailer stand out; its absence makes them feel dull. Genre alone (e.g. 'multiplayer party game') stops being a hook once oversaturated.

units.title: Comfort zone trades efficiency for uniqueness
units.detail: Stepping outside your genre costs learning time but can yield outsider-perspective ideas. For speed and reliability, build in genres you already know; blend genres only with heavy prototyping.

units.title: Manage finances to survive flops
units.detail: Save the earnings from hits so a flop game doesn't ruin you. Code Monkey survived a 90% income drop between games because he didn't squander his first game's profits.

units.title: Dissect what makes games work
units.detail: Continuously analyze why satisfying games work (moment-to-moment gameplay, not surface theme) before adapting a genre, so you know exactly what players expect.

units.title: Manually author an alpha channel in Photoshop
units.detail: Paint a black layer, select it, then Save Selection named as the alpha channel so the PSD imports with correct transparency. Recreate it after every texture edit, which gets tedious with many layers.

units.title: Flow field vs A* pathfinding
units.detail: A* computes an individual path per unit; flow field computes the whole map once toward one destination, so any number of units heading there just follow the vectors underneath them. Flow field wins when many units share a target.

units.title: Flow field node data: cost, best cost, vector
units.detail: Each grid node stores traversal cost (walls = max/255, destination = 0, walkable = 1), best cost to reach the destination, and a 2D vector pointing to the next node. Follow the vectors to reach the goal.

units.title: Flow field propagation via open list
units.detail: Seed the open list with the destination, pop nodes, examine all 4- or 8-way neighbors, compute new best cost = node best cost + neighbor cost, keep the lowest, set the direction vector, and push the neighbor. Repeat until the open list empties.

units.title: 4-way vs 8-way movement trade-off
units.detail: Choosing whether units can move diagonally changes the neighbor set and path quality; both are valid and the decision should be deliberate in any pathfinding system.

units.title: Gate systems with enable/disable components
units.detail: Structure flow field logic with a request component (enabled on move order, runs pathfinding once, then disables) and a follower component (enabled to make the unit follow the flow vectors). This keeps expensive work from running every frame.

units.title: Satisfying flying body death effect
units.detail: On enemy death spawn a dead-body prefab, fly it outward at high speed with increasing scale and fast rotation, add particles and a brief camera shake. This makes kills feel impactful and juicy.

units.title: Fly direction away from player
units.detail: Compute the launch direction as (enemyPosition - playerPosition).normalized so bodies fly away from the killer; spawn particles with the opposite direction for a trailing effect.

units.title: Destroy spawned effects after a timer
units.detail: Give flying bodies a lifetime (~1 second) and destroy the GameObject afterward, otherwise one-shot effects accumulate in the scene forever.

units.title: Normalize direction before scaling speed
units.detail: Normalize the direction vector before multiplying by speed so diagonal and axis-aligned launches move at the same speed regardless of vector length.

units.title: Scriptable objects differ between editor and build
units.detail: Scriptable objects behave like persistent state in the editor but are reset in a build, so games depending on editor-persistent behavior break mysteriously after building.

units.title: Scriptable objects support read-write state
units.detail: Scriptable objects are valid for more than read-only data containers; read-write use works. Just be aware of the editor/build persistence mismatch and pick the architecture by team size and workflow.

units.title: Reconcile editor vs build scriptable state
units.detail: If using read-write scriptable objects, either add a system that resets all values so editor behavior matches builds, or always persist changes back to file so builds match the editor.

units.title: Scriptable object architecture pros and cons
units.detail: Pros: designer-friendly, no code changes for new data/events. Cons: hundreds of assets, hard to debug, added abstraction layers, and ill-suited to games with dynamic unit counts like RTS or tycoon games.

units.title: Keep references to shared scriptable data
units.detail: Read-write scriptable object state lives in memory only; if the object is unloaded (e.g. a scene with no reference to it), state is lost. Keep a persistent reference or a persistent loading scene.

units.title: Relay solves NAT/firewall multiplayer issues
units.detail: Relay (Unity Gaming Services) makes peer-to-peer connections work through NAT and firewalls without custom dedicated servers; it integrates with lobby and netcode. Free tier is ~50 concurrent users.

units.title: Lobby replaces a hand-built master server
units.detail: A lobby service creates public/private lobbies so players find each other without exposing direct IPs. Building your own master server is a ton of work and often fragile.

units.title: Use cloud diagnostics for crash reports
units.detail: Automated crash reporting with customizable events beats asking players for logs - players can't tell you what happened. Implement it for any released game; it shows errors in real time on a dashboard.

units.title: Remote config and cloud content delivery
units.detail: Store game parameters and assets in the cloud so you can tune values or ship limited-time events without pushing a client build update.

units.title: Server-side cloud code prevents cheating
units.detail: Running logic (enemy spawning, economy, boss AI) as serverless cloud functions instead of in the client stops cheaters from hacking it, and lets you update behavior without a client patch.

units.title: Authentication is security-critical to outsource
units.detail: User authentication is easy to get wrong; use a managed service that also supports anonymous sign-in so players don't need to create accounts, then tie cloud save and economy data to the authenticated user.

units.title: A/B test changes before keeping them
units.detail: Create custom player audiences, apply different game overrides, analyze the analytics data, then roll out the winning variant to everyone. Also lets you target updates at specific regions/events.

units.title: Make many small games instead of one big one
units.detail: Learning every gamedev discipline at once is overwhelming and leads to abandoned projects. Make many small complete games, learning a handful of skills per project, and take them to completion rather than only prototyping so you hit end-of-project challenges.

units.title: Plug skill gaps with assets
units.detail: Instead of building everything from scratch, buy or download assets (characters, animations, health systems, save systems) to cover the skills you don't have, so you can focus on your core strength such as programming.

units.title: Assets save time even when you have the skill
units.detail: Even experts buy assets like pathfinding to save thousands of hours. If time is worth more than money, paying a few dollars for something someone spent hundreds of hours building is worth it.

units.title: Players don't care about asset use
units.detail: Players only care if a game is fun, not whether assets were bought or built from scratch. Use every tool at your disposal to make the best game possible.

units.title: Templates speed up prototype validation
units.detail: Starting from a game template lets you quickly validate a game idea before investing months or years. Prototype with templates, then either build on the prototype or rebuild from scratch.

units.title: Multi-world travel via save/load, not parallel worlds
units.detail: Instead of keeping two worlds running simultaneously (which breaks instance lists, UI, and performance), save the current world's state when leaving, load the destination's state, and reload on return. Requires separating global data (unlocks) from world data.

units.title: Backwards-compatible save loading
units.detail: For save-file format changes, keep the old structure in code and try loading with it first; on failure, fall back to the new format so existing players' saves aren't broken.

units.title: JSON serializes null objects as initialized defaults
units.detail: A JSON-based save can store an 'empty' object as a zero-initialized default (e.g. HQ at 0,0,0) instead of null. A plain null check won't catch it — validate that contents are not the complete defaults before treating the data as valid.

units.title: Instantiated prefabs are copies, not references
units.detail: When you Instantiate a prefab in Unity, the hierarchy object is a copy of the original prefab asset. Network objects inside that copy are not the original prefabs on the NetworkManager's prefab list, so clients reject spawning them. Fix: hold a reference to the original prefab and spawn from it.

units.title: Network objects persist between scenes by default
units.detail: Unity Netcode's NetworkObject has destroyOnLoad defaulting to false, the opposite of normal GameObjects, so spawned objects survive scene changes and cause errors. Set destroyOnLoad to true (or manually destroy) when changing scenes.

units.title: Network objects cannot be nested children
units.detail: In Netcode for GameObjects, you cannot have a child NetworkObject inside another NetworkObject. Spawn the parent as a plain object, then iterate children and spawn each as a NetworkObject individually.

units.title: Debug sync mismatches with server-to-client RPC logs
units.detail: To figure out why server and client receive different objects, add an RPC that sends logs from the server to the client. Comparing hash codes revealed objects were different copies of the same prefab.

units.title: Multiplayer multiplies difficulty — start single player
units.detail: Every mechanic is harder to build and debug in multiplayer. Beginners should build single-player games first and only move to multiplayer with experience.

units.title: Bugs are a normal part of the process
units.detail: Even experienced devs hit bugs that break everything repeatedly. Don't get frustrated — accept it as normal, improve your debugging skills, and over time bugs become things you've seen before with known fixes.

units.title: Start with a rough paper outline
units.detail: Write a high-level outline of what the feature should be (not detailed specs), sketch the UI elements, then start prototyping and iterating on the design.

units.title: Enum-driven entity type identification
units.detail: Store an enum on the guest/entity class to identify VIP type, selecting the correct name, sprite, and special messages from it. Add a simple class to wrap special behavior and check for it on the shared base entity.

units.title: Iterate on designs after seeing them in-game
units.detail: A planned VIP intro animation on the status window wasn't visible enough, so it was moved to a larger dead-center window. Validate designs in real play and change them based on visibility.

units.title: Reuse systems and content across games
units.detail: Reusing the same animation system and sprites from previous games means features like new VIPs are quick to add. Building new systems from scratch every time is the expensive path.

units.title: Exit summary window shows player what to fix
units.detail: For special guests, show a window when they leave with their final happiness, a reward tier, and every thought they had. Thoughts reveal exactly what guests are angry about, guiding the player's fixes.

units.title: A curated research pipeline for gamedev news
units.detail: Gather article sources from YouTube channels (gamedev/game design), newsletters (GameDiscoverCo, howtomarketagame.com), blogs (Unity blog, GameDeveloper.com, GamesIndustry.biz, Hacker News), and subreddits (r/gamedev, r/Unity3D), then pick a few items weekly.

units.title: Passive learning on a second monitor
units.detail: Watch gamedev/programming YouTube on a second monitor while doing low-focus tasks (rework, editing, thumbnails). Random stumbling on interesting content is a main research source.

units.title: Forced weekly publishing keeps skills sharp
units.detail: Committing to a weekly newsletter forces constant research and prevents skills from atrophying. A regular deadline is a self-imposed learning mechanism.

units.title: Build features one by one, no upfront design
units.detail: Production games are built step by step: a rough paper outline, then a working prototype with plain cubes/capsules, adding feature after feature. Don't define classes/interfaces or UML up front — start building and adjust as you go.

units.title: Code is not fixed — refactor constantly
units.detail: Write code expecting to improve it later. Refactoring is a natural part of the process; e.g. start a prototype with the simple Input Manager then refactor to the full Input System mid-project. Never be afraid to rewrite.

units.title: Skip unit tests but keep code testable
units.detail: Game code changes constantly during iteration, so tests must be rewritten each rework and are more effort than value. Instead write clean, decoupled code so tests could be added later if wanted.

units.title: Delay visuals until the idea is validated
units.detail: In real projects leave visuals/post-processing until late, using boring cubes and capsules to test logic first. Courses implement visuals early only to stay engaging — that's the exception, not the norm.

units.title: Tutorials hide all the mistakes
units.detail: Courses and tutorials show only the final working product; all prototyping mistakes and back-and-forth are cut. Making mistakes in your own projects doesn't mean you're worse — that part simply isn't recorded.

units.title: Steam review buckets gate visibility
units.detail: Steam has four review tiers: under 10 reviews (score not visible, terrible), 10-49 (visible but poor visibility), 50+ (target zone), and 500+ (enables 'Overwhelmingly Positive' type scores).

units.title: Get 50 reviews as fast as possible
units.detail: Aim to hit 50+ reviews within the first days after launch. Failing to reach 50 even months after release makes attracting large player numbers very difficult.

units.title: Find your MVP early and leave time for polish
units.detail: Cut the game to the absolute minimum that works as a complete game, and reach that MVP well before launch. A smaller highly-polished game beats a huge unpolished one.

units.title: Don't launch during festivals or Steam sales
units.detail: Pick a launch date avoiding upcoming festivals and Steam sales, which will drown your game. Find the one clear window and treat that date as fixed to force completion.

units.title: Don't ignore localization
units.detail: English speakers are a small portion of Steam's audience. Skipping localization ignores a huge number of potential players.

units.title: Wishlists drive launch visibility even if unearned
units.detail: A high wishlist count boosts the initial launch surge and Steam visibility regardless of whether those wishlists convert. After the surge, Steam checks conversion rate to decide whether to keep promoting.

units.title: Trailer and capsule art make or break wishlists
units.detail: A good trailer and capsule art drive wishlists significantly, so invest in making them as good as possible before release.

units.title: Ability as static manager class
units.detail: Implement a game ability (like Dead Eye) as a static class with init, Start, End, and IsActive functions rather than a MonoBehaviour, keeping it simple and callable from anywhere.

units.title: Animate effects with a per-frame updater
units.detail: Use a function updater utility that runs an action every frame and self-destructs when the action returns true. Interpolate post-processing weight and timeScale from start to end over an animation time for smooth slow-motion transitions.

units.title: TimeScale scaling for slow motion
units.detail: Slow motion is implemented by animating Time.timeScale (e.g. to 0.2) while the effect is active, using unscaled delta time to drive the transition so it animates smoothly.

units.title: Staggered delayed shots with index * rate
units.detail: When shooting at multiple stored target positions, fire each with a delay of fireRate * index so the first fires immediately and the rest follow at even intervals. Reset the tag list on each activation to avoid leaking previous tags.

units.title: World-to-UI coordinate conversion for overlay markers
units.detail: For world-anchored UI markers, convert the world position to a screen point via the main camera, then screen-to-world via the UI camera, then inverse-transform into the canvas' local space. Recompute every frame so markers track moving objects.

units.title: Target-tracking tags via collider overlap
units.detail: On click, use a physics overlap point to detect if a target was hit, check for a dummy marker component to confirm it's an enemy, then store a local contact position (inverse transform point) so the tag follows the enemy as it moves.

units.title: Diegetic 3D UI in the world space
units.detail: Switch a Canvas render mode from Screen Space Overlay to World Space so UI exists in the 3D world (like Dead Space or Firewatch). It reads as more polished and can be positioned/rotated anywhere.

units.title: World space UI needs an event camera
units.detail: Buttons in a world-space canvas don't respond to hover unless an Event Camera is assigned on the Canvas (the warning tells you). Assign the main camera and hover/click events work normally.

units.title: World space UI uses world units, not pixels
units.detail: In world-space canvases, sizes are in world units so default 100-pixel UI elements become massive; shrink sizes dramatically and increase pixels-per-unit on sliced sprites to get correct proportions.

units.title: Reverse-engineer success into concrete numbers
units.detail: Define your revenue goal (e.g. $50k = top 10% of Steam), pick a price, then back out required copy counts, week-one sales, and pre-release wishlists using published median conversion multipliers.

units.title: Price games at $10-15, not $3-5
units.detail: Selling too cheap means you need 3x more sales for the same revenue, and reaching players — not price — is the real bottleneck. Higher price also leaves room for discounts (people always prefer a sale) and signals quality.

units.title: Wishlist-to-launch conversion math
units.detail: Median stats: week-one sales ≈ 20% of pre-release wishlists, and year-one revenue ≈ 3x week-one revenue. So for a $50k/$15 game, target ~3,333 copies year one, ~1,111 copies week one, ~7,000 wishlists before launch.

units.title: Popular upcoming/new-and-trending kickstarts the algorithm
units.detail: ~7,000 wishlists before release lands you on Popular Upcoming, and good launch sales land you on New & Trending; those lists snowball visibility. Missing them makes hitting revenue goals very unlikely.

units.title: Visuals communicate value — price must match
units.detail: Players judge a game's worth primarily by its visuals, so a $15 game needs professional capsule art, meshes, and graphics. You can't charge a quality price for programmer art or an asset flip.

units.title: Time-based factory theme for jam
units.detail: Set a countdown clock; when it hits zero, the player goes to an upgrade screen, then returns to building. This gives the factory loop purpose without a fragile balance mechanic.

units.title: Brainstorm with others or AI
units.detail: Don't jump to your first idea. Generate 10 ideas with chat/AI, teammates, or live chat; even if half are bad, one will spark something. Write headline notes on a whiteboard rather than jumping into code.

units.title: Choose an idea that plays to your strengths
units.detail: In a 48-hour jam there is no time to learn new skills. Pick a genre you already know (e.g. programming-heavy factory games) so you can confidently finish, not explore something entirely new.

units.title: Don't sacrifice sleep during a jam
units.detail: Game jams encourage unhealthy all-nighters. Plan for a decent night of sleep; time away from the computer produces better design ideas.

units.title: Refactor enums into Scriptable Objects
units.detail: Enums can only store a single piece of data. When an item type needs more flexibility, refactor to a Scriptable Object asset per type. Refactoring is a natural, expected part of the process.

units.title: Clean code is faster than quick and dirty
units.detail: For skilled developers, writing clean architecture is generally faster than writing throwaway code, because it makes the next system trivial to add on top.

units.title: Build games system by system
units.detail: Implement and test one system at a time (belts, then miners, then crafting) instead of attempting the whole game at once. Prototype gameplay with cubes before worrying about visuals.

units.title: Can't serialize GameObject references in save data
units.detail: When saving building connections (belts linked to miners), a GameObject reference cannot be serialized. Solution: assign each object a random ID, store IDs in save data, load all objects first, then rebuild connections by matching IDs.

units.title: Start polish with post-processing
units.detail: Post-processing via a Volume component is quick to add and gives a massive visual improvement, so do it first before other polish work.

units.title: Use a to-do list to beat analysis paralysis
units.detail: Keep a written list of tasks; whenever you don't know what to do next, grab the next item. This prevents getting stuck deciding and keeps progress moving.

units.title: Write down your goals
units.detail: Simply writing goals down massively increases your odds of achieving them. Review past goals periodically and assess honestly what was hit and missed.

units.title: It's okay to pivot your plan
units.detail: Analyze your current situation; if it differs from when you made the plan, adapting to a smaller achievable goal still counts as success. Just avoid constantly abandoning ideas the moment they get hard.

units.title: Don't punish yourself for failed goals
units.detail: If you miss a goal for valid reasons, accept it and move on rather than dwelling. Punishing yourself is a poor use of time and energy; aim to achieve it later.

units.title: Fitness prevents burnout in sedentary dev work
