units.detail: Game dev is a desk job; regular exercise and walks are key to avoiding burnout even when working long hours. Protect gym/walk time as non-negotiable.

units.title: Separate visuals from underlying logic
units.detail: Keep grid/state logic in one class and a visual class that smoothly moves transforms toward the logical positions. Logic then has no animations, and visuals just follow state changes.

units.title: Reusable generic grid class
units.detail: A pre-built generic grid class lets you stand up a match-3 board in minutes. Build reusable infrastructure once and reuse it across projects to move fast.

units.title: Match detection by counting grid neighbors
units.detail: For each gem, count consecutive same-type neighbors in each of the four directions; if 3+ match horizontally or vertically, it's a valid match.

units.title: Gems fall by scanning upward from empty cells
units.detail: Cycle the grid and for each gem check positions below; if empty, move the gem there. Repeat until settled, then spawn new gems in remaining empty cells.

units.title: Events decouple UI, visuals, and logic
units.detail: Fire events when gems clear, spawn, or score changes; the visual and UI layers listen independently. The core logic works with or without UI attached.

units.title: Separate input so a bot can drive the game
units.detail: Make the core script expose swap methods with no input awareness. A bot listens for the idle state and calls the exact same swap function the manual input uses, so it only moves when the player could.

units.title: Brute-force move finder for game bots
units.detail: Test swapping each grid position with its four neighbors, simulate the result, and rank moves by score gained or glass destroyed depending on the goal type. Simple and effective.

units.title: Level editor backed by Scriptable Objects
units.detail: Store level data (width, height, per-cell gem type, glass flags, available gem types) in Scriptable Objects, and let an editor script paint cells under the mouse.

units.title: Match-4 explosion cascades neighbors
units.detail: When 4+ gems match, grab the first gem, collect its neighbors' positions, and destroy them too. A cheap way to add a satisfying bonus mechanic.

units.title: Jam with genres you already know
units.detail: Attempting a genre you've never built (a car controller) ate most of the first night of the jam. In time-limited jams, reuse skills you already have; save experimentation for normal projects.

units.title: WheelCollider is far more than a collider
units.detail: Unity's WheelCollider bundles suspension and motors, and configuring it correctly takes a lot of time. For a jam, a simple rigidbody that moves forward and rotates (stuck to a plane, perfect traction) is good enough.

units.title: AI built on a shared driver script
units.detail: Both player and AI use the same underlying car driver script. AI computes the angle toward its target and sends forward/backward/turn commands to the driver, so behaviors layer cleanly on top.

units.title: Hotfix stuck AI with random rotation
units.detail: Without pathfinding, an AI car jams into obstacles. Check if it's stuck and apply a random rotation so it can drive around. Don't forget a timer on the rotation or it re-rotates every frame.

units.title: Minimap via a second camera on a layer
units.detail: Put map icons on a dedicated layer, render it with a second camera into a RenderTexture, and display it in the UI. Simple and performant.

units.title: Never make the player switch input types
units.detail: Mixing racing (controller) and RTS (mouse) inputs is bad. Since the UI avoided the mouse, place a world-space canvas near objects that shows context UI on button presses instead of a screen-space UI.

units.title: Use the simplest winning condition for a jam
units.detail: With limited time, pick the easiest goal: destroy all spawners and enemies. Add a timer to preserve the racing identity instead of building a complex scoring system.

units.title: Generic resource manager with dictionary
units.detail: Define resource types as Scriptable Objects and track amounts in a dictionary-backed singleton manager with add/remove/canAfford functions. A pattern you'll reuse in nearly every game.

units.title: Arrow pointer tutorial system
units.detail: Place a flat arrow object on the ground and rotate it toward the target with simple math; a tutorial script sequences states (gather resource, build, attack) that re-point the arrow.

units.title: Persistent GameData across scenes
units.detail: Keep one GameData class in memory holding the character list, story state, health, and currency so state (damage, party members) carries between overworld and battle scenes.

units.title: Type-based character constructor
units.detail: A Character class takes a type in its constructor and initializes stats (health, attack) from a switch on that type. Instantiate all party characters once and reuse them everywhere.

units.title: Story state variable drives cutscenes
units.detail: Store a simple game-state variable; a switch on it decides which cutscene, dialogue, or enemy encounter fires when the player interacts with an NPC. Scenes are wired as prefab position+type markers.

units.title: Linear sequential cutscene system
units.detail: Build cutscenes as an ordered list of actions (show dialogue, position enemies, play particles, hide/show characters) executed one after another with a function timer, rather than a complex director.

units.title: Dynamic armor via sprite pixel copy
units.detail: Implement equipment by replacing pixels on the player's sprite sheet with copied pixels from the armor sprite. Enables visually equipping items with no new models.

units.title: Speed comes from reusing clean elements
units.detail: A complex game in 7 days is possible not by working 20-hour days but by assembling many previously-built, cleanly-written elements into one experience. Writing reusable code pays off project after project.

units.title: Standing out is the hardest indie problem
units.detail: Marketing and unique visuals/mechanics are the main success factors for indies. You don't need art skill if you can combine assets and shaders into an original look.

units.title: Smooth-shade shaders need high-poly meshes
units.detail: Anime/toon shading shaders rely on smooth shading, so they look wrong on intentional low-poly assets (highlights change drastically). They shine on high-polygon models.

units.title: Pixelize shader as a cheap cel-shade look
units.detail: Applying a pixelize shader to low-poly assets creates an outline plus stylized shading; tune pixel size down to avoid heavy pixel art. Applies uniformly to all meshes and VFX for a cohesive style.

units.title: Start from a microgame or base project
units.detail: Using Unity's FPS microgame (or your own base project with URP and helper scripts) as a foundation lets you build a full short game in days instead of weeks, ideal for prototypes and jams.

units.title: Mission briefing via render texture
units.detail: A camera flying around the level renders into a RenderTexture displayed on a UI panel, giving an in-fiction mission briefing cheaply.

units.title: Shield transformers as boss gating
units.detail: Connect a boss shield to external 'transformer' power lines; players can't shoot through the shield but must destroy transformers to cut power, then damage the boss. Clear objective-following puzzle.

units.title: Group nodes to keep big scripts readable
units.detail: Large visual scripts stay manageable by grouping related logic and keeping multiple flow machines per object so each concern (input, interact, attack) is separated.

units.title: Events make interaction systems modular
units.detail: Fire events instead of direct calls; any object listening can respond. A generic interactable fires a stored target event, so one button system opens doors, disables cannons, or spawns enemies without changes.

units.title: Identify colliders by layer
units.detail: In trigger-collision logic, identify what the player touched by checking its layer (keys vs doors), then check the player's key list for the matching key to open the door.

units.title: State machine for enemy AI
units.detail: Enemies use a state machine (patrol, chase, attack) with transition conditions (distance to player within detection radius, then attack range). Clear and easy to tune.

units.title: Reuse the same systems across entities
units.detail: Use one health system script on both player and enemies; sharing scripts across entities greatly increases productivity and keeps behavior consistent.

units.title: Shop sims: 90% same, theme is the differentiator
units.detail: Shop-simulator games are almost all identical interaction gameplay (first-person look around, grab, stock, checkout). You only need to be original in the last 5-10% by applying a unique theme (car parts, games, grocery).

units.title: Shop sim genre is achievable and hot
units.detail: Shop simulators are among the most profitable Steam genres, are easy for solo devs to build, and share 90% of their mechanics. The core loop is look around, interact, scan, earn money.

units.title: Prototype to validate your tools
units.detail: Build a real genre prototype using your own toolkits/assets to prove they work in a real project; it doubles as a demo and a starting base for others to expand into a full game.

units.title: Visual scripting teaches programming logic
units.detail: Visual scripting (e.g. Bolt) teaches core programming logic — how execution flows and how objects/scripts interact — without writing code. Learners can later transition to real programming or stick with visual scripting.

units.title: Multi-genre progression builds transferable skills
units.detail: Building games across genres in rising complexity (platformer → action RPG → FPS) creates a smooth learning curve; each game reuses and deepens skills from the previous one. Applying one skill set to any genre is the real goal.

units.title: Visual scripting scales from basics to full games
units.detail: Start with simple mechanics (movement, physics, collisions, jumping) and layer features on top; visual scripting can produce complete feature-rich games without writing a single line of code.

units.title: Shield absorbs damage before health
units.detail: A two-layer health system: shield/armor depletes first and health only drops once the shield is gone; shield segment count scales with armor quality. Damage bars are depleted in this order for the familiar shooter feel.

units.title: [Serializable] exposes custom classes in inspector
units.detail: By default the Inspector only shows built-in types (int, bool, enum). Adding the [Serializable] attribute to a custom class (e.g. a spawn-position class) lets it show up grouped in the Inspector.

units.title: Debug.DrawLine visualizes logic for debugging
units.detail: Beyond Debug.Log, drawing lines in world space helps debug systems like pathfinding — you literally see the path that was calculated. Lines can be toggled on/off with the Gizmos button.

units.title: Context-sensitive single-button interaction system
units.detail: One button can trigger many context-dependent actions: click = normal action, double-click = alert, hold = radial wheel with more options, click-on-target = contextual ping. Detecting context (target + input gesture) keeps controls simple while staying versatile.

units.title: Save generation params to reload identical assets
units.detail: When generating a random asset (e.g. procedural sprites), store the exact parameters in a save object; loading the saved parameters reproduces the identical asset every time.

units.title: Persist high scores as JSON in PlayerPrefs
units.detail: Store a serializable list of score entries (score + player name) as JSON in PlayerPrefs so data survives between runs; polish with trophies and highlighting for the top player.

units.title: Break-even math: revenue needed = expenses × dev time
units.detail: Longer development means more expenses to recover: at $2k/month, a 6-month game needs $12k revenue (~top 22% of Steam) while a 2-year game needs ~$50k (~top 12%). Longer dev dramatically raises the difficulty of turning a profit.

units.title: Make small games to iterate faster
units.detail: Complete beginners should cap projects at ~2 weeks, then scale up to 1/3/6-month games as skills grow; 6 months to 1 year is the indie sweet spot. Making four games in two years teaches more and gives four chances at success than one long project.

units.title: Cut dream-game scope to essentials
units.detail: Almost any dream game can be reduced to something buildable: 20 missions instead of 100, 20 cars instead of 500, a small town instead of a giant metropolis. Scope cutting is almost always possible while keeping the core fantasy.

units.title: Small-game scale depends on skill
units.detail: What counts as a 'small game' grows with experience — a beginner's month-long project may be Flappy-Bird-sized while an experienced dev can build a large game (factory automation + colony sim) in 7 months.

units.title: Years-long dev rarely pays off
units.detail: Content rarely takes a game from $10k to $100k — the concept/idea matters far more. Only extend dev beyond a year with validated demand (e.g. 30–50k wishlists) and never go past the two-year mark.

units.title: Prototype many ideas before committing
units.detail: Instead of building the first idea that comes to mind, make several quick prototypes across genres to find what has promise; the one that clicks at prototype stage is worth investing in. This underused skill is behind major hits.

units.title: Cost of living decides indie profitability
units.detail: Indie success is far easier in low-cost-of-living areas: a $2k/month dev needs $12k per 6-month game, while a $10k/month dev needs $60k. Cost of living is the closest thing to an industry cheat code.

units.title: Genre choice outweighs visual polish
units.detail: A normal game in a hot genre (simulators) can massively outsell a gorgeous game in a niche genre (platformers). Picking the genre is one of the most important early decisions — it can make the work 10x easier.

units.title: Estimate dev time at 4x your guess
units.detail: Beginners (and pros) consistently underestimate: a game you think takes a week realistically takes a month. Define what 'small' is and then cut it smaller to account for estimation error.

units.title: Keep shipping games; knowledge compounds
units.detail: Your first game likely earns ~$0, but each game removes the mistakes of the previous one; knowledge accumulates across a portfolio. Most studios stop after one game — persisting through several raises success odds.

units.title: Small games aren't just Flappy Bird clones
units.detail: Six months is a lot of time; with experience you can build substantial, complex games (a full multiplayer automation sim was built in 7 months). 'Small' is relative to your current skill level.

units.title: Multi-floor grids enable vertical levels
units.detail: Support multiple grid layers at different elevations (floors) in grid-based games; units move between floors via pathfinding links rather than freely, giving interesting vertical level layouts.

units.title: Author complex data with editor scripts
units.detail: Build small editor tools/scripts to make linking data (e.g. floor-to-floor pathfinding links) easier to create in the editor, reducing manual error-prone setup.

units.title: Clean low-dependency code makes features cheap
units.detail: Adding multi-floor support was easy because the codebase had few dependencies and clean architecture — AI and vision/detection systems needed no changes. Good architecture makes future expansions nearly free.

units.title: Swap visuals without touching logic
units.detail: Separate movement logic from animation visuals so you can replace placeholder animations (e.g. a simple jump/drop) with a proper clip without changing any code.

units.title: Invert UI mask via stencil comparison
units.detail: The standard Unity UI Mask shows pixels where the mask shape exists; inverting the stencil comparison (NotEqual instead of Equal) turns it into a cutout mask that shows everything outside the shape.

units.title: Copy shared material before modifying
units.detail: Never mutate the base/shared UI material directly when tweaking shader properties — duplicate it first, modify the copy, and return it, or you'll corrupt every object using the default material.

units.title: Override materialForRendering per object
units.detail: Extend a UI class from Image and override materialForRendering to swap the rendered material at runtime, enabling effects like an animated circle transition mask.

units.title: AI-generated code needs experience to fix
units.detail: AI code is functional but full of sneaky bugs; a zero-coding user spent hours (e.g. 4+ on a jump bug) feeding errors back. Working with AI output still requires the ability to identify and fix issues.

units.title: Token limits block AI from full codebase context
units.detail: AI assistants can't hold an entire codebase (e.g. 1000+ lines) as context, so managing many interacting systems (enemy AI, inventory, save system) becomes impractical with AI-generated code.

units.title: Use AI as instant private tutor
units.detail: AI gives instant feedback when learning: ask questions and get immediate responses instead of waiting days for forum answers. Learning by correcting AI output builds genuine logic understanding.

units.title: AI amplifies devs, doesn't replace them
units.detail: AI is best used to boost productivity and brainstorm (titles, thumbnails, metaphors), not as a replacement. Developers who learn to use AI alongside their skills will surpass those who refuse to learn it.

units.title: One-button constraint sparks creative designs
units.detail: Designing a game around a single input (tap = jump, double-tap = attack, hold = special, or one tap = one thing) forces creative, focused game concepts — a deliberate limitation that drives invention.

units.title: Behavior bricks: logic without scripting
units.detail: Modular logic blocks — individual bricks each doing one simple behavior (move a platform, fire bullets, look at an object) — compose into complete game logic without custom code; great for beginners.

units.title: Track launched process lifecycle
units.detail: Store the Process reference returned by Process.Start and poll HasExited in Update to react when the launched game closes — e.g. show/hide a 'game running' message or restore the launcher window.

units.title: Launcher steals resources while game runs
units.detail: A resource-heavy launcher (videos, complex UI) running in the background slows the launched game; set runInBackground=false so it pauses when unfocused, and cap targetFrameRate to avoid runaway fps.

units.title: Windowed launcher, fullscreen games
units.detail: Run the launcher itself in a windowed 720p mode while launched games run fullscreen, cleanly separating the menu app from the games it launches.

units.title: Visual scripting exposes programming syntax
units.detail: In Bolt, choosing 'programmer naming' shows nodes as their underlying C# syntax, so even non-programmers passively absorb basic programming knowledge (types, names) while building graphs.

units.title: Branch node for conditional execution
units.detail: A Branch node takes a boolean and a flow input and routes to true/false outputs — the visual-scripting equivalent of an if statement. Nodes not connected into the flow stay transparent/inactive.

units.title: Review old projects to see growth
units.detail: Open an old finished project and compare it to your current code. You'll instantly spot bad practices you've since fixed, which makes learning visible and proves you're actually improving.

units.title: Never make fields public
units.detail: Public fields let any class in the codebase read and write them, creating countless breakage points. Keep fields private and expose behavior via methods; if you need editor access in Unity, use [SerializeField] on a private field instead.

units.title: Stay consistent with naming conventions
units.detail: Mixed camelCase and PascalCase for the same kind of member signals low quality. Any style is fine, but define one and apply it consistently everywhere.

units.title: Always write access modifiers explicitly
units.detail: Omitting an access modifier defaults to private in some contexts but protected/internal in others. Writing it explicitly guarantees intent and removes all doubt.

units.title: Magic numbers are unreadable
units.detail: A raycast mask built from literal layer numbers like 10, 11, 12 means nothing to a reader without checking Unity. Replace magic numbers with named constants (e.g. ObjectsLayer) so intent is obvious.

units.title: Delete commented-out code
units.detail: Leftover commented code leaves readers guessing whether it's a future plan or dead experiment. Commenting while trying approaches is fine, but clean up the losers once you settle on a method.

units.title: Never use strings to identify types
units.detail: Strings like "pistol" are typo-prone (case, spaces, similar-looking characters) and fail at runtime, not compile time. Use an enum so invalid values cause compile errors and the type system protects you.

units.title: Avoid string-based Find for references
units.detail: Find() by name breaks silently if the string or object name has a typo or hidden character. Wire references directly (e.g. drag a private [SerializeField] in the Unity editor) instead of searching by string.

units.title: Don't dump data into a global data class
units.detail: Stuffing demo flags, map nodes, armies, and survivors into one GlobalData class hides what belongs where. Put data in the specific class that uses it (CityGenerator, Game, etc.) and reserve globals for true cross-cutting state.

units.title: Use descriptive member names
units.detail: Single-letter or cryptic names like 'I' say nothing; prefer names like 'infectedHandler'. Full names are barely longer and make the code self-documenting.

units.title: Game dev is smoke and mirrors
units.detail: Players believe what they perceive, not what is technically happening. Focus on simulating the bare minimum needed to sell the illusion rather than faithfully simulating reality, which kills performance.

units.title: Render effects only in the camera's view
units.detail: An intense snowstorm can be a small particle cloud fixed in front of the player's field of view instead of a world-wide system — the player can't tell the difference, and the game stays fast.

units.title: Move the world, not the player
units.detail: In cutscenes it's often easier to keep the player still and move the world and camera around them. The player's point of view is identical, and the code is much simpler.

units.title: Endless road as a spinning donut
units.detail: Endless-runner movement can be a looping donut rotating around itself rather than an infinitely generated road — looks infinite, trivial to build.

units.title: Fake tunnels with scrolling textures
units.detail: Space/hyperspace travel can be a fixed camera and a scrolling texture on a rotating shape. Nothing actually moves, so there's no astronomical-scale map to build.

units.title: Waves from a few moving triangles
units.detail: Wind Waker's ocean is just a handful of triangles bobbing up and down — indistinguishable from a real mesh wave at gameplay distance but nearly free to render.

units.title: Train = hat on a running NPC
units.detail: Fallout 3's train was an NPC wearing a train-shaped hat running fast. Absurd from the outside, perfect from the player's view — a reminder that plausibility inside the player's view is all that counts.

units.title: Fake 2D with flat 3D meshes
units.detail: Survival Squad looked 2D while running on flat 3D meshes and 3D physics because Unity lacked 2D tools. Top-down views are easy to fake; the player only sees the flat sprite-like result.

units.title: Making games as a hobby is valid
units.detail: You define success: finishing a game or just enjoying the process counts even with zero sales. Both hobby and career approaches are legitimate, so pick yours and act accordingly.

units.title: Talent is a multiplier, not a gate
units.detail: Natural talent makes learning easier, but hard work can compensate — anyone with the desire can learn game dev. Don't let perceived lack of talent stop you.

units.title: Frustration is part of learning
units.detail: Hitting errors and bugs is a normal part of learning anything. Accept frustration as expected, don't let it stop you, and move on.

units.title: Paid courses are convenience, not secrets
units.detail: No paid course holds hidden knowledge you can't find free. You're paying for a guided, structured path — Code Monkey's free course is the same quality as his paid ones.

units.title: Beware fixed learning timelines
units.detail: Claims like 'C# in 2-3 weeks' ignore that everyone learns at their own pace. Timelines don't matter if you end up with the knowledge, so ignore rigid benchmarks.

units.title: Anyone guaranteeing six-figure games is lying
units.detail: Even a skilled, experienced dev can't guarantee their own game's success, only raise the odds. Anyone selling guaranteed success is just selling courses.

units.title: Indie success is a tough arms race
units.detail: A solo dev must be good at many disciplines, and making a lucrative game is extremely hard — most indie games sell almost nothing. Treat big success as an exception, not the baseline.

units.title: If money is the only goal, skip game dev
units.detail: For pure money, a stable software job beats indie dev: higher pay, no crunch, reliable 40-hour weeks. Make games because you enjoy making games.

units.title: Publish a game in one month
units.detail: Commit to picking a tiny game idea and publishing it within 30 days. Finishing on a deadline breaks development hell and teaches that shipping is a normal, repeatable process — finishing games is a muscle you train.

units.title: Everyone over-scopes; pick a week-and-a-half idea
units.detail: If you estimate a game at 1 month, plan for 3-4. For a one-month release, pick an idea you'd estimate at ~1.5 weeks, then budget a week of polish and half a week for the Steam backend.

units.title: Choose a marketable genre and theme
units.detail: Unicycle Pizza Time succeeded on ~300 wish lists because rage-games are a hot, streamer-friendly genre with a silly name and premise. Don't make the first idea that pops into your head — pick one that could go viral.

units.title: Cancel projects that get no traction
units.detail: A few hundred wish lists after a Next Fest is a strong signal the idea isn't resonating with players. Canceling is hard but often right; analyze what went wrong and apply it to the next project.

units.title: Consistency beats sprints
units.detail: Do a tiny bit of game dev every single day rather than burning out in multi-day sprints. Take breaks and work from a list to stay on track — this is a lifelong journey.

units.title: Low cost of living enables self-funding
units.detail: Living where ~750 EUR/month covers rent, food, and utilities means a year-long game only needs ~8k to turn a profit. Self-funding is far easier when your monthly burn is small.

units.title: Use AI for brainstorming, not code
units.detail: ChatGPT is great for ideation — the name 'Dinky Guardians' came from AI-suggested creature words — but poor for generating code. Keep it in the creative corner.

units.title: Execution matters more than the idea
units.detail: Two devs starting from the same design doc produce completely different games because thousands of tiny decisions diverge quickly. Seeing a similar idea elsewhere should not stop you from building yours.

units.title: Define your game's hook
units.detail: Identify why someone plays your game over alternatives. A weak hook is tolerable for a ~4-month project but unacceptable for a 3-year one — short dev cycles allow weaker hooks, long ones demand strong ones.

units.title: Don't price games under $10
units.detail: A $5 game needs double the reach of a $10 one for the same revenue, and discount shoppers buy at 50% off regardless of the base price. Charge at least $10 unless you're prioritizing experience over money.

units.title: Wish lists predict sales
units.detail: Wish lists correlate strongly with sales, so ask people to wish list your game and wish list others' games to help them. It seems small but genuinely matters.

units.title: Outsource logos you can't draw
units.detail: Pay ~$70 on Fiverr for a logo; results far exceed anything a non-artist can make, and your Steam capsule is important marketing.

units.title: Using assets doesn't make an asset flip
units.detail: Players only care if the game is fun. Buying models and shaders to bring your vision to life is fine regardless of 'asset flip' fears.

units.title: Building for a course is ~8x slower than solo
units.detail: The trailer took ~2 weeks to build alone but would take ~4 months as a step-by-step tutorial, so you can't realistically make tutorials while developing. Reuse systems you've already taught rather than re-teaching everything.

units.title: Research government grants for games
units.detail: Several countries fund art projects including video games, but expect heavy bureaucracy — it can be a nightmare in practice. Worth researching if you need funding, though it's an option, not a guarantee.
